(assuming oxygenation remains adequate), re- evaluate the patient,
and create a different anesthetic and airway management plan. If
the patient is apneic, every effort should be made to rapidly intubate
the trachea. The most experienced individual should attempt intu-
bation and additional personnel should be summoned to collect the
supplies outlined above for a difficult intubation. The decision to
transition to emergency surgical airway access should be based on
procedural and patient status criteria [72]. Multiple unsuccessful
attempts at orotracheal intubation by an experienced veterinarian
in a patient that is rapidly desaturating and/or apneic should signal
the need to immediately proceed with a surgical approach.
Maintenance
Airway obstruction in an intubated patient during the maintenance
phase of anesthesia may arise if the endotracheal tube becomes
occluded or compressed. Potential causes include foreign material
(e.g., mucus plugs, especially with small diameter endotracheal
tubes), kinking of the endotracheal tube, overinflation of the cuff
leading to compression of the tube lumen, asymmetric cuff inflation
leading to obstruction of the bevel end of the tube, and external
compression or obstruction between the tube and the breathing sys-
tem. Procedures which hyperflex the atlanto-occipital joint (e.g., cer-
ebral spinal fluid collection and ocular procedures) are particularly
prone to causing a kinked endotracheal tube [73]. Obstruction of the
endotracheal tube may be identified by observation of increased res-
piratory effort, thoracic excursions without effective air movement
(e.g., breathing bag not moving), or by changes to or loss of the cap-
nographic waveform. Attempts to provide positive-pressure ventila-
tion are met with resistance and the patient’s thoracic movement
does not match the pressure being delivered. Spirometry may be
helpful to diagnose an occluded endotracheal tube [74]. Recognition
of an occluded endotracheal tube requires prompt intervention.
Patient positioning should be checked and modified to address a
kinked tube, cuff inflation should be evaluated, and other external
compressions or obstructions removed. If the tube is potentially
occluded with mucus, a stylet or catheter can be introduced to clear
the lumen. If that fails to resolve the obstruction, the endotracheal
tube may need to be exchanged.
Inadvertent endobronchial intubation (i.e., advancement of the
endotracheal tube beyond the thoracic inlet and into a mainstem
bronchus) is possible if tube length is excessive. This may occur
with initial tube placement at induction, or when a tube that was
correctly placed initially moves distally, most often with changes in
patient positioning. Endobronchial intubation results in atelectasis
and impaired oxygenation in the non-intubated lung. Healthy
patients are usually able to compensate for this if the F I
O2 is ~ 1.0
and hypoxemia may not result. Mechanical ventilation may predis-
pose to volutrauma in the intubated lung. This complication is best
prevented by determining the correct endotracheal tube length for
the patient, cutting it to the correct size, and confirming correct
placement by auscultating breath sounds on both sides of the chest.
Recovery
If airway obstruction occurs after extubation, it may make reintuba-
tion difficult or impossible. Using a delayed extubation technique,
where the patient is extubated only once they are lifting their head
and have regained normal muscle tone, may decrease the likelihood
of obstruction occurring after extubation in certain high-risk
patients (e.g., brachycephalic dogs). Patients with a potentially com-
promised airway should be carefully monitored after extubation
and preparations should be in place to reintubate in the face of
respiratory difficulties. If the patient appears stable and the airway
remains patent after extubation, placement in a high FI
O2 environ-
ment for several hours may help reduce the work of breathing,
ensure adequate alveolar oxygen concentrations, and improve the
chance of a successful recovery.
In cats, their small size and susceptibility to laryngospasm
may increase the risk of airway trauma during intubation, which
may manifest as airway obstruction at recovery. Similarly, in horses,
laryngospasm/laryngeal dysfunction associated with intubation
may also precipitate acute, catastrophic airway obstruction at recov-
ery. In addition to partial airway obstruction due to nasopharyngeal
congestion (routinely treated with topical phenylephrine), complete
airway obstruction may occur in horses due to physical blockade of
the nostrils (e.g., in the corner of a recovery stall). In cases of com-
plete airway obstruction, the horse may thrash violently as hypox-
emia causes significant distress. Unconsciousness may result, and
negative-pressure pulmonary edema may occur [75]. Orotracheal
intubation may not be successful in such cases, and an emergency
tracheostomy is indicated if an airway cannot be rapidly established.
Bronchospasm
Bronchospasm may result from airway irritation or stimulation
(e.g., endotracheal intubation in at-risk patients), anaphylactic
reactions, underlying disease (e.g., asthma), or drugs (e.g., non-
selective β- adrenergic blockers). In general, anesthetic maintenance
with isoflurane or sevoflurane is usually well tolerated in patients
with reactive airways as these agents promote bronchial relaxation.
Bronchospasm narrows the small airways and increases resist-
ance to ventilation. In the most severe cases, this may progress to
apnea and acute desaturation. In patients with pre-existing risk fac-
tors, bronchospasm should be suspected if a change in pulmonary
resistance is noted (e.g., it becomes more difficult to provide
positive-pressure ventilation), with or without an accompanying
decrease in SpO 2
. Changes to the capnographic waveform (i.e., the
characteristic “shark fin” or “saw tooth” pattern) indicating uneven
alveolar emptying, as well as increased peak airway pressures dur-
ing mechanical ventilation, are typically observed. In some patients,
wheezes may be appreciated on thoracic auscultation. Examination
of pressure–volume loops created by spirometry will aid the diag-
nosis of changes in resistance and compliance. In the event of a
change in pulmonary resistance, acute airway obstruction or pneu-
mothorax should also be considered as rule-outs and investigated.
Any underlying conditions that may precipitate bronchospasm
should be treated if possible (e.g., epinephrine administration for
an anaphylactic reaction). Symptomatic treatment of bronchos-
pasm involves administration of bronchodilators (e.g., aminophyl-
line, terbutaline, and albuterol) and positive-pressure ventilation
with 100% oxygen.
Accidental extubation
Unexpected intraoperative extubation is particularly problematic
if the patient was difficult to intubate initially, if patient positioning
is not conducive to reintubation, and when extubation is not
immediately recognized due to surgical drape coverings or other
obstructions. An unexpected extubation means the airway is
unprotected and the patient is not receiving oxygen or inhalant
anesthesia. Creation of an oxygen-rich pocket under the surgical
drapes due to an unexpected and unobserved extubation can
precipitate a fire [76].
Determining if extubation has happened can be challenging if it
is unobserved. Routine, continuous use of capnography is the best

-- 79 of 1450 --

64 	Section 1: General Topics
tool to detect accidental extubation as the patient’s capnographic
waveform will be lost with complete tube displacement or modified
with partial displacement. Failure to observe breathing bag excur-
sions or one-way valve movements (in a rebreathing circuit), a
sudden decrease in resistance when providing positive-pressure
ventilation, and/or detection of inhalant agent odor may indicate
that an extubation has occurred. If the patient is being maintained
with an inhalant agent and extubation is not promptly recognized,
decreases in SpO2 may be noted and anesthetic depth will lighten,
potentially resulting in patient movement.
If patient movement is noted, restraint and deepening of the anes-
thetic plane with a rapid-acting injectable agent is required prior to
attempting reintubation. Assistance is typically required, and addi-
tional injectable drugs should be available if reintubation is challeng-
ing. If extubation is recognized promptly, it may be possible to
reintubate the patient without interrupting the ongoing procedure. If,
however, intubation is not possible with the patient in the current
position, the procedure may need to be paused and the patient re-
positioned. A bougie (endotracheal tube introducer) may be particu-
larly useful for intubation in unusual positions, as it is often easier to
introduce into the airway than an endotracheal tube. In the event that
a patient with a difficult airway becomes unexpectedly extubated, a
rapid transition to surgical airway access (e.g., a tracheostomy) is
essential if orotracheal intubation cannot be quickly achieved.
Iatrogenic tracheal injury
A tracheal tear can occur when excessive force or torque is applied
to the trachea or larynx. Cats are particularly sensitive to tracheal
tears sustained during anesthesia [77–79]. Overinflation of the
endotracheal tube cuff, changing body position with the patient’s
endotracheal tube connected to the anesthetic circuit, and forceful
intubation are the most common causes of tracheal tears. Clinical
signs associated with a tracheal tear include subcutaneous emphy-
sema in the cervical region (which may be substantial), pneumo-
mediastinum, and/or pneumothorax. If a tracheal tear is suspected
under anesthesia, the patient should be managed without positive-
pressure ventilation and pneumothorax may need to be treated via
thoracocentesis. If possible, the procedure should be stopped so the
patient can recover from anesthesia. Tracheostomy or bronchos-
copy may be performed to confirm the diagnosis, although a tear is
not always visible. Most tracheal tears typically heal without any
active surgical intervention.
Acute or undiagnosed pneumothorax
While other types of pleural space disease (e.g., pleural effusion)
may have adverse impacts under anesthesia, acute pneumothorax
may manifest unexpectedly and has the potential to be life-
threatening, especially if it develops into tension pneumothorax.
Pneumothorax may arise because of a procedure (e.g., cranial
abdominal or diaphragmatic surgery), excessive airway pressure
(e.g., closed APL valve or incorrect ventilator settings), trauma to
the airways, or the presence of abnormal pulmonary structures
(e.g., bullae) [80]. The diagnosis is one of exclusion, as initial
changes in vital signs (cardiorespiratory decompensation and dif-
ficulty with ventilation) are non-specific, and other causes of such
changes (e.g., airway obstruction, bronchospasm, and endobron-
chial intubation) occur more commonly and must be ruled out.
Increased pulmonary resistance is not a reliable indicator of pneu-
mothorax [80]. It may be difficult to appreciate local clinical signs
(e.g., diminished breath sounds) in the anesthetized patient without
full access to the thorax, and other diagnostics (e.g., thoracic
radiography) may not be available intraoperatively. If the patient’s
condition warrants immediate intervention, bilateral thoracocente-
sis should be performed even if the diagnosis has not been con-
firmed. Discontinuing positive-pressure ventilation may be
warranted if there is suspicion that the air entered the thoracic cav-
ity from the airways (e.g., ruptured pulmonary bulla) with or with-
out progression to a tension pneumothorax.
Pulmonary aspiration
Aspiration of foreign material, most often gastric contents, into the
trachea and lungs can precipitate airway obstruction, bronchos-
pasm, and/or pneumonia. In rare cases, the endotracheal tube itself
may be aspirated, for example, in a horse recovering with the tube
in place, or in a small animal patient that bites the tube prior to
extubation and inhales part of it. This clearly constitutes an anes-
thetic emergency and requires immediate intervention to clear the
airway. In small animal patients, the risk of endotracheal tube aspi-
ration can be minimized by recovering patients slowly in a con-
trolled environment. If they do regain consciousness suddenly and
begin biting the endotracheal tube, the mouth should be held closed
until extubation is possible. If recovering a horse with the endotra-
cheal tube in place, ensuring the tube is well secured and interven-
ing to extubate in the event the tube is displaced from the interdental
space will prevent it being bitten. Alternatively, maintaining the
airway with a nasotracheal tube in recovery will prevent any risk of
the tube being bitten.
Brachycephalic patients, patients with laryngeal dysfunction
(e.g., laryngeal paralysis), esophageal dysfunction (e.g., megaesoph-
agus), neurologic disease, and those undergoing upper airway
surgeries may be at higher risk for developing aspiration pneumo-
nia [81]. Regurgitation of gastric contents during or after anesthesia
puts the patient at a higher risk for developing pneumonia [81].
Development of aspiration pneumonia may progress to respiratory
failure resulting in death or, due to expense of treatment and/or poor
prognosis, euthanasia may be elected [82]. In dogs, a large-scale ret-
rospective multicenter study reported the incidence of postanes-
thetic aspiration pneumonia to range between 0.04% and
0.26% [81]. The rate is unknown in cats, but in one study, 40% of
the cats diagnosed with aspiration pneumonia had undergone
recent anesthesia [83].
Diagnosis of pulmonary aspiration may be made if regurgitated
material is visualized in the oropharynx and the airway is unpro-
tected. Even in anesthetized patients that are intubated, regurgi-
tated fluid may pass by an inadequately inflated endotracheal tube
cuff and enter the lungs, and this may not be recognized until days
later when pneumonia develops [81]. Aspiration pneumonia is typ-
ically diagnosed on the basis of thoracic radiographs and physical
examination.
Ensuring that the oropharynx is cleared of debris and that there
are no small objects near the patient’s mouth during recovery will
reduce the risk of aspiration. If there is concern that fluid may
remain in the trachea proximal to an inflated endotracheal tube
cuff, extubation is sometimes performed with the cuff partially
inflated to remove excess fluid. One study involving canine cadavers
found that extubation with an inflated high-pressure low-volume
endotracheal tube cuff reduced but did not completely eliminate
intratracheal fluid [84]. This study did not evaluate potential
adverse effects of this practice such as damage to the tracheal wall
or larynx.
Reducing the risk of regurgitation and postanesthetic aspiration
pneumonia is possible, but complicated. In the study by Ovbey

-- 80 of 1450 --

et al., the incidence of aspiration pneumonia in dogs varied consid-
erably depending on the institution [81]. It was speculated that this
may be related to different anesthetic practices, but it was unclear
what those differences were. In another study involving dogs under-
going anesthesia for radiation treatment, procedural changes
including decreasing the use of anticholinergics and pure μ-opioid
receptor agonists, minimizing changes in body position, prophylac-
tically treating nausea, maintaining the endotracheal tube cuff
inflated until immediately before extubation, and improved aseptic
handling of equipment used for endotracheal intubation reduced
the incidence of postanesthetic aspiration pneumonia from 13% to
1.3% [85]. Thus, taking steps to reduce the risk of gastroesophageal
reflux (GER) and regurgitation seems warranted, particularly in
high-risk patients.
Volutrauma and barotrauma
Pulmonary volutrauma and/or barotrauma may occur as a result of
equipment maloperation (i.e., a closed APL valve as discussed in
the equipment section) or associated with positive-pressure ventila-
tion (in humans, this is often referred to as “ventilator-associated
lung injury” or “ventilator-induced lung injury”). Excessively high
airway pressures (barotrauma) and/or volume overexpansion
(volutrauma) can directly damage the lung leading to extra-alveolar
air accumulation (potentially pneumothorax) as well as pulmonary
edema and hemorrhage. The consequences of damage induced by
positive-pressure ventilation may not be appreciated during the
course of anesthesia as it takes time for the inflammatory response
to develop in the lower airways. Frank hemorrhage or fluid within
the endotracheal tube, changes to pulmonary compliance or resist-
ance, and evidence of ventilation–perfusion mismatch may be
observed. If pulmonary damage due to positive-pressure ventilation
is suspected, adjustments to the ventilation strategy should be made
with relatively low peak inspiratory pressure indicated in these
cases [86]. Barotrauma and volutrauma are best prevented by avoid-
ing excessive airway pressures and volumes in the first place. In
patients with atelectasis, a recruitment maneuver with addition of
positive end-expired pressure (PEEP) may be preferable to avoid
delivering large volumes and pressures over a long period of time.
In patients with chronic atelectasis (e.g., a congenital pericardial-
peritoneal diaphragmatic hernia or other chronic pleural space
disease), even modest increases in positive airway pressure may
precipitate re-expansion pulmonary edema and hypoxemia. This is
a rare phenomenon in people [87], and the incidence in animals is
unknown. Shear forces exerted by positive-pressure ventilation are
thought to initiate an inflammatory response that increases vascular
permeability and causes microvascular damage resulting in edema.
Every effort should be made to prevent re-expansion pulmonary
edema in patients with chronic lung collapse by using relatively
low inspiratory pressures and volumes and allowing the lung to
re- expand gradually over time. If re-expansion pulmonary edema
occurs, it can be treated with diuretics, oxygen supplementation,
and supportive care.
Wooden chest syndrome
Chest wall rigidity (wooden chest syndrome) is observed when a
patient’s intercostal muscles and diaphragm become rigid, signifi-
cantly impairing ventilation. The phenomenon is associated with
the use of fentanyl and its analogues and has been reported in peo-
ple [88]. There are no reports of wooden chest syndrome in the
veterinary literature, although it has been noted anecdotally in dogs
receiving fentanyl. Clinical signs are consistent with a rigid thoracic
cavity including failure of the chest wall to expand, higher than
expected inspiratory airway pressures, and ventilatory failure in
patients breathing spontaneously or being mechanically ventilated.
In the face of these clinical events, it is important to distinguish pos-
sible chest wall rigidity due to fentanyl from more common causes
of inability to ventilate or abrupt changes to thoracic compliance,
such as bronchospasm, acute airway obstruction, and pneumotho-
rax. If these more common causes are ruled out, chest wall rigidity
due to fentanyl may be considered, and a neuromuscular blocking
agent may be administered to decrease skeletal muscle tone and
facilitate positive-pressure ventilation [88]. Reversal with naloxone
alone does not resolve chest wall rigidity in people, although chang-
ing to a different opioid for continued surgery may be warranted.
Airway fire
Airway fire is a rarely reported but devastating complication in
human anesthesia and, despite the increasing use of laser therapy
in veterinary medicine there are very few reports in the veterinary
literature [89]. Heat, fuel, and an oxidizer can occur together in the
operating room, so it is important to be careful when cautery or
laser energy is used around the endotracheal tube or other source of
oxygen [90]. In patients that are not intubated (e.g., small exotics),
care must be taken to ensure that an oxygen-rich environment does
not occur in proximity to an ignition source [76].
The risk of a fire can be minimized by using an endotracheal
tube not made of hydrocarbons (e.g., steel), ensuring that the cuff
is properly inflated, filling the cuff with dye-colored water (to visu-
alize if it has been damaged during the procedure), using less than
100% oxygen (i.e., an FI
O2 of 33% by mixing with medical air),
avoiding nitrous oxide, and packing the area around the surgical
site with wet gauze. Simply wrapping an endotracheal tube in reflec-
tive foil may be insufficient to protect it from laser energy. In the
event of a fire, it should be extinguished as quickly as possible using
water, a fire extinguisher or, if neither of those are available, suffoca-
tion. The source of oxygen should be discontinued and physically
removed from the fire. Extubation of the patient is not always the
correct course of action but is recommended if the patient does not
have a difficult airway that would complicate reintubation. In the
event of a larger fire, the oxygen source should be removed entirely
(e.g., the oxygen supply line shut down) and personnel evacuated.
Additional information is available in Chapter 4.
Anesthetic drug- related complications
Medical error resulting in overdose
Medical errors present a significant problem in human medicine
and are estimated to be the third leading cause of death in the
United States [91]. In one veterinary teaching hospital, drug errors
were the most common type of error reported [92]. The events that
lead to a drug error are complex and are examined in Chapter 3.
Drugs may be inadvertently given at the wrong dose, to the wrong
patient, by the wrong route, at the wrong time, or the wrong drug
may be given [92]. In the face of a drug error, the most immediate
step is to try to withdraw as much drug as possible from the patient
(i.e., for intravenously administered drugs, aspirate any drug
remaining in the catheter). The next step is to determine if the over-
dose constitutes a risk to the patient and, if so, take steps to mini-
mize patient harm.
Certain drugs used in veterinary anesthesia (e.g., opioids, benzo-
diazepines, α2 -adrenergic receptor agonists, and dissociatives)
have relatively wide therapeutic margins and, depending on the

-- 81 of 1450 --

66 	Section 1: General Topics
magnitude of the overdose, may not constitute a threat to patient
safety. Other drugs (e.g., propofol and bupivacaine) have narrower
therapeutic margins, and overdose may have more serious adverse
consequences. The patient’s physiologic parameters should be
evaluated and monitored following an overdose to determine if
there is any clinically relevant impairment. If not, the procedure
may proceed cautiously. If the patient is adversely affected by the
drug overdose, administration of a specific antagonist is warranted
if one is available. For local anesthetic toxicity, a lipid emulsion
provides a depot for the drug to enter and minimizes systemic
local anesthetic effects [93]. Overdose with a non-steroidal
anti-inflammatory drug may be treated with plasmapheresis [94].
Excessive sedation caused by acepromazine may be managed with
doxapram [95]. Further information about specific anesthetic, anal-
gesic, and antagonist drugs is available in the relevant pharmacol-
ogy chapters. Symptomatic support, including maintenance of body
temperature, fluid administration, and cardiorespiratory support,
may be necessary to give the patient time to clear the drug. The
patient’s status should be evaluated after treatment and, if possible,
a delay in the procedure may be necessary if the patient’s status is
still unknown or unstable.
Patient arousal
Acute arousal is usually the result of human error (i.e., underdosing,
inattention, judgment errors, or other knowledge gaps related to
injectable drugs, inhalant agents, or anesthetic machine operation)
and requires immediate intervention. Patient arousal and movement
can result in injury to personnel, injury to the patient, prolongation of
the procedure for which the patient was anesthetized, and damage to
equipment. Significant movement in anesthetized large animals (e.g.,
adult horses) can have potentially devastating consequences.
Underdosing during inhalant anesthesia may arise due to an inade-
quate fresh gas flow rate (e.g., flowmeter not turned on, compressed
gas cylinder empty, and oxygen supply line disconnected), a vaporizer
that is empty or not turned on, a tubing disconnection, and/or inef-
fective ventilation. In the face of movement during inhalant
anesthesia, the patient should be restrained and then rapidly
reanesthetized. Administration of an injectable agent is typically used
for this purpose, but in some cases, delivery of a high oxygen flow rate
and vaporizer setting may be employed. Once the patient’s anesthetic
plane has been stabilized, a thorough investigation into the cause of
acute arousal must be undertaken, including evaluation of the anes-
thetic machine, and corrective action taken to prevent re-occurrence.
Anesthetic equipment-related complications
The reader is directed to Chapter 6 for further details about equip-
ment function.
Adjustable pressure-limiting valve closure or
malfunction
Occlusion of the adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) (i.e., pop-off)
valve or exhaust tubing can result in a buildup of pressure within
the anesthetic circuit and is a common anesthetic-related adverse
incident [96]. An activated charcoal canister (e.g., F/air canister)
placed on the ground preventing outflow of gases can also cause
pressure to build up. Once the volume capacity of the breathing sys-
tem has been reached (i.e., once the elastic limits of the breathing
bag are exceeded), pressure in the breathing circuit climbs rapidly.
This increasing pressure may result in airway injury (i.e., volu-
trauma, pneumothorax), and compromised venous return decreases
cardiac output and may precipitate cardiovascular collapse and
arrest if not addressed in time. Loss of a palpable peripheral pulse
may be appreciated as the pressure in the breathing circuit is build-
ing. If excessive pressure has accumulated, it must be rapidly
relieved by opening the APL valve or, if occlusion or dysfunction of
the valve is suspected, disconnecting the circuit at any location.
Prevention of inadvertent APL valve closure can be minimized by
confirming its function and status during preanesthetic testing of
the breathing circuit, having a second individual routinely pressure-
check the circuit [96], using an APL valve with a momentary clo-
sure function either built-in or added to facilitate manual
intermittent positive-pressure ventilation (Fig. 5.3A), and incorpo-
rating a pressure-relief valve in the anesthetic circuit (Fig. 5.3B).
(A) 	(B)
Figure 5.3 A. Addition of a momentary closure valve adjacent to a standard adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) valve in a small animal breathing circuit.
This momentary closure function facilitates intermittent positive-pressure ventilation while minimizing the risk of the APL valve being inadvertently left
closed. B. Addition of a pressure-relief valve to a standard small animal breathing circuit. This device will vent excess gases into the environment at a
preset pressure in the event the APL valve is left closed and prevent pressure being transferred to the patient’s airway. Source: Dr. Erik Hofmeister, with

Oxygen supply failure
An empty oxygen tank or failure of the oxygen supply line results
in no fresh gas flow to carry inhalant anesthetic to the patient
and, potentially, a hypoxic mix of inspiratory gases. Failure of the
flowmeter indicator to register gas flow, patient arousal and
movement during inhalant anesthesia, and decreases in hemo-
globin saturation (SpO 2 ) may all indicate an oxygen supply prob-
lem. It is important to realize that the flowmeter may initially
register some oxygen flow if an oxygen tank was turned on to
pressurize the line between the tank and flowmeter and then sub-
sequently turned off. Therefore, the amount of oxygen remaining
in the tank should always be confirmed by observing the tank
pressure gauge prior to use. In the event of oxygen supply failure,
with no readily available remedy (e.g., all available oxygen tanks
empty), anesthesia may be maintained with total intravenous
anesthesia, with the understanding that an F I O 2 of 0.21 may pre-
dispose to hypoxemia.
Breathing system malfunction
A variety of accidents can occur involving the anesthetic breathing
system. The carbon dioxide absorbent may be exhausted but the
canister may not show an obvious color change due to channeling
of gases through the interior of the cylinder. The inner tube in a
coaxial breathing circuit (e.g., Bain or F-piece) may become twisted
and occlude inspiratory flow [97]. In-circuit filters may become
saturated with moisture and cause an obstruction [98]. A tear
may occur in coaxial circuits leading to rebreathing of CO2 [99].
One- way valves may become stuck or warped in rebreathing
circuits, resulting in rebreathing of CO2
. When the anesthetist is
faced with a confounding problem that could possibly be related to
the anesthetic machine, changing machines and breathing circuits
may be warranted until a thorough investigation of the original
machine can be undertaken.
Vaporizer-related complications
In addition to the vaporizer being empty or not turned on which
will lead to underdosing and patient arousal, the vaporizer may be
filled with the incorrect anesthetic agent, may be tipped, or may not
be secured to the manifold properly. Each vaporizer is designed to
function with a specific inhalant anesthetic, as the saturated vapor
pressure (SVP) of each inhalant is unique. Filling an isoflurane
vaporizer (SVP 240 mmHg) with sevoflurane (SVP 160 mmHg)
will result in underdosing, and filling a sevoflurane vaporizer with
isoflurane will result in overdosing. If a vaporizer is tipped from the
horizontal plane (e.g., if a machine falls over), the channel may fill
with inhalant, resulting in a substantial overdose of the inhalant
agent. If the vaporizer is not secured to the manifold, the circuit
may pass a leak test but a leak will exist between the flowmeter and
the common gas outlet. Use of an anesthetic agent analyzer to meas-
ure inspired inhalant concentrations may facilitate diagnosis of a
vaporizer malfunction.
Other complications
Gastroesophageal reflux and regurgitation
Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) is the phenomenon of fluid passively
moving from the stomach into the esophagus and, potentially, into
the oropharynx. It is estimated to happen in a significant number of
dogs under anesthesia with a reported incidence rate as high as
88% in one study [100]. GER also occurs in cats, though less often
than in dogs, with rates up to 33% in one study [101]. Esophageal
reflux is a risk factor for aspiration and can cause esophageal
stricture formation [102,103]. Regurgitation into the oropharynx is
associated with a fourfold increased risk of developing pneumonia
after anesthesia [81]. While the exact incidence of esophageal
stricture formation postanesthesia is unknown it appears to be rare.
However, it is a potentially catastrophic adverse anesthetic event,
which can have a significant impact on the patient’s and client’s
quality of life [102,103].
Once GER has occurred, there are several treatment approaches
to minimize potential damage to the esophagus. Although none of
the treatments have documented an impact on the development
of esophagitis, esophageal strictures, or aspiration pneumonia, it is
expected that removing as much refluxate as possible and neutral-
izing any acidic or basic elements in the refluxate would minimize
damage to the esophagus. In anesthetized dogs with persistent
acidic esophageal pH despite repeated cycles of suctioning, lavaging
with tap water, and further suctioning, the instillation of 20 mL of
4.2% sodium bicarbonate into the distal esophagus was effective in
increasing esophageal pH [104]. A subsequent study indicated that
the lavage with water may be an unnecessary step and suggested
sole treatment with 4.2% sodium bicarbonate at 0.6 mL/kg after
suctioning was sufficient [105]. Further information on GER is
available in Chapters 2 and 41.
Ruminal tympany
In ruminants, distension of the rumen (i.e., bloat) due to inability of
gas to escape through the esophagus may complicate anesthesia and
increase the risk of regurgitation. Development of bloat compresses
the diaphragm, decreases functional residual capacity, and causes
respiratory compromise. Significant bloat may limit venous return
and impair cardiac output. Appropriate fasting (i.e., 24–48 h)
reduces the risk of bloat in adult ruminants. Passing a stomach tube
via the esophagus into the rumen will help prevent bloat in patients
that have not been fasted. In the event that bloat develops during a
procedure, a stomach tube can be passed to relieve the pressure.
If a stomach tube cannot be passed, possibly due to excess pressure
at the cardiac sphincter, transcutaneous decompression (similar to
trocharization in dogs with gastric dilatation-volvulus) can be
performed. Further information is available in Chapters 53 and 64.
Cerebral herniation
Cerebral herniation describes the displacement of brain structures
across anatomical boundaries within the calvarium (e.g., brainstem
protruding through the foramen magnum). During anesthesia,
abrupt increases in intracranial pressure (ICP) precipitated by
intubation, hypercapnia, hypertension, hypoxemia, jugular occlu-
sion, changes in head elevation, and/or exacerbation of intracranial
disease (e.g., hemorrhage, swelling) increase the risk of cerebral
herniation in at-risk patients. Cerebral herniation may stimulate a
Cushing reflex, apnea, cardiovascular collapse, and/or failure to
recover from anesthesia. A Cushing reflex manifests as an acute
increase in arterial blood pressure and a reflex bradycardia in an
attempt to maintain cerebral perfusion in the face of an increased
ICP [106]. In at-risk patients, the risk of cerebral herniation may be
reduced by maintaining PaCO2 (or PET
CO2
) in the low normal range
(e.g., 32 mmHg), keeping the head elevated, avoiding jugular occlu-
sion and hypoxemia, and potentially considering propofol rather
than an inhalant for maintenance of anesthesia [107]. If cerebral

-- 83 of 1450 --

68 	Section 1: General Topics
herniation is suspected, the patient can be hyperventilated (target
PET
CO2 of 25 mmHg), and mannitol (0.5–1 g/kg IV over 10 min)
and/or hypertonic saline (2–4 mL/kg IV over 10 min) can be
administered. Prednisone (1 mg/kg IV) may help reduce inflamma-
tion. Patients with acute cerebral herniation have a grave prognosis
and failure to recover from anesthesia is not an unexpected out-
come. Further information is available in Chapter 39.
Hyperkalemia
Development of acute hyperkalemia during general anesthesia in
a patient with normal serum potassium prior to anesthesia is a
rare but potentially life-threatening complication. In dogs and cats,
while there have been reports of intraoperative hyperkalemia, and a
definitive cause has not been identified, dexmedetomidine use has
been implicated as a risk factor [108,109]. Horses diagnosed with or
suspected to have hyperkalemic periodic paralysis may be at an
increased risk of developing hyperkalemia under anesthesia [110].
Hyperkalemia may be identified by changes to the ECG, notably
bradycardia (which is often resistant to treatment with antimus-
carinics), absent P waves, and tented T waves [108,109]. Horses
may exhibit muscle fasciculations [110]. Typical treatments for
hyperkalemia that reduce the risk of fatal arrhythmias (e.g., calcium
gluconate) and lower serum potassium concentrations (e.g., insulin,
dextrose, and sodium bicarbonate) are indicated [109]. Hyperkalemia
identified prior to anesthesia (e.g., due to urethral obstruction or
uroperitoneum) should be corrected before induction of anesthesia
if at all possible. Further information is available in Chapter 43.
Hypo- or hyperthermia
Hypothermia is a common event under anesthesia in dogs and cats,
affecting up to 89% of dogs [111,112] and 98% of cats [113]. Dogs
and cats with an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) status
of III or more are at increased risk of developing intraoperative hypo-
thermia [114]. Other risk factors identified in dogs include body
weight < 6 kg, receiving an α2
-adrenergic receptor agonist, receiving
an opioid, having an anesthetic episode lasting > 1 h, having surgery
for an orthopedic or neurologic condition, or undergoing an
MRI [112]. A variety of strategies have been investigated to minimize
intraoperative hypothermia, and the reader is directed to Chapter 17
for more information. Once hypothermia develops, active warming
strategies (e.g., forced warm air and resistive polymer heating) are
indicated although there is a lag period between implementation of
active warming and changes to core temperature [115].
Hyperthermia during general anesthesia is much less common
than hypothermia, affecting only 3–9% of dogs [111,112] and 1% of
cats [113]. Hyperthermia during anesthetic maintenance is often
iatrogenic, due to excessive warming, particularly in small patients.
Postanesthetic hyperthermia has been documented in up to 47% of
cats within 24 h [116]. It is associated largely with opioid adminis-
tration [117], although cats receiving only medetomidine and
either ketamine or propofol can also develop hyperthermia [118].
Postanesthetic hyperthermia in cats is typically self-limiting [117];
however, if the temperature is excessively high, naloxone 0.01 mg/kg
IM or IV can be administered. Body temperature often rapidly
returns to normal following opioid reversal. Further information is
available in Chapter 17.
Malignant hyperthermia
The phenomenon of malignant hyperthermia is characterized by a
rapid increase in body temperature caused by skeletal muscle con-
traction. This contraction is caused by an abnormal, excessive
influx of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum due to a defective
calcium channel, most commonly the ryanodine receptor (RyR1).
This abnormal influx is most commonly induced by anesthetic
drugs, notably halogenated inhalant anesthetic agents (not gases
such as nitrous oxide and xenon) and succinylcholine. Other trig-
gers, such as stress and exercise, may rarely precipitate malignant
hyperthermia. While malignant hyperthermia is extremely rare
overall and is less common with modern inhalant anesthet-
ics [119], it has been documented in dogs [120], cats [121], and
horses [122] using isoflurane or sevoflurane. Pigs are the most
commonly affected species and have been used as an animal model
for the disease for decades [123]. Further information about malig-
nant hyperthermia in pigs is available in Chapters 53 and 65.
Clinical signs of malignant hyperthermia vary by species and can
manifest from induction through to recovery. Typically, evidence of
a hypermetabolic syndrome predominates, particularly increased
PET
CO2
, heart rate, arrhythmias, and body temperature [120].
Muscle rigidity, changes to skin color due to vasodilation, metabolic
acidosis, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, sweating, and dissemi-
nated intravascular coagulation can also occur [123]. Because the
treatment for malignant hyperthermia is specific to that diagnosis, it
is important to distinguish it from other hypermetabolic causes,
such as hyperthermia [124], sepsis/endotoxemia [120], or thyrotoxi-
cosis [125]. Any patient exhibiting an abrupt increase in PET
CO2 or
body temperature should be considered for malignant hyperther-
mia. If suspected, inhalant anesthetics should be discontinued, the
patient changed to a “clean” machine and circuit without recent
inhalant exposure, and anesthesia maintained with an injectable
protocol (e.g., propofol infusion). The specific treatment for malig-
nant hyperthermia is the calcium channel blocker dantrolene at
2 mg/kg IV with additional doses as required up to 10 mg/kg IV.
Because dantrolene is rarely available at most veterinary hospitals,
symptomatic treatment and other calcium channel blockers may be
used but are rarely successful [120–122]. Symptomatic treatment
may include administration of sympatholytics (e.g., β-adrenergic
blockers), insulin and dextrose to treat hyperkalemia, procainamide,
neuromuscular blocking agents, hyperventilation, active cooling,
and fluid support. Lidocaine and exogenous calcium administration
may worsen the outcome [120]. Without acute dantrolene treat-
ment, malignant hyperthermia is typically fatal [120–122].
Myoclonus
Myoclonus is the rhythmic contraction of skeletal muscles and can
range from a small single-muscle tick to a whole-body contraction
that resembles a seizure. In people, the electroencephalogram
(EEG) of patients experiencing anesthesia drug-related myoclonus
is not typical of seizure activity; therefore, myoclonus appears to be
distinct from a seizure [126]. Myoclonus has been reported
in dogs administered etomidate [127], epidural morphine [128],
propofol [129], and ketamine [130]. Administering additional
drugs, such as propofol or benzodiazepines, does not reliably
stop the myoclonus [127,129], but pretreatment with an opioid or
benzodiazepine may reduce the incidence [127,131]. Myoclonus
occurring after induction typically subsides if no additional
treatment is given and does not seem to be associated with adverse
clinical effects for the patient [130].
Postanesthetic complications
Prolonged anesthetic recovery
The time to recover from anesthesia depends on the species,
the drugs used and their route of administration, the duration of

-- 84 of 1450 --

Chapter 5: Anesthetic Emergencies, Resuscitation, and Adverse Events 	69
anesthesia, and patient characteristics [132,133]. In small animal
patients, the time from termination of inhalant anesthesia to extu-
bation of the patient is usually expected to be less than 30 min [134].
In equine patients in a university teaching hospital setting, the
time from inhalant anesthesia termination to standing is typically
expected to be less than 60 min [133]. If the patient’s recovery
exceeds these times (or those defined by the institution), it may be
considered prolonged. A prolonged recovery may indicate physio-
logic disturbances, which must be corrected and is, therefore, a
potential anesthetic emergency.
Common differential diagnoses for a prolonged recovery include
hypothermia, hypotension, hemorrhage, hepatic incompetence,
renal dysfunction, hypoglycemia, neurologic disease, hypocalcemia,
and drug overdose. The potential for prolonged anesthetic recovery
should be anticipated in patients where preanesthetic patient
evaluation indicates hepatic incompetence (e.g., liver failure), renal
dysfunction, and/or neurologic disease and their anesthetic proto-
cols should be adjusted accordingly. In patients experiencing a
prolonged recovery that was not expected, their physiologic status
should be thoroughly evaluated, specifically temperature, blood
glucose, ionized calcium, blood pressure, and packed cell volume
if hemorrhage from a surgical procedure (e.g., postoperative ovari-
ohysterectomy) is a possibility. Any physiologic derangements
should be corrected. If no physiologic abnormalities are identified,
a relative drug overdose should be considered, even if the drug dose
was apparently appropriate for the patient. Opioids may be reversed
with low-dose naloxone (0.01 mg/kg IV) and benzodiazepines with
flumazenil (0.01 mg/kg IV). α2
- Adrenergic receptor agonists may
be reversed with atipamezole, tolazoline, or yohimbine. Excessive
sedation due to acepromazine may be treated with doxapram
(1.25 mg/kg IV). In exceptional circumstances, recovery from
inhalant anesthesia may be expedited with doxapram [135] or phys-
ostigmine [136]. If drug effects have been reversed and recovery
still has not progressed, persistent neurologic dysfunction, possibly
due to intraoperative hypotension, hypoperfusion, and hypoxia,
should be considered. Administration of corticosteroids, mannitol,
and/or hypertonic saline may be indicated if there is concern for
increased ICP secondary to the patient’s disease or suspected
cerebral hypoxia.
Patient injury during recovery
Injuries may be incurred by patients during recovery from anesthe-
sia. In small animals, thrashing body motions may cause trauma to
the head and limbs, necessitating further medical care (e.g., wound
care, fracture repair, and dental extraction). In horses, fractures sus-
tained during recovery account for up to 64% of all anesthesia-
related fatalities [137]. In addition to appropriate analgesia, sedation
prior to recovery, particularly in patients expected to be anxious or
aggressive, may help minimize the risk of injury. In an emergency
situation where an animal is thrashing and may injure itself, serious
consideration must also be given to the risk of injury to personnel.
In a survey, up to 43% of equine hospitals reported injury to
personnel in recovery, and most respondents felt those assisting
with equine recovery were at greater risk of personal injury [138].
In small animal patients experiencing violent recoveries, the use of
physical restraint aids where possible (e.g., leash, wooden board,
and rabies pole) should be considered to minimize the risk to
personnel and facilitate administration of injectable IM sedation
(e.g., dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and/or tiletamine–zolazepam).
In adult equine cases, there is little a single individual can do for the
thrashing patient in recovery. Often the anesthetist must wait until
the patient becomes calm enough to approach and handle and this
may be due to exhaustion or asphyxiation and loss of conscious-
ness. Once the equine patient can be handled, sedation and analge-
sia may be warranted. If the equine patient is unconscious due to
airway obstruction, a tracheostomy should be rapidly performed
and drugs readied to maintain the patient in an anesthetized or
sedated state until an airway is re-established and the patient is
stabilized.
Postanesthetic blindness
Postanesthetic blindness can occur due to decreases in cerebral
perfusion during anesthesia or occlusion of the maxillary artery,
particularly in cats. Cats suffering from hypoxia due to cardiac
arrest or profound hypotension can develop cortical blindness [139].
Blindness may also be caused by decreased maxillary artery blood
flow due to mouth gag placement for dental, oral, or endoscopic
procedures [140,141]. Cortical blindness may be permanent, or
vision may return with time [140]. Avoiding the use of spring-
loaded mouth gags and minimizing any gag opening to 30 mm or
less should prevent occlusion of the maxillary artery in cats [142].
As blindness is diagnosed after the hypoxic event has already
occurred and the patient has recovered from anesthesia, therapeutic
intervention is not possible and prevention remains the best course
of action.
Postanesthetic neuropathy, rhabdomyolysis, or
myelomalacia
Large animals, particularly horses, undergoing general anesthesia
may experience complications related to nerve, muscle or, rarely,
spinal cord damage that become apparent during recovery. Further
information on these complications is available in the Chapters 52
and 61.
Rhabdomyolysis (i.e., postanesthetic myopathy) in horses
occurs due to decreased perfusion of large muscles and subse-
quent reperfusion injury combined with increased muscle com-
partment pressure [143]. It can result in lameness, poor recovery
quality, fracture, death, euthanasia, renal failure due to myoglobi-
nuria, and/or failure to recover from anesthesia [137,144].
Postoperative rhabdomyolysis is one of the most common causes
of morbidity and mortality associated with anesthesia in the
horse, accounting for 7% of deaths [144] and 31% of non-fatal
complications [56]. Prolonged duration of anesthesia, hypoten-
sion, and lateral recumbency are risk factors for the development
of rhabdomyolysis [56]. The risk of developing rhabdomyolysis
can be reduced by minimizing the duration of anesthesia, mainte-
nance of MAP > 70 mmHg, provision of IV fluids, ensuring ade-
quate padding and positioning, and avoiding excess strain on
muscles [145]. Horses that develop rhabdomyolysis may have dif-
ficulty standing in recovery, exhibit lameness once standing, have
swollen or hard muscles, and display signs of pain such as shaking,
sweating, tachycardia, and/or tachypnea [146]. If rhabdomyolysis
is suspected, the presence of myoglobinuria and/or a significantly
elevated creatine kinase will support the diagnosis. Treatment in
the acute phase is supportive and consists of appropriate analgesia
(e.g., α2 -adrenergic receptor agonists, butorphanol, lidocaine
infusion), aggressive fluid support, anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g.,
flunixin meglumine or corticosteroids), and physical therapy such
as massage or water cooling.

-- 85 of 1450 --

70 	Section 1: General Topics
Postanesthetic neuropathy in horses occurs due to pressure on
peripheral nerves, which causes varying degrees of impairment.
Although it is rarely reported to cause fatality, it may co-occur
with rhabdomyolysis, which may mask the influence of neuro-
pathy [147]. Neuropathy may impact recovery quality and post-
operative 	morbidity, 	leading 	to 	prolonged 	recovery 	or
euthanasia [148,149]. Facial nerve injury may result from the
halter exerting pressure on superficial nerves which manifests as
facial asymmetry [150]. Distal limb peripheral nerve injury can
result from direct pressure exerted by poorly positioned poles or
other pressure points and may lead to inability to extend the
hoof. Radial nerve paralysis can occur in laterally recumbent
horses and lead to a dropped shoulder and inability to extend the
hoof [151]. Obturator nerve injury impacting anesthetic recov-
ery 	associated 	with 	parturition 	and 	dystocia 	has 	been
reported [147]. Bilateral femoral nerve paralysis has been associ-
ated with caudal extension of the hindlimbs in dorsally recum-
bent horses, but unilateral and bilateral pelvic limb neuropathies
have been reported with various body positions in both depend-
ent and non-dependent limbs [148,149,152]. The diagnosis of
neuropathy is often made by exclusion of other possible causes
of prolonged or difficult recovery, particularly rhabdomyoly-
sis [149]. Steps to minimize the risk of neuropathy are similar to
those taken to minimize the risk of rhabdomyolysis and include
sufficient padding, avoiding pressure points, maintaining ade-
quate blood flow, minimizing anesthesia duration, and pulling
the dependent forelimb forward in laterally recumbent horses to
minimize pressure on the radial nerve [149]. If neuropathy
occurs, there are few options for acute treatment beyond anti-
inflammatory drugs and physical therapy. Physical means of
support (e.g., a sling, supporting bandages) may be necessary if
the horse is unable to stand without assistance. The degree of
damage is unknown at the time of injury and can range from
neuropraxia (temporary loss of nerve conduction), to axonot-
mesis (significant axonal damage), to neurotmesis (complete
transection of the nerve) [151]. Because the prognosis is depend-
ent on the time required to recover nerve function, re-
examination is warranted to assess the patient’s progress [150].
Patients that have rapid resolution of signs likely had a mild
injury (neuropraxia), whereas those that have permanent loss of
function likely had complete disruption of the nerve fiber
(neurotmesis) [148].
Myelomalacia is a softening of the spinal cord, which leads to
catastrophic failure of spinal conducting pathways, resulting in
paralysis. It is a rare but devastating complication in horses
undergoing anesthesia [153]. Horses developing myelomalacia
will be unable to stand in recovery, may adopt a dog-sitting pos-
ture due to paraplegia, and will lack anal tone and hind limb
function [153]. The absence of anal tone, tail tone, and with-
drawal reflexes help to distinguish it from bilateral femoral
nerve paralysis. Myelomalacia most commonly occurs in horses
that were in dorsal recumbency during anesthesia and seems to
happen more commonly in draft breeds (e.g., Fresian, Morgan,
and Percheron) [153]. Other risk factors have not been identi-
fied. There is no known prevention for the development of mye-
lomalacia, and treatment has been unrewarding with a 100%
fatality rate [153]. Any horse that has abnormal hind limb func-
tion following anesthesia should be assessed for the possibility of
myelomalacia, and it should be distinguished from rhabdomy-
olysis and neuropathy, both of which may have more favorable
outcomes.
Personnel injury
Injury to personnel around an anesthetic event can result in a crisis,
which compounds or complicates patient welfare. If personnel are
injured, resources need to be diverted to caring for them, which
makes it more challenging to care for patients effectively. Injured
personnel are also unable to care for their patients, so personnel
safety should always be paramount in any veterinary setting. The
breadth of patient types encountered in anesthetic practice means
that the anesthetist may be faced with aggressive, wild, and/or ven-
omous species, which can all pose a significant threat to human
safety. Veterinary technicians working with more than six different
species reported a twofold greater risk of injury than those working
with less than four species [154]. Animals account for the majority
of accidents veterinarians encounter, up to 66% [155,156].
Veterinary staff members tend to underestimate the risk of injury
relative to an expert panel, indicating that risks exist which staff do
not perceive as such (e.g., handling an animal in recovery) [156].
Bites from dogs accounted for 35% of the injuries associated with
anesthetic procedures [157]. In one study, no survey respondents
who reported being bitten in the previous year had been engaged in
anesthesia activities, whereas 4% of those who did not report being
bitten were engaged in an anesthesia procedure, suggesting that
anesthesia activities may be safer than other activities [158]. This
may be due to the ability of veterinary anesthesia staff to use seda-
tives, which contributes to a lower overall injury risk compared
with non-veterinary workers such as groomers [159].
Risk to personnel should always be assessed, particularly in cir-
cumstances where control of the environment is limited. This is
essential in field situations or in situations where the setting is sub-
optimal (e.g., managing a horse recumbent in a trailer). A plan
should be prepared so that every individual knows their role, what
the steps of the anesthesia event will include and in what order, and
what to do if a problem occurs. Use of remote immobilization is often
preferred if an animal cannot be approached safely. Aggressive or
dangerous patients limited to a confined space (e.g., stall, corral,
or carrier) may be sedated with a blowgun, a spring-loaded syringe
pole, or a CO 2
- powered pistol. Drug combinations involving
α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists (e.g., dexmedetomidine, detomi-
dine, romifidine, or xylazine) and dissociatives (e.g., ketamine or
tiletamine) are typically used for pharmacologic restraint in domes-
tic species, and ultrapotent opioids are often used in non-domestic
species. Animals that can be physically restrained (i.e., squeeze
cage, rabies pole, or capture net) may be able to be injected by hand.
In the event of an injury to personnel, it is the anesthetist’s role to
ensure continued personnel safety and patient management. An
individual should be designated to care for the injured person so
that the anesthetist can supervise management of the patient and
environment. Once the injured person is receiving care, avoiding
further personnel injury should be the most important priority. In
some cases, this priority may have to temporarily supersede patient
welfare (e.g., releasing a thrashing cat to avoid being bitten or leaving
an enclosed space with a horse having a difficult recovery). Once
personnel safety has been established, the patient should be attended
to, and appropriate care provided. Sedation of the patient may be
required to avoid further injury to personnel or the animal.
Post- critical event debriefing
Anesthetic emergencies often occur rapidly, threaten patient well-
being and survival, and depend on the intervention of the anesthe-
sia team for a successful outcome. All of these variables can place

-- 86 of 1450 --

Chapter 5: Anesthetic Emergencies, Resuscitation, and Adverse Events 	71
significant emotional strain on care providers. This may manifest as
stress, burnout, anxiety, a feeling of helplessness, and/or depres-
sion [160]. In one study in human medical care providers, almost
half of those who answered a trauma screening questionnaire
reported one to five symptoms of psychological trauma [160].
Providers who did not have a debriefing event reported a higher
incidence of post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms than those
who did have a debriefing [160].
One study in veterinary medicine documented that debriefing
occurred in ~ 60% of CPR events [15]. Most survey respondents
indicated that a post-event debriefing tool improved team perfor-
mance. The most commonly cited points for improvement included
equipment issues, need for clinical standards, and medication
errors being made. Applications of checklists, training, and proper
organization and preparation of equipment should be considered
for any anesthetic emergency that is likely to arise [14,15,96].

Introduction
The delivery and maintenance of safe anesthesia have become
increasingly dependent upon mechanical and electrical equipment.
It is necessary for the anesthetist to have a thorough understanding
of equipment function and common failures as well as potential
patient and personnel risks before use for routine patient care.
Anesthesia equipment includes various airway support products,
oxygen delivery devices, anesthetic machines, scavenge systems,
ventilators, and many configurations of patient monitors and other
support products. The products available to the veterinary
anesthetist include nearly any human-patient product that can be
adapted for use in veterinary anesthesia, regularly produced items
specifically for the veterinary market, and many limited-production
and/or custom products that may only be occasionally available.
There are several excellent textbooks devoted to describing in great
detail the anesthetic equipment available for use in human anesthe-
sia [1–3] and, although not entirely applicable to veterinary anes-
thesia, much of the equipment used is the same (i.e., vaporizers,
laryngoscopes, endotracheal tubes, some anesthetic machines) or is
a modification of human products. As such, it would be impossible

to discuss all of the anesthetic-related equipment and products
available today in a single chapter. More recently, a veterinary-
specific anesthetic equipment textbook has been published which
details the anesthetic and monitoring equipment frequently used in
veterinary medicine [4]. This chapter intends to provide the reader
with the operating principles and a practical working overview of
common anesthetic-related products (i.e., endotracheal tubes, intu-
bating aids, etc.), the anesthetic machine, vaporizers, breathing cir-
cuits, and ventilators. In addition, there are products that have been
designed specifically for veterinary use, which are described in
more detail here.
Safety and design
Since at least 1976, human anesthetic breathing circuits (i.e., circle
system) and anesthesia machines sold in North America must
meet both mandated and voluntary regulations established by the
United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) (Medical
Device Amendments-1976, Good Manufacturing Practices-1978,
and Mandatory Device reporting-1984) and organizations such as
the International Organization for Standardization (ISO 5358-
198a), American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM F1850),
and the Canadian Standards Association (CSA). Many of these
standards are currently under re-review with updates anticipated.
Anesthetic machines designed for veterinary use are not required
to meet any specific design or safety standards beyond those asso-
ciated with basic hazards to the operator (i.e., electrical safety
requirements). Safety features are often added on an ad hoc basis
and there are no requirements for demonstrating equipment effi-
cacy. Ideally, some safety features, such as airway pressure alarms,
should be integral to the design of the anesthetic machine. The
inclusion of some of these safety systems on anesthetic machines
may help eliminate preventable anesthetic accidents. However,
until safety and design standards are adopted by the manufacturers
of veterinary anesthetic equipment, there will remain equipment
options of varying quality, efficacy, and safety available for deliver-
ing inhalant anesthetics to veterinary patients. Ancillary and sup-
port equipment for veterinary patients, including patient monitors
and ventilators, are similarly devoid of required efficacy and safety
testing. Fortunately, most reputable manufacturers and distribu-
tors readily provide the specifications, accuracy, and any available
efficacy data for their designs. Regardless of the presence of stand-
ards, it will always be incumbent upon the veterinary anesthetist to
understand thoroughly the function, principles of operation, and
use of all anesthetic-related pieces of equipment and to ensure that
the machine or piece of equipment is designed suitably well to
accomplish its functions safely.
Introduction to airway management
and support equipment
Airway management and support are vital for the safe delivery of
anesthesia. Most, if not all, anesthetics cause respiratory depression
at doses suitable for anesthesia. In addition, relaxation and/or loss
of airway reflexes make the patient more prone to upper airway
obstruction. Both of these factors put the anesthetized patient at
higher risk for the development of hypoxia. Additionally, the inhal-
ant anesthetics require delivery to the lungs while minimizing envi-
ronmental and personnel exposure to waste anesthetic gases. For
these reasons, airway management and support are critical aspects
of properly performed inhalant general anesthesia.
Endotracheal tubes, lung isolation devices,
supraglottic airway devices, laryngoscopes,
intubation aids, and techniques
Endotracheal tubes
Endotracheal tubes are commonly used to maintain an airway in
anesthetized patients. Supraglottic airway devices (SGADs) have
also been evaluated in a number of domestic species and may be
suitable alternatives in some instances [5–9]. A properly placed
endotracheal tube or SGAD with a properly inflated cuff provides a
patent airway, facilitates positive-pressure ventilation, protects the
lungs from aspiration of fluids, and prevents contamination of the
work environment with waste anesthetic gases. Occasionally, it is
desirable to limit airway management to one lung field (i.e., thora-
coscopy), and specially designed equipment is available to accom-
plish this task in dogs.
There are many styles and types of endotracheal tubes available
that can be used in veterinary medicine. Most are manufactured for
humans but can also be used in most small animal patients. There
are some veterinary-specific products available for patients requir-
ing tube sizes larger and smaller than those available for human use.
Endotracheal tubes manufactured for human patients must have
various markings and abbreviations directly on the tube describing
the tube’s characteristics as well as interval markings to measure the
depth of insertion. The markings may include the manufacturer,
internal diameter (ID), outer diameter (OD), and length of the tube,
as well as codes indicating tissue toxicity or implantation testing
(e.g., F29) (Fig. 6.1). There is no requirement for similar markings
on tubes manufactured solely for veterinary use, but it is common
for them to minimally list tube diameters and lengths. Endotracheal
tubes are often sized according to their internal diameters. For
example, a size 6.0 endotracheal tube refers to a tube with an inter-
nal diameter of 6 mm. Some tubes manufactured specifically for the
veterinary market have their sizes indicated using the French gauge/
catheter scale, and this should, but may not always, reflect the inter-
nal size of the tube. The outer diameter for any given tube size may
vary depending upon the construction of the tube. Endotracheal
tubes having thicker walls will have greater differences between the
internal and outer diameters. This can become important when
selecting tubes for very small patients. Very thick-walled tubes will
effectively reduce the internal airway diameter compared with a
thin-walled tube as ultimately, the size of the endotracheal tube that
can be placed in a patient is limited by the outer diameter of the
tube and not the inner diameter. However, very thin-walled soft
tubes are susceptible to obstruction by external compression or
kinking (Fig. 6.2).
Common endotracheal tube materials include polyvinyl chlo-
ride, silicone, or red rubber. Clear endotracheal tubes are generally
preferred so that they can be inspected visually for the presence of
mucus or blood intraoperatively, or debris within the tube lumen
after cleaning. Generally, the largest size of an endotracheal tube
that will fit without causing trauma in the patient’s trachea should
be used. Although various “rules-of-thumb” for selecting tube size
exist, it is probably easiest to estimate the most appropriate tube size
by palpating the individual patient’s cervical trachea. The tube
should not extend distally beyond the thoracic inlet and ideally
should not extend rostrally beyond the patient’s incisors, as any
additional tube length extending beyond the patient’s incisors will
increase mechanical deadspace. If the endotracheal tube is too long,
and further insertion would lead to the possibility of endobronchial
intubation, the machine end can be cut, and the endotracheal tube
connector reinserted.

The most commonly used type of endotracheal tube in both large
and small animals is the cuffed Murphy-type tube shown in Fig. 6.1.
Cole- type and guarded (spiral embedded, armored) tubes are also
occasionally used in veterinary medicine. Cole tubes are uncuffed
and have a smaller diameter at the patient (distal) end relative to
the machine (proximal) end. The distal smaller diameter portion
of the tube is inserted into the trachea to a point where the shoulder
contacts the larynx, forming a seal. However, Cole tubes will not
produce the same degree of airway security as a standard cuffed
tube and are normally used only in very small patients for short-
term intubation (see Fig. 6.3). Guarded tubes incorporate a metal or
nylon spiral-wound reinforcing wire into the endotracheal tube
wall that helps prevent tube collapse and occlusion (Fig. 6.4).
Guarded tubes are useful in situations where the tube is likely to be
compressed or kinked, such as procedures requiring extreme flexion
of the head and neck (e.g., cervical cerebrospinal fluid collection
and ophthalmic procedures) or those that involve compression of
the trachea (e.g., tracheal retraction during the ventral approach to
the cervical spinal cord).

animals and human patients is a uniform size (15 mm OD) facilitat-
ing universal connection to all standard anesthetic circuits. Tubes
designed for use in large animals typically have larger connectors,
which include metal-type and funnel-type connectors. The distal
(patient) end of the connector varies in size according to the diam-
eter of the endotracheal tube. Endotracheal tube adapters may also
incorporate gas sampling ports (Fig. 6.5). These are particularly
useful in small patients where minimizing equipment deadspace
can be important and may improve the accuracy of gas sampling in
smaller patients where non-rebreathing systems are often used.
Endotracheal tubes designed for large animals are normally
manufactured with a silicone funnel adapter attached (Fig. 6.6) that
is designed to fit over the large animal Y-piece (54 mm OD). There
are also stainless-steel Bivona endotracheal tube adapters (22 OD)
that are designed to fit the Bivona insert sometimes found on large
animal Y-pieces.
The patient (distal) end of the endotracheal tube is normally bev-
eled. Murphy-type tubes have a hole in the endotracheal tube wall
opposite the bevel, referred to as a “Murphy eye” or “Murphy hole”
(see Fig. 6.1A). The purpose of the hole is to provide an alternative
route for gas flow should the beveled opening become occluded.
Endotracheal tubes that lack a Murphy eye are referred to as Magill-
type tubes. Most endotracheal tube sizes can be found without an
inflatable cuff, although the use of cuffed tubes provides a more
reliable airway. Tubes lacking cuffs tend to be very small diameter
tubes where the addition of a cuff may not be possible or will limit
the maximum diameter tube that can be used in a patient. The cuff
is located on the machine-end side of the Murphy eye for cuffed
tubes, and can be a low-volume, high-pressure or high-volume,
low- pressure design (Fig. 6.7). In general, high-volume, low-
pressure cuffs are preferred to minimize the risk of ischemic tra-
cheal injury that may result from excessive cuff pressure against the
tracheal wall. When a properly fitting endotracheal tube with a
high-volume, low-pressure cuff is used, the pressure exerted by the
cuff on the tracheal wall is similar to the intracuff pressure. This
allows for a better estimation of the pressure on the tracheal wall
exerted by the cuff. When using a low-volume, high-pressure cuffed
endotracheal tube, the intracuff pressure does not reflect the pres-
sure on the tracheal wall but rather the pressure created by the elas-
tic recoil of the cuff, making estimates of pressure exerted by the
cuff on the tracheal wall difficult. Tracheal wall pressures exceeding
48 cmH2
O may impede capillary blood flow, potentially causing
ischemic tracheal damage, and pressure below 18 mmHg may
increase the risk of aspiration [10]. There are also several cases of
tracheal rupture or disruption reported in veterinary medicine
leading to pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and/or subcuta-
neous emphysema [11].
A reliable method for ensuring that cuff pressures are within the
recommended range is to use a cuff monitor to inflate high-
volume, low-pressure cuffs. A cuff monitor is essentially a low-
pressure manometer similar to those used for Doppler blood
pressure measurement that is attached to the pilot balloon of the
cuff and provides a measure of intracuff pressure. As noted above,
these devices are only useful when using appropriately sized high-
volume, low-pressure cuffs. If high-pressure cuffs are used or if the
endotracheal tube is markedly undersized for the patient, the
measured cuff pressure may not accurately reflect the pressure
exerted on the tracheal wall. Other commercially available cuff
inflation guides are available for the human market and can be
adapted to veterinary use (Fig. 6.8). Alternatively, it is more com-
mon to use a leak test or the minimal occlusive volume (MOV)

Recently two commercially available syringe devices specifically
designed for endotracheal tube cuff inflation have been evaluated
for use in veterinary medicine that may help reduce the incidence
of improperly inflated cuffs compared to MOV [12]. The pilot bal-
loon used for inflating the endotracheal tube cuff is connected to
the cuff via a channel incorporated into the endotracheal tube and
normally includes a syringe-activated self-sealing valve system.
However, there are also valveless pilot balloons that do not self-seal
and require occlusion using either a clamp or plug.
An uncuffed self-sealing endotracheal tube (Safe-Seal™, Innovative
Animal Products, Rochester, MN, USA, 55901) has been introduced
into the veterinary market. The tube is designed with a series of flexible
circumferential flanges at the patient end of the endotracheal tube that
deform to the contours of the trachea, forming a seal against the tra-
cheal wall eliminating the need to inflate a cuff (Fig. 6.9). There are
currently no independent research studies evaluating the effectiveness
of this tube for use in veterinary anesthesia. It is available with only a
limited number of internal tube diameters and differs from a conven-
tional endotracheal tube in that it has no Murphy eye or inflatable cuff.
Endotracheal tubes for isolating one lung
In addition to the endotracheal tubes described above, there are
tubes specially designed for isolating or ventilating one lung.
Indications for the use of these tubes include improving surgical
conditions for various thoracic procedures (i.e., thoracoscopy), the
control of contamination or hemorrhage, and use in circumstances
where unilateral pathology exists. There are generally three meth-
ods of isolating or ventilating a single lung: a double-lumen tube
(DLT), a bronchial blocker, or by using a long, standard endotra-
cheal tube as an endobronchial tube.
Figure 6.7 The upper endotracheal tube has a high-volume, low-pressure

high- pressure cuff. The bulkiness associated with some cuffs can limit the
endotracheal tube size, which can be problematic in very small patients.

Endobronchial intubation for single lung ventilation or isolation
is probably the least desirable option as it provides less direct con-
trol for making changes in the non-intubated lung. However, it does
not require specialized equipment, apart from a sufficiently long
endotracheal tube, and is relatively easy to perform. Endobronchial
intubation has been used in dogs successfully and may be an alter-
native when DLTs and bronchial blockers are not available [13,14].
DLTs tend to be the preferred option in human medicine. All
commercially available DLTs have been designed specifically for
human patients and have been adapted for use in dogs. There have
been several types evaluated in a range of dog sizes and breeds [15–
18]. DLTs consist of two single-lumen tubes bonded together and
are available as right- or left-sided tubes (Fig. 6.10), where right and
left designate which mainstem bronchus the tube is designed to fit.
Most DLTs are designed with an angled distal tip to facilitate place-
ment into either the right or left bronchus. The three most com-
monly available styles of DLTs are the Robertshaw, Carlens, and
White. The tubes have two elliptical cuffs: one occludes the trachea
and the other occludes the bronchus (Fig. 6.11). The bronchial cuff
and pilot balloon are normally colored blue for differentiation from
the tracheal cuff.
The bronchial cuffs of right-sided tubes vary in shape and design
in order to facilitate ventilation of the upper right lung lobe in
humans. The use of right-sided tubes can introduce greater place-
ment uncertainty and failures when used in dogs as the right cranial
lung lobe bronchus of the dog branches more proximally than in
humans; consequently, the bronchial cuff may occlude the bron-
chus or failure to completely isolate the hemithorax may occur. In
general, left-sided tubes are most often used and can be used effec-
tively for both right- and left-sided procedures. Even if proximal
clamping or transection of the left mainstem bronchus is required,
the left-sided tube can simply be withdrawn into the trachea so the
distal bronchial portion of the tube does not interfere with clamp-
ing. The internal lumen of the tracheal portion of the tube is oval or
D-shaped, and the sizes are designated using the French scale, rang-
ing from 26 to 41 Fr. The reduced lumen size will increase resist-
ance to breathing compared to an appropriately sized standard
single lumen tube, but this is overcome by the frequent use of inter-
mittent positive-pressure ventilation (IPPV) in these cases. DLTs
allow the anesthetist to ventilate each lung field independently of
the other or both lung fields together without replacing or moving
the tube, but it does require disconnection and reconnection of the
anesthetic circuit to the appropriate endotracheal tube adapter
(bronchial or tracheal) or both by using a Y-piece adapter (Fig. 6.12).
The ability to ventilate selectively either or both lung fields is a
distinct advantage over bronchial blocking systems or endobron-
chial intubation when surgical conditions require operating on
both sides of the chest. However, the available sizes typically limit

and White) also incorporate a carinal hook designed to aid in the
proper placement of the tube and prevent movement after position-

rather than facilitate correct tube placement [15]. Additional care
should also be taken when placing DLTs with a carinal hook to
ensure that it does not catch on any tissues or structures when
introducing the tube into the trachea. For this reason, the
Robertshaw left-sided DLT is probably the most versatile type for
use in dogs. In veterinary patients, the correct placement of a DLT
is generally confirmed by direct visualization using a small-
diameter bronchoscope. A thoracoscopic-assisted technique has
also been described [15]. Correct and complete placement is fur-
ther confirmed by ventilating both the right and left lung fields
while auscultating for lung sounds. Correct and complete place-
ment should ventilate all intended lung fields (i.e., right or left)
without ventilating any lung fields on the contralateral side.
Although blind placement is possible using some tubes, it is associ-
ated with a relatively high failure to achieve correct and complete
tube placement [15]. Small movements of the tube and/or the
patient may disrupt correct and complete placement and occasion-
ally bronchial cuffs will prolapse into the trachea, leading to com-
plete airway obstruction. Vigilance is required by the anesthetist to
recognize and correct any positional problems should they occur
(e.g., deflation of bronchial cuff).
Bronchial blockers represent another system for facilitating one-
lung isolation or ventilation in dogs (Fig. 6.13) [14,16,19–22]. In
human anesthesia, they are often used when patient size precludes
the use of a DLT or when anatomic abnormalities or differences are
present that may preclude optimal tube fit. The fact that they are
very adaptable for use over a wider range of patient sizes and are not
as anatomically specific as DLTs are distinct advantages of using
