rate and increased blood pressure. Arrhythmias may occur and the
patient’s pupils remain dilated. Palpebral and corneal reflexes remain
brisk. Nystagmus commonly occurs in horses. During this stage,
animals may briefly vocalize. In some species, especially ruminants
and cats, salivation may occur. In some species, including dogs,
cats, and goats, vomiting may be seen. The larynx of cats and pigs
is very sensitive at this stage, and premature stimulation with an
endotracheal tube may easily result in laryngospasm. Patients dur-
ing this phase retain a pedal reflex and react strongly to surgical
manipulation.
Stage 3
Stage 3 is considered the stage of surgical anesthesia. It is character-
ized by unconsciousness with progressive depression of reflexes.
This stage is the targeted anesthetic level for procedures requiring
general anesthesia. Muscle relaxation develops and ventilation
becomes slow and regular. Vomiting and swallowing reflexes are
lost. In humans, this stage has been further divided into planes I–IV
for finer differentiation. Others have suggested the simpler classifi-
cation of light (plane I), medium (plane II), and deep (plane III)
planes are more appropriate.
Light anesthesia persists until eyeball movement ceases. Medium
anesthesia is characterized by progressive intercostal paralysis, and
deep anesthesia by diaphragmatic respiration. A medium depth of
anesthesia has traditionally been considered a light to medium
plane of surgical anesthesia (stage 3, plane II), characterized by
stable respiration and pulse rate, abolished laryngeal reflexes, an
absent palpebral reflex, a strong corneal reflex, and adequate muscle
relaxation with absent response to surgical stimulation. Deep surgical
anesthesia (stage 3, plane III) is characterized by decreased inter-
costal muscle function and tidal volume, increased respiration rate,
profound muscle relaxation, diaphragmatic breathing, a weak corneal
reflex, and a centered and dilated pupil.
Patients in stage 3 have their heart rates return to normal ranges
and may experience progressive bradycardia. Blood pressure nor-
malizes and begins to decrease as anesthetic depth is deepened.
The frequency of arrhythmias decreases. Patients in light planes of
anesthesia may react to surgical manipulation and have a pedal
reflex, while these traits are lost in medium-to- deeper planes. In
general, patients will progressively lose jaw tone and limb muscle
tone, although this can vary depending on species and patient age.
For example, young dogs may have minimal jaw tone even at light
anesthesia planes, while other species such as ruminants and swine
may maintain a high degree of jaw tone even at deep planes. Eyeball
position will also vary depending on the species. In dogs and cats,
for example, the globe will rotate to a ventromedial orientation. In
other species such as horses, however, the globe will remain cen-
trally oriented. In ruminants, the globe may rotate ventrally in light
and medium anesthesia planes showing only the sclera and then
returning centrally during deep anesthesia planes.
Stage 4
Stage 4 is that of extreme CNS depression and overdose. In this
phase, cardiopulmonary function fails. The patient may exhibit
marked hypotension, weak pulses, bradycardia or transient tachy-
cardia, prolonged capillary refill time, and other cardiac arrhyth-
mias. Patients will hypoventilate and respiration itself may cease or
become irregular. Pupils will acutely dilate. All reflexes are blunted,
and muscle tone is absent. The corneal reflex ceases. In dogs and
cats, the eyeball position will rotate to a central position. In this
stage, death quickly occurs unless immediate resuscitative steps are
taken, including lessening the patient’s anesthesia depth.
Electrophysiologic monitoring
Electroencephalography is the recording of spontaneous electrical
brain activity from scalp electrodes [14–16]. Traditionally,
these electrodes are placed at standard positions according to
the International 10–20 system [14,16,17]. The electrical signals
obtained from the surface of the scalp represent the summation of
neuronal activity within the cerebral cortex, and result from excita-
tory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (PSPs) in large pyrami-
dal neurons located in the lower layers, such as layer V, of the
cerebral cortex [14,18–20]. The EEG amplitude and frequency
are influenced by afferent inputs from sensory-specific thalamic
nuclei serving as gates between peripheral receptors and the cortex,
and by epicenters within the cerebral cortex [21].
In 1934, Hans Berger proposed that the appearance of α waves
in the EEG may represent cerebrocortical events associated with
consciousness in the awake man [22]. It is believed that EEG
activity associated with consciousness is generated from pacemaker
neurons within the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS),
and then mediated and modulated through thalamic connec-
tions [19,21,23–25]. These pacemaker neurons oscillate in the
frequency range of 8–12 Hz and synchronize the excitability of cells
in the thalamocortical pathways. Small cerebrocortical areas appear
to also act as epicenters from which α activity spreads through
cortical neuronal networks, generating the α rhythm that dominates
the resting EEG. In the awake state, consciousness is maintained by
a circulating activity among the ARAS, intralaminar nuclei, and
the cerebral cortex [21]. Additional sensory stimulation will cause
cortical arousal that is characterized by the desynchronization of
α oscillators with the appearance of a faster rhythm in the β frequency
range (12–25 Hz) [21,25–28]. The term “desynchronization” is
characterized by a shift in the EEG pattern from high-voltage,
slow-wave activity to low-voltage, fast-wave activity [19,23,29].
As early as 1937, Gibbs and colleagues reported that anesthetic
agents altered electroencephalogram (EEG) activity from low-voltage
fast waves to high-voltage slow waves and proposed that the EEG
could be used clinically to measure the effects of anesthesia [30].
In 1959, Martin and colleagues first described hypnotic general
anesthetics as producing a biphasic EEG effect [31]. They observed
that during light anesthesia, there was EEG desynchronization,
which changed to progressive synchronization, slowing, and
increased amplitude as anesthesia deepened (Fig. 10.3A–C). With
further increases in anesthetic depth, the EEG displayed burst
suppression and lengthening periods of EEG silence (Fig. 10.3D).
Furthermore, a topographic distributional change from occipital
lobe dominance to frontal lobe dominance was observed.
More specifically, the EEG frequency bands utilized for assessment
of anesthetic depth are the δ (0–4 Hz), θ (4–8 Hz), α (8–13 Hz), and
β (13–30 Hz) bands [32,33]. During induction and maintenance of
anesthesia, there is a progressive decrease in EEG frequency content
characterized by a shift from a low-voltage, fast-wave pattern
to a high-voltage, slow-wave pattern [34–37]. As anesthetic depth
increases, the predominant EEG pattern is characterized by a
decrease in β activity and a concomitant increase in both α and
δ activity [38]. As anesthesia deepens further, EEG activity in the
θ and δ frequency bands appears initially in centroposterior
regions with subsequent anterior spread [39]. Lastly, very deep

-- 195 of 1450 --

180 	Section 2: Patient Monitoring
levels of general anesthesia are first indicated by flat periods
interspersed with periods of α and β activity, known as a “burst
suppression pattern,” followed by a complete loss of electrical
discharge known as “isoelectricity” or “electrical silence” [35,36,40].
Upon reducing the dose of the anesthetic agent, these patterns
reverse, and lighter levels of anesthesia are indicated again by a
decrease in amplitude and an increase in frequency content.
Depth- of-anesthesia devices
Today we recognize the EEG as a continuous non-invasive indicator
of cerebral cortical function in awake and unconscious patients
alike. The EEG is thought to be a potential measure of anesthetic
depth because it represents cortical electrical activity derived from
summated inhibitory and excitatory postsynaptic activity resulting
from subcortical events, including those that pass through subcor-
tical thalamic nuclei. Additionally, the degree of measured EEG
activity is associated with cerebral blood flow and metabolism,
which can be altered by anesthetic drugs and surgical stimulation.
Noxious stimulation during inadequate anesthesia ascends the
reticular activating system (RAS) of the brainstem and results in
EEG activation. These EEG changes vary with individual anesthet-
ics and with the nature of the noxious stimulation. Clinical assess-
ment of raw EEG signals to assess anesthetic depth is challenging
to learn, subjective to interpret, and influenced by confounders
such as electrical interferences. For these reasons, computer analysis
techniques have been utilized to distill the EEG into a condensed,
easy-to- interpret format known as the “processed” EEG which,
in turn, may be useful in assessing general trends in clinical
anesthetic depth.
Shortly before the turn of the last century, Aspect Medical
Systems undertook research efforts to develop the EEG as a general
measurement of anesthetic depth and developed the first depth-of-
anesthesia device. Their original EEG monitor, known as the
“Bispectral Index™” (BIS™) monitoring system, quantitates the effect
of hypnotic anesthetics on the human brain. Several other competi-
tors have manufactured similar depth-of-anesthesia devices over the
past three decades based upon this general technology. While the
details of each company’s algorithms often remain proprietary, these
devices and their development share several common principles.
These devices present a continuous EEG parameter, or index, that
usually ranges from an awake non-anesthetic drug-influenced state
(value of 100) to isoelectricity or electrical silence (value of 0).
These devices then use multiple EEG signal-processing approaches
to capture incremental information. Clinically relevant data (e.g.,
response to verbal commands, plasma drug concentration, and
recall) is then gathered from a large population of human subjects,
and advanced multivariate statistical analysis is used to correlate the
index value with the clinically relevant measure. Cumulatively,
these monitoring devices generally display progressively decreasing
index values from 100 to 0, which reflect a progressive increase
in anesthetic depth and provide a framework for the titration of
anesthetic agents.
The Bispectral Index™
The Bispectral Index (BIS™) is a proprietary EEG parameter devel-
oped by Aspect Medical Systems. The United States Food and
Drug Administration approved the commercial use of the device
to monitor the effect of anesthetics on the brain in 1996. A self-
adhesive index sensor is placed on the patient’s forehead. This
sensor then obtains live raw EEG signals and transmits them to a
BIS monitor via an interface cable. The BIS monitor then displays
real-time EEG as well as a dimensionless BIS value for interpreta-
tion. In humans, BIS values between 40 and 60 represent adequate
general anesthesia for surgery with values below 40 representing a
deep or over-anesthetized state (Fig. 10.4).
In humans, however, numerous limitations influence the reliabil-
ity of the BIS. The BIS appears strongly influenced by the anesthetic
technique. Certain anesthetics such as ketamine and nitrous oxide
may actually increase BIS values [41,42]. The BIS may also be influ-
enced by patient age. In children under 6 months of age, emergence
and recovery measures were unaffected by BIS titration; children
between the ages of 6 months and 3 years also showed no differences
in anesthetic use or recovery measures when BIS was compared to
standard practice monitoring [43]. This may be due to differences in
brain maturation and synapse formation resulting in differences
in the EEG in this population. Hypothermic human patients show
a wide variation in BIS values as body temperature decreases.
Specifically, BIS appears to decrease by 1.12 units for each degree
Celsius reduction in body temperature [44]. Interference with other

generally have lower pre-existing BIS values [46].
The BIS has been evaluated in veterinary anesthesiology with
conflicting results and interpretations of clinical utility (Fig. 10.5).
Bleijenberg et al. evaluated 65 dogs undergoing anesthesia for
surgery. Individual BIS values measured at light and surgical levels
of anesthesia overlapped considerably. The authors concluded that
BIS values and clinical depth of anesthesia had low specificity,
sensitivity, and predictive values, and thus the use of BIS as a sole
method to determine anesthetic depth in dogs was imprudent [47].
Campagnol et al. evaluated the correlation between BIS and
end- tidal isoflurane concentration and also compared the use of
three different BIS sensor positions in dogs. They proposed that
frontal-temporal sensor positioning provided a better correlation
with isoflurane depth of anesthesia in dogs compared to the other
sensor configurations tested [48]. Additionally, their work suggested
that BIS values might not reflect changes in depth of isoflurane
anesthesia in the absence of noxious stimulation [48]. Previous
work also identified that the use of subdermal needle electrodes was
a reliable and practical alternative to the use of patch electrodes for
the measurement of BIS in dogs [49]. The work of Ubiali et al.

in dogs evaluating BIS during propofol infusion suggested that BIS
values for humans should not be considered for classifying anes-
thetic and hypnotic depths in dogs [50]. Van Soens et al. concluded
that BIS was of limited use in titrating sedation and anesthesia
during transcranial magnetic stimulation in dogs [51].
Other work in dogs has shown a correlation between BIS and the
expired anesthetic fraction in halothane, isoflurane, and sevoflurane-
anesthetized dogs [52]. An increase in propofol infusion rates
appears to decrease BIS in dogs [53]. Like humans, other anesthetic
agents appear to have variable effects on BIS in dogs. For example,
the use of morphine–lidocaine–ketamine and dexmedetomidine–
morphine–lidocaine–ketamine constant rate infusions increased
BIS values in six healthy dogs anesthetized with isoflurane [54].
Morphine did not cause clinically significant changes in the BIS of
unstimulated dogs during isoflurane anesthesia [55]. Atracurium
also appeared to have minimal clinical effect on the BIS in anesthe-
tized dogs [56]. BIS levels appear to be lower in puppies than in
adults at the same alveolar concentration of sevoflurane [57]. Lastly,
in 31 dogs with altered levels of consciousness, Saenubol et al.
identified a significant correlation between modified Glasgow coma
scale (MGCS) scores and BIS values, suggesting that BIS values
could also be used as an alternative to MGCS monitoring in the
veterinary intensive care unit, and like in humans with neurologic
disease, might be influenced by other CNS factors beyond anesthetic
depth [58].
Less data is available in other animal species. Values of BIS are
inversely and linearly related to end-tidal sevoflurane and isoflu-
rane concentrations in anesthetized cats [59,60]. In horses, BIS
values were measured at multiple stages of sevoflurane anesthesia
in five thoroughbred horses anesthetized with guaifenesin and
thiopental following premedication with xylazine. BIS values were
lower during anesthesia than in awake or sedated horses; however,
no significant difference between BIS values was recorded at end-
tidal sevoflurane concentrations of 2.8% and 3.5% [61]. During the
recovery phase, the BIS values gradually increased over time but did
not significantly increase until the horses showed movement [61].
Haga et al. identified that BIS was an imprecise indicator of CNS
depression in isoflurane-anesthetized horses undergoing castra-
tion [62]. Belda et al. found that BIS approximated the level of
unconsciousness in halothane and sevoflurane-anesthetized horses;
however, it did not predict intraoperative movement, which would
be a major shortcoming associated with BIS monitoring in this
species [63]. Yamashita et al. also identified that BIS did not
indicate the degree of CNS depression during propofol anesthesia
in horses [64]. BIS monitoring has additionally been evaluated in
numerous other species, including goats, sheep, pigs, cows, elk,
rabbits, dolphins, alpacas, and chickens [65–73].
Spectral entropy
In chemistry, entropy is used as a measure of how the energy
of atoms and molecules becomes more spread out in a process.
For example, as a substance changes from a solid to a liquid, the
mobility and potential for interactions among atoms increases and,
consequently, so does its entropy. Mathematician Claude E. Shannon
applied these concepts in 1948 to information theory and proposed
that entropy could describe the complexity, irregularity, or unpre-
dictability of a signal [74]. For example, a pure sinusoidal wave
would have no entropy because of its regular and predictable nature,
whereas a wave containing hugely variable frequencies would have
a high entropy. As EEGs exhibit chaotic and non-linear behavior,
it followed that entropy could be applied to their interpretation.
The GE Healthcare Entropy ™ Module was released in 2003 as an
index of anesthetic depth and is available as part of some Datex
multiparameter monitors. The device uses a similar self-adhesive
frontotemporal sensor as the BIS which connects to a monitor via
an interface cable. In humans, facial electromyography (EMG) has
a frequency range (> 20 Hz) that overlaps with that of the EEG
(0.8–32 Hz). The facial EMG changes with levels of consciousness

and the use of neuromuscular blocking agents. The device assesses
two indices: State Entropy (SE) and Response Entropy (RE). SE is
computed from the EEG in the 0.8–32 Hz range and is thought to
encompass mainly the hypnotic elements of the EEG. RE, on the
other hand, is computed from EEG signals in the 0.8–47 Hz range,
which includes elements from the facial EMG. When EMG activity
is low, SE and RE should be identical. However, with arousal and an
increase in facial EMG, RE should increase [75].
Data in humans would suggest that the GE Healthcare Entropy
Module produces results comparable to that of BIS when tested
with intravenous and inhaled anesthetics [76–78]. The monitor dis-
plays the SE, RE, a raw EEG, as well as other monitored variables.
The displayed SE range is 0 (no EEG activity) to 91 (full awake) and
the RE range is 0–100. Numbers close to 100 mean that the patient
is conscious, and numbers close to 0 denote very deep anesthesia.
The manufacturer recommends that an SE between 40 and 60 is
appropriate for general anesthesia and that values outside this range
may require a dosing adjustment. In horses undergoing isoflurane
and medetomidine general anesthesia, SE values of 27.4 ± 4.8 and
RE values of 35.1 ± 7.1 were present during a surgical plane of
anesthesia. There appeared to be a poor correlation between this
technique and BIS [79]. Morgaz et al. evaluated entropy in
sevoflurane-anesthetized dogs. Their work concluded that RE and
RE-SE differences were not adequate indicators of antinociception,
and SE and RE were unable to detect deep planes of anesthesia in
dogs, although they were able to distinguish the awake and uncon-
scious states [80].
Patient state index
The patient state index (PSI) uses time, frequency, phase informa-
tion, and spatial information from the EEG to assess anesthetic
depth via a multivariate algorithm [81]. A self-adhesive five-lead
bilateral frontotemporal sensor is used. A PSI value of 25–50 is con-
sidered adequate for surgical anesthesia in humans. The index is
shown as the current value as well as the patient’s trend, which
is color-coded to indicate whether the anesthetic depth is “too
light,” “too deep,” or “just right.” Data investigating or validating the
use of PSI in veterinary species is lacking.
Cerebral state monitor
The cerebral state monitor (CSM) is a handheld portable device
that analyses the frequency content of the EEG signal. The energy
of the EEG is evaluated in specific frequency bands. These are used
to define two energy ratios called alpha (α) and beta (β). Both of
these show a shift in energy content from the higher to the lower
frequencies during anesthesia. The relationship between these
quantities is also analyzed as a separate parameter (β-α). Lastly, the
monitor evaluates the amount of instantaneous burst suppression
(BS) in each 30-s period of the EEG. This measurement quantifies
the amount of “silent” or “flat” EEG periods characteristic of the
deepest levels of hypnosis. These four parameters are used as input
to a fuzzy logic classifier system that calculates the cerebral state
index (CSI). The CSI ranges from 0 (no EEG activity) to 100 (awake
state). Values between 40 and 60 are considered adequate for surgi-
cal anesthesia in humans. Bollen and Saxtorph evaluated CSM in
dogs sedated with medetomidine undergoing dental scaling.
Undisturbed sedated dogs had a median CSI value of 43. During
dental scaling, CSI values increased to awake ranges with a median
value of 99. The authors concluded CSM to be a promising method
for monitoring the degree of sedation and hypnosis [82]. In other
work in dogs, while increasing doses of propofol showed a
correlation to CSI, no correlation was found between clinical depth
of anesthesia during propofol induction [83,84]. Bollen et al. found
good agreement between depth of anesthesia and CSI in propofol–
fentanyl-infused pigs [85].
Narcotrend® index
In 1937, Loomis and colleagues categorized the EEG during sleep
into characteristic patterns, which were assigned stages ranging
from A to E [86]. The Narcotrend® monitor by MonitorTechnik was
developed by anesthesiologists and engineers at the University
Medical School of Hannover in Germany. The system takes raw
EEG and, after artifact detection, uses a multivariate statistical algo-
rithm to categorize patients into six stages, ranging from A (awake)
to F (isoelectricity/burst suppression), and 14 substages to facilitate
greater precision in monitoring anesthesia depth [87]. In humans,
the Narcotrend index appears to correlate well with BIS analysis.
Narcotrend stages D or E appear equivalent to BIS values between
65 and 40, indicating appropriate surgical anesthetic depth. The
Narcotrend monitor is unique in that it uses standard electrocardi-
ography electrodes rather than a proprietary electrode sensor.
Limited data is available on the use of the Narcotrend index in
veterinary anesthesia. In cats, the Narcotrend index correlated to
increasing isoflurane MAC multiples, but its reliability decreased
with the addition of dexmedetomidine [88].
Index of consciousness
The index of consciousness (IoC) is a depth-of-anesthesia device
derived from a combination of symbolic dynamics, β-ratio, and EEG
suppression rate [89]. IoC ranges from 0 to 99, where 99 indicates
an awake patient, 80 is associated with sedation, the range 40–60 is
defined as the state recommended for surgical anesthesia, and
0 indicates isoelectric EEG. IoC shows a considerable time delay
before the correct index is displayed, which may limit the device’s
clinical utility [89].
Auditory evoked potentials
Auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) are electrical potentials evoked
in the auditory pathway in response to sound stimuli [90]. To gen-
erate an AEP, an auditory stimulus is repeatedly delivered to a
patient, and the EEG periods that immediately follow each stimulus
are averaged. This eliminates the non-stimulus–related portions of
the EEG and retains the specific evoked potential periods. These
potentials are then divided into several sections based on the ana-
tomical area of their origin and the time elapsed since the auditory
stimulus. The middle latency auditory evoked potential (MLAEP),
40 and 60 ms after stimulation, represents neural activity within the
thalamus and primary auditory cortex and has been used in humans
to reflect the degree of CNS depression in response to anesthetics,
and therefore general anesthetic depth [90]. One such newer device
is the aepEXplus™ made by Medical Device Management, Essex,
UK. These devices produce a dimensionless index known as the
“A-line autoregressive index” (AAI) between 0 and 100 with which
depth of anesthesia can be gauged.
In humans, AEP monitoring appears to correlate well with other
depth-of-anesthetic devices and may be preferred over BIS when
ketamine is used [91]. The use of AEP has also been evaluated
in animal species. AEPs were found to correlate with end-tidal
isoflurane concentrations and the administration of thiopental in
dogs [92,93]. Additional work in dogs premedicated with ace-
promazine and morphine and anesthetized with thiopental and
halothane found that indices generated from AEP also showed a

good correlation with anesthetic depth assessed by a trained
anesthetist [94]. Other work in dogs found that AEPs were not
statistically correlated with magnetic motor evoked potentials in
dogs undergoing transcranial magnetic stimulation and were of
limited use in titrating anesthesia in this population [51]. AEPs
were also not found to be effective in monitoring anesthetic depth
in sevoflurane-anesthetized dogs [95].
Clinical utility of depth-of-anesthesia devices
The depth-of- anesthesia devices previously discussed primarily
aim to measure the effect of injectable and inhaled hypnotic agents
on the EEG. However, numerous drugs are often administered to
patients as part of a balanced anesthesia technique and to achieve
multimodal analgesia. Not all agents impact the EEG in the same
way. Many drugs such as midazolam, dexmedetomidine, propofol,
etomidate, thiopental, isoflurane, sevoflurane, and desflurane are
thought to decrease BIS and other depth-of-anesthesia device indices
in humans. However, low concentrations of opioids, the use of neu-
romuscular blocking agents, and nitrous oxide, do not appear to
consistently change the BIS response during propofol or inhaled
anesthesia. As discussed earlier in the chapter, agents such as keta-
mine and nitrous oxide may even increase BIS depending on
dose [24,41]. Other agents administered during the perianesthetic
period that affect the sympathetic nervous system may further
influence depth-of-anesthesia devices. Administration of esmolol
has been shown to markedly decrease BIS in propofol and alfentanil-
infused humans, while sympathomimetics such as epinephrine
increase arousal and BIS values [96,97]. These drug idiosyncrasies
can easily create an inaccurate assessment of anesthetic depth and
necessitate careful individual patient interpretation. Other factors
such as patient age, hypothermia, pre-existing neurologic disease, and
electrical interference from nearby medical devices may further
influence and confound depth-of-anesthesia devices [43–45].
Is there a clear benefit to using depth-of- anesthesia devices? A
2017 systematic review and meta-analysis in humans found that the
use of BIS monitoring reduced time to extubation, to attain orienta-
tion in time and place, and to discharge from both the operating
room and postanesthetic care unit. The risk of nausea and vomiting
after surgery also was reduced by 12%. A 3% reduction in the risk of
cognitive impairment postoperatively at 3 months and a 6% reduc-
tion in the risk of postoperative delirium were also identified.
Additionally, the risk of intraoperative recall was also reduced by
1% [98]. Despite these benefits, a 2004 meta-analysis also identified
that the cost savings from reduced drug costs and time in the early
recovery period were offset by the cost of the depth-of-anesthesia
device itself and the cost of the monitoring electrodes [99].
The routine application of depth-of-anesthesia devices in animals
is questionable since their algorithms are based on data collected in
humans. March and Muir reviewed the use of BIS in animal species
and suggested that interspecies differences in the EEG features
associated with different hypnotic and amnesic states may affect the
correlation between BIS values and depth of anesthesia [100]. To
further complicate the picture, there currently is no consensus in
human or veterinary anesthesiology on how to validate depth-of-
anesthesia devices or even how best to determine depth of anesthesia.
The absence of such “gold standards” limits the present-day anesthe-
siologist’s ability to compare or judge future technologies [101]. In
2014, Schneider et al. performed a “head-to- head” comparison
in humans between electroencephalogram-based monitoring (BIS),
standard parameter-based monitoring (heart rate, blood pressure,
end- tidal anesthetic concentration, and propofol concentration), or
both strategies together, which were used to calculate an anesthesia
multimodal index of consciousness (AMIC) [102]. Their work
concluded that the use of the AMIC, including integration of
both standard monitoring and electroencephalographic parameters
more precisely reflected the depth-of-anesthesia compared to BIS
or standard monitoring alone. Ultimately, if depth-of- anesthesia
devices are to be used in veterinary anesthesia, they should be used
cautiously and only in combination with other modalities such as
Guedel’s physical signs of anesthetic depth, inhalant anesthetic
concentrations, and injectable drug plasma concentrations, and not
used as the sole mechanism of determining anesthetic depth.

Introduction
An electrocardiogram (ECG) is the graphical representation of the
cardiac electrical activity recorded over time. The ECG allows the
anesthetist to evaluate the heart rate and rhythm and, when evalu-
ated in combination with blood pressure and other indicators of
tissue perfusion and cardiac output, allows for an assessment of the
cardiovascular status of the patient. Many disease states may lead to
the development of arrhythmias (e.g., electrolyte disturbances, dis-
eases of splanchnic viscera, paraneoplastic diseases, etc.), and some
anesthetic drugs can increase the risk of spontaneous arrhythmias
in otherwise healthy animals [1–4]. Due to the widespread availa-
bility of this technology, ECG monitoring should be considered for
any patient undergoing anesthesia, even for short-duration or rou-
tine procedures.
A normal ECG is easily recognizable and represents the electrical
activity of the heart. However, to understand why and how an
abnormal rhythm may develop, it is important to understand the
basic physics behind the ECG as well as the minor species differ-
ences. It is also important to understand the limitations of an ECG
and how to differentiate common artifacts from true arrhythmias.
Electrical potentials and the lead system
There are many different systems available that can obtain an ECG;
the underlying principles remain fairly constant between machines.
Understanding the basics of electrocardiography requires integration
of multiple concepts including generation of the cardiac action
potential, the equivalent dipole theory, and the lead system. The
cardiac action potential is covered in detail elsewhere (see Chapter 33).
What follows is a brief description of the equivalent dipole theory,
cardiac vectors, and the lead system.
The equivalent dipole theory states that the heart can be approxi-
mated to a dipole (i.e., it is equivalent to a dipole when measured);
the force that is generated has a direction and magnitude and can be
represented as a vector [5,6]. A dipole is a pair of electrical charges
of equal and opposite polarity that are separated by a distance. The
electrical potential generated can be measured with a galvanometer,
which consists of two exploring electrodes placed on each side of
the system. The electrical potential measured by the galvanometer
is dependent on the intensity of the electrical force generated, the
distance the electrodes from the dipole, and the position of the elec-
trodes relative to the orientation of the dipole. Depolarization of
the myocardium generates electrical forces of varying magnitudes
and directions; this electrical activity can be thought of as vectors of
electrical activation. Electrical activity occurring simultaneously
creates a summation vector. The magnitude of these vectors is
detected on the body surface, depending on the site of the exploring
electrode and the direction of the vector. The electrode placed on a
line parallel to the direction of the vector will be able to record the
maximum amplitude of that activity [6].
When several exploring electrodes are attached on the surface of
the patient, it is possible to record the magnitude and direction of

these cardiac vectors. The ECG records the electric potential
(in mV, on the y axis) over time (in seconds, on the x axis) between
a point on the body surface and an indifferent (or reference) elec-
trode or between two recording electrodes. The lines joining these
electrodes form what we refer to as “leads” along which the cardiac
vectors are measured [6]. Leads may be defined as unipolar or bipo-
lar. If the potential is recorded between an electrode on the body
surface (exploring electrode) and an indifferent (or reference) elec-
trode, the leads are unipolar. If the difference is recorded between
two recording electrodes, the leads are bipolar.
The voltage change recorded by the leads is displayed graphically.
Each electrical wave is defined by its amplitude, polarity, and
duration. When the cardiac depolarization vector is parallel to the
lead, the wave is of maximum amplitude; a depolarization vector
perpendicular to the lead produces a wave of minimal amplitude.
Typically, a vector directed toward the positive electrode is repre-
sented as a positive wave and a vector directed toward the negative
electrode is represented as a negative wave.
Einthoven’s triangle
Due to the directionality of an ECG, the direction of electrical activ-
ity can be “seen” from different directions depending on the leads
used. A diagnostic ECG may be capable of up to 12 viewpoints in
two planes: frontal and transverse. Clinically, the frontal plane is
most commonly used.
Electrodes placed on the right forelimb, left forelimb, and left
hindlimb make up an arrangement known as “Einthoven’s triangle,”
named after Willem Einthoven, a Dutch doctor who is credited
with developing the first apparatus utilized to detect electrical
activity of the heart. The three potential differences created by this
arrangement are called leads I, II, and III (Fig. 11.1). It has been
suggested that this naming convention is largely historical, based
on Einthoven’s original description, rather than any intrinsic
meaning [7].
Bipolar, unipolar, and precordial leads
Leads I, II, and III are referred to as the “standard bipolar leads”
because they measure between two points of the electrodes
(Fig. 11.1). Lead I measures the potential difference between the
right and left forelimb with the left considered positive. Lead II, the
most common lead used clinically, is between the right forelimb
and left hindlimb with the hindlimb considered positive. Lead III is
between the left forelimb and left hindlimb with the hindlimb
considered positive [7].
As bipolar leads (and lead II specifically) are the primary leads
utilized in perianesthetic monitoring, they will be the focus of the
rest of the chapter; however, the other diagnostic leads are briefly
discussed below. Because a lead is, by nature, the potential difference
between two points, the theoretical number of leads that could exist
is nearly limitless. Cardiologists commonly use other lead systems,
such as the modified orthogonal lead system, and the descriptions
provided below should by no means be considered exhaustive,
only a summary of common configurations that may be used in the
perianesthetic period [6].
The unipolar leads are created by comparing the three electrodes
to a reference voltage created by the monitor, known as “Wilson’s
central terminal.” The signal between the three electrodes and
the reference (Wilson’s central terminal) are known as aVL
(left forelimb), aVR (right forelimb), and aVF (left hindlimb). These
are also known as the “augmented limb leads,” and they allow for a
slightly different angle of evaluation in the frontal plane [7].
The unipolar precordial leads are based on a similar concept: six
additional electrodes can be placed on the thorax near the heart and
are compared to a reference electrode (Wilson’s central terminal).

These leads (V1–V6) provide information in the transverse plane

is used with some frequency in human patients; however, it is less
commonly used in veterinary medicine during the perianesthetic

In small animals, a multilead ECG may be used to generate
targeted information about chamber enlargement, and lead II is
used predominantly to monitor patients intraoperatively. In horses,
however, it has been suggested that a multilead ECG is of less value
because of the extensive branching of the Purkinje system in the
ventricles. In these cases, a single-lead system is typically sufficient
to optimize the signal along the direction of the maximal deflection
of the electrical impulse generated within the heart. To accomplish
this, the electrodes are placed parallel to this impulse in what is
often referred to as the “base-apex lead” (Fig. 11.2) [8]. Although
there is some debate as to whether the base-apex lead is the most
effective lead for diagnostic evaluation of the horse, it is currently
the most well established [9]. It has also been suggested that the
base-apex lead arrangement accentuates the P wave of the equine
ECG [10]. This arrangement historically uses the lead I setting with
the negative (–) electrode (right forelimb/RA/white) placed over
the jugular furrow or near the manubrium. The positive (+) electrode
(left forelimb/LL/black) may be placed over the left apex of the
heart, on the left side of the chest at the level of the olecranon or at
the xiphoid. The ground electrode (left hindlimb/LL/red) may be
attached to either side of the neck. Some portable ECG monitors
utilize only two electrodes, which can be used to generate a single
lead; the lead that is generated (I, II, or III) depends on where the
electrodes are placed.
It is also important to note that many systems available in North
America use a standard color-coding system of right forelimb
or RA (white), left forelimb or LA (black), and left hindlimb or
LL (red). This color scheme is not always the same as that used
internationally [11].
The ECG complex
The ECG complex is a representation of the electrical activity
occurring in the myocardium during a single cardiac cycle, from
cell depolarization at the beginning of the cycle to the cell repolari-
zation at the end of the cycle. Different terminology may be used by
different sources to discuss these concepts, but terms used here
are wave, segment, and interval. A “wave” represents an electrical
event in the myocardium and is represented as a deflection above
or below baseline. A segment is a line joining two waves, and an
interval is the time (or graphical distance) between two events.
The primary deflections in an ECG are the P wave, the Q, R, and
S waves (often referred to as the “QRS complex”), and the T wave
(Fig. 11.3) [12].
In a normal heart, the cardiac cycle begins at the sinoatrial (SA)
node, a small group of cells located in the right atrium that act as the
dominant pacemaker of the heart. This event is not represented by
a wave on the ECG due to the small number of cells that make up
the SA node and, therefore, the very small amount of voltage
this event produces. However, immediately following SA node acti-
vation, a wave of depolarization travels across the atria facilitated by
the atrial conduction system, including Bachmann’s bundle [13].
The depolarization of the atria is represented by the P wave on the
ECG. As the wave of depolarization sweeps across the atria, it
eventually reaches the atrioventricular (AV) node. The wave of
depolarization propagates through the AV node and along the

bundle of His before following the right and left bundle branches
and, finally, through the Purkinje network on its way to the contrac-
tile cardiac myocytes. The time it takes for the wave of depolariza-
tion to propagate from the atria through the ventricular conduction
system is represented by the PQ (also referred to as PR) interval
and is defined as the time from the onset of the P wave to the onset
of the QRS complex [12]. The extensive Purkinje network spreads
the impulse to the contractile cardiac myocytes starting at the apex
of the heart and begins the formation of the QRS complex (i.e., the
three waves representing ventricular depolarization: Q, R, and S).
It should be noted that most individuals refer to the complex
that represents ventricular depolarization as the QRS, regardless
of whether the complex contains a distinct Q, R, and S wave.
Mechanical contraction of the myocardium follows electrical depo-
larization. After depolarization, repolarization of the ventricles
follows to reestablish the cellular electrical potential that allows for
the next electrical depolarization and mechanical contraction. The
electrical repolarization of the ventricle is represented as the T wave
on the ECG. The atria also experience repolarization which is
sometimes represented as the Ta wave on the ECG; however, this
wave normally occurs during the depolarization of the ventricles
(i.e., the QRS complex) and, therefore, is obscured due to the larger
electrical potential of ventricular depolarization. The ST segment,
defined as the segment between the end of the QRS complex
(sometimes referred to as the J point) and the T wave, corresponds
to ventricular systole during which the membrane potential of
ventricular myocytes is equal and is, therefore, normally represented
as a horizontal line [12]. The J wave and U wave are two underap-
preciated waves that may represent early and late ventricular repo-
larization, respectively. In humans, the J wave may be appreciated
in a normal heart but can also appear as result of hypothermia,
hypercalcemia, or myocardial ischemia [14,15]. The U wave, theo-
rized to originate from repolarization of the mid-myocardial cells
(M cells) or Purkinje cells, may be seen in patients who are brady-
cardic or suffer from hypokalemia [15].
The line that occurs between the end of the T wave and the
beginning of the next P wave is generally called “baseline” or the
“isoelectric line” and is associated with the absence of electrical
activity. This becomes important when considering the pauses that
occur during a single cardiac depolarization and the time between
the cardiac cycles.
Evaluating an ECG
Evaluation of an ECG during anesthesia can give valuable informa-
tion about the patient’s heart rate and can lead to early recognition
of dysrhythmias that could become pathologic if left untreated.
However, perianesthetic ECG interpretation may come with
limitations, such as patient positioning, limited sites for electrode
placement, and operating room artifacts. Therefore, ECG tracings
recorded as part of continuous anesthetic monitoring may not
meet all the recommendations for standardization associated with
a fully diagnostic ECG. Regardless, there is still crucially important
information that may be obtained from perianesthetic ECG
monitoring.
When evaluating the ECG, it is important to note that the horizon-
tal axis of an ECG printout (also referred to as a strip or tracing)
is time in seconds while the vertical axis is voltage, displayed in
millivolts (mV). It is also important to note the underlying paper
or sweep speed, the rate at which the ECG paper or screen travels
while the ECG is being traced, commonly 25 mm/s or 50 mm/s.
At a faster paper speed (50 mm/s), each small box (1 mm) on the
horizontal axis represents 0.02 s and the ECG complex will appear
wider. At a slower speed (25 mm/s), each small box represents 0.04 s,
and the ECG complex will appear narrower comparatively.
Heart rate calculation
The ECG can be used as a source for determining the patient’s heart
rate; however, it can be susceptible to artifact and interference,
which may make automated heart rate calculation by the monitor
less accurate. There are multiple methods available to manually cal-
culate a heart rate from a printed ECG. The simplest, albeit least
accurate, way to calculate the heart rate is to determine the number
of R waves within 3 s and multiply by 20 to obtain beats per minute
(Fig. 11.4) [16].
A more useful method, especially in patients with an irregular
rhythm, is calculation of an “instantaneous” heart rate using only
one R-R interval, defined as the distance between two sequential
R waves of the QRS complex. This method requires knowledge of
the underlying paper or sweep speed. The R-R interval can be
counted in terms of small boxes (mm); the number of boxes counted
can then be multiplied by s/mm (0.02 for 50 mm/s paper speed
and 0.04 for 25 mm/s paper speed) to obtain the amount of time
(seconds) per beat. To convert this into beats per minute, simply
divide 60 (s/min) by the number of seconds per beat. For example,
an R- R interval that was counted to be 18 small boxes at a paper
speed of 25 mm/s would be:

paper speed). In this example, the R-R interval is ~18 mm and (1500/18 = 83.3); therefore, the heart rate is estimated to be 83 beats/min. This second
method is often referred to as the “instantaneous heart rate” method. Source: Dr. Kyle Bartholomew, with permission.

Rhythm evaluation
There are many approaches to systematically evaluate an ECG, but
many of them follow the same general pattern: evaluate the heart
rate, recognize the presence of all the normal waves that make up
the ECG complex, and evaluate if there are any beats that do not
belong. A simplified algorithm can be found in Box 11.1 and is
described below. An algorithm such as this is not meant to diagnose
a specific condition; rather, it is to be used to help guide localization
of where an issue might be arising. For example, if the QRS mor-
phology is abnormal, one should consider that ventricular conduc-
tion may be abnormal, but it is up to the user to determine what the
specific problem is and how to appropriately act.
First, determine heart rate as previously described. Then, deter-
mine if the ventricular and atrial rates match. Normally, there is a
fixed interval between the P waves and QRS complexes (PQ interval);
however, in some cases, the ventricular rate (R-R interval) may not
match the atrial rate (P-P interval), and a separate heart rate assess-
ment may be needed for atrial and ventricular rates in some circum-
stances. Next, assess if every P wave has an associated QRS omplex.
Normally, there is a fixed relationship of one P wave preceding
every QRS complex, while ectopic (or abnormal) QRS complexes
often originate without a preceding atrial depolarization. Premature
complexes occur before the next anticipated sinus beat, while
escape complexes generally occur significantly later than the next
expected sinus beat. Next, determine if every QRS complex has an
associated P wave. In normal sinus rhythm and sinus arrhythmia,
there will be a P wave preceding every QRS complex, and the inter-
val between the P waves and QRS complexes will be consistent.
However, in some instances, the electrical impulse is blocked at
the AV node or His–Purkinje system, preventing propagation and
depolarization of the ventricles (e.g., AV block). Finally, determine
if the QRS complexes appear supraventricular or ventricular. In dogs
and cats, if the electrical impulse originates from the sinus node,
atrial myocardium, or AV node, the QRS complex will generally
be tall, upright, and narrow, otherwise referred to as “supraven-
tricular” [16]. If the electrical impulse originates from the ventricle,
the QRS complex will be wide and abnormal in appearance
(sometimes used synonymously with the term “ventricular”) because
it does not utilize the normal His–Purkinje system [17–19].
Systematic assessment of the ECG by this method will allow for a
rapid and accurate diagnosis of heart rate and rhythm. A dysrhyth-
mia (also often referred to as arrhythmia) denotes an irregularity
in the cardiac rhythm. In-depth discussions of the diagnosis of
dysrhythmias along with underlying mechanisms and treatments
are covered elsewhere [13]. In short, dysrhythmias are often charac-
terized by the anatomic place of origin, rate, and/or regularity.
Supraventricular arrhythmias arise from the atria or AV node, while
ventricular arrhythmias arise from the ventricles. When dysrhyth-
mias originate from the AV node, they are sometimes more specifi-
cally classified as junctional. When further characterized by rate, slow
rates are referred to as bradyarrhythmias (e.g., sinus bradycardia,
AV block, and sinus arrest), while rapid rates are referred to as
tachyarrhythmias (e.g., sinus tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia,
and supraventricular tachycardia). Common arrhythmias that
occur at normal rates are respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and acceler-
ated idioventricular rhythm. Dysrhythmias may also be classified
according to their regularity. For example, fibrillation is an irregu-
lar, chaotic rhythm (e.g., atrial fibrillation), while tachycardia is a
regular (non-irregular) rhythm [17]. Once the rate and rhythm are
characterized, further decisions on alterations of anesthetic man-
agement or treatment course can be made as needed.
Mean electrical axis
The mean electrical axis (MEA) refers to the direction and orien-
tation of ventricular depolarization and refers solely to the QRS
complex. It may be thought of as the average vector of ventricular
depolarization. Even though MEA can be measured in any plane,
its characterization for ventricular evaluation occurs mainly in the
frontal plane using a hexaxial reference system, a graphical arrange-
ment of the three bipolar and three unipolar leads together [12].
The MEA may be determined to identify the presence of ventricular
dilatation or hypertrophy and to detect intraventricular conduction
defects. For example, in a normal heart, the left ventricle is the domi-
nant ventricle; therefore, the normal MEA is generally to the left.
However, if there is significant right ventricular hypertrophy, the
MEA will be shifted to the right.
It is important to note that MEA is not only related to the mass
that is being depolarized but also to the timing of the myocardial
depolarization. Variations in MEA can occur due to abnormalities
in the direction, magnitude, and timing of myocardial depolariza-
tion and may indicate hypertrophy of cardiac tissue or a conduction
disturbance [12].
In describing the MEA, a degree system is used with 0° directed
to the left, 90° directed down, and 180° directed to the right
(Fig. 11.5). The MEA in the normal dog lies between 40° and 100°;
in the cat, the MEA is more variable, from 0° to 160°. The MEA is
typically determined by using the six standard ECG leads (three
bipolar and three unipolar) and may be calculated by several
different methods. First, if there is a lead with an isoelectric QRS
complex (i.e., the deflection of the R and S complexes are equiva-
lent), the MEA lies on the axis perpendicular to the isoelectric lead.
If the net QRS amplitude is positive on that perpendicular lead
(i.e., the deflection of the R complex is greater than that of the S),
then the MEA points toward the positive pole. If the net QRS ampli-
tude is negative on that perpendicular lead (i.e., the deflection if the
R complex is less than that of the S), then the MEA points toward
the negative pole. A slightly more cumbersome but more accurate
method involves plotting the net amplitude of the QRS complex of
leads I and aVF and the intersection will provide the vector equal to
the MEA. The MEA can also be estimated (i.e., right versus left)
simply by assessing the net deflection in lead I. If the net deflection
of the QRS in lead I is positive, then the MEA lies to the left, and if
the net deflection of the QRS in lead I is negative, then the MEA lies
to the right [17].

Regardless of technique, it is important to note that consistency
in technique may be important. For instance, there have been discus-
sions comparing calculation of MEA using both the base-apex lead
and alternative lead positioning systems in equine patients [9,20].
Although the focus of these studies has been on which system is the
most clinically useful for determination of abnormalities, one thing
is made clear by these investigations – the methodology used to
determine the MEA can significantly change the established nor-
mal. Care must be taken to ensure comparisons are made between
measurements obtained using the same standards [9,17,20].
Species- specific variations
There is an obvious difference in the morphology of the QRS
complex between certain species that can be appreciated by even
the most novice observer (Fig. 11.6). In some veterinary species, the
normal QRS complex has a largely positive deflection from baseline
in lead II. These include dogs, cats, primates, rats, and many other
domestic mammals. In other veterinary species, namely horses,
pigs, and ruminants, the QRS complex has a largely negative deflec-
tion in lead II, as well as in the more commonly used base-apex lead
for horses. The basis for this was initially suggested by Hamlin and
Smith in 1965 who proposed that species in their first category
(category A; dogs, cats, and primates) had three “fronts” or vectors
of depolarization during the classic QRS complex, while species in
their second category (category B; horses, pigs, and ruminants) had
only two fronts of depolarization (Fig. 11.7). In category B species,
more general penetration of the Purkinje fibers into the epicardium
results in a single burst of depolarization and simultaneous excita-
tion of the majority of the mass in both ventricles [21]. In compari-
son, Purkinje fibers in category A species are distributed mainly in
the subendocardial layer, leading to the classically recognized
pattern of ventricular depolarization [21].
More deeply penetrating and diffuse Purkinje fiber distribution,
similar to category B species, have also been recognized in other
species including whales, dolphins, and birds [22]. It is important
for anesthetists to be aware that these differences exist to avoid
mistaking a normal QRS complex in a category B species with an
ectopic ventricular beat in a category A species, as this could impact
clinical case management. For example, avian species commonly
have negatively deflected QRS complexes and rates exceeding
200–300 beats/min; this morphology may appear similar to ventric-
ular tachycardia in other species, which could lead to misdiagnosis
that would significantly change anesthetic management of the
patient (Fig. 11.6D).
Canine
The normal heart rate of an adult dog is between 60 and 160 beats/
min and, in addition to a normal sinus rhythm, healthy adult dogs
may have a prominent respiratory sinus arrhythmia that is charac-
terized by cyclic variations in heart rate approximately synchronous
with the phase of respiration and the accompanying fluctuations in
vagal tone [23,24]. The rate appears to accelerate during inspiration
and decelerate during expiration, and the effect begins to diminish
at higher heart rates. In dogs, the parasympathetic nervous system
has pronounced effects on the modulation of heart rate [25]. It has
been hypothesized that an increase in heart rate during inspiration
increases cardiac output and, therefore, pulmonary perfusion dur-
ing a period with increased lung volume, and this subsequently
improves ventilation–perfusion ratios [26].
Normal P wave morphology and timing may vary from cycle to
cycle in some dogs; this cyclic variation is a characteristic often
referred to as a “wandering pacemaker” and is due to changes in
the site of impulse origin within the sinus node and/or changes
in the exit pathway from the sinus node [24].
Feline
The normal heart rate of cats can vary significantly from roughly
120–240 beats/min, although, anecdotally, it is uncommon to
identify a cat with a heart rate near the lower end of the range in
a hospital setting. Unlike dogs, respiratory sinus arrhythmia is
uncommon in healthy adult cats in a hospital setting, but it has been
recognized when recordings of heart rate and rhythm were gener-
ated remotely in cats at home [24,27].
Feline ECGs can be difficult to interpret due to their high heart
rates and the low voltage of their ECG complexes detected by the
surface electrodes (Fig. 11.6A). Lower voltage potentials lead to
smaller amplitudes on an ECG, and this increases the likelihood
of artifacts and interference, which complicates interpretation. This
complication applies to most small animals including small mam-
mals and birds.
Equine
Much like the dog, the underlying heart rate and rhythm of horses
are heavily influenced by parasympathetic tone at rest. Cardiac
arrhythmias due to high vagal tone (e.g., sinus arrhythmia, sinus
block, sinus arrest, sinus bradycardia, wandering pacemaker,

As mentioned earlier, there are differing opinions regarding
the optimal technique for performing equine electrocardiography.
The most common methodology among veterinary anesthetists
in North America appears to be the base-apex lead system;
however, utilization of the Dubois lead positioning system has
been suggested [9]. This includes a 12-lead rather than two-lead
system and is thought to compensate for the limitations of using
the frontal plane in horses. As opposed to humans, for whom the
majority of the lead placement systems have been developed,
the orientation of the long axis (and axis of depolarization) of the
equine heart tends to be perpendicular to the spine as opposed to
parallel to it [20].
ECG equipment
The most basic modern ECG machines consist of electrodes, a
screen to display waveforms, and a microprocessor to make evalua-
tions, calculations, and adjustments; some may also have a printer
to create physical copies of the ECG (Fig. 11.8). ECG machines can
vary significantly in their sophistication, ranging between 2 and 10
electrodes capable of many different leads. As the ECG is a graphi-
cal representation of voltage over time, many monitors allow altera-
tion of the scale on both the x axis (time, mm per second) and the y
axis (voltage, mV). Common time intervals are 25 and 50 mm/s.
Some monitors will automatically scale the y axis (voltage) to opti-
mize the image; increasing the scale may allow the user to evaluate
the waveform but will also make artifacts more prominent. For
example, the ECG complex of a cat often appears significantly
smaller than that of dog due to the smaller voltage detected by the
ECG surface electrodes (Fig. 11.6A) [17].
Small, portable, single-lead ECG monitors are also available
(Fig. 11.8B). These units often have just two electrodes and, while
they are not as useful for diagnostic purposes, they can be useful for
monitoring sedated or anesthetized patients in remote locations or
areas in which larger equipment may be impractical. Cardiac telem-
etry monitors can also be used to monitor the ECG of a patient
from a short distance such as a cage or stall without the need for
cables connected to the display. Smartphone-based ECG monitoring
units have also been used with success for monitoring of patients
outside the hospital setting [29].
ECG electrode cables also come with a variety of different
attachments for attaching to a patient (Fig. 11.8C). Metal “alligator”
clips are often less desirable during prolonged sedation or anesthe-
sia because they can cause discomfort or focal tissue ischemia and
often require alcohol or electrode gel to improve the ECG signal.
Care should be taken when applying alcohol to ECG electrodes on
the skin of a patient immediately prior to defibrillation due to the
risk of combustion [30]. Alternatives include adhesive ECG pads
that can be placed on any non-haired or shaved skin surface; these
are less likely to cause tissue damage but may still cause skin irrita-
tion upon removal. Another alternative for very small animals is the
use of small-gauge needles placed through the skin as an anchor
point for metal ECG clips. Hypodermic needles are often used, and
metal clips may be attached to the needle after it is passed through
the skin; the ends of the needle can be covered with rubber or
the needle cap to reduce the likelihood of an inadvertent needle
puncture. Commercially available specialized ECG needles are also
available.
Artifacts and filters
The ECG is designed to detect very subtle changes in the electrical
potential between two points on the body. This means that the ECG
is also predisposed to outside influence in the form of “artifacts” or

-- 210 of 1450 --

Chapter 11: Electrocardiography 	195
electrical noise; these can occur in both the low- and high-frequency
ranges [11]. Almost all the modern ECG monitors have filters built
into their design to remove these artifacts prior to displaying them
on the screen or printout. Modern ECG machines employ what is
referred to as a “bandpass filter,” a filter that allows signal frequen-
cies within a specific range to be displayed while removing electrical
activity above and below this frequency. Bandpass filters have two
components: the low-pass filter and the high-pass filter. The low-pass
filter (or high-frequency filter) allows signals with a lower frequency
than the cutoff frequency to be transmitted, while those with a higher
frequency are attenuated. A high-pass filter (or low-frequency filter)
does the opposite, attenuating signals with frequencies lower than
the cutoff value.
Examples of low-frequency artifacts include respiration or
patient movement. Some monitors not designed for use in veteri-
nary medicine have a low-frequency filter setting of 0.5 Hz
(30 beats/min), and some horses and reptiles may have heart rates
that reasonably fall below this threshold, creating challenges in
monitor interpretation [11,31].
High-frequency artifacts can be caused by muscle fasciculations,
shivering, and, importantly, 60-cycle (Hz) electromagnetic interfer-
ence from electrical equipment in the perioperative area. Most
modern ECG machines include an additional notch filter to specifi-
cally attenuate artifacts within the 60-Hz frequency range. This may
help limit the interference from surrounding electrical equipment.
Types of electrical equipment that can commonly lead to artifacts
include MRIs, flexible bronchoscopes or endoscopes, nerve stimu-
lators, and, in some situations, cell phones [11].
Electrosurgery units are another potential source of ECG
artifacts (Fig. 11.9). Electrosurgery units based on the concept of
creating heat using a flow of electrical current through a small area
of tissue can lead to changes in the ECG waveform that can be both
overt and subtle [32,33]. Care must be taken to ensure that the
patient is properly grounded, as there have been incidences of
burns associated with electrosurgery units and ECG electrodes
where grounding has been inadequate [34]. There is at least one
documented case of severe esophageal burns caused by an esopha-
geal ECG probe in a dog where grounding became inadequate
during surgery [35].
Effect of anesthesia
The ECG is a useful diagnostic tool for monitoring patients
undergoing sedation and anesthesia. It is especially important for
patients with comorbidities that put them at risk for development
of dysrhythmias, as well as for healthy patients whose risk of dys-
rhythmias may increase with anesthetic medications. Dysrhythmias
may occur under anesthesia in the absence of underlying cardiac
disease. In a study of 50 healthy young dogs undergoing elective
procedures, 26 out of 50 had at least one instance of second-degree
AV block, 22 out of 50 had ventricular premature contractions, and
2 out of 50 experienced ventricular tachycardia perioperatively;
however, some of these dogs were anesthetized with halothane,
which is known to sensitize the heart to certain arrhythmias
[36–38]. In a study of 49 healthy cats without structural heart dis-
ease undergoing inhalant anesthesia with isoflurane or sevoflurane,
5 cats had at least one ventricular premature complex throughout
the anesthetic period [4]. It has been suggested that healthy horses
without underlying cardiac disease may have a prevalence of dys-
rhythmias as great as 25%, even when awake [28], with some of the
most common arrhythmias being first and second-degree AV block.
Horses undergoing inhalant anesthesia for colic and non-colic
procedures had high incidences of arrhythmias postoperatively,
exceeding 75% in both groups [39]. The causes of these cardiac
rhythm disturbances under anesthesia are addressed elsewhere,
but an understanding of the equipment used, the common artifacts
encountered, and the species differences that occur can help the
anesthetist differentiate a normal ECG from a life-threatening
dysrhythmia and allow appropriate intervention and educated
decision-making regarding patient care.

Introduction
Blood pressure (BP) is a vital sign that is relatively easy to measure
in most veterinary patients. Perfusion of organs and tissues is vital
in delivering oxygen and nutrients as well as removing metabolic
byproducts. While the measurement of BP does not directly meas-
ure perfusion, pressure is required to bring blood to tissues and
vital organs including the heart, brain, and kidneys. Trauma and
surgical interventions may cause hemodynamic shifts, while the
administration of sedation and general anesthesia results in altera-
tions in cardiac function and vasomotor tone, thereby affecting BP
(Box 12.1). BP monitoring should be a part of the care and manage-
ment of all patients undergoing sedation and anesthesia, as outlined
in both the American Animal Hospital Association and American
College of Veterinary Anesthesia and Analgesia monitoring
guidelines [1,2].
Blood pressure determinants and definitions
BP measurement is traditionally expressed as a series of three values:
systolic arterial pressure (SAP), diastolic arterial pressure (DAP),
and mean arterial pressure (MAP), each with their own importance
in patient assessment. SAP is the pressure exerted by blood against
the arterial walls during systole of the cardiac cycle. DAP represents
the amount of pressure that blood exerts on the arterial walls during
cardiac relaxation (diastole). MAP is of great importance in anes-
thetized patients, as it determines perfusion pressure in the tissues
and is directly influenced by cardiac output (CO) and systemic vas-
cular resistance (SVR). Conversely, pulse pressure (PP) is simply
the difference between SAP and DAP and does not indicate appro-
priate tissue perfusion. Since most sedative and anesthetic agents
affect vasomotor tone, digital pulse palpation should not be used as
a substitute for accurate measurement of BP in anesthetized patients.
Mean arterial pressure
MAP represents the area under the arterial pressure/time curve
divided by the cardiac cycle duration. Modern invasive blood pres-
sure measurement systems accurately calculate MAP based on anal-
ysis of the arterial waveform, while most non-invasive oscillometric
systems measure MAP as the greatest cuff pressure amplitude vari-
ation. In addition, MAP may be roughly estimated by the following
formula, though this equation has a number of limitations:
MAP 	DAP 	/ 	SAP 	DAP	1 3
Factors that influence MAP include CO and SVR:
MAP 	CO SVR
Cardiac output
CO is a product of heart rate (HR) and stroke volume (SV):
CO 	HR SV

A more in-depth discussion of CO may be found in elsewhere in
this text (Chapter 33). Briefly, HR is influenced by chronotropy,
lusitropy, and dromotropy, whereas SV is influenced by volume
(inotropy, preload, and total blood volume) in addition to afterload.
Chronotropy defines the physiologic timing of HR. Lusitropy is
the period of cardiac relaxation that occurs during diastole when
cardiac myocytes have a decreased level of cytosolic calcium, as
opposed to inotropy when increased calcium uptake causes posi-
tive contractile effects in the cardiac myocytes. Dromotropy is the
actual conduction of an impulse, usually through the AV node,
which in turn influences HR.
Systemic vascular resistance
SVR, also known as “total peripheral resistance,” is influenced by
vascular size (1/∞) and blood viscosity and is defined by the
amount of force that the vasculature system exerts on circulating
blood, excluding pulmonary circulation. SVR influences BP via
three factors: vessel length, vessel diameter, and the viscosity of the
blood [3]. Alterations in vessel diameter have an enormous effect on
vessel flow, as defined by the Hagen–Poiseuille equation, whereby a
reduction of vessel diameter by 1/2 decreases flow to only 1/16th of
the original flow:
P 	Q L	8 	4

where ∆P is the pressure difference between the two ends of the
vessel, Q is the volumetric flow rate, L is the length of vessel, η is the
dynamic viscosity, r4 is the vessel radius to the fourth power, and 8/π
is a constant of proportionality.
Normal ranges of blood pressure
A consensus statement by the American College of Veterinary
Internal Medicine (ACVIM) details guidelines for the identifica-
tion, evaluation, and management of systemic hypertension in dogs
and cats [4]. This statement cites difficulty in determining a single
value or range acceptable for all cats and dogs and that normal
ranges of BP will vary by species and patient factors, including tem-
perament, age, breed, body condition, and sex. Measurement tech-
nique and location will also affect the values obtained. Numerous
studies have attempted to investigate and define normal ranges of
BP in various species with variable results. In general, prehypertension
is defined as SAP 140–150 mmHg, hypertension that may lead to
potential target organ damage as SAP > 160–179 mmHg, and severe
hypertension as SAP > 180 mmHg.
Difficulties in defining a universally acceptable range of BP
emphasize the importance of obtaining baseline BP values in
patients prior to an anesthetic event, especially if concerns exist for
target organ damage and/or underlying risk factors are identified
(Box 12.2).
Hypotension-related morbidity and mortality is difficult to
determine and most likely depends on a number of individual
factors. In a study of over 30,000 humans undergoing non-cardiac
surgery, hypotension (defined as MAP < 55 mmHg) for as little as
1–5 min was associated with increased risk of acute kidney
injury [5]. While large-scale trials in veterinary medicine are lack-
ing, the importance of maintaining perfusion during anesthesia
should nonetheless be prioritized. For instance, use of excessive lev-
els of inhalant leads to a significant decrease in SVR and a relative
hypovolemia [6]. Hypotension is one of the most common compli-
cations of anesthesia and can have serious consequences if left
unmanaged [1]. In horses, postanesthetic myopathy is a complex
and potentially fatal consequence of inadequate tissue perfusion
pressure during anesthesia. Multiple studies in horses have demon-
strated increased risk of complications when MAP < 60 mmHg [7,8];
as such, common practice is to ensure that MAP is greater than
70 mmHg at all times [9]. Current information indicates that,
although maintenance of MAP is important, maintaining global
perfusion without increasing SVR should be prioritized, and vaso-
active support agents should be selected accordingly [10].
Autoregulation of blood pressure
The ability of organs to maintain a relatively constant blood flow
despite changes in perfusion pressure is known as “autoregulation.”
Organs perform this task intrinsically via three main mecha-
nisms [11]. Metabolic regulation of blood flow occurs when changes
in metabolism result in the release of vasodilatory substances such as
adenosine, carbon dioxide, and lactic acid. An example of such meta-
bolic regulation would be the vasodilation that occurs in muscle beds
in response to hypoxia. Myogenic (pressure-dependent) mechanisms
autoregulate blood flow via smooth muscle-lined vessels; increased
pressure within the vessels leads to vasoconstriction, and decreased
pressure is followed by vasodilation in smaller arteries and arterioles.
Myogenic regulation of blood flow is observed in renal tissues. Shear-
stress-dependent (endothelial) mechanisms regulate blood flow via
the endothelial release of vasoactive factors such as nitric oxide and
prostacyclin, causing vasodilation of smooth muscle-lined vessels, as
well as endothelin, which modulates vasoconstriction [12]. Such
regulation may be observed in brain and cardiac tissue.
Organs that demonstrate the greatest ability for autoregulation
of blood flow include the brain, heart, and kidneys. The brain
maintains autoregulation largely by metabolic means along with
myogenic and endothelial responses. Recall that cerebral perfusion
pressure (CPP) is the difference between MAP and intracranial
pressure (ICP); it is critical to maintain constant CPP and cerebral
blood flow (see Chapter 39). In humans, cerebral perfusion is

autoregulated within an MAP range of 60–160 mmHg, where, in
the dog, autoregulation of cerebral perfusion has been reported to
occur with the MAP range of 70–140 mmHg [13,14]. In the kid-
neys, autoregulation of blood flow protects them from injury due to
fluctuations of arterial BP and maintains the perfusion necessary
to meet metabolic needs. Myogenic mechanisms of autoregulation
allow for maintenance of constant renal blood flow (RBF) within
the MAP range of 90–150 mmHg in rats, 70–130 mmHg in humans,
and 40–100 mmHg in dogs [15,16]. Interestingly, RBF and glomer-
ular filtration rate are maintained independently of renal perfusion
pressure (RPP) via intrarenal autoregulatory mechanisms in the
defined range of 80–180 mmHg in humans [17]. This safeguard is
provided by a combination of myogenic and tubuloglomerular
feedback that buffers transmission of changes in RPP to the capil-
laries of the glomeruli, protecting them from potential barotrauma
while preserving renal function.
During anesthetic events, the maintenance of systemic BP within
ranges of autoregulation ensures consistent blood flow to the vital
organs, including the kidneys, heart, and brain. Various studies in
differing species and physiologic states demonstrate slight differ-
ences in ranges, so one recommended approach is to maintain BP
within 20% of measured baseline BP taken prior to arrival in the
operating room [18].
Invasive blood pressure measurement
Invasive blood pressure (IBP) monitoring is considered the gold
standard for BP measurement in anesthetized veterinary patients
and allows for continuous, beat-by- beat assessment of BP and pulse
waveform analysis. As this technique requires catheterization of an
artery (thus the name “invasive”), it also facilitates sampling for
arterial blood gas analysis. The term “direct” BP measurement is
sometimes also used to describe this method; however, almost all
IBP systems incorporate a transducer (see below) to convert the
kinetic energy produced by changes in arterial pressure into electri-
cal energy. SAP and DAP are directly measured with this technique,
and MAP is calculated as the area under the arterial waveform over
the cardiac cycle (Fig. 12.1). Careful setup and specialized equip-
ment are needed to obtain the graphical display of the arterial pres-
sure waveform and the numeric values; accuracy relies upon factors
including the arterial catheter, the saline-filled tubing connecting
the catheter to the transducer, the transducer itself, and the electri-
cal components.
Patients where IBP monitoring should be considered for perio-
perative care include those where continuous monitoring of BP
and/or repeated arterial blood gas/electrolyte sampling is necessary.
These include high-risk surgical and critically ill patients with
anticipated rapid changes in hemodynamic status. Patients with
comorbidities such as cardiac, pulmonary, or renal disease, signifi-
cant risk of hemorrhage, and/or those receiving vasoactive sub-
stances (e.g., inotropes, vasopressors) should also be considered for
IBP monitoring.
Disadvantages of this technique include the cost or availability of
advanced monitoring equipment and the need to catheterize a
peripheral artery as well as potential risk of local pain, hemorrhage,
hematoma formation, infection at the catheterization site, embo-
lism, or ischemia/thrombosis (Fig. 12.2). A retrospective study
examining the catheterization sites of 267 dogs and cats found loss
of palpable pulse postoperatively in 22.3% of animals without
evidence of associated tissue ischemia [19]. Care should always be
