where ρ is the resistivity of blood, L is the mean distance between the
inner electrodes (the thoracic length), VET is the ventricular ejec-
tion time, (dZ/dt)max is the maximum value of the first derivative
during systole, and Z0 is the basal thoracic impedance. Bioimpedance
provides real-time estimation of SV and cardiac output, along with
measures of thoracic fluid content, left ventricular ejection time, sys-
temic vascular resistance, and left cardiac work index [108].
Bioreactance has been developed from the bioimpedance tech-
nique but measures changes in frequency of electrical currents,
rather than voltage, potentially making it less prone to noise-
derived errors [110]. Both techniques are non-invasive and can be
applied quickly. However, the biggest concern with these techniques
is the accuracy and precision of the measurements. Physiological
studies in healthy humans showed good reliability of the results, but
this was not consistent in critically ill patients, particularly in the
presence of pulmonary edema and/or pleural effusion. In addition,
electrical interference may also occur from other anesthesia moni-
toring devices connected to the patient [111–113].
Little or no evidence exists on the accuracy and reliability of
these techniques in veterinary species [114,115]. Therefore, bioim-
pedance and bioreactance cardiac output determination should not
be considered as a valid and reproducible method at present. A
shortcoming of both bioimpedance and bioreactance mathematical
models is the approximation of the shape of the chest as a cylinder
or a cone for stroke volume determination. These represent over-
simplifications of the electrical events occurring inside the thorax
during the cardiac cycle and are sources of technique inaccuracy. It
seems unlikely that the algorithms designed for human patients
would be sufficiently accurate for use in various veterinary species.

Standard capnography as an indicator of cardiac
output
A simple and practical indicator of cardiac output in any anesthe-
tized patient is end-tidal carbon dioxide (PET
CO2
) measured by cap-
nography. PET
CO2 is determined by CO2 production (VCO2 ),
alveolar ventilation, and pulmonary perfusion. Assuming stable
conditions of patient minute ventilation and body temperature, and
in absence of airway obstruction or extra-metabolic sources of CO 2
(e.g., laparoscopic surgery or sodium bicarbonate administration),
a sudden change in PET
CO2 has been shown to reflect a proportional
alteration in cardiac output [116,117]. Studies on preload optimiza-
tion have demonstrated that percentage changes in PET
CO2 induced
by intravascular volume expansion linearly reflect percentage
increases in cardiac output [118].
In practical terms, the simultaneous decrease in systemic blood
pressure and PET
CO2 in an anesthetized patient (with constant min-
ute ventilation) may reflect a primary reduction in cardiac output.
In such conditions, if sinus rhythm and normal HR are confirmed,
therapeutic interventions should focus on optimization of preload
and myocardial contractility to support SV.
In contrast, a decrease in blood pressure with no reduction in
PET
CO2 suggests a decrease in systemic vascular resistances rather
than a decrease in cardiac output, indicating that vasopressor ther-
apy is the most appropriate intervention to correct the
hypotension.
In clinical scenarios of drastically decreased blood flow such as
hemorrhagic shock or impending cardiac arrest, the correlation
between changes in PET
CO2 and cardiac output is no longer linear.
In cases where oxygen consumption becomes supply dependent
(critical O2 delivery), the drop in PET
CO2 is also accompanied by a
decrease in VCO2 . In dogs, it was demonstrated that the relation-
ship between percentage changes in PET
CO2 and cardiac output
during hemorrhagic shock is best determined by the following log-
arithmic function:
y 	x	3 3617 	31 854	. 	ln 	.
where y represents cardiac index (mL/min/kg) and x represents

CO2 (mmHg). This implies that the greatest decrease in PET

occurs at the lowest cardiac output [119].

Introduction
Since William Thomas Green Morton’s demonstration of ether use
in 1846, the delivery of anesthesia and the monitoring of anesthe-
tized patients have undergone significant transformation [1].
Today, vigilant perianesthetic care necessitates the assessment of
cardiovascular, ventilatory, and metabolic status. Among these,
monitoring ventilation plays a role in providing crucial patient- and
equipment-related information. During anesthesia, the patient’s
ability to maintain proper ventilation may be compromised by
anesthetic and analgesic drugs, muscle relaxation, and changes in
respiratory drive. Monitoring ventilation allows assessment of
carbon dioxide production, delivery to the lungs, and elimination
via gas exchange, thereby preventing complications and ensuring
patient well-being [2,3]. It is imperative for an anesthetist to under-
stand the physiologic principles of ventilation and various assess-
ment methods to ensure patient safety and optimize anesthesia
delivery.
Physiology of aerobic respiration
Although occasionally used interchangeably, ventilation and respi-
ration can be viewed as two separate physiologic functions.
Ventilation refers to the movement of gases, specifically oxygen and
carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), in and out of the alveoli in the lungs.
Respiration refers to the cellular utilization of oxygen in the process
of generating energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
In aerobic respiration, glycolysis of carbohydrates occurs in the
cytoplasm in the presence of oxygen. Pyruvate moves into
mitochondria and enters the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle after
conversion to acetyl-CoA (Fig. 14.1). The final step in aerobic res-
piration is oxidative phosphorylation, including the electron trans-
port chain and the process of chemiosmosis.
This series of reactions generates ATP, which is the primary
source of energy for cells. For efficient aerobic respiration to occur,
there must be an adequate supply of glucose and oxygen-rich blood
to the mitochondria in the tissues. Carbon dioxide is generated as a
by-product of aerobic respiration. The partial pressure of carbon
dioxide (PCO2
) is highest within the mitochondria, from which it
passes through the cytoplasm to the blood, and then is carried to the
lungs for excretion. Carriage of CO2 within the blood occurs primar-
ily as bicarbonate, as a dissociation product from the buffering of
CO2 with water to form carbonic acid, and, to a lesser extent, as car-
bamino compounds bound to hemoglobin and plasma proteins or
dissolved gas (see Chapter 37). Once delivered to the lungs, alveolar
ventilation allows for gas exchange between the alveoli and circula-
tion resulting in the acquisition of oxygen and expiration of CO2
.
Alveolar CO2 (PA
CO2
) is directly proportional to the amount of CO2
produced by metabolism (VCO2
) and subsequently delivered to the
lungs and inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation (VA

Carbon dioxide and acid–base implications
Carbon dioxide and its equilibration between the intracellular and
extracellular environments are critical to acid–base homeostasis
and can provide valuable information about respiratory status and
compensatory mechanisms. The concentration of CO 2 in the blood
is directly related to the regulation of pH. Increased levels of CO2
result in higher carbonic acid (H 2 CO3 ) formation and thus the gen-
eration of H + ions, leading to a decrease in blood pH (acidemia) and
a compensatory increase in blood bicarbonate (HCO3
-) concentra-
tion. Conversely, decreased CO 2 levels reduce carbonic acid forma-
tion, resulting in an increase in blood pH (alkalemia) and
compensatory decrease in blood HCO3
-. Respiratory alkalemia
(hypocapnia) and acidemia (hypercapnia) result in rapid equilibra-
tion between the extra- and intracellular fluids, causing more dra-
matic shifts in pH during these conditions when compared to
metabolic acidemia or alkalemia [5].
There are many potential physiologic consequences of hypercap-
nic acidemia including catecholamine release (may lead to tachyar-
rhythmias), increased cardiac output, electrolyte shifts (e.g.,
hyperkalemia), rightward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissocia-
tion curve, and cerebral vasodilation [6–8]. In the face of severe
hypercapnia (> 80 mmHg), central nervous system signs including
narcosis and coma can occur [9,10]. When decreases in the arterial
partial pressure of CO2 (PaCO2
) result in pH greater than 7.6, the
physiologic consequences may include cerebral and myocardial
vasoconstriction with resulting decreases in blood flow, decreased
cardiac output, leftward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissocia-
tion curve, hypokalemia, and predisposition to arrhythmias [11].
Importance of monitoring ventilation
Perianesthetic mortality trends appear to be decreasing in veteri-
nary patients over time, though remain significantly higher than in
humans [12–23]. Given the wide array of physiologic consequences
of ventilatory derangements, early detection of respiratory events
through advanced monitoring, including capnography, allows for
timely intervention and enhanced patient safety throughout the
perioperative period [24–27].
Monitoring standards
The American College of Veterinary Anesthesia and Analgesia
(ACVAA) published its stance on anesthetic monitoring of small
animal patients in 2009 [28]. Within those recommendations, mul-
tiple ventilation monitoring techniques are mentioned, including
subjective measurements, such as visualization of chest wall expan-
sion or movement of an attached reservoir bag, and thoracic auscul-
tation via external or esophageal stethoscope, or the use of an audible
respiratory monitor. These techniques indicate a binary endpoint
(i.e., absence or presence) and do not allow for objective measure-
ments, as they do not provide a carbon dioxide value. Partial

) with a capnograph or
blood gas analysis to obtain PaCO2 or partial pressure of venous car-
bon dioxide (PvCO2
) are the major objective monitoring methods
for ventilation. The use of spirometry is mentioned for measurement
of tidal volume and investigation of respiratory mechanics, and
while this is an objective measurement, it does not provide partial
pressure of carbon dioxide. The subjective measurements are con-
sidered essential or required by the ACVAA. Capnography is recom-
mended, and blood gas analysis recommended as needed on a
patient-specific basis. The Small Animal Monitoring Guidelines are
in the process of being updated as of 2023.
The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) has dictated
since 1989 that any procedure in which endotracheal intubation or
laryngeal mask airway is used requires the use of capnometry, cap-
nography, or mass spectroscopy to quantify expired carbon dioxide.
The requirement for quantitative monitoring of carbon dioxide was
extended to sedated patients in 2010 [29]. It is recommended that
alarms associated with abnormal carbon dioxide are audible in the
operating room. A closed claims analysis at the end of the last cen-
tury determined that of respiratory events, including inadequate
ventilation, esophageal intubation, and difficult airway, 72% could
have been prevented using better respiratory monitoring, and spe-
cifically, that the combination of pulse oximetry and capnography
could have prevented > 90% of claims for inadequate ventilation and
esophageal intubation [2].
The value of capnography in veterinary anesthesia and critical
care settings is such that its use should be encouraged in primary
care practice settings and an expectation in a specialty or tertiary
care setting.
Physical methods of monitoring ventilation
The most accessible methods to monitor ventilation are the subjec-
tive assessment of breathing by visualization and auscultation of all
lung fields and the trachea with a stethoscope. These methods
should be included in every preanesthetic assessment, should
accompany other monitoring techniques throughout the anesthetic
event, including the recovery period, and should be utilized diag-
nostically in the event of a respiratory complication. Additionally,
auscultation of lung sounds bilaterally directly after intubation is a
highly recommended technique to confirm appropriate endotra-
cheal tube (ETT) placement and aid in early diagnosis of endobron-
chial or esophageal intubation.
The lung sounds, as well as respiratory rate, effort, and quality, can
indicate various causes for a change in ventilation. For example, a
patient with a fixed airway obstruction will tend toward a decreased
respiratory rate with a longer inspiratory phase. A patient with an
alveolar disease or pleural space disease will often experience an
increase in respiratory effort and could have increased (e.g., crackles
in pneumonia) or decreased (e.g., absence due to pleural fluid) lung
sounds. Respiratory disease may negatively impact ventilation; anes-
thetic management requirements of specific respiratory conditions
vary and are discussed in Chapter 38.
Apnea monitors
Apnea monitors are simple respiratory monitoring tools that have
been used historically in veterinary medicine and persist in some
practice settings. Apnea monitors attach to the circuit between the
distal end of the ETT and the patient end of the breathing circuit.
The major information gained from an apnea monitor is the
presence of inhalation/exhalation and a respiratory rate. Their
design can be as simple as a low-profile plastic attachment that cre-
ates a “whistle” noise during the breathing cycle. They also come in
a more sophisticated design with a circuit attachment and separate
digital display that alerts the user with an audible and visual respira-
tory “beep” with each breath, displays the time between breaths,
and provides an alarm that is triggered by a preset apnea duration
(Fig. 14.2). Most models are equipped with battery power, making
them highly portable. These monitors give a binary response (i.e.,
movement of gas or not) but do not provide any information about
the effectiveness of respiratory efforts. In addition, like any adapter
between the ETT and the breathing circuit, they add mechanical
deadspace.
Quantitative monitoring of carbon dioxide
The use of quantified carbon dioxide as a monitoring tool in gen-
eral anesthesia has multiple merits and can be accomplished in sev-
eral forms (Table 14.1). In addition to the ability to provide
information about metabolism, lung perfusion, and adequacy of
ventilation, detection of carbon dioxide in respiratory gases can
indicate integrity of the ETT and breathing circuit. Continuous CO 2
monitoring provides real-time data and allows for immediate detec-
tion of changes in ventilation and prompt intervention. It is primar-
ily used to confirm ventilatory status (including respiratory rate,
PET
CO2
, and inhaled CO2 [PI
CO2 ]). Importantly, capnometry/cap-
nography is the most reliable primary method for identifying
whether an endotracheal tube is correctly placed within the airway
instead of the esophagus.

Capnometry/capnography can also be instrumental in detecting
life threatening cardiorespiratory complications. For example, the
rapid decline in PET
CO2 as detected by a capnograph may be the first
and only reliable indicator of cardiopulmonary arrest in the anesthe-
tized patient, as detailed below.
Methods of carbon dioxide measurement
Like other forms of patient monitoring in veterinary medicine, the
implementation of CO2 measurement requires equipment that
meets specific criteria to ensure its regular use and effectiveness. It
is important for monitoring equipment to be affordable and readily
available. Cost-effective options enable wider accessibility, allowing
veterinary professionals to incorporate CO 2 monitoring into their
standard protocols. Equipment should be easy to use and should
not require extensive training or complex setup procedures.
Additionally, lightweight, portable, and durable equipment offers
flexibility for the rigors of daily use and enables monitoring in dif-
ferent areas of the veterinary hospital or during transport. In the
case of monitoring ventilation, equipment should be ideal for the
properties of CO 2 and be able to distinguish it among other gases
that are present with minimal interference.
Blood gas analysis
The gold standard for determination of PaCO 2 is arterial blood
gas analysis. An arterial sample is obtained either via puncture or
from an indwelling catheter into a preheparinized syringe. Air
bubbles are expelled, and the sample should be analyzed within
30 min or stored on ice. Both laboratory-based and patient-side
blood gas analyzers are available that utilize a glass electrode cov-
ered with a CO 2 permeable membrane (the Severinghaus elec-
trode) to ascertain CO 2 concentrations. Carbon dioxide from
the blood sample diffuses across the membrane into a bicarbonate
solution. Carbonic acid is created and devolves into H + and
HCO 3
– . The generation of H + ions, and therefore pH, is logarith-
mically related to the concentration of CO 2 in the sample, creating
a voltage difference between the glass electrode and the reference
electrode [31].
Disadvantages of arterial blood gas analysis include intermittent
sampling and the need to puncture an artery. In addition, the
required equipment may not be available in all veterinary clinical
settings.
Chemical detection (colorimetry)
Chemical detection is based on the principle that when CO 2 is
combined with water, carbonic acid is formed, which then disso-
ciates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate. In turn, the pH is
decreased, and this change acts as a surrogate marker for detec-
tion of CO 2 when using a pH-sensitive indicator. These devices
typically house a color changing, pH-sensitive indicator within a
clear window, which can be connected to standard endotracheal
tube and breathing circuit components. For each device, a chart
will reference which color change correlates with a range of CO 2
measurements. Though the measurements are not precise, they
have proven to be successful at detection of endotracheal intuba-
tion, prediction of return of spontaneous circulation in resuscita-
tion, and monitoring of ventilation for many hours where
quantitative methods are not available [32–34]. Advantages for
this type of device include its light weight and low cost.
Disadvantages include generation of semiquantitative results,
conditional interpretation of color change, short-term usability,
and added resistance to flow.
Infrared spectroscopy
The widely used technology that possesses a majority of the
aforementioned qualities is infrared (IR) spectroscopy. IR spectros-
copy involves the analysis of the interaction between IR radiation
and asymmetric, polyatomic molecules at distinct spectra.
Homogeneous molecules, such as oxygen, do not absorb IR radia-
tion, and techniques for oxygen measurement are discussed in
Chapter 15. IR radiation consists of a range of wavelengths that fall
between the visible and microwave regions of the electromagnetic
spectrum. When a sample is exposed to IR radiation, the molecules
within the sample absorb energy at specific frequencies that are
characteristic of the chemical bonds present. The wavelength at
which CO2 has the strongest absorption band is approximately
4.3 μm, which allows reasonable discrimination from other
molecules that also absorb IR radiation and are commonly found
in an expired breath (i.e., inhalant anesthetics). Notably, two
molecules with IR absorption bands close to CO 2 that may cause
cross-interference are water vapor and nitrous oxide (N2 O).
Once the absorption of IR radiation by CO2 in a sample of expired
breath is measured, the principles of the Beer–Lambert law are
applied:
A 	lc
where A is the absorbance, ɛ is the molecular absorption coefficient,
l is the length of the optical path, and c is the molecular concentra-
tion. Absorption of IR radiation at the specified wavelength is pro-
portional to the concentration of the molecule (CO 2 ) being
measured. When the absorbance is compared to a known standard,
the amount of CO2 present in respiratory gases can be quantified as
a partial pressure (representative of the number of molecules pre-
sent) or converted to a percent concentration (expressed as a pro-
portion of the total).
The essential elements for IR spectroscopy include: a source of IR
radiation, a sample cell, and a photodetector [35]. IR capnographs
may use an optical filter to transmit only the desired wavelength
(nondispersive) or may separate the wavelengths spatially with
prisms or diffraction (dispersive). Nondispersive IR spectroscopy is
most commonly in use as it is more efficient.
Infrared radiation source
In general, IR radiation sources may be considered broad- or
narrowband. One example of a broadband source is a heated ele-
ment known as a “blackbody emitter.” In this case, filters are uti-
lized to eliminate IR that is outside the desired range, and the
constant source is mechanically chopped by a spinning wheel.
The spinning wheel alternately blocks and allows the IR radia-
tion to pass through to the sample or detector. This chopping
action creates a time-varying signal, which is important for sep-
arating the desired IR signal from any background noise or
interference. Multigas analyzers employ several specific narrow-
band filters to allow for the measurement of halogenated agents
along with CO 2 and may also include integrated technology for
measurement of oxygen.
An example of a narrowband IR source is laser-based molecular
correlation spectroscopy, or Microstream technology. This uses a
unique approach to emit a band of IR radiation that is highly precise
for CO2
. In Microstream technology, a glass electrode that contains
several gases, including nitrogen and CO2
, is exposed to a radio fre-
quency voltage. Consequently, the nitrogen molecules experience
excitation and their interaction with CO2 causes excitation of those
molecules. When CO2 returns to its resting state, it emits radiation,

-- 239 of 1450 --

which is used as the narrow spectrum IR source. This IR source
is then electronically modulated in order to allow sampling
every 25 ms.
Ultimately, the IR light is transmitted through the sample cham-
ber, and the filtered and modulated signal reaches a detector where
the intensity is measured, processed, and directed to the user inter-
face where it is displayed.
Problems with infrared spectroscopy
The IR absorption band for CO 2 lies between two strong water
vapor absorption bands, and water vapor can interfere with CO 2
measurement in several ways. When exhaled breath passes through
the respiratory system, it picks up water vapor, which can signifi-
cantly contribute to the total gas volume. Water vapor can condense
at the sample cell, where it will absorb IR radiation, leading to a
falsely increased CO 2 reading. Heating of sensors, water traps,
absorbent filters, and specialized permeable (e.g., Nafion) tubing
are a few solutions utilized to limit this interference. In sidestream/
diverting monitors (see below), the cooling of the sampled gas will
affect the concentration of water vapor and lead to slight overesti-
mation of PET
CO2 [36]. Water vapor and secretions can also cause
full or partial occlusion of sampling lines leading to altered meas-
urements or even no measurement at all.
Another phenomenon known as “collision broadening” causes
apparent increases in CO2 due to the molecular interaction with
gases such as N2
O and O2
, which can result in widened absorption
spectra.
Mainstream capnometry/capnography
Mainstream (non-diverting) CO2 devices utilize IR technology with
the sensor placed between the patient and the breathing system.
The sample cell (cuvette) functions as the airway adapter and the IR
source and detector are all housed within the sensor. The transmit-
ted signal may be displayed directly on the sensor housing, or a
cable may be used to connect to an external monitor. Advantages to
mainstream devices include rapid response times, higher accuracy
with small tidal volumes and faster respiratory rates, no need to
separately scavenge sampled gases, and no waste of inhalant agents.
Disadvantages to mainstream devices include added weight and
mechanical deadspace to airway with limited adaptability, suscepti-
bility to damage, and secretions on the windows of the cuvette caus-
ing interference with readings. Many of the noted disadvantages to
mainstream technology are historical and have been minimized
with contemporary solid-state technology [35,37].
Sidestream capnometry/capnography
Sidestream (diverting) CO 2 devices use a variety of airway adapters
attached to a long sampling line to connect to the sample cell
housed within a distant monitor. Samples are constantly aspirated
at variable rates (typically 50–200 mL/min). A combination of
water permeable tubing, filters, and water traps may be used to limit
water vapor contamination. Advantages to sidestream devices
include the lightweight nature of the ETT adapter, potential to min-
imize deadspace by connecting sampling tubing directly to a spe-
cialized ETT adapter, the protected status of the sensor within the
monitor housing, and the ability to monitor PET
CO2 in non-
intubated patients with nasal catheters. Disadvantages include delay
time (based on sampling rate), the need for rerouting of sampled
gas (scavenged or returned to circuit), and the potential for issues
with the sampling line or water trap devices (e.g., leaks, kinks, or
occlusions) [38].
Raman spectroscopy
Historically, another form of spectroscopy has been used that takes
advantage of the phenomenon called “Raman scatter.” In this tech-
nology, a high-intensity argon laser is applied to a gas sample. The
laser causes excitation of the molecules within the sample, creating
an altered energy state. When the molecules return to their stable
state, energy is emitted in a signature specific to that molecule,
known as “Raman scatter radiation.” It provides a fingerprint-like
spectrum that represents the specific vibrational and rotational
modes of the molecules present. This technology is not currently
used in clinical settings for capnometry as smaller, lighter, and less
expensive technology has prevailed [39].
Mass spectrometry
Mass spectrometry measures components of a gas mixture based on
their mass and charge. A sample is drawn into a vacuum chamber
where it is exposed to an electron beam. The ionized fragments are
then accelerated by an electrical field and separated by a magnetic
field. Detectors are then able to measure individual components of
the sample. While mass spectrometry remains a valuable analytical
tool for research and specialized applications, the size, complexity,
and cost limitations make it impractical for routine patient moni-
toring in clinical settings. More accessible and cost-effective tech-
nologies are currently preferred for continuous patient monitoring,
especially in veterinary medicine [40,41].
Transcutaneous measurement
Transcutaneous measurement of carbon dioxide (P TC CO 2 ) is a
non-invasive method used to measure CO 2 by placing heated elec-
trochemical sensors on the skin. The technique relies on the prin-
ciple that CO 2 can diffuse through the skin, allowing its
measurement at the skin surface. As in arterial blood gas analysis,
a Severinghaus electrode is used to assess CO 2 concentrations.
While P TC CO 2 measurement could be particularly useful in situa-
tions involving non-intubated patients, or where frequent blood
sampling is impractical or stressful, there remain many limita-
tions to its use in veterinary clinical practice. In rabbits, it was
demonstrated that P TC CO 2 was able to reasonably approximate
PaCO 2 [42]. However, in cats [43], sheep [44], and dogs [44,45],
P TC CO 2 consistently overestimates PaCO 2 and cannot be used as a
reliable surrogate. Development of optical detection technology
may offer an alternative to electrochemical-based means in the
future [46].
Time-based capnography
A capnogram wave is most commonly plotted as CO 2 partial pres-
sure in millimeters of mercury (mmHg) against time. In this for-
mat, there are four phases to the capnogram, one that represents
inhalation and three that represent phases of exhalation. Of note,
there is still disagreement within the literature as to the correct
labeling system in phase number for the capnogram. While the
numbering system might vary, the actual phase of inhalation or
exhalation represented by the component of the graphical image
remains the same.
The normal capnogram
A normal time capnogram, as described below, is shown in Fig. 14.3.
Phase 0 = inspiratory phase or inspiratory downstroke.
Represented by a rapid downswing in expiratory CO2 partial

pressure. In a normal waveform, the CO2 partial pressure rapidly
reaches zero.
Phase I = respiratory baseline. It marks the start of expiration and
represents emptying of anatomic deadspace, which is CO2 free.
Phase II = expiratory upstroke. Continued exhalation of a mixture
of alveolar gas and deadspace gas from the conducting airways.
The expired CO2 partial pressure rapidly increases.
Phase III = the alveolar plateau. Continued exhalation of alveolar
gas creates a gradually elevating line due to uneven alveolar emp-
tying. The peak of the plateau represents the PET
CO2 at the end of
the exhaled tidal volume.
Alpha (α) angle = the transition from phase II to III. In normal
states, this angle should be approximately 100°. The α angle rep-
resents the transition from airway gas to alveolar gas.
Beta (β) angle = the transition from phase III to phase 0. In normal
states, it should be approximately 90°. It is at this point in the
capnogram waveform that a PET
CO2 value is measured.
Abnormal capnograms
In the process of critically evaluating a capnogram waveform, there
are multiple pieces of information to gather, all of which lead to a
clinical picture of respiratory status: (1) respiratory rate and con-
sistency of rate; (2) PET
CO2 value; and (3) waveform appearance. A
change in respiratory rate or a change in the consistency of the res-
piratory rate provides information related to anesthetic depth, noci-
ceptive signaling, or brainstem status or pathology, among other
states. Capnography is a powerful tool in helping to estimate, with
good accuracy in healthy patients, the PaCO2
; however, PET
CO2
typically underestimates PaCO2 by approximately 1–7 mmHg in
small animals, and this underestimation may be greater in large ani-
mals during general anesthesia. This is due to two major factors: the
presence of a constant anatomic deadspace and the concentration
gradient of CO 2 between the pulmonary capillary and alveolus.
There are abnormal states that can lead to a larger gradient between
PaCO2 and PET
CO2
, and those will be discussed briefly later [47,48].
As a surrogate of PaCO2
, PET
CO2 reliably provides information on
the status of metabolism, pulmonary perfusion (and therefore car-
diac output), and ventilation, as described above. In addition, a
change in PET
CO2 can provide information about the integrity and
function of anesthesia equipment, including the breathing circuit
and ETT, and, when combined with interpretation of the capnogram
waveform, can provide a targeted focus for intervention. Examples
of waveforms commonly encountered in veterinary clinical practice
are presented in Fig. 14.4.
Specific clinical indications and uses of time-based
capnography
The continuous and real-time measurement of PET
CO2 provides
important insight into respiratory and metabolic status. While cap-
nography is always useful for monitoring clinical status, it is also a
critical tool in certain disease processes and case presentations.
Differential diagnosis of hypoxemia
A major strength of the quantitative measurement of P ET
CO 2 is the
ability to detect clinical situations that may lead to hypoxemia as
well as to focus the differential diagnosis for hypoxemia when it
has occurred. For example, a capnogram with an obtuse α angle
(“shark swimming to the left”) indicates an obstruction to exhala-
tion that could be due to upper airway (partial endotracheal tube
obstruction or kinking) or lower airway (severe bronchospasm)
issues (Fig. 14.4B). Another example is the absence of a waveform
that could indicate apnea, esophageal intubation, complete airway
obstruction, or disconnection of the patient from the anesthesia
circuit. A capnogram with an elevated baseline can point to
rebreathing of carbon dioxide, which indicates equipment issues
with clearance of exhaled CO 2 , including a dysfunctional one-way
valve in the breathing circuit, an exhausted carbon dioxide absor-
bent canister, a significant amount of mechanical deadspace, or
insufficient oxygen flow rate in a non-rebreathing circuit, many of
which could lead to a hypoxemic gas mixture if left unattended
(Fig. 14.4D).
Intracranial disease
In patients at risk for elevated intracranial pressure, it is crucial that
cerebral blood flow is maintained in a normal range. Carbon diox-
ide partial pressure has a significant and linear effect on cerebral
vascular reactivity and tone, causing cerebral vasodilation as local
CO2 partial pressure increases, and cerebral vasoconstriction as it
decreases [49]. In these patients, identification of a normal arterial
to expired carbon dioxide [P(a-et)CO 2
] gradient via blood gas
analysis, followed by continuous monitoring of capnography, is
imperative. Maintenance of PaCO2 at or slightly below a normal
partial pressure (35–40 mmHg) will significantly reduce the likeli-
hood of brain herniation, an irreversible and devastating patient
outcome [50]. Information related to anesthetic management of
patients with intracranial disease is available in Chapter 39.
Acid–base derangements
In patients that are suffering from diseases that predispose them to
acidemia, the close monitoring and maintenance of PaCO2 is
imperative to focused care. An increase in PaCO2 causes a decrease
in pH as discussed earlier, and therefore, hypoventilation precipi-
tated by anesthesia may add to a pre-existing metabolic acidemia.
Additionally, many patients that have a chronic metabolic acid–base
disorder will have enlisted respiratory compensation as a mecha-
nism to maintain favorable physiologic status. As a non-invasive
estimate of PaCO2
, PET
CO2 can be utilized to avoid compounding
an acid–base abnormality.
Hyper- and hypokalemia
An increase in CO2 leads to an increase in H+ concentration in the
blood. Hydrogen ions are exchanged across the cell membrane for
potassium ions (K+
) in the cell to maintain electroneutrality, leading
to an increase in serum K+ concentrations. The result is a precipitous
increase in K+ in the blood, which can have multiple negative conse-
quences that will quickly and significantly affect patient outcome,

to hypokalemia, which can also precipitate arrhythmias as well as
muscle weakness [51–53].
Difficult airway and lower airway disease
During routine, emergent, and difficult endotracheal intubation
scenarios, capnography can be an important tool for verifying cor-
rect placement of the ETT. Confirmation that the ETT is properly
positioned in the trachea rather than the esophagus will reduce the
risk of complications related to misplacement [2]. Furthermore,
changes in the capnogram, as outlined in the capnogram section
above, may indicate developing or worsening airway obstruction
and can demonstrate response to interventions (e.g., bronchodila-
tor therapy).

Cardiopulmonary arrest
The capnograph is arguably the most useful monitor during cardio-
pulmonary arrest (CPA) and resuscitation, as it reflects pulmonary
perfusion, and therefore cardiac output, in real time. It is non-
invasive, easy to connect, and does not require any adjustment.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) scenarios result in a degree
of patient movement that creates significant artifacts for almost all
other monitoring equipment, while the capnograph suffers little to
no artifact due to thoracic compressions [54,55].
The PET
CO2 is related to cardiac output both in normal scenarios
and during a CPR event. It can help to determine the quality of
ongoing chest compressions or internal cardiac massage because the
amount of blood returning to the lungs will largely determine the
amount of CO2 delivered to the lungs. For the same reason, capnog-
raphy will be the first monitor to reliably convey if the patient has
experienced cessation of blood flow and therefore CPA, and it is also
extremely useful in identifying return of spontaneous circulation
(ROSC) quickly. Finally, capnography is a powerful prognostic tool
during the CPR event. Hofmeister et al. found that in instances
where PET
CO2 was measured during CPR, dogs experiencing sus-
tained PET
CO2 > 15 mmHg during a CPR event had an 86% chance
of ROSC, while patients who did not sustain a PET
CO2 > 15 mmHg
had a 94% chance of non-survival [56].
Cardiac output measurement
As mentioned above, PET
CO2 is directly related to cardiac output
due to the fact that the cardiovascular system is circular, and there-
fore, almost the entire cardiac output passes through the lungs. This
means the PET
CO2 sampled at the end of the endotracheal tube is
correlated with cardiac output if metabolism and ventilation are
held constant. Due to this correlation, PET
CO2 can be used to effec-
tively measure trends in cardiac output, if not the exact value. It can
be argued that clinically, knowing trends in cardiac output as
opposed to the exact amount is more valuable, because the relative
change in cardiac output in response to intervention might change
patient outcome.
The relationship between carbon dioxide and cardiac output can
be used to non-invasively measure cardiac output via the indirect
Fick method. This is based on the Fick principle, which states that the
quantity of gas (oxygen or CO2
) delivered to or taken away from the
lungs is equal to the amount of gas absorbed by the pulmonary circu-
lation or diffused from circulation to the alveoli and respiratory bron-
chioles. While the Fick principle-derived cardiac output measurement
method relies on oxygen uptake by the patient, which can be difficult
to measure, the indirect Fick method relies on partial rebreathing of
carbon dioxide. The Non-Invasive Cardiac Output (NICO®) monitor
is a piece of equipment that creates periods of partial rebreathing to
estimate arterial and mixed venous CO2 partial pressures based on
PET
CO2 [57]. It is attached to the circuit in between the endotracheal
tube and the circle system. Unfortunately, this monitor can only be
used for patients with a tidal volume of 200 mL or more [58,59].
Cardiac output monitoring is covered in detail in Chapter 13.
Nasal catheter
The use of CO2 measurement for veterinary patients can be critical
in patients that are not intubated and where continuous blood sam-
pling is not ideal. Use of a nasal catheter for the measurement of
PET
CO2 has been investigated in dogs and foals [60–62], and dis-
plays reasonable correlation with paired CO2 values. While correla-
tion is better for those patients who are not simultaneously receiving
oxygen therapy through the catheter, correlation was acceptable in
both scenarios. More importantly, these results were clinically rele-
vant and indicate that nasal catheters might be used to measure
PET
CO2 non-invasively in patients pre- and postoperatively and in
critical care settings.
Species considerations
While mammalian respiratory anatomy and function share similarities
across species, there are variations that reflect adaptations to size, envi-
ronment, and physiological needs. Furthermore, the adaptations of
non-mammalian species warrant consideration, but do not preclude
the use of capnography in these animals. It is important to remember
that the rationale for use of non-invasive PET
CO2 monitoring in veteri-
nary medicine is the assumption that it will correlate closely with
PaCO2 and, therefore, be a good surrogate for ventilatory adequacy.
Dogs and cats
There is reasonable evidence in anesthetized dogs with a closed
chest that PET
CO2 correlates well with PaCO 2 in a variety of differ-
ent ventilation modes [63–66]. However, during thoracotomy,
PET
CO2 was found not to be a reliable indicator of PaCO2 and, thus,
adequacy of ventilation [66]. There is little published information
examining the differences in PET
CO2 and PaCO2 in cats. In one
study that included six ventilated cats, the authors found that
PET
CO2 was generally lower than PaCO 2 and was a good predictor
of hypoventilation, but direct arterial sampling for the measure-
ment of PaCO2 was still recommended [67].
Horses
Measurement of PET
CO2 in horses is primarily focused on side-
stream monitoring in anesthetized horses, but it has been shown
that there is a relatively small difference in P(a-et)CO2 in horses
that are standing and healthy [68]. In anesthetized and recumbent
horses and ponies, there can be significant changes in ventilation–
perfusion (V/Q) matching resulting in wide variation in P(a-et)
CO2
, although differences are improved when controlled ventila-
tion is instituted compared to spontaneous ventilation [69–74].
Capnometry has significant limitations in the anesthetized horse
unless it is paired with blood gas analysis.
Birds and reptiles
The significant anatomic and physiologic differences in non-
mammalian respiratory systems are discussed elsewhere (Chapters 57
and 58). Notably, in birds, gas flow is unidirectional and gas
exchange occurs through a cross-current mechanism. This adapta-
tion can result in a negative P(a-et)CO 2 gradient. In mechanically
ventilated African Gray Parrots (Psittacus erithacus), a strong
correlation was found between PET
CO2 and PaCO2
, with PET
CO2
consistently overestimating PaCO 2 by about 5 mmHg [75]. In anes-
thetized raptors, correlation between PET
CO2 and PaCO 2 was seen,
but agreement varied with high, low, and normal PET
CO2 val-
ues [76]. During air sac insufflation in chickens, PET
CO2 often
exceeded PaCO 2 , but there was not a strong correlation between the
two [77]. Finally, a study in anesthetized Amazon parrots (Amazona
ventralis) also found that PET
CO2 overestimated PaCO 2 during
spontaneous ventilation, but this difference reversed over time with
mechanical ventilation [78].
In reptiles, the adaptation of intracardiac shunting may have a sig-
nificant impact on the interpretation of capnometry. In a study of
anesthetized and ventilated green iguanas (Iguana iguana), differ-
ences in the P(a-et)CO2 gradient were relatively minimal, but as
time passed, this difference significantly increased [79].

Volumetric capnography
Volumetric capnography (VCap) plots exhaled CO2 against expired
volume, allowing for the determination of physiologic deadspace
(the sum of anatomic and alveolar deadspace), effective alveolar
tidal volume, and volume of CO2 eliminated per breath [80]
(Fig. 14.5). Volumetric capnograms have a similar waveform as
time-based capnograms, excluding the inspiratory segment. Phase I
of the volume capnogram starts at zero as the first gas exhaled is
from airway (anatomic) deadspace and is free of CO2
. The slope at
phase II rises sharply as a mixture of gas from the anatomic dead-
space and alveoli is exhaled. The slope at phase III is determined by
the distribution of ventilation and perfusion within the alveoli and
usually escalates until the end of the breath. The area under the
curve of this capnogram is the amount of carbon dioxide exhaled
within a tidal volume. The point-of-care ability to ascertain dead-
space and investigate V/Q abnormalities provides valuable informa-
tion about the effectiveness of ventilation. It can better focus
treatment of hypoxemia or impending hypoxemia, revealing
whether the problem is primarily a ventilation or a deadspace
issue [81–83]. Due to its ability to quantify pulmonary perfusion,
and therefore cardiac output, this is a useful non-invasive tool for
anesthetized patients [84]. To date, the use of Vcap in veterinary spe-
cies of interest has been mostly limited to research settings [85–87].

Introduction
The goal of physiologic monitoring during anesthesia is to ensure
an adequate oxygen supply to maintain mitochondrial aerobic
metabolism and, ultimately, cellular function. Several techniques
have been developed to monitor oxygenation for clinical and
research purposes. Currently, there is no gold standard technique
for monitoring oxygenation that combines quick response time,
suitability for in vivo assessment, ease of use, inexpensiveness, and
ability to evaluate local and regional tissue oxygenation. The avail-
able techniques provide information reflecting the status of the
whole body, making them unsuitable to detect regional and local
alterations until they are well established and may have resulted in
irreversible organ damage. On the other hand, many techniques
that specifically investigate oxygen concentrations at the cellular
level are only applicable in vitro, on prepared isolated tissues, or are
poorly applicable to the clinical setting due to cost of the equip-
ment, difficulty of use, and limited experience in veterinary patients.
This chapter describes the techniques available for real-time
monitoring of tissue oxygenation and metabolism in living animals,
with a focus on the technical aspects, clinical use, and limitations.
Hypoxia versus hypoxemia
Although the terms hypoxia and hypoxemia are often used inter-
changeably, they are not the same (Table 15.1). Hypoxia is a condi-
tion in which the supply of oxygen to tissues fails to ensure normal
cellular metabolism, whereas hypoxemia describes a state of low
arterial oxygen tension (interchangeably referred to as “oxygen par-
tial pressure”). Hypoxemia is a frequent cause of tissue hypoxia, but
it is not the only one, with other major causes being anemia, histo-
toxicity, and reduced forward blood flow. The causes of hypoxemia
are classified in various ways in the literature and include low
inspired oxygen partial pressure, hypoventilation, and venous
admixture. Venous admixture represents all the ways venous blood
can move from the right to the left side of the circulation without
being oxygenated, including low ventilation–perfusion (V/Q)
ratios, anatomic or physiologic shunt, and diffusion impairment.
Some authors will also include reduced venous oxygen content sec-
ondary to either low cardiac output or high oxygen extraction by
the tissues (e.g., seizures) [1].

Oxygen content, delivery, and consumption
The following equations are fundamental in the evaluation of
oxygen transport and utilization.
Oxygen content
Oxygen content of arterial blood (CaO2
) is the total amount of
oxygen in arterial blood and is calculated as follows:
CaO 	mL/dL 	Hb SaO 	PaO	2 	2 	2	1 34 	0 0031	. 	.
where Hb is the total hemoglobin concentration and SaO 2 is the
arterial saturation of hemoglobin with oxygen (see discussion of
functional versus fractional oxygen saturation below). The first
term of the equation represents the amount of oxygen bound to
hemoglobin, and the second term characterizes the quantity of
oxygen dissolved in plasma. The vast majority of the oxygen in
blood is carried by hemoglobin (~98%), whereas only a small
amount is dissolved (~2%).
Oxygen delivery
Oxygen delivery ( DO2
) is the amount of oxygen delivered to the
tissues each minute and is calculated as follows:
DO 	mL/minute 	CO CaO	2 	2
where CO is cardiac output in L/min. It is important to note that
adequate oxygen delivery is dependent on adequate cardiac output,
hemoglobin concentration, and PaO2 . This calculation does not
consider abnormal hemoglobin species such as methemoglobin or
carboxyhemoglobin.
Oxygen consumption
Oxygen consumption ( VO2 ) is the amount of oxygen used for met-
abolic processes per minute and is calculated via the Fick equation:

where C(a–v)O2 is the difference between systemic arterial and
mixed venous (i.e., pulmonary arterial) oxygen content. If both DO2
and VO2 are known, the oxygen extraction ratio can be calculated.
Oxygen extraction ratio
The oxygen extraction ratio (O 2

:
O ER 	VO /DO	2 	2 	2
 	 	.
Causes of increased O 2
ER include anything that increases oxygen
consumption (e.g., seizures, hyperthermia, and sepsis) or decreases
oxygen delivery (including hypoxemia and anemia). A low O 2
ER is
usually due to decreased oxygen consumption as caused by anes-
thesia, mechanical ventilation, and hypothermia. A major factor
limiting routine clinical use of O 2
ER is that it requires measurement
of mixed venous O2 via a pulmonary arterial catheter.
Visual assessment of oxygenation
Gray to blue mucous membrane discoloration (cyanosis) indicates
the presence of deoxygenated blood in the observed tissue. The
detection of cyanosis may be unreliable as a measure of tissue oxy-
genation, however, as it depends upon both the visual acuity of the
observer and the local concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin;
moreover, it may be affected by lighting conditions [2]. A minimal
concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin (5 g/dL) is required to
cause a degree of cyanosis sufficient to be detected visually [3].
Therefore, an anemic animal might be hypoxemic without showing
cyanosis because the decreased hemoglobin concentration would
be saturated with oxygen even in the presence of considerably
reduced partial pressures of oxygen in the blood. Drug-induced
peripheral vasoconstriction (e.g., as caused by α2
- adrenergic recep-
tor agonists) can cause peripheral cyanosis. When peripheral blood
flow slows down due to vasoconstriction, oxygen can diffuse into
the tissues over a longer time (i.e., oxygen extraction increases),
leaving more deoxygenated hemoglobin in the capillary bed [4].
Measuring oxygen partial pressure
The partial pressure of oxygen (PO2
) can be measured in a liquid
(e.g., blood), a gas (e.g., inspired gas), or at the skin using technol-
ogy based on the polarographic Clark electrode, which is composed
of a silver anode, a platinum cathode, and a gas-permeable mem-
brane through which oxygen molecules can diffuse freely. When a
polarizing voltage is applied to the cathode, a current that is propor-
tional to the partial pressure of oxygen is generated between the
anode and the cathode, where oxygen is reduced. The following
information focuses on the measurement of PO2 in arterial blood,
mixed venous blood, or diffusing through the skin. Measurement of
oxygen in inspired and expired gas will be discussed in a separate
section later in this chapter.
Arterial blood gas analysis
Analysis of arterial blood gases includes the measurement of partial
pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the arterial blood,
reported in North America in mmHg. Partial pressures are often
misinterpreted as a measure of how much oxygen and carbon diox-
ide are in the blood; however, instead, they indicate the pressure
exerted by the dissolved, unbound molecules of each gas against the
measuring electrode. The only parameter that quantifies the amount
of oxygen in the blood, expressed as mL/dL, is the CaO2
, which is
calculated from both SaO 2 and PaO 2 values as outlined above.

Chapter 15: Monitoring Oxygenation 	233
Arterial oxygen saturation of hemoglobin is a function of PaO 2
, and
their relationship is expressed by the oxygen–hemoglobin dissocia-
tion curve. Arterial blood gas analysis remains the most popular
method for advanced monitoring of oxygenation in animals, with
PaO 2
, SaO 2
, and the calculated alveolar–arterial (A-a) gradient used
clinically to assess oxygenation. The A-a gradient is the measured
arterial PO2 (PaO2 ) subtracted from the PA
O2
, calculated from the
alveolar gas equation. A normal A-a gradient is less than 20 mmHg.
As the A-a gradient widens during oxygen supplementation, the
ratio of PaO2 to fractional inspired oxygen (PaO 2
/FI
O2
), also known
as the “Horowitz index,” may be calculated instead. At sea level, the
normal PaO 2
/FI
O2 ratio is approximately 400–500; values below 400
suggest the presence of gas exchange abnormalities. The PaO2
/FI
O2
ratio is a widely used clinical indicator of pulmonary function; nev-
ertheless, its reliability is controversial. The main disadvantages of
using the PaO2 /FI
O2 ratio to guide clinical decisions are its depend-
ence on barometric pressure and its inability to distinguish alveolar
hypoventilation from other causes of hypoxemia, such as V/Q mis-
match and shunt [5,6]. Moreover, the PaO 2
/FI
O2 ratio does not
indicate CaO 2 , which depends on hemoglobin concentration, nor
does it provide information on oxygen delivery to tissues [5,6].
The biggest limitation of arterial blood gas analysis is its inability
to detect regional or local changes in tissue oxygenation. The non-
continuous nature of monitoring and the costs associated with
repeated testing also represent clinically relevant limitations. In
addition, arterial blood gas analysis requires anaerobic sampling
and either immediate analysis or special handling.
There are no unanimous guidelines with respect to the frequency
of arterial blood sampling and analysis for proper monitoring of the
oxygenation status in animals. In human patients undergoing thora-
coscopy, it takes only 5, 10, or 20 min for the arterial partial pressure
of oxygen to change by 10%, 20%, or 40% of its initial value, respec-
tively [7]. This finding may suggest that frequent sampling would be
necessary for prompt detection of severe changes in blood oxygena-
tion in animals with compromised respiratory function. Another
potential disadvantage of monitoring oxygenation through arterial
blood gas analysis is the need for placing an indwelling arterial cath-
eter to facilitate frequent blood sampling. Although this procedure is
usually performed in animals with no or minor complications,
hematoma formation, hemorrhage, vasculitis, and thrombus forma-
tion are possible sequelae. Moreover, obtaining arterial samples can
be technically challenging in very small animals, and frequent blood
sampling from small patients may result in iatrogenic anemia.
Mixed venous oxygen partial pressure
Mixed venous blood refers to blood in the pulmonary artery and is
representative of venous blood from all organs and tissues. The par-
tial pressure of oxygen in mixed venous blood (PvO2 ) reflects meta-
bolic activity and oxygen consumption. The normal PvO2 while
breathing room air is around 40 mmHg, corresponding to a satura-
tion of around 70% (see discussion of mixed venous O 2 saturation
below). The PvO2 can be used to calculate mixed venous O 2 con-
tent, VO2
, and O2
ER; however, the measurement of PvO2 requires
placement of a pulmonary arterial catheter. This procedure is rarely
performed in veterinary patients and has fallen out of favor in criti-
cally ill human patients [8].
Transcutaneous measurement of blood gases
Transcutaneous blood gas monitoring systems are commercially
available and have been used in dogs, sheep, mice, rats, and cats [9–
12]. Blood gases diffusing through the skin can be detected and
quantified by a sensor applied to the body surface. The digital sen-
sors used to measure transcutaneous gases incorporate a Clark elec-
trode for PO2 measurement and a Severinghaus-type sensor to
detect PCO 2
. There are models that incorporate pulse oximetry
instead of the Clark electrode [13]. The PCO 2 is measured from the
pH of an electrolyte solution separated from the skin by a mem-
brane that is highly permeable to CO 2
; the changes in pH of the
electrolyte solution are proportional to the logarithm of the changes
in PCO2
. The sensor must be heated to 41 °C/105.8 °F prior to use
to enhance local blood perfusion and CO 2 diffusion though the
intact skin.
The main advantage of transcutaneous monitoring is that this
technique is suitable for continuous and non-invasive monitoring
of oxygenation and ventilation. It provides real-time information
on partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide, enabling clini-
cians to detect changes in respiratory status more quickly than with
intermittent blood gas analysis. Moreover, its use avoids the draw-
backs and costs associated with frequent arterial blood sample col-
lection and analysis.
Transcutaneous blood gas monitoring is widely used in human
medicine, especially in neonatal patients, to obtain non-invasive
and continuous blood gas measurements during mechanical venti-
lation or procedures potentially resulting in impaired gas exchange,
such as bronchoscopy and bronchial lavage [14]. Other applications
include monitoring of respiratory function associated with sleep
apnea or other conditions potentially resulting in hypoxemia and
hypercapnia [15]. In the veterinary literature, however, information
pertaining to transcutaneous blood gas monitoring is limited and
seems to suggest that transcutaneous measurement of PCO2 lacks
accuracy [10–12,16–19]. In dogs, transcutaneous PCO2 overesti-
mated PaCO 2 by more than 10 mmHg; moreover, quick changes in
PaCO 2 caused by alterations of the breathing pattern were detected
by transcutaneous monitoring with a 6-min delay [12]. It was,
therefore, concluded that, while transcutaneous PCO 2 monitoring
might be useful for detecting changes or trends in PaCO2
, it was not
sufficiently accurate to be used as a valid surrogate of PaCO2 . Very
similar conclusions were drawn from a study conducted in rats,
whereas in mice a good correlation was established between trans-
cutaneous PCO2 and PaCO2 [10,11]. An experimental study con-
ducted on anesthetized dogs demonstrated that decreases in cardiac
output caused by iatrogenic hemorrhage resulted in less accurate
PCO2 readings; however, correlation with PaO2 values improved
after fluid resuscitation [16]. In critically ill dogs, the level of agree-
ment between transcutaneous and arterial readings was lower than
that reported in human patients, and the transcutaneous monitor
consistently overestimated both PaO2 and PaCO2 [19]. In a slightly
different application, some studies report the use of transcutaneous
PCO2 to evaluate skin graft viability in experimental dogs [17,18].
One study investigated the use of transcutaneous oxygen monitor-
ing in Louisiana pine snakes [20].
Measuring hemoglobin saturation
with oxygen
The percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen is measured
clinically either by CO-oximetry or pulse oximetry. It is important
to note that these methodologies report slightly different values.
A CO-oximeter can measure all forms of hemoglobin, including
the abnormal forms that cannot bind oxygen: carboxyhemoglobin
(COHb), methemoglobin (MetHb), and sulfhemoglobin (SulfHb).
Consequently, CO-oximeters report the fractional hemoglobin

Hb), that is, the percent of total hemoglobin that is
saturated by oxygen:

In most patients, FO 2

exist, the FO2
Hb is the correct parameter to use in the calculation of
CaO2 and DO2
.
Historically, the direct measurement of hemoglobin saturation
with oxygen in blood was accomplished via the volumetric or man-
ometric methods in which the volume of gas or the pressure exerted
by that gas was directly measured. Modern methodology incorpo-
rates spectrophotometers that detect the absorbance of light by the
molecules of interest. Moreover, pulse oximeters non-invasively
measure hemoglobin saturation with oxygen using spectrophotom-
etry. The following discussion will address both invasive and non-
invasive techniques for SO2 measurement.
CO-oximetry
CO- oximetry (also known as “hemoximetry”) reports total Hb,
saturation of arterial or venous Hb by oxygen, as well as concentra-
tions of abnormal hemoglobins. CO-oximeters utilize spectropho-
tometry with multiple wavelengths of light. A blood sample placed
in the machine is heated and hemolyzed. Light is fractionated and
filtered, with specific wavelengths directed through the blood sam-
ple and onto photodiode sensors. According to the Beer–Lambert
law, the absorbance of light of a specific wavelength is logarithmi-
cally related to the concentration of molecules in a solution that will
absorb that wavelength. Most modern blood gas analyzers now
have an integrated CO-oximeter such that the reported saturation is
measured (i.e., FO 2 Hb). Some older analyzers, however, do not have
this capability, and the reported saturation may be calculated based
on the measured PO 2 using an idealized oxygen–hemoglobin
dissociation curve. If the resulting estimated saturation is used in
various calculations of oxygenation (e.g., CaO 2 or DO2
), clinically
important error may be introduced.
Arterial hemoglobin saturation
Direct measurement of arterial hemoglobin saturation with oxygen
(FaO2
Hb) is achieved with CO-oximetric analysis of a properly
handled arterial blood sample. As described above, the CO-
oximetric FaO 2
Hb is the proportion of total hemoglobin that is oxy-
genated, as all species of hemoglobins are investigated.
Mixed venous hemoglobin saturation
Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2
), that is the saturation by
oxygen of hemoglobin as measured in the pulmonary artery, can be
used to assess the adequacy of systemic oxygen delivery versus
consumption. While breathing room air, SvO2 in the healthy patient
is expected to be between 65% and 80%. A low SvO2 indicates
that DO2 is not meeting metabolic oxygen demands, helping to
guide clinical decision-making in critically ill patients. Continuous
measurement of SvO2 can be achieved with a fiberoptic catheter
equipped with a CO-oximeter [21]. However, as previously men-
tioned, placement of pulmonary arterial catheters has fallen out of
routine use in human medicine and is rarely performed in veteri-
nary clinical practice. Blood obtained from the cranial vena cava
may be used as a reasonable clinical surrogate of mixed venous
blood to assess central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO 2 ) [22–24].
Jugular venous saturation (SjvO2
) is used mostly to monitor
brain oxygenation. Venous samples can be obtained through an
indwelling jugular catheter and analyzed intermittently; alterna-
tively, for continuous monitoring of SjvO 2 , the use of specific fiber-
optic jugular catheters equipped with an oximeter is required.
Measured SjvO 2 is used to assess the balance between cerebral
oxygen delivery and cerebral oxygen demand and is therefore used
as an indirect marker of the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen
(CMRO 2
). The therapeutic target for this purpose is generally to
maintain SjvO2 values greater than 50%. Increased oxygen supply or
decreased oxygen demand will increase SjvO2
, whereas decreased
supply and increased demand will have the opposite effect. Clinical
scenarios that cause decreased SjvO 2 include generalized hypox-
emia, local or systemic hypoperfusion, and increased cerebral
metabolism or oxygen extraction resulting from conditions such as
pyrexia and seizures [21,25]. In contrast, increased SjvO2 may result
from reduced cerebral metabolism, alteration in oxygen diffusion
or extraction due to neuronal infarction or inflammation, or cere-
bral hyperemia.
The arteriovenous difference in oxygen (AVDO 2 ) can be extrap-
olated from SaO 2 and SjvO2
. It is postulated that, while SjvO2 is
accepted as a measure of oxygen delivery, AVDO 2 may better repre-
sent cerebral extraction of oxygen [26]. As a measure of oxygen
extraction, low AVDO 2 may suggest the presence of neuronal
infarction, with resulting metabolic derangement and mitochon-
drial injury.
On a balance of risk and benefit, SjvO 2 monitoring is considered
a safe and valuable tool. However, it has several limitations. First, it
relies on several assumptions, including static SaO2 , hemoglobin
concentration, and hemoglobin dissociation over time. Second, it
cannot be used to detect focal brain ischemia as the gained informa-
tion rather reflects the generalized brain perfusion and oxygenation
status. Finally, although placement and maintenance of central
venous catheters is a relatively simple procedure in dogs and has
been associated with a low incidence of life-threatening seque-
lae [27], puncture of the carotid artery, hematoma formation, infec-
tion, thrombosis, and raised intracranial pressure remain possible
complications in animals as well as in humans. Pitfalls of measure-
ments may result from positional changes of the head, micro-
thrombi formation at tip of the catheter, and the necessity for
frequent calibrations whenever fiberoptic catheters are used [21].
Pulse oximetry
Pulse oximetry is based on the principle that O2
Hb and HHb hemo-
globin differentially absorb red and near-infrared light, with O 2
Hb
absorbing greater amounts of near-infrared light and lower amounts
of red light than does HHb. This is consistent with clinical observa-
tion, as well-oxygenated blood, with its higher concentration of
O 2
Hb, appears bright red to the eye because it scatters more red
light than does HHb. Traditional pulse oximeters emit two wave-
lengths of light, red light (at 660 nm), and near-infrared light (at
940 nm) from light-emitting diodes located in one arm of the
probe [28]. The light that is transmitted through the tissues is then
detected by a photodiode on the opposite arm of the probe

(transmittance). In the case of reflectance probes, the sensing diode
is placed next to the transmitting diode. The relative amount of red
and infrared light absorbed are used to determine the proportion of
hemoglobin bound to oxygen (SpO2
), based on the Beer–Lambert
law which logarithmically correlates the concentration of a sub-

length (Fig. 15.1). The signal is divided into an AC component
(representative of greater light absorption during pulsatile arterial
flow) and a DC component (the baseline light absorption by venous
blood and tissue) (Fig. 15.2). The pulse oximeter analyzes the
absorption of light by measuring the increase in light absorption
due to the increase in arterial blood volume during systole, calculat-

Pulse width correlates with the systemic vascular resistance,
whereas systolic amplitude has been related to stroke volume and
was found to be directly proportional to local vascular distensibility
over a wide range of cardiac output values. Moreover, the position
of the dicrotic notch is used as an indicator of systemic vascular
resistance [30,31]. The plethysmographic variability index is a non-
invasive dynamic indicator of fluid responsiveness based on heart–
lung interactions over the respiratory cycle that some pulse
oximeters display, and it is described in more detail in Chapter 12.
Many of its features, particularly ease of use, non-invasiveness,
and the continuous nature of monitoring, have made pulse oxime-
try very popular in veterinary practice, and it has been a standard of
basic anesthetic care in people since the 1980s. Despite its wide-
spread use, however, several studies indicate that many general
practitioners do not know the basic principles behind pulse oxime-
try technology, a knowledge that is fundamental to appreciate its
limitations and to recognize erroneous readings [32,33].
In anesthetized animals, erroneous SpO 2 readings are commonly
caused by poor peripheral perfusion, resulting from vasoactive
drugs, hypotension, and hypothermia. Dysrhythmias, arterial com-
pression caused by the sphygmomanometer cuff, and peripheral
vascular disease can also affect the quality of pulse oximetry wave
tracings [34–36]. Additionally, venous pulsations may result in
falsely low SpO2 readings because they cause venous O 2
Hb satura-
tion to be added to the signals coming from arterial blood [37].
Excessive movement becomes an issue mostly in non-anesthetized
animals that require frequent or continuous assessment of their
respiratory function. Another important limitation of pulse oxime-
try is that the PaO 2 is estimated from SpO 2 values based on the
assumption that the relationship between the two variables is
consistent with that described by the equation for the oxyhemo-
globin dissociation curve. However, this may not be the case in
anesthetized animals, in which alterations in pH, temperature, and
partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2
) are expected to shift the
curve [38]. One study performed in critically ill dogs concluded
that pulse oximetry sensitivity for the detection of hypoxemia was
poor and that SpO2 was not a clinically suitable surrogate for PaO 2
,
although the correlation between measured and predicted (based
on SpO 2
) PaO 2 values was higher in anesthetized and mechanically
ventilated dogs compared to awake dogs [39]. Another group
reported delayed detection of hypoxemia, defined as SpO 2 lower
than 90%, following endotracheal tube cuff herniation in two
dogs [40]. Finally, pulse oximetry may be a late indicator of respira-
tory impairment during oxygen supplementation, providing a false
sense of security as SpO2 as detected by pulse oximetry may remain
within normal ranges despite a declining PaO2 [41,42]. This is due
to the sigmoid shape of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve,
wherein saturation is nearly complete at PaO2 values as low as
90–100 mmHg and increasing the PaO2 above this level will no
longer affect the SpO 2
. Therefore, when SpO 2 is ≥ 97%, the PaO 2
could be anywhere between 90 and 600 mmHg [43,44].
Within the last couple of decades, more sophisticated, multi-
wavelength pulse oximeter devices have become commercially
available [45,46]. Besides providing non-invasive and continuous
readings of SpO 2 , pulse CO-oximetry allows the detection of
COHb and MetHb, as well as evaluation of derived variables,
including hemoglobin concentration, perfusion index, plethys-
mogram variability index, oxygen reserve index (ORI), non-
invasive FO 2 Hb, and CaO 2 [47]. One study conducted in dogs
compared values of SpO 2 , CaO 2 , and hemoglobin concentration
obtained from a pulse CO-oximeter with those measured
invasively using a spectrophotometric-based blood gas analyzer
and found that calibration of the device using a measured
hemoglobin concentration was necessary to improve the accu-
racy and precision of pulse CO-oximetry when used to monitor
hemoglobin [48]. In anesthetized pregnant sheep, Masimo pulse
CO-oximetry was a useful and reliable tool for monitoring
SpO 2 during phases of clinically significant cardiovascular and
respiratory dysfunction [49]. The ORI is useful to assess the
oxygenation status during oxygen supplementation and states of
moderate hyperoxia (PaO 2 of approximately 100–200 mmHg),
which represents a significant limitation for traditional pulse
oximetry. 	As 	mentioned 	previously, 	supplemental 	oxygen
administration increases the PaO 2 to values ranging from 100
to 600 mmHg, while SpO 2 reaches a maximum of 100% at a PaO 2
around 100 mmHg. Simultaneously, the venous oxygen saturation
(SvO 2 ) will progressively increase until the PaO 2 reaches about
200 mmHg, and it will stabilize at about 80%. The simultaneous
evaluation of changes in PaO 2 , SpO 2 , and SvO 2 over time is the
basis for the ORI calculation, which results in a number ranging
between 0 and 1 [44]. Decreases in ORI to near 0.24 may provide
advanced indication of declining PaO 2 when SpO 2 is still
> 98% [50].
Inspired and expired oxygen concentrations
Measurement of inspired oxygen concentrations in the anesthetic
circuit, accompanied by a low concentration alarm, is required
standard monitoring in human anesthesia care as it allows the
detection of delivery of hypoxic gas mixtures. It is less commonly
performed in veterinary anesthesia, however, due to associated
expense and lack of training. Inspired and expired oxygen concen-
trations can be measured with paramagnetic, polarographic, and
electrochemical oxygen analysis [51,52]. Infrared analysis cannot
be used because oxygen is a nonpolar molecule. Most current oxy-
gen analyzers employ paramagnetic analysis, which relies on the
fact that unpaired electrons in the outer shell of an oxygen atom
cause it to be attracted to the strongest part of an inhomogeneous
magnetic field, whereas all other common respiratory gases move
to the weakest part of it. Sampling and reference chambers sepa-
rated by a pressure transducer are subjected to a switched electro-
magnetic field, and the resulting pressure difference is converted to
a voltage that is directly proportional to the concentration of oxy-
gen in the sample gas. Most of the commercially available paramag-
netic analyzers are accurate and not affected by anesthetic gases,
although the response time is limited by the maximal gas flow rate
through the measuring cell [53].
Polarographic oxygen analysis, as described earlier in this chap-
ter, is based on a modified, battery-powered Clark-type elec-
trode [51]. Traditional electrochemical oxygen analyzers are based
on the galvanic cell. Briefly, the oxygen sensor is composed of a
membrane, a cathode, and an anode surrounded by an electrolyte
solution. Oxygen diffuses through both the anode and membrane
and reaches the cathode, where it is reduced, generating a current
that is proportional to its partial pressure. While traditional electro-
chemical analyzers respond slowly to changes in oxygen and, there-
fore, are not suitable for measuring end-tidal oxygen concentrations,
novel electrochemical imaging systems with integrated microelec-
trode arrays seem to offer an attractive means of measuring oxygen
consumption rate in real time [52].
Measuring inspired and end-tidal oxygen concentrations may be
used to estimate the level of oxygenation in the body and the

-- 252 of 1450 --

Chapter 15: Monitoring Oxygenation 	237
effectiveness of ventilation. While a 4–5% difference between
inspired and expired oxygen concentrations is considered normal,
one study conducted in pigs found that a difference greater than 5%
after having reached a steady state is a sensitive indicator of
hypoventilation [54]. In this study, the decrease in oxygen end-tidal
concentrations was promptly followed by a decrease in PaO 2
,
whereas changes in SpO 2 were not detectable until ventilation was
decreased to 37% of the initial value. Moreover, studies conducted
in humans determined that the difference between inspired and
expired volumes of oxygen can be used as an estimate of the patient’s
oxygen consumption [55,56]. Low end-tidal oxygen levels are use-
ful indicators of hypoventilation and low inspired oxygen concen-
trations can alert the anesthetist to inadequate fresh gas flow
delivery and oxygen supply malfunctions [57].
Near- infrared and Raman spectroscopy
Near-infrared and Raman spectroscopy are used in human medi-
cine for non-invasive continuous monitoring of regional tissue
perfusion and oxygenation, and several studies demonstrate ben-
efit in monitoring cerebral, intestinal, and renal perfusion to
detect tissue ischemia and hypoxia [58,59]. These technologies
share with pulse oximetry its basic principles, as both techniques
are based on the differential light absorption of oxygenated and
deoxygenated hemoglobin [60,61]. However, while pulse oxime-
try can only provide readings of the percentage of oxyhemo-
globin in pulsatile blood, spectroscopy is capable of measuring
oxyhemoglobin in non-pulsatile environments, such as the
peripheral microcirculatory system. The “optical window” of
near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) includes wavelengths of 650–
950 nm. Light below 650 nm is too strongly absorbed by hemo-
globin, whereas light above 950 nm is mostly absorbed by water.
On the contrary, light in the near-infrared optical window can
propagate relatively deeply, usually a few centimeters, into bio-
logical tissue, as absorption from water, hemoglobin, collagen,
and proteins is negligible at these wavelengths. Instruments spe-
cifically developed for brain functional analysis use two (usually
780 and 830 nm) or more wavelengths [59,61–63]. Raman spec-
troscopy relies on the detection of a shift in frequency of light
inelastically scattered following the excitation of a molecule of
interest [64]. The fundamental differences between NIRS and
Raman techniques lie in the nature of the molecular transitions
taking place (change in molecular polarizability for Raman and
dipole moment change for NIRS), in the type of monochromatic
light used (within the near-infrared range for Raman and within
the infrared range for NIRS), and in the strength of absorbance
and transmittance (weaker for Raman compared to NIRS) [65].
Investigation into Raman spectroscopy for monitoring tissue
oxygenation is mostly preclinical in nature, and no literature sur-
rounding their use in veterinary patients exists.
Practical use of NIRS devices requires the user to switch on the
light source, direct the emitted light into the tissue to be analyzed,
and then measure the reflectance re-emerging from that tissue, a
few centimeters distant from the light source. Engineering sophisti-
cation has led to the development of miniaturized spectrometers,
making notable impact on the applicability of NIRS to the human
clinical setting. There are a wide variety of commercially available
devices in the market, with system complexity ranging from few
sources and detectors, suitable to imaging small areas, to systems
covering wider regions of the body. The sources and detectors can
be placed directly onto the skin (Fig. 15.3) or, alternatively, the light
can be guided to the target tissues through a system composed of
optical fibers and receiving probes, to be applied to the area of inter-
est. To reduce the running costs, most devices employ reusable sen-
sors that can be disinfected.
Variables measured by NIRS include local or regional hemo-
globin oxygen saturation and the oxygenation/deoxygenation
hemoglobin ratio, but also the oxygenated/deoxygenated myoglo-
bin ratio in skeletal muscle [63]. Spectroscopy has been used to
study a range of diverse conditions, including epilepsy, metabolic
myopathy, and diabetes mellitus [63,66,67]. The most common
clinical and experimental application of NIRS in humans remains
the analysis of brain function and cerebral blood flow. Local cere-
bral blood flow typically increases as a result of enhanced neural
activity; because blood flow increases more than cerebral oxygen
extraction, during phases of increased cerebral metabolism, there
is a localized rise in oxygen levels and, therefore, in oxygenated
hemoglobin. Consequently, the ratio of oxygenated/deoxygenated
hemoglobin is used to estimate neural activity [68].
The first report on the use of spectroscopy to assess oxygenation
was conducted in cats [60]. Several more recent studies investi-
gated the use of NIRS in both clinical and experimental dogs [69–
75]. One study found that, in Chihuahuas, changes in cerebral
oxygenation levels were associated with the administration of
anesthetics [75]. Another investigation reported the use of near-
infrared technology to monitor myocardial oxygenation during
ischemic preconditioning [69], while other investigators used
spectroscopy for monitoring of skin, subcutaneous tissue, and
skeletal muscle oxygenation status [71,74]. In a study of dogs
presented for acute hemorrhage, NIRS was able to differentiate
those in a clinically determined state of shock from those without
shock [76]; moreover, lower tissue oxygen saturation as deter-
mined by NIRS was associated with more severe shock in a
different population of dogs [77].
