In dogs, morphine is commonly administered during the periop-
erative period and can provide analgesia for thoracotomy [398],
tumor removal [399], orthopedic [400], mastectomy [401], neuter-
ing [402], or laparotomy [187] procedures. Morphine analgesia has
been reported in dogs with a variety of routes of administration (e.g.,
parenteral, epidural, intrathecal, intra-articular), as well as nontradi-
tional techniques such as nebulization, topical application, and injec-
tion into acupoints (pharmacopuncture) [15,144,381,403–405].
However, the analgesic efficacy of morphine administered by nebuli-
zation or topical ocular application, as well as the extradural route via
gel-foam remains questionable [381,406,407]. The effective dose
(ED50
) of IV morphine in dogs is 0.71 mg/kg with an onset and dura-
tion of analgesia of 10 min and 2–4 h, respectively [396,397,408].
When administering morphine as a CRI in dogs, doses of 0.15 ±
0.02 mg/kg/h were required to maintain significant antinociception
as assessed by von Frey thresholds [397]. Interestingly, it has been
reported that the use of 0.5 mg/kg IV boluses may provide more con-
sistent and effective analgesic plasma concentrations of morphine
when compared to a CRI [397]. Epidurally or intrathecally adminis-
tered morphine has provided long-lasting analgesia for up to 24 h
following administration in dogs undergoing laparotomy, thoracot-
omy, and orthopedic procedures with minimal adverse effects.
Intravenous morphine provides moderate to marked dose-
dependent sedation with an onset of 2–5 min, a peak effect at
15–30 min, and a duration of up to 2 h at higher doses (e.g., 1.0 mg/kg)
[161,203]. The onset of action for sedation with IM morphine
administration can take as long as 30 min [161]. Behavioral adverse
effects are also dose-dependent and include dysphoria and vocaliza-
tion following IV administration in dogs [203,235,313]. Dysphoria
may occur less commonly in dogs administered morphine when
compared to other opioids such as methadone [203,235].
Morphine reduces HR in dogs by 26% for up to 2 h following IV
administration, with minimal negative changes in CI [203]. Dogs
may experience a transient (< 10-min duration) elevation in mean
arterial pressure 5 min following IV administration [203]. Morphine
has very little effect on arterial pH, PaCO2
, and PaO2 values [203].
Increases in minute ventilation via increased respiratory rate (e.g.,
panting) without effects on tidal volume are often observed follow-
ing administration [203].
Morphine has been reported to cause systemic histamine release
in dogs following IV administration [235]. Maximum plasma hista-
mine concentrations reached 440 ng/mL and 589 ng/mL following
0.5 and 1.0 mg/kg of morphine, respectively [235]. Flushing of the
skin is most notable at the higher dose within 1 min following
administration. Cardiovascular parameters are minimally affected
following these doses of morphine despite the release of histamine.
In a previous study, hypotension was noted in one of five dogs at 2
and 5 min following 1.0 mg/kg morphine corresponding to hista-
mine concentrations of 589 and 351 ng/mL, respectively [235].
Clinically used infusion doses result in insignificant cardiovascular
effects associated with morphine-induced histamine release [235].
Following IM morphine administration, nausea and emesis
have been reported in 30–80% and 50–75% of dogs, respectively
[234,244,245,409]. The emetic effect of morphine generally occurs
within 10 min following IM administration and time to cessation
is approximately 1–3 min [234,244]. Salivation and defection are
also commonly observed shortly after administration. Urinary
retention, pruritis, myoclonus, and rarely priapism, have been
noted following epidural or intrathecal morphine administration in
dogs [284,285,410]. Priapism is self-resolving within 7–8 h follow-
ing intrathecal morphine, but supportive interventions such as
lubrication and massage are advised to minimize trauma to the

penis. Urinary retention generally resolves within 24 h but has been
reported to persist for 7 days following epidural morphine admin-
istration [283,286]. Manual expression of the urinary bladder is rec-
ommended if this happens. These side effects are more commonly
observed with intrathecal administration and/or when using mor-
phine with preservatives [284,286].
Cats
Morphine is effective in treating moderate to severe pain in cats and
should be administered every 4–6 h at doses of 0.2–0.4 mg/kg
[137,182,379,411]. Early studies using extremely high doses
(> 5–10 mg/kg) resulted in neuroexcitatory behaviors consisting of
excitement, motor agitation, and aggression (i.e., “feline mania” or
“morphine mania”). At the time, these observations led to the erro-
neous conclusion that cats were poor subjects for future opioid
investigations [184–186]. At clinically relevant doses (0.2 mg/kg),
however, cats generally do not show signs of dysphoria, but rather
euphoria (e.g., purring, kneading, rolling, and or affectionate
behavior) or mild sedation, which can last up to 3 h following IM
administration [182,412].
Similar to dogs, the half-life and apparent volume of distribution
of morphine is 76.3 min and 2.6 L/kg, respectively, following a
0.2 mg/kg IV bolus in cats [68]. However, clearance is about half
that of dogs at 24.1 mL/kg/min. Cats lack the enzyme UDP-
glucuronosyltransferase 2B7 (UGT 2B7), which is responsible for
the glucuronidation of morphine in humans [413]. This enzyme
deficiency may contribute to the lack of metabolites produced fol-
lowing morphine biotransformation in cats [68]. To compensate for
slow glucuronidation, morphine undergoes extensive sulfation in
cats [115,413]. Like dogs, no detectable concentrations of morphine-
3- glucuronide were noted following morphine administration in
cats, and in one study, the metabolite morphine-6- glucuronide was
detected in only 3 of 11 cats [68].
Horses
Morphine provides excellent analgesia in horses, but its use remains
controversial due to the potential for gastrointestinal ileus, excite-
ment, and increased locomotor activity [194,414,415]. The dra-
matic adverse effects published in earlier studies utilized morphine
doses of 0.5–1.0 mg/kg and even up to 2.4 mg/kg [193,416]. For
example, morphine sulfate at 0.5 mg/kg IV can produce muscle
fasciculations, pawing, and pacing for 2–4 h post-administration
[417,418]. In contrast, lower doses of morphine (0.05–0.1 mg/kg)
may not induce any excitatory effects or only minimal, transient
(< 5 min) pawing, head shaking, and circling [310,418]. Furthermore,
in a clinical setting, preoperative doses of 0.1–0.2 mg/kg have not
been shown to increase the incidence of postoperative gastrointes-
tinal complications or produce excitement during the anesthetic
recovery period [419–421]. The epidural route in particular (either
lumbosacral or cervical) is associated with a very low risk of excita-
tion when similar doses are administered [228,422,423].
Morphine administered at doses of 0.5 mg/kg and greater can
result in reduced cecocolic motility that may be prolonged, lasting
for up to 360 min [416,417,424]. A single lower dose of morphine at
0.05 mg/kg IV did not induce alterations in gut motility. Abdominal
auscultation scores and the number of borborygmus events were
reported to be decreased for up to 60 min following 0.05 and
0.1 mg/kg IM and 0.1 mg/kg IV [310]. Borborygmus frequency was
also reduced at 120 min following the 0.1 mg/kg IV dose [310].
Mean weight of feces collected was not different for 48 h following
administration of IM and IV doses of 0.05 and 0.1 mg/kg, and
horses did not show evidence of colic [310]. Repeated morphine
doses every 4 h of 0.1 mg/kg or higher can produce signs associated
with colic in horses [417]. Despite the apparent dose-dependent
effects on gastrointestinal motility reported when comparing low
and high doses of morphine in horses, analgesia was not detected
via thermal and electrical threshold testing [310,425]. Epidurally
administered morphine at 0.1 mg/kg can provide long-lasting anal-
gesia with minimal gastrointestinal or behavioral effects when com-
pared to systemically administered morphine [105,229]; however,
higher epidural doses may impact gastrointestinal motility [228].
A minimum of 0.1–0.2 mg/kg of IV morphine can provide anal-
gesia in horses, with the higher dose producing a more consistent
effect [423,426]. At these doses, antinociception can be provided
from 120–240 min [423,426]. Horses produce both morphine-3-
glucuronide and morphine-6- glucuronide following morphine
administration, and these metabolites may contribute to sedation
and thermal antinociceptive effects in this species [81,418].
Administration of these metabolites, rather than the parent com-
pound, could prove beneficial during the perioperative period.
In one study, morphine administered as an IV bolus of 0.15 mg/
kg follow by a CRI at 0.1 mg/kg/h provided analgesia in horses with
carpal synovitis; however, increased HR, respiratory rate, and
systolic blood pressure as well as decreased gut sounds were
observed [427]. Another study using a similar dosing regimen did
not significantly alter cardiopulmonary variables [428]. Infusion
rates of 0.1–0.3 mg/kg/h can be used intraoperatively for pain man-
agement in horses undergoing general anesthesia and surgery with
minimal negative consequences on recovery quality [429]. Similarly,
two systematic reviews published in 2022 reported that morphine
administration at clinically relevant doses has minimal effect on
recovery in horses and in some instances can improve recovery
quality [430,431]. Morphine (120 mg) administered intra-
articularly also provides significant pain relief in horses with syno-
vitis with few adverse effects [432]. Oral morphine has been recently
studied in horses and is associated with fewer adverse behavioral
effects. At doses of 0.2–0.8 mg/kg PO, it has a bioavailability of
approximately 30% [433]. Additional studies are required to deter-
mine the analgesic benefit of orally administered morphine in this
species. In donkeys, morphine at 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg IV produced
dose-dependent mechanical antinociceptive effects for 60 and
300 min, respectively, with minimal adverse effects [434].
Food and fiber animals
Opioids are not commonly utilized for pain management in
farm animal species due to withdrawal times (i.e., the need to
ensure no drugs are present in meat and milk) and the need for
controlled substance record keeping [435]. Morphine provides
dose-dependent thermal antinociception in cattle at doses as low as
0.15 mg/kg, increasing the thermal threshold by 10 °C. Increased
locomotor activity is generally not observed in cattle at IV doses of
0.5 or 1.0 mg/kg [436]. Epidural morphine at 0.1 mg/kg can be a
cost-effective technique to provide adequate analgesia in cows
and pigs undergoing surgical procedures or experiencing acute
pain [437–439].
Morphine administration has been recently evaluated in goats.
When comparing morphine plasma concentrations to those associ-
ated with effective analgesia in humans (> 16 ng/mL) [440], mor-
phine administered at 0.25 mg/kg IV to goats would be expected
to provide a brief period of analgesia lasting approximately
30 min [95]. A higher dose of 0.4 mg/kg IV appears to provide little

-- 392 of 1450 --

Chapter 23: Opioids 	377
additional benefit. IM dosing at 0.25 and 0.4 mg/kg may provide
analgesia for 1–3 and 3–4 h, respectively [95]. SC administration
provided a similar duration of analgesia compared to IM doses of
0.25 mg/kg and 0.4 mg/kg, with durations of approximately 1–2 and
2–3 h, respectively [95].
In llamas, morphine had minimal cardiovascular effects and
induced dose-dependent decreases in respiratory rate and increases
in sedation and body temperature when administered at 0.05, 0.25,
and 0.5 mg/kg IV [441]. Following administration of morphine at
0.5 mg/kg IM, bioavailability was 120% with a significantly longer
mean terminal half-life (342 min) in llamas compared to both dogs
(81 min) and cats (93 min) [441]. The metabolite morphine-6-
glucuronide was infrequently detected and remained at concentra-
tions < 40 ng/mL following 0.5 mg/kg IM and IV [441]. Morphine
at 0.5 mg/kg IV may produce muscle tremors, hyperexcitability, and
sedation lasting up to 1 h following administration in llamas [441].
Morphine can be dosed at 0.25 mg/kg IV every 4 h to produce
analgesia in llamas [441].
Hydromorphone
Dogs and cats
Hydromorphone is a full μ-opioid receptor agonist that provides
similar dose-dependent magnitude and duration of analgesia and
sedation, with reduced histamine levels, compared to IV mor-
phine [235,442,443]. It is 5–10 times more potent than morphine
on a milligram basis with similar cardiopulmonary adverse effects.
The duration of analgesia provided by IV hydromorphone at
0.1–0.2 mg/kg is at least 2 h with the potential to last up to 4 h in
dogs and 4–8 h in cats [236,443]. Lower IV doses of 0.05 mg/kg
hydromorphone provided a significantly shorter duration of anal-
gesia (up to 80 min) in cats [442]. Following 0.1 mg/kg IM admin-
istration in cats, analgesia onset occurred in 15 min and duration
of action was 345 min [183]. SC administration in cats resulted in
a much slower onset to peak analgesic effect of (105 min) with a
duration of action of 210 min [98]. The duration and magnitude
of analgesia was less when hydromorphone was administered to
cats 6 months of age compared to adult cats; therefore, it should
be dosed more frequently in younger animals [237]. Liposomal
encapsulated hydromorphone administered SC also provided
long-lasting analgesia for up to 24 h in dogs undergoing limb
amputation [444]. Repeated administration of hydromorphone
within a 4-h period can result in excitation or prolonged anesthetic
recovery [236]. Duration of sedation is up to 3 h following 0.2 mg/
kg SC administration [213], but may be unreliable at lower doses
in clinically healthy dogs [445]. When evaluating its analgesic
efficacy as a CRI, 0.03 mg/kg/h can provide pain relief similar to
fentanyl [446]. Hydromorphone has also been administered
epidurally in cats, but its duration of analgesia is significantly
shorter than that provided by epidural morphine (i.e., 5 h versus
24 h) [447].
Horses
In horses, hydromorphone administered at 0.02–0.08 mg/kg IV
provides analgesia for up to 12 h [311]. Increases in respiratory
rate, HR, and body temperature were also observed [311].
Hydromorphone 0.04 mg/kg IM was shown to have high bioavail-
ability in horses (217%) and can provide similar duration and
magnitude of analgesia when compared to IV administration [80].
Hydromorphone increased arterial pressure and decreased borbo-
rygmi without altering fecal output when administered at 0.025 and
0.05 mg/kg IV [448]. Reductions in borborygmi may persist for
90–120 min at these doses and routes [448]. Horses may experience
excitement (e.g., pacing, vocalizing, rearing, and kicking) for 1–2 h
following administration [80]. Hydromorphone administration
was not shown to increase the incidence of postanesthetic signs of
colic in horses [449]. Hydromorphone at 0.04 mg/kg IV may pro-
vide better analgesia in horses undergoing elective arthroscopy
compared to butorphanol at 0.02 mg/kg IV [450].
Methadone
Dogs and cats
Methadone, a phenylheptylamine (Table 23.6), is a full μ-opioid
receptor agonist that also has effects at monoamine and NMDA
receptors. It is commonly used in the perioperative period in
dogs and cats. It can be administered via a variety of routes; how-
ever, more variability in plasma concentrations was noted with
the standard formulation when administered SC. Methadone
produces more potent dose-dependent cardiovascular depressant
effects on HR when compared to that of morphine (reductions of
32–46% with methadone versus 15–26% with morphine) [203].
Methadone may hinder the feasibility of gastroduodenoscopy
when compared to butorphanol [203] and potentially should be
avoided in non-painful patients undergoing these procedures.
Vomiting is generally rare following methadone administration;
however, it can still occur.
Methadone alone provides mild sedation in dogs, but they may
occasionally whine [314]. When administered with acepromazine,
it can provide dose-dependent sedation of greater magnitude than
morphine–acepromazine or butorphanol–acepromazine [162,451].
Oral transmucosal methadone at 0.4 mg/kg in dogs can also pro-
vide sedative effects; however, sedation is less than that observed
following IM administration of a similar dose [241].
Methadone possesses both opioid and monoamine effects
(mediated by the levo- or R(–)-enantiomer) as well as NMDA
antagonistic effects (mediated by the dextro- or S(+)-enantiomer)
[452–454]. The latter could be beneficial in patients with chronic
pain, hyperalgesia, and central sensitization [455]. In cats, metha-
done at 0.3 mg/kg IV and 0.6 mg/kg OTM produced antinocic-
eption for greater than 2 and 4 h, respectively [456]. IM methadone
also provided a 4-h duration of antinociception [457]. Methadone
can be administered as a CRI at 0.1 mg/kg/h in dogs and provided
analgesia up to 2 h following its discontinuation [458]. Methadone
also provides superior analgesia when compared to buprenor-
phine for dogs undergoing orthopedic and ovariohysterectomy
procedures [149,459]. Similar findings were reported in cats
undergoing neutering procedures [150]. Chloramphenicol and
fluconazole act as enzyme inhibitors of CYP2B11 in dogs and can
alter the pharmacokinetics of opioids [460]. The combination
of methadone–fluconazole administered SC twice within a 6-h
period was shown to provide safe and effective postoperative
analgesia for up to 12–24 h following the second dose in dogs
with minimal adverse effects [461]. In Greyhounds, the dose
to maintain analgesic plasma concentrations of 40 ng/mL is
1.5–2 times higher than that observed in Beagle dogs [454].
Therefore, a dose of 1–1.5 mg/kg is recommended every 3–4 h in
this breed [454].
Horses and ruminants
Methadone provides some sedation in horses, but less than that
associated with butorphanol [462]. When administered as a sole

-- 393 of 1450 --

378 	Section 3: Pharmacology
agent to horses, dysphoria, euphoria, and spontaneous locomotor
activity can be observed for up to 2 h post-administration [463].
This is particularly evident at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg [464]. When
combined with detomidine, sedation and analgesia is enhanced,
but there is a marked increase in ataxia [465]. The combination of
methadone with detomidine may be a more suitable premedication
to maintain cardiovascular stability (e.g., less depressant effects on
blood pressure) than the combination of methadone and aceprom-
azine [466]. Methadone also produces more pronounced antinocic-
eptive effects when combined with detomidine than when combined
with acepromazine [467]. Increases in blood pressure and respiratory
rate and decreases in gut sounds are noted following methadone
administration [427]. Methadone has little effect on arterial blood
gas values in horses [463].
Methadone may be an effective analgesic addition when admin-
istered via parenteral or epidural routes to horses for standing
procedures or for surgical procedures requiring general anesthe-
sia [468,469]. Methadone was effective in providing analgesia for
lipopolysaccharide-induced carpal synovitis when administered as
a 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus followed by a CRI of 0.25 mg/kg/h [427].
Lower infusion rates (0.05 mg/kg/h) have also been used in
combination with detomidine for standing procedures [470].
Inconsistent antinociceptive effects have been reported with
doses of 0.2 mg/kg IV, with more reliable antinociception at
0.5 mg/kg [464]; however, negative behavioral side effects may
be observed. Oral administration of the injectable and lipid
nanocarrier formulations of methadone does not provide antino-
ciception in horses [471]. Epidurally administered methadone
(0.1 mg/kg) provides effective analgesia for up to 5 h with no
appreciable side effects [468]. As with any analgesic intervention,
horses should be monitored closely to ensure adequate pain relief
when administering methadone.
Methadone at 0.3 mg/kg IV provides effective analgesia in small
ruminant species and reduces autonomic responses associated with
noxious stimuli [472]. Methadone can also be administered epidur-
ally to sheep and cows for pain management [473,474]. Additional
research pertaining to the use of methadone in ruminants would
provide a better understanding of the drug’s pharmacodynamic
effects in these species.
Oxymorphone
Oxymorphone is approximately 10 times more potent than mor-
phine and acts primarily at the μ-opioid receptor. Oxymorphone
is metabolized mainly via conjugation, with small amounts
excreted as intact drug or other metabolites in dogs. Its adverse
effects are similar to those of other opioids (e.g., whining, panting,
sedation, dysphoria, and bradycardia) and, though vomiting is
rarely observed with IV administration, it can occur following SC
administration [371]. Oxymorphone provides 90 min of antinoci-
ception following 0.2 mg/kg IM in dogs [475] and up to 5–6 h of
clinical analgesia in dogs and cats following 0.05 mg/kg IV [476].
Like other full μ-opioid receptor agonists, oxymorphone provides
more effective postoperative analgesia compared to butorphanol
in dogs [477]. Oxymorphone did not demonstrate antinociceptive
effects in cats when administered via the OTM route at 0.1 or
0.25 mg/kg due to its low bioavailability, which is approximately
half that of OTM methadone (19% versus 44%) [238,478].
Pharmacokinetic data suggest a dose of 0.03 mg/kg followed by
0.02 mg/kg every 2 h would maintain therapeutic analgesic con-
centrations in cats. However, this will create high- but short-lived
peak concentrations, which could predispose cats to transient
adverse behavioral effects [479]. An alternative would be to
administer a 0.005 mg/kg bolus followed by a CRI of 0.005 mg/kg/h
[479]. Pharmacokinetic data in dogs recommend dosing at
0.1 mg/kg every 2–4 h or 0.006–0.012 mg/kg/h as a CRI [371].
Due to the associated costs, few reports exist regarding the use of
oxymorphone in large animal species.
Fentanyl
Dogs and cats
Fentanyl is a highly protein-bound, lipophilic phenylpiperidine
derivative (Table 23.6) with a rapid onset, short duration of action,
and a potency 75–100 times greater than morphine. It is often
administered as CRI due to its short duration of action which is
attributed to its rapid redistribution from the central to the periph-
eral compartment following injection [61]. In humans, the context-
sensitive half-time for fentanyl increases substantially following 3 h
of administration which may contribute to cumulative effects [480].
This effect has not been reported in dogs following a 4-h infusion
which makes fentanyl CRIs clinically useful for prolonged pain
management in this species [61,351,481,482]. In dogs, fentanyl is
rapidly absorbed following SC administration, and pharmacokinet-
ics are comparable to the IV route of administration [483,484].
Significant pain occurs following subcutaneous injection, and the
addition of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate to fentanyl (1:20 ratio) prior
to injection abolishes discomfort [483]. Fentanyl does not induce
vomiting in dogs [485] and may be associated with fewer adverse
effects compared to morphine [486].
Fentanyl can produce sedation and recumbency in dogs and
increased locomotor activity and euphoria in cats [487]. The latter
effects are more commonly observed at doses > 20 μg/kg IV [487].
It was reported that 25% of healthy dogs undergoing orthopedic
procedures administered a fentanyl CRI developed dysphoria fol-
lowing extubation [188]. The administration of a low bolus dose
(0.5 μg/kg) of dexmedetomidine given slowly IV may improve
recovery quality in dogs administered prolonged fentanyl CRIs
(e.g., > 2 h) [189]. Fentanyl has been reported to cause “woody chest
syndrome” in humans which results in reduced chest wall compli-
ance and impaired ventilation [488]; however, similar findings have
not been reported in dogs [489]. At high doses > 20 μg/kg IV, fenta-
nyl can cause hypoventilation and cyanosis. Severe bradycardia and
asystole have been reported following a 3 μg/kg IV bolus of fentanyl
in two dogs [490].
Fentanyl provides adequate analgesia for acute pain management
in dogs and cats [276,446,491,492]. In cats, a fentanyl CRI at 5 μg/kg/h
produced significant thermal and mechanical antinociception
that was short-lived following cessation of the infusion [493,494].
A lower infusion rate of 3 μg/kg/h, however, did not significantly
increase thermal thresholds in cats [494].
Fentanyl can be administered via transdermal patch to provide
postoperative pain relief for up to 72–96 h. In dogs, the recom-
mended dose is approximately 4 μg/kg/h, and in cats greater than
2 kg, application of one 25-μg/h patch is recommended. Marked
individual variability in drug absorption has been reported in both
dogs and cats using reservoir (gel pouch) patches; however, higher
bioavailability and less variability is observed in dogs compared to
cats [71,495] (Fig. 23.6). Adverse effects are the same as those
observed following parenteral administration. The thickness of the
epidermis may delay the onset of action without disrupting peak
plasma concentrations [496]. Body temperature also influences
serum fentanyl concentration in cats [497]. In general, the onset of
analgesia following application in dogs and cats is approximately

-- 394 of 1450 --

Chapter 23: Opioids 	379
24 and 7–12 h, respectively [498]. When transdermal fentanyl
patches remain in contact with the skin, they can provide analgesia
for up to 72 h; however, there is the potential for plasma fentanyl
concentrations to fall below analgesic levels in cats by 72 h (Fig. 23.6B).
Transdermal patches are generally safe, but accidental ingestion and
exposure resulting in serious adverse effects have been reported in
dogs, pigs, and children [499,500]. Treatment requires naloxone or
naltrexone [500]; however, clinicians must be aware of the potential
for renarcotization following administration of an antagonist. To
minimize adverse effects and illegal use, the original formulation of
a particular transdermal patch (Duragesic®) was modified, and the
gel pouch containing a reservoir of liquid drug was replaced by a
“drug-in- adhesive matrix” designed to minimize fentanyl leakage
and potential for abuse (Duragesic® package insert 2014) [379].
After use, the FDA recommends promptly disposing of patches by
folding them in half with the sticky sides together and then flushing
them down a toilet [501]. The FDA recommends this method of
disposal because a patch could be harmful and possibly fatal in a
single dose if used by someone other than the individual for whom
it is intended. It is recommended that patches not be placed in
household trash cans where children or pets can have access. When
prescribing transdermal fentanyl patches, veterinarians should be
aware of potential complications, absorption variability, liability
issues in the event of accidental human exposure through ingestion
or contact, considerations for extra-label use during acute or inter-
mittent postoperative pain, and potential adverse effects associated
with their use [379].
Horses and food animals
Fentanyl at clinically relevant doses may not provide analgesia in
horses and results in dose-dependent adverse behavioral effects
(e.g., head and eye movement, fine muscle fasciculations, and shift-
ing of forelimbs) [502]. A minimum dose of 10 μg/kg IV provided
thermal antinociception in horses between 10 and 30 min [503].
This equates to minimum fentanyl plasma concentrations of 6.1–
6.8 ng/mL, which is approximately six times what is required in
dogs and cats [23,504]. Intravenous fentanyl is well tolerated in
foals 1–6 weeks of age. Increased locomotor activity was observed
in foals at doses of 8 and 16 μg/kg, while mild and heavy sedation
was observed at 4 and 32 μg/kg, respectively [505]. Plasma concen-
trations associated with analgesia were comparable to those
reported for adult horses; thus, the clinical utility of IV fentanyl in
horses remains somewhat unclear at this time [505]. In sevoflurane-
anesthetized piglets, intravenous fentanyl at 10 μg/kg produces
transient and spontaneously resolving muscle tremors [506]. This
could pose significant issues in specific research surgical settings. In
isoflurane-anesthetized adult pigs, infusions of 5, 10, and 20 μg/kg/h
also produced “shivering” [507].
Transdermal fentanyl patches have been used in horses for long-
term analgesic therapy [508]. The onset of action is rapid with peak
plasma fentanyl concentrations occurring 8–15 h post-application.
Plasma concentrations are maintained between 1 and 3 ng/mL for
up to 48 h [309]; bioavailability is high and reported to be approxi-
mately 96% [309]. Despite these advantages, peak concentrations
did not exceed 3 ng/mL; therefore (based on a previous study),
transdermal fentanyl may not provide adequate analgesia when
administered as monotherapy.
Transdermal fentanyl application in goats produces variable
plasma concentrations (0.83–16.69 ng/mL) with an onset of peak
plasma concentrations similar to horses [94,509]. Sheep, however,
demonstrated more stable plasma concentrations (0.62–2.73 ng/
mL) with peak effects at 12 h following application [89]. Application
of fentanyl patches to calves, even at doses as low as 1–2 μg/kg/h,
resulted in neuroexcitation and tachycardia suggesting that caution
is warranted [510]. In pigs, transdermal fentanyl is well tolerated
and is potentially a better analgesic option than buprenorphine
following surgical procedures [507].

Remifentanil
Remifentanil is a μ-opioid receptor agonist that is structurally
similar to fentanyl (Table 23.6). It has an extremely short half-life
(e.g., 6 min in dogs) and duration of action [511]. Remifentanil is
metabolized via ester hydrolysis by nonspecific esterases in blood
and tissues. This unique pharmacokinetic feature is attributed to
its propanoic acid methyl ester linkage on the piperidine nitro-
gen [512]. Recovery from remifentanil is rapid regardless of dose
and infusion duration, as the context-sensitive half-time remains
unchanged at less than 5 min [512,513].
In cats, a minimum dose of 0.3 μg/kg/min may be required to
prevent the generation of a motor response from an electrical nox-
ious stimulus [514]. In a clinical study in isoflurane-anesthetized
cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy, 0.4 μg/kg/min provided more
appropriate analgesia when compared to 0.1 and 0.2 μg/kg/min
infusion rates [515]. Species differences in the antinociceptive
effects of remifentanil at the level of the spinal cord have been
observed between dogs and cats. For example, remifentanil’s inhibi-
tory effect on nociceptive transmission at the spinal cord was shown
to be less pronounced in cats compared to dogs [516]. Presumably,
this is due to the differences in Aδ fiber distribution within the
CNS, which may account for additional species-level differences in
the antinociceptive effects of μ-opioid receptor agonists [516].
Remifentanil has been associated with acute opioid tolerance and
opioid-induced hyperalgesia in rats, mice, and rabbits [517–519].
Evidence to support similar findings in dogs is lacking [520].
Remifentanil increases arginine vasopressin concentrations in
anesthetized dogs [521]. As with other opioids, this may be a physi-
ologic compensatory response to bradycardia-induced hypotension
or result from direct stimulation of μ-opioid receptors in the neuro-
hypophysis [522,523]. There are limited studies comparing the
adverse effects associated with remifentanil and fentanyl in dogs
and cats. A prospective randomized multicenter study in humans
reported that the frequency of adverse effects was similar between
remifentanil and fentanyl; however, hypotension occurred more
commonly in patients receiving remifentanil [524]. Other clinical
trials found similar results pertaining to blood pressure, but also
reported lower HRs in patients administered remifentanil com-
pared to fentanyl [525]. Remifentanil, however, may be a better
alternative to fentanyl when early and frequent postoperative neu-
ral and motor function assessments are required [526]. Remifentanil
has been used successfully as part of a multimodal protocol in a
horse undergoing a 13-h surgical procedure [527]. It has also been
used as part of an equine sedation protocol at 6 μg/kg/h in conjunc-
tion with a xylazine CRI [528]. In isoflurane-anesthetized horses
also receiving dexmedetomidine, peak blood remifentanil concen-
trations occurred at 45–50 min after starting an IV remifentanil
CRI at 6 μg/kg/h [529].
Sufentanil
Sufentanil is a highly lipid soluble μ-opioid receptor agonist that is
10–15 times more potent than fentanyl. It is a thienyl analogue of
4-anilinopiperidine (Table 23.6). In isoflurane-anesthetized cats,
the clearance, volume of distribution, and terminal half-life of
sufentanil is longer than that of fentanyl and alfentanil [530]. Like
fentanyl, sufentanil has been administered for intraoperative anal-
gesia and constitutes a good alternative during times of fentanyl
shortages. Recovery quality in dogs undergoing ovariohysterec-
tomy was significantly better in dogs administered a sufentanil
infusion when compared to fentanyl, with comparable degrees of
analgesia and respiratory depression [531]. Similar effects on
recovery quality were reported when sufentanil was compared to
fentanyl and administered in combination with lidocaine and keta-
mine in dogs undergoing total ear canal ablation and bulla osteot-
omy [532]. Recovery quality following general anesthesia in cats is
similar between sufentanil and fentanyl [533]. Sufentanil can be
combined with bupivacaine and administered epidurally in dogs
and has been reported to provide a greater degree of analgesia in the
postoperative period when compared to fentanyl and bupiv-
acaine [534]. A novel long-lasting sufentanil formulation has been
evaluated in dogs and can be administered intramuscularly for pro-
longed postoperative pain relief (e.g., approximately 24 h) [535].
Despite its antinociceptive effects, a high incidence of intraopera-
tive respiratory and cardiovascular complications currently pre-
cludes use of this product in clinical scenarios [535]. Limited data
are available regarding the use of sufentanil in large animal species.
Meperidine (pethidine)
Meperidine (pethidine) is a phenylpiperidine synthetic opioid
(Table 23.6) and μ-opioid receptor agonist. Meperidine provides
good but short-duration analgesia lasting approximately 60–90 min
post-administration in dogs [536,537] and cats [538,539]. An active
metabolite, normeperidine, is produced following metabolism by
N- demethylation via hepatic cytochrome P450. Normeperidine is a
CNS excitotoxic agent and can produce agitation, noise sensitiza-
tion, and muscle twitching in dogs with inappropriate dosing [540].
Benzodiazepines, but not naloxone, are recommended to treat these
adverse effects [540]. Meperidine possesses vagolytic properties at
medium doses, but bradycardia is observed at very high doses due
to its local anesthetic-like actions resulting in direct myocardial
depression [541,542]. Tachycardia may also be a result of histamine
release following IV administration. Meperidine’s effects on HR
do not attenuate dexmedetomidine-induced bradycardia [196].
Meperidine can induce pain during IM injection, which may be
related to its acidic pH (3.5–6.0) [196]. Meperidine administered to
conscious dogs at 10 mg/kg IV stimulates peripheral mast cells
resulting an acute and transient period of vocalizing, flare reaction,
scratching, hypersalivation, urination, defecation, and tachypnea
[543]. It also can result in local edema and erythema due to cuta-
neous histamine release following IM injection [242]. Despite
these local effects, meperidine generally does not result in clinically
significant systemic histamine concentrations following IM
administration [544].
Meperidine administered IV, SC, and IM at 1 mg/kg does not
produce thermal antinociceptive effects in horses [311,545].
However, there may be some short-term analgesic benefit with alle-
viation of equine lameness at a dose of 1 mg/kg IM [546]. Meperidine
can, however, provide long-lasting analgesia (240–300 min) with a
quick onset (12 min) following caudal epidural administration with
minimal sedation and ataxia and no adverse cardiopulmonary
effects [547].
Carfentanil, etorphine, alfentanil, and thiafentanil
Carfentanil, a fentanyl analogue that is 20–30 times more potent
than fentanyl and 10,000 times more potent than morphine, was
approved for veterinary use in 1986 as an intramuscular large ani-
mal tranquilizer. In the US, veterinarians must receive authoriza-
tion and be placed on an “Approved Carfentanil Users List” with
special Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) registration class
approval. In Canada, carfentanil is considered a Schedule I sub-
stance, meaning that it serves no accepted medical use and has high
abuse potential. Currently, its only approved use in humans is as a

-- 396 of 1450 --

Chapter 23: Opioids 	381
radiolabeled isotope, [11C]-carfentanil, to aid in mapping the
μ-opioid receptor via positron emission tomography in research
settings.
Veterinarians must handle carfentanil with extreme caution as
very small quantities (0.01 mL) can be lethal. Accidental carfentanil
intoxication in humans can lead to miosis, respiratory and CNS
depression, and potentially death. It is best to handle highly potent
opioids (i.e., thiafentanil, etorphine, and carfentanil) with at least
two people present, to wear protective clothing, gloves, and a face
shield, and have an opioid receptor antagonist (e.g., naloxone, nal-
trexone, or diprenorphine) readily available. The first confirmed
human accidental overdose exposure associated with carfentanil
occurred when a veterinarian accidentally splashed carfentanil cit-
rate 1.5 mg and xylazine 50 mg from an immobilization dart into
his eyes and mouth [548]. Despite irrigation, sedation occurred
within 2 min and the subject was administered naltrexone 100 mg
parenterally (supplied in the same package as carfentanil) prior to
arrival at the hospital [548]. The veterinarian was discharged a day
later after a complete recovery [548]. Etorphine and thiafentanil
carry similar concerns and are discussed elsewhere (Chapter 55).
Hydrocodone, oxycodone, and codeine
Hydrocodone is a μ-opioid receptor agonist and undergoes N-
demethylation and N-oxidation to norhydrocodone and N-oxide
metabolites (major metabolites) as well as hydromorphone and
hydromorphone 	glucuronide 	(minor 	metabolites) 	[549].
Hydrocodone is predominately used in dogs as an antitussive agent
(0.22–0.5 mg/kg PO every 6–12 h) and exerts its antitussive proper-
ties via simulation of μ-opioid receptors on sensory nerve endings
that initiate cough as well within the CNS [550]. Hydrocodone is
often formulated with an anticholinergic drug (homatropine), non-
steroidal anti-inflammatory agent, or acetaminophen (paraceta-
mol). The latter combination should not be used in cats because
acetaminophen is toxic in this species. Codeine has also been used
as an antitussive agent in dogs; however, sedation may be more
prominent than with hydrocodone.
Previous studies evaluating oral administration of opioids such
as hydrocodone and codeine have demonstrated low bioavailability,
large individual variability, erratic gastrointestinal absorption, and
limited analgesic effect, particularly in dogs [551–553]. One study,
however, evaluating hydrocodone at 0.5 mg/kg PO in Greyhound
dogs reported that plasma concentrations of the metabolite hydro-
morphone did exceed those previously reported to provide analge-
sia from 0.5 to 8 h [554]. A clinical trial compared the analgesic
efficacy of oral extended-release hydrocodone (3.0 mg/kg) to firo-
coxib in dogs undergoing tibial plateau leveling osteotomy
(TPLO) [555]. In this study, dogs administered hydrocodone had
higher pain scores and lower limb function than dogs administered
firocoxib. Similarly, pain relief was considered unacceptable in
dogs administered hydrocodone–acetaminophen PO for TPLO
surgery [556]. In dogs, differing metabolic and elimination path-
ways along with a more vigorous first-pass effect [557–560] may
explain the lack of bioavailability and analgesic efficacy of these
drugs compared to other species.
Codeine is classified as a μ-opioid receptor agonist and can be
administered IV, IM, SC, PO, or as a CRI. Oral bioavailability of
codeine is extremely low in dogs (4%) [551]. Metabolism of codeine
generates many metabolites including morphine, codeine, and
codeine-6- glucuronide [561]. Codeine at 1–3 mg/kg SC provides
dose-dependent antinociceptive effects for 1–3 h based on the elec-
trical dental pulp stimulation model in dogs [562]. While
postoperative codeine at 2 mg/kg SC every 8 h for 24 h alone pro-
vided adequate analgesia in 6/9 (66%) dogs undergoing maxillec-
tomy or mandibulectomy [563], pain assessment in this study
involved numeric rating and simple descriptive scales rather than a
validated multidimensional pain scale. In cats, codeine at 2 mg/kg
PO failed to produce thermal antinociceptive effects [564]. Orally
administered codeine in horses is rapidly metabolized to morphine,
morphine-3- glucuronide, 	morphine-6- glucuronide, 	codeine-6-
glucuronide, and norcodeine [565]. Plasma concentrations of
morphine-6- glucuronide following codeine at 0.6 mg/kg PO were
comparable to those following an analgesic dose of morphine in
horses [81,565]. Codeine is generally well tolerated in horses but
lacks the ability to provide antinociception when administered PO
at doses of 0.3, 0.6, and 1.2 mg/kg [78].
More studies are required to prove the analgesic efficacy of these
drugs in veterinary medicine. Due to the lack of evidence support-
ing clinical efficacy of orally administered codeine, oxycodone, or
hydrocodone, the authors do not recommend their use as mono-
therapies for treatment of pain in dogs or cats [379].
Partial opioid agonists
Buprenorphine
Dogs and cats
Buprenorphine is a μ-opioid receptor partial agonist. It is available
as a hydrochloride salt in various formulations approved for use in
humans, cats, and dogs depending on the jurisdiction. In the US, in
addition to the human 0.3 mg/mL preservative-free injectable solu-
tion (Buprenex®), two concentrated buprenorphine formulations
are commercially available for use in cats for postoperative analge-
sia. One contains 1.8 mg/mL buprenorphine (Simbadol®) and is
administered SC once daily for up to 72 h. The other formulation
contains 20 mg/mL buprenorphine (Zorbium®) for single transder-
mal administration providing analgesia for up to 96 h. In Europe,
Canada, and Australia, 0.3 mg/mL multidose injectable formula-
tions are available for IM or IV administration and provide analge-
sia for 6–8 h in dogs [566] and 4–8 h in cats [20]. In the following
discussion, if not specifically noted, statements pertain to the
0.3 mg/mL injectable formulation, which will be referred to as the
“traditional” injectable formulation where applicable.
In dogs, premedication with buprenorphine (0.02 mg/kg IM)
produces inferior postoperative analgesia compared to methadone
(0.3 mg/kg IM) for ovariohysterectomy [149]. However, when
administered IV as a CRI (0.015 mg/kg loading dose and 0.0025 mg/
kg/h for 6 h), buprenorphine provides satisfactory postoperative
analgesia for elective ovariectomy [567]. Buprenorphine transder-
mal patches (0.005–0.006 mg/kg/h applied 40 h before anesthesia)
or IV buprenorphine (0.02 mg/kg administered 30 min before the
induction of anesthesia and then every 6 h for 24 h) provided simi-
lar intra- and postoperative analgesia following unilateral mastec-
tomy [566]. The addition of buprenorphine (0.1 mL of 0.3 mg/mL
solution) to bupivacaine (0.3 mL of 5 mg/mL solution) for infraor-
bital nerve blocks enhanced the duration of analgesia in dogs with
acute dental pain [568].
A commercially available concentrated buprenorphine solution
(1.8 mg/mL, Simbadol®) has been investigated in dogs. Used as pre-
medication at 0.02 mg/kg, it provided adequate postoperative anal-
gesia following ovariohysterectomy when administered IV or IM,
but not when administered SC [372]. The authors attributed this to
erratic drug absorption after SC administration. However, a larger
dosage (0.12 mg/kg IV, SC) in awake dogs demonstrated complete

-- 397 of 1450 --

382 	Section 3: Pharmacology
SC absorption [59]. After intranasal or OTM administration at
0.03 mg/kg, buprenorphine bioavailability was 58% and 41%,
respectively; and plasma drug concentrations associated with anal-
gesia were maintained for up to 5 h [21]. Sedation, panting, whining,
hypersalivation, ataxia, decreased rectal temperature, reduced
appetite, and diarrhea have been observed in awake dogs [21,59].
These effects may limit the clinical utility of Simbadol® as an analge-
sic in dogs. A lipid encapsulated, extended-release buprenorphine
formulation (0.2 mg/kg SC) provided sustained analgesic plasma
drug concentrations and antinociception for up to 72 h [569].
In cats, the traditional formulation of buprenorphine adminis-
tered at 0.02 mg/kg IM preoperatively did not provide postopera-
tive pain relief after ovariohysterectomy; however, an additional
buprenorphine dose administered during wound closure was asso-
ciated with adequate analgesia [153]. Concurrent administration of
meloxicam (0.2 mg/kg SC) or gabapentin (50 mg PO) also seemed
to improve the analgesic effect of preoperative buprenorphine
(0.02 mg/kg IM) for ovariohysterectomy [570]. Similarly, preopera-
tive buprenorphine (0.02 mg/kg IM) in conjunction with intrates-
ticular lidocaine block (2 mg/kg) and postoperative meloxicam
(0.3 mg/kg SC) induced good postoperative analgesia after
orchidectomy in cats [571]. Thus, repeated doses of the traditional
(0.3 mg/mL) injectable formulation of buprenorphine or its use as
part of a multimodal analgesic protocol is required to provide ade-
quate postoperative analgesia after neutering in cats.
The need for outpatient pain control in cats has encouraged the
investigation of alternative formulations and routes of administra-
tion for buprenorphine. For instance, both commercially available
and compounded formulations of injectable buprenorphine are
absorbed by the OTM route. However, individual variation in
buprenorphine absorption and poor palatability associated with
some formulations (those with preservatives) may preclude clinical
utility of this route of administration [572,573]. The commercially
available concentrated buprenorphine formulation (1.8 mg/mL;
0.24 mg/kg SC, Simbadol®) provided similar analgesia to the tradi-
tional injectable formulation (0.3 mg/mL; 0.02 mg/kg IM) follow-
ing dental extractions [20]. The concentrated formulation has the
advantage of longer lasting analgesia compared to the traditional
formulation and, therefore, less frequent dosing and potential aver-
sion to drug administration. However, the concentrated buprenor-
phine formulation produced a higher prevalence of postoperative
hyperthermia than morphine (0.1 mg/kg SC) following ovariohys-
terectomy [307]. A single administration of a compounded liposo-
mal encapsulated buprenorphine formulation (0.2 mg/kg SC)
maintains putative analgesic drug concentrations for 96 h [574]. A
novel transdermal buprenorphine formulation (20 mg/mL;
Zorbium®) also provides 96 h of analgesia when applied topically to
the cervical skin (8 mg to cats 1.2–3 kg, and 20 mg to cats > 3–7.5 kg)
1–2 h prior to both elective surgical reproductive sterilization and
forelimb onychectomy [29].
Horses
In horses, preoperative buprenorphine (0.005 mg/kg IV) provides
better intraoperative analgesia than butorphanol (0.025 mg/kg
IV) [154], and a larger dose (0.01 mg/kg IV) induces effective post-
operative analgesia for surgical castration [575]. Buprenorphine
(0.0075 mg/kg IV) also induces good sedation for cheek tooth
extraction [576]; however, postoperative locomotor stimulation
may occur [154,576]. Attempts to induce long-lasting analgesia
with a single administration of a compounded buprenorphine for-
mulation (0.1 mg/kg SC or IM) failed due to the severity and duration
of adverse gastrointestinal effects and behavioral excitation [577]. A
single off-label administration of a commercially available concen-
trated buprenorphine formulation (1.8 mg/mL; 0.0025 and
0.005 mg/kg SC, Simbadol®) induced antinociception but only at
the lower dose rate and for a duration comparable to that achieved
with traditional concentration buprenorphine (0.3 mg/mL; 0.005–
0.01 mg/kg IV) [76,575]. The gastrointestinal and behavioral
adverse effects may preclude the use of doses greater than 0.005 mg/
kg SC for the concentrated buprenorphine formulation. Alternative
routes of administration have been explored in attempts to prolong
the analgesic effects of buprenorphine. For instance, buprenorphine
concentrations are detectable for at least 24 h in inflamed joints
after a single intra-articular administration (0.005 mg/kg), but the
chondrotoxic effects may preclude clinical use of this route of
administration [107,578].
Mixed opioid agonist–antagonists
Butorphanol
Butorphanol is structurally classified as a morphinan (Table 23.6)
and exhibits antagonist to partial agonist activity at μ-opioid recep-
tors, and agonist activity at κ-opioid receptors. It is approved for use
as an antitussive in dogs and an analgesic in cats and horses, but
approval varies among countries. It is available as butorphanol tar-
trate and may be administered via IV (bolus and CRI), IM, SC, or
PO routes. There are also reports of alternative routes of adminis-
tration such as intravenous regional limb perfusion in horses [579]
and intranasal administration in parrots and rabbits [580,581].
Butorphanol tablets, despite producing antitussive and mild seda-
tive effects, have low oral bioavailability and do not induce effective
analgesia. Extravascular parental administration may be painful on
injection [582].
Dogs and cats
In dogs, butorphanol induces opioid effects measured as decreased
rectal temperature following IV bolus (0.4 mg/kg), IV CRI (0.2 mg/
kg IV followed by 0.2 mg/kg/h), and SC injection of butorphanol
(0.8 mg/kg) with bicarbonate (forming a poorly-water-soluble sus-
pension), but not after SC administration of butorphanol (0.4 mg/
kg) alone [582]. Lower butorphanol doses may be used for sedation
than those required for analgesia. Procedural sedation with butor-
phanol (0.4 mg/kg IV) allows easier and faster endoscopic duode-
nal intubation compared to methadone (0.3 mg/kg IV) [583]. When
combined with dexmedetomidine (2 μg/kg IV), butorphanol
(0.2 mg/kg IV) also induces rapid onset of deep sedation that facili-
tates positioning for radiographic examination [584]. When admin-
istered as premedication or immediately after completing surgery,
butorphanol (0.4 mg/kg IV or IM) provides insufficient postopera-
tive analgesia after ovariohysterectomy, laparotomy, or shoulder
arthrotomy in dogs [477,585,586]. However, the criteria for rescue
analgesia in the Gomes et al. study [585] was set below the validated
intervention point for the scale used (i.e., Glasgow Composite
Measure Pain Scale total score > 3.5/20 instead of > 5/20).
In cats, butorphanol (0.1–0.4 mg/kg IM) induces good quality
sedation, but potentially inferior to that achieved with full μ-opioid
receptor agonists [587]. Butorphanol also prevents vomiting and
reduces the incidence and severity of nausea induced by dexmedeto-
midine [588,589]. Compared to buprenorphine (20 μg/kg IM), the
incidence of vomiting is less with butorphanol [589]. Butorphanol
(0.4 mg/kg IM) combined with medetomidine (15 μg/kg IM) for

-- 398 of 1450 --

Chapter 23: Opioids 	383
premedication failed to induce postoperative analgesia after ovario-
hysterectomy; even after adding another dose of butorphanol dur-
ing wound closure [153]. In contrast, butorphanol (0.3 mg/kg IM)
as part of a multimodal analgesic protocol with dexmedetomidine,
lidocaine, and meloxicam provided effective postoperative analge-
sia after orchidectomy [571]. The requirement of isoflurane is
also reduced with butorphanol compared with buprenorphine in
cats [571], and butorphanol IV CRI dose-dependently reduced the
MAC of isoflurane by 23–68% [359].
Horses
Administered alone to healthy, non-painful horses, butorphanol
increases locomotor activity. Locomotion is prevented by pre-
administering a sedative (e.g., an α2
-adrenergic receptor agonist)
and/or a tranquilizer (e.g., acepromazine) [590]. Increased locomo-
tion with butorphanol is not noted in newborn foals, but sedation
and increased nursing is observed [591]. Mild sedation induced by
a combination of butorphanol (0.01 mg/kg IV) and detomidine
(0.01 mg/kg IV) does not affect the grade of laryngeal function in
horses undergoing endoscopic examination of the upper respira-
tory tract [592]. When administered as part of a premedication
protocol, butorphanol (0.02–0.1 mg/kg IV) induces acceptable
postoperative analgesia in horses undergoing elective surgical pro-
cedures [155]. Acceptable postoperative analgesia is also achieved
when butorphanol (0.02 mg/kg IV) is administered just before skin
incision in horses undergoing elective arthroscopy [450]. However,
premedication with detomidine (0.01 mg/kg IV) followed by butor-
phanol (0.1 mg/kg IV) may not provide adequate postoperative
analgesia following castration in ponies [593].
Interactions with full opioid agonists
Butorphanol decreases some of the effects induced by μ- opioid
receptor agonists while still inducing analgesia via μ- and κ-opioid
receptor activation. Thus, butorphanol (0.2 mg/kg IV) decreases
but still preserves some of the antinociception induced by hydro-
morphone (0.1 mg/kg) in cats [239]. Butorphanol (0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV)
partially reverses oxymorphone-induced respiratory depression
and bradycardia in the early postoperative period in dogs [218]. It
also attenuates respiratory depression and decreases immobilizing
effects induced by etorphine (0.1 mg/kg IM) in goats [594]. In the
case of a prolonged recovery or relative μ-opioid receptor agonist
overdose, titrating butorphanol IV to effect is recommended over
bolus administration [218,239].
Nalbuphine
Nalbuphine is a κ-opioid receptor agonist and μ-opioid receptor
antagonist. It remains the only narcotic analgesic not controlled
under the Controlled Substances Act in the US. An injectable for-
mulation containing nalbuphine hydrochloride at 10 or 20 mg/mL
is approved for use in humans in the US. Nalbuphine alone induces
sedation and analgesia in dogs, but both effects are less potent than
with pure μ-opioid receptor agonists. Also, the sedation and anal-
gesia may not be sufficient to perform some clinical procedures
(e.g., clipping/prepping and catheterization) or alleviate some
types of pain [595]. Both sedation and analgesia exhibit ceiling
effects [596,597]. Deeper sedation is achieved when nalbuphine is
administered in neuroleptanalgesic combinations with aceproma-
zine or α2 - adrenergic receptor agonists [163,595,597]. However,
nalbuphine (0.5 mg/kg or 1 mg/kg IV) combined with aceproma-
zine failed to provide sufficient intra- or postoperative analgesia in
dogs undergoing ovariohysterectomy (as was also the case for
butorphanol and morphine in this study) [585]. Administration of
IV nalbuphine (0.75 mg/kg) every 4 h or less or as a CRI has
been recommended for postoperative analgesia in dogs [598].
Epidural nalbuphine administration (0.3–0.6 mg/kg) induces
MAC-sparing effects and long-lasting postoperative analgesia and
sedation [599]. However, data on the analgesic effects of nalbuphine
CRI and the safety of epidural nalbuphine in dogs are lacking.
Compounded nalbuphine applied topically to the cornea at 0.8–1%
had no effect on pain scores in experimental dogs with surgically
damaged corneas [600], or dogs undergoing phacoemulsification
cataract surgery [601], or on corneal sensitivity in clinically nor-
mal horses [602]. Thus, topical ophthalmic nalbuphine cannot
be recommended as an analgesic. Nalbuphine induces minimal
cardiovascular changes in healthy dogs after IV bolus adminis-
tration (1–2 mg/kg), after an IV loading dose (0.3 mg/kg IV) fol-
lowed by a CRI (0.4 mg/kg/h), or after epidural administration
(0.3–0.6 mg/kg) [597,599,603,604].
There is limited information on nalbuphine in other domestic
animal species. For instance, mild sedation has been reported with
a neuroleptanalgesic combination of nalbuphine (0.5 mg/kg IV or
IM) and acepromazine (0.05 mg/kg IV or IM) in cats, and sedation
was similar to that achieved with butorphanol (0.4 mg/kg IV or IM)
and acepromazine [605]. Similarly, nalbuphine (0.15 mg/kg IM)
is not inferior to butorphanol (0.15 mg/kg IM) when used in
combination with dexmedetomidine and tiletamine–zolazepam
for induction of anesthesia to perform gonadectomy in cats [606].
When administered as an IV premedication in horses, nalbuphine
(0.75 mg/kg) combined with xylazine (1.1 mg/kg) alone or xylazine
(0.5 mg/kg) and acepromazine (0.02 mg/kg) induced smoother
inductions and recoveries from anesthesia, longer duration of
anesthesia, and increased analgesia compared to xylazine alone
(1.1 mg/kg) [607]. This is in contrast to another study that reported
similar analgesia with xylazine alone (1.1 mg/kg IV) or combined
with nalbuphine (0.75 mg/kg IV) in experimental horses during
electrical stimulation of the dentine of a canine tooth [608].
Nalbuphine (0.4 mg/kg IV) reduced some pain-related behaviors
but did not eliminate physiological signs of distress in calves
after surgical castration [87]. Compared to ketamine alone
(10 mg/kg IV), nalbuphine (0.5 mg/kg IV) combined with keta-
mine (5 mg/kg IV) induced smoother induction and recovery from
anesthesia and better postoperative analgesia in goats [609].
Nalbuphine (1 mg/kg SC) induced sedation and analgesia without
affecting cardiovascular function in sheep [610]. Further studies are
required to determine the true clinical utility of nalbuphine in
domestic animal species.
Measuring thermal nociceptive thresholds in Hispaniolan
Amazon parrots, nalbuphine hydrochloride (12.5 mg/kg IM, but
not 25 and 50 mg/kg IM) induced antinociception compared to
saline control and all three doses induced antinociception for up to
3 h compared to baseline values. However, the two larger doses
induced less antinociception than the lowest dose. This is consistent
with a bell-shaped dose–response curve demonstrating a ceiling
effect [611]. Antinociception for up to 12 h was obtained with nal-
buphine decanoate (37.7 mg/kg IM) [612]. Differences in the dura-
tion of antinociception are due to differences in the pharmacokinetic
profile of these two nalbuphine salts [613,614].
When nalbuphine is used concurrently with μ-opioid receptor
agonists, both μ- and κ-opioid receptor-mediated analgesia
may be achieved while decreasing the severity of μ-opioid receptor-
mediated adverse events. This has been partially demonstrated in

384 	Section 3: Pharmacology
dogs where the administration of nalbuphine (0.3–1 mg/kg IV)
decreased the degree of sedation induced by a combination of
morphine (0.5 mg/kg IV) and acepromazine (0.05 mg/kg IV) [596],
and decreased the adverse cardiovascular effects induced by fenta-
nyl (50 μg/kg IV) [615]. Also, in goats, nalbuphine (0.8 mg/kg IV)
decreased the level of immobilization but had minimal effects
on the respiratory depressant effects induced by etorphine
(0.1 mg/kg IM) [594].
Opioid antagonists
Naloxone, naltrexone, and methylnaltrexone
Naloxone is a short-acting opioid receptor antagonist that is rapidly
absorbed after IV and IM administration. A dose of 0.04 mg/kg IV
is recommended for opioid reversal during cardiopulmonary arrest
in dogs and cats [616]. Intranasal naloxone (administered with an
atomizer) is also an effective route in dogs, particularly for emer-
gency use in working canines accidentally exposed to opi-
oids [617,618]. The required dose of intranasal naloxone is four
times higher than the IV dose, with an approximately 50% reduc-
tion in maximum plasma concentrations. Naloxone is often used to
reverse the sedative effects associated with pure μ-opioid receptor
agonists. Patients should be closely monitored as renarcotization
may occur following IV and IM naloxone administration [217]. In
dogs that received oxymorphone, this may occur within 20–40 and
40–70 min following IV and IM naloxone administration, respec-
tively [619]. Similar findings were reported in cats 1 h following
0.04 mg/kg IV naloxone administration to reverse the effects of
0.1 mg/kg IV hydromorphone [239]. Studies have reported that
rapid administration of IV naloxone can result in depressed menta-
tion and blepharospasm [126,620]. The etiology of this adverse
effect is yet to be determined but may be associated with acute opi-
oid withdrawal [126,620], alterations in cerebral vascular tone [621],
or systemic hypertension [622]. In humans, the administration of
IV naloxone did not ablate the analgesic effect of epidural mor-
phine [623]; however, it may reduce the effects of epidural mor-
phine on urinary bladder function [624]. Naloxone also may
attenuate some of the cardiovascular responses associated with
shock. For example, naloxone administered at 0.04 mg/kg IV sig-
nificantly lowered endotoxin-induced increases in right ventricular
pressure and HR in horses [625].
Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist at μ-, κ-, and δ-opioid recep-
tors. Naltrexone is often administered to reverse the sedative effects
of carfentanil and etorphine in wildlife and zoo animals but would
also be effective in reversing other opioids as well. The dose of nal-
trexone is 100 mg per 1 mg of carfentanil administered; typically,
one-quarter of the dose is administered IV and the remainder is
administered SC. Naltrexone’s longer duration of action, at least
twice that of naloxone in some species, makes it desirable in wildlife
and zoo animals where repeat dosing may not be feasible. In dogs,
however, the duration of action of naltrexone may not differ signifi-
cantly from that of naloxone. Serum half-life during the elimination
phase (mean ± SE) was reported to be 71.2 ± 8.9 min for naloxone
and 85.1 ± 9.0 min for naltrexone in dogs [626]. Therefore, while
naltrexone may be longer acting compared to naloxone in other
species, its effects dissipate quickly in the dog [626]. In cats, naltrex-
one at 0.6 mg/kg IV should be administered every 60–120 min to
reverse high-dose opioid agonists [627].
Methylnaltrexone is a quaternary derivative of naltrexone and is
a selective peripherally-acting μ-opioid receptor antagonist [628].
Methylnaltrexone does not bind with δ-opioid receptors but binds
μ-opioid receptors with an eightfold higher potency than κ-opioid
receptors [629]. The addition of the methyl group forms a positively
charged compound with greater polarity and lower lipid solubility
compared to naltrexone [629]. At clinically relevant doses, meth-
ylnaltrexone is restricted from crossing the blood–brain barrier in
animals. This property allows for reduced peripheral adverse effects
while maintaining the central analgesic effects of opioid agonists.
For example, methylnaltrexone can prevent or treat postoperative
opioid-induced gastrointestinal ileus [630]. This could be of
particular benefit in horses administered morphine [631,632]. Its
effects on reducing the gastrointestinal effects associated with
buprenorphine may be limited [633].
Multitargeting molecules
Tramadol
Between 2014 and 2019, tramadol was the most widely prescribed
opioid by veterinarians in the US [37]. Tramadol is a racemic mix-
ture of (+)-tramadol and (–)-tramadol. The positive enantiomer
has low μ-opioid and α2
- adrenergic receptor affinity and inhibits
neuronal serotonin reuptake. The negative enantiomer binds to α2 -
adrenergic receptors and inhibits neuronal norepinephrine reup-
take [634]. Tramadol is extensively metabolized by cytochrome
P450 enzymes and the profile and extent are species- and individual-
specific [634]. The metabolite O-desmethyltramadol, or M1
, has lit-
tle intrinsic activity at μ-opioid receptors but has a 200-fold affinity
compared to tramadol [634]. The opioid-mediated analgesic effi-
cacy of tramadol relies on O-desmethyltramadol. The serotoniner-
gic and noradrenergic effects of tramadol may also contribute to
analgesia by augmenting descending inhibitory pathways. Tramadol
is available in oral formulations in North America, Europe, and
Oceania, and in injectable formulations in parts of Europe and
Latin America.
Dogs produce very low concentrations of O-desmethyltramadol,
and the clinical utility of tramadol has been questioned in this
species. Tramadol (1–10 mg/kg IV) induces minimal, short-lived
mechanical antinociception and no thermal antinociception
[408,635]. A meta-analysis concluded low certainty of tramadol’s
analgesic evidence for postoperative pain management [636]. The
need for rescue analgesia with tramadol is reduced compared to
no treatment, placebo, codeine, buprenorphine, butorphanol, or
nalbuphine, increased compared to methadone, and similar com-
pared to morphine [636]. Administered before surgery, tramadol
(3 mg/kg SC) induced postoperative analgesia similar to that of
morphine (0.5 mg/kg IV) in dogs undergoing surgical neuter-
ing [402,637]. However, when administered postoperatively,
tramadol (3 mg/kg IV every 4 h) induced insufficient analgesia
following surgical tumor removal [399]. When administered
during anesthesia, tramadol (1.5 mg/kg loading dose followed by
1.3 or 2.6 mg/kg/h CRI) had no meaningful sevoflurane MAC-
sparing effect (5% and 8%) [638,639]. Thus, tramadol should be
used judiciously in dogs and the potential for analgesic failure
is high. Tramadol monotherapy is unlikely to have meaningful
benefits for pain control in dogs.
Compared to carprofen (2.2 mg/kg PO every 12 h), tramadol
(5 mg/kg PO every 8–12 h) provided less effective postoperative
analgesia following enucleation in dogs [640]. It had no clinical
benefit for dogs with osteoarthritis of the elbow or stifle [641].
Similarly, the combination of tramadol (4 mg/kg IV) and meloxi-
cam (0.2 mg/kg IV) administered as premedication is not superior
to meloxicam alone at inducing postoperative analgesia following

-- 400 of 1450 --

Chapter 23: Opioids 	385
surgical neutering [642]. Adequate analgesia for up to 30 days fol-
lowing TPLO is achieved with cimicoxib (2 mg/kg PO every 24 h)
and tramadol (2 mg/kg PO every 12 h), but only cimicoxib improved
limb function and range of motion and reduced the occurrence of
hock edema [643]. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs seem to
be superior to tramadol for inducing analgesia in dogs suffering
from painful clinical conditions.
In cats, oral tramadol (0.5–4 mg/kg) induced dose-dependent
thermal antinociception with doses of at least 2 mg/kg necessary to
induce a significant analgesic effect, and doses of 4 mg/kg every 6 h
associated with maintenance of a near maximal antinociceptive
effect [644]. Preoperative oral tramadol (6 mg/kg) provides at least
equivalent analgesia to that of IM tramadol (4 mg/kg), which in
turn is more effective than IM meperidine (6 mg/kg) following
ovariohysterectomy [645,646]. Oral tramadol (2 mg/kg PO every 12
h for 5 days) improves mobility and activity in geriatric cats with
osteoarthritis but adverse effects were reported [647]. Although
tramadol may be a useful drug for acute and chronic pain in cats,
oral formulations are rarely palatable and induce profuse salivation
and poor treatment compliance. This has led to exploration of alter-
native routes of administration in this species. Epidural administra-
tion of tramadol (1 mg/kg) plus lidocaine (2 mg/kg) induced better
postoperative analgesia than either drug alone following orchidec-
tomy [648]. A tramadol gel product (1.9–3.2 mg/kg) has been
investigated for transdermal administration but plasma drug con-
centrations were low or undetectable [649].
Adverse effects have been reported after tramadol administra-
tion in cats and clinical signs include increased neuromuscular
activity, tachycardia, fever, tachypnea, and agitation related to
excessive levels of serotonin [650]. The risk of serotonin syndrome
should be considered when serotonin antagonists and/or reuptake
inhibitors (e.g., trazodone and fluoxetine), monoamine oxidase
inhibitors (e.g., selegiline), or tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., ami-
triptyline and clomipramine) are co-administered with tramadol.
In horses, IV bolus tramadol administration (2 mg/kg) induced
no thermal antinociception [651], and a tramadol IV CRI (1 mg/kg
bolus followed by 3 mg/kg/h) induced no mechanical antinocicep-
tion [652]. However, tramadol co-infused with acetaminophen
(6 g/h IV) induced mechanical antinociception 20 min after start-
ing the infusion that persisted for 15 min after stopping the
infusion [652]. Oral tramadol administration (5 mg/kg PO every
12 h for 1 week) produced minimal analgesia in horses with
chronic laminitis, whereas co-administration of a subanesthetic
dosage of ketamine (0.6 mg/kg/h IV for 6 h on each of the first
3 days of tramadol administration) induced immediate and
lasting analgesia [653]. Intra-articular administration of tramadol
(4 mg/mL) produced no postoperative analgesia following
arthroscopic surgery [654]. Tramadol alone may not induce clinical
analgesia in horses.
Tapentadol
Tapentadol has a dual mechanism of action as a μ-opioid receptor
agonist and a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. Current investi-
gations have focused on determining if tapentadol is an effica-
cious analgesic alternative in dogs and cats. Immediate and
extended-release PO formulations are available in the US and
Europe, and an injectable formulation is also available in Europe.
After PO administration to dogs and cats, tapentadol undergoes
extensive first-pass metabolism [65,655,656]. The major metabo-
lite in dogs is tapentadol-O-glucuronide and in cats it is
tapentadol-O-sulfate [655,656].
In dogs, IV (1.4 –6.8 mg/kg) but not PO (5.7–30 mg/kg) admin-
istration of tapentadol induced sedation, salivation, panting, ataxia,
and diarrhea [65,408,655]. Thermal antinociception, similar to that
of morphine (0.5–1.0 mg/kg IV), has been documented with tapen-
tadol (4.6–6.8 mg/kg IV) [408]. Clinical cases of unilateral cranial
cruciate ligament rupture improved in subjective (simple descrip-
tive scale) but not objective (pressure sensitive walkway system)
lameness evaluations at 4 h following tapentadol (30 mg/kg PO)
administration [657]. However, in the latter study, the assessor was
not blinded to treatment and no negative control group was included.
In cats, IV, IM, or SC administration of tapentadol (5 mg/kg)
induced mild sedation, salivation, and panting, with the effects
being less intense and of shorter duration following IM and SC
administration. The bioavailability of IM and SC tapentadol is 94%
and 90%, respectively [73]. Oral tapentadol (5.7 and 11.4 mg/kg)
induced salivation and thermal antinociception with the higher
dosage inducing a similar duration of antinociception as buprenor-
phine (0.02 mg/kg IM) and twice as long as the lower tapentadol
dosage [658].
Although experimental studies indicate potential analgesic ben-
efits of tapentadol in dogs and cats, more research is needed before
any recommendations can be made regarding its use in clinical
veterinary practice.

Introduction
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are among the
most important drugs used in all species of animals. They have the
advantage of producing both analgesic and anti-inflammatory
effects in animals. Because they are not controlled or scheduled
drugs, they can be easily prescribed and dispensed. There are a vari-
ety of formulations and routes of administration to choose from
that include oral tablets, oral caplets, oral liquids, chewable tablets,
paste (for horses), oral transmucosal mist, transdermal, and inject-
able solutions for intravenous (IV) or subcutaneous (SC) adminis-
tration (Table 24.1, Box 24.1).
This chapter will focus primarily on the most common drugs
used in most countries, but the reader should appreciate that avail-
ability, registration, licensing, and approvals by regulatory authori-
ties vary greatly around the world. There are drugs available in
some countries that are not available in others and some older
drugs on the market that have been replaced by newer approved
animal drugs in some countries. Some older drugs for which new
information has not been generated in many years (aspirin for
example) will not be covered in this chapter, but details of their
pharmacology may be found in previous editions of this and other
older textbooks. Although this chapter focuses primarily on the
major veterinary species of dogs, cats, horses, and cattle, the use of
NSAIDs in other animals should not be overlooked. There has been
extensive work in zoo and exotic species, particularly new work
published in non-mammalian species. Surprising differences in
both activity (e.g., cyclo-oxygenase [COX] activity) and pharma-
cokinetics exist among these other species. But it is beyond the
scope of this chapter to address all the other animal species in which
NSAIDs are administered; therefore, the reader is encouraged to
consult species-specific publications for more guidance.
Information on the pharmacology of these agents has been pro-
vided by Lees [1] as well as many other authors [2–5]. Guidelines
for clinical use in dogs [2,6–8], cats [7–11], horses [12], and food
animals [13] are available in species-specific reviews. A description
of the chemistry, mechanism of action, and clinical use of the coxib
class of NSAIDs is also available [14,15]. Because these extensive
and complete reviews are available, these details will be abbreviated
for this chapter.
Mechanism of action
Metabolism of arachidonic acid
As shown in Fig. 24.1, arachidonic acid, a fatty acid consisting of 20
carbons, is released from cell membranes by the enzyme phospho-
lipase A2 (PLA2 ). Arachidonic acid is the predominant fatty acid in
animal cell membranes. The products of arachidonic acid biotrans-
formation are referred to as “eicosanoids” because of their structure

These products act locally via G-protein-coupled receptors to gen-

responsible for important physiological functions. A group of LOX
products, the leukotrienes, are also responsible for inflammation,
but are not inhibited by the traditional drugs covered in this chapter
and will not be further discussed.
The action of traditional NSAIDs is to inhibit COX enzymes and
alter the formation of the prostanoids [16]. The significant develop-
ment that improved the understanding of NSAIDs’ mechanism of
action occurred in the early 1990s when new details about the tar-
gets of these drugs emerged [17,18]. It was elucidated that there are
two isoenzymes (isoforms) of COX (also known as “prostaglandin
synthase”) that are responsible for synthesis of prostaglandins.
Prostaglandin 	synthase-1 	(COX-1) 	is 	usually 	simplistically
described as a constitutive enzyme expressed in tissues [17,18].
Prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxane synthesized by this
enzyme are responsible for normal physiologic functions.
Prostaglandin synthase-2 (COX- 2), on the other hand, is inducible
(upregulated) and synthesized by macrophages and inflammatory
cells after stimulation by cytokines and other mediators of inflam-
mation. In 2002, a third isoenzyme of COX was described [19,20].
The COX-3 enzyme is a splice variant from the COX-1 gene, which
