humans for sleep disorders arising from a variety of causes. Despite
widespread use, there is limited peer-reviewed veterinary literature
available.
In an experimental cat study (n = 6), trazodone reduced activity
(assessed via accelerometry) to 43–86% of pre-dosing values, with
doses of 50, 75, and 100 mg/cat (corresponding to 10.6–16.7 mg/kg,
16–25 mg/kg, and 21–33 mg/kg PO, respectively) [266]. The highest
dose (100 mg/cat) was most effective in reducing activity, with a peak
effect at 2.5 h after dosing, but considerable interindividual variability
in baseline and post-trazodone activity was reported. However,
behavioral responses to a comprehensive physical examination
(including abdominal palpation, otoscopic and ophthalmic examina-
tion, and mock venipuncture and cystocentesis with needle penetra-
tion of skin) performed 90 min after dosing were unchanged
compared to placebo. Similarly, a stress score did not identify differ-
ences between placebo and the 100 mg/kg treatment. Heart and res-
piratory rates were unaffected by trazodone compared with placebo.
In a double- blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized crossover
study (n = 10 cats) evaluating the effect of trazodone on transport
and handling, trazodone (50 mg/cat, approximately 11 mg/kg PO)
reduced signs of stress during transport and improved ease of han-
dling [267]. Reduced stress (from “very tense” to “weakly relaxed”)
and improved tractability (from “restraint needed to examine
safely” to “easy/relatively easy to examine”) were identified.
Sleepiness was identified as an adverse effect. Trazodone was given
approximately 1–1.5 h before transport to the clinic and 1.5–2 h
before physical examination.
As with cats, data from dogs is from a small number of studies,
with variability in reported responses to trazodone. A randomized,
placebo-controlled, double-blinded study did not identify differ-
ences in behaviors between treatments [268]. Dogs (n = 29)
received either placebo or trazodone (2.8–10.8 mg/kg PO, every 12
h) with trazodone dose adjusted according to owner’s wishes dur-
ing a 4-week period following elective orthopedic surgery, during
which activity restriction and confinement were prescribed.
Behavioral assessments included greeting behavior, calmness,
behavior on leash, and tolerance of confinement. The authors sug-
gested several reasons for trial failure, including selection bias
toward calmer dogs, caregiver placebo effect (owners performed
behavioral assessments), placebo-by-proxy effect (owner beliefs
altered interaction with their dog leading to a change in dog behav-
ior), and lack of sensitivity in the behavioral assessment instru-
ment. By contrast, a recent double-blinded, placebo-controlled
crossover study in dogs (n = 20) found that trazodone (9–12 mg/kg
PO) given 90 min before transport to a veterinary clinic was asso-
ciated with reduced stress scores in the clinic, with most owners
(18/20) correctly identifying when trazodone had been given [269].
Two earlier studies in dogs showed efficacy with trazodone, though
both had limitations in study design, limiting data interpretation.
A study of 36 dogs admitted for elective orthopedic surgery all
received trazodone postoperatively for 4 weeks, with a subset of
owners requesting a dose increase after week 2 (to 7 mg/kg PO
every 8 h) [270]. Owners assessed behaviors (greeting behavior,
calmness, behavior on leash, and tolerance of confinement).
Compared to preoperative behavioral assessments, trazodone was

-- 445 of 1450 --

430 	Section 3: Pharmacology
associated with reduced intensity of greeting and overall calmness,
but not response to owner commands or tendency to pull on leash
walks. Trazodone was assessed as improving tolerance of postop-
erative confinement. Most owners reported an onset of drug effects
within 45 min of dosing (16–90 min for 90% of owners) and a
median duration of action of > 4 h (upper limit of observation
period). A study of hospitalized dogs (most dogs were admitted to
the surgery service) evaluated a convenience sample of 59 dogs
prescribed trazodone (4.7 ± 1 mg/kg PO) by the supervising veteri-
narian, with a comparison group of dogs not prescribed trazodone
(n = 58) [271]. Stress-related behavior scores were higher in the
trazodone treatment group at baseline compared with the untreated
group, but there was a significant reduction in these scores when
assessed approximately 110 min following trazodone administra-
tion. One dog showed signs of aggression 60 min after trazodone
administration.
In horses, 6 mg/kg PO induced mild sedation (based on a simple
descriptive scale) in 7/8 horses, which lasted between 0.5 and 8 h
after trazodone administration, with 4/8 horses remaining sedated
at 12 h and no signs of sedation apparent at 24 h [272]. Higher doses
(7.5 and 10 mg/kg PO) caused sedation within 20–30 min of admin-
istration that was generally mild (3/6 horses were heavily sedated at
the higher dose) and lasted a few hours [273]. In the latter study,
arrhythmias diagnosed by thoracic auscultation, without an ECG,
were noted in 2/6 horses that received 10 mg/kg PO.
In goats, intended as a model for wild ruminants, a dose of
10 mg/kg PO resulted in a five- to sixfold increase in time spent
sleeping and lying down, with reduced activity lasting approxi-
mately 4 h [274]. Eating and ruminating were unaffected.
Two studies have evaluated the effect of trazodone on the propo-
fol requirement for induction of general anesthesia in dogs [275,276].
A retrospective study of dogs (n = 15) undergoing radiotherapy
treatment showed a significant reduction in propofol dose (approx-
imately 25%) when trazodone was given approximately 2 h before
anesthesia (4.8 [2.9–7.3] mg/kg PO) [275]. Dogs were premedi-
cated with alfentanil and atropine and served as their own controls.
A prospective, randomized, unblinded study did not find an effect
of trazodone (5–7 mg/kg PO 2 h before anesthesia) on the propofol
dose requirement (dose administered over 20–30 seconds) com-
pared with acepromazine (0.01–0.03 mg/kg IM 30 min before anes-
thesia) [276]. All dogs (n = 15 per treatment) were also given
morphine (1 mg/kg IM 30 min before anesthesia). A MAC-sparing
effect has been identified in dogs, with a 17% reduction in isoflu-
rane MAC following trazodone (8 mg/kg PO) [277].
Trazodone is metabolized to an active metabolite, meta-
chlorophenylpiperazine, which has agonist activity at the 5-HT 2C
receptor, though its significance in animal species is unknown
[273,278]. The primary route of elimination is renal (approximately
75%) with the remainder undergoing fecal elimination.
Pharmacokinetics have been described in dogs (PO, IV, per rec-
tum), horses, pigeons, and goats [272,274,278–281]. Time to peak
effect appears to vary markedly between individual dogs, with peak
plasma concentrations achieved 445 ± 271 min after 8 mg/kg PO
(n = 6 dogs), though onset of signs may be apparent within
45 min [270,280]. Pharmacokinetics have not been described in
cats, but variability in behavioral responses may also reflect interin-
dividual pharmacokinetic differences [266].
Adverse effects appear uncommon in dogs following PO dosing,
with one report of hepatotoxicity in a dog attributed to trazodone
(4 mg/kg PO once or twice daily) and reports of aggression follow-
ing IV (3/6 dogs) and PO (1/59 dogs) administration [271,280,282].
Trazodone at doses between 1 and 30 mg/kg IV results in transient,
dose-dependent reductions in heart rate and arterial blood pres-
sure [283]. In cats (n = 12) given trazodone (approximately 11 mg/kg
PO) 90–120 min before echocardiography, sedation was observed
but there were minimal changes in cardiac measurements [284]. In
horses, 4/8 horses exhibited sweating following oral trazodone
(6 mg/kg), while IV dosing was associated with aggression, ataxia,
tremors, and circling (2/2 horses, 2 mg/kg) and ataxia, tremors,
circling, and sweating (1.5 mg/kg) [272,278].
Reported doses in dogs range from 3 to 12 mg/kg PO every 8–12 h
[268,269,271,280] and those in cats range from 8 to 30 mg/kg
PO [266,267,284]. Available formulations include 50, 100, 150, and
300 mg tablets.
Vasopressin (arginine vasopressin, antidiuretic
hormone) and desmopressin
The primary perioperative indication for vasopressin is in CPR and
refractory hypotension [84,285–288]. It is a potent vasoconstrictor,
acting on V1a receptors located in vascular smooth muscle, though
it also displays activity at V1b (anterior pituitary) and V2 (renal col-
lecting duct) receptors, and inhibits nitric oxide produc-
tion [289,290]. Its analog, desmopressin (DDAVP), is used in the
treatment of central diabetes insipidus [291–293] and management
of coagulopathy [294–296].
Vasopressin is an alternative vasopressor to epinephrine for use
during CPR, though there is no clear evidence supporting its role as
a replacement for epinephrine. Recent veterinary CPR guidelines
suggest its use (0.8 U/kg IV) on alternating rounds of CPR instead
of epinephrine, though there is no evidence that it confers a benefit
over epinephrine in humans [84,297]. Due to the lack of
β1
- adrenergic receptor activity, it may reduce the risk of myocardial
ischemia compared with epinephrine, though it will still cause cor-
onary vasoconstriction. An additional potential advantage over epi-
nephrine is that V 1 receptors, unlike α1
- adrenergic receptors,
remain responsive in an acidic environment [298]. Reports of clini-
cal use in the veterinary literature are mixed [285,287], with vaso-
pressin showing no benefit over epinephrine in a randomized
comparison using a standardized CPR technique [287] but associ-
ated with an improved rate of return to spontaneous circulation in
a hospital-wide study [285]. A meta-analysis demonstrated a poten-
tial improvement in return of spontaneous circulation associated
with its use, though contributing studies were predominantly in
porcine models of ventricular fibrillation [288].
Vasopressin can be administered via the endotracheal route, if
necessary, with one animal study suggesting that the same dose as
that recommended for IV use is effective [299].
What has become clear from the Reassessment Campaign on
Veterinary Resuscitation (RECOVER) initiative [300] is that there
is wide variability in study design and reporting of animal models
of CPR, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions from cur-
rently available experimental evidence. Anecdotal reports suggest
the use of vasopressin in cases of refractory hypotension, though
the available veterinary literature is sparse and human studies are
contradictory [286,290,301–304]. This is likely a reflection of the
heterogeneity of clinical and experimental studies [303]. Infusion
rates of 0.5–5 mU/kg/min and 0.1–2.5 mU/kg/min have been sug-
gested in dogs and foals, respectively [286,290,301]. Users should
be aware of the potential for detrimental hypoperfusion of vascu-
lar beds resulting from the resultant vasoconstriction [305].
Desmopressn acetate (DDAVP), a synthetic analog of vasopres-
sin with reduced vascular effects, is used for perioperative

-- 446 of 1450 --

Chapter 25: Anesthetic and Analgesic Adjunctive Drugs 	431
management of patients with von Willebrand disease [295,306,307]
and management of central diabetes insipidus [291–293,308].
von Willebrand disease, the most common canine hereditary
defect of hemostasis, is classified according to one of three sub-
types, with type 1 being the least severe and most common, espe-
cially in Doberman Pinschers [309]. Management consists of both
non-transfusion and transfusion therapy, based on disease severity
and clinical presentation. Non-transfusion therapy includes appro-
priate patient management (i.e., good surgical technique, minimiz-
ing use of drugs with antiplatelet activity, careful handling) and
DDAVP. Administration of 1 μg/kg SC or IV 30 min before surgery
may support hemostasis, but the response is more variable in dogs
than humans [295,306]. Administering DDAVP intranasally or into
the conjunctival sac is commonly performed, but there is limited
supporting evidence of its efficacy via this route in von Willebrand
disease.
Other reported uses for DDAVP include support of hemostasis
following administration of aspirin before surgery [310,311], as a
prophylactic measure to manage postoperative diabetes insipidus
following hypophysectomy [296], and administration to canine
blood donors to increase von Willebrand factor production before
blood collection for cryoprecipitate [312].
Injectable vasopressin is available as a 20 U/mL solution. DDAVP is
available as a 4 μg/mL injectable solution, 0.1 and 0.2 mg tablets,
100 μg/mL spray, and a 0.01% solution for intranasal administration.
Analgesic adjuncts
Amantadine and memantine
The dopamine agonist and N-methyl-D- aspartate (NMDA) recep-
tor antagonist amantadine was originally used as an antiviral
agent [313,314] but has entered clinical use in human medicine for
diseases and presentations as varied as Parkinson’s disease [315],
traumatic brain injury (TBI), and pain. Its continued use in the
management of Parkinson’s disease arose serendipitously from a
patient with Parkinson’s disease noticing an improvement in motor
function wtaking amantadine for influenza [316]. Recent meta-
analysis and systematic reviews have indicated a potential role for
amantadine in TBI though further studies are required to confirm
promising earlier findings [317,318]. Human studies have demon-
strated improved arousal when amantadine was administered
between 3 days and 4 weeks following TBI, and purported mecha-
nisms are through CNS stimulation mediated by amantadine’s
dopaminergic activity and reduced neurotoxicity through its
NMDA receptor antagonism [319,320]. Its use in animals is cur-
rently limited to an experimental model of TBI in rats where learn-
ing and hippocampal neuron survival were improved with
amantadine administration 1 h following TBI [321].
Memantine, a derivative of amantadine, has similar pharmaco-
logical properties [322]. It has been used in dogs for compulsive
disorders, though there is currently limited evidence of its use in
pain management [265].
Amantadine has been used for analgesia, acting via NMDA
receptor antagonism [323]. Its role as an analgesic appears to be
limited to chronic pain, particularly where central sensitization
may play a role, such as in chronic arthritis and limb amputation,
though its efficacy appears variable [324–327]. In dogs with pelvic
limb lameness and pain that was not alleviated by NSAID use,
activity increased following 3 weeks of therapy combining meloxi-
cam (0.1 mg/kg PO once daily) and amantadine (3–5 mg/kg PO
once daily) [324]. Doses of 2–10 mg/kg PO 2–3 times daily have
also been suggested. At these higher/more frequent doses, there is a
possibility of CNS excitation. Pharmacokinetic data (from a single
dose study) are supportive of 5 mg/kg PO twice daily dosing in dogs
(a dose of 10 mg/kg PO twice daily was predicted to result in plasma
levels associated with adverse effects in humans), though more
work is needed to confirm this prediction [328,329]. Amantadine
(14 mg/kg PO once daily with meloxicam 0.1 mg/kg PO) has also
been reported as successful in managing chronic pain following
bilateral pelvic fractures that was not responsive to meloxicam and
gabapentin [330].
In cats, amantadine at a dose of 3–5 mg/kg PO once or twice daily
has been suggested in cases of chronic arthritis [323,328,331]. A
blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized crossover study of 13 cats
with osteoarthritis found that amantadine (5 mg/kg PO once daily)
was associated with reduced activity (as assessed via accelerometry)
but improved owner-assessed outcomes (client-specific outcome
measures) [331]. Amantadine was also associated with a higher pro-
portion of owners reporting an improved quality of life for their cat.
Over the course of the 3-week treatment period, the only adverse
effect was vomiting, which occurred with a similar frequency in the
amantadine and placebo groups. The study did not include a wash-
out period between treatments, justified based upon the short half-
life in cats [331,332]. In a thermal threshold testing model in healthy
cats given oxymorphone to induce antinociception, amantadine did
not result in any further antinociception; however, it may be that an
acute nociception model in otherwise healthy cats may not be
appropriate for assessing amantadine [333,334].
Amantadine (3 mg/kg PO twice daily) was associated with marked
improvements in activity and interaction in a rhinoceros with sus-
pected chronic osteoarthritis and neuropathic pain of the thoracic
limbs that showed limited response to, or adverse effects associated
with, phenylbutazone, pentosan polysulfate, and gabapentin [335].
Pharmacokinetic data are available for dogs, cats, and par-
rots [329,332,336]. In Greyhounds, the short half-life (approximately
5 h) indicates that twice daily oral dosing (5 mg/kg) may be prefer-
able to once daily [329]. No adverse effects were reported. In cats,
amantadine has high oral bioavailability and a half-life similar to
that reported in dogs (approximately 5.5 h) following a dose of 5 mg/
kg PO [332]. As for dogs, this suggests that twice daily dosing may be
needed to maintain appropriate plasma concentrations. In orange-
winged Amazon parrots (Amazona amazonica), a 5 mg/kg PO dose
of amantadine, once daily, produced plasma concentrations consid-
ered therapeutic in dogs without causing adverse effects [336]. There
is currently no species-specific pharmacodynamic data to support
this dose. Based on renal elimination of minimally/partially metabo-
lized drug in other species, the authors suggested that birds with
renal disease may be at increased risk of developing toxicity [336].
Amantadine undergoes primarily renal excretion in dogs [337], and
there are limited dose-response data from rats [338].
More work is required to clarify the potential role of amantadine
and memantine in chronic pain, with a recent meta-analysis identi-
fying a lack of strong evidence for its use in people with a range of
neuropathic pain etiologies [327].
As a result of its dopaminergic properties, CNS stimulation is a
predicted side effect from overdose, and caution should be exer-
cised in patients receiving other dopamine agonists (e.g., the mono-
amine oxidase inhibitor selegiline), or agents inhibiting the reuptake
of serotonin (e.g., the tricyclic antidepressants such as amitripty-
line, and the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxe-
tine). Such combinations risk the occurrence of serotonin
syndrome, a potentially fatal syndrome characterized by signs of

-- 447 of 1450 --

432 	Section 3: Pharmacology
CNS stimulation, muscular tremors, and autonomic stimulation
including tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypertension [339–342]. The
risk is likely increased in the presence of hepatic insufficiency as
monoamine oxidase inhibitors and selective serotonin reuptake
inhibitors are metabolized by the CYP450 pathway. Specific to
anesthesia, there is evidence from human medicine that the phenyl-
piperidine opioids (meperidine, fentanyl, and fentanyl’s congeners,
tramadol and methadone) all increase the CNS concentration of
serotonin to varying degrees and in some instances have contrib-
uted to serotonin syndrome, although the risk to veterinary patients
remains unknown [343,344].
A less studied use of amantadine and memantine involves their
use as local anesthetics. Local anesthesia appears to be mediated
through sodium channel-blocking properties in addition to NMDA
receptor antagonism [338,345]. It remains to be seen if there are
significant advantages over traditional local anesthetics such as
lidocaine and bupivacaine.
It is possible that amantadine availability for animal use may
become restricted in some jurisdictions [346].
Amantadine is available as 100 mg tablets and capsules and as a
10 mg/mL syrup. Memantine is available as 5 and 10 mg tablets and
as a 2 mg/mL oral formulation.
Amitriptyline and nortriptyline
The tricyclic antidepressant amitriptyline is indicated for behavio-
ral disorders (e.g., obsessive-compulsive disorder) [347], idiopathic
feline lower urinary tract disease (IFLUTD) [348,349], and more
recently, neuropathic pain states [350–352]. Tricyclic antidepres-
sants are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, increasing synap-
tic levels of serotonin and norepinephrine. This appears to be the
primary mechanism mediating their useful behavioral modifica-
tion effects. However, other less well-understood mechanisms of
action may also contribute to their clinical potential as analge-
sics [350]. These include sodium channel blockade [353], NMDA
receptor antagonism [354], and antihistamine activity [355], but
not opioid receptor activity [356].
Amitriptyline (1–2 mg/kg/day) is commonly prescribed for
management of IFLUTD, though which mechanism(s) of action
result in improved clinical signs is unclear: serotonin reuptake
inhibition, antihistamine, and anticholinergic activity may be
involved [348,349,357].
Use of amitriptyline in treating neuropathic pain remains largely
anecdotal [207,350–352]. One case series of three dogs with neuro-
pathic pain reported a positive response to amitriptyline (1.1–
1.3 mg/kg PO twice daily) in two of the dogs [350]. Of these, one dog
had signs consistent with mechanical allodynia and dysesthesia over
the facial dermatome innervated by the infraorbital branch of the
right trigeminal nerve. Following no apparent response to gabapen-
tin (12.5 mg/kg PO twice daily), there was an improvement associ-
ated with amitriptyline (1.3 mg/kg PO twice daily), with clinical
signs resolving over 6 weeks. Owner-initiated discontinuation of
treatment was associated with a rapid return of clinical signs (in
3 days), leading to reinstitution and maintenance use of amitripty-
line therapy. A second successful use of amitriptyline (1.1 mg/kg PO
twice daily) was for management of intermittent lumbar pain with
diffuse mechanical allodynia. Clinical signs improved within a week
of initiating treatment and were resolved within one month. Again,
discontinuing therapy was associated with a return of pain (in
2 days), resulting in long-term amitriptyline therapy. In the third
case, in which there was mechanical allodynia secondary to ulnar
and median nerve lesions, amitriptyline (1.4 mg/kg PO twice daily)
did not improve clinical signs; however, there was improvement
with gabapentin (14.3 mg/kg PO twice daily). Sedation, a common
adverse effect of amitriptyline, was reported by the owners. In each
of these three cases, initial trials with NSAIDs, steroids, and opioids
for pain management were unsuccessful. It is also interesting that
when one therapy fails, the addition of or switch to another may prove
successful. This illustrates the potential complexity and challenge of
treating these cases. A study of 13 dogs diagnosed with osteosar-
coma receiving a combination of therapies (cimicoxib 2 mg/kg PO
once daily; amitriptyline 1–1.5 mg/kg PO once daily; gabapentin
10 mg/kg PO every 8 h) and a battery of nociceptive tests (including
investigator and owner behavioral assessments, quantitative sensory
testing, activity level and quality of life assessment) failed to identify
a clear benefit from the prescribed analgesics [358]. This highlights
the difficulty in studying complex, dynamic, naturally occurring
pain states, which is further complicated by use of poorly established
effective analgesic therapies. Attributing analgesia to a single drug is
often complicated in reported case series when animals are given
multiple drugs concurrently [207,352].
A feline case of suspected neuropathic pain was thought to have
developed following an initial femoral fracture repair, iatrogenic
sciatic 	nerve 	trauma, 	and 	subsequent 	amputation 	[351].
Approximately 1 month after amputation, the cat was observed fre-
quently shaking the stump though there were no signs associated
with pain when the stump was palpated. This was believed to be a
case of phantom limb pain. Initial treatment consisted of an IV
infusion of morphine, ketamine, and lidocaine for 37 h, followed by
oral transmucosal buprenorphine (approximately 0.03 mg/kg twice
daily) and oral amitriptyline (approximately 2 mg/kg twice daily).
The cat was ambulating normally at discharge. At follow-
up 10 months later, no further shaking of the amputation stump
was reported. There is increasing evidence of neuropathic pain in
cases of Chiari-like malformation and syringomyelia [359], and it
may also be implicated in some cases of head shaking in horses [360].
Hepatic metabolism of amitriptyline results in production of the
active metabolite nortriptyline in dogs and humans [361]. Both
amitriptyline and nortriptyline are also excreted unchanged in
urine, and caution should, therefore, be exercised in animals with
renal insufficiency. Nortriptyline is used clinically as a treatment for
neuropathic pain in humans [362], though its use in animals has
not been reported.
The recommended route of administration is oral [363]; trans-
dermal application is not effective at raising plasma drug levels and
intrathecal administration resulted in marked spinal cord pathol-
ogy [354]. The pharmacokinetics of amitriptyline have been
described in dogs and horses [329,364,365]. Further work is
required to further understand the pharmacokinetics in horses as
there is evidence of oral transmucosal absorption [364]. In a study
of six horses, amitriptyline (1 mg/kg PO) administration was asso-
ciated with significant reductions in heart rate (remaining within
normal limits) and intestinal motility (for 2 h post-administration),
with no respiratory changes observed [364]. One horse developed
transient second-degree AV block at 30 min post-administration,
which lasted for 2 h. Another horse developed ventricular prema-
ture contractions (1 per min) at 30 min post-administration (dura-
tion not reported). In dogs, amitriptyline pharmacokinetics may be
altered depending on whether dogs are fed or fasted at the time of
oral administration, with possible important differences in bioa-
vailability, though limited sample sizes prevent firm conclusions
from being drawn [329,365,366]. Fed Greyhounds given 4 mg/kg
PO had low bioavailability (6%) and peak plasma levels below those

-- 448 of 1450 --

Chapter 25: Anesthetic and Analgesic Adjunctive Drugs 	433
considered therapeutic in humans [329]. In contrast, at a similar
dose in fasted mixed-breed dogs, plasma levels were within the
therapeutic range for humans [366]. Breed differences may also
play a role in pharmacokinetic differences. Two fasted dogs vom-
ited following oral amitriptyline administration, though it was
unclear if this was drug related [329]. When given at 4 mg/kg IV to
Greyhounds, the following adverse effects were observed: sedation,
ataxia, transient tachycardia, polyphagia, and vomiting [329].
Adverse effects on the heart include tachycardia mediated via
inhibition of cardiac sodium channels and an anticholinergic effect
and potential fatal ventricular tachyarrhythmias from overdose
(greater than approximately 15 mg/kg IV) in dogs and cats [367–
369]. Ventricular tachyarrhythmias are preceded by prolongation of
the QRS complex. No ECG abnormalities were detected in dogs
receiving appropriate doses of amitriptyline (0.74–2.5 mg/kg PO
every 12 h) for behavioral disorders [370]. Other signs of toxicity in
conscious dogs include hypersalivation and vomiting. Common
adverse effects at therapeutic doses are weight gain and seda-
tion [357]. While there is a theoretical risk of triggering serotonin
syndrome with the concurrent use of tricyclic antidepressants and
monoamine oxidase inhibitors, this risk (at least in humans) is
believed to be low with amitriptyline [344]. Treatment of amitripty-
line toxicity includes alkalinization (with sodium bicarbonate) and
lipid emulsion therapy [369].
Available formulations of amitriptyline include 10, 25 , 50, 75 ,
100, and 150 mg tablets. Available formulations of nortriptyline
include 10, 25, 50 , and 75 mg tablets and a 10 mg/5 mL oral
solution.
Cannabinoids
Use of the cannabis plant, Cannabis spp., has spanned thousands of
years, for both its psychoactive and medicinal properties. There has
been a renewed interest more recently as it has become legalized
(under varying conditions, according to jurisdiction) and more
readily accessible [371,372]. This is reflected in a rapid growth in
the published human and veterinary literature, with several veteri-
nary reviews available [373,374].
The active molecules of interest that derive from Cannabis are
delta-9- tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD). A
somewhat simplified view is that THC exerts psychoactive effects
and CBD exerts therapeutic effects. These cannabinoids act via can-
nabinoid receptors, primarily CB 1 and CB2
, which exist as part of an
endogenous cannabinoid system with the following endogenous
ligands 	(endocannabinoids): 	anandamide 	(N-arachidonoyl),
2-arachidonoyl glycerol, and 2-arachidonoyl ether. In addition to
endocannabinoids, cannabimimetics (endogenous fatty acids)
modulate the endogenous cannabinoid system [375,376]. CB 1 and
CB 2 receptors are widely distributed in the body, including the cen-
tral and peripheral nervous systems, the immune system, intestines,
and skin, among others [374]. Receptor and ligand expression is
likely to vary in different disease states and may present a route for
therapeutic modulation of disease response [374]. To date, most
clinical veterinary studies have focused on osteoarthritis, epilepsy,
behavioral disorders, and atopic dermatitis, with varying quality of
evidence [373,377]. Compounding the limited number of high-
quality trials is variation in the cannabinoid or cannabimimetic
molecules studied, methods of administration, and poorly estab-
lished doses [374].
In osteoarthritis, there are a small number of higher quality clini-
cal trials reported in a mix of dog breeds [207,378–380]. In a double-
blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized, crossover trial of dogs
with osteoarthritis (n = 16 dogs), CBD in oil (with measurable levels
of THC but no evidence of psychoactive effects during the study) at
a dose of 2 mg/kg twice daily PO for 4 weeks resulted in a significant
reduction in pain scores (Canine Brief Pain Inventory and veteri-
nary assessment) and increase in activity levels, but no improvement
in lameness score or weight-bearing [378]. In this study, dogs also
received a variety of other drugs including NSAIDs and nutritional
joint supplements, with no change to treatment regimens during the
study. Reported adverse effects included an increase in alkaline
phosphatase (ALP) (mean of 323 versus 160 U/L in 9/16 dogs). A
double-blinded, placebo-controlled, parallel group, randomized
study in dogs with osteoarthritis compared three treatments (0.5 mg/
kg CBD PO, 1.2 mg/kg CBD PO, and 0.5 mg/kg liposomal CBD PO,
once daily; n = 5 dogs per treatment group) against placebo (n = 5
dogs), with each group treated for 4 weeks [379]. Pain was evaluated
with the Helsinki Chronic Pain Index and veterinary assessments.
No adverse effects were reported based on the evaluation of hemato-
crit and serum chemistry. There was a dose-dependent reduction in
pain and increase in mobility in the 1.2 mg/kg CBD and 0.5 mg/kg/
day liposomal CBD treatment groups. A double-blinded, placebo-
controlled, crossover trial of dogs with osteoarthritis (n = 23), given
a CBD-rich hemp oil (2.5 mg/kg twice daily PO, which also con-
tained 0.3% THC) for 6 weeks (with no washout period, based on
predicted half-life < 4 h), did not identify any improvement in the
recorded outcome measures (activity, Canine Brief Pain Inventory,
Liverpool Osteoarthritis in Dogs questionnaire, and gait analy-
sis) [380]. In this study, approximately 50% of the dogs were also
receiving an NSAID. Adverse effects included vomiting (2/23 dogs)
and elevated ALP, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), or alanine
transaminase (ALT) (14/23 dogs). It has been suggested that dosing
follows an escalation schedule, with treatment for at least 14 days
before a dose increase, if necessary [374]. Brioschi et al. compared
CBD (2 mg/kg twice daily via oral transmucosal route for 12 weeks)
combined with multimodal analgesia (gabapentin, amitriptyline,
prednisone, or firocoxib) against multimodal analgesia alone in dogs
with osteoarthritis in a randomized, parallel group study design (n =
9 receiving CBD protocol, n = 21 receiving multimodal analgesia
protocol) [207]. Pain was assessed with the Canine Brief Pain
Inventory, with scale items significantly lower in dogs during CBD
treatment. No adverse effects in CBC or serum biochemistry param-
eters were noted, with observed somnolence and ataxia attributed to
concurrent gabapentin, and some ptyalism associated with CBD
administration. In all these studies, some of the reported improve-
ments reflect statistical significance but fairly small changes in
assessment scale scores. This may reflect multiple factors, including
heterogeneity of osteoarthritis in the studied population, assessment
scale sensitivity, interindividual variability in response to treatment,
and small sample sizes, all of which underline the need for addi-
tional well-designed studies.
Similarly, high-quality evidence is also currently limited in stud-
ies of cannabinoids for the treatment of epilepsy, behavioral disor-
ders, and atopic dermatitis [381–383].
The pharmacokinetics for some cannabinoids have been pub-
lished for dogs, pigs, horses, and guinea pigs [378,384–393].
However, variations in formulation can affect absorption and bioa-
vailability and, in dogs, cannabinoid absorption varies according to
fasting state, so care should be taken when selecting a formulation
and dose [387]. Oral bioavailability of CBD in dogs is low (approxi-
mately 19%), with extensive first pass metabolism and primarily
fecal elimination [393–395]. Active metabolites are formed follow-
ing hepatic metabolism in humans, though more work is required

-- 449 of 1450 --

434 	Section 3: Pharmacology
to understand their presence and effects in animal spe-
cies [374,392,393,396]. Following oral administration of CBD in
dogs, peak plasma levels are achieved between 1.5 to 5 h, with
results varying between studies and with dose [378,384,387,391,392].
Importantly, there can be wide variability between cannabinoid
product labels and actual content [397].
With the expansion of access to cannabinoids, there is increasing
information available on toxicity and its management [394,398].
Toxicity manifests as a combination of clinical signs involving the
neurologic, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal systems, with com-
mon signs in dogs including ataxia, dullness/disorientation, mydri-
asis, 	urinary 	incontinence, 	hyperesthesia, 	tremors/shaking/
twitching, bradycardia, and vomiting [394,398,399]. Prognosis fol-
lowing intoxication is generally good, with a reported LD 50 exceed-
ing 3000 mg/kg PO for THC [400]. The LD50 for CBD has not been
described, though available reports suggest mortality is low follow-
ing exposure [394,399]. A safety and tolerability study of CBD
(doses up to 30.5 mg/kg PO), THC (doses up to 41.5 mg/kg PO),
and CBD-THC combination (doses up to 13:8.4 mg/kg PO) in cats
reported lethargy, hypothermia, ataxia, and protrusion of the nicti-
tating membrane as the most common adverse effects, primarily
associated with THC and CBD–THC [401]. A similar study in dogs
suggests better tolerability of cannabinoids in this species compared
to cats [396]. Cardiovascular changes (pale mucous membranes,
bradycardia, and tachycardia) and tachypnea were similarly
reported for each treatment.
Gabapentin and pregabalin
Gabapentin and pregabalin are structural analogs of γ-aminobutyric
acid (GABA). Historically, gabapentin has been prescribed as an
anticonvulsant in humans and veterinary species, but is being used
increasingly for neuropathic, chronic, and perioperative pain.
Previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses identified some
promising results for a role in chronic and neuropathic pain, but a
more recent meta-analysis shows that the evidence supporting their
use for chronic postoperative pain remains unclear [402–406]. For
acute postoperative pain in humans, current evidence indicates that
any statistically significant reductions in pain scores are not clini-
cally significant [407]. There is a growing body of veterinary litera-
ture describing its use in dogs [350,358,408–412], cats [413–417],
horses [418–421], and cattle [422–424], though questions remain
regarding its efficacy and appropriate dosing regimens.
The mechanism of action of gabapentin and pregabalin is not
fully understood. They do not appear to interact with GABA,
NMDA, or dopamine receptors, with most evidence indicating
inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels, with an intracellular
site of action that requires active uptake [425–427]. Inhibition leads
to a reduction of calcium influx, in turn reducing the release of a
range of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, altering chan-
nel trafficking, and stimulating movement of channels away from
neuronal cell membranes [426].
Pharmacokinetic data, primarily for gabapentin, are available for
dogs [411,428], cats [414,429], horses [418,419,430], cattle [422–
424], pigs [431], and horses [432]. In dogs, a short terminal half-life
suggests the need for frequent dosing; this is supported by limited
clinical evidence indicating that the therapeutic dose is in the range
of 10–20 mg/kg PO two to three times daily [408,410].
Approximately 30% of the drug undergoes hepatic metabolism (to
N-methyl-gabapentin), followed by renal elimination [428]. In
humans, pregabalin shows favorable pharmacokinetics over gabap-
entin, with greater binding affinity for the voltage-gated calcium
channel, linear pharmacokinetics, and non-saturable absorption
from the gastrointestinal tract [433]. It remains to be seen to what
extent these differences are present in animal species [429,432].
Since the previous edition of this textbook was published, several
randomized, double-blinded clinical trials have been published and
the following discussion will focus on these [434–436]. The most
common population for these studies has been Chiari-like malfor-
mation and syringomyelia in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels, which
is associated with neuropathic pain secondary to caudal cerebellar
herniation and development of syringes in the spinal cord [434–
436]. A randomized, placebo-controlled, double- blinded clinical
trial in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels with Chiari-like malforma-
tion and syringomyelia (n = 8 dogs) found significant reductions in
owner-rated pain scores using a numerical rating scale (including
spontaneous vocalizations, phantom scratching, and exercise
impairment) and improvement in quantitative sensory testing
(reduced mechanical hyperalgesia, cold hyperalgesia, and allo-
dynia) in dogs receiving pregabalin [434]. The mean difference in
pain scale scores was 1 (scale range 0 to 10). Dogs were given prega-
balin (5 mg/kg PO twice daily) or placebo for 14 days and all dogs
also received an NSAID throughout the study period. Two dogs
showed signs of sedation. Another study of Cavalier King Charles
Spaniels with Chiari-like malformation and syringomyelia, using a
randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded crossover design,
reported reduced scratching and pain intensity (both owner and
investigator assessed) and fewer scratching events (84% reduction)
associated with pregabalin treatment (n = 12 dogs) [435]. All own-
ers stated a preference for the period in which their dogs received
pregabalin. Dogs received 150 mg pregabalin PO twice daily (13–
19 mg/kg) for 21 days with a 2-day dose escalation, 2-day dose
tapering, and 2-day washout period between treatments. The main
adverse events reported were increased appetite (did not result in
significant increase in body mass) and transient ataxia. A third ran-
domized, blinded, crossover study in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels
with Chiari-like malformation and syringomyelia (n = 33) found a
significant improvement in quality of life associated with gabapen-
tin (approximately 11.5 mg/kg PO three times daily) combined
with carprofen (approximately 2.2 mg/kg PO once daily), in com-
parison with baseline scores or carprofen therapy alone [436].
Quality of life was owner-assessed using a visual analog scale (VAS)
and showed a 10-mm reduction on the scale. A similar result was
found with administration of the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor,
topiramate (approximately 11 mg/kg PO three times daily).
Blinding to treatment was incomplete as capsules containing gabap-
entin were labeled as such, limiting control of a placebo effect.
Reported adverse effects were mild and self-limiting and included
sedation, polyphagia, vomiting, diarrhea, and inappetence in four
dogs. One dog in the gabapentin-carprofen group died, but the
cause of death could not be determined (no necropsy performed).
Pharmacokinetic data for the use of pregabalin for analgesia in
dogs suggest that plasma concentrations associated with analgesia
in humans are achieved with a single dose of 4 mg/kg PO [437].
A randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study of pregabalin
(4 mg/kg PO three times daily) in 46 dogs (predominantly
Dachshunds) initiated immediately before surgery for interverte-
bral disc herniation and continued for 5 days postoperatively found
a significant reduction in pain scale scores (using a composite
measure pain scale; mean reduction of 2.5 units on a 0–20 scale)
and an increase in mechanical nociceptive thresholds [438]. Rescue
analgesia requirements were low and similar in both treatment
groups, and all dogs also had a fentanyl patch in place during the

-- 450 of 1450 --

Chapter 25: Anesthetic and Analgesic Adjunctive Drugs 	435
assessment period. Serum concentrations of pregabalin (sampled
shortly before the next dose was administered) were highly variable,
showing an approximately 30-fold difference between individuals.
A randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled clinical trial evaluat-
ing gabapentin in 29 dogs undergoing thoracic limb amputation did
not identify an advantage of gabapentin over placebo (gelatin cap-
sule) for postoperative pain [410]. Dogs received varying combina-
tions of other analgesics (methadone, fentanyl, and NSAIDs),
which may have made it difficult to identify a small treatment effect
(the authors suggested the trial was underpowered) and the gabap-
entin dose (10 mg/kg total daily dose) may have been insufficient. A
randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled clinical trial in a popula-
tion of dogs undergoing hemilaminectomy surgery (n = 63 dogs
total) included gabapentin (10 mg/kg PO twice daily) as an adjunc-
tive analgesic (alongside levomethadone and a fentanyl patch) [408].
Compared to placebo, there was a non-significant reduction in pain
scores. These mixed outcomes of gabapentin/pregabalin therapy
may also reflect its mechanism of action in relation to the disease
state, as voltage-gated calcium channels are upregulated following
nerve injury and there is a delay for this to occur [439,440]. This
could explain the lack of support for a role in acute postoperative
pain in humans [407]. Further clinical studies are needed to better
understand when gabapentin therapy is warranted.
In contrast to cats, gabapentin (20 mg/kg PO, 2 h before general
anesthesia) has an isoflurane MAC-sparing effect (20% ± 14%
reduction) in dogs, with no impact on cardiovascular varia-
bles [441]. Gabapentin (25–30 mg/kg PO) reduces fear behaviors in
dogs with storm phobia when given approximately 90 min before
exposure, with ataxia reported as an adverse effect [442].
Pharmacokinetic data for gabapentin in cats shows a high oral
bioavailability (approximately 90%) and terminal half-life of around
3–4 h, with a suggested a dosing regimen of 8 mg/kg PO every 8 h,
or 3 mg/kg PO every 6 h, in order to achieve plasma concentrations
associated with analgesia in humans [414,443,444]. However, an
increase in thermal threshold did not occur when gabapentin was
administered orally at 5, 10, or 30 mg/kg in healthy cats [413].
These doses resulted in plasma drug concentrations in excess of
those associated with analgesia in humans, leaving the authors to
question the utility of gabapentin in healthy cats and the adequacy
of the pain model. Sedation was not associated with gabapentin in
this study at any dose, though it is a common adverse effect in dogs.
The same investigators were not able to show a MAC-sparing effect
of gabapentin on isoflurane despite achieving plasma drug concen-
trations almost double those reported to be effective in humans,
though this does not rule out an analgesic effect [415]. In the pres-
ence of chronic kidney disease, plasma levels of gabapentin (10 mg/
kg PO) were elevated to twice the concentration observed with the
same dose in healthy cats and positively correlated with serum cre-
atinine and serum symmetric dimethylarginine concentrations,
indicating that dose reduction is necessary in cats with chronic kid-
ney disease [444]. A randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study
in cats undergoing ovariohysterectomy (n = 15–19 cats per treat-
ment group) did not identify a benefit of gabapentin (approximately
17 mg/kg PO twice daily) over meloxicam [417]. Rescue analgesia
was required in all treatment groups as follows: gabapentin (25% of
cats), meloxicam (13% of cats), and placebo (50% of cats). Two
doses of gabapentin were given preoperatively, and a single dose of
meloxicam (0.2 mg/kg SC) was given shortly before surgery. All cats
also received buprenorphine perioperatively. Despite a lack of clear
supporting evidence, it appears to be a popular choice for chronic
musculoskeletal pain in cats [443]. The successful use of gabapentin
(10 mg/kg PO every 8 h) was reported following polytrauma in two
cases of road traffic accidents [416]. In each case, clinical signs were
consistent with mechanical allodynia. Gabapentin was initiated
when mechanical allodynia was observed 24–48 h following the
surgical procedure and, in both cases, clinical signs resolved within
24 h, allowing a reduction of all administered analgesics.
Importantly, a multimodal analgesic approach was used in both
cases with cats also receiving opioids, NSAIDs, and locoregional
analgesia. Chronic use of gabapentin in three cats (polytrauma or
osteoarthritis) for between approximately 100–350 days (6.5 mg/kg
PO twice daily) has been reported, without apparent adverse
effects [445]. Pharmacokinetic data for pregabalin in cats indicate a
longer terminal half-life compared to gabapentin which, along with
linear pharmacokinetics, may make pregabalin preferable to gabap-
entin in this species [429,446]. Pregabalin (2 mg/kg PO twice daily)
was associated with superficial dermatitis lesions in a cat with squa-
mous cell carcinoma and clinical signs of neuropathic pain [447].
Lesions resolved with cessation of treatment and recurred when
pregabalin was re-started (in response to recurrence of clinical neu-
ropathic pain signs).
There has been increasing interest in gabapentin (13–30 mg/kg
PO 1 to 1.5 h before transport) and pregabalin (5–10 mg/kg PO 1.5
h before transport) for anxiety and fear reduction in cats with both
drugs appearing to be effective and associated with minimal, self-
limiting adverse effects (sedation, ataxia, hypersalivation, and vom-
iting) [448–450]. Pregabalin is approved in Europe and the United
States as a single oral dose (5 mg/kg 1.5 h before travel) to reduce
anxiety before travel and veterinary visits [450].
In a study of gabapentin, reporting pharmacokinetic and behavio-
ral data in horses, following 20 mg/kg PO or IV, no significant
changes in heart rate or mean arterial blood pressure were
recorded [419]. Sedation, scored as mild to moderate, occurred in all
horses for 1 h following IV gabapentin. The frequency of drinking
and standing at rest increased and decreased, respectively, over the
11-h observation period. Oral dosing of gabapentin had a lower bio-
availability in horses (16%) compared to dogs (80%), which is likely
to influence dosing requirements. No metabolites were detected in
equine plasma, indicating that metabolism may be similar to that
reported in humans, with the majority of drug excreted unchanged
in urine. These pharmacokinetic data were in broad agreement with
those previously reported in this species [418]. Oral dosing of gabap-
entin, up to 120 mg/kg PO twice daily, was not associated with seda-
tion or ataxia, and vital signs and serum biochemistry values
remained within the reference ranges [432]. By contrast, pregabalin
appears to have considerably higher oral (nasogastric tube) bioavail-
ability (> 90%) in horses, with a terminal half-life of 8 h [430].
There are few clinical reports of gabapentin use in horses
[420,421,451]. In one randomized, blinded, crossover study (n = 14
horses) of chronic thoracic limb lameness (navicular syndrome,
osteoarthritis, or collateral cartridge ossification), no advantage of
including gabapentin (20 mg/kg in grain twice daily) in addition to
an NSAID was identified [451]. Horses were evaluated with a subjec-
tive lameness score and various force plate measurements.
Gabapentin (2–3.3 mg/kg PO every 8 to 12 h) was included as
part of a multimodal analgesic plan (with opioids, NSAIDs, locore-
gional analgesia, α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists, and ketamine at
various times) in a horse following initial debridement of subsolar
seromas, followed by infection and ongoing chronic laminitis and
tendonitis [420]. Though difficult to specify the contribution of
gabapentin, pain scores improved with initiation of gabapentin
(along with concurrent perineural administration of bupivacaine)

-- 451 of 1450 --

436 	Section 3: Pharmacology
and no adverse effects were noted. In another reported case involv-
ing a pregnant mare following colic surgery, continuing signs of
pain (circling and pawing with the affected hoof) were associated
with femoral neuropathy and pelvic limb paresis [421]. Following a
lack of response to xylazine, butorphanol, flunixin, and a lidocaine
CRI, with adverse effects (marked sedation) during a detomidine
CRI, gabapentin was begun (2.5 mg/kg PO every 8 h for 24 h, then
every 12 h). Two h after giving gabapentin, during which time deto-
midine CRI (3 μg/ kg/h IV) and acepromazine (0.03 mg/kg IV
every 6 h) were continued, the mare was less agitated and clinical
signs improved over the following 36 h.
Pharmacokinetic and some pharmacodynamic data are available
in adult cows [424] and calves [422,423]. A comparison of gabapen-
tin (15 mg/kg PO once 1 h before dehorning) with flunixin, meloxi-
cam, and meloxicam with gabapentin did not result in significant
differences between groups or compared with placebo in plasma
cortisol concentrations or eye temperature [423]. The results for
mechanical nociceptive threshold were equivocal. Weight gain was
the only parameter to show a difference between analgesic treat-
ments and placebo. Average daily weight gain was greater in calves
treated with meloxicam and gabapentin than placebo, gabapentin
alone, or meloxicam alone. A combination of gabapentin (15 mg/kg
PO) and meloxicam (0.5 mg/kg PO) resulted in plasma levels of
gabapentin greater than 2 μg/mL (which is the threshold associated
with analgesia in humans) for 15 h [422]. Compared with horses
and dogs where maximal plasma concentrations were achieved
within 2 h, peak concentrations in calves were not reached until 7 h
post-administration. In adult Holstein-Friesian cows, the time to
achieve maximal plasma concentrations of gabapentin (10–20 mg/
kg PO co-administered with meloxicam 1 mg/kg PO) was also slow,
taking over 8 h [424]. Both gabapentin and meloxicam concentra-
tions in milk took 3 days to drop below the level of detection.
In dogs, approximately 30–35% of an administered dose of
gabapentin undergoes hepatic metabolism while unchanged drug is
excreted by the kidneys [428]. The metabolism of gabapentin has
not been reported in the cat.
Gabapentin is available as tablets and capsules (100, 300, 400,
600, and 800 mg) and as a 50 mg/mL oral formulation. Pregabalin
is available as capsules (25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 225, and 300 mg)
and as an oral solution (20 mg/mL).
Tapentadol
The analgesic agent tapentadol was designed with the aims of com-
bining μ-opioid receptor agonism and norepinephrine reuptake inhi-
bition without dependency on generating active metabolites, as is the
case with tramadol [452,453]. Tapentadol has a higher affinity
(approximately 50-fold) for the μ-opioid receptor compared to tram-
adol, but lower affinity compared to the M1 metabolite of tramadol.
Compared to tramadol, it has similar potency for inhibition of nor-
epinephrine reuptake, and lesser potency (approximately fivefold) at
inhibiting serotonin reuptake inhibition [452]. These activities, with-
out a reliance on metabolism to an active metabolite, make tapent-
adol an attractive analgesic option though evidence of its use in
veterinary species is limited. The pharmacokinetics have been
described in dogs and cats [454–456]. In dogs, it has a low oral bioa-
vailability (approximately 4%) and, as in humans, is expected to
undergo extensive hepatic metabolism (glucuronidation) to generate
inactive metabolites, of which tapentadol-O-glucuronide appears
most important in dogs [455,456]. Oral dosing at 10, 20, and 30 mg/
kg showed rapid absorption, with a terminal half-life of 3.5–4 h [456].
In a canine pharmacokinetic study, dose-related adverse effects
(salivation, sedation, and panting) were described more frequently
after IV administration [454]. The dose ranges were 1.4–3.9 mg/kg
IV and 5.7–15.8 mg/kg PO. This contrasts with an oral pharmacoki-
netic study in which no adverse effects (no change in heart or respira-
tory rates and no sedation) were reported at doses of 10, 20, and
30 mg/kg PO [456]. In cats, bioavailability appears high after IM
(94%) and SC (90%) injection with a terminal half-life of 2–3 h.
Adverse effects (salivation, agitation, and panting lasting around
15–20 min) were reported at a dose of 5 mg/kg but were more com-
mon following IV rather than IM or SC administration [455].
Effective doses in dogs and cats are not well established [457,458].
In an acute pain model (thermal withdrawal latency; tail flick) in
healthy Beagles, tapentadol (6.8 mg/kg IV) induced a significant
increase in withdrawal latency that was similar to morphine
(1.0 mg/kg IV) and lasted around 40 min with peak effect at
10 min [457]. In the same study, tramadol (6.8–10 mg/kg IV) had
no effect on thermal thresholds. Tapentadol was associated with
sedation, ataxia, hypersalivation, and diarrhea. An unblinded clini-
cal study of 18 dogs with cranial cruciate rupture assessed 4 h after
tapentadol (30 mg/kg PO) showed an improvement in subjective
lameness assessment, with no change in gait analysis variables [459].
No sedation was reported. In a randomized, blinded, crossover,
experimental study in healthy cats (n = 6), two different doses of
tapentadol (approximately 6 and 11 mg/kg PO) increased thermal
thresholds from baseline for 1- and 2-h post- administration,
respectively; however, thermal thresholds were not significantly
different from placebo. The 2-h duration of effect observed with the
higher tapentadol dose was comparable to that observed in the
buprenorphine (0.02 mg/kg IM) group [458]. Most cats hypersali-
vated following tapentadol administration, and this effect lasted up
to 20 min.
Tapentadol is classified as a controlled substance in most juris-
dictions. Oral formulations include 50, 75, and 100 mg tablets and a
20 mg/mL solution.
Tramadol
Tramadol is a racemic mixture and has been described as an “atypi-
cal” opioid due to the potential provision of analgesia via opioid and
non-opioid (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition)
mechanisms [460]. Interestingly, both enantiomers of the parent
compound and the M 1 metabolite (O-desmethyltramadol) contrib-
ute to analgesia. Norepinephrine reuptake inhibition results from
activity of the (– or levo)-enantiomer of tramadol, serotonin (5-
HT) reuptake inhibition results from activity of the (+ or dextro)-
enantiomer of tramadol, and μ-opioid receptor agonism results
from activity of the (+)-enantiomer of the M 1 metabolite and the
(+)- enantiomer of tramadol [460–462]. It is, therefore, clear that
the potential for interindividual as well as inter- and intraspecies
variation in analgesic potency may occur as a result of variations in
metabolism.
The pharmacokinetics of tramadol have been described in the
dog [463–469], cat [468,470,471], horse [472–475], alpaca [476],
llama [477], goat [478], piglet [479], and rhesus macaque [480].
In humans, metabolism of tramadol to the active M1 metabolite is
mediated by CYP2D6. In the dog, there appears to be limited produc-
tion of the M1 metabolite, indicating that analgesia is largely depend-
ent on activity of the parent compound, concentrations of which
display considerable interindividual variability (> 10-fold variation in
plasma concentrations) [461,463–466,481]. A canine hepatic micro-
somal study has identified CYP2D15 as contributing to M1 formation
and CYP2B11/CYP3A12 as contributing to the predominant inactive

-- 452 of 1450 --

Chapter 25: Anesthetic and Analgesic Adjunctive Drugs 	437
M2 metabolite (N-desmethyltramadol) [469]. While the therapeutic
plasma concentration of M1 is unknown in the dog, measured levels
are typically substantially below those associated with analgesia in
humans. This may explain the variability in efficacy observed clini-
cally, with a similar pattern observed in a subsection of humans who
are “poor metabolizers” (i.e., those lacking the CYP2D6 isozyme) and
consequently experience substantially lower analgesia from trama-
dol [482]. There is also evidence of genetic polymorphism in thor-
oughbred horses, which may explain the variation in plasma
metabolite concentrations in this species [483]. As tramadol is
excreted largely unchanged in urine, hepatic dysfunction would not
be expected to result in complications with therapeutic dosing.
In cats, metabolism of tramadol is significant, resulting in M 1
metabolite concentrations associated with analgesia in humans
[468,471,484]. Clearance was lower than reported in dogs, indi-
cating that less frequent dosing may be effective. Excretion of
parent drug and metabolites is suspected to be renal.
Tramadol may prove an effective analgesic in llamas as signifi-
cant concentrations of the M 1 metabolite were detected following
IV and IM administration, but clearance was similar to that
reported in horses, which could make frequent dosing neces-
sary [477]. In alpacas, a study of six adult animals discovered wide
interindividual variation in oral absorption (ranging from 6% to
20%) and rapid clearance, with variable detection of the M1 metab-
olite [476]. At doses of 3.4–4 mg/kg IV, adverse effects such as head
tremor, ataxia, and star gazing were observed. A lower rate of infu-
sion (i.e., the same dose but administered over 10 min) or oral dos-
ing was not associated with side effects. Further work is needed to
identify an effective dose in alpacas.
Lumbosacral epidural administration of tramadol (3 mg/kg) pro-
vided less effective and shorter acting analgesia than lidocaine
(4 mg/kg) in adult goats undergoing castration with a rubber ten-
sion band [485].
Since the previous edition of this book, a systematic review and
meta-analysis has been published on the use of tramadol for post-
operative analgesia in dogs [486]. In reviewing 26 randomized clin-
ical trials, including 848 dogs, the authors found that the certainty
of evidence (a reflection of quality of evidence) supporting the use
of tramadol for postoperative analgesia, specifically rescue analge-
sia requirement, was low or very low based on a four-point scale
(high, moderate, low, and very low). Studies published up to
2020 were included in this analysis and grading reflects the poor
quality of reporting, risk of bias, and imprecision, all of which are
recognized and ongoing problems in the veterinary literature [487–
491]. Disappointingly, none of the included studies performed a
power calculation to estimate sample size and most (25/26) were
designed as superiority trials, to identify a benefit of tramadol use.
Together, this makes interpretation of existing data challenging,
though evidence that tramadol does not make an important contri-
bution to either postoperative analgesia or experimental nocicep-
tive models continues to grow [457,481,492–494]. While there is
probably some benefit to providing tramadol versus no analgesia
(relative risk [RR]: 0.47; 95% CI: 0.26–0.85), its efficacy in reducing
the highest pain score observed is questionable (standardized mean
difference: –1.09; 95% CI: -2.34–0.16) [486]. When compared with
different opioids (methadone, morphine, butorphanol, buprenor-
phine, codeine, and nalbuphine), there was no clear benefit associ-
ated with tramadol, with a possible exception for nalbuphine
(tramadol may perform better; low certainty of evidence). There is
some evidence that tramadol is less effective than NSAIDs, though
the 95% CI for the RR is wide (RR: 2.27; 95% CI: 0.68–7.60).
Unfortunately, weaknesses in study design, limitations of using dif-
ferent pain assessment scales, and inconsistencies in their applica-
tion all contribute to difficulties in interpreting these data. The
ongoing popularity of tramadol for chronic osteoarthritis pain
management raises major concerns regarding the efficacy of anal-
gesia provided [492,495]. A 26–36% sevoflurane MAC-reduction
effect has been reported in dogs [496].
In horses, several pharmacokinetic studies of tramadol have been
performed [471–473,475,483,497]. In contrast to humans, and simi-
lar to dogs, production of the unconjugated M1 metabolite in horses
is low, below the threshold associated with analgesia in humans [474].
However, in contrast to dogs, this does not represent a limitation of
metabolism but rather very efficient glucuronidation (glucuronide-
conjugated M1 metabolite is rapidly produced following IV and PO
dosing) [473,474]. The role of the glucuronide-conjugated M1
metabolite in analgesia in horses is unclear. Similar to other species,
large interindividual variability in M1 metabolite production is also
present in horses, with some of this variability perhaps explained by
genetic polymorphism in CYP2D50 [473,474,483,497]. In addition
to low concentrations of the M1 metabolite, rapid clearance and
short terminal half-life (approximately 2–3 h) may limit the trama-
dol’s use in this species [473,474,483,497]. Repeated oral dosing (5
and 10 mg/kg every 12 h) resulted in accumulation of plasma trama-
dol (and extended terminal half-life) but not of its M1 metabolite,
though plasma concentrations continued to reflect widespread
interindividual variability [497]. One horse, with a high plasma con-
centration, developed signs of colic though a clear causal relation-
ship could not be established. Tramadol pharmacokinetics in foals
(6–43 days old, administered 3 mg/kg IV) differed from that of adult
horses, with a larger volume of distribution and faster clearance,
though glucuronidation capability was reduced and different adverse
effects were observed [475]. Between 13 and 43 days of age, transient
inactivity and sedation were observed.
Dose-dependent adverse behavioral effects (muscle tremors, agi-
tation, and circling) are observed following IV (1.5–3 mg/kg) but
not oral administration (3–10 mg/kg) in horses [473,474,497].
Doses of tramadol greater than 3.1 mg/kg IV in horses were associ-
ated with significant (approximately 100%) increases in respiratory
rate, 50% reductions in borborygmus, and trembling [498]. At
lower doses (0.3 mg/kg IV), signs associated with CNS stimulation
(i.e., head nodding) were observed.
Clinical data are increasingly available for both chronic and acute
pain conditions. In four horses with chronic laminitis given oral
tramadol (5 or 10 mg/kg twice daily), the higher dose resulted in a
modest improvement in comfort (using a proxy measure of off-
loading frequency) [499]. Extradural administration (0.5–1 mg/kg)
shows promise and may be a useful alternative route, providing
analgesia and limiting CNS stimulation [500,501]. The extradural
administration of tramadol has also been reported in cattle and
lambs [502,503]. In horses, a dose of 2 mg/kg IV did not result in
significant reductions in skin twitch latency or hoof withdrawal
reflex during exposure to thermal stimulation [498]. While higher
doses may have resulted in analgesia, the 2 mg/kg dose was selected
as adverse effects were observed with higher doses.
Sedation was observed with tramadol doses greater than 2 mg/kg
IV and at 4 mg/kg IM in dogs [466,504,505]. In cats, 1 mg/kg SC had
variable behavioral effects with six of eight cats exhibiting signs of
euphoria and two cats appearing dysphoric [506]. Reliance on renal
excretion of parent drug and the active M1 metabolite implies that
renal dysfunction might result in increased adverse effects [507],
though none have been reported in veterinary species.

-- 453 of 1450 --

438 	Section 3: Pharmacology
In cats, the limited evidence available shows some promise for
an analgesic effect of tramadol, which may reflect the increased
production of the M 1 metabolite in this species [413,471]. Further
research is needed to confirm these initial findings and establish
effective doses. Oral administration at 8.6–11.6 mg/kg was effec-
tive at reducing the MAC of sevoflurane by approximately
40% [508]. Doses between 2 and 4 mg/kg PO have been associated
with an increased thermal threshold in cats, and a dose of 4 mg/kg
PO every 6 h has been proposed for providing analgesia [413]. An
oral dose of 6 mg/kg provided similar levels of analgesia as 4 mg/
kg IM for ovariohysterectomy surgery, though the author recog-
nized a limitation of small sample size [509]. A comparison of
meperidine (pethidine) and tramadol (2 and 4 mg/kg IM) found
similar levels of analgesia, with an increased requirement for res-
cue analgesia in the meperidine group [510]. A 2 mg/kg IM dose
of tramadol appeared to provide similar levels of analgesia as both
morphine and control comparison groups (all cats also received
medetomidine and ketamine) though the group sample size was
estimated based on cardiovascular changes rather than pain
assessment [511]. In cats exposed to mechanical stimulation,
extradural administration of tramadol (1 mg/kg) was more effec-
tive than saline control but shorter lasting than extradural mor-
phine [512]. A 2 mg/kg SC dose was no more effective than
placebo following ovariohysterectomy when assessed with an
interactive VAS and composite pain score, though there was a
lower requirement for rescue analgesia compared with pla-
cebo [513]. A comparison of oral tramadol (3 mg/kg every 12 h)
combined with a meloxicam spray to placebo with meloxicam
spray in cats with osteoarthritis did not identify any advantage of
including tramadol [514]. Similarly, 1 mg/kg SC did not substan-
tially increase either pressure or thermal threshold responses in
cats [506]. An important barrier to the use of tramadol in cats is
the very low palatability of oral suspensions, which can trigger
considerable hypersalivation. Formulating oral doses as capsules
circumvents this problem [509,515]. A proprietary transdermal
formulation of tramadol (200 mg/mL tramadol), administered at
approximately 3 mg/kg either did not result in detectable plasma
tramadol concentrations or concentrations greater than 100 times
lower than an oral dose of 1 mg/kg [516]. Furthermore, the pro-
prietary metered-dose applicators delivered an amount that
exceeded the intended dose by up to 39%. In a randomized,
placebo-controlled, blinded comparison of different doses of
tramadol, in cats with osteoarthritis (0, 1, 2, and 4 mg/kg PO),
activity and owner-assessed outcomes improved at the 2 mg/kg
dose [515]. The frequency of adverse events was dose dependent,
with mydriasis, euphoria, agitation, sedation, decreased appetite,
and diarrhea observed most frequently. A case report of acciden-
tal tramadol overdose (80 mg/kg PO instead of 4 mg/kg PO)
resulted in agitation, hypersalivation, head jerking, and hyperten-
sion after the first dose, followed by obtunded mentation, lateral
recumbency, hypertension, tachycardia, abdominal distension,
and pain after a further dose [264]. These signs were attributed to
serotonin toxicity resulting from tramadol’s effects as a serotonin
reuptake inhibitor. The cat responded to supportive therapy (flu-
ids, analgesia), an enema to relieve abdominal distension, and
cyproheptadine (a serotonin receptor antagonist, 2 mg/kg PO
once daily), with resolution of clinical signs over several days.
Tramadol is classified as a controlled substance in most jurisdic-
tions. Available oral formulations include 50 and 100 mg tablets and
a 5 mg/mL oral solution. Injectable formulations are approved in
some countries.

History of neuromuscular blocking agents
Long before its introduction to medical practice, curare was extracted
primarily from plants, such as Chondrodendron species, by native
South American aboriginal populations for use in quivers, arrows,
or spears to hunt animals. Curare’s site of action, the neuromuscular
junction (NMJ), was described by Claude Bernard as early as 1844
through his well-known experiments using frog nerve–muscle
preparations, demonstrating that direct muscle stimulation could
be achieved while evoked contractions were abolished when motor
nerves were stimulated in the presence of curare. This discovery
was preceded by observations by Benjamin Brodie in 1812 who
described that animals injected with curare could be kept alive
if their lungs were ventilated. Later, in 1934, Henry Dale described
the role of acetylcholine (ACh) in neuromuscular transmission.
A multitude of studies that followed those original observations
described the anatomy and function of the NMJ and the neuro-
transmitters involved. The NMJ and the events that result in neu-
romuscular transmission are now well understood and an immense
amount of information has been made available since those initial
reports.
Curare was first introduced to medical practice as a potential
treatment for convulsive seizures and spasticity and as part of shock
therapy. It was then recognized that the effects of curare could be
useful in providing muscle relaxation during general anesthesia.
The first report of the agent being used for this purpose occurred in
1942 by Dr. Harold Randall Griffith and his resident, Dr. Enid
Johnson, during an appendectomy [1]. The synthesis of the alkaloid
agent tubocurarine followed and its use during anesthesia began to
gain traction. Further studies by Drs. John Halton and Cecil Gray
with tubocurarine in 1946 laid the foundation for development of
what became known as the “Liverpool anesthetic technique” – the
first example of the concept of balanced anesthesia. The technique
became popular and the practice of using deep planes of anesthesia
to avoid movement was largely abandoned [2–4]. Within the next
10 years, the use of neuromuscular blockade for anesthesia in
people had spread throughout the world.
Neuromuscular blocking agents in veterinary
anesthesia
Possibly owing to more limited access to mechanical ventilators, or
because most intubations and surgeries can be performed in veteri-
nary species without the need for muscle paralysis, the uptake on
incorporating neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) into vet-
erinary anesthesia has been much slower and more limited than in
human anesthesiology. The depolarizing agent succinylcholine was
first used for canine anesthesia in 1952 [5] and in 1954, Hall and
Weaver described the use of the nondepolarizing agent gallamine
coupled with positive-pressure ventilation as part of balanced anes-
thesia in the dog and cat [6]. Since those initial reports, a significant
body of evidence relating to the effects, clinical use, monitoring,
and antagonism of neuromuscular blockade in veterinary anesthesia
has now accumulated. While our understanding of these agents has
grown exponentially, NMBAs remain part of only a small proportion
of all cases in veterinary anesthesia [7].

Anatomy and physiology of the
neuromuscular junction
NMBAs exert their actions by interrupting transmission through
the NMJ. The NMJ is composed of a presynaptic motor neuron
and a postsynaptic skeletal muscle cell separated by the synaptic
cleft (Fig. 26.1). The presynaptic cell originates in the spine and
travels uninterrupted to the target muscle. It loses its myelin sheath
when it approaches the synapse and branches to contact several
muscle cells, composing what is known as a “motor unit.” This
presynaptic cell synthetizes and stores ACh in vesicles; both a
reserve and a readily available population of ACh vesicles are
found within this cell. Depolarization of the motor neuron results
in an influx of Ca 2+ via voltage-gated channels that triggers the
mobilization of vesicles and the release of a large amount of ACh
into the cleft. When two molecules of ACh interact with both α
subunits of a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) located in
the folds of the postsynaptic cell, a conformational change occurs
within the receptor, allowing an influx of Na + into the skeletal
muscle cell. Depolarization of the endplate terminal triggers the
activation of voltage-gated Na + channels that propagate the action
potential along the cell, signaling the process for muscular contrac-
tion [8,9]. The interaction between ACh and the nAChR is very
brief, with its effects terminating almost immediately. Free ACh is
promptly hydrolyzed by the acetylcholinesterase enzyme into cho-
line and acetic acid [10]. The sudden and drastic reduction in the
concentration of ACh in the cleft favors the movement of ACh
away from the nAChR.
The amount of ACh released by the nerve is affected by the con-
centration of extracellular Ca2+
. The absence of Ca2+ would result in
the absence of ACh release and muscular contractions, while dou-
bling the concentration of Ca2+ would result in a 16-fold increase in
the amount of released ACh. Under normal circumstances, only a
fraction of the available vesicles of ACh are released; however, this
fraction is more than sufficient for effective neuromuscular trans-
mission. Moreover, only a small number of available nAChR need
to be activated to cause maximal depolarization of the muscle cell.
These redundancies in the process of neuromuscular transmission
provide the NMJ with a substantial margin of safety and an immense
reserve [11].
Pentameric nAChRs are found postsynaptically in the shoulders
of the primary clefts, and presynaptically in the motor nerve. The
postsynaptic receptor contains two α1 subunits, which are the bind-
ing sites of ACh (and NMBAs). The fetal and mature forms of this
receptor vary by only one subunit: a γ subunit in the fetal subtype,
and the ε subunit in the mature form. β1 and δ subunits complete
the receptor. The fetal subtype, and a third subtype composed of α7
subunits, are found during development, and are replaced by the
mature form soon after birth; the adult form remains for life. The
fetal and α7 subtypes can also proliferate in abnormal situations
that result in decreased muscle activity, such as poor innervation,
prolonged immobilization, or increased muscle catabolism (e.g.,
inflammation). Opening time of the sodium channel and sensitivity
to specific ligands are altered in these receptors. This explains in
part why increased sensitivity to succinylcholine and decreased
potency of nondepolarizing agents are observed in neonates or dur-
ing abnormal states when other subtypes of the nAChR proliferate.
Upregulation of receptors may also be involved in the differences
observed during neuromuscular pathologies [12,13].
Presynaptic nAChR are also found in the NMJ. Through positive
and negative feedback loops, presynaptic receptors control the
mobilization and release of ACh. A negative feedback loop stops
further release of the transmitter when the concentrations of ACh

may play a key role in the development of fade during repeated
nerve stimulation when nondepolarizing NMBAs are used (discussed
in the section on monitoring neuromuscular transmission). The
depolarizing agent succinylcholine does not inhibit this receptor,
explaining why no fade is observed when that agent is used [14].
Neuromuscular blockade
Neuromuscular transmission can be interrupted, producing paralysis,
and thereby providing one of the main components of anesthesia
(relaxation/immobility) without the need for excessively profound
depression of the central nervous system. NMBAs do this through
one of two main mechanisms: depolarization of the postsynaptic
cell (depolarizing NMBA) or competitive antagonism of the nAChR
(nondepolarizing NMBA).
Pharmacology and nomenclature
The effects of NMBAs are measured by quantitating the reduction
in the evoked force of contraction (or a surrogate). Potency is deter-
mined by constructing a dose-response curve, which is composed
of the responses to several submaximal doses (Fig. 26.2A). From
that relationship, the effective doses that produce 50% and 95%
depression of force of contraction (ED 50 and ED 95
, respectively) can
be identified. The ED95 can be used to compare agents given at equi-
potent doses, or to compare the characteristics of multiples of the
ED 95
. The onset time is the interval between administration and a
predetermined effect, typically 95% depression. Duration of action
(sometimes called “duration of clinical or surgical block”) is the
time between injection and the return of 25% (sometimes 10%) of
force of contraction. The recovery index is the time between 25%
and 75% recovery of the evoked force of contraction and describes
the slope (or speed) of recovery. Complete recovery of neuromus-
cular transmission requires more time and is reached when no
residual weakness can be measured (Fig. 26.2B).
Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents
Nondepolarizing NMBAs exert their action through competitive
antagonism of the nAChR receptors. The binding of a nondepolar-
izing NMBA with at least one α1 subunit of the nicotinic receptor
prevents the conformational change produced by ACh. Therefore,
Na+ influx, depolarization, and contraction do not occur. In general,
nondepolarizing NMBAs are large, water-soluble molecules, with
relatively low volumes of distribution (typically 0.2–0.4 L/kg) that do
not cross the placenta or the blood–brain barrier. No sensory
