Resistance
Factors opposing blood flow (i.e., afterload) are described and quan-
titated in terms of resistance, hindrance, and impedance. These
terms are frequently conflated but are not the same and should not
be used interchangeably. The Hagen–Poiseuille equation is the pop-
ular method employed for reporting vascular resistance (R):
R 	L 	r	8 	4
	/
R is usually derived by dividing the change in pressure by flow
(i.e., R = (P1 – P2
)/Q) and although convenient is arguably the least
accurate since, as stated previously, blood is not a Newtonian fluid,
vessels are not rigid tubes, and blood flow is not laminar in all parts
of the arterial tree. The rheological term that characterizes blood
flow conditions (i.e., blood flow velocity) is “shear rate,” which is
a function of blood flow velocity and vascular geometry. Blood vis-
cosity is shear rate (i.e., blood flow velocity) dependent. Viscosity
decreases as shear rate increases according to this equation:
shear stress dynes/cm 	/shear rate s	2 	1
where η is viscosity and shear stress is the force applied during pul-
satile blood flow between theoretic parallel layers of blood in the
blood vessel [221,222]. Shear rate gradually increases and blood vis-
cosity decreases as large arteries become smaller and is greatest in
the capillaries regardless of low blood flow rates [223,224]. This phe-
nomenon (decreased blood viscosity in smaller vessels) is known
as the “Fåhræus–Lindqvist effect” and is attributed to the centrali-
zation (i.e., central streaming) of RBCs, reduced RBC numbers
(Fåhræus effect) at the vessel wall (“plasma skimming”), and RBC
deformability. Rephrasing, as the diameter of the vessel decreases,
the concentration of RBCs decreases (Fåhræus effect) and blood
viscosity also decreases (Fåhræus–Lindqvist effect) [225]. Viscosity
in capillaries is low because RBCs pass through capillaries single file
in the center of the capillary. Blood viscosity is, therefore, dependent
upon the RBC concentration (hematocrit), RBC deformability and
aggregability, plasma viscosity, temperature, and blood flow condi-
tions [226,227]. Notably, blood viscosity is rarely measured or calcu-
lated in most studies reporting vascular resistance although it can be
responsible for significant effects in smaller blood vessels, during
hemodilution, and in low blood flow states. Maintaining normal
blood viscosity sustains microcirculatory blood flow and supports
coherence between macrovascular and microvascular perfusion
(i.e., hemodynamic coherence) [228–231].
Vascular hindrance (Rh ) varies with blood viscosity (η) and vessel
geometry (i.e., radius, length) and the number of blood vessels
arranged in parallel over which the resistance measurement is being
made [232]. Vascular hindrance (Rh ) is

An increase in viscosity is known to produce compensatory

Impedance (Z) is defined as the ratio between the frequency com-
ponents of the local blood pressure and blood flow waveforms [235].
Impedance includes both the resistance (R) and reactance (i.e.,
changes in vessel compliance or stiffness) of the vessel wall to pul-

where ZL represents longitudinal impedance, which is the sum of
the pulsatile (Rp

conditions, the steady resistive non-pulsatile component (R) repre-
sents approximately 85–90% of the total impedance to blood flow
while the pulsatile component (Rp

10–15%. This fact (R = 85–90% of ZL

investigators and clinicians are usually satisfied with the determina-

(i.e., Hagen–Poiseuille equation: R = P/Q). The components of Z
change substantially, however, during heart failure or pharmaco-
logical manipulation [237]. Aortic input impedance (Zi) is the ratio
of pressure and flow at the aortic root and is dependent upon aortic
elastance or compliance [235,236]. Impedance to blood flow, there-
fore, is viewed as having a resistive (steady-state [R]) component
due primarily to the arterioles and a reactive (pulsatile [Rp
]) compo-
nent due to vessel wall properties (i.e., compliance, elastance, and
pulse-wave reflection). Low systolic arterial pressure enables more
complete ventricular ejection, maintains low myocardial oxygen
demands, and provides little stimulus for producing hypertrophy.
High diastolic pressure ensures adequate coronary blood flow and
myocardial perfusion because most of myocardial blood flow
occurs during ventricular relaxation. Increases in systolic and dias-
tolic pressures increase myocardial work, oxygen consumption, and
energy requirements and decrease myocardial perfusion [215].
Ideally, the best match between the heart’s pumping activity and the
vascular response to the ejection of blood (ventricular–vascular
coupling) is obtained when myocardial work is kept as low as pos-
sible (i.e., relatively low systolic pressure), while adequate myocar-
dial and peripheral tissue perfusion (i.e., higher diastolic pressure)
is maintained [238]. Anesthesia and fluid therapy generally decrease
hematocrit and plasma protein concentrations leading to decreases
in blood viscosity, which, when combined with a decrease in imped-
ance (i.e., vasodilation and vessel smooth muscle relaxation),
favorably affect ventricular–vascular coupling, providing that
hypotension (e.g., Pm < 60 mmHg) does not occur [239–242].
The optimum hematocrit for transporting oxygen varies among
species and generally ranges between 30% and 45% [243]. Splenic
contraction (e.g., dogs and horses) provides additional RBCs (i.e.,
increases hematocrit) and oxygen-carrying capacity during times of
stress or exercise [244]. Excessively elevated hematocrits (e.g., poly-
cythemia; > 65%) and hyperproteinemia (e.g., dehydration) dra-
matically increase blood viscosity and myocardial work due to an
increase in RBC aggregability and rouleaux formation resulting in
an increase in Rp (i.e., Z) and a decrease in oxygen delivery to tis-
sues. Hemodilution (e.g., isovolumic hemodilution) can be benefi-
cial in reducing blood viscosity and is used during anesthesia to
improve oxygen delivery to tissues [245,246]. Blood flow is more
dependent upon plasma viscosity in smaller vessels (< 100 μm) and
capillaries [246]. The viscous properties of plasma and its effects on
wall shear stress, nitric oxide production, and functional capillary
density, therefore, are particularly significant for maintaining
microcirculatory flow [247,248]. Hematocrit values less than 30%,
however, jeopardize blood oxygen content, microcirculatory blood
flow, and tissue oxygenation. Anesthesia and fluid therapy generally
produce favorable effects on hematocrit, RBC deformability, and

plasma protein concentration, leading to alterations in blood vis-
cosity, which decrease impedance and improve ventricular–vascular
coupling [241,242].
Preload and afterload
Preload is the stretch (i.e., increased muscle length) or load imposed
on a muscle fiber or the myocardial wall at the end of diastole just
before contraction begins (Box 33.3) [249]. End-diastolic muscle
length (i.e., in vitro), end-diastolic volume (EDV), end-diastolic
pressure (EDP), and ventricular wall stress have all been used as
measures of preload. Sarcomere length provides the most meaning-
ful measure of preload but is impossible to measure in vivo. The
EDV is directly related to the degree of stretch imposed on myocar-
dial sarcomeres and, therefore, provides the most accurate in vivo
preload determinant. Preload is usually explained in terms of the
Frank–Starling relationship where the force generated by ventricu-
lar contraction occurs in direct relation to the end-diastolic fiber
length (i.e., heterometric autoregulation) [250]. Increases in cardiac
muscle resting tension likely increase sensitivity to calcium, result-
ing in an increase in contractile force [251]. The Frank–Starling
relationship serves as an important compensatory mechanism for
maintaining SV when afterload or contractility is acutely changed
(Fig. 33.32) [252]. Notably, preload is affected by afterload [253].
Increases in afterload decrease the volume of blood pumped by
the heart with each beat (i.e., SV), which results in increased end-
systolic volume (ESV) that augments EDV (i.e., preload).
Afterload is the force opposing ventricular ejection (Box 33.3)
[249]. Although conceptually straightforward use of the term
“afterload” suffers from multiple definitions and incomplete under-
standing of what the term represents. Afterload in isolated muscle
tissues (i.e., in vitro) is the external force that inhibits the muscle
(i.e., sarcomere) from shortening [200]. In contrast, afterload
in intact animals changes continuously throughout ventricular
ejection and is more accurately described by the hindrance or
impedance to blood flow during ventricular ejection. An acute
increase in arterial blood pressure increases ventricular EDV and
decreases SV. The increased ventricular EDV increases ventricular
wall stretch and contractile force via the Frank–Starling mechanism
(i.e., heterometric autoregulation). This, however, is followed by a
progressive decrease in the EDV to near-normal values and a sus-
tained increase in SV (i.e., homeometric autoregulation; von Anrep
effect; Box 33.3). Multiple mechanisms are responsible for this
response including release of angiotensin II and endothelin, activa-
tion of the mineralocorticoid receptor and myocardial Na + –H+
exchanger, increase in intracellular Na+ concentration, and aug-
mentation of the Ca 2+ transient amplitude through the Na +
–Ca2+
exchanger (NCX). The net effect of all of these mechanisms is an
increased SV at a lower diastolic volume [254]. The major reason
for interest in afterload is because of its inverse relationship with
SV in failing hearts and its direct correlation with myocardial
oxygen consumption (i.e., MVO 2
) as a result of an increase in ven-
tricular wall tension (Fig. 33.31) [215]. The effects of anesthetic
drugs on afterload and homeometric autoregulation require further
investigation.
The cardiac cycle and pressure–volume loop
Detailed illustrations of the cardiac cycle (i.e., Wiggers diagram) are
used to explain the time-related relationships among the various
electrical, mechanical (e.g., pressure, volume, and flow), and acous-
tic (Table 33.9) components of cardiac contraction and relaxation
(Fig. 33.33A) [255]. The diagram provides a pictorial representa-
tion of all the major events that occur during one cardiac cycle.
Similarly, the ventricular pressure–volume (PV) loop provides a
real-time image of changes in ventricular pressure plotted against
ventricular volume (Fig. 33.33B) [256,257]. Changes in the PV loop
are used to illustrate and quantitate changes in cardiac function:
preload, afterload, contractility, and ventricular–vascular cou-
pling [256–258]. Various components of the cardiac cycle and PV
loop for both the right and left ventricles are qualitatively similar,
although quantitatively different.
The P wave of the surface ECG is a reasonable starting point to
begin a description of the cardiac cycle since electric activity pre-
cedes mechanical activity (Fig. 33.33A). Electrical impulses origi-
nating in the SA node are rapidly transmitted from the right to the
left atrium by atrial specialized fibers (i.e., Bachmann’s bundle)
causing generation of the P wave and almost simultaneous contrac-
tion of the right and left atria. Bifid P waves representing electrical
activation of the right and then left atria are frequently observed in
ECGs obtained from larger animals (e.g., horses and cattle) due to
the increased size and volume of the atria, and the time required to
traverse the increased muscle mass. Atrial contraction increases
intra-atrial pressure, producing the “a” wave of the atrial pressure
curve. Both right and left atria function as reservoirs and conduits
for blood transfer and, upon contraction (i.e., atrial kick), prime the
ventricles contributing approximately 10–30% of the ventricular
blood volume at resting HRs and becoming more important at
faster HRs. The reflected pressure wave from the atrial kick and
structural vibrations in the AV valves prior to ventricular contrac-
tion are responsible for the fourth heart sound (S 4
, atrial gallop) that
generally remains inaudible in small animals (e.g., dogs and cats)
but is frequently auscultated in larger animals (e.g., horses and cat-
tle) or in animals with dilated and stiffened ventricles (Table 33.9).
Ventricular contraction is signaled by the R wave and begins after a
variable delay (i.e., PR interval), during which the electrical impulse
traverses the AV node. Once the ventricle is electrically activated,
ventricular contraction raises intracavitary pressure to a value
greater than in the atrium closing the AV (i.e., tricuspid and mitral)
valves. The AV valves bulge into their respective atria due to the

increased pressures in their respective ventricles, thereby decreas-

sure curve. The AV valves are prevented from completely prolapsing
into the atrial chambers by cord-like fibrous structures (i.e., chor-
dae tendineae) that connect ventricular papillary muscles to the
edges of the tricuspid and the mitral valves. The sudden develop-
ment of tension in the contracting ventricular myocardium and
tensing of the chordae tendineae coincident with AV valve closure
are responsible for the first heart sound (S 1
; Table 33.9). The rapid
increase in ventricular pressure while both the AV and semilunar
(i.e., aortic and pulmonic) valves are closed produces isovolumic
contraction (Fig. 33.33A,B). Once ventricular pressure exceeds that
in the aorta or pulmonary artery, the semilunar valves open and
ventricular ejection begins (Fig. 33.33A). The initial portion of the
ejection phase of the cardiac cycle coincides with an abrupt decrease
in ventricular volume, a large increase in aortic flow velocity, and a
decrease in the venous pressure curve since the AV valves are drawn
toward the apex of the heart thereby increasing the volume of the
atria (i.e., the “x descent” following the “c” wave of the atrial pres-
sure curve; Fig. 33.33A). Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pres-
sure during the first one-third of ventricular ejection (i.e., the rapid
ejection period), reaches equilibrium with aortic pressure, and
thereafter declines more rapidly than aortic pressure because of the
onset of ventricular relaxation. Once the ventricular pressure
decreases to values below the arterial pressure, the semilunar valves
close. Closure of the semilunar valves is associated with the devel-
opment of an incisura (i.e., dicrotic notch) in the arterial pressure
waveform, the second heart sound (S2
), and the end of ventricular
systole. The second heart sound is composed of both aortic (A2
)
and pulmonic (P 2
) components and is frequently split (10–15 ms)
during slow HRs and in larger species (e.g., horses and cattle) [259].
The volume of blood ejected by the ventricle (i.e., SV) is the differ-
ence between ventricular EDV and ESV
SV 	EDV ESV
The period between closure of the semilunar valves and open-
ing of the AV valves and the beginning of ventricular filling is
termed “isovolumic relaxation” (Fig. 33.33A,B). Isovolumic relax-
ation is characterized by a rapid decrease in ventricular pressure
and no change in ventricular volume. Once ventricular pressure
falls below atrial pressure, the AV valves open, initiating a phase of
rapid ventricular filling and producing the third heart sound (S 3 ;
ventricular gallop; Table 33.9). The third heart sound is believed
to be caused by vibrations in the ventricular walls once they reach
their elastic limit during ventricular filling. The third sound is fre-
quently heard in larger species (horses and cattle) or in dogs and
cats with dilated ventricular chambers due to cardiac disease [260].
Ventricular filling proceeds more gradually after the initial rapid
filling phase, whereas ventricular pressure and volume increase
nonlinearly during late diastole (Fig. 33.33B). The slope of the PV
curve (dP/dV) during ventricular filling is an index of ventricular
elasticity, and its inverse (dV/dP) is used to assess ventricular
compliance [257]. The ventricular filling phase continues as blood
returns to the atria from the systemic and pulmonary circulations
until the cardiac cycle is reinitiated by the next SA nodal electrical
impulse.

A PV loop represents the simultaneous changes in pressure and
volume that take place during a single cardiac contraction and is
represented as an irregular rectangle, inscribed in a counterclock-
wise fashion, in which intraventricular pressure is plotted on the y-
axis against ventricular volume on the x-axis [257,261]. Analysis of
the PV loop begins at point (B) and occurs at end-diastole (i.e., at
the onset of systole as demarcated by closure of the AV valves and
the first heart sound; Fig. 33.34A). The coordinates of this point are
EDV and EDP. The ratio of EDV to EDP is a measure of static ven-
tricular compliance, and the ratio of EDP to EDV is a measure of
static ventricular stiffness. The relative slope of the ventricular fill-
ing line from A to B (Fig. 33.34A) is an estimate of dynamic ven-
tricular compliance (Cdynamic
) and the steepness of the slope is a
measure of dynamic stiffness.
Ventricular pressure increases rapidly from B to C once the AV
valves close, but there is no change in volume (i.e., isovolumetric
contraction) until the semilunar valve opens at C (Fig. 33.34A) and
blood begins to be ejected into the aorta. Ventricular pressure
changes minimally during the ventricular ejection from C to D (i.e.,
isotonic contraction; Fig. 33.34A) but ventricular volume decreases.
The change in ventricular volume represented by the horizontal
distance between BC and DA (Fig. 33.34A) is the SV, and the ratio
(SV/EDV) is the ejection fraction (EF).
EF 	SV/EDV
The EF is the percentage of the EDV the ventricle pumps into the
aorta during each contraction and ranges from 50–60% in healthy
animals. The EF is considered a “gold standard” for assessing the
general health of the cardiovascular system [262,263].
Closure of the semilunar valves (i.e., point D) indicates the end of
systole. The ratio of end-systolic pressure (ESP) to ESV (ESP/ESV)
is a measure of end-systolic elastance or stiffness of the ventricle
contracting from any given EDV. The slope of the end-systolic
pressure–volume relationship (ESPVR) obtained from ventricular
contractions during decreases in ventricular volume is a load-
independent measure of myocardial contractility [261]. This slope

(Ees
) is believed to be the most useful and accurate load-independent
estimate of cardiac contractility currently available (Fig. 33.34B).
The ventricular pressure falls quickly once the semilunar valves
close (i.e., D to A; isovolumetric relaxation; Fig. 33.34A) and the
ventricles begin to fill once the AV valves open.
Arterial elastance (Ea
), a measure of the opposition to ventricular
ejection (i.e., afterload), is the slope of a line that starts at the EDV
and goes through the end-systolic PV point (Fig. 33.34B). Ea can
also be calculated (i.e., Ea = Pes
/SV) [261]. The Ea
/Ees ratio is a meas-
ure of ventricular–arterial coupling and is normally close to 1.0
implying that the ventricular and arterial systems are optimally
coupled (Fig. 33.34C) [264,265]. Ventricular–arterial uncoupling
occurs when the Ea
/Ees ratio is > 1.0.
The total area within the PV loop represents the total work per-
formed by the ventricle against the opposition to ejection (i.e., after-
load) imposed by arterial pressure and the stiffness (i.e., elastance)
of the arterial wall. Total work is comprised of both internal work
(i.e., cycling of heavy meromyosin heads and stretching the series
elastic elements) and external work (i.e., moving a volume of blood
against a resistance). Total work is a measure of myocardial oxygen
consumption (MVO2
) and, along with oxygen delivery (DO2
), is
used to estimate energetic balance (MVO2 /DO2 ) and oxygen extrac-
tion ratio (O2
ER = MVO 2
/DO2
) [215].
Thus, ventricular PV loops allow calculation of: (1) intracardiac
ventricular pressures, (2) ventricular compliance, (3) myocardial
contractility, (4) SV, and (5) myocardial oxygen consumption. In
addition, the ratio of pulsatile aortic pressure to SV is an estimate of
arterial stiffness and, like Ea
/Ees
, can be used to monitor changes in
ventricular–vascular coupling [266].
The cardiac cycle and PV loop illustrate the hemodynamic events
that occur during cardiac contraction and relaxation (Figs. 33.33
and 33.34). Clinically, M-mode echocardiography and two-
dimensional color-flow Doppler echocardiography provide a
dynamic representation of cardiac function (Fig. 33.35) [267]. For
example, CO can be quantitatively estimated non-invasively (e.g.,
via echocardiography) as the product of HR and SV:
CO 	HR SV
SV 	LVOT area LVOT VTI
where LVOT area is the left ventricular outflow tract area and LVOT
VTI is the velocity time integral.
Assessment of cardiac function
Assessment of cardiac contractile function (i.e., systolic function)
encompasses multiple physical and image-based methods for deter-
mining performance (i.e., CO), inotropy (i.e., force), and contractil-
ity (i.e., force and velocity) (Box 33.4) [268–270]. Measurements of
CO and inotropy are load-dependent and, therefore, must account
for changes in either preload or afterload to explain hemodynamic
and cardiovascular functional changes. Cardiac contractility is
load-independent and, therefore, requires methods of measure-
ment that are not sensitive to changes in preload, afterload, or
HR [69,206]. Contractility is generally described by shifts of the
force–velocity–length relationship, shifts in the ventricular func-
tion curve (e.g., shifts in the Frank–Starling relationship) when
preload and afterload are held constant, or by changes in Ees
(Fig. 33.36) [89,257,261,265]. Available indices used to evaluate car-
diac contractile function generally fall into one of four broad cate-
gories: (1) isovolumic contraction phase indices, (2) ejection phase

techniques used to manipulate preload or afterload are important.
Changes in preload induced by administering IV fluids or removal
of blood, occlusion of the caudal vena cava, or by changing after-
load via physical constriction of the aorta produce a different result
than changing preload or afterload pharmacologically (e.g., meth-
oxamine, phenylephrine to increase afterload; nitroprusside, isoflu-
rane to decrease preload). Differences arise due to the additional
vasoactive, inotropic, clinotropic, lusitropic, chronotropic, and
dromotropic properties that these drugs produce [202,263]. The PV
loop produces more information about contraction and relaxation
of the ventricle than any other method of expressing either systolic
or diastolic function. It allows direct measurement of EDV
(preload), ESV, SV, and EDP and permits calculation of EDP/EDV
(elastance), PRSW, Ees
, Ea
, Ea
/Ees
, and the slope of the PV curve dur-

between the interruptions could be used to calculate dLVP/dtmax
,

inversely to EF, can be obtained non-invasively, and is considered to
be the “gold standard” of ventricular systolic function in clinical
cardiology [274].
Less invasive assessment of Ees has been approximated by myo-
cardial stress, magnetic resonance elastography, or from a single
PV loop for which volume is estimated non-invasively by echocar-
diography and pressure is estimated indirectly from peak systemic
systolic arterial pressure using sphygmomanometry [275]. Despite
arithmetic “corrections,” estimates of volume (by echocardiogra-
phy) and pressure (e.g., sphygmomanometer) are at best esti-
mates. “True” ESV obtained by echocardiography is limited by
geometrical considerations, precision, and reproducibility, while
“true” ESP differs from peak pressure in non-central arteries with
peripheral arterial peak pressure variably and significantly higher
than that realized by the ventricle at end-systole [276]. Regardless,
evaluation of contractility estimated from a single PV loop
obtained by non-invasive measurements has produced accurate
predictions of patient outcomes [276,277]. In addition, segmental
strain curves obtained non-invasively by trans-diaphragmatic
two-dimensional echocardiographic images and speckle tracking
analysis have been demonstrated to produce a load-independent
measure of the cardiac contractile state [278]. The PV relationship
has been used to assess the effects of most anesthetic drugs on
cardiac function [279–281].

coupling and is fundamentally important to an understanding of
cardiac performance [112,282]. The most popular and clinically rel-
evant definition of diastole states that relaxation begins with the
closure of the aortic valve, which is indicated by the second heart
sound (S 2
, Fig. 33.33A). Diastole is thereafter divided into four
phases: (1) isovolumic relaxation, (2) early rapid ventricular filling,
(3) slow (i.e., reduced) ventricular filling (diastasis), and (4) atrial
systole (during sinus rhythm). Mechanical factors, loading factors,
inotropic activity, HR, and synchronicity (patterns of relaxation)
are the major determinants of lusitropy [112,283–285]. Factors and
interventions that alter relaxation are of special interest because of
their importance in determining ventricular compliance or stiff-
ness. A partial list of methods used to quantitatively describe relax-
ation includes pressure, volume-derived, and interval indices
(Box 33.4). Indices of isovolumetric relaxation (i.e., the rate of ven-
tricular pressure decline; –dP/dt) and the time constant for relaxa-
tion (τ) are useful for measuring the active phase of relaxation and
reflect the dissociation of actin–myosin linkages because of reup-
take of cytoplasmic calcium by the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Both
indices are influenced by myocardial systolic function, ventricular
loading conditions (preload and afterload), and HR and are, there-
fore, considered to be load-dependent.
Drugs used as preanesthetic medication or for intravenous or
inhalation anesthesia often produce profound effects on the cardio-
vascular system and indices of cardiac function (Table 33.10).
While the arterial effects of anesthetic dugs are well-recognized,
consideration should also be given to effects on venous physiology,
unstressed vascular volume (Vus
), and venous return. The venous
vascular effects of anesthetics on the effective or stressed circulating
blood volume (Vs
) are much more complex than originally sur-
mised and can be responsible for precipitous and dramatic decreases
in venous return and cardiac function [286,287].
Oxygen delivery and oxygen consumption
The importance of adequate oxygen delivery (DO2 ) cannot be over-
emphasized because reduced oxygen consumption (VO 2 ) and the
development of increasing oxygen debt are directly linked to increased
morbidity and mortality [288–291]. Once DO2 falls below the mini-
mum threshold for tissue metabolic requirements an oxygen supply–
demand imbalance occurs (Fig. 33.36). Inadequate DO2 increases
oxygen debt and promotes anaerobic metabolism [289]. The severity
of oxygen debt and anaerobic metabolism can be quantitated by their
metabolic correlates, lactic acid and negative base excess (i.e., base
deficit) [291]. Lactate accumulation and base deficit are used clini-
cally, to quantitate the onset and severity of oxygen debt, the probability
of death (LD50
), and the therapeutic reversal of oxygen debt [292].
Tissue oxygen consumption (VO 2 ) is determined by cellular
metabolic rate. The VO2 can be determined by the Fick, or oxygen
consumption, equation [293]:
VO 	CO CaO 	CvO	2 	2 	2

Decreased Hb concentration (e.g., parasitism, hemorrhage, and
hemodilution) causes OE to increase to maintain the requisite
oxygen delivery required by metabolizing tissues. The critical Hb
concentration, DO2Crit
, and OERCrit are approximately 4 g/dL,
5–7 mL/kg/min, and 0.6 (60%), respectively, in normal healthy
dogs (Fig. 33.36) [294,295]. Higher concentrations of most anes-
thetics, including ketamine, are known to decrease tolerance to ane-

anesthetic-induced blunting of CO and alterations in blood flow
distribution among organ systems [296,297]. It is important to rec-
ognize that most experimental studies detailing anesthetic drug
effects in animals and humans frequently include additional derived
or calculated variables (e.g., CO, SVR, stroke work, and MVO 2
) that
provide additional information regarding drug-related effects.
Mathematic coupling occurs when one variable either directly or
indirectly contains the whole or components of a second varia-
ble [298,299]. This can lead to erroneous results and invalid conclu-
sions in studies involving these derived and/or calculated
variables.
Neurohumoral and local control mechanisms
Blood flow is regulated by the integration of supraregional (i.e.,
CNS), regional, and local factors (Box 33.5). These regulatory
elements coordinate immediate and long-term adjustments in total
vascular resistance, vascular capacitance, blood volume, blood
pressure, and CO. CNS regulation depends on three components:
afferent input, central integration and processing, and efferent out-
put [300]. Continuous adjustments in cardiovascular system
function and reflex responses help to modulate and buffer changes
in blood volume, pressure, and flow in order to sustain oxygen and
nutrient delivery to tissues (Fig. 33.37; Box 33.6). The autonomic
nervous system exerts a major influence on the regulation of cardi-
ovascular function [301]. Peripheral receptors, including barore-
ceptors, mechanoreceptors, and chemoreceptors, sense and respond
to changes in blood flow, blood pressure, blood volume, and blood-
gas tensions. These sensory signals are integrated in “control cent-
ers” located in the hypothalamus, pons, and medulla from which a
host of neurohumoral responses are elicited. The autonomic nerv-
ous system regulates the release of neurotransmitters (e.g., norepi-
nephrine and acetylcholine) that activate adrenergic and cholinergic
receptors that modify cardiac performance and vascular tone
(Table 33.11). Minute-to-minute changes in blood flow are also
regulated by local control mechanisms, which integrate with nerv-
ous system activity [302]. Many of the cardiac and vasoactive
effects produced by neurotransmitters and circulating substances
are mediated by the activation of G-protein- coupled receptors
(GPCRs) 	[303]. 	GPCRs 	are 	transmembrane 	heterotrimeric

the membranes of cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells,
and vascular smooth muscle cells. They convert extracellular sig-
nals into intracellular responses and are activated by neurotrans-
mitters, neuropeptides, hormones, glycoproteins, and a variety

Most anesthetic drugs blunt the neurohormonal and sensory
(input), neural integration (processing), and effector (output)
mechanisms that control cardiovascular function [305–308].
Inhalation anesthetics in particular blunt compensatory responses
to blood loss, trauma, fluid administration and resuscitative drugs
(e.g., catecholamines and/or vasopressors) and, when administered
in excessive amounts, can totally abolish homeostatic control mech-
anisms [308–312]. Normally, a decrease in arterial blood pressure

Box 33.6 Cardiovascular and pulmonary reflexes and effects.
Abdominocardiac reflex: Mechanical stimulation of the abdominal viscera
causes changes in heart rate, usually slowing; rarely causes extrasystoles.
Anrep effect: Increases in aortic pressure results in a positive inotropic
effect, augmented resistance to outflow in the heart.
Atrial stretch-receptor reflex: Atrial distension causes the release of atrial
natriuretic peptide (ANP) from the atria, resulting in diuretic activity,
vasodilation, inhibition, and aldosterone secretion. ANP is an endogenous
antagonist of angiotensin II. Sinus and supraventricular tachycardias are
common stimuli for this response.
Bainbridge reflex: An increase in heart rate initiated by stretch-sensitive
mechanoreceptors in the great veins and right and left atria. The reflex is
primarily attributed to an increase in venous return and withdrawal of vagal
tone. A reverse Bainbridge reflex is used to explain a decrease in heart
rate during an acute decrease in venous return.
Baroreceptor reflex (i.e., high-pressure baroreceptor [mechanoreceptor]
reflex): Stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch
decreases heart rate in response to increases in arterial blood pressure. A
decrease in arterial pressure produces hyperventilation, and an increase in
arterial blood pressure causes respiratory depression and ultimately apnea.
Bayliss effect: A mechanism by which vessels keep organ blood supply
constant. Increased blood pressure induces reactive vasoconstriction thereby
limiting increases in blood flow and vice versa.
Bezold–Jarisch reflex: Afferent and efferent pathways in the vagus nerve
stimulation of cardiac, primarily ventricular, chemoreceptors or stretch
receptors (mechanoreceptors), induce sinus bradycardia, hypotension, and
peripheral vasodilation. Stretch of ventricular mechanoreceptors is
responsible for syncope when standing.
Branham’s sign: Slowing of the heart rate following compression or
excision of an arteriovenous fistula (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus ligation).
Chemoreceptor reflex: Systemic hypoxia or hypercarbia cause bradycardia,
coronary vasodilation, and systemic vasoconstriction.
Cough reflex: Stimulation of the larynx, trachea, or main bronchi or
chemical stimulation throughout the respiratory tree result in cough or
endotracheal tube precipitates bradycardia.
Craniocardiac reflex: Stimulation of cranial nerves (olfactory, ophthalmic,
and trigeminal), resulting in bradycardia and hypotension (depressor effects).
Cushing reflex: Increases in intracranial pressure result in Cushing’s triad
(i.e., increasing systolic blood pressure and widened pulse pressure,
bradycardia, and irregular respiration) theorized to be caused by increased
sympathetic and parasympathetic (i.e., vagal tone) activation form increases
in cerebral and peripheral blood pressures, respectively.
Diving reflex (i.e., oxygen-conserving reflex): Stimulation of the
trigeminal nerve (i.e., cranial nerve five) by cold temperature, pressure of
immersion) causes activation of the vagus nerve and sympathetic chain
causing bradycardia, systemic vasoconstriction, and cerebral vasodilation.
Hering–Breuer reflex: Effects of the vagus in the control of respiration –
lung inflation arrests inspiration, and lung deflation initiates inspiration
Low-pressure baroreceptor reflex: Low-pressure baroreceptors in the
large systemic veins, pulmonary vessels, and walls of the right atrium and
ventricles sense changes in wall tension and are involved with the regulation
of blood volume. Increases in blood volume increases atrial natriuretic
peptide (ANP) and antidiuretic hormone secretion, inhibits constriction of
renal arterioles and increases heart rate (see: Bainbridge reflex).
Oculocardiac reflex (Aschner’s reflex): Pressure on the eyeball causes
bradycardia, vasoconstriction, and cerebral vasodilation
Pulmonary chemoreflex: Stimulation of C-fiber endings (juxtapulmonary
capillary receptors [J receptors]) by tissue damage. Fluid accumulation of cytokines
produces sinus bradycardia, hypotension, shallow breathing and apnea,
bronchoconstriction, and mucous secretion (e.g., isoflurane administration).
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia: Cyclical changes in heart rate coincident
with normal respiration. Heart increases during inspiration and decreases
during expiration.
Vagovagal reflex: Afferent and efferent pathways in the vagus nerve.
Stimulation or irritation of the larynx or trachea by a laryngoscope or
endotracheal tube precipitates bradycardia.
Vasovagal reflex (Barcroft–Edholm reflex): Initiated by a decrease in
venous return to the heart (e.g., hypovolemia, orthostasis, compression of
the inferior vena cava, micturition, increased intrathoracic pressure, and
regional analgesia), causing sinus bradycardia and vasodilation. The term has
come to include neurocardiogenic syncope, carotid sinus syndrome, and
micturition syncope in human patients.
Venorespiratory reflex: Increases in right atrial pressure stimulate increases
in respiration.

vascular receptors (i.e., baroreceptors), which are the most impor-

from these receptors triggers readjustments in CNS autonomic out-

sure. Local myogenic autoregulation also helps to protect the brain,
heart, liver, mesentery, and skeletal muscle from small changes in
blood pressure. If arterial blood pressure is reduced to a point that
tissue blood flow is negatively affected, baroreceptor-triggered
responses produce increases in HR, cardiac contractility, and vas-

adrenal gland during severe decreases in mean blood pressure (<
40–60 mmHg) exacerbating these effects. In addition, blood flow is
redistributed to the lungs, heart, and brain (i.e., central circulation)
and away from the skin, skeletal muscle, kidney, and splanchnic vis-
cera (i.e., from the unstressed vascular volume [Vus
] to the effective
or stressed vascular volume [Vs
]) [313]. Similarly, peripheral chem-
oreceptors sense changes in blood gases (i.e., PO 2
, PCO 2 ) and the
acute onset of hypoxemia or hypercarbia (i.e., respiratory acidosis)
activates autonomic responses that induce tachycardia and periph-
eral vasoconstriction.
Neurohormonal mechanisms
Neurohormonal factors, including osmoreceptors in the hypothala-
mus, antidiuretic hormone released by neurons in the supraoptic
and paraventricular nuclei, aldosterone secreted by the adrenal cor-
tex, renin and erythropoietin produced by the kidney, and atrial
natriuretic peptide released by stretch-sensitive atrial muscle cells,
are all integrally involved in maintaining plasma volume, the pro-
duction of RBCs, and preserving blood volume (Fig. 33.37) [314,315].
Arterial baroreceptors are stretch receptors (mechanoreceptors)
located in the carotid sinus and aortic arch which respond to
decreases in arterial blood pressure and the rate of change of
blood pressure by incremental increases in the rate of electrical
impulses (i.e., baroreceptor reflex). Impulses from the carotid sinus
baroreceptors are carried by the carotid sinus and glossopharyngeal
nerve (cranial nerve IX), while impulses from the aortic arch are
carried by the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) to the nucleus tractus
solitarius in the brain. The signals are processed and initiate an
effector response that adjusts parasympathetic and sympathetic
outflow returning arterial blood pressure to its normal range. For
example, parasympathetic nervous system activity increases and
sympathetic nervous system activity decreases when arterial pres-
sure increases above the normal set point. The increased parasym-
pathetic activity to the SA node decreases HR. Simultaneously,
decreased sympathetic activity reduces HR and myocardial con-
tractility and results in vasodilation in arterioles and small veins.
Baroreceptor activity is minimal at mean arterial blood pressures
below 60 mmHg but progressively increases as mean arterial pres-
sure rises above 60 mmHg, reaching a maximum at approximately
180 mmHg. Most baroreceptors have a set point of approximately
100 mmHg. Decreases in arterial blood pressure (Pm < 60 mmHg)
decrease the firing rate of the carotid sinus nerve which decreases
parasympathetic activity to the heart and increases sympathetic
activity to the heart and blood vessels, thereby increasing HR and
blood flow, and redistributing blood volume from Vus to Vs
.
Anesthetic drugs interfere with the baroreceptor reflex [316].
Inhalation anesthetics depress normal baroreflex responsiveness
and diminish sympathetic output from the CNS [308,309]. The
degree of baroreceptor depression depends upon the rate of drug
administration and the depth of anesthesia produced.
Low-pressure cardiac mechanoreceptors located in the atria,
ventricles, and pulmonary veins help to minimize changes in sys-
temic blood pressure in response to changes in blood volume [314].
These cardiac stretch receptors respond to comparatively small
changes in pressure or stretch. The atria contain two types of low-
pressure receptors located at the venoatrial junctions. An increase
in atrial volume activates both types of atrial mechanoreceptors,
sending impulses to the medulla via vagal afferents. Depending on

the prevailing HR, arterial blood pressure, and venous return, HR
may increase or decrease [317]. Increases in venous return and
atrial distension usually cause a withdrawal of vagal tone and
enhancement of sympathetic outflow increasing HR (i.e., Bainbridge
reflex) and vice versa (i.e., reverse Bainbridge reflex; Box 33.6).
Atrial distension also decreases sympathetic output to renal afferent
arterioles resulting in vasodilation and decreases in vasopressin
(antidiuretic hormone) release, thereby reducing fluid reabsorption
in the renal tubular collecting ducts and increasing urine flow. The
rapid loss of free water into the urine helps return circulating blood
volume to normal values. In addition to these neural responses,
atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and brain natriuretic peptide
(BNP) are released into the bloodstream (Fig. 33.37) [318]. ANP is
produced in atrial cardiomyocytes in response to atrial distension
and increases sodium excretion by the kidney with an accompany-
ing increase in water loss. BNP has a similar effect to ANP and is
produced by ventricular muscle cells in response to increases in
myocardial stretch [319].
Ventricular mechanoreceptors located in the ventricular endo-
cardium discharge in parallel with changes in ventricular pressure
and produce effects that help to regulate systemic blood pressure
and myocardial work. Ventricular distension, however, also stimu-
lates powerful depressor reflexes that decrease HR and peripheral
vascular resistance, resulting in bradycardia and hypotension (i.e.,
Bezold–Jarisch reflex) [320–322]. Impulses initiated by either ven-
tricular distention or the injection of select chemicals (e.g., capsai-
cin or serotonin) into the coronary arteries can produce the
Bezold–Jarisch reflex, which is also called the “coronary chemore-
flex” (Box 33.6) [322].
The carotid artery and aortic arch contain specialized sensory
chemoreceptors termed the “carotid and aortic bodies” [323]. The
carotid and aortic bodies are innervated by the glossopharyngeal
(i.e., cranial nerve IX) and vagus (i.e., cranial nerve X) nerves and
receive the highest blood flow per gram of tissue weight of any
organ within the body. They are sensitive to changes in arterial oxy-
gen tension below 60 mmHg, increases in carbon dioxide tension
greater than 45 mmHg, and pH less than 7.30 [323]. They are
depressed by hypothermia. Increases in afferent activity from the
chemoreceptors increase minute ventilation, restoring arterial
blood pH, carbon dioxide, and/or oxygen to normal.
The kidney is the major site for activation of the renin–angiotensin–
aldosterone system (RAAS) [324,325]. The RAAS produces pep-
tides that demonstrate autocrine (i.e., on the cells where they are
being produced), paracrine (i.e., on neighboring cells), or endo-
crine (i.e., on a distant organ or tissue via systemic circulation)
effects. Renin is produced by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney
and is secreted into the circulation during hypotension or hypov-
olemia [324]. This enzyme cleaves angiotensinogen, produced by
the liver, to angiotensin I, thereby initiating an enzymatic cascade
that generates peptides that regulate blood pressure, cell growth,
apoptosis, and electrolyte balance. Angiotensin I is hydrolyzed by
angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE1) producing the octapep-
tide, angiotensin II. Angiotensin II acts on angiotensin II type 1 and
type 2 receptors (i.e., AT1R and AT2R) promoting vasoconstric-
tion, inflammation, salt and water reabsorption, and oxidative
stress via AT1R activation [325]. Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2
(ACE2) is expressed in various organ systems including the cardio-
vascular system, kidneys, lungs, and brain, and exerts important
actions to maintain cardiovascular homeostasis. ACE2 activa-
tion is the dominant mechanism for counter-regulating the effects
of angiotensin II by metabolizing it into the beneficial peptide
Angiotensin-(1–7). Angiotensin-(1–7) binds to Mas 1 receptors
(i.e., ACE2/Ang-(1–7)/MasR axis) present on cardiomyocytes, car-
diac fibroblasts, and endothelial cells limiting the oxidative and
inflammatory effects of angiotensin II and producing cardioprotec-
tive effects (Fig. 33.39) [326]. The impact of anesthesia and anes-
thetic drugs on the RAAS and homeostasis requires further
investigation [327].
The hypothalamus is directly involved in the hormonal control of
cardiovascular responses. Arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hor-
mone) is produced in the hypothalamus and is transported through
nerve cell axons to the posterior pituitary [328,329]. Under normal
circumstances, the pituitary releases vasopressin in response to
increases in plasma solute (Box 33.5). Vasopressin acts on the col-
lecting ducts of the kidney, where it stimulates water conservation,
thereby returning plasma osmolality (and volume) to normal.
Vasopressin is a vasoconstrictor, especially in mesenteric vessels;
therefore, the presence of circulating vasopressin is influential in

Local mechanisms
Autoregulation is the ability of blood vessels to adjust blood flow in
accordance with metabolic needs despite changes in tissue perfu-
sion pressure [331–333]. Mechanisms that contribute to changes in
vascular tone include responses to intraluminal pressure (myogenic
response), the effects of blood flow on the endothelial lining of
vessels (shear-dependent response), and the concentrations of met-
abolic factors on vessels (metabolic response). The myogenic mech-
anism is a type of autoregulation that responds almost immediately
to changes in arterial blood pressure by increasing smooth muscle
contraction in response to increases in arterial pressure and vice
versa. The vasoconstriction or dilation helps to maintain a constant
tissue blood flow. Similarly, increases in blood flow velocity increase
wall shear stress and the release of nitric oxide from the vascular
endothelium producing vasodilation and vice versa [334]. The met-
abolic response occurs after longer periods (30 s) of low tissue
blood flow. Increases in tissue oxygen demand or decreases in oxy-
gen tension release vasodilatory substances (e.g., CO2
, H +
, K +
) and
vasodilatory prostaglandins (e.g., PGI 2
) that relax vascular smooth
muscle, thereby improving blood flow until normal oxygen tension
is reestablished [335].
In summary, vascular tone and tissue perfusion are modulated by
host neurogenic, neurohumoral, and local factors that determine
tissue blood flow [336–339]. Collectively, these factors determine
the number of perfused (RBC-containing) capillaries, known as the
“functional capillary density.” Whether a given capillary remains
open or closed depends on the contractile state of the terminal arte-
rioles located near the entrance to the capillary bed.
Special circulations
Special circulations include those organs that control or modulate
their own blood flow using methods that override those described
by Poiseuille’s law (see section on hemodynamics and cardiac func-
tion) [340]. Active hyperemia is the concept that organ blood flow
is proportional to metabolic activity and the production of
vasodilator metabolites (CO 2
, H +
, K +
, lactate, and adenosine).
Reactive hyperemia occurs in response to a prior period of
decreased blood flow (i.e., ischemia). The coronary, cerebral, pul-
monary, and splanchnic circulations are primarily dependent on
local metabolic activity for regulation of blood flow while renal
blood flow is primarily determined by myogenic tone and tubulo-
glomerular feedback (Table 33.12). Skin and skeletal muscle blood
flow are primarily determined by changes in sympathetic tone. Skin
arterioles have a high density of α1
- adrenergic receptors that when
activated cause vasoconstriction. It is noteworthy that anesthetic
drugs and anesthesia blunt all normal compensatory responses and
autoregulatory mechanisms that mobilize and redistribute blood to
tissues that are in highest demand. These effects are due to their
direct vasodilatory effects and depression of sympathoadrenal
activation [160,161,341].
Coronary circulation
The heart has the highest oxygen consumption per tissue mass of all
organs in the resting body and receives most of its blood flow during
diastole (Fig. 33.40). Myocardial arterial oxygen extraction is 70–80%,
compared with 25% for most other organs. The heart receives
approximately 5% of the CO and possesses a rich capillary network,
three to four times denser than skeletal muscle, to achieve this high
extraction [342–346]. Species differences in coronary artery anatomy
and its regulation are responsible for different patterns of myocardial
perfusion and the heart’s response to ischemia [347–349].
Flow across the resting myocardium is usually dependent upon
the pressure gradient between the aortic root (“coronary driving
pressure”) and the right atrium although coronary perfusion pres-
sure in the left ventricle is more accurately determined as the differ-
ence between the aortic diastolic pressure and left ventricular
end-diastolic pressure. Under normal conditions the driving pres-
sure is fully maintained along epicardial conduit vessels with little
pressure loss in the distal epicardial arteries. Intracoronary arterial
pressure declines in the microvasculature (< 100 μm) reaching a
value of 20–30 mmHg across the capillaries [346]. The majority of
coronary blood flow occurs during diastole and decreases by 50%
or more during isovolumic contraction in intramyocardial vessels
compared to epicardial arteries (Fig. 33.40) [346]. Blood flow
resumes during isovolumic relaxation. The primary determinants
of resistance to blood flow in the myocardium include extravascular
compression of intramural coronary vessels (30–40% of total resist-
ances), the contractile state of the myocardium, and HR [343]. In
addition, systolic ventricular torsion also increases coronary

resistance to a point that systolic flow within the myocardium may
be zero or negative during systole.
Coronary blood flow is mainly determined by local metabolic
activity, oxygen demand, and HR (Table 33.12) [351]. Autoregulatory
myogenic and metabolic mechanisms coordinate the interaction
between intracoronary driving pressure and microvascular resist-
ance to maintain adequate flow across capillaries for substrate
delivery and metabolite removal. The vascular endothelium is the
final common pathway controlling vasomotor tone (coronary
autoregulation) and, like all other vessels, nitric oxide production
plays a major role [352–353]. Local regulatory mechanisms main-
tain blood flow within the physiologic range but fail during hypo-
tension when flows become strongly dependent on the driving
pressure. Coronary arteries receive their innervation through bilat-
eral vagal (parasympathetic) fibers from the cardiac plexus at the
base of the aorta and sympathetic nerves from the stellate gan-
glion [354]. Factors that lower arterial blood pressure (hypov-
olemia), increase ventricular diastolic pressure (heart failure), or
decrease diastolic time (tachycardia) lower the subendocardial to
subepicardial flow ratio predisposing to subendocardial ischemia,
ST segment changes, and cardiac arrhythmias. Increases in HR
impinge on diastolic time more than systolic time thereby decreas-
ing perfusion time. Anesthesia and anesthetics drugs decrease
myocardial perfusion by increasing HR, lowering arterial blood
pressure, and impairing ventricular function.
Cerebral circulation
The brain has little capacity for anaerobic metabolism or storing
energy and is therefore dependent upon an uninterrupted blood
flow. Cerebral autoregulation maintains stable cerebral blood flow
during changes in arterial blood pressure (i.e., cerebral perfusion
pressure [CPP]) ranging from 50–150 mmHg [355]. Cerebral blood
flow (CBF) is dependent on CPP and inversely proportional to cer-
ebrovascular resistance (CVR):
CBF 	CPP/CVR 	MAP ICP /CVR
where MAP is the mean arterial pressure and ICP is the intracra-
nial pressure. If intracranial pressure is stable, CPP is replaceable
by MAP. Both myogenic and local metabolic factors determine
CBF, with local metabolic factors being the most important.
For example, increases in the arterial partial pressure of carbon
dioxide (PaCO 2 ) of 1 mmHg decrease CVR and increase CBF
by approximately 3–4%, and vice versa (Table 33.5) [356–358].
Severe hypocapnia can, therefore, markedly increase CVR and
decrease CBF, predisposing to brain ischemia. Myogenic tone
decreases in response to decreased pressure and vice versa. If CPP
increases or decreases, the myogenic reflex results in vasocon-
striction or vasodilation, respectively [355]. Cerebral vasoreac-
tivity is also modulated by astrocytes and microglia that secrete
neurotransmitters with vasoactive properties [356]. Such neuro-
transmitters include acetylcholine and nitric oxide that are
potent vasodilators, and serotonin and neuropeptide Y that
cause vasoconstriction [356]. Endothelial mechanisms also
include the cellular secretion of the vasodilator nitric oxide as
well as the vasoconstrictors thromboxane A 2 and endothelin-1.
Inhalation and dissociative (e.g., ketamine and tiletamine) anesthetics
have been demonstrated to increase CBF, while most hypnotics
and sedatives (e.g., propofol, alfaxalone, etomidate, and dexme-
detomidine) reduce CBF [359].
Pulmonary circulation
The lung is unique among all organs in that it receives the entire
CO, contains approximately 10–15% of the total blood volume, and
serves as an important blood reservoir stabilizing left ventricular
SV and CO (Fig. 33.1) [360,361]. The primary purpose of the pul-
monary circulation is gas exchange [362]. The right ventricle and
pulmonary circulation buffer dynamic changes in blood volume
and flow resulting from respiration, positional changes, and changes
in left ventricular CO [360]. This low-pressure system has limited
ability to control the regional distribution of blood flow resulting in
the potential for the pulmonary capillaries to collapse [363]. Mild
increases in pulmonary arterial blood pressure normally distend
and recruit pulmonary capillaries, decreasing pulmonary vascular
resistance. Pulmonary blood flow is determined by the difference
between inflow and outflow pressures unless the surrounding pres-
sure (i.e., alveolar pressure) is greater than the outflow pres-
sure [363]. Pulmonary blood flow, therefore, is often described in
terms of a “Starling resistor” where the pressure surrounding a col-
lapsible tube influences the fluid flow through it. Low vascular pres-
sure also predisposes the lung to the so-called “waterfall effect”
wherein pulmonary venous pressure may be below alveolar pres-
sure and therefore only intermittently permits blood flow.
Pulmonary blood flow is particularly influenced by gravity in larger
animals (e.g., adult horses and cattle) resulting in the regional redis-
tribution of pulmonary blood flow during anesthesia [362,363].

mechanical ventilation can markedly reduce or stop pulmonary
blood flow leading to marked reductions CO and arterial blood
pressure [364].
The bronchial circulation (i.e., bronchial arteries) supplies oxy-
genated arterial blood to the lung parenchyma. Although physical
factors have an important role in determining both pulmonary and
bronchial blood flow, local vasoactive metabolites and low alveolar
oxygen tension (PA
O2
) determine pulmonary parenchymal blood
flow (Table 33.12). Low PA
O2 produces vasoconstriction of intrapul-
monary arteries [365]. Alveolar hypoxia activates mitochondrial
sensors increasing the production of reactive oxygen species that
depolarize pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells leading to the
activation of voltage-gated calcium channels, increases in cytosolic
calcium, and vasoconstriction [365]. The primary site of action is in
small extra-alveolar vessels. During hypoxic conditions the pulmo-
nary vessels constrict increasing pulmonary arterial pres-
sure [366,367]. This response distends and recruits under-perfused
pulmonary vessels effectively shunting blood to better ventilated
alveoli and resulting in an improved ventilation–perfusion ratio.
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) functions as a nega-
tive feedback mechanism for matching ventilation and perfusion
and is minimally inhibited by recommended doses of anesthetic
drugs, including propofol [368,369].
Splanchnic circulation
The splanchnic circulation includes multiple organs, contains
approximately 20% of total blood volume, and receives approxi-
mately 25% of the CO (Table 33.8) [370,371]. Splanchnic vessels,
particularly veins, are highly compliant and serve as one of the
body’s largest blood volume reservoirs. Local metabolites regulate
tissue perfusion during normal resting conditions (Table 33.12).
Splanchnic veins and the spleen, however, also contain a high popu-
lation of α1
- and α2
-adrenergic receptors that are highly sensitive to
adrenergic stimulation [148,150,151,372–374]. For example, the
volume of blood that can be mobilized from the spleen, liver, and
intestine of hemorrhaged dogs ranges from 6% to 30% of their total
blood depending upon the severity of hemorrhage [375]. If arterial
blood pressure decreases substantially, sympathoadrenal stimula-
tion causes splanchnic arterial constriction, increasing the pressure
in capacitance vessels and expelling splanchnic blood into the sys-
temic circulation [152]. Active mobilization of splanchnic blood
volume is almost entirely the result of β2
- and α1
-adrenergic recep-
tor activation [373]. Both β2
- and α1
- adrenergic receptors act in
concert to maximally shift blood from the splanchnic vasculature
into the systemic circulation by decreasing splanchnic vascular
capacitance and intrahepatic vascular resistance [375–377]. These
processes deliver blood to the systemic circulation and can effec-
tively compensate for up to 50–60% of lost blood volume. Inhalant
and injectable anesthetic drugs including benzodiazepines (e.g.,
midazolam) blunt the ability of the splanchnic circulation to mobi-
lize blood [378–380]. This effect may be more important than the
arterial vasodilatory or negative cardiac inotropic effects of anes-
thetic drugs when considering the potential causes for arterial
hypotension and/or low CO during anesthesia.
Renal circulation
Myogenic tone and tubuloglomerular feedback are the two most
important mechanisms that regulate renal blood flow during rest-
ing conditions (Table 33.12) [381,382]. Increases in arterial blood
pressure stretch smooth muscle cells in the walls of afferent arteri-
oles perfusing the glomerulus causing them to contract, thereby
increasing vascular resistance and minimizing a change in glomer-
ular blood flow. Decreases in arterial blood pressure cause the
smooth muscle cells to relax, decreasing vascular resistance and
maintaining blood flow.
The juxtaglomerular apparatus is a specialized structure formed
by the glomerular afferent arteriole and the distal convoluted
tubule. Renin is the key regulator of the renin–angiotensin–
aldosterone system and is critically involved in salt, volume, and
blood pressure homeostasis. Renin is mainly produced and released
into the circulation by juxtaglomerular epithelioid cells (i.e., macula
densa) located in the walls of the distal nephron and constricts
renal afferent arterioles as they enter the glomerular capillary net-
work [382]. Elevated sodium concentration in the distal tubule
triggers the macula densa to release ATP and adenosine that stimu-
lates the juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole to contract,
thereby decreasing glomerular blood flow and filtration rate,
and vice versa. The vasodilator, nitric oxide, modulates this
response [383]. Changes in sympathetic tone also modulate renal
blood flow during resting conditions. Increases in sympathetic tone
reduce renal blood flow, filtrate formation, and urine output while
decreases in sympathetic tone result in vasodilation, increased
blood flow, and increased urine output.

Introduction
The term “cardiopulmonary bypass” is broadly applied to the
procedure by which blood is diverted away from the heart and
lungs while also providing oxygenated blood to other organs to sus-
tain viability. There is a long history of the use of animals, predomi-
nantly pigs and sheep, for cardiovascular surgical training and
research. Additionally, over the past three decades, animals, most
notably dogs (albeit there are occasional reports of cats [1]), have
been anesthetized with varying frequency in the clinical arena to
facilitate surgical procedures involving the heart (and lungs) [2–15].
Although perioperative morbidity is common (e.g., dysrhythmias,
bleeding, phrenic nerve damage, hypoventilation, and hypoxemia),
acute survival (off pump to recovery) percentages from the
aforementioned reports are generally high, even 100%. Longer-term
survival, however, is variable, with wide-ranging complications
including hemorrhage, thromboembolism, pleural effusion, heart
failure, and sudden death being reported.
The focus of this chapter is to introduce the reader to cardiopul-
monary bypass as used to facilitate cardiac surgery in canine
patients. Challenges associated with this as a clinical tool have been
reviewed [16]. Although anesthesia management is reviewed here,
much of the chapter is devoted to introducing the basics of circuitry
and instrumentation used to facilitate cardiopulmonary bypass
and the considerations (e.g., cardiac protection and management of
coagulation) that arise as a result. As the reader is no doubt aware,
many cardiac procedures may be performed on the beating heart,
sometimes with the added utilization of inflow occlusion and
hypothermia. This chapter is limited to a discussion of the manage-
ment of clinical canine patients where cardiopulmonary bypass is
necessary to facilitate cardiac surgery.
The circuitry and patient cannulation
The external circuit
The circuit external to the patient consists of a reservoir for blood
and fluids used to prime the pump, a membrane (versus bubble) [17]
oxygenator of appropriate size (pediatric size is commonly used for
small- to medium-sized dogs), ventilating system, pumps (roller
or centrifugal) [18,19] of varying number (three to five) to facilitate
circulation of blood, a heat exchanger, and circulating heating/
cooling water bath to permit initial cooling and subsequent warm-
ing of the patient (Fig. 34.1). Tubing appropriate to the patient’s size
(so that excessive hemodilution resulting from excessive prime
volume, exposure to circuit components, and subsequent red blood
cell trauma can be minimized) connects these parts and is attached
to lines from/to the patient. As the lung is no longer functional dur-
ing this process, an oxygen flowmeter (or oxygen and air flowme-
ters along with an oxygen blender to vary the oxygen fraction) and
vaporizer are connected to the circuit to facilitate the delivery of
inhaled anesthetic as needed. Maintenance of anesthesia with par-
enterally administered injectable drugs has also been described [14].
Newer bypass circuits have an independent pump and tubing
mechanism for the delivery of cardioplegic solutions, arterial and/
or venous in-line monitors (to record temperature, hematocrit,

sensors). A more complete description and diagram of bypass cir-
cuitry available for human cardiopulmonary bypass are available in
other medical texts [20].
Although the personnel responsible for the anesthetic manage-
ment of the patient should have a general understanding of the
external circuitry used, the author’s experience has been that an
individual with specialized training in perfusion should be respon-
sible for ensuring functionality of the external circuitry and bypass
equipment. The anesthesia personnel will, however, need to be in
constant communication and provide the perfusionist with patient-
specific information, such as the hematocrit and calculated blood
volume. This information will be used to determine the pump prime
volume with a target hematocrit of 25–30% to optimize capillary
flow and oxygen-carrying capacity during bypass when hypother-
mia causes an increase in blood viscosity [21]. The perfusionist may
request crystalloid fluids, synthetic colloids, blood, plasma or
packed red cells (usually in smaller patients), and additives such as
mannitol, sodium bicarbonate, and heparin to add to the pump
prime. Steroids are added to the pump prime in some circum-
stances but with decreasing frequency. The perfusion team may
also request a vaporizer and inhalant anesthetic consistent with
what the anesthesia team is using for the patient. Additional details
regarding types and sizes of oxygenators, calculation of pump prime
volume, components of prime solution, types and sizes of tubing,
etc. may be found elsewhere [21–23].
Patient cannulation
Patient cannulation is performed by the surgical team. A lateral
thoracotomy is the preferred approach in the dog if the cardiac
procedure to be performed allows for this; a median sternotomy
approach is a feasible alternative. Commonly, arterial (oxygenated)
blood is actively returned (using a pump) to the patient via a can-
nula placed in the femoral or carotid artery. It is important that the
anesthesia team is aware of which site will be used and, specifically
for the femoral vessels, which limb will be utilized, so they do not
place the arterial catheter to monitor systemic arterial blood pres-
sure in the same limb. The arterial cannula is either placed first or
at the same time as the thoracotomy is performed if there are two
surgeons. Early placement facilitates a quicker connection to the
bypass circuitry if the patient’s status deteriorates during placement
of the venous cannula(e).
Bicaval or atrial venous cannulation is performed by the surgical
team depending on the procedure to be performed. For procedures
involving the right heart, bicaval cannulation is preferred to mini-
mize blood in the surgical field and minimize compromise to
venous drainage if the heart is retracted during the procedure
(Fig. 34.2). The venous line connected to the cannula passively
drains the majority of blood returned to the heart into the reservoir
of the bypass circuit. Blood returning from the thebesian veins,
coronary sinus, and systemic collaterals can usually be drained by
appropriate (depending on the nature of the surgery) placement of
these cannulas to reduce the risk of right ventricular distention.
As this is a gravity-dependent process, the height of the patient
above the reservoir is an important consideration. Suction may be
cautiously applied to venous drainage if needed. An additional left
ventricular vent line may be placed to minimize left ventricular
distention and warming resulting from drainage of systemic, peri-
cardial, and bronchopulmonary collaterals and thebesian veins [20].
A surgical suction cannula is also available and may be connected
with a line to the reservoir.
Placement of the aforementioned cannulas facilitates extracor-
poreal circulation and a bloodless surgical field but does not offer a
mechanism for myocardial protection. An additional cannula is,
therefore, placed for administration of cardioplegia. This cannula
may be placed such that flow of cardioplegic solution is anterograde
via an aortic root cannula located on the cardiac side of the aortic
cross clamp, or retrograde via a balloon catheter in the coronary
sinus. Cardioplegic solutions are administered to stop cardiac
activity once the aortic cross clamp is placed to reduce energy
requirements, protect myocardial cells, and scavenge free radicals.
Cardioplegic solutions may be blood-based (sanguineous) or
crystalloid-based, with additives for cardiac protection (e.g., mannitol
or lidocaine) and high levels of potassium to stop electrical activity.
Figure 34.1 Standard and pediatric cardiopulmonary bypass pumps.
