causes hypoventilation, hypoxemia, and hypercapnia [23,41].
In general, there is tight physiologic control over PaCO 2 with a
quasi-linear relationship between V̇E and PaCO2 (and end-tidal
CO2 partial pressure [PET
CO2
]), with higher CO 2 levels increasing
V̇E as illustrated in Fig. 37.4A [48]. Species differences in response
to progressive increases in PaCO2 or PET
CO2 induced by increasing
inspired CO2 exist, with horses being slightly less responsive and
burrowing or diving animals being much less responsive than
humans [48–50]. Unlike the quasi-linear relationship between V̇E
and increasing CO 2 levels, the change in V̇ E evoked by changes in
PaO2 is curvilinear. While V̇E remains relatively constant with PaO2
values above 70 mmHg, an exponential increase in V̇ E occurs as
PaO2 falls below 60–70 mmHg in mature animals [44,46,49].
As illustrated in Fig. 37.4B, when the FI
O2 in conscious horses was
decreased from approximately 1 (100% inspired oxygen concentra-
tion) to 0.16 (16% inspired oxygen concentration), there was no
substantial change in V̇E
; however, as FI
O2 was decreased below 0.16,
an inspired oxygen concentration that would result in PaO2 <
60 mmHg, V̇ E increased exponentially [50].
Metabolic acid–base disturbances trigger a compensatory response
in ventilation through peripheral chemoreceptors. A decrease in
plasma pH originating from non-respiratory causes stimulates
peripheral chemoreceptors and increases V̇ E . The decrease in
PaCO2 secondary to the increase in ventilatory drive reduces the
impact of metabolic acidosis on blood/extracellular pH. The com-
pensatory decrease in PaCO 2 in animals with metabolic acidosis is
self-limiting because of a decrease in central chemoreceptor activity
associated with the alkalinization of CSF pH, which limits further
reductions in PaCO 2 . Therefore, respiratory compensation of meta-
bolic acidosis may only partially offset the impact of the metabolic
acid–base disturbance on pH [46,51]. The decreased V̇ E and com-
pensatory increase in PaCO2 during metabolic alkalosis is also
limited because rising PCO 2 levels within the CNS increase the
ventilatory drive [51].
The respiratory compensation of metabolic acid–base disturbances
can be estimated in dogs. To date, there is limited data to allow cal-
culation of the expected respiratory compensation of metabolic
acid–base disturbances in cats, but it appears that the feline species
have a limited ability to reduce the impact of metabolic acidosis on
pH through an increase in pulmonary ventilation [51]. In dogs with
primary metabolic acidosis, for each mEq/L of decrease in plasma
HCO3
− from normal values (e.g., 20 mEq/L), a compensatory
decrease in PaCO 2 of 0.7 mmHg is expected to occur [51,52].
Changes in PaCO 2 of the same magnitude but in an opposite direc-
tion occur during metabolic alkalosis. Calculating the expected
respiratory compensation to metabolic acid–base derangements is
useful to differentiate simple from mixed acid–base disturbances
and the reader is referred to the specialized literature for further
details [51,52]. From an anesthesiologist’s perspective, it is impor-
tant to understand that anesthetic drugs may decrease central and
peripheral chemoreceptor activity, increasing PaCO 2 and inhibiting
the respiratory compensation to metabolic acidosis.
The cerebral cortex also provides input to the medullary respira-
tory center, mediating behavioral/voluntary changes in pulmonary
ventilation (Fig. 37.3). Behavioral changes such as fear, anxiety,
excitement, and pain are thought to be particularly important in
small animal species and will often increase ventilatory drive and
cause hypocapnia (low PaCO2
)/primary respiratory alkalosis because
of increased V̇ E and V̇ A [53]. Heat stress/hyperthermia may also
increase the ventilatory drive, particularly in animals with limited
ability to sweat through the skin, such as dogs. In these species,
panting is an important thermoregulatory mechanism. Panting is
characterized by a controlled increase in f and a decrease in V T with
the purpose of increasing evaporative heat loss through the upper
airways [54]. Although V̇E is increased in animals that are panting,
such change results mainly from increased deadspace ventilation
(increased ventilation to the conducting airways). Therefore, PaCO2
may be close to normal because the decrease in V T prevents V̇A
from increasing.
Pulmonary inputs to the medullary respiratory center include
the pulmonary stretch receptors (also known as “slowly adapting
stretch receptors”), J receptors, and irritant receptors (also known as
“rapidly adapting stretch receptors”) (Fig. 37.3) [44,46]. The pulmo-
nary stretch receptors, located in the smooth muscle of the airways
(trachea and bronchi) [55], are stimulated by distension of airway
smooth muscle (enlargement of airway cross-sectional area) as lung
volume increases during inspiration [56]. As there is an increase in
the frequency of depolarization from these receptors caused by
the conditions described above, a negative feedback mechanism
(the Hering–Breuer reflex) determines termination of inspiration
and prevents lung over-inflation [44,46]. Although the role of pul-
monary stretch receptors in controlling inspiration in adult humans
is now believed to be minor, in several veterinary species including
dogs, cats, and rabbits, it appears to play a significant role in the
regulation of V T [44,57]. The J receptors are nerve endings located
in the pulmonary interstitium and the conducting airways.
Stimulation of J receptors by inflammation results in rapid, shallow
breathing, mucus production, and bronchoconstriction [44].
Irritant receptors are nerve endings located in the epithelial cells of
the conducting airways that are activated by noxious stimuli such as
gases/chemicals and suspended particles [44]. Activation of these
receptors will alter the ventilatory rhythmic pattern and may lead
to rapid/shallow breathing. Sniffing and sneezing are caused by
the presence of irritants in the nasal cavity, whereas stimulation
of laryngeal and pharyngeal irritant receptors may cause cough,
mucus secretion, or, in severe situations, laryngospasm, bronchos-
pasm, and apnea.
Pulmonary ventilation
Physics of respiratory gases and the alveolar gas equation
Respiratory gases (oxygen, CO2
, and nitrogen) can be measured as
percent of total volume represented by each gas in the mixture (%)
or according to their partial pressure in millimeters of mercury
(mmHg) or kilopascals (1 kPa = 7.5 mmHg). Gases dissolve in
fluids and diffuse across membranes (e.g., alveolar–capillary mem-
brane) according to their partial pressures [58]. Dalton’s law states
that the total partial pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the
partial pressure of each gas. The partial pressure of each gas is
calculated by multiplying the percent volume of each gas in the
mixture by the barometric pressure (PB
), that is, the pressure exerted
by the atmosphere, and is expressed in mmHg or kPa (Fig. 37.5).
Because the degree of collision among gas molecules is influenced
by the gravitational forces exerted by the earth, the partial pressure
of a single gas or gas mixture will vary according to the altitude in
relation to sea level [58]. While the partial pressure of a gas or gas
mixture decreases in proportion to the decrease in barometric pres-
sure at higher altitudes, the percent volume of gas in the mixture
remains constant with changes in altitude and barometric pressure.
As such, FI
O2 is the same at sea level or the top of Mount Everest
(21%), the highest peak on earth (8848 meters above sea level).
However, because PB at Mount Everest is about one-third of that at

-- 718 of 1450 --

sea level (253 mmHg and 760 mmHg, respectively), oxygen partial
pressure in inspired gas (PI
O2
) at this altitude will be markedly low
(53 mmHg, calculated as FI
O2 × PB
), leading to a degree of hypox-
emia that is incompatible with life. While extremely high altitudes
(above 5500 meters or 18,000 feet) generally cannot sustain devel-
oped forms of life due to the low PI
O2
, another more realistic example
of the impact of altitude on inspired gases is illustrated in Fig. 37.5.
Compared to Rio de Janeiro (Brazil), located at sea level, the PI
O2 in
Fort Collins (United States), located 1525 meters above sea level, is
reduced from 160 mmHg to 134 mmHg due to altitude. Oxygen
partial pressure in alveolar gas (PA
O2
), calculated on the basis of the
alveolar gas equation, will be approximately 105 mmHg and
85 mmHg at sea level and an altitude of 1525 meters, respectively.
Assuming that the alveolar to arterial oxygen gradient (P(a-a)O2
) is
normally between 5 and 15 mmHg, normal PaO 2 levels in Rio de
Janeiro and Fort Collins are estimated to be approximately
95–100 mmHg and 75–80 mmHg, respectively.

should be subtracted from the altitude-based barometric pressure if

PB minus PH O2

altitude (Table. 37.4). While water vapor partial pressure in inspired
gas is probably zero in a patient receiving 100% medical oxygen
without humidification, this simplification may stray from reality if
relative air humidity and ambient temperature are elevated. If the
relative air humidity is 51%, water vapor pressure of ambient air is
9 mmHg at 20 °C [58].

The respiratory quotient is influenced by the diet/source of
energy metabolism and varies with the percentage of carbohy-
drates, proteins, and fats being oxidized. Oxidative metabolism of
carbohydrates, proteins, and fats results in R values of 1, 0.8, and
0.7, respectively [58]. The reason for this difference is that when
oxygen fuels carbohydrate metabolism, one molecule of CO2 is
formed for each molecule of oxygen consumed; during oxidative
metabolism of fats, a large share of the oxygen combines with
hydrogen atoms from the fats to form water instead of CO2
. In
humans consuming a Western diet, R has been determined to be
0.8 while studies in healthy conscious dogs report an R-value of
0.9 [43]. The respiratory quotient can be altered by species, breed,
nutritional state, hormonal circadian rhythm, and level of activity.
Because of changes in the energy metabolism, R values ranging
from 0.7 to 0.8 have been reported in critically ill dogs [59].
Kinetics of carbon dioxide elimination
The ideal gas exchange between pulmonary capillary blood and the
alveoli is illustrated in Fig. 37.2. As the CO 2 in mixed venous blood
(CO2 partial pressure in mixed venous blood [PvCO2
]) reaches the
pulmonary capillaries, it equilibrates with PA
CO2 . The rate of CO2
removal from the alveoli to ambient air, and consequently the
PA
CO2 and the CO 2 partial pressure in end-pulmonary capillary
blood (Pc´CO 2
), is determined by the volume of air flowing in and
out of alveoli over 1 min, that is, V̇A [9]. The PaCO 2 , which averages
CO2 of the end-capillary blood from all alveoli, indicates the adequacy
of V̇A . It is important to understand the variables that influence CO2
removal to manage V̇ A and PaCO2 in the perianesthetic setting.
The flow of gas in and out of the lungs is an essential component
of gas exchange between alveoli and the pulmonary capillary blood.
As explained before, V̇E
, is determined by the breathing frequency (f )
and by the volume of gas that enters and leaves the mouth or nostrils
in each breath, that is the tidal volume (V T
) (Fig. 37.2, Table 37.3).
VE 	T	V	f
Gas exchange takes place only at the level of the alveolar–capillary
barrier, more specifically in alveoli that are ventilated and perfused.
Areas of the respiratory tract that receive ventilation but that do not
participate in gas exchange, are referred to as “deadspace.” Because
the upper airways and tracheobronchial tree do not participate in
gas exchange, the relative volume necessary to fill these structures
during tidal breathing is termed “airway deadspace” (VDaw
). The
conducting airways are not the only component of the respiratory
system responsible for deadspace ventilation, however, ventilated
but not perfused alveoli also contribute to deadspace. The volume
of these alveolar units is referred to as “alveolar deadspace” (VDalv
).

From this equation, it is evident that V̇A is inversely correlated
with PaCO 2
. If V̇ A is reduced by 50%, and V̇ CO2 is unchanged
( stable metabolism), PaCO2 will double and vice versa. Pulmonary
ventilation (V̇ E and V̇ A ) in the resting state should match the CO 2
production at the basal metabolic rate, which may vary among ani-
mal species and breeds [60]. Because energy expenditure and basal
metabolic rate are significantly higher at birth and progressively
decrease as aging occurs [60], V̇E and V̇A are significantly higher in
neonatal and pediatric patients than in adult animals. The clinical
implication of higher V̇ E and V̇ A in younger patients is that respira-
tory depression caused by anesthetic agents can rapidly lead to
severe hypercapnia and hypoxemia in these individuals.
Based on the second formula above (V̇A = V̇E – VD phys
), isolating V̇E
on one side of the equation shows that V̇E is the sum of VD phys
and V̇A .
However, during a single breath, gas exchange will depend on the
fraction of V T that goes beyond the VD phys
, and effectively ventilates
alveoli that are perfused. While both fractions of a V T are useful to
consider as independent variables, over time, there is some mixing
between the gas in the VDaw
and the alveolar gas due to diffusion of
gases, a phenomenon facilitated by the movement created by the
beating heart [61]. This “mixing” action probably explains why
PaCO 2 levels are usually not all that elevated in smaller dogs or cats
showing a very shallow tachypneic breathing pattern wherein V T
must be near VDaw
. It probably also explains why insufflation of
15 L/min oxygen deep into the trachea in an apneic horse will main-
tain PaO2 values in the 50–60 mmHg range (Dr. Wayne McDonell,
personal observation).
Experimentally, VD phys
has been evaluated in animals using several
techniques that are influenced to varying degrees by pulmonary
ventilation and perfusion abnormalities (V̇A /Q̇ mismatch and shunt).
As clinicians and researchers, it is important to consider the meth-
odology and the factors influencing the measurement as it may
alter the interpretation of the results [62–64]. Initial studies in
humans measured VDaw
using the single-breath nitrogen washout
test (Fowler’s technique), which involves plotting the partial pressure
of nitrogen in expired gas of a single breath after a maximal voluntary
inspiration of 100% oxygen [9,65]. However, the Fowler technique
is technically challenging to perform in conscious animals due to
the need for voluntary maximum inspiration.

The diagram in Fig. 37.6A shows the composition of deadspace

, lowers CO 2 in mixed expired gas (PE

and increases the gradient between PA

The kinetics of CO 2 elimination assessed by the volumetric cap-
nography curve has three distinct phases (Fig. 37.6B). Phase I repre-
sents exhaled gas from the upper airways, which does not contain
CO 2 . Phase II represents expired gas from the lower portions of the
airways mixed with CO2
- rich alveolar gas, which causes a rapid rise
in CO2
. Phase III is the expired volume that represents pure alveolar
gas as the CO 2 curve flattens and plateaus. The slope of phase III
reflects the emptying of alveoli with different time constants. In
patients with small airway disease/bronchoconstriction, or with
lung disease, resistance to gas flow may differ substantially among
alveolar units [71]. During expiration, alveoli where the conducting
airways offer low resistance to gas flow empty first (“fast” alveoli),
whereas poorly ventilated alveolar units due to increased resistance
to gas flow take longer to empty. Because alveoli with different
time constants differ in the speed they are emptied during expira-
tion, the slope of phase III increases [71]. The area under the CO 2
curve represents the total amount of CO2 exhaled during a single
breath (V T
CO2,br
). The CO2 eliminated per minute, which is assumed
to be equivalent to CO2 production per minute (V̇ CO2
), is calculated
by multiplying the respiratory rate (f) by the V T
CO2,br
.
The airway–alveolar interface, identified as the inflection point
of phase II, is the limit between exhaled gas from lower conducting
airways (bronchioles) and CO2 - rich alveolar gas (Fig. 37.6C). The
expired volume below and above the inflection point represents
the airway deadspace (VDaw
) and the alveolar tidal volume (VTalv
),
respectively. The CO 2 level at the midpoint of phase III slope,
starting at the inflection point and ending at the end-tidal partial
pressure of CO 2 (PET
CO2 ), represents the average CO 2 of all alveolar
units (PA
CO2
) [64,66,72]. Studies measuring PA

Effects of altered alveolar ventilation
While changes in deadspace may not necessarily impact the ability
to achieve adequate gas exchange, when V̇A is altered significant
changes in PA
CO2 and PA
O2 can occur (Fig. 37.2, Table 37.5). As
previously discussed, V̇A is inversely correlated with PaCO2 as
described by the alveolar ventilation equation (V̇ A = K × V̇ CO2
/
PaCO 2
). Hyperventilation occurs when V̇A is excessive relative to
metabolic rate; as a result, PaCO2 is reduced. An increase in f,
referred to as “tachypnea,” may not result in hyperventilation if a
decrease in V T prevents V̇ E and V̇A from increasing. Hypoventilation
is present when PaCO2 rises because V̇A is low relative to V̇CO2 . The
effects of hypoventilation on PA
O 2 and PaO 2 in a healthy dog
breathing ambient air or 100% oxygen are illustrated in Table 37.5.
In an individual breathing ambient air at sea level with normal V̇ A
(e.g., PaCO 2 = 36 mmHg), PA
O2 is predicted to be approximately
110 mmHg by the alveolar gas equation. If there is a decrease in V̇ A
(e.g., PaCO 2 increases from 36 mmHg to 72 mmHg), PA
O2 decreases
from 110 mmHg to approximately 70 mmHg because of rising CO 2
levels within the alveoli. Considering that the alveolar to arterial
oxygen gradient (P(a-a)O 2
) is 5–15 mmHg for a healthy individual
breathing ambient air, PaO 2 can be predicted to be decreased from
95–105 during normal ventilation to 55–65 mmHg during
hypoventilation. If air is replaced by 100% oxygen in inspired gas
(FI
O2 = 0.97), PA
O2 will be markedly increased (612 mm Hg) despite
severe hypoventilation. Although P(a-a)O 2 may increase over
time due to absorption atelectasis caused by elevated FI
O2 , PaO2 can
be estimated to be approximately 500 mmHg in the presence of
severe hypoventilation with an F I
O2 close to 1.0.
Pulmonary mechanics
Fluctuating pressure gradients between the airway opening and the
alveoli cause air to flow in and out of the lungs. The factors that
contribute to these pressure gradients and the measurement of their
magnitude are referred to as “pulmonary mechanics.” During spon-
taneous breathing, a negative pressure gradient between the airway
opening (mouth, nostrils, or the interface between the breathing
circuit and the endotracheal tube) and the alveoli/pleural cavity is
responsible for the inflow of gas to the lungs. In anesthetized
patients, a mechanical ventilator is commonly used to create a posi-
tive pressure gradient between the airway opening (endotracheal
tube) and the alveoli to generate flow of gases into the lungs during
inspiration. Factors that influence the development of a pressure
gradient between the airway opening and the alveoli include the
elasticity of the lungs, thoracic cage, and diaphragm (chest wall),
in addition to the resistance to flow between these two regions.
These properties determine the normal distribution of airflow
within the lung and the energy expended to achieve optimal venti-
lation (work of breathing). Both anesthesia and disease can alter
the elastic properties and resistance of the respiratory system,
impacting the ability to achieve adequate alveolar ventilation. While
pulmonary physical characteristics are generally measured on the
whole lung in the clinical setting, regional differences in physical
properties are also important in determining normal distribution of
ventilation.

With initiation of inspiration, as active muscular effort enlarges the

plays a part in normal expiratory activity, producing a biphasic
mode of exhalation. As the Ppl becomes less negative, Palv may
slightly increase above atmospheric pressure. Reversal of the pres-
sure gradient during expiration (Palv > Pao
) causes air to flow from
the alveoli to the airway opening/atmosphere [49,79].

pressure transducer connected to the airway opening to measure Pao
(face mask or endotracheal tube) and to an esophageal balloon
placed in the thoracic esophagus to provide a surrogate measure of
P pl
. The change in lung volume (or V T ) can be measured using a
spirometer, a body plethysmograph, or a pneumotachometer [10].

anesthetized individuals receiving positive-pressure ventilation,
Palv−Ppl provides an assessment of the positive pressure applied to
the lung tissue per se, excluding the effects of the chest wall and
abdomen [80].

Prior to the advent of spirometry, in anesthetized patients receiv-

and end-expiration were used for pressure determinations, and

different components (lung and/or chest wall) to total compliance
needs to be considered when interpreting values and when imple-

Compliance is further characterized as either dynamic, static, or
quasistatic. In spontaneously breathing animals, dynamic compli-
ance describes changes in lung volume per unit change in pleural
pressure in the presence of airflow. If the patient is receiving
mechanical ventilation in a volume-controlled mode without an
inspiratory pause (period of zero flow at the end of inspiration),
then dynamic compliance is measured as the change in lung volume
per unit change in airway pressure (peak inspiratory pressure minus
end-expiratory pressure) (Fig. 37.10A). Dynamic C RS is altered by
changes in the elastic properties of the respiratory system and
by changes in airway resistance (R aw ). Static and quasistatic C RS
describes changes in lung volume per unit change in pressure dur-
ing a brief pause at end-inspiration (zero airflow). Because patient
cooperation is required, static compliance measurements are often
performed in anesthetized animals receiving mechanical ventila-
tory support with an inspiratory pause (Fig. 37.10B) [30,83–85].

(substituting Hagen–Poiseuille’s determinants of flow into Ohm’s
law), the resistance to laminar gas flow can be established:
Resistance viscosity length of tube
radius
8 4
Resistance to laminar flow therefore increases with an increase in
the tube length or a reduction in tube radius. The significance of
this equation for the anesthetist is the impact of the diameter of a
patient’s airway on the resistance to gas flow. An increase in resistance
can result from a variety of conditions such as bronchospasm, con-
genital or acquired anatomic abnormalities in the airway, and/or
the presence of mucus, exudates, foreign bodies, or tumors within
the airway lumen [89,90]. If a narrow endotracheal tube is used in a
patient with an already increased airway resistance due to respiratory
disease (e.g., tracheal collapse or brachycephalic airway syndrome),
there may be a dramatic increase in resistance to airflow during
anesthesia with spontaneous ventilation. For example, if the diam-
eter of the upper airway is reduced by 50% due to pathology or
secondary to the placement of a small endotracheal tube, the R aw
goes up 16-fold. Of note, with laminar flow, viscosity is the only gas
property to influence resistance.
While the above relationship between gas flow, pressure gradient,
and resistance is valid during laminar flow, when flow rate exceeds
a critical velocity, it becomes turbulent as gas molecules swirl
and turn in a chaotic pattern rather than in an orderly manner.
In this circumstance, the relationship between the pressure gradient
as gas flows through a straight tube (∆P) and the flow rate is no
longer linear. Fig. 37.11B shows the physics of turbulent flow. In
this case, ∆P will depend on gas density and the squared flow as
follows [89,90]:
P 	constant gas density flow 2
With turbulent flow, the change in pressure is inversely propor-
tional to the fifth power of the radius of the tube (Fanning equa-
tion); therefore, airway radius has an even greater impact on air
flow than with laminar flow [91]. In a straight unbranched tube, the
transition from laminar flow to turbulent flow can be estimated by
the Reynold number (Re), a nondimensional number that is derived
from gas velocity, tube diameter, gas density, and gas viscosity.
Re linear gas velocity tube diameter gas density
gas viscosiity
As the Reynolds number increases above 2000, air flow becomes
progressively more turbulent. While airway resistance and its deter-
minants are generally explained in terms of laminar flow, the struc-
ture of airways results in a mix of laminar and turbulent flow in the
major airways. In addition to the variables included in calculating
the Reynolds number, branching and/or irregularities in the tube
predispose to turbulent flow. In general, resistance to gas flow is
significantly greater with turbulent flow relative to laminar flow and
turbulent flow is dependent on gas density and not viscosity.
Because flow may become turbulent during pathological conditions
that include narrowing/partial obstruction of the airways, incorpo-
rating helium, a gas with less density relative to oxygen or air, as a
carrier gas with oxygen (mixture of 70% helium and 30% oxygen)
may reduce resistance to gas flow [92,93]. As gas flow is usually
laminar in the distal airways (and therefore not influenced by gas
density), helium, which has a viscosity similar to air, may be less
useful in animals with mild-to-moderate bronchoconstriction of
the distal airways but it may have a positive impact in the presence
of severe bronchospasm affecting the whole bronchial tree, as gas
flow is likely turbulent under these circumstances [89]. In anesthe-
tized horses, an alveolar recruitment maneuver with a mixture of
70% helium and 30% oxygen increased dynamic CRS and improved
pulmonary oxygen exchange (decreased P(a-a)O2
) when compared
to 100% oxygen [93]. However, dynamic CRS is altered by the resis-
tive and elastic properties of the respiratory system, and it remains
to be demonstrated that the use of helium as a carrier gas would
improve pulmonary mechanics by reducing resistance to gas flow in
horses [93].

despite the narrow radius, airflow velocity in bronchioles is very
low and follows a laminar pattern. Therefore, the relative
contribution of the small airways and bronchioles to total R aw is low
(< 10%) unless marked lower airway disease/bronchospasm is
present [79]. As with lung compliance, resistance to airflow changes
with lung volume. As lung volume decreases, R aw increases, with
dramatic increases occurring at lung volumes below FRC.
Presence of turbulent flow and increased R aw directly impact the
work of breathing, which is the energy spent by respiratory muscles
(measured in joules) for air to flow in and out of the lungs. Work of
breathing is measured as the product of pressure changes across the
respiratory system (Pao − Ppl in spontaneously breathing animals)

-- 727 of 1450 --

712 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
and the volume of gas moved (V T
) [89,90]. Because inspiration is an
active process that involves contraction of the diaphragm and chest
wall muscles, most of the work done occurs during inspira-
tion [89,90]. Respiratory work is further divided into elastic work
(required to overcome the recoil of the lung) and resistive work
(required to overcome the frictional opposition or resistance to air-
flow) [89,90]. As is discussed in Chapter 38, turbulent flow and
increased R aw are likely to be present in dogs with brachycephalic
airway syndrome or collapsed trachea and horses with severe bron-
chospasm secondary small airway disease (heaves). The consequent
increase in the respiratory work may lead to fatigue of inspiratory
muscles, therefore, mechanical ventilatory support may be required
in these patients.
Distribution of ventilation
The distribution of inspired gases during inspiration is not
completely homogenous throughout the lung, with gravity playing
a major role in regional pulmonary ventilation. Specifically, due
to the weight of the lung in the thorax, P pl is more negative
(sub-atmospheric) in the uppermost part of the thorax relative to
the lowermost portion and the negative pressure gradient between
the alveoli and the pleural cavity (Palv − P pl
) is greater in dorsal lung
compared to ventral lung areas. Therefore, the average alveolar size
is larger in the uppermost areas and smaller in the lowermost
areas of the lung at end-expiration (Fig. 37.12A) [94,95]. Since
larger alveoli have lower compliance (they are less distensible), they
expand less on inspiration, and air preferentially enters the more
compliant lowermost alveoli (Fig. 37.12B), producing a vertical
gradient of ventilation distribution in standing animals breathing
quietly [96–98]. This tendency for preferential ventral ventilation
in the lung may also be associated with regional chest wall and
diaphragmatic movement. During anesthesia, the distribution of
ventilation becomes more uneven and may even reverse so that the
uppermost lung of a laterally recumbent horse is receiving most of
the ventilation.
Local resistance to air flow and compliance are the two major
determinants of regional distribution of ventilation [79] (Fig. 37.13).
Alveoli within regions with normal resistance and compliance com-
pletely fill during slow and fast tidal breathing, while alveoli that are
poorly complaint due to inflammation/fluid accumulation in the
interstitium (e.g., in pneumonia) only partially fill during inspira-
tion. If there is increased resistance to airflow due to narrowing of
the small airways caused by mucus, bronchoconstriction, or foreign
material, these alveolar units take longer to fill and empty during
tidal breathing and are referred to as “slow” alveoli. Slow alveoli also
tend to be under-distended during inspiration (less ventilated than
perfused), especially at faster respiratory frequencies [79]. Slow
alveoli contrast with alveoli that completely fill regardless of the
breathing pattern (“fast alveoli”). Uneven distribution of ventila-
tion, leading to areas of low V̇ A /Q̇ and gas exchange impairment
(lower- than- expected PaO 2 values) occur in lung disease due to
areas with poor compliance or increased resistance to airflow.

Pulmonary perfusion
The pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure system composed of
highly compliant arterial vessels that offer low resistance to blood
flow. Because pulmonary arterial tree vessels are relatively thin-
walled and compliant, the pulmonary circulation can accommodate
large increases in blood flow without an appreciable increase in
mean pulmonary arterial pressure (MPAP) under physiological
conditions. One notable exception is horses, where MPAP increases
from 25–30 mmHg at rest to values above 80 mmHg during gallop-
ing because the pulmonary vasculature cannot dilate to accommo-
date the large increase in pulmonary blood flow/CO that occurs
during high-intensity exercise [99]. The pulmonary hypertension
caused by the increase in pulmonary blood flow is considered a
major factor that contributes to exercise-induced pulmonary
hemorrhage in equine species [100]. The extensive branching of the
pulmonary arterial tree increases the vascular surface area available
for gas exchange. Although this is followed by a progressive reduc-
tion in the diameter of arterial vessels, when the multiple arterial
branches are arranged in parallel, the total cross-sectional area of
the pulmonary arterial tree is greatly increased; hence, vascular
resistance is lower in the pulmonary than in the systemic circula-
tion even though it accepts the same volume of blood per unit of
time. Interestingly, there are differences among species, with horses
having higher pulmonary artery pressures at rest than humans and
dogs [101,102]. Typically, MPAP values in resting conscious horses
are in the range of 25–30 mmHg while in dogs MPAP values are
approximately 15 mmHg [101–103]. Higher pulmonary artery
pressure values observed in large animal species are necessary to
overcome the large vertical hydrostatic pressure gradient and
provide perfusion to the uppermost areas of the lungs.
In the absence of intracardiac shunting, the pulmonary blood
flow generated by the right ventricle equals the aortic blood flow
generated by the left ventricle. The total blood flow to the lungs
(Q̇T
), is determined by the gradient between arterial MPAP and left
atrial pressure (LAP) and by pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR),

Distribution of pulmonary perfusion
For many years, it was believed that gravity was a primary determi-
nant of the distribution of pulmonary blood flow. Specifically, a
vertical perfusion gradient was thought to direct more blood flow
to lower lung regions compared to upper lung regions in both
conscious and anesthetized animals [96,105]. Current evidence
suggests that distribution of pulmonary blood flow is governed by
other factors, such as the branching pattern of the pulmonary arte-
rial tree and regional differences in PVR, with little gravitational
dependence in quadrupeds [106–108]. While some of the conflict-
ing results can be attributed to inaccurate methods of determining
blood flow distribution, a heterogeneous pattern of lung perfusion
has been documented in conscious standing horses, with a larger
proportion of the blood flow being directed toward the uppermost
(caudo-dorsal) lung regions, against gravitational forces [106].

Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
Unlike smooth muscle in systemic arteries, which dilates in
response to hypoxia, pulmonary arterial smooth muscle contracts
when exposed to low oxygen partial pressures, a response referred
to as “hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction” (HPV). The contractile
response of pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells to hypoxia has
been shown to be an inherent characteristic, with endothelial cells
now regarded as modulators of the response [112–114]. Activation
of a mitochondrial sensor in the smooth muscle cell in response
to hypoxia results in closure of potassium channels, opening of
calcium channels, and subsequent activation of the contractile
apparatus within the smooth muscle cells [113]. This local response
diverts mixed venous blood from poorly ventilated lung areas to
better-ventilated alveoli, thus helping to minimize the increase in
venous admixture and oxygenation impairment caused by low
V̇A
/Q̇ and shunt (Fig. 37.16) [112,115]. HPV develops when the
alveolar oxygen partial pressure falls to less than 100 mmHg in
the normal lung, and the response is maximal when the oxygen
tension is approximately 30 mmHg [112]. There is an apparent
difference in the strength of the HPV response to whole lung
hypoxia in various species [116], based on exposure of animals to
high altitude and excised lung studies [117–119]. Cattle and swine
have a strong reflex, whereas ponies, cats, and rabbits have an
intermediate response, and sheep and dogs show less response. It
appears, however, that under normal conditions even species with a
weak hypoxic pulmonary reflex are capable of considerable blood
flow diversion in response to regional areas of low alveolar oxygen
partial pressure [116,118]. Interestingly, the response varies with time
and repeat exposure to low oxygen conditions [112]. While HPV

Pulmonary hypertension
Understanding the factors that cause an abnormal increase in
pulmonary artery pressure is important because anesthesia of
animals with conditions leading to pulmonary hypertension
may be required. Although a pulmonary artery catheter (Fig. 37.14)
is the gold standard method for evaluating pulmonary hyperten-
sion, diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension in dogs is based on the
measurement of tricuspid regurgitation velocity using Doppler
echocardiography and on echocardiographic signs of pulmonary
hypertension [120]. Fig. 37.17 illustrates the pathophysiological
changes that may result in pulmonary hypertension in animals.
Pulmonary hypertension has been classified according to its
origin as precapillary, postcapillary, or mixed (pre- and postcapillary).
Precapillary pulmonary hypertension, also known as “pulmonary
arterial hypertension,” is caused by abnormalities on the arterial
side of the pulmonary circulation and occurs when MPAP is
abnormally increased because of an increase in PVR secondary
to lung disease associated with arterial vasoconstriction, and/or
pulmonary thromboembolism. Precapillary pulmonary hyperten-
sion also occurs in severe forms of heartworm disease in dogs
(dirofilariasis) [120,121]. Lung disease leading to alveolar hypoxia
(low alveolar PO2
) also has the potential to cause pulmonary hyper-
tension (defined in humans as MPAP > 25 mmHg) because of a
vasoconstrictive response (increased PVR) in alveoli exposed to
low PO2
, that is, HPV. In dogs, pulmonary hypertension is associated
with a diverse spectrum of respiratory diseases, most commonly
obstructive disorders, and estimates of systolic pulmonary artery
pressures > 47 mmHg using Doppler echocardiography were
associated with non- survival [122].
Congenital cardiac defects leading to increased total pulmonary
blood flow (Q̇ T ) may also cause pulmonary arterial (precapillary)
hypertension (Fig. 37.17) [120,121]. Because pressures on the left
side of the heart are higher than on the right side of the circulation,
persistent ductus arteriosus (PDA), ventricular septal defect (VSD),
and atrial septal defect (ASD) often result in arterial blood being
added to mixed venous blood (left-to- right shunt) in dogs. If the
shunted flow is relatively small (e.g., PDA with small ductal diam-
eter, small VSD), the resulting increase in blood flow through the
pulmonary artery may not result in significant pulmonary
hypertension because the pulmonary vasculature is highly
compliant and can accommodate the increase blood volume.
However, in their most severe forms, these congenital defects may
be associated with significant pulmonary arterial hypertension
ultimately resulting in shunt reversal.
PDA is one of the most common congenital cardiac defects in
dogs, accounting for up to 30% of congenital defects in this species.
Direction of blood flow through the PDA is determined by the pres-
sure gradient between the aorta and the pulmonary artery. Usually,
when PDA is detected in young dogs, there is a continuous left-to-
right shunt because pressures and vascular resistance are higher in
the aorta than in the pulmonary artery. Blood flow though the duct
is dependent on ductal diameter. In case of a very large PDA caus-
ing excessive increases in Q̇T
, hypertrophy of smooth muscle from
small pulmonary arteries/increased PVR occurs to protect pulmo-
nary capillaries from volume overload. Precapillary pulmonary
hypertension secondary to increased PVR can precipitate reversal

incidence of pulmonary hypertension estimated by Doppler echo-

dogs (median age) to 22% in animals older than 5 years [124],
pulmonary hypertension is more frequently associated with PDA
in cats with up to 46% of animals presenting with this complica-
tion [126]. Right-to- left shunting associated with severe pulmonary
hypertension may also occur more frequently in cats than in
dogs [125,126]. Anesthesia is unlikely to be performed in animals
with PDA and right-to-left shunting because ductal closure may be
contraindicated under these circumstances. Although there might
be a concern that decreases in SVR/hypotension induced by general
anesthesia could reverse the shunt from left-to- right to right-to- left
because aortic pressures could fall below pulmonary artery pres-
sures, precipitating cyanosis, there are no complications related to
shunt reversal (hypoxemia/cyanosis) reported in dogs anesthetized
with isoflurane for transvascular PDA occlusion [127]. However,
the absence of studies reporting shunt reversal in dogs undergoing
anesthesia for PDA correction must be interpreted with care.
If anesthesia is performed in animals with severe pulmonary
hypertension where pulmonary artery pressures approach aortic
pressures, drug-induced hypotension could in theory reverse the
shunt and precipitate cyanosis/hypoxemia.
Pulmonary hypertension of postcapillary origin (also known as
“pulmonary venous hypertension”) (Fig. 37.17), is characterized by
elevated pressures on the venous side of the pulmonary circulation
(PAOP > 15 mmHg in humans). Postcapillary pulmonary hyperten-
sion caused by left-sided congestive heart failure is the result of
passive backward transmission of elevated left ventricular filling
pressures (LVEDP and LAP) increasing pressures in the pulmonary
veins, capillaries, and arteries. Chronic left-sided congestive heart
failure secondary to myxomatous mitral valve disease or dilated
cardiomyopathy is a common cause of postcapillary pulmonary
hypertension in dogs with at least 40–70% of cases affected
[128,129]. At this time, the incidence of postcapillary pulmonary
hypertension secondary to left-sided congestive heart failure is
smaller in cats (17%) than in dogs (> 70%) [130].
Pulmonary edema
Pulmonary edema is defined as an increase in pulmonary extravascular
water. In its more severe form, alveoli are flooded with transudate
(hydrostatic pulmonary edema) or exudate fluid (increased
permeability pulmonary edema) [131,132]. Movement of fluid across
capillary membranes was first described by Starling and has since
been refined and described by the following equation [131,132]:
J 	K 	P 	P	v 	cap 	cap	int 	int
Where Jv is the flow rate of transudated fluid across the
endothelium which, in equilibrium, will be equal to the lymphatic
drainage; K is the filtration coefficient or leakiness of fluid from
the endothelium to the interstitium (also known as “hydraulic
conductance”); Pcap is the hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary
capillary; Pint is the hydrostatic pressure in the interstitial space;
σ (sigma) is the protein reflection coefficient, which is an expres-
sion of the permeability of the endothelium to albumin; πcap is the
oncotic pressure in the pulmonary capillaries (mainly determined
by albumin); and πint is the oncotic pressure in the interstitium
[131–133]. In the normal lung Pint is slightly negative compared to
Pcap
, which results in the movement of fluid from the microvascula-
ture to the interstitium. However, interstitial edema does not occur
under normal circumstances because this is matched by lymphatic
system’s ability to remove the filtrate from the interstitium. If there
are no changes in the normal endothelial structure, intravascular
oncotic pressure (πcap
) is higher than in the interstitium (πint
), which
also helps to retain fluid within the intravascular space [131–133].
It has been traditionally accepted that the fluid balance in the
lungs and other tissues obeys the classical Starling equation
described above. However, with the evolving knowledge of the role
of the endothelial glycocalyx in fluid dynamics across the capillaries,
this classical view has been reassessed as it may not fully reflect the
transvascular movement of fluid at the capillary level [133,134].
The glycocalyx, which is a layer of proteoglycans and glycoproteins
lining the luminal aspect of capillaries, serves as a barrier to the
efflux of plasma proteins (albumin) and therefore helps to maintain
the Starling forces that prevent pulmonary edema. In the revised
Starling equation, the oncotic pressure gradient is between the
intravascular space and the protein-free space beneath the glycoca-
lyx. In this construct, pulmonary edema develops as Pcap and Jv
increase and/or lymphatic drainage decreases [133,134]. Damage to
the endothelial glycocalyx by shear stress induced by fluid resusci-
tation, or by inflammatory mechanisms associated with sepsis may
increase the risk of pulmonary edema caused by excess fluid admin-
istration in hypovolemic and septic animals [135,136].
There are three basic mechanisms responsible for pulmonary
edema: (1) increased hydrostatic forces within the microvasculature,
(2) increased microvascular permeability, and (3) low plasma
oncotic pressure (hypoalbuminemia). The third mechanism does
not appear to play an important role in causing lung edema per se.
However, hypoalbuminemia may contribute to pulmonary edema
when it occurs concomitantly with the other two mechanisms.
Hydrostatic pulmonary edema occurs when increased Pcap causes
fluid accumulation within the interstitium and leakage of fluid floods
alveoli with transudate fluid [131,132]. Hydrostatic pulmonary
edema occurs in animals presenting in advanced stages of left-sided
congestive heart failure (e.g., degenerative mitral valve disease and
dilated cardiomyopathy in dogs, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in
cats) or animals receiving excessive amounts of intravenous
fluids [128,137,138]. Left-sided heart disease leading to severe
diastolic dysfunction may precipitate hydrostatic pulmonary edema
as excessive LAP and LVEDP will increase pressures in vessels
located proximally in the pulmonary circulation (pulmonary vein,
and pulmonary capillary pressures) [128]. Doppler echocardiog-
raphy is an important tool to evaluate the degree of diastolic dys-
function and risk of pulmonary edema in the latter patients [128,139].
A restrictive fluid therapy strategy should be adopted during
anesthesia if a restrictive pattern of diastolic function (suggested
by elevated LVEDP) is identified by Doppler echocardiography in
small animals [128,137,139,140].
Although less common, pulmonary edema can occur secondary
to upper airway obstruction, a condition referred to as “negative-
pressure pulmonary edema” or “postobstructive pulmonary edema.”
The etiology is likely multifactorial; however, excessively negative
intrathoracic/alveolar pressures, generated by contraction of inspir-
atory muscles against an obstructed upper airway, lead to an increase
in venous return to the right side of the heart and an increase in
hydrostatic pressures in the pulmonary vasculature. In combination
with greater negative alveolar pressures under these circumstances,

transvascular fluid filtration is increased, precipitating interstitial
and alveolar edema [141,142]. In one retrospective study of noncar-

lung edema resulting from airway obstruction was recorded in 8
animals [143]. Hemorrhagic/negative-pressure pulmonary edema
is a rare but potentially fatal complication reported in horses with
acute upper airway obstruction during recovery from anesthesia
[142,144]. The hemorrhagic nature of pulmonary edema (presence
of pink frothy fluid in the airways) in this species is likely a result of
injury to pulmonary capillaries and alveolar membranes caused by
the extremely negative intrathoracic/airway pressure [142,144].
Increased permeability pulmonary edema occurs when damage to
the microvascular endothelial surface layer and alveolar epithelium
leads to leakage of protein-rich fluid from the microvasculature
to the interstitial compartment and alveoli [131,132]. In humans,
increased permeability pulmonary edema is a characteristic of
acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Direct causes of acute
lung injury (ALI) leading to ARDS in humans include pneumonia,
aspiration of gastric contents, inadequate ventilator settings leading
to alveolar overdistension, inhalation injury, pulmonary contusion,
pulmonary vasculitis, and drowning. Humans may also develop
ARDS secondary to indirect injury to the lungs, which may occur
due to sepsis not involving the lungs, major trauma, pancreatitis,
severe burns, non-cardiogenic shock, drug overdose, and multiple
transfusions [145]. Based on the criteria for the diagnosis of veteri-
nary ARDS in small animals and foals published in 2007 [146], the
most frequent cause of lung injury leading to increased permeability
pulmonary edema and signs of ARDS was aspiration pneumonia in
dogs and systemic inflammatory response syndrome without sepsis
in cats [147]. Current evidence shows that acute necrotizing pan-
creatitis may be an important cause of indirect lung injury in dogs,
as this disease has been associated with recruitment of pulmonary
intravascular macrophages (PIMs) and histological evidence of
lung inflammation [148,149]. While anesthesia of animals with
increased permeability pulmonary edema and/or ARDS is rarely
necessary, when required, a protective ventilatory support strategy
is highly recommended to avoid further lung injury and is discussed
further in Chapter 38.
Ventilation–perfusion relationships
Ventilation–perfusion relationships and gas exchange
To achieve optimal gas exchange with the least amount of energy
expenditure, ventilation and perfusion would not necessarily be
uniform throughout the lung but rather would be matched in order
to achieve optimal oxygenation and CO 2 removal. In fact, when an
arterial blood gas sample is analyzed for efficacy of gas exchange, it
must be borne in mind that PaO 2 and PaCO 2 values reflect the
blood flow from millions of alveoli with varying V̇A
/Q̇ ratios.
A mismatch between ventilation and perfusion, more specifically
increased areas of low V̇ A /Q̇ ratio and shunt (perfusion of non-
ventilated regions), has a major impact on oxygen uptake by the
lung. Since CO 2 is more diffusible across the alveolar–capillary
barrier than oxygen, the presence of low V̇ A /Q̇ regions leads to
decreased PaO 2 levels before PaCO2 is increased [9,96,150,151].
A diagrammatic representation of V̇A /Q̇ relationships is detailed
in Fig. 37.18A. Ideal matching between ventilation and perfusion
occurs when the V̇A
/Q̇ ratio is 1. In the conscious resting animal
with normal lung function, gas exchange is optimal because the
relative distribution of V̇A /Q̇ ratios is centralized toward the preva-
lence of alveoli with a V̇A /Q̇ ratio close to 1 (Fig. 37.18B) As alveolar
units become less ventilated (areas of low V̇ A
/Q̇ ratio), there is a
progressive increase in the amount of mixed venous blood added to
end-capillary blood, known as “venous admixture.” One extreme is
to have perfused alveoli or areas of the lung with no ventilation such
that blood passing through such a region is not oxygenated. This is
referred to as “intrapulmonary shunt” and has a V̇A
/Q̇ ratio equal to
zero [150]. The major consequence of adding mixed venous blood
(PvO2 = 40 mmHg) to pulmonary end-capillary blood is a decrease
in PaO2 and arterial oxygen content (CaO 2 ). Oxygenation impair-
ment secondary to areas of low V̇ A /Q̇ ratio and shunt may be
observed in animals with pulmonary disease (pneumonia, neopla-
sia, and lung edema) or during general anesthesia. Although
arterial oxygenation can be impaired, CO2 elimination may not be
compromised during the early stages of pulmonary disease. In fact,
severe hypoxemia (PaO 2 < 60 mmHg) caused by areas of low V̇ A
/Q̇
and shunt may be associated with normal or below normal PaCO 2
(respiratory alkalosis) due to stimulation of peripheral chemore-
ceptors located in the carotid body by low PaO 2 (hypoxic drive),
which mediates an increase in V̇ A through increases in f and
V T [53,150]. This is possible because CO 2 is 20 times more diffusi-
ble across the alveolar–capillary membrane than oxygen and there
is an inverse relationship between V̇ A and PaCO 2
. In animals that
have a reduced central respiratory drive (due to disease or second-
ary to drugs including opioids and general anesthetics), low V̇ A
/Q̇
and shunt may contribute to rising PaCO 2 levels. Because areas of
low V̇ A
/Q̇ are partially ventilated, hypoxemia caused by low V̇ A
/Q̇
can be counteracted by increasing alveolar oxygen partial pressure
(PA
O2
) via oxygen supplementation (i.e., increasing F I
O2
). If a
patient that is ventilated fails to respond to an increase in FI
O2
,
shunt should be suspected as the major cause of oxygenation
impairment.
As capillary blood flow decreases in relation to the ideal in venti-
lated alveoli (areas of high V̇ A /Q̇ ratio), there is an increase in the
fraction of total ventilation that does not contribute to gas exchange,
that is wasted ventilation [150]. Alveolar deadspace (VDalv
) is an
extreme instance of a high V̇A
/Q̇ ratio, where alveoli are ventilated
but are not perfused. As explained above, VDalv
adds to the airway
deadspace (VDaw
) to form the physiologic deadspace (VD phys
). An
increase in VDalv
per se does not impact gas exchange if there is a
compensatory increase in V̇ A [150]. However, if the ventilatory
response is obliterated or reduced by anesthetic drugs, PaCO2
will increase.
Based on radioisotope studies evaluating distribution of blood
flow in pulmonary capillaries across the lung tissue, the vertical
gradient of perfusion and ventilation is minimal in standing dogs
with a horizontal lung [107,152]. Matching of vertical perfusion
and ventilation gradients in conscious horses is such that there is
little difference in V̇A
/Q̇ in different lung regions [97,106]. Studies
using a multiple inert gas elimination technique in horses suggest
that the scatter of V̇A
/Q̇ ratios in conscious horses is very similar to
that seen in people [153]. No regions of low V̇ A
/Q̇ were identified,
but a minor shunt component (less than 3% of CO) was observed.
A high V̇A
/Q̇ area was identified (constituting 3–17% of the total),
and the extent of this area was correlated with lower pulmonary
artery pressures [153] (Fig. 37.19).

O2 at high altitudes
(discussed previously). A more detailed description of the assess-

Shunt fraction is the percentage of total blood flow generated by
the right ventricle (i.e., Q̇T ) that reaches the left ventricle without
exposure to ventilated areas of the lung. Shunted flow is divided
into intrapulmonary and anatomic shunt. Intrapulmonary shunt
occurs when mixed venous (pulmonary arterial) blood perfuses
non-ventilated areas of the lung (V̇ A
/Q̇ = 0). Anatomic shunt is
blood flow that bypasses lung parenchyma (that is, the portion of
the lung where there is gas exchange), moving directly from the
right side of the heart to the left side of the heart. Anatomic shunt
can be either physiologic or pathologic, as in some congenital
cardiac diseases (e.g., PDA with right-to-left shunt, as explained
previously). Physiologic anatomic shunt corresponds to the outflow
from bronchial and Thebesian veins (a network of vessels that
irrigate the myocardium in mammals) that drains directly into the
left heart [150,151,155,156]. The presence of a small physiologic
anatomic shunt (2 to 5% of Q̇ T
) explains why, in conscious
individuals breathing ambient air, PaO2 is slightly lower than
PA
O2 [150,151,156]. As explained before, intrapulmonary shunt
(V̇A
/Q̇ = 0) plays a major role in causing oxygenation impairment in
patients with severe lung disease and in some animal species during
general anesthesia. Pathologic anatomic shunt is a major cause of
increased shunt fraction in animals with congenital heart diseases
leading to severe hypoxemia/cyanosis.
The terms “venous admixture” and “shunt fraction” do not mean
the same thing, although they are often used interchangeably in the
literature, which causes some confusion. While shunt fraction is the
percentage of Q̇ T going past non-ventilated areas of the lung, venous
admixture is the degree of admixture of mixed venous blood
(including mixed venous blood from areas of low V̇A
/Q̇ and shunted
flow) with pulmonary end-capillary blood that would be required
to produce the observed difference between the arterial and the
end-capillary oxygen partial pressure. True shunt fraction can be
calculated by the formula described above only in patients breath-
ing 100% oxygen (F I
O2 > 0.9), as the impact of low V̇ A /Q̇ units on
venous admixture is eliminated [150,151]. However, if the patient
is breathing lower inspired oxygen concentrations (e.g., F I
O2 = 0.21
to 0.6), the calculation above is better referred to as “venous
admixture” as it will represent not only shunted flow but also the
blood flow going past low V̇ A /Q̇ units.

reasonably accurate estimate of the magnitude of pulmonary shunt
flow (Fig. 37.20) [157]. Fig. 37.20 also illustrates the poor response,

Effects of anesthesia on ventilation, pulmonary
perfusion, and ventilation–perfusion relationships
Influence of anesthetic drugs on neural control
of ventilation
Injectable and inhalant anesthetic agents and some sedative/
analgesic drugs used during the perioperative period decrease the
ventilatory response to increases in PaCO2 and decreases in PaO2 in
a dose-dependent manner. This occurs secondary to suppression of
neuronal activity in the medulla and pons, decreased central and
peripheral chemoreceptor activity, as well as inhibition of mechan-
oreceptors throughout the respiratory system [44].
The typical hypoventilation and the resulting hypercapnia
observed in spontaneously breathing anesthetized animals is not
harmful per se if extracellular/blood pH is not markedly decreased
(< 7.20) and hypoxemia is prevented by increasing FI
O2
. However, if
general anesthesia is induced in animals with uncorrected meta-
bolic acidosis, suppression of chemoreceptor activity leading to
increased PaCO2 above physiologic ranges (> 45 mmHg) has the
potential to precipitate a mixed acid–base disturbance (metabolic
acidosis and respiratory acidosis) that may result in severe acidemia
(pH < 7.10–7.20) [52]. The effects of the latter on homeostasis
during general anesthesia may be translated into poor cardiovascu-
lar function and hypotension refractory to catecholamines [158]. In
addition to metabolic disease, in patients with pre-existing impaired
gas exchange prior to sedation/anesthesia, appropriate selection of
drugs and the management of the clinical consequences associated
with the effects on the neural control of ventilation will improve
outcomes.
To determine drug effects on the neural control of ventilation
in vivo, the change in V̇E in response to alterations in environmental
conditions (hypoxia, hyperoxia, hypercapnia, and hypocapnia)
can be measured in experimental settings. In conscious normal
mammals, the CO 2 response curve, which is the graphic representa-
tion of the change in V̇ E in response to increases in PaCO 2 or PET
CO2
is relatively linear (Fig. 37.4A). The effects of drugs on the neural con-
trol of ventilation are determined by measuring changes in respira-
tory pattern (most notably frequency) and the degree of respiratory
depression as assessed by PaCO 2
, in addition to the ventilatory
response to increased CO 2 and decreased PaO 2 with different drug
doses or combinations.
Inhalant and injectable anesthetic drugs
The anesthetic index, calculated by dividing the end-tidal anes-
thetic concentration that induces apnea (cessation of breathing for
60 s) by the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC), provides an
assessment of the central respiratory depressant effects of inhalant
anesthetics [159,160]. Inhalant anesthetics in current use cause
progressive increases in PaCO 2 as the anesthetic dose is increased
from 1 MAC to 1.5 and 2 MAC multiples [4]. Although the degree
of hypercapnia observed with equipotent concentrations of
sevoflurane and isoflurane, ranging from 1 to 2 MAC is similar [4],
the anesthetic index was reported to be larger for sevoflurane
(3.45 MAC) than for isoflurane (2.65 MAC) in dogs, suggesting that
sevoflurane causes less respiratory depression at higher equipotent
anesthetic concentrations than does isoflurane [161].
As noted above, CO2 is a major determinant of ventilatory drive
in normal mammals under typical environmental conditions.
All inhalant general anesthetic agents in current use produce a
dose-dependent decrease in the ventilatory response to CO2
.
Therefore, for any given PaCO 2 , the V̇ E is lower than in a conscious
animal and the CO 2 response curve is shifted downward and to the
right as illustrated in Fig. 37.21A [162]. The reduced sensory input
and central sensitivity to CO2 produce a marked fall in V̇ E , usually
through a dose-related decrease in V T
, with a variable effect on
breathing frequency depending on the inhalant anesthetic. As a
result of these changes, PaCO 2 levels increase as the anesthetic dose
is increased when animals breathe spontaneously [2,4,163,164].
The degree of hypercapnia at equipotent doses of inhalant anesthetic
agents varies with the species and the degree of surgical stimulation
[4,160,163–165]. Afferent sensory input from surgical stimulation
will stimulate the respiratory center in the brainstem and increase

the ventilatory drive. Therefore, the respiratory depression induced
by general anesthetics is usually less in the presence of surgical
stimulation. Noxious stimulation however will not alter ventilatory
drive during general anesthesia if afferent sensory input is blocked
by local/regional anesthesia techniques. Of the inhalant anesthetics,
halothane produces the least increase in PaCO 2 during spontaneous
respiration, whereas, at equipotent doses, isoflurane, sevoflurane,
and desflurane produce somewhat higher and similar PaCO2 levels
in most species [4,163,166–168]. In ruminants, the degree of
hypercapnia is greater with equipotent inhalant anesthetic doses
than for horses, and horses show more respiratory depression than
monkeys, cats, and dogs [4,160,163,165,169,170]. Clinically, swine,
ferrets, rabbits, and rats also seem to be more prone to hypercapnia,
whereas deep-diving seals may become totally apneic during light
levels of anesthesia or with opioid-only sedation [167,171,172].
The apneic threshold can be defined as the PaCO 2 level at which
spontaneous ventilatory effort ceases due to loss of central respira-
tory drive (e.g., low PaCO2 or high CSF pH [relative to the set-point]).
A PaCO 2 reduction of 5–9 mmHg from normal resting values
through voluntary hyperventilation in conscious humans, or by
artificial ventilation of deeply sedated or anesthetized animals, pro-
duces apnea. The distance between the resting normal PaCO 2 level
and the apneic threshold is relatively constant (i.e., 4–6 mmHg less
than the normal resting level) irrespective of the anesthetic
depth [174,175]. Because inhalant and injectable anesthetics reset
the apneic threshold to a higher level, PaCO2 must be higher than
the normal range for the animal species for spontaneous breathing
efforts to occur during general anesthesia [176]. It is a common
practice to provide mechanical ventilation in anesthetized animals
simply by adjusting the number of mandatory breaths (f) and the V T
(or inspiratory pressure) delivered by the ventilator (i.e., V̇ E
) to
maintain PaCO2 levels within normal ranges (35–45 mmHg), with-
out having to resort to neuromuscular blocking agents to abolish
spontaneous respiratory efforts. This technique may not be effec-
tive, however, if V̇ E delivered by the mechanical ventilator is less
than necessary to maintain eucapnia. On the other hand, if the
ventilator is adjusted to deliver a relatively large V̇ E
, the resultant
decrease in PaCO 2 (hypocapnia) can lead to a more prolonged
period of apnea after discontinuation of mechanical ventilation at
the end of anesthesia. One practical way of reducing the period of
apnea following mechanical ventilation is to decrease V̇E by lower-
ing the ventilator respiratory rate to allow PaCO 2 to increase above
the apneic threshold toward the end of anesthesia. In anesthetized
horses, adjusting controlled mechanical ventilation to allow higher
PET
CO 2 values (60 mmHg) results in a more rapid return of spon-
taneous ventilation at the end of anesthesia when compared to
animals where mechanical ventilation was adjusted to achieve a
PET
CO2 of 40 mmHg [177]. When weaning a patient from ventila-
tory support, if the animal is apneic for more than 30 s to 1 min,
the anesthesiologist can intermittently provide manually assisted
breaths while allowing PaCO 2 to rise to a level where the apneic
threshold is again exceeded, and spontaneous ventilation resumes.
Depending on the residual analgesic or anesthetic drug levels, the
latter typically occurs at elevated PaCO2 levels.
Among the contemporary injectable anesthetic agents, propofol
is known for inducing respiratory depression and transient apnea in
a similar fashion as thiopental in small animals [178]. The injecta-
ble anesthetic alfaxalone, may also cause respiratory depression/
apnea after rapid intravenous administration. In dogs sedated with
dexmedetomidine–methadone, incidence of post-induction apnea
did not differ between induction of anesthesia with propofol and
alfaxalone [179]. However, when both agents were administered at
a faster rate to induce anesthesia (2 mg/kg/min and 4 mg/kg/min
for alfaxalone and propofol, respectively) 100% of animals devel-
oped apnea lasting for at least 30 s; while a slower rate of adminis-
tration (0.5 mg/kg/min and 1.0 mg/kg/min for alfaxalone and
propofol, respectively), reduced the incidence of apnea to 25% for
both anesthetic agents [179]. In dogs, current evidence therefore
favors the slow titration of injectable anesthetics to achieve the
desired depth of anesthesia to minimize post-induction respiratory
depression/apnea [179,180]. Use of propofol as part of a total intra-
venous anesthesia technique often results in significant respiratory
depression/apnea that requires mechanical ventilatory support in
animals [181,182]. There is some evidence that total intravenous
anesthesia with alfaxalone might be favored when mechanical ven-
tilation is not available in cats because of less respiratory depression
relative to that observed with propofol [182]. However, evidence in
dogs undergoing elective surgery points out that maintenance of
anesthesia with propofol (mean infusion rate 0.37 ± 0.09 mg/kg/min)
or alfaxalone (mean infusion rate 0.11 ± 0.01 mg/kg/min) results in
a similar degree of hypoventilation [183].
Although ketamine may be associated with less respiratory
depression than other injectable anesthetics, when dissociative
anesthetics are used in combination with other drugs during clinical
anesthesia, they may also contribute to apnea or reduced V̇E . For
example, post-induction apnea was more common in dogs after
administration of propofol–ketamine (2 mg/kg each) than after
propofol (4 mg/kg) alone [184]. Similarly, induction of anesthesia
with propofol–ketamine in dogs for laryngeal examination resulted
in lower hemoglobin saturation (87%) than propofol alone (94%),
an observation attributed to a reduced central ventilatory drive and
associated hypoventilation [185]. In cats, pulmonary ventilation
may be decreased when supratherapeutic doses of ketamine are
used, but the slope of the CO2 response curve is not altered in
comparison to the conscious state [186]. In horses, short-term
anesthesia with α2
-adrenergic receptor agonists and ketamine alone
or in combination benzodiazepines and/or guaifenesin induces
some degree of respiratory depression (increased PaCO2
), although
less than that observed with inhalant anesthetics [187–189]. During
anesthesia produced with tiletamine–zolazepam or halothane in
horses, PaCO2 levels will increase by 5–10 mmHg if the inspired
oxygen concentration is increased from 21–30% to 90–100%
[190,191]. The latter is attributed to a reduction in chemoreceptor
activity associated with higher PaO 2 levels [44]. Other studies have
shown a trend toward greater respiratory depression (i.e., higher
PaCO2 levels) in spontaneously breathing, isoflurane-anesthetized
horses inhaling an inspired oxygen concentration approaching
100% compared to 50% oxygen [192]. Greater respiratory depres-
sion associated with high F I
O2 has been reported in other species
under general anesthesia, including the rabbit [193]. Although
there is a decrease in respiratory drive observed in spontaneously
breathing animals during anesthesia with increased FI
O2 levels,
oxygen supplementation is still recommended to minimize the risk
of hypoxemia, particularly in the equine [187,188,190,192,194,195].
As described previously, in conscious individuals V̇E steeply
increases when PaO 2 falls below 60 mmHg, with the slope of the
curve approaching infinity as PaO 2 falls to 30–40 mmHg [196]
(Fig. 37.4B). Compared to the conscious state, most general anes-
thetics suppress peripheral chemoreceptor activity and inhibit the
hypoxic ventilatory drive in a dose-related fashion (Fig. 37.22)
[197–202]. Early studies demonstrated that isoflurane causes less
suppression of the hypoxic ventilatory drive compared to halothane

-- 738 of 1450 --

Chapter 37: Respiratory Physiology and Pathophysiology 	723
and enflurane (Fig. 37.22) [198]; and sevoflurane appears to cause
less 	suppression 	of 	the 	hypoxic 	ventilatory 	drive 	than
isoflurane [202]. While barbiturates (thiopental and pentobarbital)
are known for inhibiting the hypoxic ventilatory drive, intravenous
ketamine (10 mg/kg, followed by 0.5 mg/kg/min) was shown to
preserve the ventilatory response to low PaO2 levels in dogs under
experimental conditions (Fig. 37.22) [197]. In human subjects,
propofol inhibits the hypoxic ventilatory response even when
administered at subanesthetic doses to produce sedation without
loss of consciousness [201].
Anesthetic drugs that suppress the hypoxic ventilatory drive
should be used cautiously for induction of anesthesia in animal
species where endotracheal intubation is associated with a greater
degree of difficulty, such as lagomorphs (rabbits) and rodents, or if
the equipment necessary to perform endotracheal intubation and
artificially ventilate the lungs is not readily available. If prolonged
apnea occurs during induction of anesthesia, failure to establish a
patent airway for oxygen supplementation and positive-pressure
ventilation will quickly precipitate an episode of severe hypoxemia/
tissue hypoxia, and an anesthetic fatality. For anesthesiologists
who are less experienced with endotracheal intubation in rabbits,
a species-specific supraglottic airway device (laryngeal mask)
may facilitate more rapid establishment of a patent airway for
oxygen supplementation and artificial ventilation of the lungs if
necessary [203,204].
Sedatives and hypnotics
Mild to moderate sedation with α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists
alone usually does not result in clinically relevant changes in
arterial blood gases in most species. However, when relatively high
doses of α2 - adrenergic receptor agonists are combined with opioids
or ketamine to produce deeper levels of sedation/chemical restraint,
some degree of gas exchange impairment (increased PaCO 2 and
decreased PaO 2 ) can be observed in small animal species breathing
room air (Fig. 37.23A,B) [205–208]. In ruminants, the degree of
impaired gas exchange associated with α2
- adrenergic receptor ago-
nists alone, administered at doses sufficient to induce recumbency,
can be marked [7,209]. When arterial blood gas changes associated
with α2
- adrenergic receptor agonist combinations are observed,
they cannot be explained only by a centrally mediated decrease in
V̇ E and V̇A
, as the increase in PaCO2 per se does not justify the
decrease in arterial oxygenation observed after administration of
these drug combinations. While the decrease in V̇E and increase
in PaCO2 induced by injectable/inhalant anesthetics appears to be
related to the CNS depressant effects of these drugs, V̇A
/Q̇ mismatch
likely contributes to the decrease in PaO 2 in animals receiving

Experimental data in dogs suggests that high doses of medetomi-
dine administered intravenously (20 μg/kg) inhibit the ventilatory
response to increased CO 2 levels in comparison to the awake state,
but such effect is less than that observed during isoflurane anesthe-
sia (Fig. 37.21A) [162,198]. Dexmedetomidine-induced sedation
has also been shown to impair the ventilatory response to hypox-
emia and hypercapnia in humans [210]. In dogs that were receiving
a fentanyl infusion (5 μg/kg/min) during recovery from isoflurane
anesthesia, intravenous dexmedetomidine administration (2.5 μg/kg)
resulted in significant respiratory depression (PaCO 2 > 45 mmHg)
when compared to placebo or acepromazine (0.05 mg/kg) [207].
Therefore, caution should be exerted when α2 - adrenergic receptor
agonists are used to provide sedation during recovery from general
anesthesia because of the potential for respiratory depression par-
ticularly when oxygenation will not be monitored or the ability to
provide oxygen supplementation is not available. Relatively low
doses of α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists are commonly adminis-
tered after discontinuation of inhalant anesthesia in horses with
the goal of improving the quality of recovery [211,212]. However,
administration of α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists and other anes-
thetic adjuvants to horses in the recovery room should be delayed
until strong spontaneous breathing efforts are present, if measures
to support ventilatory support are not available, as apnea may be
precipitated if these drugs are administered to animals that are in a
deep plane of anesthesia.
Phenothiazines (acepromazine) and butyrophenones (droperidol)
may increase the hypoxic ventilatory drive, possibly by blocking
the effects of endogenous dopamine on peripheral chemoreceptors
[50,213,214]. Interestingly, in humans and cats, intravenous dopa-
mine (3–5 μg/kg/min) inhibits the ventilatory response to low PaO2
due to depression of peripheral chemoreceptor (carotid body)
output [215,216]. In human patients with heart failure breathing
ambient air, intravenous dopamine has also been shown to decrease
V̇ E despite decreased oxygen saturation and increased PET
CO2
,
although the clinical significance of this in the management of
clinical veterinary patients is unknown [217].
Opioids
Opioids are known for inducing respiratory depression. In knockout
mice lacking μ-opioid receptors, morphine and other pure μ-opioid
receptor agonists do not induce respiratory depression, demon-
strating that the adverse ventilatory effects induced by these drugs
are largely mediated by stimulation of μ-opioid receptors [218,219].
Experimental evidence obtained in conscious human subjects pro-
vides ample evidence that pure μ-opioid receptor agonists suppress
the ventilatory response to hypercapnia [220]. Contrasting with
pure μ- opioid receptor agonists, drugs that act as μ- opioid receptor
antagonists and κ-opioid receptor agonists (butorphanol and nal-
buphine) have a limited (ceiling) effect on the ventilatory response
to increasing CO 2 levels [221,222] and can reverse the respiratory
depression induced by pure μ-opioid receptor agonists [223–225].
