) is further aggravated by use of high
F I
O2 [226]. However, the clinical significance of respiratory depres-
sion caused by hyperoxia associated with high FI
O2 in animals
receiving opioids is presently unclear.
Opioids may induce panting in some species, most notably
dogs [227–229]. In conscious dogs, panting is more frequently
observed after administration of pure μ-opioid receptor agonists
(oxymorphone) than after μ-opioid receptor antagonists/κ-opioid
receptor agonists (butorphanol) [230]. This reaction is thought to
be mediated by the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center that
resets as if the body temperature was increased (though it is not).
Because panting is an important thermoregulatory mechanism
in canine species, opioid administration to conscious dogs may
decrease body temperature [54]. Interestingly, an increase in body
temperature leading to clinically relevant hyperthermia is
observed after opioid administration in cats, which is attributed to
drug-induced changes in the thermoregulatory center [231].
Although panting is commonly observed after opioid adminis-
tration in canine species, relatively high doses of methadone
(0.5–1 mg/kg) or morphine (1.0 mg/kg) administered intravenously
do not cause clinically relevant changes in arterial blood gases in
healthy conscious dogs [232]. Administration of hydromorphone
(0.2 mg/kg) subcutaneously, or liposome-encapsulated hydromor-
phone (2.0 mg/kg, subcutaneously), increased PaCO 2 and decreased
PaO2 from baseline values in dogs [233]. However, blood gas
changes were mild in the latter study, and in most cases, PaCO 2 val-
ues were not increased above the high normal range (45 mmHg),
and PaO 2 values were not decreased below the low normal range
(80 mmHg) [233]. Butorphanol does not induce significant changes
in arterial blood gases when administered to conscious dogs at a
dose of 0.3 mg/kg intravenously [234], or even when larger doses
(up to 0.8 mg/kg) are administered in spontaneously ventilating
dogs anesthetized with halothane [235]. However, in human sub-
jects anesthetized with 50% nitrous oxide in oxygen, butorphanol
was shown to inhibit the increase in V̇E in response to increasing
CO2 levels [236]. While administration of opioid analgesics to con-
scious non- painful horses may result in excitatory behavior, arterial
blood gases are unaltered [237–239]. In isoflurane-anesthetized
horses, morphine administered intravenously at doses, ranging
from 0.15 to 0.25 mg/kg does not induce respiratory depression,
while supratherapeutic doses (2.0 mg/kg) cause significant
respiratory depression/hypercapnia [240,241].
Pure μ-opioid receptor agonists (methadone, 0.25–0.75 mg/kg;
morphine, 0.25–1.0 mg/kg) combined with intramuscular aceprom-
azine (0.05 mg/kg) induce sedative effects with minimal evidence of
respiratory depression based on arterial blood gases in healthy
dogs [242,243]. Intravenous or intramuscular administration of
acepromazine (0.05 mg/kg) combined with butorphanol (0.4 mg/kg)
or nalbuphine (0.5 mg/kg) in cats induces mild sedation without
evidence of respiratory acidosis based on venous blood gases [244].
In animals, the respiratory depressant effects of opioids are evident
when these drugs are administered intravenously during general
anesthesia [240,245–247]. Respiratory depression/apnea associated
with intraoperative opioid administration often requires mechanical
ventilatory support in anesthetized animals [245,247,248]. Constant
rate infusion of short-acting pure μ-opioid receptor agonists
(e.g., sufentanil) in isoflurane-anesthetized dogs causes the CO2
response curve to become nearly flat, suggesting that these drugs
produce marked inhibition of central chemoreceptor activity
during general anesthesia (Fig. 37.21B) [173]. Studies in cats under
light anesthesia with α-chloralose and urethane have shown that
morphine (0.15 mg/kg) depresses ventilation at hyperoxia but does
not alter the ventilatory response (increase in V̇ E
) to hypoxia [249].
Administration of μ-opioid receptor agonists as premedication
may also impair ventilation during recovery from anesthesia. Clinical
evidence in healthy dogs undergoing surgery (ovariohysterectomy
and castration) indicates that premedication with hydromorphone
0.2 mg/kg, intramuscularly may result in higher PaCO2 in compari-
son to the use of butorphanol 0.4 mg/kg, intramuscularly [250].
When μ-opioid receptor agonists are used as premedication, the
degree of respiratory depression is usually mild and well tolerated
by healthy animals undergoing elective surgeries [250]. However,
caution should be exerted when these drugs are administered to
sick animals or patients with respiratory disease, as they may have a
greater impact on ventilation and lead to clinically relevant hyper-
capnia and hypoxemia. During recovery from general anesthesia in
dogs, persistent respiratory depression caused by opioids resulting
in low hemoglobin saturation (e.g., pulse oximetry < 94%) can occur
while the patient is breathing ambient air and is often accompanied
by excessive residual sedation and delayed extubation (lack of return
of swallowing reflex). These signs can be reversed by slow intrave-
nous titration of a μ-opioid receptor antagonist (naloxone 1–5 μg/kg)
or a μ-opioid receptor antagonist/κ-opioid receptor agonist (butor-
phanol 0.05–0.1 mg/kg). In dogs, intravenous naloxone at 1 μg/kg
increments every 2 min can be administered until the breathing
frequency and amplitude of spontaneous respiratory efforts are
increased to the point of normalizing pulse oximetry saturation
(≥ 95%), and there is an improvement in the levels of consciousness/
return of the swallowing reflex allowing orotracheal tube removal.
Because respiratory depression and analgesia are clinical effects
associated with μ-opioid receptor stimulation, slow titration until
achieving the desired effect is important to avoid reversal of the
analgesic effects. The elimination half-life of intravenous naloxone
is relatively short in dogs (37 min) [251]. Therefore, clinicians
should be aware of possible recurrence of respiratory depression
and the need for additional opioid reversal over time [252]. In the
case of opioid intoxication, much higher doses of naloxone (40 μg/kg)
are necessary to reverse the adverse effects/respiratory depression
induced by the opioid and there may be the need for repeated
administration of high doses in case of an inadequate response.
Pharmacokinetic studies in dogs suggest that the intranasal route
(4 mg via a commercially available fixed-dose naloxone atomizer;
mean dose of 0.17 mg/kg) may represent an effective alternative to
intravenous naloxone administration in emergency situations of
opioid intoxication [251].
Effects of sedation and anesthesia on pulmonary
ventilation and mechanics
In addition to reducing central respiratory drive as discussed above,
sedation and anesthesia can alter pulmonary ventilation by chang-
ing the volume of the lung, absolute or relative amount of deadspace
(physiological and apparatus deadspace) in relation to V T
, and the
mechanical properties of the respiratory system. While the changes
associated with anesthesia can be considered individually, it is
important to recognize that alterations in individual components of
the respiratory system are not independent. For example, changes
in lung volume influence the mechanical properties of the respira-
tory system, and vice versa.
Ventilation and lung volumes
A reduction in lung volume, specifically the lung volume at end-
expiration (FRC), is one of the major physiologic changes associated

-- 741 of 1450 --

726 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
with general anesthesia and recumbency [61,253–256]. While not
extensively studied in all species, a reduction in FRC observed with
general anesthesia has been demonstrated in several species,
including humans, horses, and dogs [27–29,256,257]. In recumbent
humans, FRC is reduced by about 20% with the induction of general
anesthesia [256,257]. While a reduced FRC does not necessarily
result in atelectasis, it is a commonly recognized sequela to the
reduction of lung volume associated with recumbency and
relaxation/paralysis of respiratory muscles induced by anesthesia.
Atelectasis has been reported to occur in up to 90% of adult human
patients with normal cardiopulmonary function undergoing general
anesthesia, with up to 20–25% of the lung becoming atelectatic or
poorly ventilated as assessed by computed tomography [254,258].
One study in beagle dogs showed no change in FRC associated
with thiopental anesthesia; however, sedation and both sternal
and lateral recumbency have been shown to reduce FRC in deep-
chested dogs [29,259]. While measurement of FRC has rarely been
performed in dogs, with advances in thoracic imaging, specifically
computed tomography, changes in lung volume and the develop-
ment of atelectasis during anesthesia have been evaluated more
extensively. In dogs sedated and maintained in sternal recumbency,
minimal atelectasis is evident on computed tomography images;
however, mild attenuation of aeration/atelectasis occurs in lateral or
dorsally recumbent dogs during sedation and/or general anesthesia
breathing spontaneously or receiving mechanical ventilation
[260–263]. In horses and cows, the decrease in FRC with the onset
of recumbency and general anesthesia may be marked, as much as
50–70%. This has been directly measured by helium dilution [27,264]
and open-circuit nitrogen washout [28] and is consistent with imag-
ing studies showing reduced lung aeration [265,266]. The reduction
in FRC seems to be primarily related to the positional change
from an upright posture to recumbency and, in horses, is greater in
lateral or dorsal recumbency compared to sternal positioning [28].
Laterally recumbent horses and cows have a smaller FRC compared
to the conscious state and radiographic images indicate that the
dependent lung is poorly aerated [265,266]. Studies using nuclear
scintigraphy and computed tomography have clearly demonstrated
that there is markedly less ventilation of the dependent lung of
horses in lateral and dorsal recumbency during anesthesia [267,268].
In horses, the reduction in lower lung volume is accompanied by
atelectasis and may be influenced by the degree of obesity or body
conformation, a finding consistent with studies in humans [269,270].
The acute reduction in FRC and development of atelectasis asso-
ciated with anesthesia has been primarily attributed to three factors:
(1) alterations in chest wall (thoracic wall and diaphragm) function
and configuration with a resultant increase in P pl (globally with
regional differences), (2) low distal airway/alveolar pressures (Palv
),
and (3) loss of functional surfactant. The former two mechanisms
are believed to be the major mechanisms contributing to the devel-
opment of atelectasis in healthy humans and in some animal species
under anesthesia while surfactant dysfunction is recognized to
contribute to the development of atelectasis in patients with pre-
existing lung injury and/or patients receiving long-term mechanical
ventilatory support [257,271].
Alterations in chest wall function and configuration are respon-
sible for most of the reduction in FRC associated with anesthesia,
particularly in large animal species such as horses and cows. In
conscious animals, the outward recoil of the chest wall results in
a sub-atmospheric pressure within the pleural cavity (P pl ). The
pressure difference between the inside (alveoli) and the outside of
the lung (pleural cavity) (Palv − P pl
), is responsible for maintaining
the alveoli open throughout the respiratory cycle (inspiration and
expiration). Induction of anesthesia results in relaxation of the chest
wall (thoracic wall and diaphragm), which in turn increases Ppl
(it becomes less negative) and decreases the outward pull on the
lung. Cranial migration of the diaphragm, increased transfer of
pressure from the abdominal cavity to the thorax, and the weight
of the lung within the chest wall also contribute to an increased
(less negative) P pl
, most notably in the dependent lung regions.
When the pressure outside the lungs (P pl
) exceeds the pressure
within the airways and alveoli (Palv
), compression atelectasis develops.
Because of their long-sloping diaphragm (notably horses), anatomy
of their gastrointestinal tract, and their body mass, large animal
species are more prone to compression of the lungs and atelectasis
in dependent zones when recumbent relative to small animal species.
In horses and cows, with the onset of anesthesia and movement into
lateral recumbency, there is radiographic evidence of a marked
change in the two-dimensional lung silhouette and the position of
the diaphragm [265,266]. In ponies anesthetized with halothane,
the diaphragmatic outline moved forward in both sternal and lateral
recumbency, although the forward shift was considerably greater in
lateral recumbency [265]. When the ponies were positioned in
dorsal recumbency, the diaphragmatic outline moved toward the
dependent spine region. With minor variations, observations of
315–400 kg cattle were very similar [266]. The positional alteration
of the diaphragmatic silhouette concurs with the reduction in FRC
noted by Sorenson and Robinson when ponies were moved from
sternal to lateral or dorsal recumbency [28]. In addition to changes
in position of the diaphragm, the tonic activity of the lateral chest
wall, especially that provided by the serratus ventralis muscle, may
be decreased in anesthetized horses, and it is postulated that this
phenomenon reduces the stabilization of the lateral chest wall and
likely contributes to the loss of FRC in this species [272].
In addition to loss of lung volume secondary to compression,
distal airway and alveolar pressures (Palv
) may also contribute to the
loss of lung volume and atelectasis during anesthesia [271].
Reduction in airway radius or even obstruction of small airways
secondary to compression (as described above), constriction, or the
presence of intraluminal material (e.g., mucus) may reduce ventila-
tion to distal lung units. Absorption of gases from the regions of
lung that are poorly ventilated but still perfused may subsequently
result in the development of absorption atelectasis. The development
of the latter is influenced by the characteristics of the gases in the
distal lung unit. In individuals breathing ambient air, alveolar gas
contains approximately 79% of nitrogen (Table 37.4). Because
nitrogen is insoluble in blood, it is not absorbed from the alveoli to
capillary blood and may have a role in preventing alveolar units
with low V̇ A
/Q̇ ratio from collapsing (acting as a “nitrogen skele-
ton”). If alveolar nitrogen is largely replaced by oxygen by using
high F I
O2 (> 0.8), the flow of oxygen from alveoli to capillary blood
in low V̇A
/Q̇ units exceeds flow of inspired gas (oxygen) entering
these alveoli, causing these lung units to become progressively
smaller until they collapse [154]. High FI
O2 in the perianesthetic
period has been demonstrated to lead to a greater degree of
atelectasis in horses, dogs, cats, and humans, an observation
consistent with absorption of gases in distal airways and alveoli
[61,191,253,261,262,273].
There are several important consequences resulting from a
decrease in lung volume at end-expiration. Most importantly, a
reduced FRC predisposes a patient to V̇ A
/Q̇ mismatching and
intrapulmonary shunting of blood secondary to the development of
atelectasis [256]. Due to compression of lung parenchyma during

-- 742 of 1450 --

Chapter 37: Respiratory Physiology and Pathophysiology 	727
anesthesia, a portion of blood supplying the lung will flow by
collapsed (V̇A
/Q̇ = 0) and/or poorly ventilated alveoli (V̇ A /Q̇ ratio
between 0.01 and 0.1) without achieving adequate oxygenation
(assuming HPV does not divert blood to well-ventilated lung units),
thereby contributing to a reduction in oxygen levels in the blood
leaving the lung (i.e., increased venous admixture) [274], as
discussed previously. Although oxygenation impairment/low PaO 2
is the major consequence of atelectatic lung areas, an increase in
Q̇ s/Q̇ T through the lung also adds CO2
- rich mixed venous blood to
oxygenated blood, further aggravating hypercapnia caused by a
decrease in V̇A during anesthesia. In addition to impacting gas
exchange function of the lung, changes in lung volume also influ-
ence pulmonary mechanics, with pulmonary resistance increasing
and compliance decreasing with a reduction in FRC/atelectasis.
To minimize the loss of lung volume and the development of
atelectasis associated with anesthesia and recumbency, several
strategies have been investigated including the use of negative-
pressure ventilation, positive-pressure ventilation, and varying
inspired gas composition. Early mechanical ventilators were designed
to create a negative (sub-atmospheric) pressure around the thorax
to enlarge the chest wall and pull gas into the lungs by creating a
negative intrapleural pressure. This was achieved by encasing the
whole body (except the head) inside a cylinder that intermittently
generated a sub-atmospheric pressure. These early ventilators, also
called “iron lungs,” were widely used during the 1950s to provide
mechanical ventilation in patients who suffered from paralysis of
diaphragm caused by poliomyelitis. Due to the required equipment
and limited access to the patient’s thorax, ventilatory support
using negative-pressure ventilation is not in common use today.
Application of intermittent positive pressure to oxygen or air/oxy-
gen mixtures supplying the lungs is now commonly used during
veterinary medicine to maintain alveolar ventilation. Depending on
the strategy, positive-pressure ventilation may establish a positive
pressure gradient between the alveoli and pleural space such that
loss of lung volume and atelectasis does not occur. However, the
level of applied positive pressure and its resulting Palv may not be
enough to overcome the increased Ppl in the dependent lung zones,
therefore the latter may remain closed throughout the respiratory
cycle. Even if inspiratory pressures are set to a level that is high
enough to open up atelectatic lung areas during inspiration, if there
is no positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) or if the level of PEEP
is inadequate to keep the alveoli open during expiration, the inter-
mittent opening and closure of alveoli (tidal recruitment) will lead
to ventilator-induced lung injury, specifically atelectrauma [275,276].
Reversal of atelectasis during anesthesia may require an alveolar
recruitment maneuver, that is, the temporary application of high
inspiratory airway pressures to open up atelectatic lung areas,
followed by mechanical ventilation with an adequate PEEP level
to prevent loss of lung volume and recurrence of atelectasis
[93,262,277,278]. As high FI
O2 levels have been shown to contribute
to absorption atelectasis, the use of varying inspired F I
O2 and/or
supplementation of inspired gases with less soluble gases such as
helium have been investigated [93,194,279,280]. Inspired gas con-
centrations, alveolar recruitment maneuvers, and PEEP adjustment
during mechanical ventilation are discussed in greater detail in
Chapter 38.
Ventilation and deadspace
As previously discussed, V̇A and the maintenance of normal PaCO2
levels can be influenced by alterations in deadspace and the VD phys
/V T
relationship. In anesthetized patients, deadspace can be altered
through a change in either VD phys
(airway or alveolar) or mechanical
(apparatus) deadspace. Airway deadspace can increase with
positional changes such as extension of the head and neck, high
airway pressures associated with positive-pressure ventilation, and
bronchodilation [281,282].
While bypassing the upper airways through use of a tracheos-
tomy or placement of an endotracheal tube (of appropriate length)
decreases total deadspace (physiologic and apparatus deadspace),
anesthetic equipment, including facemasks, excessively long endotra-
cheal tubes that protrude outside the mouth/nostrils, and airway
adaptors placed between the breathing circuit and the endotracheal
tube for airway gas sampling/analysis or spirometry can dramati-
cally increase apparatus and total deadspace, with possible clinical
relevance, particularly in small patients [283]. While an increase in
deadspace will not alter V̇ A if a compensatory change in V T and/or f
occurs, as one may expect to occur in a conscious healthy individual,
an increase in deadspace due to anesthesia equipment, combined
with an unchanged or decreased V T associated with general
anesthesia, can significantly increase VD phys
/V T
, reduce V̇ A , and
contribute to hypercapnia.
As previously discussed, changes in expired nitrogen concentra-
tion over a single breath after the patient inhales 100% oxygen can
be used to estimate deadspace values in an experimental setting
(single-breath nitrogen washout), while volumetric capnography is
the current clinical gold standard to determine VD phys
, VDalv
, VDaw
, and
effective alveolar ventilation per minute [V̇A = (V T – VD phys
) × f ]. In
general, VD phys
does not change significantly in healthy human patients
during general anesthesia with either spontaneous or artificial ven-
tilation [257]. In healthy spontaneously breathing horses with nor-
mal cardiovascular function placed in dorsal recumbency, VD phys
/V T
ratio measured according to the Bohr equation by volumetric
capnography was approximately 0.35–0.39 and remained relatively
stable over 3 h of general anesthesia [68]. In anesthetized dogs
receiving positive-pressure ventilation, VD phys
/V T ratio calculated
using the Bohr–Enghoff equation, was approximately 0.6, and
remained stable throughout a 60-min period [69]. Use of high air-
way pressures (typically with high PEEP levels) during mechanical
ventilation can, however, result in an increase in Palv and VDalv
by
impairing alveolar perfusion [284]. A decrease in pulmonary perfu-
sion from a variety of causes including a reduced CO associated
with anesthesia or an embolic event, can also lead to an increase
in VDalv
[281]. In hemodynamically compromised small animal or
large animal patients, an increase in P(a-et)CO 2 may not reflect
only impaired pulmonary perfusion if there is significant oxygena-
tion impairment secondary to areas of low V̇A
/Q̇ and intrapulmonary
shunting of blood.
Ventilation and lung mechanics
As previously described, the mechanical properties of the respira-
tory system, specifically regional compliance and resistance,
determine the normal distribution of airflow within the lung and
the energy expended to achieve optimal ventilation. Changes in the
upper and lower airways, thoracic cage, and diaphragm associated
with anesthesia produce marked changes in airway resistance and
pulmonary compliance. While thoracic and lung tissues contribute
to overall pulmonary resistance, the relative change over time in
healthy subjects is believed to be minor relative to the airways.
While changes in lung mechanical properties are significant with
anesthesia, interpretation of measurements of both pulmonary
resistance and compliance during anesthesia is difficult because
changes in lung volume per se will alter these values [79,257].

-- 743 of 1450 --

728 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
The latter is particularly relevant when considering the etiology of
such changes. Absolute values for pulmonary resistance and com-
pliance are influenced by many factors including the method of
measurement, airway device and diameter, patient size, and method
of ventilation. Further discussion regarding the measurement of
pulmonary mechanics during anesthesia is provided in Chapter 38.
At rest under normal circumstances (nasal breathing), the upper
airways (nasal cavity, pharynx, and larynx) are responsible for more
than 50% of the total R aw
. With sedation and anesthesia in horses,
alar and pharyngeal muscles relax, reducing the diameter of the
upper airways, further increasing the resistance to breathing and
increasing the relative contribution of the upper airways to total
R aw [285–287]. In some patients, the consequences of an increase in
upper airway resistance may be limited to an increase in the patient’s
effort to achieve alveolar ventilation. This is typically characterized by
an increase in abdominal movement during inspiration with minimal
or paradoxical (inward-moving) chest wall movement. The latter
respiratory pattern is due to a greater impact of anesthetics on the
function of intercostal muscles versus the diaphragm. Upper airway
obstruction following sedation or induction of general anesthesia
may also occur, particularly in patients with structurally abnormal
upper airways, such as in brachycephalic dogs and cats, or patients
with pathology of the upper airways. In the equine placed in dorsal
recumbency for prolonged periods, congestion and tissue swelling
of the nasopharyngeal structures are particularly common. For
obligate nasal breathers (e.g., cats and horses), bypassing the naso-
pharynx by placing an orotracheal tube, nasotracheal tube (horses),
or supraglottic airway device (cats) reduces upper airway resistance
and the work of breathing, ensuring a patent airway during anes-
thesia [287]. Further discussion regarding the relative risk and
benefits of different airway devices is provided in chapters dedicated
to specific species management. In contrast to the upper airways,
most currently used injectable and inhalant anesthetics result in a
dose-dependent bronchodilation in addition to inhibiting airway
vagal reflexes and bronchoconstriction [175,288–291]. One notable
exception is desflurane, which may cause an increase in R aw due
to bronchoconstriction at higher doses (1.5–2.0 MAC) [290,292].
Airway resistance is, however, influenced by lung volume, with
lower lung volumes resulting in an increase in resistance, particu-
larly as lung volumes approach RV [293].
In general, in humans, an overall increase in R aw (excluding the
effect of upper airways) occurs with anesthesia. It is unknown if this
is due to the reduction in lung volume or change in airflow rates,
two variables that impact resistance measurements [61]. During an
anesthetic period, however, R aw generally remains stable in healthy
human patients receiving ventilatory support [61]. There are few
studies evaluating conscious versus anesthetized respiratory mechan-
ics in veterinary species using consistent methodology that take into
consideration the effect of lung volume and airflows, therefore it is
difficult to make conclusions regarding the effects of anesthesia
alone. In one study evaluating cows anesthetized for 3 h with halo-
thane, R aw tended to increase, however, the degree of change was only
significant in fed cows [294]. The latter also was reported to become
tympanic, therefore, it is possible that the change over time in R aw was
related to a loss of lung volume. In anesthetized mechanically venti-
lated healthy dogs placed in lateral or dorsal recumbency for ortho-
pedic procedures, R aw did not significantly increase over a 120-min
period [295]. Resistance was also unchanged in healthy sedated
recumbent foals receiving ventilatory support over a 24-h period [296].
Similar to the decrease in lung volumes with anesthesia, total
respiratory system compliance (CRS
) is reduced during anesthesia. It
is important to emphasize that decreased C RS in anesthetized
animals may be the result of decreases in lung (C L
) and chest wall
(C CW ) compliance. Development of anesthesia-related atelectasis
and severe lung disease will reduce C RS because of poor CL
. Factors
that are external to the lung, such as loss of respiratory muscle tone/
muscle paralysis (diaphragm and intercostal muscles) induced by
anesthetic drugs, obesity, increased intra-abdominal volume and
pressure, and chest wall conformation (barrel-chested dogs) will
result in a less compliant chest wall (decreased C CW ) and contribute
to a reduced CRS during anesthesia [297]. Although an independent
assessment of C L and C CW would allow the anesthetist to identify the
cause of decreased CRS and to direct the clinical conduct to improve
overall compliance, as described previously, in the clinical setting
CRS is often measured during anesthesia with positive-pressure ven-
tilation. Specifically, total C RS (either dynamic or static/quasistatic
C RS
), is calculated as the ratio between the V T (mL) and the driving
pressure (cm H2
O) (inspiratory minus end-expiratory pressures)
during mechanical ventilation. However, comparison of compliance
measurements among veterinary species requires indexing values
to ideal body weight (mL/cmH2
O/kg). Analysis of CRS measurements
indexed to body weight shows that adult horses present signifi-
cantly lower CRS (0.4 mL/cmH2
O/kg) than dogs (1.3 mL/cmH2
O/kg)
during anesthesia and positive-pressure ventilation [93,297].
In healthy human patients, the decrease in C RS with anesthesia is
believed to be due to the reduction in lung volume [257]. The time-
line of changes in lung volume with changes in compliance, are con-
sistent with the latter etiology. In healthy dogs maintained under
general anesthesia in a clinical setting, quasistatic CRS has been
shown to be relatively stable over time, but it is reduced in obese
animals and animals with a barrel-shaped chest [295,297]. Although
there is a paucity of data in the literature, adequate preoperative
fasting appears to be important to minimize the decrease in CRS and
improve gas exchange during general anesthesia in ruminants. In
one study, a progressive decrease in dynamic C RS was recorded dur-
ing a 90-min period of halothane anesthesia in nonfasted cows and
in cows that were deprived of food for 48 h and water for 12 h prior
to anesthesia [294]. However, dynamic CRS was decreased to a
greater extent in nonfasted than in fasted cows and these changes in
pulmonary mechanics were associated with progressive worsening
of gas exchange (higher PaCO2 and lower PaO2 values), probably
because of a greater degree of atelectasis associated with the devel-
opment of abdominal tympany in cows that were not fasted before
anesthesia [294].
Effects of anesthesia on pulmonary perfusion and hypoxic
pulmonary vasoconstriction
Pulmonary perfusion is driven by the gradient between MPAP and
LAP. Inhalant anesthetics have a major impact on the perfusion of
systemic organs due to dose-dependent decreases in mean arterial
pressure (MAP) and/or CO. The effects of inhalant anesthetics on
pulmonary circulation, however, are less obvious as increasing doses
of inhalant anesthetics (from 1.0 to 1.5–2.0 MAC) did not cause
significant changes in MPAP in spontaneously breathing dogs,
despite reduction of MAP in a dose-related manner (Fig. 37.24A) [4].
In mechanically ventilated horses anesthetized with sevoflurane,
MPAP was significantly decreased from values observed in conscious
animals, although changes in MPAP were not observed between MAC
multiples (Fig. 37.24B) [298]. Absence of changes in MPAP occurred
despite dose-related decreases in MAP and CO (Fig. 37.24B) [298].
Ventilated but poorly perfused lung areas (high V̇ A /Q̇ ratio), appar-
ently caused by low MPAP, appear to be relatively common finding

-- 744 of 1450 --

Chapter 37: Respiratory Physiology and Pathophysiology 	729
in standing conscious horses [153,299]. Although general anesthe-
sia decreases CO and MPAP compared to the conscious state in
equine species, areas of high V̇ A /Q̇ ratio are paradoxically decreased
from values recorded during the conscious state in dorsal recum-
bency anesthetized horses [299].
Major changes in CO during anesthesia will influence arterial
and mixed venous blood oxygenation. In a patient with a relatively
large intrapulmonary shunt (e.g., 50% of shunted flow leading to
hypoxemia/low PaO2 ), arterial oxygenation will be further impaired
if CO is significantly decreased by anesthesia or hemorrhage. This
effect is secondary to a decrease in mixed venous blood PO 2 and
not to a direct effect of low CO on gas exchange within the
lungs [300,301]. Because oxygen delivery is decreased by low CO, a
compensatory increase in oxygen extraction by tissues reduces the
PO2
/hemoglobin saturation in mixed venous blood. As the pulmo-
nary artery blood with lower-than-normal PO 2 and hemoglobin
saturation (e.g., 30 mmHg and 57%) reaches ventilated alveoli, it
will not be fully oxygenated and the blood leaving these alveolar
units will further aggravate the oxygenation impairment caused by
the intrapulmonary shunt [300,301]. Based on this physiologic con-
cept, the anesthesiologist should consider means to improve CO
(e.g., inotropic and/or fluid administration) in patients where poor
hemodynamic function is coinciding with hypoxemia caused by
intrapulmonary shunting during anesthesia.
General anesthesia and mechanical ventilation may decrease
perfusion in specific areas of the lung through decreases in Q̇T
,
which may contribute to an increase in VDalv
if perfusion is
completely abolished in some lung areas. As previously discussed,
ventilated lung areas where capillary blood flow is absent because
Palv is greater than arterial and venous pressures (West zone I)
(Fig. 37.15) can be increased in anesthetized patients receiving
mechanical ventilation, especially if high inspiratory pressures and/
or high levels of PEEP are used. Due to relationship between PET
CO2
and PaCO 2 in mammalian species with normal lungs, monitoring
P ET CO 2 provides a quick and non-invasive tool to assess the
adequacy of ventilation in patients under general anesthesia.
Under normal circumstances, the P ET CO 2 (which represents the
CO 2 eliminated from alveoli that are ventilated and perfused) is
up to 5 mmHg less than PaCO 2 , as alveolar CO 2 is diluted with gas
from the airways, which does not contain CO 2 [302]. However, in
the event of decreased lung perfusion during anesthesia contrib-
uting to an abnormally high VDalv
, the P(a-et)CO 2 will often
increase above 5 mmHg. As previously noted, the anesthesiologist
should also be aware that the use of P(a-et)CO 2 as an index
that reflects solely pulmonary/alveolar deadspace is limited in
the presence of significant low V̇ A /Q̇ areas and intrapulmonary
shunting [62,68]. Mixed venous blood bypassing ventilated alveoli
(shunted flow) and areas with low V̇ A /Q̇ ratios adds CO 2 -rich
blood to the arterial side leading to an increase in PaCO 2 and
overestimation of pulmonary/alveolar deadspace based on the
Enghoff method [62,68]. For practical purposes, the anesthesiolo-
gist may suspect that intrapulmonary shunting is increased, and
therefore bears a greater influence on P(a-et)CO 2 calculations, by
evaluating PaO 2 values while the animal is breathing an inspired

In hemodynamically unstable patients, if P(a-et)CO 2 is elevated
or increases over time, there could be an increase in pulmonary/
alveolar deadspace secondary to poor pulmonary perfusion, which
should be investigated. Identification and resolution of the cause of
abnormally high P(a-et)CO2 is paramount to avoid the development
of further complications during anesthesia. For practical purposes,
in anesthetized small animals presenting a clearly distinguishable
phase III (alveolar plateau) in the capnogram, an increased discrep-
ancy between PET
CO2 and PaCO 2 (P(a-et)CO 2 > 5 mmHg) may
provide a rough estimate that VDalv
/V T is increased. In otherwise
healthy anesthetized animals receiving constant volume mechani-
cal ventilation, a temporal increase in P(a-et)CO 2 may suggest
poor pulmonary perfusion secondary to low CO caused by surgical
factors such as intraoperative hemorrhage/shock [75,76]. Similar
changes secondary to low CO caused by obstruction of venous
return (vena cava) or aortic flow during surgical manipulation of
the abdominal cavity may be observed in small animal anesthesia.
In anesthetized horses, P(a-et)CO2 gradients of 10 mmHg or
higher are a common finding and this difference historically was
thought to arise as consequence of increased pulmonary/alveolar
deadspace in this species [67,303]. The degree of underestimation
of PaCO2 by PET
CO2 in dorsally recumbent horses is higher during
emergency colic surgery than during elective arthroscopic surgery
(Fig. 37.25A,B) [303]. High airway pressures (> 30 cmH2 O) are
frequently necessary to provide mechanical ventilation in colic
horses with poor chest wall compliance associated with a distended
abdomen; the elevated Palv generated by mechanical ventilation
under these circumstances likely has a negative impact on lung per-
fusion because of compression of pulmonary capillaries. However,
because of the significant increase in shunted flow observed during
routine anesthesia in horses, P(a-et)CO2 and VDalv
/V T calculations
based on the Enghoff method may not only reflect an increase in
pulmonary/alveolar deadspace but should be considered global
indices of gas exchange efficiency (Fig. 37.25A,B) [68]. Therapeutic
measures to improve CO/pulmonary perfusion (e.g., initiating
or increasing dobutamine infusion rate) should be considered
if P(a-et)CO2 is excessively increased. In the case of high airway
pressures observed during anesthesia for colic surgery, the surgeon
should expedite abdominal decompression to minimize the negative
impact of distended bowel on chest wall compliance. An
improvement in lung perfusion in these cases may also be associated
with increases in PaO 2 due to better V̇A
/Q̇ matching.
Besides influencing gas exchange, pulmonary perfusion is an
important factor to consider when evaluating the pharmacokinetics
of injectable anesthetics/anesthetic adjuvants, as drugs are subject to
first-pass pulmonary uptake, that is, the instantaneous extraction of
a drug from the circulation by lung tissue [304]. Pulmonary retention
is related to the percentage of the injected dose that remains in the
lungs after the first-pass period [304]. While metabolism will not
necessarily occur in the lungs, drugs that are substantially retained

Propofol undergoes significant first-pass pulmonary retention in
animals and man but there is no definitive evidence that this drug
is metabolized in the lung. Although studies have suggested that
the lungs take part in the metabolism/elimination of propofol
in humans [305], this has been a matter of dispute [306,307]. In
human surgical patients, propofol was shown to undergo extensive
first-pass pulmonary retention (28.4%) but was released back into
the circulation, as indicated by comparable propofol concentration
versus time curves obtained from blood entering the lungs (mixed
venous blood collected from a pulmonary artery catheter) and from
blood exiting the lungs (arterial blood collected from a radial artery
catheter) [306]. In sheep, 30% of a propofol dose was eliminated
during first-pass through the lungs [308]. However, the study could
not determine if elimination was attributed to true drug metabolism
in the lung or to distribution into a deep lung compartment [308].
In pentobarbital anesthetized cats, first-pass pulmonary retention
of propofol is relatively large (60%) and is significantly reduced
when fentanyl is administered 30 s before propofol injection, but
not when fentanyl is administered 3 or 10 min before propo-
fol [309,310]. Propofol and its metabolites are mainly excreted in
urine and an extremely small fraction of propofol is exhaled though
the lungs. Because the concentration of propofol in expired gas
correlates well with plasma concentrations, monitoring of expired
propofol concentrations may have a clinical application in the
future [311–313]. Other drugs used during anesthesia such as
thiopental, ketamine, opioids, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines,
and catecholamines (norepinephrine and dopamine) can be taken
up by the lungs and more specific details on handling of these
drugs by lung tissue in humans and animal species are available
elsewhere [304].
Anesthesia and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
As discussed previously, HPV is a physiologic mechanism whereby
a decrease in alveolar PO2 causes constriction of adjacent arterioles.
In the presence of gas exchange impairment/hypoxemia due to
areas of low V̇A /Q̇ ratio or shunt, HPV may improve arterial
oxygenation by diverting pulmonary blood flow to better-aerated
regions of the lung. Comparison of the effects of anesthetic drugs
on PaO 2 and shunt fraction during one-lung ventilation has been
used extensively to indirectly assess the effects of inhalant or
intravenous anesthetics on HPV in humans, but this model fails to
evaluate the effects of lung regions with low PaO2 on the vascular
tone of adjacent arterioles. On the other hand, in vitro studies using
isolated lung preparations ventilated with low FI
O2 may be able to
demonstrate drug effects on HPV but may not be directly extrapo-
lated to clinical situations.
Attenuation of HPV by some anesthetic drugs may in part
explain the lower than expected PaO 2 values observed during
general anesthesia. Early experimental studies in the 1970s using a
perfused lung model in cats and dogs originally postulated that
inhalant anesthetics could inhibit HPV, and that this could lead to an
increase in the proportion of mixed venous blood flowing through
areas of low V̇A /Q̇ ratio or non-ventilated lung areas (shunt), thereby
contributing to a decrease in PaO2 during anesthesia [314]. This
postulation was later confirmed using isolated rat lung prepara-
tions, which showed that HPV was inhibited by inhalant agents
(halothane, methoxyflurane, and ether), but remained unaffected
by injectable anesthetics (barbiturates and ketamine) [315]. Other
in vitro studies supported the observation that all contemporary
inhalant anesthetics (isoflurane, sevoflurane, and desflurane) would
block HPV and that this effect could, at least in part, explain the
absolute or relative hypoxemia observed in animals receiving inhal-
ant anesthesia [316–318]. Although isoflurane was reported to
inhibit HPV [316,319–321], some early studies failed to show a
consistent effect of this inhalant on HPV/arterial oxygenation in
anesthetized animals and humans due to methodological issues,
including lack of comparison of the HPV response to that of
non-anesthetized individuals, the confounding effect of other
concurrently administered drugs (e.g., pentobarbital anesthesia), or
the lack of comparison of the pressor response to alveolar hypoxia
at a fixed pulmonary artery flow [322–325]. Because the pressor
response of pulmonary arterial vessels to low alveolar PO 2 (i.e.,
HPV) is also flow dependent, the effects of drugs on HPV should be
compared at a similar pulmonary artery flow [326,327].
The effects of inhalant anesthetics on HPV are controversial at
best. Studies performed during one-lung ventilation in humans have
suggested that sevoflurane and desflurane inhibit HPV in a similar
fashion as isoflurane because of absence of differences in PaO2
among these drugs [328–331]. However, sevoflurane and desflu-
rane did not inhibit the pressor response to low alveolar PO2 at a
similar CO/pulmonary flow range in piglets [332]. In chronically
instrumented dogs, the increase in pulmonary artery pressure in
response to alveolar hypoxia (due to low FI
O2 ) at a similar pulmo-
nary artery flow indicates that isoflurane, but not sevoflurane or
desflurane, inhibits HPV in comparison to the HPV observed in the
conscious state (Fig. 37.26A,B) [327,333]. Based on the same meth-
odology, ketamine did not alter HPV while propofol potentiated
HPV in comparison to the HPV observed in conscious state in dogs
(Fig. 37.26C,D) [334].
Although some experimental models provide evidence that the
pressor response to low alveolar PO 2 is maintained by propofol,
ketamine, desflurane, and sevoflurane [327,332–334], there is no
evidence that any one anesthetic drug is associated with better arte-
rial oxygenation during one-lung ventilation, with the exception of
propofol [328–331,335,336]. In conscious animals presenting with
lung disease associated with areas of low V̇ A /Q̇ ratio and shunt,
HPV may represent an important mechanism that prevents further
oxygenation impairment. Under these circumstances, the anesthe-
siologist could opt for drugs that are more likely to preserve the
HPV response observed during the conscious state (i.e., propofol,
ketamine, sevoflurane, and desflurane).
Effects of anesthesia on ventilation–perfusion
relationships
All forms of general anesthesia are associated with some degree
of deterioration in pulmonary gas exchange. A decrease in arterial
oxygenation that cannot be explained by hypoventilation/
hypercapnia is commonly observed in otherwise healthy animals
undergoing general anesthesia. An increased P(a-a)O 2 resulting in
lower- than-expected PaO2 levels is usually attributed to a mismatch
between ventilation and perfusion of the lungs (V̇ A
/Q̇ mismatch);
more specifically due to areas of low V̇A /Q̇ ratio (between 0.01
and 0.1) or areas of the lungs that are perfused but not ventilated
(V̇A /Q̇ ratio = 0). Development of atelectasis of dependent lung
regions resulting in shunted flow to the lungs (V̇A /Q̇ ratio = 0) com-
bined with the inhibition of HPV is the main cause of oxygenation
impairment during general anesthesia. As previously discussed,
factors such as body mass, obesity, type of recumbency, intrab-
dominal volume/pressure, and inspired oxygen concentration, may
contribute to development of atelectasis and poor lung compliance

-- 747 of 1450 --

732 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
during anesthesia [27,28,261,268,337]. There are species differences
in the development of V̇A
/Q̇ mismatch and shunt. Horses are
particularly prone to develop a large shunt (> 15–20% of CO) due to
the presence of large areas of alveolar collapse during anesthesia,
with body positioning in dorsal recumbency resulting in larger
areas of atelectasis and shunt when compared to lateral recumbency
(Figs. 37.27 and 37.28) [268,299]. As previously noted, because of
their body mass, large animal species are more prone to compres-
sion of the lungs leading to atelectasis than small animals. More
specifically, in horses, compression of the lungs by gravitational
forces acting on the chest wall, and by abdominal viscera pushing
the diaphragm forward, are of greater magnitude than in dogs and
cats, explaining why this species develops more atelectasis/shunted
blood flow during anesthesia (Figs. 37.27 and 37.28).
In humans, atelectasis that develops after induction of anesthesia
may extend into the postoperative period and cause some degree
of oxygenation impairment after recovery and has been associated
with a higher incidence of postoperative complications (e.g.,
pneumonia) [338,339]. Evidence of the negative impact of intraop-
erative atelectasis in the postanesthetic period in veterinary species
is currently lacking.
The gold standard method for assessing the matching between
ventilation and perfusion of the lung (V̇A /Q̇) is the multiple inert
gas elimination technique, which has advanced the understanding
of the mechanism of gas exchange impairment during anesthesia in
humans and animal species [299,301,340,341]. In normal conscious
humans, a bimodal distribution of V̇A
/Q̇ ratios has been identified,
with one mode centered around the ratio of 1 and another, smaller
mode, within low V̇A /Q̇ regions [341].
Fig. 37.29 shows changes in ventilation and perfusion matching
evaluated by a multiple inert gas elimination technique in conscious
and anesthetized horses [299]. The relative distribution of ventila-
tion and perfusion in conscious standing animals with normal
lungs is centered around 1, which is the ideal matching between
ventilation and perfusion to achieve optimal gas exchange. A small
area of high V̇A
/Q̇ ratio (between 10 and 100) and of shunted flow
(V̇ A
/Q̇ = 0), which represents < 3% of total pulmonary blood flow
(Q̇ S
/Q̇T < 3%), may also be observed in healthy horses in a quadru-
pedal position (Fig. 37.29A) [153,299]. After induction of anesthe-
sia in horses breathing spontaneously, there is a marked increase in
shunt flow, which often exceeds 30% of total pulmonary blood flow
(Q̇S
/Q̇T > 30%) when animals are positioned in dorsal recumbency.
Such increases in shunt flow result in oxygenation impairment
characterized by marked increases in P(a-a)O 2 (Fig. 37.29B). Use of
conventional mechanical ventilation with zero end-expiratory
pressure (ZEEP) or 10 cm H2 O of PEEP does not consistently
decrease the shunt in dorsally recumbent horses and may contribute
to further decreases in PaO2 if inotropic support is not used to
counteract the negative effects of positive-pressure ventilation on
pulmonary blood flow (CO) (Fig. 37.29C,D).

high F I
O2 still is safer in spontaneously breathing horses because it
may prevent hypoxemia under these circumstances. Experimental
studies carried out during conventional mechanical ventilation
in dorsally recumbent horses (V T = 15 mL/kg and f adjusted to
maintain eucapnia) have shown that inhaling a 50% oxygen
concentration does not reduce the Q̇S
/Q̇T in comparison to a > 95%
oxygen concentration (n = 5 per group) [194]. Contrasting with the
high incidence of hypoxemia during anesthesia with lower F I
O2
(0.3–0.5) in spontaneously breathing horses, use of 40% inspired
oxygen in isoflurane-anesthetized cats not receiving mechanical
ventilatory support resulted in greater optimization of oxygen
transfer from alveoli to capillary blood (P(a-a)O2 = 24 ± 11 mmHg
with F I
O2 = 0.4 versus P(a-a)O2 = 163 ± 31 mmHg with F I
O2 > 0.9)
and was not associated with hypoxemia (Fig. 37.30B) [273].
Computed tomography images confirmed that decreases in FI
O2
from > 0.9 to 0.4 decreased atelectatic areas of the lungs, likely
because of decreased absorption atelectasis (Fig. 37.30C). In
mechanically ventilated isoflurane-anesthetized dogs, computed
tomography also showed that 40% inspired oxygen reduced poorly
aerated and non-aerated lung areas in comparison to 100% oxygen,
probably because of decreased absorption atelectasis [261]
(Fig. 37.28B). Reduction of atelectasis with 40% oxygen in dogs
resulted in lower P(a- a)O2 than with 100% oxygen (36 ± 12 mmHg
versus 177 ± 49 mmHg). Use of lower FI
O2 may reduce lung collapse
without increasing the risk of hypoxemia in small animal species
(dogs and cats). However, at present, there is no evidence to support
the potential benefits of preventing absorption atelectasis during
the early recovery phase and postanesthetic period in normal
veterinary patients.
In 	contrast 	to 	other 	species, 	intravenous 	injection 	of
α2 -adrenergic receptor agonists has been reported to cause moder-
ate (PaO 2 < 60 mmHg) to severe (PaO2 < 40 mmHg) hypoxemia in
sheep [209,344]. The severity of hypoxemia is highly variable
among different breeds and among individual animals of the same
breed [345]; however, it may be life-threatening in animals with
pre-existing respiratory disease or in individual animals that have
greater sensitivity to this adverse reaction. In addition to low PaO 2
levels, PaCO 2 may be normal or below normal values [209];
hypocapnia observed concurrently with hypoxemia is likely caused
by an increase in VE secondary to activation of peripheral chemo-
receptors by low PaO2 levels (hypoxic ventilatory drive).
Experimental evidence shows that hypoxemia caused by sedation
with α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists in sheep is the result of an
increase in shunted flow (Q̇ S /Q̇T
) secondary to an inflammatory
response in the lungs/pulmonary edema [345,346]. Studies using a
pulmonary artery catheter (Fig. 37.14), have shown that the oxy-
genation impairment caused by α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists
in anesthetized sheep is associated with pulmonary hypertension
(MPAP > 25 mmHg) and significant increases in PAOP, which often
exceeds the threshold associated with pulmonary edema caused by
increased hydrostatic pressure (PAOP > 15–18 mmHg) [345,346]
(Fig. 37.31A). The marked increase in PAOP (> 15–18 mmHg),
reported 2 min after intravenous dexmedetomidine (2 μg/kg) in
sevoflurane-anesthetized sheep, suggests that early development
of oxygenation impairment/pulmonary edema is secondary to
increased hydrostatic pressure in the microcirculation, which leads
to the movement of fluid from the intravascular compartment to
the alveolar interstitium/alveolar lumen [345] (Fig. 37.31A).
Sheep are particularly susceptible to the adverse effects of
α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists on the pulmonary circulation
where significant increases in MPAP and PAOP are observed after
relatively small cumulative doses of medetomidine (1.5 μg/kg,
intravenously) [346]. Based on the pathophysiology of pulmonary
hypertension discussed previously, cumulative doses of medeto-
midine (0.5 to 4.0 μg/kg/min) likely cause pre- and postcapillary
pulmonary hypertension (increases in MPAP secondary to
increases in PVR and PAOP, respectively) [346]. This response
contrasts with a study evaluating progressively increasing doses
of medetomidine (1 to 20 μg/kg intravenously) in conscious dogs,
where only a high dose (20 μg/kg) significantly increased PAOP and
MPAP [347] (Fig. 37.31B). However, even when medetomidine was
administered at doses that may cause clinically relevant increases in
pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure (PAOP > 15–18 mmHg),
there was no evidence of pulmonary edema as PaO 2 was not sig-
nificantly altered in healthy dogs (Fig. 37.31B). Collectively, these
results suggest that elevated hydrostatic pressure is not the only
factor that triggers the pulmonary edema/oxygenation impairment
observed following α2 - adrenergic receptor agonist administration
in sheep.
Damage of the capillary endothelium and type-1 alveolar cells,
intra-alveolar hemorrhage/edema, and interstitial edema has been
reported 60 min after intravenous xylazine (0.15 mg/kg) adminis-
tration to sheep [348]. Besides the pulmonary edema of hydrostatic
origin, it has been proposed that damage to lung parenchyma/pul-
monary edema may also result from an inflammatory component
that involves activation of pulmonary intravascular macrophages
(PIMs) [348]. These are phagocytic cells that play an important role
in removing particulate material from the circulation in some ani-
mal species (ruminants, pigs, and cats) [349]. It appears that PIMs
are activated early during the course of pulmonary edema, as these
cells present morphological changes 3 min after α2
- adrenergic
receptor agonist injection in sheep [348].
Besides damage to lung parenchyma in vitro, studies have also
shown that α2 -adrenergic receptor agonists induce airway smooth
muscle contraction in sheep but not in other species such as cattle
and horses [350–352]. Bronchoconstriction, combined with lung
edema, may be responsible for the increase airway resistance (R aw )
observed following intravenous medetomidine administration in
halothane-anesthetized sheep receiving mechanical ventilation [346].
Increased R aw /bronchoconstriction might be caused by proinflam-
matory mediators (cytokines) secondary to lung damage or by
direct stimulation of α2
- adrenergic receptors located in airway
smooth muscle [351]. Besides increasing R aw
, α2
- adrenergic recep-
tor agonists also decrease dynamic compliance of the respiratory
system (C RS
), which can be attributed to a decrease in lung compli-
ance due to pulmonary hemorrhage/edema, although dynamic C RS
may also decrease if resistance to gas flow (R aw ) is elevated, as
explained previously.
α2
-Adrenergic receptor agonists that cannot cross the blood–brain
barrier and are devoid of sedative/analgesic effects also induce
hypoxemia and pulmonary inflammation/edema, providing evidence
that these adverse effects are mediated by peripheral α2
- adrenergic
receptor stimulation [344,346,348]. Intravenous administration of
vatinoxan (0.75 mg/kg), a peripheral α2
- adrenergic receptor antag-
onist that does not cross the blood–brain barrier, can prevent
hypoxemia caused by a high dose of xylazine in sheep (0.5 mg/kg,
intravenously) without an apparent effect on sedation [353]
(Fig. 37.32). Although these results suggest that vatinoxan may be
a promising option to prevent the adverse pulmonary effects of
α2 -adrenergic receptor agonists in this species, its use was associ-
ated with more severe histopathological changes in the lung
which requires further investigation [353]. α2
- Adrenergic receptor

agonists are potent sedatives and analgesics that are useful as

Oxygen transport
Arterial oxygen content
Oxygen is transported from the lungs to tissues largely in chemical
combination with hemoglobin, with only a small fraction of total
arterial oxygen content (CaO2 ) dissolved in plasma (PaO2
).
Mammalian hemoglobin consists of four-unit molecules. Each
unit molecule contains a heme group, which is a protoporphyrin
consisting of four pyrroles with a central ferrous ion (Fe 2+
). Oxygen
combines reversibly with the Fe2+ in proportion to the PO2
.
At complete saturation, each gram of hemoglobin combines with
approximately 1.36 mL of oxygen. This is the total carrying capacity
of hemoglobin, or four oxygen molecules combined with each
hemoglobin molecule [355,356]. The total oxygen content of
arterial blood, in mL of oxygen per deciliter (100 mL) of blood, is
calculated as follows:

hemoglobin saturation in arterial blood (expressed as fraction),
Hb is the hemoglobin concentration (g/dL), and 1.36 is the
maximum oxygen-carrying capacity of fully saturated hemoglobin.
The second part of the equation corresponds to the amount of
oxygen dissolved in blood (mL/dL), calculated as PaO 2 multiplied
by the solubility coefficient of oxygen in 1 deciliter of blood
(0.0031) [355,356].

738 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve and the Bohr effect
As most of the oxygen is carried by hemoglobin, it is important
to understand the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, which
describes the relationship between hemoglobin saturation and PO 2
(Fig. 37.33A). The ability of hemoglobin to combine with oxygen
depends on the PO2 in the surrounding environment. The sigmoidal
shape of the oxyhemoglobin curve reflects its physiologic role in
uploading oxygen in the lungs and offloading oxygen to the tissues.
At the pulmonary capillary level, hemoglobin has a high affinity to
oxygen, being almost fully saturated in a normal conscious animal.
This affinity translates into a tendency for the oxyhemoglobin curve
to become flat as PO2 in arterial blood increases above 70 mmHg,
which corresponds to a hemoglobin saturation above 94% [355,356].
At the systemic capillary level, transfer of oxygen from blood to
tissues is facilitated by the decrease in hemoglobin’s affinity for
oxygen. This is reflected by the steeper slope of the oxyhemoglobin
curve at PO2 values less than 60 mmHg. At a PO 2 of 40 mmHg,
which is the oxygen tension typically found in mixed venous blood
draining systemic capillaries, the hemoglobin saturation falls to
approximately 75% and the total oxygen content in mixed venous
blood is approximately 24–25% less than in arterial blood [355,356].
The position of the oxyhemoglobin curve is dynamic and is
modified according to changes in metabolic status. Physiological
conditions that signal an increase in metabolic activity such as
increased temperature, high PCO2, and low pH decrease the affinity
of hemoglobin for oxygen and cause a rightward shift of the
oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (Fig. 37.33B). Physiological
changes that signal decreased metabolic activity (decreased
temperature, low PCO2, and increased pH) increase the affinity of
hemoglobin for oxygen and cause a leftward shift of the
oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve [355,356]. Certain enzyme
systems aid the dissociation of oxygen from hemoglobin, the most
completely 	studied 	being 	the 	enzyme 	system 	producing
2,3- diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG). This enzyme is a byproduct of
glycolysis within the red blood cells that enhances the dissociation
of oxygen from hemoglobin by competing with oxygen for the
binding site. Anemia, chronic hypoxemia, and acclimation to high
altitude reduce oxygen content in blood and stimulate glycolysis.
Increased glycolysis and 2,3-DPG production during these clinical
conditions facilitate unloading of oxygen at the tissue level. A
lowered level of this enzyme, as occurs with stored blood used for
transfusion, increases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen and
shifts the dissociation curve to the left [355,356]. While changes in
2,3-DPG levels are a major factor influencing the loading and
unloading of oxygen in humans, in some animal species, including
cats and ruminants, hemoglobin affinity for oxygen is less affected
by 2,3-DPG. In these species, chloride ions (Cl−) play a greater role
in modifying hemoglobin oxygen affinity [357–359]. As red blood
cells reach the capillaries of the systemic circulation, rising CO 2
levels originating from tissue aerobic activity form HCO 3

these cells. In a mechanism named “chloride shift” or “Hamburger
effect” (see further details below), the HCO 3
− is driven out of red
blood cells to plasma in exchange for Cl−. The increase in Cl− inside
the red blood cells, in a similar fashion as 2,3-DPG, reduces affinity
of hemoglobin for oxygen, facilitating the unloading of oxygen to
tissues [357–359].
In 1904, the Danish physiologist Christian Bohr first showed
that increased PCO 2 decreases the affinity of hemoglobin for
oxygen [360]. The effects of changes in pH and PCO 2 on the affinity
of hemoglobin for oxygen (Bohr effect) play an important role in
facilitating the uploading of oxygen in the lungs and its subsequent
transfer to tissues (Fig. 37.33B) [361]. As CO 2 is eliminated by
alveolar ventilation, the decrease in PCO 2 and increase in pH at the
pulmonary capillary level augments the affinity of hemoglobin for
oxygen (leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve), facilitating the
uploading of oxygen to pulmonary capillary blood. In the systemic
capillaries, as CO 2 produced by metabolic activity is transferred
from tissues to capillary blood, the resultant increase in PCO 2 levels
and decrease in pH reduces the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen
(rightward shift of the dissociation curve), facilitating the unload-
ing of oxygen from hemoglobin to tissues [361].
The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curves are not superimposed in
all mammals but have a similar sigmoidal shape among mamma-
lian species (Fig. 37.34) [356,362]. The oxygen partial pressure at
which hemoglobin saturation is 50% (P50
) provides a comparative
measure of the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, and this value
varies between species. Slightly higher P 50 values are found in dogs
and rabbits in comparison to horses, cattle, and elephants suggest-
ing that small animals are better adapted to oxygen delivery at the
tissue level than large animal species (Fig. 37.34A) [356,362]. Also,
P50 is reduced in septic patients and carbon monoxide poisoning,
whereas the reverse has been encountered in chronic anemia. Since
tissues require a given volume of oxygen per unit time, the hemo-
globin concentration of blood has a significant influence on oxygen
content and delivery to the tissues.
South American camelids (e.g., llamas and alpacas), have geneti-
cally coded changes in hemoglobin that increase its affinity for oxy-
gen and result in lower P 50 values in comparison to other mammal
species (Fig. 37.34B) [363–365]. The relatively low P 50 in Andean
camelids is an important adaptation for life in their natural
environment, where altitudes above 4000 meters decrease PI
O2
from 160 mmHg (sea level) to 95 mmHg or less. Because of their
relatively low P50 (22.7 mmHg), denoting high affinity of hemo-
globin for oxygen, llamas were reportedly able to maintain a high
SaO 2 (> 92%) when PaO 2 values were already at hypoxemic levels
(51–53 mmHg) due to the high altitude (PI
O2 = 107 mmHg at 3420
meters where PB is 511 mmHg) [363]. By comparison, in humans,
SaO2 is reduced to 86–87% at a PaO2 of 51–53 mmHg. While
increased hemoglobin affinity for oxygen is physiologically advan-
tageous because CaO 2 is maintained despite hypoxemic conditions/
low PaO2
, unloading of oxygen at the tissue level may be reduced.
However, high-altitude camelids present a very effective mechanism
of oxygen transfer to tissues [363,364].
Hypoxemia
“Hypoxemia” is a term that specifically refers to abnormally low
PaO2 or hemoglobin saturation in arterial blood. Hypoxemia can be
caused by low PI
O2
, hypoventilation, and anything that causes
venous admixture (including low V̇ A
/Q̇ ratio, shunt, and diffusion
impairment). As explained before, hypoxemia caused by hypoven-
tilation, low V̇A /Q̇ ratio, and shunt are of particular interest to the
anesthesiologist. Another important factor that may contribute
to hypoxemia in anesthetized animals, that is not related to gas
exchange impairment across the alveolar–capillary membrane, is a
decrease in mixed venous oxygen saturation secondary to low
CO during anesthesia in the face of a large pre-existing shunt, as
discussed previously [300,301]. Diffusion limitation across the
alveolar–capillary membrane may play an important role in the devel-
opment of hypoxemia in some circumstances. Diffusion of oxygen
to capillary blood can be limited by interstitial edema or fibrotic
thickening of the alveolar–capillary membrane (interstitial lung dis-
ease), or when there is an extremely short capillary transit time [151].
In humans with interstitial lung disease, diffusion limitation most
commonly causes hypoxemia during exercise as under these
circumstances the decrease in capillary transit time does not allow
enough time for oxygen to equilibrate between the alveolar gas and
end- capillary blood [150,366]. Mild hypoxemia (PaO 2 between 60
and 80 mmHg) observed during heavy exercise in horses is the

result of diffusion limitation, which is precipitated by the shorter

Based on PaO2 and SaO2 values, hypoxemia can be classified as
mild, moderate, or severe (Table 37.6). Classification of the severity
of hypoxemia considers the magnitude of the change in PaO2 on
SaO 2 and the impact on oxygen content. For instance, if PaO 2
decreases from 100 (SaO 2 = 0.977) to 50 mmHg (SaO 2 = 0.85),
hypoxemia is classified as moderate because CaO2 decreases by only
13% (e.g., from 20.2 to 17.5 mL/dL) as 85% of hemoglobin is still
saturated. However, if PaO2 falls below 40 mmHg, critical hemo-
globin desaturation is observed because of the steep slope of the
oxyhemoglobin curve (Fig. 37.33). If PaO2 falls to approximately
27 mmHg, hemoglobin saturation is only 50%. At this level of desat-
uration, hypoxemia is classified as severe since CaO2 falls by nearly
50% of the normal value (from 20.2 to 10.3 mL/dL).
As explained before, an increase in F I
O2 by 100% oxygen admin-
istration can markedly increase PaO 2 if intrapulmonary shunt is not
the source of oxygenation impairment. However, this increased
PaO2 results in a relatively small increase in CaO2 if hemoglobin
saturation is already close to 100% while the animal is breathing
ambient air. In a conscious individual breathing ambient air
(F I
O2 = 0.21) with a PaO2 (100 mmHg), 1 deciliter (100 mL) of
blood will hold 0.3 mL of oxygen dissolved in solution. If oxygen
bound to hemoglobin is considered (hemoglobin saturation = 97.7%
at a PaO2 of 100 mmHg and hemoglobin concentration = 15 g/dL),
total oxygen content increases to approximately 20.2 mL of oxygen
per 100 mL of blood, or about 70 times as much as plasma.
An increase in FI
O2 from 0.21 to > 0.9 increases PaO2 by fivefold
(from 100 to 500 mmHg), but CaO 2 will increase only by 9% (from
20.2 to 22.0 mL/dL), as nearly all hemoglobin is already saturated
when PaO2 is 100 mmHg (97.7%). Although this increase in oxygen
content is relatively small, it may be of clinical relevance in patients
whose oxygen-carrying capacity is already compromised by severe
anemia (e.g., hematocrit < 15% or hemoglobin < 5 g/dL). The PaO2
level is also of some importance because oxygen transfers from
blood to tissues by diffusion, and the process occurs at a rate pro-
portional to the difference in oxygen tension between plasma and
tissues. Preoxygenation of the lungs, preferentially via a sealed face
mask attached to a breathing circuit filled with 100% oxygen, is
recommended for added safety before induction of anesthesia in
anemic animals, as the decrease in CaO2 is more likely to achieve
critical levels if mild-to-moderate hypoxemia occurs in patients
with an already reduced oxygen-carrying capacity.
As hypoxemia becomes severe, cyanosis (blue-purple tinge) of
mucous membranes can be observed because deoxygenated hemo-
globin is dark red. However, cyanotic mucous membranes may not
be perceived if the animal is anemic. Blood gas analyzers directly
measure PO2 in plasma through polarographic electrodes, while
hemoglobin saturation is often calculated from PO2 based on the
human oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve. A more accurate meas-
urement of hemoglobin saturation would require the use of species-
specific algorithms, or the direct measurement of hemoglobin
saturation via a blood gas analyzer equipped with a CO-oximeter.
Pulse oximeters are non- invasive tools that measure hemoglobin
saturation by absorption and transmission of two wavelengths of
light (red and infrared light) through the tongue or other anatomic
structures in animal species. Conventional pulse oximeters, however,
are unable to detect other forms of hemoglobin that cannot bind to
oxygen and will provide erratic hemoglobin saturation values in the
presence of carboxyhemoglobin or methemoglobin [368,369].
Similarly, calculation of hemoglobin saturation from PO 2 using a
blood gas analyzer not equipped with a CO-oximeter will lead to
an erroneous estimation of hemoglobin saturation under these
circumstances. If dyshemoglobinemias are suspected (e.g., methe-
moglobinemia or carboxyhemoglobinemia due to carbon monox-
ide poisoning), or if there is a discrepancy between PaO2 measured
by blood gas analysis and hemoglobin saturation measured by
conventional pulse oximetry, an accurate measure of hemoglobin
saturation can be obtained via CO-oximetry, which can measure
concentrations of oxyhemoglobin, deoxyhemoglobin, and other
forms of hemoglobin (including methemoglobin and carboxyhemo-
globin), or via non-invasive multiple wavelength pulse CO-oximetry
technology [370–372].
Carbon dioxide transport
Carbon dioxide is 20 times more soluble in water than oxygen. Its
solubility coefficient is 0.0308 mmol/mmHg, which corresponds to
0.066 mL/mmHg/100 mL of blood. Therefore, the amount of CO2
dissolved in 100 mL of venous and arterial blood is approximately
3 mL (PvCO 2 = 46 mmHg) and 2.5 mL (PaCO 2 = 40 mmHg),
respectively; the difference is eliminated by alveolar ventilation [373].
Because CO2 has a much higher solubility and diffusing capability
when compared to oxygen, its partial pressure in pulmonary capillary
blood and the alveoli will be virtually the same [373]. This rapid
equilibration ensures that CO2 elimination by the lungs is not
impaired in the face of a large intrapulmonary shunt if the ventilatory
response in alveoli that are ventilated and perfused is preserved.
Arterial CO2 levels are a function of CO 2 elimination and
production, and under normal circumstances, PaCO2 levels are
maintained within narrow limits. During high-intensity exercise,
the production of CO2 is increased enormously, whereas during
anesthesia, production likely decreases. Elimination of CO2 depends
on pulmonary blood flow (Q̇ T
) and alveolar ventilation (V̇ A ).
Normally, CO 2 production (V̇ CO 2 ) parallels oxygen consumption
(V̇ O2 ) according to the respiratory quotient (R). As explained previ-
ously, the ratio between V̇ CO 2 and V̇ O2 varies according to the diet
and source of energy metabolism [58]. Although the value varies
depending on the diet, R equals 0.8 at steady state in humans and
may differ in animals. Due to the blood buffer systems, CO2 trans-
port to the lungs for excretion occurs with little change in blood pH.
Carbon dioxide content in blood and the Haldane effect
The total amount of CO 2 produced in tissues by aerobic metabolism
is transported to the lungs in three ways: (1) as gas dissolved in
blood; (2) as HCO3
−; and (3) as carbamino compounds [356,373].
Carbon dioxide produced by the tissues diffuses down a concen-
tration gradient to capillary blood in the systemic circulation in a
process that is coupled with the transfer of oxygen from capillary

summarized in Fig. 37.35. Typically, the PCO2 of mixed venous
blood draining tissues and organs of the systemic circulation is
slightly higher than the PCO2 of arterial blood (Pv CO2 = 46 mmHg
versus PaCO 2 = 40 mmHg). However, most CO2 is transported in
mixed venous blood as plasma HCO 3
- or combined with hemo-
globin as carbamino compounds, with CO2 dissolved in blood repre-
senting a smaller fraction of total CO2 content. Because CO 2 is a
nonpolar molecule, it readily diffuses across the lipid membrane of
red blood cells, where carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the hydration
of CO2 to H 2
CO3 and its dissociated form (HCO3
− and H +
). This
reaction occurs within red blood cells but not in plasma of verte-
brates, which does not contain carbonic anhydrase. A buildup of
hydrogen within the cell would prevent further conversion of
HCO 3
− from H 2
CO3 . However, as oxyhemoglobin (HbO 2
) releases
oxygen to tissues, deoxyhemoglobin (Hb−) buffers the hydrogen
ion released by H2 CO3 , further shifting the reaction toward the gen-
eration of HCO 3
−, which increases the total CO2 content in blood.
The newly formed HCO3
− anion is exported from the red blood cell
to plasma in exchange for Cl− in a mechanism named the “chloride
shift” or “Hamburger effect.” Approximately 60% of total CO2 content
in venous blood is transported as HCO 3
− [373]. As hemoglobin
unloads oxygen to tissues, total CO2 content increases because CO2
reversibly binds to the amino groups (-NH 2
) of deoxyhemoglobin
to form carbamino compounds (HbCO 2 ), which is the second most
important form of CO 2 transport and corresponds to 30% of total
CO2 content in mixed venous blood. Finally, the remaining 10% of
the total CO 2 content is present in venous blood as CO2 dissolved in
solution [373]. The Haldane effect is the increase in CO2 carrying
capacity (total CO2 content) that occurs with a decrease in PO2
. At
the tissue level, the Haldane effect is explained by: (1) the buffering
action of deoxygenated hemoglobin which combines with hydro-
gen ions released by H 2
CO3 and contributes to an increase in plasma
HCO3
− and (2) the reversible combination between deoxyhemo-
globin and CO2 forming carbamino compounds. The interplay
between the Bohr (effect of changes in pH and PCO2 on hemo-
globin’s affinity for oxygen) and Haldane effects at the tissue level is
detailed in Fig. 37.36.

Once mixed venous blood reaches the lung, the partial pressure
of CO 2 decreases from 46 mmHg to approximately 40 mmHg in
end-capillary blood. The difference corresponds to the amount of
CO 2 eliminated by alveolar ventilation. However, CO 2 transported
as gas dissolved in plasma is not the only source of CO 2 eliminated
by alveolar ventilation. A large proportion of exhaled CO 2
originates from carbamino compounds (HbCO 2 ) and HCO 3
−. As
illustrated in Fig. 37.37, as CO 2 is eliminated by alveolar ventilation,
the relative contribution of CO 2 dissolved in plasma to total CO 2
content is reduced from 10% in venous blood to 5% in arterial
blood, whereas the carbamino compounds have their relative
contribution to total CO 2 reduced from 30% in venous blood to 5%
in arterial blood; the remaining CO 2 (90%) is transported in
arterial blood as HCO3
−. As CO2 is transferred from plasma to
ventilated alveoli, the decrease in pulmonary capillary PCO 2 shifts
the H 2 CO 3 ⇌ HCO 3
− reaction toward the formation of CO 2 and
H 2 O. Additionally, as oxygen is transferred from alveoli to capillary
blood, an increase in HbO 2 reduces CO 2 carrying capacity by
decreasing the amount of Hb− available to form carbamino
compounds. In summary, the Haldane effect in the lungs
(decreased total CO 2 content at high PO 2 levels in pulmonary
capillary blood) is explained by: (1) decreased amount of Hb−
which limits the buffering of hydrogen ions released by H 2 CO 3 and
shifts the equation toward the formation of H 2 CO 3 with its
subsequent dissociation into CO 2 and H 2 O, and (2) decreased
availability of Hb− to combine with CO 2 and form carbamino
compounds. The interplay between the Bohr and Haldane effects
at the alveolar–capillary barrier is detailed in Fig. 37.38.

produce respiratory acidosis and alkalosis, respectively, because

The normal pH is slightly more acidic in venous blood
(7.34 to 7.43) than in arterial blood (7.35 to 7.45) because of higher
PCO2 in venous blood. Acidemia and alkalemia are defined as a
plasma pH below or above, respectively, the normal range for the
species in question. Concurrent metabolic acid–base disturbances
and the presence or absence of renal compensation of the respira-
tory acid–base disturbance will determine the actual degree of pH
change accompanying hypocapnia or hypercapnia.
During acute respiratory acidosis (e.g., general anesthesia in a
spontaneously ventilating patient), there can be a small compen-
satory increase in plasma HCO 3
−. In dogs and cats with acute res-
piratory acidosis, HCO 3
− has been estimated to increase by
0.15 mmol/L for each mmHg increase in PCO 2 above normal
(e.g., PCO 2 = 36 mmHg) [52,53]. Hemoglobin contributes to the
increase in HCO3
− during acute respiratory acidosis, as deoxygen-
ated hemoglobin (Hb−) will neutralize the hydrogen ions released
from H 2
CO3
, shifting the H 2
CO3 ⇌ HCO 3
− equation toward the
formation of HCO3
−. If hypercapnia persists for several days,
chronic respiratory acidosis is associated with a renal compensatory
response. The kidneys eliminate the excess acid load via excretion
of ammonium chloride (NH4
+
Cl−) [53]. Increased excretion of Cl−
is paralleled by increased reabsorption of HCO3
− by renal tubular
cells, resulting in a state of hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
(decreased plasma Cl− and increased plasma HCO 3
−), which may
be able to minimize or neutralize the impact of chronic respiratory
acidosis on pH. The compensatory renal response to chronic acido-
sis is estimated to increase plasma HCO3
− by 0.35 mmol/L for each
mmHg of increase in PCO2 in dogs but current data does not allow
the estimation of the renal compensation to chronic respiratory
acidosis in cats [53].
