mode may be selected in intubated patients to achieve an elevated
airway pressure for a short period of time (e.g., 30 cmH 2 O for 20 s),
before returning to a standard mechanical ventilation protocol and
post-recruitment 	PEEP, 	which 	aims 	to 	keep 	the 	alveoli
opened [38,101,136] (Fig. 38.26B). However, most anesthesia
machines do not have the option for CPAP. In this case, with the
spontaneous mode selected, the rebreathing bag is manually
squeezed with the pop-off (APL) valve closed/semi-closed to
achieve the target airway pressure for the desired length of time.
This technique may be used to improve oxygenation and expand
the lungs in small animal species (dogs and cats) with diaphragmatic
hernia. In this case, the increase in airway pressure should be
applied after reduction of the visceral contents herniated into the
thoracic cavity, while the surgeon is guiding the increase in airway
pressure by visually assessing lung expansion within the thoracic
cavity (see discussion below regarding re-expansion pulmonary
edema). The maximum airway pressure can be limited to
30 cmH 2 O or less, pending the severity of cardiovascular depression
(e.g., hypotension) observed during the recruitment maneuver.
Cats with a diaphragmatic hernia may be more sensitive to the
negative cardiovascular effects of ARMs, therefore a reduced
maximum airway pressure is initially recommended (≤ 20 cmH 2 O).
Alveolar recruitment may also be performed using cycling
maneuvers, which have three distinct phases: (1) hemodynamic
conditioning; (2) recruitment; and (3) decremental PEEP trial
(Fig. 38.26C and 38.27). During the hemodynamic conditioning
phase, before the lung’s opening pressure is achieved, inspiratory
pressures and PEEP are progressively increased with ventilation in
PCV mode while the driving pressure (gradient between Pmax and
PEEP) is held constant. Theoretically, pulmonary tissue stress is less
than during CPAP maneuvers. Stepwise increases in airway pres-
sure may reduce the possibility of overdistension of ventilated lung
areas as it progressively spreads across the collapsed lung tissue,
opening atelectatic alveoli in a more controlled manner than with
CPAP maneuvers [101,135]. Stepwise increases in airway pressures
also identify individuals with occult hypovolemia, who may not
tolerate the higher airway pressures that are necessary to open
collapsed lung areas [135]. If severe hypotension is identified dur-
ing this phase, the procedure is interrupted, and intravenous fluid
boluses and/or sympathomimetics are administered before the
cycling maneuver is reinstituted. During the recruitment phase,
while PEEP is maintained at the maximum target level (e.g.,
15 cmH 2 O for 30 s), the driving pressure can be temporarily
increased by adjusting Pmax to achieve inspiratory pressures that are
necessary to open collapsed lung areas (e.g., 30 cmH 2 O). The
decremental PEEP trial is the last phase of a cycling maneuver and
aims to determine the lowest PEEP level that will prevent de-
recruitment or re-collapse of lung tissue. As PEEP is progressively
reduced in 2 cmH2 O steps, it will reach the closing pressure, that is
the pressure at which alveoli collapse [135]. Identification of the
closing pressure can be performed by measuring the quasistatic CRS
at the end of each stepwise decrease in PEEP during VCV with an
inspiratory pause. The post-recruitment PEEP level can be adjusted
based on the PEEP that resulted in highest quasistatic CRS during
the decremental PEEP trial + 2 cmH 2
O [135,137–139].
Effects of mechanical ventilation on cardiovascular
function
In general, greater cardiovascular depression occurs in anesthetized
animals receiving positive-pressure ventilation compared to
anesthetized animals that are permitted to breathe spontaneously.
Mechanical ventilation alters cardiovascular function directly through
changes in intrapleural and alveolar pressures. Cardiovascular
function is also indirectly modified by mechanical ventilation via
changes in PaCO2 levels. A decrease in V̇E due to low respiratory
frequency and/or low V T set on the ventilator will cause varying
degrees of hypercapnia. In conscious dogs and humans, hypercap-
nia increases endogenous catecholamine levels leading to a cardio-
vascular stimulant effect (increased heart rate, cardiac output, and
arterial blood pressure, and decreased systemic vascular resistance
[SVR]). Although general anesthetics can potentially blunt the
sympathetic stimulation caused by high PaCO2 levels, studies in
anesthetized mechanically ventilated horses have shown that
hypercapnia increases circulating plasma epinephrine and norepi-
nephrine levels and results in cardiovascular stimulation [140,141].
In humans under general anesthesia, mild hypercapnia (PaCO 2 up
to 60 mmHg) during mechanical ventilation increases subcutane-
ous tissue oxygen tension, which may contribute to oxidative killing
of surgical pathogens by neutrophils and reduce the rate of surgical
infection [142]. However, cardiovascular depression/poor respon-
siveness to exogenous catecholamines can occur in the face of
severe acidemia (pH < 7.2).
In most patients, mechanical ventilation depresses cardiovascu-
lar function by decreasing venous return. The blood flow entering
the heart through the vena cava (VR) is directly proportional to the
gradient between the mean circulatory filling pressure (MCFP) of
the venous circulation and right atrial pressure (RAP) divided by
the resistance to blood flow in the venous circulation.
VR MCFP RAP
Venous resistance
The MCFP is determined by the stressed volume (Vs
), which rep-
resents the blood volume that exerts pressure inside the veins and
effectively contributes to VR; while the unstressed volume (Vus ) is
the blood that keeps small veins and venules minimally opened and
does not contribute significantly to VR [143,144]. Changes in VR
during spontaneous breathing and during mechanical ventilation
are illustrated in Fig. 38.28. During spontaneous breathing, VR
transiently increases because the gradient between MCFP and RAP
increases as P pl become more negative during inspiration. In con-
trast, mechanical ventilation decreases the gradient between MCFP
and RAP as Ppl increases during inspiration. According to the
Frank–Starling mechanism, as VR and preload are decreased, RV
stroke volume decreases on the next heartbeat. Under normal cir-
cumstances, decreases in preload/stroke volume induced by
mechanical breaths are relatively small. However, in hypovolemic
animals, the inspiratory rise in Ppl caused by mechanical ventilation
induces larger decreases in VR/preload, which may result in signifi-
cant cardiovascular depression. An excessively large V T delivered by
the ventilator may also induce greater decreases in VR/preload,
mimicking the effects of hypovolemia.
In addition to the effects on VR, distension of the alveolar wall
caused by the rise in alveolar pressure (Palv
) increases RV afterload
because of compression of pulmonary capillaries in West zones I
and II. The increase in RV afterload opposes RV ejection and may
contribute to the decrease in RV stroke volume (Fig. 38.29) [116,145].
On the left side of the circulation, increases in pleural (P pl )
and alveolar (Palv ) pressures induced by mechanical breaths
cause intermittent increases and decreases in aortic blood flow
and left ventricular (LV) stroke volume (Fig. 38.29). Aortic
blood flow and LV stroke volume transiently decrease because of
the inspiratory decrease in preload/RV stroke volume as
discussed before; however, the maximum decrease in aortic

flow/LV stroke volume caused by this mechanism will only be
detected a few heartbeats later, during expiration, reflecting the
time needed for blood to travel through the pulmonary
circulation. On the other hand, an inspiratory increase in aortic
flow/LV stroke volume occurs because of increased LV preload
and decreased LV afterload caused by increased Palv and by
increased P pl , respectively, as illustrated in Fig. 38.29. Because
patients that are hypovolemic have larger variations in aortic
flow/LV stroke volume induced by mechanical breaths, heart–
lung interactions during mechanical ventilation provide the
physiologic basis for assessment of fluid responsiveness, that is,
the determination of whether a patient will respond or not to
intravascular volume expansion with increases in stroke volume/
cardiac output [116,145].

that there are four basic mechanisms that contribute, either alone or
in combination, to lung injury associated with mechanical ventilation:
barotrauma, volutrauma, atelectrauma, and biotrauma. Barotrauma,

initially defined as excessively high airway pressures/Palv causing lung
damage, was the first proposed mechanism of ventilator-induced lung
injury (VILI). However, experimental studies in the 1980s showed
that VILI occurs when excessively high airway pressures/Palv causes
excessive alveolar expansion (volutrauma) [146,147]. Therefore,
elevated inspiratory pressure (equivalent to Palv
) is more likely to result
in VILI if it results in excessive increases in lung volume. This
fundamental 	concept 	was 	shown 	by 	experimental 	studies
demonstrating that mechanical ventilation with high airway pressures
(Ppeak of 45 cmH2
O) did not result in evidence of lung damage/
inflammation when lung expansion was limited by low chest wall
compliance (Fig. 38.30) [146]. Barotrauma is currently defined as lung
injury caused by high transpulmonary pressures, that is the pressure
difference between inside (Palv
) and outside the lung (Ppl
), which effec-
tively results in alveolar overdistension [148]. Although barotrauma
may occur during VCV because of high inspiratory pressures, the
anesthesiologist should consider that elevated inspiratory pressures
(high Palv
) may not result in excessive increases in transpulmonary
pressure (alveolar overdistension) if Ppl is also increased because chest
wall compliance is markedly reduced, as in morbidly obese animals or
animals with marked increases in intra-abdominal pressure. As an
example, standard mechanical ventilator settings (V T of 12–15 mL/kg)
in horses with colic and severe abdominal distension may, on some
occasions, result in Ppeak values that exceed 45 cmH2
O. Although no
specific measurements of transpulmonary pressures have been per-
formed in horses under these circumstances, the decrease in Ppeak that
is noticeable after the surgeon removes the distended bowel from the
abdominal cavity suggests that the cause of vof the chest wall by
abdominal viscera. Therefore, high inspiratory pressures under these
conditions are less likely to be harmful to the lungs.
Besides 	barotrauma 	and 	volutrauma, 	atelectrauma, 	and
biotrauma are now recognized as mechanisms of VILI [148].
Atelectrauma is caused by high shear forces from cyclic opening
and closure of atelectatic alveoli, which can trigger a local
inflammatory response and injure the alveolar–capillary mem-
brane [148]. The alveolar instability caused by the intermittent
opening and closure of atelectatic lung areas, named “tidal recruit-
ment,” occurs when the level of inspiratory pressure is large
enough to open atelectatic alveoli, but these alveoli subsequently
collapse during expiration because the level of end-expiratory pres-
sure is insufficient to keep them open throughout the ventilatory
cycle [149–151]. Biotrauma has been recognized as an important
mechanism of VILI in ARDS. It is characterized as a biological
response, including activation of a pro-inflammatory cytokine
cascade that promotes injury even in lung areas not subjected to
mechanical stress and in extrapulmonary organs [148]. Although
data are lacking in veterinary medicine, it has been recognized
that a lung-protective ventilation strategy in humans with ARDS,
aimed at minimizing mechanical stress to the lungs by use of
low V T
s, may attenuate the systemic inflammatory response and
associated multiple organ failure, contributing to a decrease in
mortality [123,152–154].
Mechanical ventilation during anesthesia
in humans and veterinary species
Experimental animal models of ARDS show that application of
PEEP with a relatively small V T is less injurious to the lung than
ventilation with a large V T in the absence of PEEP [147]. In the
medical field, the importance of VILI and its negative impact
on clinical outcomes was first established in humans with
ARDS [123,153–155]. Historically, routine anesthesia in humans
was performed with relatively high V T (10–15 mL/kg) without
PEEP in most instances [156]. While the concept of lung-protective
ventilation with low V T (≤ 6 mL/kg) and high PEEP (> 12 cmH 2
O)
has been a standard procedure for long-term ventilation in humans
with ARDS in the ICU setting for more than 20 years [157], ventila-
tion strategies for routine anesthesia in humans only started to
change with advances in the understanding of mechanisms of VILI,
where lung damage is closely related to the amplitude of cyclic stretch
of lung parenchyma induced by mechanical ventilation [158].
In human patients without lung disease undergoing anesthesia for
elective surgeries, mechanical ventilation with lower V T (6 mL/kg)
and 10 cmH2 O PEEP may reduce lung inflammation compared to a
higher V T (12 mL/kg) [159]. A reduction in V T from values
≥ 10 mL/kg to < 8 mL/kg also improves the clinical outcome (lower
incidence of postoperative pneumonia/respiratory failure and
shorter duration of hospital stay) in human patients without ARDS
in the operating room [160,161]. To prevent postoperative pulmo-
nary complications, current guidelines for protective mechanical
ventilation in human patients undergoing surgery recommend
targeting a V T of 6–8 mL/kg based on predicted (ideal) body weight
and an initial PEEP level of 5 cmH2
O [162].
Ventilator settings in veterinary species cannot be directly
extrapolated from recommendations in humans for several reasons
including: (1) minute ventilation (V T × f) should be adjusted
according to the CO2 production (metabolic rate), which can vary
among animals and man; (2) the V T adjusted on the ventilator may
vary among species because of differences in airway deadspace

and VD phys
, which could also impact extrapola-

(calculated using a correction

The use of low V T (8 mL/kg) has been evaluated in anesthetized
dogs; however, a real benefit in terms of improved clinical outcome
(decreased postanesthetic respiratory complications) has not been
identified [167,168]. In addition, one canine study showed that a V T
of 8 mL/kg results in less than ideal V̇A leading to hypercapnia/
respiratory acidosis despite the use of high breathing rates (> 30
breaths/min) [167]. In this same study, computerized tomography
also provided evidence that the low V T (8 mL/kg) resulted in a
greater degree of atelectasis/poorly aerated lung areas in compari-
son to a V T of 15 mL/kg plus 5 cmH2
O of PEEP [167]. As VDaw
tends
to remain relatively constant, VD phys
can be further increased by an
increase in VDalv
during clinical anesthesia. Under these circum-
stances, mechanical ventilation with V T in the range that approaches
the deadspace represented by the conducting airways (6–8 mL/kg)
could result in even higher degrees of hypercapnia despite attempts
to maintain V̇A by increasing the number of mandatory breaths (f).
While data are lacking for most species, current evidence still sup-
ports the use of V T
s in the range of 10–15 mL/kg during routine
anesthesia in most species as no real benefit has been shown with
V T
s recommended in humans to provide “protective lung ventila-
tion.” If anesthesia ventilators that incorporate flow sensors that
allow accurate adjustment of V T are not available, Ppeak is often
adjusted along with respiratory rate to maintain eucapnia based on
capnography in small animal practice.
During PCV, the target airway pressure (Pmax
) will vary according
to the species as they differ in their CRS
. Also, specific conditions
such as decreased CRS due to obesity, pneumoperitoneum, or
thoracic shape (barrel-chested dogs) may require a higher Pmax to
provide effective alveolar ventilation. The Pmax can be initially set at
5–7 cmH2
O in cats with healthy lungs receiving PCV with zero end-
expiratory pressure (driving pressure between 5–7 cmH2 O) [169].
Setting the Pmax
/driving pressure at 5–7 cmH2
O was recommended
because when Pmax values were increased above this range there
were progressive increases in overinflated pulmonary parenchyma
upon computed tomography [169]. To date, there are no published
studies evaluating the Pmax during PCV in canine species; however,
clinical experience has shown that in non-obese medium-sized
dogs with healthy lungs, the Pmax can be initially set at 8–10 cmH2
O;
taking into consideration that there is an intrinsic PEEP of at least
2 cmH 2
O in a bellows-type ventilator, this level of Pmax will result in
a driving pressure of 6–8 cmH2
O.
In humans, avoidance of 100% oxygen as carrier gas and mainte-
nance of PEEP during mechanical ventilation are strategies used to
reduce atelectasis and improve oxygen transfer from alveoli to arte-
rial blood (decrease the P(A-a)O 2 and increase PaO2 /FI
O2 ratio). As
explained in Chapter 37, collapse of poorly ventilated alveolar units
(V̇A /Q̇ < 0.15) is precipitated by high F I
O2 (> 0.8) because the trans-
fer of oxygen to pulmonary capillary blood exceeds the inspired gas
flow entering these alveoli [170]. As the predominant mechanism
responsible for the increase in intrapulmonary shunt during anes-
thesia in humans with normal lungs is compression atelectasis, the
use of lower FI
O2 by mixing oxygen and air in inspired gas per se
does not abolish atelectasis during anesthesia and surgery [171].
However, current guidelines for lung-protective mechanical venti-
lation in anesthetized human patients include the recommendation
to set the FI
O2 after intubation to ≤ 0.4 with subsequent adjustments
in FI
O2 to the lowest value necessary to maintain oxygen saturation
monitored by pulse oximetry ≥ 94% (strength of recommendation:
weak) [162].
A reduction in the inspired oxygen concentration from 100% to
40% during VCV (V T adjusted to 15 mL/kg) in dogs reduced atelec-
tasis and poorly aerated lung areas, recognized as dense lung areas
upon computed tomography, and improved oxygen transfer from
alveoli to arterial blood (decreased P(A-a)O2
) despite lower PaO 2
values in comparison to animals receiving 100% oxygen [15].
During VCV in dogs (V T adjusted to 12 mL/kg), a reduction in
inspired oxygen from 100% to 40% while maintaining zero end-
expiratory pressure or the use of 100% oxygen with PEEP (5 cmH2
O)
after an ARM (CPAP of 40 cmH2
O applied for 20 s) resulted in
higher PaO 2
/FI
O2 ratio, improved pulmonary mechanics (increased
compliance), and increased lung aeration in comparison to 100%
oxygen and zero end-expiratory pressure [38]. While the use of
lower FI
O2 may be a feasible alternative to improve lung function
during mechanical ventilation in dogs with healthy lungs, reducing
the FI
O2 from values > 95% to 50% during conventional VCV did
not reduce the large shunt fraction/venous admixture that develops
in dorsally recumbent, isoflurane-anesthetized horses [35].
Anesthesia for bronchoscopy
While lower airway procedures in large animals can be performed
using sedation and topical anesthesia, general anesthesia is required
to permit bronchoscopy in companion animals. General considera-
tions when performing anesthesia for bronchoscopy include the
impact of the patient’s underlying condition on respiratory function,
potential for bronchospasm, overall impairment of gas exchange
function of the lung during and following the intervention, reduction
in airway lumen by the bronchoscope increasing R aw and the work
of breathing, and a potential lack of a sealed airway throughout the
bronchoscopy procedure, which could lead to environmental pollu-
tion and impair efficacy of positive-pressure ventilation. Reported
complications associated with bronchoscopy (with or without
bronchoalveolar lavage) in companion animals include hypoxemia,
hemodynamic changes (bradycardia, tachycardia, hypotension, and
hypertension), pneumothorax, bronchospasm, prolonged anesthetic
recovery, and death [172–177]. Most complications that occur
during anesthesia are transient and improve over time with oxygen
supplementation, ventilatory support, and/or specific interventions
such as thoracocentesis; however, mortality during anesthesia in
feline patients undergoing bronchoscopy may be higher compared
to that observed with other interventions [172].
Management of anesthesia
Most canine and feline patients scheduled for bronchoscopy have
clinically significant underlying respiratory disease that warrants
a thorough history, preoperative physical examination, and
diagnostic work up, including chest radiography. In general,
sedation of small animal patients with opioid analgesics is routinely
performed 	due 	to 	their 	mild 	sedative 	and 	antitussive
properties [172]. Inclusion of anticholinergics in premedication
protocols may not prevent bronchospasm; however, they can be
included based on other indications [178]. Preoxygenation of
patients prior to induction of anesthesia with injectable anesthetics
and subsequent delivery of oxygen using an anesthetic breathing
circuit is recommended. Methods used to secure the airway prior
to bronchoscopy in cats include a sterilized standard endotracheal
tube or a supraglottic airway device [172,179], while sterilized
standard orotracheal tubes are generally used in dogs. Anesthesia
may be initially maintained with either an inhalant anesthetic or an

-- 798 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	783
injectable anesthetic. As the patient’s cardiopulmonary status can
change rapidly during endoscopic airway procedures, it is
recommended that monitoring devices such as an electrocardiogram
(ECG), blood pressure monitor, pulse oximeter, and capnograph
are in use prior to initiation of any airway procedure.
Several different strategies can be used to facilitate oxygen
delivery during airway examination and sample collection. A bron-
choscope swivel adapter placed between the patient’s end of the
breathing circuit and endotracheal tube permits use of an endo-
scope with an endotracheal tube or supraglottic device (Fig. 38.32).
Use of a bronchoscope adapter avoids the need to disconnect an
intubated patient from the breathing circuit during the exam,
allowing more effective oxygen supplementation/high FI
O2 levels to
be provided throughout the procedure. Of concern for the anesthe-
siologist is the narrowing of the trachea (in non-intubated patients)
or of the endotracheal tube by the bronchoscope, which will increase
R aw and the work of breathing. Therefore, intubation should be per-
formed with an endotracheal tube with the largest internal diameter
possible and if possible, mechanical ventilation should be consid-
ered to improve gas exchange and reduce the work of breathing,
especially in patients that are already dyspneic and experiencing
respiratory muscle fatigue due to increased work of breathing.
Providing oxygen (from the anesthesia machine or alternative
oxygen source) via a catheter that is suitable for insertion into the
trachea with or without an orotracheal tube in place is an alterna-
tive option. In patients that are too small to permit passage of a
scope through an endotracheal tube and/or placement of a catheter
beside the scope, it may be possible to deliver oxygen through one
of the endoscope channels. With the latter technique, low oxygen
flows should be used, and care taken to ensure adequate expiratory
airflow to prevent gas trapping in the lungs and development of a
pneumothorax. To minimize potential environmental contamina-
tion and personnel exposure to inhalant anesthetics, injectable
agents such as propofol or alfaxalone, administered as an infusion
or intermittent boluses are generally preferred to maintain anesthesia
during bronchoscopy if it is not feasible to use a bronchoscope
swivel adapter with a breathing circuit. During anesthetic recovery
following bronchoscopy, continued supplementation of inspired gases
with oxygen and monitoring of the patient’s adequacy of oxygenation
is highly recommended. Further recommendations regarding
preanesthetic patient preparation and anesthetic management for
patients with specific respiratory diseases are provided below.
Anesthesia for intrathoracic procedures
Indications for thoracic exploration in companion animals typically
include spontaneous pneumothorax, lung lobe torsion, intrathoracic
or thoracic mass lesions, traumatic lesions to the thorax, diaphrag-
matic hernia, congenital vascular anomalies such as persistent right
aortic arch or persistent ductus arteriosus, pericardial disease, chy-
lothorax, and pyothorax [180–185]. In addition, esophageal foreign
bodies and/or esophageal perforations are relatively common in
companion animals, and in some instances, they may require
thoracic exploration for removal and repair, respectively [186].
Although less common, in the equine and bovine, pleuropneumonia,
pericarditis, and traumatic injuries to the thorax, resulting in a
pneumothorax and/or diaphragmatic hernia may be indications for
thoracic exploration and surgical repair [187–190]. Diagnostic or
therapeutic interventions related to intrathoracic structures may be
performed using an intercostal thoracotomy, median sternotomy in
small/medium-sized animals, or a thoracoscopic approach. In some
instances, more than one surgical technique may be required to
achieve the desired outcome, particularly when thoracoscopy is the
initial technique employed, therefore, the anesthetist should be pre-
pared for multiple surgical approaches [183,184,191,192].
In most species, intrathoracic procedures are performed under
general anesthesia; however, in adult cows and horses, both thora-
cotomy and thoracoscopy have been performed in standing sedated
animals using local anesthetic techniques [187,190,193]. Although
an incomplete mediastinum is possible in large animal species, in
mature horses and cattle, the mediastinum is commonly reported to
be complete [190,193,194]. As such, despite lung collapse on the
side of surgery, adequate gas exchange can be maintained due to the
function of the contralateral lung when the surgery is performed
with the horse or cow standing, assuming it does not have similar
pathology. Like large animals, dogs and cats generally have a

complete mediastinum; however, when any veterinary patient is
under general anesthesia, ventilatory support is generally required
once the pleural space is entered even if the contralateral thoracic
space and lung are normal. Traditional two-lung ventilation is gen-
erally used during intrathoracic procedures under general anesthe-
sia; however, as will be discussed below, one-lung ventilation (OLV)
is feasible in dogs and may provide optimal surgical conditions for
some intrathoracic procedures. Thoracoscopy under general anes-
thesia with two-lung ventilation may be performed with or without
intrathoracic CO 2 insufflation to facilitate visualization of intratho-
racic structures [180,185,194,195]. In the cat during general anes-
thesia, CO 2 insufflation pressures greater than 3 mmHg result in
significant cardiovascular side effects and are not recommended in
this species [196–198]. In the horse and dog during general anes-
thesia, use of thoracic CO 2 insufflation is described, and the cardio-
pulmonary effects can be marked. Insufflation of the thoracic cavity
should not be undertaken unless required and in-depth cardiopul-
monary monitoring is recommended [187,199–202].
Complications and outcomes associated with thoracic interven-
tions are dependent on the primary disease and concurrent condi-
tions; however, in general, major intraoperative concerns include the
potential reduction in pulmonary gas exchange both during and
following the procedure, iatrogenic injury to intrathoracic structures,
as well as a deterioration in cardiovascular performance associated
with ventilatory support, reduced venous return, vasodilation, and/
or hemorrhage [183,191]. Postoperatively, pneumothorax and pleu-
ral effusion are frequently reported, particularly if patients have
clinical signs associated with pulmonary or pleural disease preop-
eratively [181,186,191]. Cellulitis and abscessation of the thoracot-
omy site have been reported in horses with pleuropneumonia
following thoracic exploration [189]. Commonly encountered
conditions involving the respiratory system that require either
thoracoscopy or thoracotomy are discussed further below.
Management of anesthesia
Prior to anesthesia, the surgical approach should be reviewed with
the surgical team to facilitate planning for patient positioning,
management of ventilation, including the need for OLV or thoracic
insufflation, as well as a postoperative patient management plan,
including the optimal approach to analgesic management.
Intrathoracic procedures are major surgeries with potential for
considerable reduction in respiratory and cardiovascular function
intraoperatively and a thorough preoperative assessment of the
patient is strongly recommended. In addition, a complete blood
count (CBC), serum biochemistry, and thoracic radiographs are
highly recommended in all patients undergoing intrathoracic pro-
cedures with additional diagnostic imaging such as ultrasound and
computed tomography as appropriate. In patients with pre-existing
respiratory disease, preoperative arterial blood gas analysis can pro-
vide information regarding lung function if it is available. Patients
with intrapulmonary masses should be evaluated for metastasis,
and changes in hepatic or renal function, in addition to the effects
of the mass on respiratory function. Cardiovascular assessment
with an ECG, echocardiographic evaluation, and blood pressure
measurement are appropriate for patients with pre-existing cardiac
disease. For patients with a history of trauma, an ECG and arterial
blood gas are also highly recommended preoperatively due to the
potential presence of arrhythmias and gas exchange impairment.
Whenever possible, patients should be normovolemic with ade-
quate hemoglobin concentrations prior to intrathoracic procedures
as blood loss is a potential complication [184]. Preoperative fluid
therapy may therefore include crystalloid, artificial colloid, and/or
blood product administration. In cases where significant hemor-
rhage is anticipated, preoperative blood typing or crossmatching is
warranted. Medications aimed at optimizing cardiopulmonary
function should be maintained preoperatively. In patients with pre-
existing pneumothorax or pleural effusion, air and/or fluid should
be removed from the intrathoracic space immediately prior to anes-
thesia, to minimize the patient’s work of breathing and improve gas
exchange during anesthetic induction. In cases with rapidly accu-
mulating intrathoracic air or fluid, measures to permit repeated
chest evacuation, such as a chest tube should be in place prior to
induction of anesthesia.
The specific anesthetic protocol used for thoracic procedures
should be tailored to the individual patient. Systemic administration
of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs), sedatives,
and opioid analgesics, with regional anesthesia (paravertebral or
intercostal nerve block) or infiltration of local anesthetic at surgery
sites, generally provides suitable conditions for thoracoscopy in the
standing adult horse or cow [187,189,190,193,194,203]. Monitoring
of the patient’s PaO2 is recommended and oxygen administration
through nasal catheter(s) is indicated if hemoglobin saturation falls
below 95% [190,203].
Recommendations for small animal patients undergoing general
anesthesia include preoxygenation of the patient if there is any pre-
existing impairment of pulmonary function, use of rapid induction
strategies to secure a sealed airway quickly, use of mechanical
ventilatory support during the thoracic procedure or earlier if
indicated, providing hemodynamic support as required (inotrope/
vasopressor infusions and antiarrhythmic medications), employing
active warming strategies to maintain the patient’s body tempera-
ture, and using multiple approaches to manage postoperative pain.
In general, a balanced anesthetic technique using a combination of
inhalant anesthetics and infusions of minimum alveolar concentra-
tion (MAC)-reducing agents such as opioids, lidocaine (except cats),
and ketamine can be used to maintain a suitable plane of anesthesia
while providing intraoperative analgesia and minimizing the car-
diovascular depression induced by inhalant anesthetics. In cases
where pulmonary tissue is being resected or there is a risk of air
leak, inhalant agents are ideally avoided to prevent environmental
contamination. Neuromuscular blocking agents are not routinely
used in veterinary patients undergoing intrathoracic procedures as
adequate muscle relaxation is typically achieved with the protocols
discussed above.
Critical to the success of intrathoracic procedures performed
during general anesthesia is the use of appropriate ventilatory
support techniques. While ventilation can be supported manually
for a short period of time, mechanical ventilation should be
available for any intrathoracic intervention planned under general
anesthesia. This will permit consistent ventilation using set volumes
or pressures while freeing up the anesthetist to monitor and manage
other aspects of anesthesia such as providing appropriate and timely
hemodynamic support. In cases with significant pulmonary
parenchymal disease or pleural effusion, the clinician should be
prepared to provide ventilatory support immediately after
anesthetic induction while in some patients, spontaneous
ventilation may be feasible before thoracotomy or thoracoscopy. In
patients undergoing a thoracotomy or thoracoscopy, once the
thoracic cavity is open to the atmosphere and intrapleural pressure
equilibrates with atmospheric pressure, the patient’s breathing
effort will not be able to create a negative intrapleural pressure and
normal airflow into the ipsilateral lung. As previously noted, in

-- 800 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	785
most healthy dogs and cats, the mediastinum is complete; however,
it may be disrupted in cases with thoracic disease and entry to the
chest may impact both lungs. For some intrathoracic procedures in
canine patients, controlling ventilation to the right and left lungs
independently may be desirable, and techniques to achieve such
conditions are discussed below. In most cases requiring separation
of the lungs, ventilation is initiated using a standard orotracheal
tube, and therefore whole lung ventilation is conducted until the
patient is prepared and positioned for surgery. Placement of an
endobronchial blocker or performing selective endobronchial
intubation to initiate OLV is then performed to minimize lung
movement and improve surgical visualization.
With traditional (non-PEEP) ventilatory support, opening of
the pleural cavity via a thoracotomy or thoracoscopy typically results
in a decrease in PaO2 because of venous admixture associated with
V̇A
/Q̇ mismatch and intrapulmonary shunting of blood [190,193,203–
207]. The latter is attributed to a decrease in FRC (to below closing
capacity) associated with the loss of the elastic recoil of the chest wall
and its associated negative intrapleural pressure [204]. The
significance of the fall in PaO2 will be dependent on the patient’s
baseline oxygenation; however, in most companion animals without
primary lung disease, hemoglobin oxygen saturation is generally well
maintained during intrathoracic procedures. While the use of PEEP
and conservative V T settings (< 15 mL/kg) may not influence
outcomes in patients with healthy lungs, in patients with lung injury,
the use of ventilatory strategies that minimize lung collapse and
maintain alveolar recruitment, as discussed above, should be
employed to prevent further lung injury. In terms of lung mechanical
properties, as FRC is reduced, the compliance of the lung will
decrease; however, the overall impact on the patient may be variable
depending on the contribution of the chest wall, as total respiratory
compliance (CRS
) is the sum of both lung and chest wall compliance.
For example, during thoracoscopy, CRS may not change significantly,
while it may increase in a patient undergoing a median sternotomy
because the constraint imposed by the chest wall on total CRS has
been removed. In the latter circumstance, if the patient is receiving
ventilatory support with a preset pressure target (PCV mode) and the
Pmax is not decreased once the thorax is open, PaCO2 will generally fall
due to excessive alveolar ventilation associated with an increase in V T
.
Irrespective of the surgical approach, if the V T delivered to the patient
is maintained (VCV mode), changes in PaCO2 will be minimal after
the thorax is opened [205,208].
Recommended monitoring during intrathoracic procedures
under general anesthesia includes pulse oximetry, capnography,
ECG, direct arterial blood pressure, blood gas analysis, and body
temperature. While end-tidal CO2 monitoring may be a useful tool
to adjust mechanical ventilation in healthy dogs, PET
CO2 may not
reliably assess adequacy of ventilation in dogs undergoing thora-
cotomy [209,210]. Despite its limited ability to evaluate adequacy of
ventilation, PET
CO2 monitoring and determination of P(a-et)CO 2
by serial arterial blood gas analysis may provide important infor-
mation related to changes in alveolar deadspace and lung perfusion
in patients undergoing thoracic surgery.
Arterial blood gas analysis will provide an accurate measure of
PaCO 2 as well as information regarding the patient’s oxygenation
and degree of intrapulmonary shunting of blood. In terms of lung
mechanical properties, airway pressure should also be monitored
and if available, spirometry will provide additional information
regarding pulmonary mechanics to help guide ventilatory support
as described above. In small animal patients, if it is not possible to
monitor blood pressure invasively, a Doppler blood pressure
monitor is recommended in addition to an oscillometric technique,
as it can be used repeatedly over a short period of time, and it has an
audible signal permitting the anesthesiologist to continuously
evaluate the pulse rate, rhythm, and quality of peripheral perfusion.
Arrhythmias are relatively common in patients undergoing thoracic
procedures due to underlying cardiovascular disease, hemodynamic
alterations associated with the intervention, or direct myocardial
irritation, therefore the clinician should monitor the ECG continu-
ously and have antiarrhythmics available.
Small animal patients with chronic pleural space disease (e.g.,
chronic diaphragmatic hernia or chylothorax) may have concurrent
pulmonary parenchymal disease and/or lung lobe collapse, which
will be further injured by rapid re-expansion during surgery.
The pathophysiology of pulmonary re-expansion injury (i.e.,
re-expansion pulmonary edema) is complex but includes mechanical
stress leading to increases in the pulmonary microvascular
permeability secondary to the abrupt re-expansion of the lungs, and
infiltration of immune cells [211,212]. In humans, re-expansion
pulmonary edema is a rare but potentially fatal complication that
may occur after rapid re-expansion of chronically collapsed/
atelectatic lungs secondary to pneumothorax, hemothorax, and
pleural effusion [211,212]. Although objective data are lacking in
the veterinary literature, rapid re-expansion of the lungs during
surgery in cats with chronic diaphragmatic hernia may carry high
risk of fatality because of re-expansion pulmonary edema [213].
Therefore, in cases of diaphragmatic hernia where chronic alveolar
collapse is suspected, extra caution should be exerted when applying
progressively increasing inspiratory pressures and increased PEEP
levels to reopen collapsed alveoli. Visual assessment of the reopening
of collapsed lung (which changes from a dark color to a light pink)
by the surgeons may help to guide the anesthesiologist when
recruiting collapsed areas. Pulmonary edema has been observed in
some individuals in the early postoperative period, which has led
to various recommendations such as limited crystalloid volume
administration, use of colloids, administration of diuretics, and
administration of corticosteroids. Despite the lack of published
evidence, gradual re-expansion of chronically collapsed lung might
carry a lower risk of complications compared to rapid re-expansion
of the lung intraoperatively. When considering alveolar recruitment
maneuvers (ARMs) previously discussed in this chapter, a stepwise
increase in airway pressures by using a cycling maneuver approach
could be an option to minimize sudden re-expansion of the collapsed
lung after the abdominal viscera are removed from the thorax.
Placement of at least one thoracic tube prior to chest closure is
routine in patients at risk of intrapleural air or fluid accumulation
following thoracoscopy or thoracotomy. At the end of the surgical
intervention, the anesthesia-surgery team needs to communicate
when the chest is closed to ensure removal of intrapleural air and
closure of the chest tubes prior to recovery from anesthesia.
Recommended analgesic techniques used in patients undergo-
ing a thoracotomy include regional anesthesia techniques (e.g.,
intercostal nerve block, serratus plane block, paravertebral nerve
block, and placement of bupivacaine liposomal injectable sus-
pension at wound closure), epidural analgesia with opioids,
and systemic analgesia with opioids, ketamine, lidocaine, dexme-
detomidine, and NSAIDs. In clinical patients, using more than
one approach is highly recommended. Epidural morphine admin-
istration is an effective means of providing analgesia for thora-
cotomies in small animals [214,215]. As morphine is more soluble
in water than in fat, epidural administration of this opioid at
the level of the lumbosacral space results in relatively high

-- 801 of 1450 --

786 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
concentrations in the cerebrospinal fluid, which favors its cranial
spread within the medulla and the extension of its analgesic effects
up to the level of thoracic dermatomes [216].
More recently, an ultrasound-guided erector spinae block adopted
in humans for pain control in thoracic surgery has been evaluated
in cadaveric studies performed in dogs (level of the ninth thoracic
transverse process) [217,218]. A bilateral erector spinae block has
been used in anesthetized dogs undergoing sternotomies [219],
whereas another case series not including a control group reported
that epidural morphine, combined with an ultrasound-guided
erector spinae plane block with bupivacaine, provided adequate
intra- and postoperative pain control for lateral thoracotomies in
dogs [220]. A serratus block is another interfascial plane block that
provides analgesia for thoracotomies in humans [221] that has been
evaluated in cadaveric studies in dogs [222]. However, like the erec-
tor spinae block, published evidence of its effectiveness for control-
ling pain in thoracic surgery is based on a case series study with a
small number of animals [223].
Intrapleural instillation and infiltration of local anesthetic around
chest tube insertion sites have also been shown to be safe and improve
postoperative analgesia in dogs [224–226]. When local anesthetic
techniques are employed, bupivacaine or ropivacaine are generally
preferred due to the longer duration of action relative to lidocaine.
Due to potential toxicity, the total dose of bupivacaine should not
exceed 2 mg/kg in dogs, whereas the dose of ropivacaine should
not exceed 3 mg/kg in this species.
Separation of the lungs and one-lung
ventilation (OLV)
Functional separation of the lungs can be performed during anes-
thesia for a variety of indications. In veterinary medicine, the most
common indications are to facilitate thoracoscopic or minimally
invasive thoracic surgery or to isolate one lung from another when
contamination from one lung to the other is undesirable [227]. In
the latter instance, patients are generally undergoing lung lobectomy
to remove the affected lobe [192,228–231]. Controlling the
distribution of ventilation in patients with a bronchopleural fistula,
pulmonary bullae, disruption of the tracheobronchial tree, or other
severe unilateral lung disease are less common indications for
isolation of the lungs during ventilatory support [227,229].
Theoretically, the need for ventilation of both lungs versus selective
ventilation of one lung influences what strategy is optimal for the
intended procedure. To achieve independent ventilation of the right
and left lungs, placement of a double-lumen endotracheal tube is
necessary. When ventilation of one lung and collapse of the
alternative lung will provide the necessary conditions, options
include selective endobronchial intubation using a single-lumen
endotracheal tube, placement of a double-lumen endotracheal tube,
or use of a bronchial blocker (Fig. 38.33) [227,232,233].
With some bronchial blockers and double-lumen endotracheal
tubes, it is also feasible to ventilate one lung and maintain static lung
inflation using CPAP with varying FI
O2 levels in the alternate
lung [227,229]. In veterinary medicine, determination of the best
strategy for an individual patient will be dependent on the size of the
patient, available equipment (endoscopic equipment and specialized
airway devices), surgical approach, and experience of the anesthesia
and surgical team. Irrespective of the type of equipment used,
fiberoptic 	bronchoscopy 	is 	recommended 	either 	during 	or
immediately following placement to ensure the correct location of the
double-lumen tube or blocker, although this may not be feasible in
very small patients. When the latter is not feasible, video-assisted
thoracoscopic verification of airway device placement has been used
and fluoroscopic guidance of airway devices suitable for OLV has been
described in an experimental setting [230,234]. A brief description of
the technique and physiologic consequences of selective lung
ventilation is provided below. Depending on the planned intervention,
patients may be placed in lateral recumbency, with the ventilated lung
in the dependent position, or dorsal recumbency.
As noted, placement of a double-lumen endotracheal tube creates
functional separation of the right and left lung, permitting either
independent ventilation of both lungs, ventilation of one lung, and
either application of CPAP or zero airway pressure on the alternative
lung. Several different double-lumen tube designs exist; however, due
to anatomical differences in humans and veterinary species, patient
size, and airway configuration, their use is generally limited to
medium-sized dogs (10–25 kg) that can be managed with standard
