orotracheal tubes with internal diameters of 6.5 to 10 mm. Double-
lumen endotracheal tubes are supplied in varying configurations,
lengths, and internal and external diameters, variables that must be
considered on an individual patient basis. In general, left-sided
double-lumen tubes, which have a longer tube that fits into the left
mainstem bronchus and a shorter tube terminating above the carina,
are commonly used due to the anatomy of the right mainstem
bronchus and right apical lobe in humans as well as veterinary
species. Specifically, the short distance from the tracheal carina to the
right apical lobe, as well as anatomical variation between individual
patients, make consistent blocking of the right lung more challenging
and prone to failure in both humans and dogs [227,235].
Endobronchial blockers, which are also available in different
sizes and configurations, are long catheters with inflatable cuffs at
the distal tip designed to occlude an airway. The blocker can be
placed before the endotracheal tube so that they both reside within
the trachea independently, or it can be placed through an endotra-
cheal tube under bronchoscopic guidance once the patient is intu-
bated (Fig. 38.33). Verification of the position of the device is similar
to that described for double-lumen endotracheal tubes. Once in
place, the cuff on the blocker can be inflated, isolating the portion
of the lung distal to the endobronchial blocker cuff from the tra-
chea. Some blockers have a lumen within the catheter that permits
application of either negative pressure or positive pressure to the
isolated lung region. The former facilitates collapsing the lung and
the latter permits delivery of continuous airway pressure to maintain
lung volume without fluctuations in lung size. In cases where use of
a double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker is not possible (unsuitable
or unavailable), advancement of an endotracheal tube, of sufficient
length, into a mainstem bronchus can create isolation of a lung lobe
and OLV. This procedure has been described for use in large dogs
due to the limitations in length of double-lumen endotracheal tubes
and bronchial blockers [231].
The physiologic effect of separate lung ventilation strategies will
vary depending on how each lung is managed. While physiologic
effects of ventilation are anticipated to be equivalent to that
observed with traditional ventilation when independent ventilation
of both lungs is provided (e.g., with a double-lumen endotracheal
tube and two separate ventilators), a decrease in PaO2 is observed
when ventilation is limited to one lung [208,236–239]. The latter is
a result of continued perfusion of the non-ventilated lung (shunted
blood flow). As explained in Chapter 37, hypoxic pulmonary vaso-
constriction (HPV) can minimize the oxygenation impairment
caused by the increase in shunted flow during OLV because mixed-
venous blood is redirected from non-ventilated lung regions with
low PA
O2 to ventilated lung areas. Numerous factors have been
shown to reduce HPV during OLV, including underlying lung dis-
ease, sepsis, hypocapnia, hypothermia, Trendelenburg position,
and systemic vasodilators [235,240]. While inhalant anesthetic
agents were historically considered to be inhibitors of HPV, when
delivered at doses at or below 1 MAC they have been demonstrated
to result in a similar degree of intrapulmonary shunting compared to
injectable anesthetic regimens; therefore, they are no longer consid-
ered contraindicated for clinical use during OLV [235,239,240].
Factors that may potentiate HPV include hypercapnia, hyperthermia,
metabolic acidosis, and hypertension [235]. The clinical implications
of the latter variables in controlling HPV have not been studied in
veterinary medicine to date.
In addition to the continued perfusion of the non-ventilated
lung, alteration of V̇A
/Q̇ relationships in the ventilated lung can also
contribute to a reduction in PaO 2 in patients undergoing OLV. The
latter may be influenced by underlying disease, ventilatory strategy,
patient hemodynamics, and positioning [235,240,241]. One of the
best predictors of the ability of a patient to tolerate OLV, is their
PaO2 while receiving two-lung ventilation in the position required
for surgery [235]. Patients with severe lung dysfunction may not
have adequate capacity of the non-surgical lung to permit safe OLV.
Ensuring adequate PaO2 levels prior to initiation of OLV with arte-
rial blood gas analysis is highly recommended. The ventilatory
strategy used for the ventilated lung may also impact patient arterial
oxygen levels. A recruitment maneuver at the start of OLV is rec-
ommended in humans to minimize atelectasis in the ventilated
lung and has been used in clinical veterinary patients [229,235].
Decreased pulmonary perfusion due to hemodynamic causes (e.g.,
hypotension) may be associated with pre-existing V̇A /Q̇ abnormali-
ties in both lungs even before initiation of OLV, and this will further
impair gas exchange and exacerbate hypoxemia after the lung is iso-
lated. In terms of patient positioning, the incidence of hypoxemia is
higher when human patients are in a supine position (equivalent to
dorsal recumbency in quadrupeds) [235,240]. As the right lung is
larger (about 55% of the total volume) than the left lung (45%),
human patients that are positioned in right lateral recumbency for
OLV of the right lung (left thoracotomy) present better arterial oxy-
gen levels than individuals positioned in left lateral recumbency for
OLV of the left lung (right thoracotomy). Similar discrepancy in
lung sizes exists in animals, and it is anticipated that patients having
OLV of the right lung while positioned in right lateral recumbency
for left thoracotomy would be at less risk of hypoxemia compared to
animals positioned left lateral recumbency (ventilation of the left
lung) for right thoracotomy.
Investigations of the cardiopulmonary effects of closed-thorax
OLV have been carried out in healthy experimental dogs anesthetized
with isoflurane positioned in lateral recumbency, with and without
PEEP of the dependent ventilated lung [236–238]. Consistent with
reports in other species, including humans, a substantial decrease in
PaO2 is observed with initiation of OLV. These studies found that
tissue oxygen delivery was not significantly different during OLV
versus the control bilateral lung ventilation, despite the large increase
in P(A-a)O2 gradients, and the increase in venous admixture. The
maintenance of tissue oxygen supply occurred because CO was
maintained and because the use of 100% oxygen as the inhalational
carrier gas resulted in PaO2 levels during OLV that were high enough
to produce nearly full hemoglobin oxygen saturation, despite the
increase in P(A-a)O2 gradient. Similar findings have been reported
in normal dogs undergoing OLV with an open thoracic cavity [208].
Although it did not affect oxygen delivery in the healthy dogs studied,
the use of PEEP in the ventilated lung did improve PaO2 levels,
consistent with reducing intrapulmonary shunting and the inclusion
of PEEP was therefore recommended in clinical patients [238]. The
delivery of CPAP to the non-ventilated lung has also been shown
experimentally to maintain PaO2 in dogs undergoing OLV while
placed in right lateral recumbency [239].
In many of the experimental studies described to date, the V T and
respiratory rate were maintained at similar levels before and after
initiation of OLV with VCV and PaCO2 increased in all studies,
although the values remained within acceptable limits, an effect
likely due to the creation of increased deadspace ventilation with
the relatively large V T
s delivered to the one lung [208,236,237].
With PCV, as expected, conversion to OLV without changing venti-
latory variables resulted in an increase in PaCO 2 [239].
In veterinary medicine, numerous case series and case reports of
patients undergoing OLV for a variety of procedures, including

-- 803 of 1450 --

788 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
lung lobectomy for pulmonary mass removal, thymoma removal,
correction of persistent right aortic arch, and pericardial fenestra-
tion, have been published [182,183,228,229,231,242–244]. In clinical
patients, balanced anesthetic protocols that include local anesthesia
and injectable analgesics that permit inhalant anesthetics to be
maintained below 1 MAC or injectable anesthetic regimens
(propofol) are recommended. Ventilatory strategies that include
PEEP levels of 3–5 cmH 2
O and reduced V T
s (< 10 mL/kg) when
converting from two to OLV to prevent overinflation of the venti-
lated lung are suggested, although the specific V T should ideally be
adjusted to the individual patient based on gas exchange and
pulmonary mechanics measurements as discussed.
In the event of hypoxemia during OLV: (1) the FI
O2 to the venti-
lated lung should be maximized; (2) placement of the endobronchial
blocker/double-lumen endotracheal tube/endotracheal tube should
be verified; (3) patient hemodynamics should be supported
to achieve normotension; and (4) lung recruitment of the ventilated
lung with subsequent application of PEEP, if not in use, should be
initiated. If PaO2 levels do not increase to satisfactory levels (gener-
ally considered a PaO2 above 60 mmHg), two-lung ventilation
should be resumed. If a double-lumen endotracheal tube or bron-
chial blocker with lumen to the blocked lung is in place, CPAP can
be delivered to reduce atelectasis in the non-ventilated lung [229,239].
Complications reported during OLV in veterinary patients
include inability to achieve OLV or displacement of the airway
devices and subsequent failure of OLV during surgery, in addition
to inadequate PaO2 [180,227]. In some instances, surgical access
is inadequate despite OLV, and conversion to a thoracotomy is
required. Inadvertent entrapment of an endobronchial blocker tip
by a surgical stapler has also been reported [245].
Anesthetic management of patients
with respiratory disease
Patients with respiratory disease may require anesthesia for proce-
dures related or unrelated to their respiratory disease. Unfortunately,
sedation and anesthesia of these patients are associated with an
increased risk of anesthetic morbidity and mortality. To reduce
such risks, when developing an anesthetic plan, it is important for
clinicians to understand (1) the underlying pathophysiology of the
condition and its consequences as they relate to anesthesia; (2) the
presence and nature of any concurrent conditions; and (3) the pro-
posed diagnostic and/or therapeutic intervention and its potential
complications. Knowledge of the required positioning of the patient
during interventions will also assist with anesthetic preparation and
case management.
Patients presenting to a veterinary hospital in respiratory distress
may need to be triaged and supported prior to obtaining a history
and complete physical examination. In some instances, additional
specific information in the history relative to the respiratory disorder
is relevant to anesthesia as discussed below; otherwise, it is assumed
that standard history and physical examination are appropriate. In
general, proactive review and discussion of possible complications
and challenges among veterinary team members will increase pre-
paredness and improve patient outcomes. Respiratory diseases with
substantial implications related to anesthesia will be discussed in
detail below, and while all potential disorders are not covered, the
principles and practices applied to these conditions are often trans-
ferrable to other situations. As previously noted, when specific
aspects of anesthetic management are not discussed, it is assumed
standard practices including balanced anesthetic protocols with
appropriate supportive therapies and analgesic strategies are
appropriate.
Anesthesia and upper respiratory disease
Anesthesia may be indicated in patients with upper airway disease
or dysfunction for procedures that may or may not be associated
with their airway. In animals with upper airway disease, resistance
to airflow (R aw ) and the work of breathing are often increased.
These changes can be exacerbated due to the relaxation of the upper
airways induced by sedation and anesthesia. Of greatest concern is
the potential for severe hypoventilation and/or airway obstruction;
however, numerous other factors should be considered depending
on the patient’s underlying condition, as discussed below.
General approach to the management of animals with a
difficult airway
Securing an airway to maintain its patency, minimize the risk of
aspiration, and permit administration of oxygen, with or without
an inhalant anesthetic, is a key component of anesthetic manage-
ment. Differences in degree of difficulty in securing an airway exist
among species; however, access to appropriate equipment and pre-
anesthetic preparation result in successful airway management in
most patients. Unfortunately, challenges in establishing an airway
can occur in patients with normal airways due to laryngospasm or
in patients with abnormalities secondary to a variety of factors
including anatomic conformation (e.g., brachycephalic breeds),
foreign bodies, structural abnormalities (e.g., temporomandibular
joint disease), masses intrinsic or extrinsic to the airway, inflam-
mation, and/or fluid accumulation. Successful management of the
patient, including prevention of hypoxemia caused by induction of
anesthesia with injectable agents and rapidly securing a patent air-
way, may be impacted by preoperative planning and emergency
preparation.
The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) has published
guidelines for the management of the difficult airway [246]. While
no definitive guidelines exist in veterinary medicine, the principles
of preparing in advance of anesthetic induction, providing oxygen
supplementation during attempts at establishing an airway, enlist-
ing assistance, and attempting alternative strategies or awakening
the patient can be applied to the veterinary situation. More detail on
management of the difficult airway can be found in Chapter 5.
Further recommendations for airway management of animals with
pre-existing respiratory diseases are discussed below.
Canine brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome
Characteristics and pathophysiology
Individuals identified as being affected with brachycephalic airway
syndrome, or brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS),
have a combination of primary and secondary abnormalities that
result in a reduced airway diameter and partial to complete airway
obstruction [247,248]. Not all brachycephalic dogs are affected by
BOAS; however, a large percentage of dogs within certain breeds,
most notably English and French Bulldogs, Pugs, and Boston
Terriers, meet the criteria for classification as being affected by
BOAS [249–251]. Common primary abnormalities in dogs affected
with BOAS include stenotic nares, abnormal nasal turbinate mor-
phology, elongated soft palate, redundant pharyngeal soft tissues,
macroglossia, and hypoplastic trachea [250,251]. As anticipated
based on the turbulent airflow characteristics of the upper airways
and the relationship of luminal radius to resistance to airflow
(Chapter 37), the reduction in upper airway diameter results in a

-- 804 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	789
dramatic increase in airway resistance (R aw ) and the work of breath-
ing. To compensate for the upper airway obstruction, a greater
transpulmonary pressure gradient (Pao – P pl
) is required to generate
adequate inspiratory flow. Unfortunately, greater negative intralu-
minal pressure can exacerbate collapse of the upper airway struc-
tures into the air passages and further increase R aw
. Secondary
structural alteration to the airways as a result of the changes in
intraluminal pressure and flow that are observed in BOAS patients
include soft palate hyperplasia, pharyngeal hyperplasia, laryngeal
collapse, tonsillar hyperplasia, and eversion, eversion of laryngeal
saccules, and bronchial collapse [247,252–256].
Clinical signs reported in dogs with BOAS include increased
respiratory noise, snoring, stridor, inspiratory dyspnea, exercise
intolerance, heat intolerance, syncope, cyanosis, and collapse. Case
presentation to the veterinary hospital may vary tremendously.
In some instances, clinical signs may be evident during elective
physical examination with owners unaware of any abnormalities,
while in other instances, dogs may present on an urgent basis with
life-threatening hypoxemia and/or hyperthermia. An increase in
thoracic and abdominal muscular effort associated with inspiration
is often present at rest during physical examination and it is exac-
erbated with exercise or when the animal is placed in a stressful
environment. Longer inspiratory times, and shorter expiratory
times are also characteristic of the condition [257]. Severely affected
dogs may develop respiratory obstruction during sleep when
pharyngeal muscles relax, resulting in altered sleep patterns [258].
The latter has drawn comparisons between this condition and
obstructive sleep apnea in humans, with the English Bulldog
being considered a naturally occurring animal model of the human
condition [258].
The presence of lower airway or pulmonary parenchymal disease
is highly variable in dogs with BOAS. Although large prospective
studies have not been performed, higher PaCO2 and lower PaO2
values have been reported in French Bulldogs presenting for BOAS
surgery in one investigation as well as in a group of brachycephalic
dogs presenting to a referral hospital for a variety of procedures
[259,260]. In both studies, PaCO 2 was elevated above normal values
suggesting chronic habituation to hypoventilation while changes in
PaO 2 were relatively mild and consistent with reduced alveolar
ventilation. As mentioned, however, some dogs may present with
cyanosis, indicative of severe reductions in PaO 2 , which may be
secondary to reduced alveolar ventilation, V̇A
/Q̇ mismatch, or
intrapulmonary shunting associated with pulmonary parenchymal
disease [261]. Aspiration pneumonia was reported as an underlying
cause of hypoxemia in one retrospective study assessing brachyce-
phalic dogs admitted to a referral hospital [261]. Post-obstructive
pulmonary edema, also known as “negative-pressure pulmonary
edema,” as reported in other species, including humans and horses,
has also been suggested to be a contributing factor in cases with
acute severe hypoxemia [262]. Excessive negative airway pressures
caused by severe upper airway obstruction increase venous return
to the right side of the heart and increase pulmonary artery pressure.
This effect, in combination with decreased left heart function,
results in excessive increases in pulmonary capillary hydrostatic
pressures leading to pulmonary edema as fluid moves out of
pulmonary capillaries into the lung interstitial tissue and alveolar
lumen [262]. Early experimental models of upper airway
obstruction (nasal and laryngeal) in dogs reported impaired
oxygenation over several weeks postoperatively and it was
concluded that both hypoventilation and V̇A
/Q̇ disturbances
contributed to the hypoxemia [263]. In the latter study, however,
dogs were noted to have difficulty eating; therefore, aspiration
pneumonia may have contributed to the hypoxemia observed.
In addition to abnormalities related to the respiratory system,
gastrointestinal signs including gagging, ptyalism, regurgitation,
and vomiting are reported in many BOAS patients, with the severity
of signs correlating with the severity of respiratory compromise
[264–266]. The nature of the gastrointestinal abnormalities may
vary with breed, with French Bulldogs having a higher prevalence
of gastrointestinal signs compared to English Bulldogs and Pugs
[265–268]. Further investigation into the gastrointestinal dysfunc-
tion in this group of patients has shown the presence of gastritis,
esophagitis, gastroesophageal reflux, atony of the lower esophageal
sphincter, and sliding hiatal hernia [265,268,269]. Regurgitation
and vomiting are of particular concern in the perioperative period
as they are associated with aspiration pneumonia, esophagitis,
esophageal stricture, and airway obstruction [270–272]. Reported
incidence of regurgitation in patients hospitalized for surgical cor-
rection of BOAS ranged from 9.1% to 34.5% [264,267,273] with
postoperative rates being higher than preoperative rates in one ret-
rospective study [273]. Large negative intrathoracic pressure cre-
ated during inspiration secondary to partial airway obstruction is
believed to contribute to the increased incidence of gastrointestinal
dysfunction in this group of dogs [269]. Underlying gastroesopha-
geal junction abnormalities, hiatal hernia, and/or esophageal dys-
motility likely also contribute to the presence of gastrointestinal
disease [269,273–276]. Reduction in frequency of gastrointestinal
events, such as regurgitation and vomiting reported by owners, and
improvement in gastrointestinal lesions, as assessed by endoscopy,
following surgical interventions to alleviate the upper airway
obstruction have been reported, strengthening the relationship
between respiratory dysfunction and gastrointestinal disease in
dogs with BOAS [265–267,277].
Brachycephalic dogs have also been shown to have a higher rest-
ing vasovagal tone than dogs of other breeds, which may predispose
them to bradycardia [278]. In a sample of brachycephalic dogs,
arterial blood pressure assessed using an oscillometric technique
was demonstrated to be higher than in control dogs [259]. Others
have reported higher packed cell volume and indices compatible
with hypercoagulability, potentially due to the low PaO2 levels and
chronic inflammation [259]. Ocular conformation in brachycephalic
dogs, and particularly those with BOAS, predisposes them to
corneal injury [249,279].
Surgical interventions have consistently been shown to reduce
undesirable respiratory and gastrointestinal signs and improve
the quality of life, as judged by owners and physical examination
findings, in a large percentage of brachycephalic dogs [250,264,
267,280–283]. Techniques currently performed for BOAS include
staphylectomy, alarplasty, turbinectomy, vestibuloplasty, laryngeal
sacculectomy, and tonsillectomy [247]. Brachycephalic dogs have a
higher reported incidence of complications, including death, in the
perioperative period compared to non-brachycephalic breeds when
anesthetized for a variety of procedures [273,277,284–287]. The
reported perioperative morbidity and mortality associated with air-
way surgery in this patient population range from 6 to 51.1% and 0
to 6.6%, respectively [250,264,277,287–290]. English Bulldogs were
reported to have a higher anesthetic complication rate, including
death, when compared with other brachycephalic dogs in one
retrospective study [290]. Reports on the impact of brachycephalic
dog age on anesthetic outcomes associated with airway surgery
have been variable. Young dogs were reported to have a higher
incidence of regurgitation in one study, and a higher complication

-- 805 of 1450 --

790 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
rate in another; however, it is recognized that dogs with more severe
disease may present at a younger age [273,291]. Anesthetic risk in
brachycephalic dogs that had undergone corrective airway surgery
was reduced in one study; however, the risk relative to non-
brachycephalic dogs was not assessed prospectively and it may
remain higher in the brachycephalic population [287]. A preopera-
tive risk score, based on preoperative data, to predict the risk
of major complications or death for dogs presenting for surgical
treatment of BOAS syndrome was created based on retrospective
data from two centers and subsequently validated in a third
center [292]. Risk of a negative outcome was successfully predicted
based on a 10-point score (BRisk score), determined by assigning a
score to the animal’s breed (English or French Bulldog versus other
brachycephalic breeds), surgical history, procedures planned, body
condition score, level of compromise at admission, and rectal tem-
perature upon admission [292]. Based on highly accessible data,
the BRisk score, can help inform owners regarding the risk of a
negative outcome as well as prepare staff and resources prior to
corrective surgery [292].
Management of anesthesia
Overall, the specific concerns related to BOAS during the perianes-
thetic period include the potential development of respiratory
distress, hypoxemia, and/or airway obstruction (partial or complete),
and the predisposition to regurgitation and aspiration [262,293].
The surgical location also makes anesthetic monitoring of the
patient’s depth of anesthesia using jaw tone or eye reflexes more
challenging as well as poses a greater risk of unobserved airway
disconnection or gastric regurgitation. Maintaining hemodynamic
stability and preventing corneal trauma, are also of concern and
may prove more challenging than in non-BOAS patients. Having a
clearly communicated perioperative plan developed with the entire
veterinary team, that extends for at least 24 h postoperatively, is
highly recommended [262,277,294].
Prior to anesthesia, it is important that a thorough history,
including the owner’s perception of their animal’s condition is
obtained. Unfortunately, owners are often unaware of their dog’s
abnormalities and risks associated with surgery and anesthesia [279].
Specific questions regarding the dog’s respiratory noise, exercise
tolerance, activity levels, and gastrointestinal signs should therefore
be included rather than interpretive questions that rely on the
owner’s opinion regarding normal canine behavior (activity levels)
and physical symptoms (e.g., respiratory noise and heat tolerance).
Current medications including NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and
gastrointestinal medications are particularly relevant as they will
influence perioperative patient medical management.
Physical examination including auscultation of the laryngeal
region and thorax should be performed, although referred upper
airway sounds can make auscultation challenging in many dogs.
Inspiratory stridor over the laryngeal region is an indicator of
laryngeal dysfunction which may impact the ease of intubation as
well as the planned surgical intervention [295]. Hyperthermia may
be present in patients presenting in respiratory distress and should
be considered during initial patient stabilization; however,
acquisition of rectal temperature can be stressful, and it may be
prudent to stabilize the animal prior to obtaining this measurement.
Several investigators have used scoring systems to characterize
the severity of respiratory symptoms and facilitate prediction of
outcomes and/or complications following surgical intervention
[264,265,292]. The BRisk score provides risk of mortality or major
complications during the period of hospitalization [292]. Inclusion
of a 3-min trot test and evaluation of pulmonary mechanics using
whole-body plethysmography can provide further information
regarding the patient’s airflow obstruction [295,296]. The latter is
not routinely available for clinical use, but it has been used to objec-
tively assess other measures of respiratory dysfunction in BOAS
patients as well as the outcome associated with different surgical
and medical treatments [291,295,297].
Although patients may be systemically healthy, routine presurgi-
cal diagnostic testing should include a CBC, serum biochemistry,
and thoracic radiographs to screen for inflammatory lung disease
and to provide baseline values in the event of complications postop-
eratively. Additional tests such as esophageal contrast studies, ultra-
sound, or fluoroscopy are recommended based on individual
clinical signs. Patients showing a marked increase in respiratory
effort and/or signs of impaired oxygenation should have further
assessment of respiratory function performed. Arterial blood gas
sampling and analysis is ideal; however, if this is not feasible, meas-
urement of hemoglobin oxygen saturation with pulse oximetry is
informative in some patients. While the latter tool is readily availa-
ble, the limitations of pulse oximetry need to be considered when
interpreting individual patient measurements [298]. In patients
presenting with severe disease, an ECG and blood pressure meas-
urement may also provide additional useful information preopera-
tively. Because of the high incidence of pulmonary hypertension in
animals with clinical signs of BOAS, echocardiographic evaluation
should be considered. For elective procedures, overweight dogs
should have a nutritional consultation and weight loss plan imple-
mented prior to surgery as obesity has been associated with severity
of clinical signs in Bulldogs and Pugs with BOAS [296].
To date, no large prospective clinical study has been performed
to assess the optimal perioperative medical management of gastroin-
testinal dysfunction in BOAS patients. Due to the high prevalence of
gastric and esophageal disease in most dogs with BOAS, routine pre-
operative administration of a proton pump inhibitor is recom-
mended [269,299–301]. While the treatment may not prevent
gastroesophageal reflux and regurgitation in all dogs, it will increase
the gastric pH and may prevent secondary esophageal lesions from
developing. The duration of treatment may vary based on the
individual patient’s clinical signs as well as ease of treatment. Patients
with a history of regurgitation have an increased incidence of
perioperative regurgitation and may benefit from a longer preoperative
course of therapy if feasible [268,273]. The prokinetic cisapride has
shown positive effects in BOAS dogs and is currently recommended
over metoclopramide, which has shown variable effects on
gastroesophageal reflux and regurgitation; however, it may not be
readily available. Many clinicians include metoclopramide despite a
lack of strong evidence supporting its use at clinically recommended
doses [251,300,302]. Maropitant, a neurokinin-1 (NK1
) receptor
antagonist, is an effective antiemetic when administered prior to
preanesthetic medication and is therefore recommended in patients
with a history of vomiting [303–306]. Routine inclusion of histamine
type-2 (H2
) antagonists/proton pump inhibitors and mucosal
protectants, such as sucralfate, in the perioperative management of
BOAS patients is more controversial; however, when used on a short-
term basis, they have a low incidence of side effects and may offer
beneficial effects in patients with severe gastrointestinal disease.
Once a procedure is scheduled, it is recommended that the
brachycephalic patient be admitted on the day of surgery with
minimal wait time before premedication to minimize the impacts
of stress and anxiety. Prescribing oral behavioral modifying drugs
to reduce pre-appointment fear may also be considered [307].

-- 806 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	791
The impact of fasting time on the risk of regurgitation, gastroe-
sophageal reflux, and/or vomiting in both normal and dogs affected
with BOAS is not known at this time. At present, there is inadequate
data to make recommendations for a universal fasting period prior
to anesthesia [308,309]. Common recommendations include over-
night fasting (minimum fasting period of 6 h) and free access to
water until premedication.
Prior to administration of preanesthetic medication, the anes-
thesia workstation should be prepared. In addition to the standard
equipment, orotracheal tubes in a range of sizes, facemasks, and
monitors including a pulse oximeter should be readily available.
Laryngoscopes with different blade sizes and/or styles, should be
available to facilitate intubation. Despite the presence of an orotra-
cheal tube, the work of breathing in brachycephalic dogs will likely
be higher than in a non-brachycephalic dog of similar weight due to
their relatively small airway radius and tendency for overweight
body condition scores. As such, it is recommended that a suitable
mechanical ventilator be available and prepared for use. Equipment
that can be used to suction the oropharyngeal area should also be
readily available in the induction and recovery areas.
In general, the choice of premedication agents will be dependent
on the patient’s temperament and co-existing medical conditions,
planned diagnostic and/or surgical intervention, and clinician
preference. When patients are scheduled for relatively non-invasive
procedures such as airway surgery only, it is recommended that
μ-opioid receptor agonists are not used due to their association with
regurgitation and vomiting, particularly when administered alone via
the intramuscular (IM) or subcutaneous (SC) route [306,310–313].
In mature quiet dogs, low doses of sedative agents alone may be
sufficient, with opioid analgesic agents added if required once the
patient is anesthetized with a secure airway. If opioid analgesics
are included in the premedication, methadone or buprenorphine are
currently recommended options as they are associated with a lower
incidence of vomiting [313]. Panting is also associated with μ-opioid
receptor agonists, which can worsen airway obstruction in patients
with severe disease. Some authors have recommended the exclusion
of α2
-adrenergic receptor agonists due to concerns related to airway
obstruction associated with profound muscle relaxation. While high
doses of α2
-adrenergic receptor agonists should be avoided,
premedication with dexmedetomidine (2 μg/kg IM) in combination
with methadone (0.3 mg/kg IM) has been shown to provide good
sedation without an increase in complications in ASA I or II
brachycephalic dogs prior to anesthetic induction when compared
to acepromazine (0.02 mg/kg IM) and methadone (0.3 mg/kg
IM) [314]. When α2
-adrenergic receptor agonists are not included in
the premedication regimen, including anticholinergics such as
glycopyrrolate in the animal’s premedication offers the advantage of
maintaining heart rate and reducing oropharyngeal secretions.
While anticholinergics have not been demonstrated to increase the
risk of aspiration pneumonia, atropine has been shown to reduce
lower esophageal sphincter tone [270,315–318]. While the decision
to include anticholinergics prophylactically in the premedication
regimen remains controversial, their use to treat bradycardia once a
secure and sealed airway is established is warranted.
Induction of anesthesia using a rapidly acting injectable anesthetic
such as propofol or alfaxalone is ideal to ensure a rapid transition to
a secure and sealed airway; however, this should be performed
following preoxygenation for 3–5 min using a facemask. The latter
has been shown to prolong the time to hemoglobin desaturation
and will permit a brief airway examination prior to intubation
should the patient become apneic [39,40]. If preoxygenation using a
mask is not tolerated, preoxygenation using a flow-by technique
can be used; however, the time to desaturation will be shorter
compared to that obtained with a mask [40]. Irrespective of the
technique used, the patient’s eyes should be well lubricated prior to
induction to minimize risk of corneal abrasion.
Prior to intubation, a rapid oropharyngeal exam should be per-
formed. Further examination may be warranted in individual
patients with signs of laryngeal dysfunction. Orotracheal intuba-
tion is generally performed using direct visualization facilitated by
use of a laryngoscope while the patient is maintained in sternal
recumbency with the head and neck elevated. The cuff on the
orotracheal tube should be inflated to create a seal as soon as
the orotracheal tube is in place and the seal should intermittently
be verified throughout anesthesia. If standard placement of an
endotracheal tube is not possible due to challenges associated with
visualization, a stylet, such as a semi-rigid urinary catheter can be
used as a guide for the endotracheal tube to facilitate intubation.
Oxygen can be insufflated through the catheter while the endotra-
cheal tube is placed. If it is not possible to place an orotracheal tube,
the catheter can be used to provide oxygen while a tracheostomy is
performed. As the catheter is rigid, care must be taken to not
damage the airways and excessive flows should be avoided if severe
airway narrowing is present. If available, a small-diameter endo-
scope can also be used as a stylet for the endotracheal tube. Because
the trachea is often hypoplastic in dogs with BOAS, it may not be
possible to insert an endotracheal tube of the same size that would
be typically inserted in a non-brachycephalic dog of similar body
mass. For example, while a 9.5 mm internal diameter endotracheal
tube would easily fit in a 20 kg mongrel dog, an English Bulldog of
similar weight may allow placement of an endotracheal tube with
an internal diameter of only 6.5 mm (Fig. 38.34A). Inasmuch as the
endotracheal tube will further reduce diameter of an already nar-
rowed airway, resulting in greater increases in R aw and the work of
breathing, providing mechanical ventilatory support during anes-
thesia is strongly advised (Fig. 38.34B). Dog breeds that are typically
diagnosed with BOAS (e.g., English and French Bulldogs, Pugs, and
Boston Terriers) have a barrel-shaped chest and often are obese,
factors that are known to decrease CRS during anesthesia
(Fig. 38.34B) [118]. In these dogs, due to their increased R aw and
decreased C RS
, VCV or PCV volume-guaranteed may be preferred
over a standard PCV mode as previously discussed in the mechani-
cal ventilation section.
Once a secure airway is in place and oxygen supplementation
initiated, a variety of techniques and anesthetic agents can be used
to maintain anesthesia, including inhalant anesthetics, infusions of
injectable anesthetics, or a combination of both. The goal should be
to use a protocol that results in a smooth, excitement-free recovery
while minimizing residual sedation and upper airway relaxation.
In terms of inhalant anesthetics, some clinicians might prefer sevo-
flurane over isoflurane because the former has a pharmacokinetic
profile that favors faster recoveries from anesthesia. However,
clinical data shows that the quality and duration of recovery are
comparable between these inhalant anesthetics in canine species
[319,320]. Use of infusions of injectable anesthetics may result in
more prolonged anesthetic recoveries when compared to inhalant
anesthetics and therefore may be less desirable unless inhalant
anesthetics are contraindicated for other reasons. If constant rate
infusions of opioids are indicated to provide intraoperative analgesia
and reduce inhalant requirements, fentanyl and remifentanil are
suitable agents [321,322]. While remifentanil is the ideal agent for
prolonged infusions because it is devoid of cumulative effects [323],

-- 807 of 1450 --

792 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
fentanyl is still an effective drug for intraoperative use in dogs with
BOAS because, differently from humans, this opioid does not accu-
mulate during prolonged infusions in dogs (i.e., its plasma sensitive
half-life is unaltered by infusion duration in this species) [324].
If prolonged recoveries are attributed to residual effects of pure
μ-opioid receptor agonists, partial reversal with a μ-opioid receptor
antagonist (naloxone) or a μ-opioid antagonist/κ-opioid agonist
(butorphanol) should be considered.
Care should be taken when positioning the patient. Even with
optimal positioning such as sternal recumbency with head elevated,
or lateral recumbency with the oropharyngeal area elevated,
the oropharynx should be surveyed routinely for gastric contents.
This is particularly important when the patient is moved repeatedly
during anesthesia [325]. If reflux is noted, the oral cavity and esoph-
agus should be cleared immediately, and the esophagus and mouth
flushed with warm water followed by gentle suctioning prior to
recovery. Intraoperatively, monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation,
and thermoregulation should be performed on a regular basis in
addition to hemodynamic monitoring tailored to the patient. Pulse
oximetry and capnography can be monitored continuously; ideally,
blood gas analysis is performed intermittently to verify accuracy
and gain further insight into potential impairment of oxygenation
in critical patients.
Irrespective of the surgical or diagnostic procedures being
performed, addition of local anesthetic techniques should be
considered to reduce the reliance on opioid analgesics in the post-
operative period. Bilateral maxillary blocks may reduce the need for
additional opioid and anesthetic drug use intraoperatively in
patients undergoing BOAS-related airway procedures [326,327].
Unfortunately, inadvertent puncture of the maxillary artery resulting
in retrobulbar hemorrhage/hematoma is a potential complication
of this block [328]. Analgesic adjuncts such as intravenous lido-
caine (50 μg/kg/min) and ketamine (10 μg/kg/min) infusions can
also be added to opioid infusions to provide additional analgesia
and improve intraoperative stability during longer procedures if
necessary. Corticosteroids are often administered in patients under-
going airway surgery and may be administered prior to anesthesia
or in the perioperative period; however, their use will preclude the
administration of NSAIDs for postoperative analgesia because of
increased risk of toxicity.
Although there is not extensive objective evidence to support
their use, vasoconstrictors such as phenylephrine or oxymetazoline,
applied topically in the upper airways, may reduce swelling prior to
recovery. Depending on the surgical procedure, a system for deliv-
ering oxygen using nasal catheters or prongs may be placed prior to
extubation, and oxygen delivered via this route. The routine pre-
placement of nasotracheal catheters has also been described
[283,329]. Normothermia should be achieved prior to initiation of
recovery to prevent shivering associated with low body tempera-
ture. Although hypothermia is often observed following prolonged
anesthesia, hyperthermia should also be avoided during the
recovery phase as panting secondary to elevated body temperature
can worsen signs of upper airway obstruction in dogs with BOAS.
Recovery from anesthesia is a particularly critical phase in
animals with BOAS as most complications related to surgery and
anesthesia are observed during this period. Dogs with BOAS who
have not had airway surgery are still at increased risk of
postoperative complications. Adverse events frequently reported
in brachycephalic dogs in the postoperative period include
respiratory distress, hypoxemia, prolonged time to extubation,
airway obstruction (partial or complete), regurgitation, vomiting,
and aspiration [250,264,277,287–289]. The recovery period is
particularly challenging in brachycephalic patients following airway
surgery due to the associated soft tissue swelling. In some cases
where severe airway swelling is present, it is appropriate to place a
temporary tracheostomy tube prior to recovery. Potentially life-
threatening events, primarily related to the patency of the airway,
have been reported up to 24 h postoperatively; therefore, intensive
monitoring is currently recommended for at least this period
following airway surgery [277]. Having a clean set of orotracheal
tubes, laryngoscope, facemask, tracheostomy tubes, and additional
short-acting injectable anesthetic available prior to initiation of
recovery will permit rapid reestablishment of general anesthesia and
a patent airway if necessary. Recovering dogs with BOAS in sternal
recumbency following airway suctioning, with their tongue pulled
out of the oral cavity, and head and neck slightly elevated, may
improve their ability to ventilate with the least amount of respiratory
effort. Dogs with BOAS tolerate the presence of an orotracheal tube
at greater levels of wakefulness when compared with normal dogs,
probably because it provides an unobstructed airway and reduces
the work of breathing. Most clinicians recommend discontinuing
oxygen supplementation while the patient still has the orotracheal
tube in place to verify that an FI
O2 of 0.21 is tolerated, as judged by
the maintenance of oxygen hemoglobin saturation (Fig. 38.34C and
D). The orotracheal tube can be maintained in place until the dog
shows resistance to the tube by pawing at the mouth or chewing the
tube. Immediately following extubation, oxygen supplementation
using a facemask or flow-by technique can be provided to increase
the F I
O 2 which will help maintain oxygenation if mild
hypoventilation or V̇A
/Q̇ mismatching are present. Ideally,
oxygenation is assessed using arterial blood gas analysis in patients
at risk of hypoxemia in recovery; however, if arterial blood gas
analysis is not available or feasible during the immediate post-
extubation period, pulse oximetry is a suitable alternative as it may
still provide additional clinically relevant information during
recovery relative to visual observation of mucus membrane
color [298]. If an acute decrease in pulse oximetry hemoglobin
saturation (SpO2
) to values below 95% and the displayed heart rate
matches the pulse rate taken by other means (palpation or blood
pressure tracing), a change in management is indicated. While SpO2
/

accurate FI
O2 is generally not available during recovery with either
facemask or flow-by oxygen delivery [330,331].
To reduce airway soft tissue swelling postoperatively, systemic
corticosteroids such as dexamethasone can be administered unless
there are specific contraindications [264,283]. Aerosolized epineph-
rine has also been shown to improve airflow in BOAS patients, with
Pugs showing a greater response relative to Bulldogs [297]. During
recovery from anesthesia, caution should be exerted to avoid
confusing an animal displaying dysphoric/excitatory behavior
associated with opioid administration from an animal that is
agitated because of an obstructed airway. If the dog becomes dys-
phoric, low doses of dexmedetomidine (1–2 μg/kg diluted in saline
and slowly titrated to effect) or acepromazine (0.01–0.02 mg/kg)
administered intravenously and titrated to effect are effective at
calming the patient; however, if the patient cannot achieve adequate
airflow, interventions are required immediately. Depending on the
facilities and clinician preference, dogs may be placed on non-
invasive ventilatory support using HFNOT, CPAP, or following oro-
tracheal 	intubation, 	traditional 	positive-pressure 	ventilation,
for a variable period to wait for airway inflammation to sub-
side [53,62,65,332,333]. Provision of CPAP in animals with

alternative option to invasive mechanical ventilation. Tracheostomy
tubes, both temporary and permanent, are associated with high
complication rates; however, they can provide a useful strategy for
short- and long-term management in select cases [335,336].
Feline brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome
Characteristics and pathophysiology
Brachycephaly is a characteristic of certain feline breeds but sub-
stantially less literature exists regarding its impact on the health and
welfare of this species relative to the canine [337,338]. To date, there
is little information regarding anesthetic morbidity and mortality in
cats affected with BOAS. Dyson et al. reported a higher anesthetic
complication rate in Himalayan cats, a breed characterized by
brachycephaly [284]. Persian, Himalayan, British Shorthair, Bernese,
Scottish Fold, and Exotic Shorthair cats are considered brachyce-
phalic breeds; however, Persian and Exotic Shorthair are considered
extreme brachycephalic breeds with associated severe symptoms
related to their altered facial conformation [339]. The reported
structural respiratory abnormalities in cats include stenotic nares
and abnormal nasal turbinates [251,340,341]. Unlike brachycephalic
dogs, an elongated soft palate appears to be very rare in cats [342].

airflow, nasal discharge, and reduced activity levels are reported
clinical signs associated with brachycephaly in cats [251,340,343].
Surgery to reduce the nasal obstruction to airflow has been
described with low rates of complication [344,345].
In addition to the respiratory abnormalities, ophthalmic disease
is very common with epiphora, corneal ulceration, corneal sequestra,
keratitis, and entropion being reported in a high percentage of
brachycephalic cats [338,343,346]. Dental malalignment, difficulty
with prehension, and hypersalivation are also reported at frequen-
cies greater than in non-brachycephalic cats, whereas regurgitation
and vomiting have not been associated with brachycephaly in the
feline [347].
To date, little information exists regarding the prevalence of
cardiovascular disease in brachycephalic cats. A report on disorders
and mortality in Persian cats under first-opinion veterinary care in
the UK reported renal disease, neoplasia, and tumor-associated
disorders as the major causes of death; however, the significance of
brachycephaly on their cat’s overall wellbeing is underappreciated
by owners [348].
Management of anesthesia
The major anesthetic concern for brachycephalic feline patients
is related to the risk of airway obstruction in the perioperative
period. Corneal trauma is also a significant risk due to their facial
conformation [346].
Preoperative history, work up, and preparation should be tailored
to the individual patient. Like brachycephalic dogs, obtaining a
thorough and complete history with client education regarding
underlying disease is recommended. Routine patient preanesthetic
preparation, including fasting times, is suitable based on the current
state of knowledge.
Prior to sedating a brachycephalic cat, the workstation should be
set up to include a variety of endotracheal tubes and facemasks. To
date, there are no comparative studies evaluating different anesthesia
protocols in brachycephalic cats and the associated outcomes. The
following recommendations therefore reflect current opinions based
on experience and the reader is referred to the literature on general
anesthetic management in feline patients [349]. The specific anesthetic
protocol should be tailored to the individual patient based on their
behavior, underlying disease(s), and proposed surgical intervention.
After premedication, cats should be monitored continuously for
respiratory obstruction. Preoxygenation will minimize the risk of
hypoxemia during oropharyngeal examination and placement of the
orotracheal tube. Anticholinergic agents decrease oropharyngeal
secretions and may indirectly reduce the incidence of laryngospasm
during induction of anesthesia; therefore, they should be considered as
part of a preanesthetic protocol if the patient is not receiving an α2
-
adrenergic receptor agonist and no other contraindications exist.
To minimize the risk of hypoxemia and laryngospasm during
induction of anesthesia brachycephalic cats should be preoxygenated
for at least 3 min with a face mask attached to a breathing circuit
with the oxygen flowmeter adjusted to deliver a high flow rate
(> 200 mL/kg/min). Intravenous agents such as propofol or alfax-
alone are suitable anesthetic induction agents as they have the
advantage of being rapid acting with a short duration of effect,
which permits titration to a suitable anesthetic depth of anesthesia
to permit intubation. Actual doses of intravenous anesthetics will
depend on the level of sedation/CNS depression achieved after pre-
medication and on the severity of systemic disease if present.
Topical administration of 2% lidocaine (0.1 mL) to the arytenoid
cartilages should be performed while visualizing the larynx with a
laryngoscope and the face mask repositioned while the anesthesi-
ologist waits for the latency period of topical lidocaine. Attempts
at intubation should only be performed once the patient is at an
appropriate depth of anesthesia. Clinical experience dictates that
intubation can be performed 45–60 s after topical lidocaine, which
appears to be the minimum latency to achieve desensitization of the
arytenoids. In the event of a failed intubation (e.g., due to anatomical
abnormalities), the anesthesiologist may attempt to pass a small
semi-rigid stylet through the arytenoids and use it as a guide for
inserting the endotracheal tube. If the cat develops laryngospasm,
the depth of anesthesia should be evaluated, and additional anes-
thetic administered if required before subsequent attempts at intu-
bation are repeated. Use of rocuronium (1 mg/kg) was reported to
reverse severe laryngospasm and produce appropriate conditions
for intubation in a cat [350], although this is rarely required if
appropriate intubation techniques are followed.
As in brachycephalic dogs, maintenance of anesthesia can be
achieved using a variety of techniques. General principles of reduc-
ing the need for intra- and postoperative opioid analgesics by incor-
porating local anesthetic techniques may offer the advantage of
reducing respiratory depression during recovery. Careful swabbing/
suctioning of the airway should be performed prior to initiation of
recovery and intensive monitoring should be performed until the
cat is showing control of the head and airflow is such that increased
inspiratory effort is not causing patient distress. To prevent laryn-
gospasm during recovery from anesthesia, extubation in the cat
should not be delayed as is practiced in the dog. Positioning the cat
in sternal or lateral recumbency with the tongue extended out of the
oral cavity and the mouth open following extubation often provides
optimal airflow until the animal has regained greater control of
laryngeal muscles. In some cases, the head may need manual sup-
port to prevent closing of the mouth. Supplemental oxygen should
be provided in the early post-extubation phase using a facemask
or by placing the cat in an oxygen-enriched environment. In
non- intubated, spontaneously breathing cats anesthetized with an
injectable regimen (intramuscular dexmedetomidine, ketamine,
and buprenorphine), non-invasive ventilatory support provided by
a helmet adjusted to deliver a CPAP of 5 cmH2
O with an FI
O2 of
0.21 improved arterial oxygen levels [351]. However, currently,
there are no studies evaluating the benefits and feasibility of CPAP
and oxygen supplementation provided by helmets in cats with
BOAS recovering from general anesthesia. Patients that have
undergone airway surgery may benefit from postoperative over-
night hospitalization with observation due to possible airway swell-
ing; however, there are no large-scale studies reporting details
related to complications following upper airway surgery in cats.
Canine laryngeal paralysis
Characteristics and pathophysiology
The upper respiratory tract, including the larynx, provides most of
the resistance to airflow at rest in the normal animal due to the
rapid (relative to that in lower airways) and turbulent airflow as
described in Chapter 37 [352]. Laryngeal dysfunction can dramati-
cally increase the resistance to breathing by reducing airway radius
and, when disease is bilateral, it can lead to complete airway
obstruction. During inspiration, contraction of the paired
cricoarytenoideus dorsalis muscle normally abducts the arytenoid
cartilages and vocal folds, thereby widening the glottis. During
swallowing, the arytenoid cartilages are adducted, and the vocal
folds are brought together though contraction of several internal
laryngeal muscles to prevent aspiration of material into the trachea.

-- 810 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	795
The caudal laryngeal nerve, a terminal branch of the recurrent
laryngeal nerve arising from the vagus nerve in the thorax,
innervates all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except for the
cricothyroideus muscle, which is innervated by the cranial laryngeal
nerve, arising from the vagus nerve in the proximal cervical region.
Congenital and acquired laryngeal paralysis have been described
in the canine [353,354]. A hereditary mode of transmission has
been reported in numerous breeds [353–355]. Acquired laryngeal
paralysis can result from damage to the neural control of the larynx
(central or peripheral lesions involving the nerves innervating the
larynx), disease affecting the laryngeal muscles, or neuromuscular
junction disorders [354]. For dogs in which a specific etiology is not
identified, the condition has historically been referred to as
“idiopathic laryngeal paralysis.” At present, Labrador Retrievers,
Golden Retrievers, Newfoundlands, Irish Setters, and Brittany
Spaniels are the most common breeds affected with acquired laryn-
geal paralysis of unknown cause [354]. More recently, it has been
recognized that, for many dogs, the disease is progressive with
generalized signs becoming evident as the dog ages. “Laryngeal
paralysis” associated with “generalized polyneuropathy,” “late-onset
laryngeal paralysis,” or “geriatric-onset laryngeal paralysis polyneu-
ropathy syndrome” are terms that are currently used to identify the
disease in dogs with progressive generalized disease [354,356].
Irrespective of the etiology, laryngeal paralysis is characterized by
impaired abduction and adduction of the arytenoid cartilages and
vocal folds, either unilaterally or bilaterally resulting in the vocal cords
assuming a paramedian position. Clinical signs of laryngeal paraly-
sis may include a change in phonation (bark), coughing, dysphagia,
or gagging, increased inspiratory sounds, decreased exercise toler-
ance, respiratory distress, cyanosis, hyperthermia, and col-
lapse [354]. Dogs are generally more severely affected in hot weather
and during or immediately after exercise; however, the severity of
symptoms associated with laryngeal paralysis can vary tremen-
dously [354]. Hypoxemia can be marked in severely affected dogs
with only minor changes in PaCO2 levels. Hypoventilation (elevated
PaCO2
) may be the underlying cause of impaired oxygenation and
cyanosis in some cases; however, pneumonia secondary to aspiration
or negative-pressure pulmonary edema caused by upper airway
obstruction may also contribute to hypoxemia by increasing the dif-
fusion barrier for oxygen at the alveolar–capillary level, V̇A
/Q̇ mis-
matching, and/or intrapulmonary shunting. As mentioned, several
other conditions may be responsible for acquired laryngeal paralysis
and dogs may have other clinically significant diseases related to
their primary condition. For example, generalized polyneuropathy
may be present and may be detected on neurological examination.
Esophageal dysmotility is present in many cases with late-onset
idiopathic laryngeal paralysis and may manifest as gastroesophageal
reflux, regurgitation, and/or aspiration pneumonia [357].
Clinical diagnosis of laryngeal paralysis is made based on laryn-
geal examination performed under heavy sedation or light planes of
general anesthesia. Examination may involve direct visual examina-
tion and/or video-endoscopy. A lack of abduction of arytenoid
cartilages during inspiration, laxity of the vocal cords, and edema of
the corniculate processes are supportive of the diagnosis [358].
Experimentally, insufflation of CO 2 to stimulate respiration with
assessment of laryngeal function using video-endoscopy through a
laryngeal mask airway has been demonstrated to be effective in
dogs with surgically created laryngeal paralysis [359]. As will be
discussed, anesthesia can influence the assessment of laryngeal
paralysis by inhibiting abduction of arytenoid cartilages and leading
to a false positive diagnosis.
Medical management including patient weight loss, anti-
inflammatory medication, and exercise restriction is recommended
for patients with unilateral laryngeal paralysis and/or mild clinical
signs. When laryngeal paralysis is bilateral and/or symptoms impact
a dog’s quality of life, surgery is recommended. Results may vary
with the underlying etiology of the disease, breed, and comorbidities
[356,360]. Unilateral arytenoid lateralization is the technique most
used currently as it has been shown to improve the quality of life in
dogs with significant presurgical symptoms [251,354,356,360–363].
The most common postsurgical complication is aspiration pneumo-
nia [361,362,364]. Rates of aspiration pneumonia of 18.6, 31.8, and
31.8% at 1, 3, and 4 years postoperatively were reported in a large
retrospective study of 232 dogs having unilateral arytenoid laterali-
zation [364]. In this study, factors predisposing to aspiration included
esophageal disease and use of opioids postoperatively [364].
Management of anesthesia
The presence of underlying respiratory disease that could predis-
pose the patient to hypoxemia, the potential for impaired airway
patency, and the risk of regurgitation and aspiration are the major
anesthetic concerns for patients with laryngeal paralysis in the peri-
operative period. As with patients with BOAS, the surgical location
makes anesthetic monitoring of patient’s depth of anesthesia using
jaw tone or eye reflexes more challenging. Surgical location also
poses a potentially greater risk of unobserved regurgitation and
disconnection or obstruction of the anesthetic breathing circuit.
A thorough history including exercise tolerance, concurrent
diseases, previous anesthetics, and current medications is required.
A physical examination including in-depth examination of the
respiratory and neurological systems is indicated. As discussed,
many patients have an associated progressive generalized neurologi-
cal disease. Megaesophagus, myasthenia gravis, hypothyroidism,
or neoplasia should be considered as possible concurrent condi-
tions [354]. CBC, serum biochemical profile, urinalysis, thyroid
function screening, and thoracic radiographs are considered
standard in mature patients. Further diagnostic procedures such as
video fluoroscopy and measurement of serum antibodies against
acetylcholine receptors to test for canine myasthenia gravis may be
indicated based on examination and preliminary diagnostic test
results.
Information to support a change in routine fasting times for
patients undergoing general anesthesia to diagnose and/or treat
laryngeal paralysis does not exist; therefore, a standard fasting
period is recommended. Medical management prior to anesthesia
to reduce the risk of aspiration pneumonia and/or gastrointestinal
complications includes antiemetics such as maropitant, proton
pump inhibitors, and prokinetics [300]. Maropitant administered
30 min to 1 h prior to preanesthetic medication has consistently
been shown to reduce the incidence of vomiting following
preanesthetic administration in healthy dogs [303,305,306]. The
prokinetic cisapride has been demonstrated to increase lower
esophageal pressure and reduce gastroesophageal reflux in normal
dogs [302,365]. It was also shown to reduce the incidence of aspi-
ration in clinical patients having unilateral arytenoid lateralization
in one relatively small study using historical controls [366]. In the
latter study, a total dose of 1 mg/kg of cisapride was administered by
an intravenous infusion over approximately 90 min prior to surgery
(increasing doses based on response to infusion). Of 50 dogs
receiving cisapride, three had reported adverse clinical signs
during the infusion; however, no further adverse effects were
reported. Metoclopramide, another prokinetic, has had variable

-- 811 of 1450 --

796 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
results on outcomes in dogs, with one study demonstrating a
reduction in gastroesophageal reflux while others have shown no
impact on gastroesophageal reflux or regurgitation and aspiration
[364,367,368]. To date, evidence to support routine administration
of metoclopramide in patients with the goal of reducing regurgita-
tion and aspiration is lacking [300,354,368].
Preoxygenation is recommended prior to and during anesthetic
induction to prevent hypoxemia during laryngeal examination.
Numerous studies, as recently reviewed by Ranninger et al. [369],
have been performed to determine the best anesthetic protocol to
permit assessment of laryngeal function by direct visualization or
video laryngoscopy. Direct comparison between studies is challeng-
ing due to differences in study design, study population, drug
doses, and drug administration techniques; however, in general,
premedication has been shown to be beneficial. This is potentially
due to reduced doses of injectable anesthetics subsequently required
to facilitate examination. The use of hydromorphone or morphine
is not recommended in patients with laryngeal dysfunction because
opioid-induced vomiting may increase the risk of aspiration.
However, methadone, butorphanol, or buprenorphine are frequently
used and have not been shown to have a deleterious effect on out-
comes. Recently, dexmedetomidine alone or in combination with
butorphanol or hydromorphone was shown to permit assessment
of laryngeal function by video laryngoscopy in normal dogs [370].
Specifically, following an initial dose of dexmedetomidine
(3 μg/kg IV), administered alone or in combination with an opioid
(0.3 mg/kg of butorphanol or 0.1 mg/kg of hydromorphone), addi-
tional dexmedetomidine (2 μg/kg doses) was administered (up to a
maximum of 15 μg/kg) to prevent jaw movement and permit evalu-
ation of the laryngeal function before and after intravenous doxapram
administration (1 mg/kg) [370]. Although no complications related
to vomiting and aspiration pneumonia were reported after
dexmedetomidine/hydromorphone in this study, it is still advisable
to avoid this opioid in dogs with laryngeal dysfunction. Vomiting is
commonly observed after dexmedetomidine in cats and emesis
may also occur following this drug in canine species and this
possibility should be considered by the anesthesiologist as it could
lead to aspiration pneumonia in animals with laryngeal paralysis.
In terms of anesthetic induction agents, thiopental was shown to
be superior to other injectable agents in early studies evaluating
impact on laryngeal function; however, it is not readily available
and propofol has consistently been shown to be a suitable alterna-
tive [371–373]. When alfaxalone has been compared to propofol,
the results have been variable with some showing equivalency while
others report a greater negative impact on laryngeal function rela-
tive to propofol [371,372,374–376]. Laryngeal function was shown
to be superior after a period of anesthesia maintained with isoflu-
rane following induction with propofol or alfaxalone relative to that
observed immediately following induction of anesthesia with either
intravenous agent, although maintenance of anesthesia with an
injectable regimen was not evaluated [377]. While assessment could
be delayed for a period after induction with injectables and orotra-
cheal intubation, the impact of intubation prior to assessment of
laryngeal function is unknown and the potential for environmental
contamination with inhalant agents should be considered.
Doxapram, a CNS stimulant, transiently increases respiratory rate
and V T in dogs and has been administered intravenously at 0.25 to
2.5 mg/kg to improve the assessment of laryngeal function in
dogs [370,372,376,378,379] (Fig. 38.35). As laryngeal obstruction
may worsen following administration of doxapram in dogs with
laryngeal dysfunction, the team should be prepared to quickly
intervene in this scenario [369,378]. Other reported side effects of
doxapram include tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias, muscle
rigidity, hyperthermia, and seizures; however, these would appear
to be rare events as they have not been reported in canine clinical
trials [369].
Following orotracheal intubation, anesthesia is generally
maintained with an inhalant anesthetic and adjunctive agents such
as systemically administered lidocaine and opioids when required
to achieve adequate analgesia and to decrease inhalant anesthetic
concentrations. As for patients undergoing BOAS-related surgery,
butorphanol, buprenorphine, or methadone are commonly recom-
mended analgesic agents with hydromorphone and morphine being
considered unsuitable due to their association with vomiting and
regurgitation. Use of NSAIDs should be based on the individual’s
history of corticosteroid use and gastrointestinal status. Prior to
discontinuing anesthesia, the oropharyngeal region should be
carefully examined and suctioned to remove any excess fluid. It is
important that the patient is normothermic to prevent shivering or
panting during recovery. Preplacement of a nasal oxygen catheter
prior to recovery should be considered in patients with underlying
lower airway or pulmonary parenchymal disease that may require
