should continue for 12–24 h postoperatively to permit rapid inter-
ventions should regurgitation and aspiration occur.
Canine tracheal collapse
Characteristics and pathophysiology
Narrowing of the tracheal lumen can occur from numerous
causes, including trauma, intraluminal tracheal masses, compres-
sive extraluminal masses, tracheal hypoplasia, and tracheomalacia.
The most common form of tracheal collapse is characterized by
softened tracheal rings resulting in dorsoventral flattening of the
trachea with collapse of the dorsal tracheal membrane, which may
be weakened or redundant, into the tracheal lumen. The extratho-
racic (cervical) or intrathoracic trachea or both may be affected as
well as the bronchial walls [380]. Although less common, mal-
formed tracheal rings, with cartilage that deviates dorsally into the
trachea into what is described as a W shape, are also present in
some dogs [381]. The underlying cause of tracheal collapse is
unknown; however, it is likely multifactorial and may vary with the
specific characteristics (malformation versus tracheomalacia).
Based on breed prevalence, genetic factors likely play a role in com-
bination with infectious and environmental contributions. Breeds
most affected by tracheal collapse are toy or small breeds including
Yorkshire Terriers, Pomeranians, Toy Poodles, Chihuahuas, Maltese,
and Pugs [381].
Clinical signs may develop at any age; however, most studies
report onset at 6–8 years of age [381]. Coughing, which is often
described as “goose-honking,” gagging, stridor, reduced exercise
tolerance, and dyspnea are commonly reported clinical signs [381].
The severity of disease on presentation for veterinary examination
can vary tremendously with some dogs appearing normal on physical
examination. In these dogs, gentle tracheal palpation can generally
elicit a cough. Other dogs may present on an emergency basis with
severe dyspnea and cyanosis. The location of the tracheal collapse
will impact the timing of the obstruction to airflow observed on
physical examination. In dogs with dysfunction of the cervical por-
tion of the trachea, the negative airway pressure generated during
inspiration causes dynamic collapse of the airway. If the intratho-
racic portion of the airway is affected, the dynamic collapse will be
observed during forced exhalation, such as occurs during coughing.
Dogs with cervical tracheal obstruction therefore present with an
increase in inspiratory effort while dogs with thoracic tracheal
disease exhibit abnormal signs during expiration. Many dogs are
affected at multiple locations and therefore exhibit signs of dyspnea
during inspiration and expiration [382]. Laryngeal paralysis has
been documented as a complicating factor in up to 30% of cases
with tracheal collapse [383]. Bronchomalacia, small airway disease,
and pneumonia are also present in approximately 20% of dogs with
tracheal collapse. Chronic inflammation and impaired mucociliary
clearance likely contribute to the lower airway disease. Pulmonary
function testing may be available to further characterize the respira-
tory obstruction but is not routinely available.
Other comorbidities reported in dogs with tracheal collapse
include obesity, cardiomegaly, pulmonary hypertension, mitral
valve disease, hepatomegaly, and endocrinopathies [381,384]. A
causal association between tracheal collapse and the mentioned
comorbidities has not been established and concurrent diagnosis
likely reflects the age and breed predisposition for cardiovascular
and endocrine disease in these dogs.
Diagnosis of tracheal collapse is based on physical examination,
diagnostic imaging, and tracheobronchoscopy [381]. Fluoroscopic
examination of patients while awake is preferred to radiographic
examination due to the dynamic nature of the collapse. Computed
tomography if available may also provide additional information
regarding the severity and extent of airway dysfunction. During
tracheobronchoscopy, a bronchoalveolar lavage may be performed
to characterize the extent of lower airway disease.
Medical management of tracheal collapse, which is regarded as
palliative not curative, involves multimodal therapy aimed at reduc-
ing inflammation and the predisposition for coughing. Antitussives,
anti-inflammatories (steroidal drugs), anxiolytics, bronchodilators,
and antibiotics are often prescribed based on the patient’s severity
of disease following diagnostic work up. In addition to medical
management, interventions currently recommended in some patients
include extraluminal tracheal prostheses or intraluminal stent
placement. General anesthesia is typically required for both a thor-
ough diagnostic work up and for therapeutic interventions. Patients
with a confirmed or suspected diagnosis of tracheal collapse may
also be anesthetized for non-airway-related reasons (e.g., dental or
abdominal procedures).
Outcomes and mean survival times of dogs presenting with vary-
ing severity of disease and subsequent medical and/or interven-
tional surgical management have been reported [382,384–387]. In
general, the disease is progressive but dogs presenting with mild-to-
moderate clinical signs show an improvement in clinical symptoms
with medical management while dogs with severe clinical symp-
toms, as judged by respiratory noise, coughing, and dyspnea, have a
superior outcome when managed with an intervention such extra-
luminal prosthesis or intratracheal stent placement. Perioperative
mortality following extraluminal prosthesis is reported to occur in
approximately 5% of cases [385,387]. The reported rate of major
complications following extraluminal prosthesis or intratracheal
stent placement is approximately 40%. Tracheal tears, laryngeal
paralysis, and pneumonia are reported with extraluminal repair
and stent fracture, while tissue ingrowth, progressive tracheal col-
lapse, and stent dislodgement are reported following intraluminal
stent placement [382,385,387].
Management of anesthesia
The potential for impaired airway patency leading to marked
increases in R aw and the work of breathing, stimulation of the cough
reflex, and augmentation of hypoxemia due to underlying respiratory
disease are the major anesthetic concerns for patients with tracheal
collapse in the perioperative period. In patients undergoing intralu-
minal stenting, the need to share the airway during the stent place-
ment and to prevent post-procedural coughing are aspects that require
consideration. For patients with pre-existing laryngeal dysfunction
and those patients developing postsurgical laryngeal paralysis,
strategies to minimize risks discussed in the laryngeal paralysis
section are applicable.
Physical examination, CBC, biochemistry profile, urinalysis,
thoracic radiographs, as well as imaging performed to characterize
the tracheal disease, should be performed prior to anesthesia.
Auscultation of the upper airways should be included during the
physical examination to screen for laryngeal disease. Further
cardiovascular diagnostic tests such as ECG and cardiac ultrasound
should be recommended based on the physical examination
and thoracic radiographic results. Patients should be maintained on

-- 813 of 1450 --

798 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
their medical management regimen up to the perioperative period
to minimize coughing and inflammation of the airways. As noted
above, general anesthesia to permit tracheobronchoscopy and/or
airway sample collection (tracheal wash or bronchoalveolar lavage)
may be performed prior to stent placement. During the exam, the
degree and location of airway collapse can be assessed (Fig. 38.36).
After careful planning and treatment of underlying conditions,
animals may undergo a second anesthetic procedure for placement
of an intraluminal stent or placement of external ring prostheses
(Fig. 38.37) [388].
In addition to the standard workstation and monitoring
equipment set up, endotracheal tubes with embedded radiopaque
markings in various sizes and lengths should be available when
intraluminal stent placement is planned. Equipment to permit
oxygen insufflation during tracheobronchoscopy should be
available as discussed above (Anesthesia for bronchoscopy).
To date, there are no studies comparing outcomes with different
protocols in patients undergoing diagnostic or therapeutic proce-
dures related to tracheal collapse. Due to their antitussive properties,
opioid analgesics are routinely included with low doses of sedative
agents in the premedication regimen. Butorphanol provides
adequate analgesia for minimally invasive procedures (endoluminal
stent placement); however, when more invasive procedures such as
extraluminal prosthesis placement are planned, a μ-opioid receptor
agonist such as methadone is recommended for perioperative
analgesia. Adding an anticholinergic to the premedication is
recommended if there are no contraindications as airway secretions,
which can elicit coughing, will be reduced.
Preoxygenation and upper airway examination should be
performed before intubation. As in patients with BOAS or laryngeal
paralysis, the intravenous agents propofol or alfaxalone are suitable
anesthetic induction agents. Lidocaine administered intravenously
at 1–2 mg/kg intravenously prior to or during anesthetic induction
with propofol or alfaxalone with subsequent intubation has variable
impact on the frequency of coughing [389–392]. In dogs premedi-
cated with methadone or acepromazine, lidocaine at 1.5–2 mg/kg
was reported to reduce the incidence of cough while dogs that had
dexmedetomidine included in the premedication prior to 2 mg/kg
of lidocaine did not demonstrate a reduced incidence of cough-
ing [389,390]. Importantly, the incidence of cough reported in dogs
receiving lidocaine systemically at induction ranges from 7 to 52%
[389–393]. Fentanyl administered at 7 μg/kg IV was shown to be
superior to 2 mg/kg lidocaine IV at suppressing cough in dogs
receiving alfaxalone for induction of anesthesia; however, 9% of
dogs were reported to have coughed during intubation [393]. In
methadone-premedicated dogs where endotracheal intubation was
performed after achieving a moderate plane of anesthesia (propofol
titrated to abolish the medial palpebral reflex), co-administration
of lidocaine (2 mg/kg IV) resulted in a relatively low incidence of
coughing (7%) [390]. Anesthetic induction with propofol alone
(43% incidence of coughing) increased the likelihood of coughing
during endotracheal intubation by 10 times in comparison to
propofol and IV lidocaine [390]. Although no studies have been
completed to date in dogs with tracheal collapse, for those dogs who
have a history of coughing, recommendations include ensuring
antitussives are continued prior to anesthesia, opioid analgesics are
included in the premedication regimen, intubation is performed at
a moderate depth of anesthesia (injectable titrated until loss of
medial palpebral reflex), and lidocaine 1.5–2.0 mg/kg is adminis-
tered as part of the induction protocol.
During airway examination and endoluminal stent placement,
maintenance of anesthesia with injectable agents (propofol or
alfaxalone), administered as boluses or as an intravenous infusion,
will reduce the potential for environmental contamination as
maintaining a sealed airway with no leaks is difficult with inhalant
anesthetics. For patients with tracheal collapse that are undergoing
extraluminal stent placement or procedures unrelated to the airway,
maintenance of anesthesia with an inhalant anesthetic regimen is
suitable with ventilatory support provided as required. Ideally,
spontaneous breathing is maintained during anesthesia for
endoluminal stent placement as there may be periods when
positive-pressure ventilation is not feasible. In patients with cervical
tracheal collapse undergoing endoluminal stent placement through
the endotracheal tube, the endotracheal tube can be extended

pneumothorax should be considered if deterioration in ventilation
or oxygenation develops.
Irrespective of the procedure undertaken, prior to anesthetic
recovery, the airway should be examined and carefully suctioned to
remove excess fluid or debris. Avoiding excitement and coughing in
addition to ensuring analgesia is critical during recovery. Low doses
of sedatives such as acepromazine (0.01 mg/kg) or dexmedetomidine
(1 μg/kg) can facilitate a smooth recovery. Butorphanol is a suitable
postoperative analgesic when minimally invasive procedures such as
bronchoscopy or endoluminal tracheal stenting are occurring or
when local anesthesia can be included in the protocol. Invasive
procedures such as extraluminal stent placement require the use of
opioid analgesics with greater analgesic efficacy such as methadone.
Including NSAIDs in the perioperative analgesic regimen if no
contraindications exist (for example, concurrent corticosteroids) is
recommended. Oxygen supplementation may be required during
anesthetic recovery. The technique used can be tailored to the
individual patient needs and resources available. As patients are
generally small, an oxygen-enriched environment created with an
oxygen hood or cage is often suitable. Patients with tracheal collapse
that are recovering from anesthesia but have not undergone airway
stabilization techniques may require oxygen supplementation during
recovery. In severe cases, nasotracheal catheterization and/or
emergency stent placement may be indicated.
Equine guttural pouch disease
Guttural pouches are extensions of the Eustachian tubes which
connect the pharynx to the middle ear. Of domesticated veterinary
species, the equine is the only species with guttural pouches. In the
adult horse, each pouch is approximately 500 mL in volume with
medial and lateral compartments. The pouches communicate with
the pharynx via a pharyngeal orifice located in the lateral and
caudal aspect of the pharynx, rostral and ventral to the dorsal
pharyngeal recess. The maxillary artery, internal and external
carotid arteries, and cranial nerves VII, IX, X, XI, and XII as well as
the mandibular nerve (branch of cranial nerve V), the sympathetic
trunk, and cranial cervical ganglion are either located in or adjacent

Equine guttural pouch tympany
Characteristics and pathophysiology Distention of the guttural
pouch, referred to as “tympany,” is generally reported in foals in the
first few weeks of life [395–400]. Arabian and Paint horse foals are
overrepresented in some regions; however, the condition has
been reported in a variety of breeds, including Warmbloods,
Thoroughbreds, Standardbreds, and Quarter horses [395–400].
Causes of the condition include alteration of the structure of the
pharyngeal opening of the pouch such that it acts as a one-way
valve to capture air and fluid within the pouch, upper airway
inflammation, persistent coughing, or pharyngeal muscle dysfunc-
tion [401]. The condition is usually unilateral but can be bilateral
and is more common in fillies than colts. A hereditary link has been
established in some breeds [401].
On physical examination, there is usually marked tympanic dis-
tention noted in the parotid region that is nonpainful on palpation.
Both sides can be affected even with unilateral disease as one pouch
may encroach medially on the other side. Stridor can range from
mild to severe depending on the degree of airway obstruction.
Severe distention can result in dyspnea and dysphagia, with secondary
aspiration pneumonia and empyema of the guttural pouches.
Diagnosis is performed by radiographic and endoscopic examination
of the pharynx and guttural pouches.
Initial patient management generally involves decompressing the
pouches by placing a catheter into the pharyngeal opening, a proce-
dure performed using endoscopy. Many patients can be managed
medically with an indwelling catheter placed into the affected
pouch; however, surgery may be required in some cases [401].
Traditional surgical techniques include creating a connection
between the affected and non-affected pouches, altering the open-
ing of the guttural pouch into the pharynx on the affected side, or
creating a new opening into the pharynx with the foal under
general anesthesia in dorsal or lateral recumbency. Alternatively, a
minimally invasive approach using transendoscopic electrocautery
or laser can be used. The latter may be performed with the foal
under general anesthesia or sedation [395,396,399]. Overall, success
following surgical interventions is high, although repeat surgeries
are frequently required to achieve complete resolution of the
condition [399,401].
Management of sedation and/or general anesthesia In addition to
standard perioperative concerns related to sedation and general
anesthesia, concerns for foals with guttural pouch tympany relate
to underlying respiratory disease, and potential development of
further compromise of upper airway airflow during the periopera-
tive period. Intraoperative damage to vessels with subsequent
hemorrhage or nerve injury is possible due to the location of major
vessels and nerves in the surgical field [397,401].
A standard history, including determination of current medica-
tions and information regarding the degree of respiratory compro-
mise and prior anesthetic events should be obtained. Preanesthetic
diagnostic work up in foals presenting with tympany should include
a thorough physical examination, CBC, biochemistry profile, and
radiographs of the pharyngeal region and thorax. Endoscopy is
generally performed as part of the diagnostic plan. In most cases,
surgery is not undertaken in the first few weeks of life; however, if
surgery is required in this period, serum IgG should be measured to
ensure adequacy of passive transfer of antibodies. In foals with
clinical signs related to pneumonia (fever, increased respiratory
effort, and/or impaired gas exchange), medical management should
be initiated, and if required, general anesthesia scheduled after res-
olution of pneumonia. Alternatively, surgery could be performed
under sedation if feasible.
Preoperative medications routinely administered include NSAIDs
such as flunixin meglumine in addition to antimicrobials. An intra-
venous catheter should be placed to facilitate sedative and analgesic
administration. Sedation with xylazine and butorphanol has been
reported to provide adequate conditions for surgery with laser in
some foals [395,396]. In patients undergoing general anesthesia,
surgery is ideally scheduled when the foal is not compromised due
to underlying pulmonary disease as previously mentioned. Medical
management, including decompression of the pouches using
indwelling catheters, can be considered while the patient is stabi-
lized. Immediately prior to general anesthesia, decompression of
tympany is recommended if pharyngeal distention is creating
upper airway obstruction. For cases undergoing general anesthesia,
preoxygenation is recommended prior to induction of general anes-
thesia if the foal has any pulmonary parenchymal disease. This can
be achieved using nasal catheters or a facemask connected to the
anesthetic breathing circuit once the foal is sedated and manually
restrained. Sedation can be accomplished with either a benzodiaz-
epine (midazolam or diazepam) or an α2
-adrenergic receptor agonist
based on the patient’s age and hemodynamic status [402]. Injectable
anesthetic induction techniques (ketamine or propofol titrated to
effect) are recommended over inhalational agents alone as the latter
has been associated with a higher morbidity in foals [403].
Maintenance of anesthesia can be achieved through a variety of
techniques including injectable, inhalant, or a combination of
techniques [398,399]. Opioids are typically used to provide intra-
operative analgesia. Monitoring of cardiovascular and respiratory
function throughout anesthesia is ideally performed with ECG,
direct blood pressure monitoring, capnography, and pulse oximetry
measured continuously, with intermittent arterial blood gas analy-
sis. As the surgical site is located near the head, the intra-arterial
catheter can be placed in the lateral metatarsal artery to facilitate
monitoring of blood pressure and sampling for gas analysis.
Monitoring of body temperature and use of warming devices to
prevent hypothermia are also recommended along with standard
fluid therapy protocols. Postoperative analgesia with an opioid
analgesic in combination with an NSAID is standard while corti-
costeroid administration may be required in some cases to reduce
soft tissue swelling [398–401]. Respiratory obstruction is generally
minimal following surgery, however, an orotracheal tube can be
maintained until the foal is standing to minimize the risk of inade-
quate airflow during recovery.
Equine guttural pouch mycosis
Characteristics and pathophysiology Mycotic infection located
within the guttural pouches can affect horses at any age but the
factors that predispose a horse to developing an infection are
unknown. [401]. Aspergillus is the most common fungus associated
with the condition. Lesions are typically located on the dorsal wall
of the guttural pouch and in most cases the disease is unilateral.
Clinical signs arise due to secondary mycotic erosion of tissues,
including nerves and vessels within and adjacent to the pouches.
Epistaxis is the most commonly reported clinical sign, however,
cranial nerve damage resulting in dysphagia, which may present as
coughing or nasal discharge with particulate food material and/or

-- 816 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	801
aspiration pneumonia is also reported either in isolation or with
epistaxis. Other clinical signs resulting from cranial nerve injury
include laryngeal hemiplegia, facial paralysis, and Horner’s syn-
drome. Pain in the head and cranial cervical region may be present.
Radiographs may reveal fluid in the guttural pouches. Definitive
diagnosis is generally determined by endoscopy.
The infection can spontaneously resolve, however, the mortality
associated with guttural pouch mycosis is high in horses with
epistaxis due to hemorrhage. Medical management involves treating
the fungal infection with oral and topical antifungal agents as well
as daily flushing of the pouches. Supportive therapy such as intrave-
nous balanced crystalloids and/or blood may be required in addition
to nutritional support and systemic anti-inflammatories to reduce
neuritis [401]. In horses with epistaxis, surgery may be undertaken
to occlude affected arteries using balloon catheters, microcoils, or
nitinol plugs with the goal of reducing the risk of mortality associ-
ated with hemorrhage [401,404]. Depending on the surgical tech-
nique used and individual circumstances, the procedures may be
performed with the horse standing or under general anesthesia.
Management of sedation and/or anesthesia The major concerns
related to sedation and/or general anesthesia of the horse with
guttural pouch mycosis for arterial occlusion relate to the hemo-
dynamic stability of the patient associated with hypovolemia,
the potential for hemorrhage, and/or neurological abnormalities
including ataxia, blindness, and collapse following arterial occlu-
sion [404–408]. In horses with dysphagia, underlying aspiration
pneumonia may be present and gas exchange impairment may be
aggravated once the horse is recumbent. Ataxia, blindness, weak-
ness, and laryngeal paralysis are all postoperative risks that could
impair recovery from general anesthesia.
In addition to a standard history including current medications
and prior surgeries, the number of episodes and the timing of any
epistaxis events should be obtained. Diagnostic work up of patients
presenting for sedation and general anesthesia should include a
thorough physical examination, CBC, and serum biochemistry.
Further work up such as thoracic radiography should be based
on results of the physical examination. In hypovolemic patients,
fluid therapy with crystalloids and blood products to reestablish
blood volume and ensure normal oxygen-carrying capacity of the
blood should be performed prior to surgery.
During sedation, restraining the head in an elevated position is
important to prevent increases in pressures in affected arteries
prior to ligation [409]. In general, sedation can be achieved by
titrating α2 -adrenergic receptor agonists to effect with an opioid
analgesic such as butorphanol or morphine included in the proto-
col. For standing procedures, additional α2 -adrenergic receptor
agonists can be administered as required by intermittent boluses or
via an infusion [405,410]. In general, infusions will reduce the total
dose of sedative administered and the variation in level of sedation.
An initial intravenous dose of detomidine (5–10 μg/kg) followed
by an intravenous infusion (5–10 μg/kg/h) provides good quality
sedation for standing surgery [411]. Opioid analgesics such as
morphine (0.05 mg/kg) or butorphanol (0.05 mg/kg) can also be
added to the protocol. While acepromazine is often administered
to horses prior to standing surgery in combination with α2 -
adrenergic receptor agonists, it should be avoided in any horse
with hypovolemia due to its vasodilating effect. Local anesthesia
can be delivered topically in the nostril to facilitate endoscopy as
well as infiltrated subcutaneously at the surgery site [405]. Horses
should be monitored throughout the procedure. The veterinary
team should be available to rapidly induce anesthesia in the horse
in the event of complications that could endanger the horse or per-
sonnel. Induction of general anesthesia may be required in an
emergency when hemorrhage cannot be controlled with the horse
standing.
For horses undergoing general anesthesia, standard anesthesia,
and supportive drug protocols are appropriate. ECG, direct arterial
blood pressure (lateral metatarsal site), capnography, and blood gas
analysis with repeated packed cell volume/total protein measure-
ments (if significant hemorrhage occurs intraoperatively) should be
included as part of the monitoring protocol. The anesthetist should
be prepared to adjust fluid therapy, including the need for a blood
transfusion, based on intraoperative blood loss.
Equine laryngeal paralysis
Characteristics and pathophysiology
Several different pathological conditions may affect the equine
laryngeal region; however, the most common condition resulting in
surgical intervention is recurrent laryngeal neuropathy. The disease
is characterized by progressive reduction in abduction and adduction
of the arytenoid cartilages, most commonly on left side, though it
can be bilateral. The severity of the laryngeal dysfunction is generally
scored using the Havermeyer laryngeal 1–4 grading system with 4
being the most severely affected. Although the cause is unknown,
progressive axonopathy, specifically loss of large, myelinated axons
in the recurrent laryngeal nerves, is responsible for neurogenic
atrophy of the musculature of the larynx [412]. Breeds commonly
reported to be affected include Thoroughbreds, Warmbloods, and
various draft breeds. Poor exercise performance and an increase in
exercise-induced stridor are typical clinical signs [413–416]. Horses
with recurrent laryngeal neuropathy generally do not have
concurrent medical conditions but laryngeal paralysis secondary to
guttural pouch mycosis, cervical trauma, neoplasia, or inflammatory
processes have been rarely described [416,417].
Definitive diagnosis of recurrent laryngeal neuropathy or
laryngeal dysfunction associated with other disease processes is
accomplished with endoscopy in the non-sedated horse at rest and/
or during exercise [416]. Both α2
-adrenergic receptor agonists and
acepromazine influence the scoring of laryngeal dysfunction via
endoscopy, therefore, physical restraint is recommended during the
initial assessment of laryngeal function at rest [418]. Ultrasound
has been added to the typical diagnostic work up of horses with
laryngeal paralysis to assess the degree of laryngeal muscle atrophy
and screen for concurrent laryngeal diseases [419].
In cases of recurrent laryngeal neuropathy, surgery may be
undertaken when performance is impaired. Laryngoplasty, ventri-
culectomy, ventriculocordectomy, reinnervation of the caudal
arytenoideus dorsalis muscle, and arytenoidectomy have all been
described with unilateral laryngoplasty and ventriculocordectomy
most commonly performed [420]. Traditionally, these procedures
are conducted during general anesthesia with the horse in lateral
recumbency. More recently, laryngoplasty and ventriculectomy
have been performed with the horse standing under sedation to
avoid the risks of general anesthesia, improve visibility, and
anatomical orientation, and permit more accurate assessment of
arytenoid abduction intraoperatively [413,421]. Overall, the
prognosis for return to performance after laryngoplasty is good,
although nonracing horses have a better prognosis. Postoperative
complications are numerous and include dysphagia leading to
coughing, chronic tracheitis and bronchitis, lung abscess formation,
and pneumonia [416].

Management of sedation and anesthesia
Preanesthetic preparation should include a thorough physical
examination with focus on the respiratory system. Standard preop-
erative diagnostic tests, such as a CBC or blood gas analysis with
packed cell volume, total protein, and blood urea nitrogen or creati-
nine are appropriate unless co-existing disease is detected on physi-
cal examination. Preoperative fasting time of 8 to 12 h with water
freely available is typically recommended. Non-steroidal anti-
inflammatories are routinely administered pre- and postoperatively.
As noted, there are several advantages to performing laryngeal
surgery with the horse standing, including the reduced risk of
neuropathy and myopathy associated with recumbency and gen-
eral anesthesia. Sedation protocols that include acepromazine
(0.03 mg/kg IV) followed by an α2 -adrenergic receptor agonist
administered as an infusion or intermittent boluses are typically
employed. Opioid analgesics, such as butorphanol (0.05 mg/kg) or
morphine (0.05 mg/kg), are added to improve the quality of seda-
tion and provide intraoperative analgesia. Local anesthesia of the
operative field can be achieved with either local infiltration of
the site or by performing a unilateral cervical plexus (C2 and C3)
block [413,422]. Placing ear plugs and a hood with a blinker on the
surgery side is also recommended [413].
In cases in which general anesthesia is required, routine anesthetic
protocols including standard monitoring and fluid therapy are suit-
able. Direct arterial pressure should be measured from the lateral
metatarsal artery and the anesthetist should ensure they have ready
access to an intravenous access port if using a jugular vein for fluid
and drug administration. Intubation can occasionally be difficult in
horses with unilateral laryngeal paralysis; therefore, the anesthetist
should be prepared to use a smaller endotracheal tube to minimize
trauma of the laryngeal structures during intubation in patients
with severe clinical signs. The surgical team may also request the use
of a small orotracheal tube if ventriculectomy is being performed to
assist with access to the surgical site. Alternatively, intermittent
extubation may be considered intraoperatively [416].
Anesthesia and lower airway disease
Patients may require sedation and/or general anesthesia for further
diagnostic work up of their airway disease or for unrelated condi-
tions. General considerations for patients undergoing bronchos-
copy are discussed above. In general, patients with lower airway
disease typically have an increase in lower airway resistance, which
may be exacerbated by anesthesia because of a decrease in muco-
ciliary clearance and accumulation of airway secretions. Feline and
equine asthma are discussed below in more detail; however, the
principles of anesthetic management also apply to canine patients
with chronic bronchitis.
Feline asthma
Characteristics and pathophysiology
Feline asthma is an inflammatory lower airway disease currently
estimated to affect 1–5% of cats [423]. Major characteristics of
asthma 	in 	cats 	include 	airway 	inflammation, 	airway
hyperresponsiveness, and airflow limitation. The etiology of the
disease is believed to be due to a Type I hypersensitivity to inhaled
allergens with genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors
involved in the pathophysiology [424,425]. Cats generally present
for clinical signs, such as coughing, wheezing, or respiratory distress
at 4–5 years of age; however, more subtle signs may be evident in
younger cats [423]. Siamese cats may be overrepresented, but the
disease has been reported in all breeds [426,427]. Fluctuations in
clinical signs are relatively common and may correlate with exposure
to allergens. As with presenting complaints, physical examination
findings may vary considerably, with some cats being asymptomatic
and others exhibiting tachypnea, wheezing, increased expiratory
effort, and open-mouth breathing [428,429]. A cough can generally
be elicited with gentle tracheal palpation. A CBC may show elevated
total leukocyte and eosinophil counts and eosinophilic inflammation
is present in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid [428,429]. Radiographic
findings can also be highly variable with some cats having normal
radiographic findings while others have bronchial, interstitial,
bronchointerstitial, or alveolar patterns. Lobar collapse may be
present in some cats which is attributed to airway obstruction with
respiratory secretions [428]. Further diagnostic testing including
thoracic ultrasound, thoracic computed tomography, and pulmo-
nary function testing may help to characterize the degree of severity
of the disease and airflow obstruction, although the availability of
the latter is limited for clinical patients. Cats with chronic bronchitis,
pulmonary parasitic disease, or heartworm-associated respiratory
disease may be confounded with asthmatic cats, and the definitive
diagnosis of asthma may not be known when the patient requires
anesthesia, particularly when scheduled for bronchoscopy and
bronchoalveolar lavage [423,428,429]. Therapy of cats with mild-
moderate asthma includes environmental management, optimiza-
tion of body weight, glucocorticoids, and bronchodilators as
required. When cats present in respiratory distress, oxygen therapy,
bronchodilators, glucocorticoids, and in some cases, sedation may
be required [423].
As noted above, asthma is a relatively common airway disease in
cats therefore anesthesia may be required for routine procedures
that do not involve the airways. In addition, general anesthesia may
also be required to permit procedures such as bronchoscopy and/or
bronchoalveolar lavage to obtain a definitive diagnosis of asthma
and rule out other diseases involving the airways. In humans,
the risk of perioperative morbidity and mortality is higher in
patients with asthma, particularly when their condition is unstable;
however, this information is currently unknown for cats [430,431].
Bronchospasm is reported to occur in about 9% of human patients
with asthma during the perioperative period [432]. Although not
specific to asthma, in cats undergoing bronchoscopy and bron-
choalveolar lavage while receiving jet ventilation (180 breaths/min
delivered by a specialized jet ventilator) a 38% complication rate
was reported, with 24% of the complications considered mild [173].
Three percent of cats in the latter investigation were reported to
develop a pneumothorax during the procedure [173]. A similar
incidence of pneumothorax development was described in a more
recent retrospective study (2.5%) [172].
Management of anesthesia
General concerns for patients with asthma include the potential
development of bronchospasm, increased R aw leading to impaired
expiration/gas trapping within the lungs, and/or hypoxemia during
or after anesthesia [430,431]. Overall, perianesthetic goals should
include minimizing airway secretions, avoidance of airway
manipulation at light planes of anesthesia, and using strategies that
minimize the risk of laryngospasm and hypoxemia.
Prior to anesthesia, the patient should have a thorough history
with documentation of current medications, followed by a diagnostic
work up including a physical examination with pulmonary and
cardiac auscultation, CBC, serum biochemistry profile, and thoracic
radiographs. The latter will help rule out other cardiopulmonary
diseases and provide further information regarding the severity of

-- 818 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	803
lung involvement. As noted, clinical signs can fluctuate, and elective
procedures should be performed when the patient is not exhibiting
signs of significant respiratory dysfunction.
Preanesthetic 	administration 	of 	terbutaline 	systemically
(0.01 mg/kg IM or SC) may be considered prior to performing
bronchoscopy and/or bronchoalveolar lavage and in cats with
asthma undergoing anesthesia for non-airway procedures [423].
Although this treatment is thought to reduce the incidence of bron-
chospasm in cats undergoing bronchoalveolar lavage, to date, no
prospective study has evaluated its efficacy [172,173,423]. Similarly,
to date, there are no studies evaluating the outcome of different
anesthetic protocols in cats with naturally occurring asthma.
General recommendations include premedicating cats with opioids
such as butorphanol or methadone, and an anticholinergic. Due to
their potential association with histamine release, morphine and
meperidine are not recommended opioid analgesics in patients
with reactive airways. Although anticholinergics may increase the
viscosity of airway secretions, they are effective bronchodilators
and may reduce the risk of laryngospasm secondary to oropharyn-
geal secretions. Additional sedation can be achieved if required by
adding acepromazine, midazolam, or alfaxalone. Experimentally,
dexmedetomidine reduced histamine-induced bronchoconstric-
tion in healthy dogs and reduced indicators of airway inflammation
in a murine model of asthma [433,434]. Although α2
-adrenergic
receptor agonists may be suitable sedatives, their use in combination
with anticholinergics, without concurrent peripheral α2
-adrenergic
receptor antagonist administration is not recommended because of
a severe hypertensive response [435]. When used in combination
with opioid analgesics, α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists can reduce
arterial hemoglobin oxygen saturation in healthy animals breathing
room air and oxygen supplementation should be available [17,436].
Preoxygenation prior to anesthetic induction, if tolerated, will
minimize the risk of hypoxemia during anesthetic induction.
Ideally, monitoring of hemoglobin oxygen saturation (SpO 2 on a
peripheral site such as the paw) is initiated prior to induction of
anesthesia, along with ECG assessment of cardiac rhythm and
rate. Induction of anesthesia with an injectable anesthetic will
provide a smooth transition to general anesthesia and propofol is
often used in asthmatic patients as it produces airway smooth
muscle relaxation and reduces R aw [432]. Ketamine has also been
shown to result in relaxation of airway musculature and may be
preferred in some hemodynamically unstable patients. Ketamine
is typically combined with a benzodiazepine to improve muscu-
loskeletal relaxation and facilitate intubation [437]. The effects of
alfaxalone on airway smooth muscle have not been reported,
however, based on its clinical effects, it is anticipated to have
similar effects as propofol and ketamine. When endotracheal
intubation is performed, lidocaine should be applied topically to
the larynx 45–60 s before intubation is attempted to avoid
laryngospasm and endotracheal tube placement should not be
attempted if the patient is at a light plane of anesthesia [438]. In
cats with asthma, an endotracheal tube with the largest internal
diameter possible should be placed to minimize the impact of the
tube on overall R aw (Fig. 38.16). Use of a feline supraglottic airway
device may also be a suitable means to protect the airway in select
patients [172]. Isoflurane and sevoflurane both consistently pro-
duce bronchodilation and reduce R aw ; however, the latter may
offer slightly greater effect and it is therefore the preferred
inhalant agent in humans with asthma [432]. Desflurane is not
recommended as it may cause airway irritation and increase R aw
at higher concentrations (2 MAC) [432].
Anesthesia can be maintained under spontaneous ventilation.
Depending on the disease severity and the associated increase in
R aw
, work of breathing, or deficits in arterial oxygenation, mechani-
cal ventilatory support may be required. In such cases, the goal
should be to provide a long expiratory phase to prevent gas trapping
associated with lower airway obstruction. The latter can be accom-
plished by using a short inspiratory time (e.g., < 1.5 s) and a small
I:E ratio (e.g., ≥ 1:3). Extubation is recommended when patients
are still at a deep plane of anesthesia unless it is specifically con-
traindicated due to other concurrent conditions. If patients are
receiving glucocorticoids, NSAIDs are contraindicated, and alter-
native strategies must be employed to ensure adequate analgesia
postoperatively.
Signs of bronchospasm, which can occur at any time during the
perianesthetic period, include an increase in respiratory effort dur-
ing spontaneous ventilation. An increased R aw and reduced dynamic
CRS (V T
/[Ppeak – PEEP]) is indicated by an increase in P peak if the cat
is receiving VCV. If an advanced anesthesia ventilator is available,
adding an inspiratory pause during VCV may facilitate identifica-
tion of increased R aw by analyzing the gradient between Ppeak and
P plat (Fig. 38.16). Otherwise, it may be possible to qualitatively
appreciate increased R aw and decreased dynamic CRS during manual
compression of the reservoir bag, as higher P peak (recorded by the
manometer of the breathing circuit) is needed to achieve adequate
chest excursion. Impaired gas exchange will be evident as cyanosis,
a decrease in SpO 2 and PaO 2
, and an increase in PET
CO2 or
PaCO2 [176,432]. A classic obstructive expiratory pattern on the
capnograph may be observed: an obtuse α angle that can be
described as a “shark fin.” The plane of anesthesia should be assessed
and deepened if the patient’s hemodynamic status permits, and aero-
solized albuterol administered via the endotracheal tube. Additional
treatments include systemic terbutaline, corticosteroids, anticholin-
ergics, or a low dose of epinephrine (0.005–0.01 mg/kg, SC or IV).
Inspired gases should be supplemented with oxygen if the patient is
breathing room air. The decision to induce general anesthesia to
reestablish an airway in a conscious (i.e., post-extubation) patient
will be determined by the severity of gas exchange impairment and
the patient’s work of breathing.
Equine asthma (non-infectious lower airway disease)
Characteristics and pathophysiology
Lower airway disease in the equine is common, with etiologic factors,
including environmental and infectious factors [439]. Recently, the
term “equine asthma” has been proposed to include horses with a
spectrum of clinical signs ranging from mild inflammatory airway
disease to those exhibiting signs of recurrent airway obstruc-
tion [440]. Horses with asthma may have a variety of clinical signs,
including a cough, reduced performance, increased work of breath-
ing and, when severe, impaired gas exchange. Physical examination
findings may be very mild or may reveal nostril flaring while the ani-
mal is at rest, an increase in abdominal expiratory effort, nasal dis-
charge, expiratory wheezes, and inspiratory crackles. Pulmonary
function tests available in some referral centers can detect an increase
in R aw
, increased maximal change in pleural pressure (∆Ppl
), and a
reduced dynamic CRS [439]. The severity of the disease is often
episodic with clinical signs precipitated by exposure to specific
antigens such as moldy hay or pasture allergens [441]. Bronchoalveolar
lavage sampling typically reveals neutrophilic inflammation.
Treatment includes environmental modification to reduce allergen
exposure, corticosteroids, and bronchodilators. Therapeutics may be
administered systemically or via inhalation [439].

Management of anesthesia
Patients with severe airway disease may have impaired gas exchange
during episodes of airway inflammation and bronchospasm. An
increased P(A-a)O2 difference leading to lower-than-expected PaO2
levels due to atelectasis is not uncommon in normal horses during
general anesthesia; however, this may be exacerbated in horses with
pre-existing V̇A
/Q̇ mismatching associated with severe asthma. In
addition, increased R aw in cases of severe asthma contributes to an
increase in work of breathing which in turn may contribute to
reduced ventilation during general anesthesia in spontaneously
breathing horses.
Preanesthetic history should include the horse’s degree of respira-
tory compromise during rest and exercise as well as medications
being administered. If the patient is exhibiting clinical signs consist-
ent with impaired gas exchange, arterial blood gas analysis prior to
anesthesia in addition to routine preoperative physical examination
and diagnostics is recommended. Pulmonary function testing if
available can provide a method to trend an individual horse’s response
to therapy and characterize the severity of their disease. Horses with
acute exacerbations of clinical signs should not undergo elective proce-
dures until stabilized and in horses with continued gas exchange
impairment (hypercapnia and hypoxemia), procedures should be
performed with the horse standing using sedation and local/regional
anesthesia rather than general anesthesia whenever possible. As
dorsal recumbency is associated with the greatest risk of hypox-
emia [2,24], if general anesthesia is required, lateral recumbency is
the preferred position if feasible for the intended procedure.
Prior to anesthesia, patients should be maintained on medica-
tions and exposure to known allergens such as dusty hay or straw
eliminated to minimize the risk of relapse in their condition.
Fortunately, sedatives and general anesthetics routinely used in
horses result in relaxation of airway smooth muscle. Xylazine was
shown to reduce R aw and increase dynamic C RS in ponies exhibiting
lower airway obstruction following a challenge with dusty
hay [442]. Ketamine, isoflurane, and sevoflurane have also been
shown to produce bronchodilation as discussed above. Monitoring
of direct arterial blood pressure, arterial blood gas, ECG,
capnography, and respiratory mechanics is ideal for prolonged
procedures performed under general anesthesia. Ventilatory
support with low rates (6–7 breaths per min) and long expiratory
times (I:E ratio of 1:3 or 1:4) should be used to avoid gas trapping
in the lungs leading to dynamic hyperinflation/intrinsic PEEP
during expiration. Modern piston-driven large animal anesthesia
ventilators allow an inspiratory pause to be set in VCV mode
(Tafonius, Hallowell EMC). In horses with severe bronchospasm
secondary to asthma, the use of an inspiratory pause could
theoretically allow recognition of an increase in R aw by an increase
in the gradient between P peak and P plat . With either spontaneous or
positive-pressure 	ventilation, 	setting 	a 	target 	PaCO 2 	of
50–60 mmHg (permissive hypercapnia) can be adopted. In humans
with severe obstructive airway disease, the development of gas
trapping can occur due to inadequate/slow emptying of the lungs
during expiration. Increased P peak during VCV, decreased V T and
hypercapnia during PCV, and increased PEEP during the
expiratory phase are all indicators of increased R aw and gas trapping
caused by severe small airway disease in humans [443].
Strategies used to address hypoxemia during anesthesia
include employing lung recruitment maneuvers as discussed
above, supporting hemodynamics, and administering aero-
solized albuterol (salbutamol) via a metered dose inhaler into
the endotracheal tube [130,134,444,445]. Adverse side effects of
the latter treatment include sweating, ventricular tachycardia, and
hypotension; therefore, hemodynamics should be monitored
during treatment [444,446].
Anesthesia and pleural space disease
Pleural space disease is relatively common in veterinary species either
in isolation or in combination with other conditions, including
pulmonary parenchymal disease (contusions, neoplasia, pneumonia,
and bullae), mediastinal masses, esophageal disease (perforation),
infectious diseases such as feline infectious peritonitis, diaphragmatic
hernia, coagulopathies, and/or cardiovascular disease. The presence
of air or fluid in the thoracic cavity, or disruption of the normal
chest wall or diaphragm anatomy (penetrating chest wound or a
diaphragmatic hernia), can dramatically influence respiratory
function. Patients may present on an urgent basis and require
immediate intervention to address the underlying condition.
Pneumothorax and/or pleural effusion
In normal patients, the pleural space is under negative pressure
relative to the atmosphere, which maintains lung volume at end
expiration, facilitates venous return (Fig. 38.28A), and influences
myocardial performance. Air can enter the chest through the
thoracic wall, esophagus, or respiratory system creating a pneu-
mothorax. Traumatic pneumothorax or pneumothorax resulting
from an esophageal foreign body is generally detected during
physical examination and diagnosed with ultrasound and radio-
graphic imaging in patients presenting with a history of trauma or
inappropriate consumption of foreign objects. Spontaneous pneu-
mothorax can occur in association with inflammatory, infectious,
or neoplastic disease of the lung. In the dog, primary spontaneous
pneumothorax has also been reported with ruptured pulmonary
bullae or blebs leading to an air leak between the lung and pleural
space [191,447,448]. In large animals, spontaneous pneumothorax
has been reported in patients with pleuropneumonia or
bronchopneumonia, presumably secondary to air leaks from the
lung parenchyma [449,450]. Irrespective of the cause of the
pneumothorax, clinical signs are dependent on the volume of air
within the thoracic space, with some patients exhibiting only
minor changes in respiratory rate and effort, while others present
in respiratory distress. Additional clinical signs consistent with
pneumothorax include cyanosis, lack of lung sounds on
auscultation of the dorsal lung fields, fever, tachycardia,
depression, 	inappetence, 	exercise 	intolerance, 	and 	cough
[447,449,450]. Diagnosis of pneumothorax is generally based on
radiographic and ultrasonographic findings [191,449–451].
A small volume of fluid (0.1–0.3 mL/kg) resides in the intra-
pleural space; however, abnormal accumulation of fluid can result
from many different conditions with the categorization of the fluid
including transudates, modified transudates (e.g., chylous effusions),
or exudates (e.g., hemorrhagic effusions). Congestive heart failure,
neoplasia, and pleuropneumonia are a few of the more common
causes of pleural effusion in veterinary species [451,452]. Cytologic
evaluation with bacterial culture of pleural fluid acquired via
thoracocentesis is required to confirm the nature of the effusion.
Major concerns for patients that require anesthesia with air or
fluid accumulation in the chest include the nature of the underlying
disease, the presence of concurrent disease, and the impact of the
air or fluid within the pleural space on cardiopulmonary function.
In many instances, when anesthesia is required, an intrathoracic
intervention is planned; however, in some cases, such as a stable or

-- 820 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	805
resolving pneumothorax post-trauma, non- thoracic injuries may
require general anesthesia to permit intervention.
Management of anesthesia
The patient’s respiratory function, hemodynamic status, level of
hydration, and cardiac performance should all be critically evalu-
ated and appropriately managed prior to anesthesia. In many
instances, patients with pleural space disease will have undergone
an extensive diagnostic work up prior to anesthesia. Animals with a
history of trauma should have an ECG performed prior to induction
of anesthesia, if possible, to investigate potential arrhythmias [453].
Measurement of serum cardiac troponin I levels may also provide
information regarding the probability of subsequent arrhythmias in
dogs with blunt chest trauma [453].
In addition to oxygen supplementation and appropriate analgesic
therapy, preoperative preparation should include removal of pleural
fluid and/or air prior to induction of anesthesia. The specific anes-
thetic protocol used can be tailored to the individual patient. If pul-
monary contusions are present, it is generally preferrable for the
patient to maintain spontaneous ventilation during anesthesia, to
avoid further injury to the lung. A means to evacuate pleural fluid
or air is ideally established prior to and maintained during anesthe-
sia, with easy access to the system by the anesthesia team members
when the patient is not undergoing an intrathoracic procedure.
Development of pneumothorax during routine anesthesia in ani-
mals and humans is a rare event, but it may occur if emphysematous
bullae or smaller blebs in the pulmonary parenchyma are ruptured
by positive-pressure ventilation [454]. In animals with traumatic
pneumothorax and/or pulmonary contusions, anesthesia for cor-
rection of other problems (e.g., fractures) should be postponed
until there is an improvement in the clinical signs related to the
respiratory system. To minimize further complications in animals
with pre-existing pneumothorax, anesthesia should be maintained
under spontaneous ventilation and animals should receive an
inspired oxygen concentration close to 100%. When mechanical
ventilation is required, adjusting the ventilator to deliver a relatively
low V T (≤ 8 mL/kg) or adjusting the volume delivered by the
ventilator to result in a relatively low Ppeak (≤ 8 cmH2
O in small
animals) is advisable to minimize the risk of positive-pressure
ventilation causing pneumothorax secondary to rupture of a
previously injured area of the lung. Aggravation of a previously
existing pneumothorax or the development of pneumothorax
during anesthesia with VCV is noticed by progressive increases in
Ppeak as lung compliance rapidly worsens. A vicious cycle known as
“tension pneumothorax” may quickly develop. Specifically, lung
volume progressively decreases as positive-pressure ventilation
causes more gas to become entrapped into the pleural cavity, and
the animal will quickly become hypoxemic/cyanotic. If the
anesthesiologist faces this scenario, mechanical ventilation should
be interrupted, and thoracocentesis and/or rapid placement of a
chest tube should be completed to prevent a cardiac arrest.
Prior to anesthetic recovery, a system to provide oxygen
supplementation and thoracic drainage should be in place. In
general, patients with pleural space disease should be monitored
intensively for at least 24 h postoperatively.
Diaphragmatic hernia
In veterinary patients, defects or rents in the diaphragm are
commonly acquired secondary to trauma, such as motor vehicle
collisions, kicks, thoracic wounds, or falls [455–457]. Although less
common, congenital defects in the diagram, such as congenital
peritoneopericardial hernia, hiatal hernia, diaphragmatic diverticu-
lum, and retrosternal diaphragmatic hernia, are also encountered
[455,458,459]. Dyspnea and an abdominal breathing pattern second-
ary to severe lung collapse are common clinical signs in small animals
presenting with acute traumatic rupture of the diaphragm. The sever-
ity of clinical signs is generally related to the degree of lung compres-
sion caused by the migration of the abdominal viscera into the
thoracic cavity. Some animals present with a chronic diaphragmatic
hernia and a history of anorexia, vomiting, or exercise intoler-
ance [456,457]. In some instances, the defect is discovered inciden-
tally on imaging studies or during abdominal exploration, or when
clinical signs develop after a known traumatic event (sometimes
years later). Clinical signs only develop when abdominal organs are
displaced into the chest cavity resulting in impaired organ function,
respiratory compromise, and/or pain. Diaphragmatic defects in large
animals are usually identified when animals present for colic or
abdominal pain due to intestinal incarceration [455,460].
Thoracic imaging generally establishes a diagnosis of a diaphrag-
matic defect in dogs and cats. In large animals, diagnosis is chal-
lenging, and it is often determined intraoperatively [455,460,461].
Results of thoracic auscultation, thoracic radiography, thoracic
ultrasonography, and rectal examination in large animals may result
in a diagnosis or suggest diaphragmatic incarceration of abdominal
viscera in the thoracic cavity [455].
Surgical correction is generally performed through a standard mid-
line laparotomy with removal of incarcerated viscera from the thorax
back into the abdomen followed by closure of the diaphragmatic tear.
Successful thoracoscopic repair of a diaphragmatic rent, however, has
been reported in the equine [455]. In general, depending on concur-
rent injuries, survival rates for dogs and cats that undergo surgery for
correction of traumatic diaphragmatic hernias are good, with reported
survival to discharge of approximately 80–90% [456,457,462]. In the
equine, overall prognosis for horses presenting with diaphragmatic
defects is poor. In horses with operable lesions, the prognosis may be
fair (approximately 70%) for survival [460,461].
Major anesthetic concerns for patients with diaphragmatic hernia
include impaired respiratory function, in particular the ability to
oxygenate throughout the perianesthetic period, re-expansion
pulmonary edema, hemodynamic depression as a result of the pres-
ence of abdominal viscera within the thorax, induction of arrhyth-
mias associated with surgical manipulations within the thoracic
cavity, hemorrhage, viscera rupture, prolonged surgical time, and
presence of pneumothorax and pleural effusion following closure of
the defect [455,463].
Management of anesthesia
Hemodynamically unstable patients should be stabilized prior to
anesthesia with appropriate fluid therapy and sympathomimetics if
necessary. Patients with impaired oxygenation or an increased
respiratory effort should receive oxygen supplementation prior to
and during the induction of anesthesia. In small animal patients,
preoxygenation with a facemask may be effective unless there is
severe hypoxemia secondary to a large increase in intrapulmonary
shunting of blood [39,40]. Consideration should be given to
maintaining the patient in a head-up position throughout induction,
surgical preparation, and the surgical approach to minimize
compression atelectasis. In large animals, intranasal or intratracheal
insufflation with oxygen can be used prior to induction of anesthesia
[47,50,464]. Intensive monitoring of the patient’s hemodynamic
status is recommended throughout anesthesia, ideally with inva-
sive blood pressure techniques and an ECG. Patients can be
