hemodynamically unstable during anesthesia and the use of bal-
anced anesthetic techniques with local anesthesia and inotropic/
vasopressor 	support 	is 	highly 	recommended 	to 	optimize
cardiovascular and respiratory status. Mechanical ventilation with
100% oxygen should be instituted immediately after orotracheal
intubation. If a VCV mode is chosen in small animals with abdominal
viscera herniated into the thoracic cavity, adjusting the ventilator to
deliver low V T
s (≤ 8 mL/kg) is initially recommended to minimize
the risk of excessive distension of pulmonary parenchyma that
remains functional/not collapsed. If a standard veterinary anesthesia
ventilator that does not allow precise measurement of V T is utilized,
it is advisable to adjust the volume delivered by the ventilator
according to the Ppeak monitored by the manometer measuring
pressure within the breathing circuit. Although there are no
published studies evaluating the clinical outcome of different
ventilation strategies in animals with diaphragmatic hernia, initially
limiting the Ppeak to 7–8 cmH2
O in cats or 10 cmH2
O in dogs should
be considered to reduce the risk of alveolar overdistention. If a
decelerating flow, pressure-targeted ventilation (PCV) mode is
adopted as a protective lung strategy, maximum airway pressures
can be adjusted as above.
In animals with acute lung collapse/atelectasis caused by the
displacement of abdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity, moderate
(hemoglobin saturation < 90%) to severe hypoxemia (hemoglobin
saturation < 75%) may persist despite the use of high FI
O2 (> 0.9) and
mechanical ventilation. Besides poor arterial oxygenation, the
presence of large areas of atelectasis (stiff lung) will also result in low
CRS
. Following removal of the abdominal organs from the thoracic
cavity (which may involve the stomach, liver, spleen, and segments of
the small intestine) the lungs should be gradually expanded by slowly
increasing maximum inspiratory pressure (directly or by small step-
wise increases in V T
; Fig. 38.26D) combined with progressively
increasing PEEP levels if possible. If an advanced anesthesia ventilator
is available for use in small animals, a cycling maneuver as described
in Figs. 38.26C and 38.27 can be performed [138,139]. A commercially
available piston-driven large animal ventilator (Tafonius, Hallowell
EMC) is also capable of performing ARMs through progressive
increases and decreases in PEEP in large animals [117]. Clinical
observations have indicated that cats with diaphragmatic hernia are
more sensitive to the cardiovascular depression-associated cycling
maneuvers; therefore, smaller stepwise increases in PEEP and
maximum inspiratory pressures (Pmax
) are preferred (e.g., 3 cm H2
O
instead of 5 cmH2
O) and the maximum increase in PEEP and Pmax in
this species can be initially limited to 10–12 cmH2
O and
20–25 cmH2
O, respectively. As explained above, slow progressive
increases in airway pressure, which can be achieved by cycling
maneuvers as previously described, are advisable to reopen collapsed
alveoli as opposed to sudden exposure of lung parenchyma to high
airway pressures (e.g., temporary administration of a CPAP of
30–40 cmH2
O; Fig. 38.26B), which could potentially lead to alveolar
rupture, lung inflammation/edema, and hemorrhage in diseased
lungs [101,125]. ARMs have been shown to improve pulmonary
oxygen gas exchange and respiratory mechanics (increased CRS
) in
healthy dogs and horses but their impact on outcomes has not been
evaluated in animals with a diaphragmatic hernia [38,117,130,134,13
6,138,139,465]. If the anesthesia ventilator in use does not incorporate
advanced methods of ventilation used in ARMs, the anesthesiologist
can manually perform a recruitment maneuver by closing the pop-
off (APL) valve and progressively increasing the airway pressures by
manually squeezing the rebreathing bag (Fig. 38.26A). This procedure
is ideally performed under the guidance of the surgeon observing the
expansion of collapsed lung areas. Contraindications of ARMs
include hemodynamic instability (e.g., hypotension), cor pulmonale
(right-sided heart failure), lung emphysema, and bronchopleural fis-
tula. If hypotension is present, animals should be properly stabilized
with fluids and sympathomimetics, if necessary, before an ARM is
initiated [466].
Following closure of the diaphragmatic rent, air should be
removed from the thorax, a procedure generally performed using a
catheter placed through the diaphragm. As oxygen supplementa-
tion and pleural fluid or air evacuation from the thorax may also be
required following recovery from anesthesia, appropriate systems
should be pre-placed prior to anesthetic recovery in small animals
and if feasible in large animals.
Anesthesia and pulmonary parenchymal disease
While general considerations related to bronchoscopy and thoracic
exploration are discussed above, further considerations related to
anesthetic management of patients with intrapulmonary masses,
lung lobe torsions, and pneumonia are provided below.
Intrapulmonary masses
Removal of primary lung tumors or metastatic lesions may be per-
formed for diagnostic purposes and to prolong and/or improve a
patient’s quality of life. Patients with intrapulmonary masses may
also require anesthesia for non-thoracic procedures. In either case,
when the type of lung cancer is known, it is recommended that
further information regarding the nature of the cancer is obtained
from current veterinary oncology texts and/or consultation with
veterinary oncologists.
Management of anesthesia
Anesthetic considerations for human patients with lung cancer
are summarized as the “4 Ms” which include (1) Mass effects;
(2) Metabolic effects; (3) Metastases; and (4) Medications [235],
which may provide a useful mnemonic to consider when presented
with veterinary patients with suspected lung cancer. In essence, a
thorough physical examination and diagnostic work up of any
patient with intrapulmonary disease scheduled for anesthesia
should be performed to detect concurrent disease including acid-
base/electrolyte abnormalities, anemia, and effects associated with
the size and location of the lung mass as well as any metastases.
In consultation with the surgical team, the surgical approach,
potential surgical complications, and perioperative analgesic plan
can be discussed and developed. Current medications should be
reviewed to determine if there are contraindications to any analge-
sics routinely used such as NSAIDs. Specific considerations related
to the intrathoracic procedure are discussed above.
Canine lung lobe torsion
Characteristics and pathophysiology
Torsion of a lung lobe along its long axis is a rare but life-threatening
disease reported in both dogs and cats [467–470]. Underlying
conditions that may predispose a patient to the condition include
pleural effusion, pneumonia, and pneumothorax; however, it may
also occur spontaneously in healthy animals. Most commonly,
middle-aged, large- breed, and deep-chested dogs such as Afghan
hounds are affected [467,471]. Pugs also appear to be predisposed
to the condition and juvenile dogs less than one year have been
reported with lung lobe torsions [472,473]. Presenting clinical signs
are variable and include lethargy, anorexia, coughing, hemoptysis,
dyspnea, vomiting, and exercise intolerance [467,469,473,474].

-- 822 of 1450 --

Chapter 38: Oxygen Therapy, Mechanical Ventilation, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Respiratory Disease 	807
Pyrexia, tachypnea, or dyspnea with increased respiratory effort
may be present on physical examination and auscultation may
reveal muffled heart sounds, harsh lung sounds, crackles and
wheezes, and decreased lung sounds over a portion of the lung
field [467,470,472–474]. Complete blood cell count, biochemistry
profile, and cytology of pleural fluid may be consistent with an
ongoing inflammatory process and/or reveal underlying concur-
rent disease. Diagnostic imaging routinely performed includes
radiography, ultrasonography, and computed tomography which
may identify the affected lobe and presence of pleural effusion.
Bronchoscopy may reveal an occluded bronchus. Diagnosis may be
challenging with differential conditions including pneumonia, neo-
plasia, and pulmonary thromboembolism, and definitive diagnosis
may occur during exploration of the thorax [475]. Surgical removal
of the affected lung lobe via an intercostal thoracotomy following
medical stabilization of the patient is required [475]. Survival for
dogs undergoing lung lobectomy appears to have risen with dis-
charge rates of up to 92% recently reported [467,474]. Cats may also
have a high rate of survival to discharge rate although fewer reports
are available [470].
Management of anesthesia
Oxygen supplementation should be provided to any patient with
signs of impaired oxygenation and thoracocentesis should be
performed to remove excess pleural fluid prior to anesthesia.
Hematology, serum chemistry, and blood gas analysis results should
be used to guide fluid and electrolyte therapy during patient stabili-
zation prior to and during anesthesia. If a large amount of pleural
fluid is present, it may be necessary to place a chest tube to achieve
adequate thoracic drainage.
Oxygen supplementation should be continued into the preanes-
thetic period. The general principles for intrathoracic procedures
discussed above should be followed with adjustments made based
on the individual patient. Ventilatory support with 100% oxygen
may be required immediately following induction of anesthesia,
due to the presence of pleural effusion. As the total lung volume
will be reduced due to loss of the affected lung lobe, V T
s that are
traditionally employed in small animal anesthesia (12–15 mL/kg
based on ideal body weight) may result in variables degrees of
hyperdistention of alveoli located in the remaining functional
lung areas. Therefore, if a VCV mode with an inspiratory pause is
adopted during anesthesia, it is suggested that the V T should be
adjusted to a normal driving pressure (gradient between P plat and
PEEP). Although there are no published studies specifically
evaluating the normal driving pressure during mechanical
ventilation in small animals, clinical experience has shown that
most healthy non-obese dogs receiving VCV with a target V T of
12–15 mL/kg require a driving pressure of approximately
7–10 cmH 2 O; healthy cats require a lower driving pressure
(5–7 cmH 2 O). Adjusting the V T according to a target driving
pressure is suggested as a means of avoiding overdistention of
aerated lung parenchyma in patients that have lost functional lung
areas due to lung lobe torsion of a lung tumor. If standard
veterinary equipment that does not allow accurate V T adjustment
is used, the volume delivered by the ventilator can be adjusted to
deliver a target P peak (limited to 7–8 cmH 2 O in cats and to 10
cmH 2 O in dogs) to minimize the risk of alveolar overdistension.
Reported intraoperative complications include cardiopulmonary
arrest, hypotension, and hemorrhage [472,474]. A thoracostomy
tube should be placed prior to recovery to facilitate removal of
pleural effusion in the postoperative period.
Pneumonia
In humans, postoperative respiratory dysfunction is extremely
common, particularly following intrathoracic surgery [476–478].
In this population, pre-existing pulmonary disease, duration of
anesthesia, advanced patient age, obesity, intrathoracic procedures,
and presence of a nasogastric tube postoperatively have been iden-
tified as significant risk factors for postoperative respiratory com-
plications [476,479]. A reduction in function of normal respiratory
defenses such as the mucociliary clearance mechanism, presence
of atelectasis, and stress- and drug-induced immunosuppression
likely all contribute to the development of impaired respiratory
function following general anesthesia and surgery [478,480]. Stress
and general anesthesia have been shown to cause immunomodula-
tion, most commonly immunosuppression, in animal models of
infectious disease [481].
Although there are no large clinical trials reporting outcomes in
veterinary patients with pre-existing pneumonia undergoing
anesthesia to date, general anesthesia, and elective surgery are not
recommended in these patients to minimize the risk of perioperative
respiratory dysfunction and potential exacerbation of disease
severity. Neonatal or pediatric equine and ruminant patients with
pneumonia may present for non-elective exploratory laparotomy,
patent urachal resection, or orthopedic procedures. Additional
comorbidities in these patients may include persistence of fetal
circulation and failure of passive transfer of colostral antibodies.
Small animals with upper airway and/or gastrointestinal disease
with pneumonia secondary to aspiration of foreign material
may 	require 	anesthesia 	for 	endoscopy 	or 	abdominal
procedures [271,354,482]. Pulmonary aspiration is defined as the
inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents into the larynx and
lower respiratory tract [483]. The latter occurs due to suppression
or dysfunction of cough and laryngeal reflexes (laryngospasm).
Aspiration pneumonia associated with frequent regurgitation is a
common finding in dogs and cats with megaesophagus. Although
this condition is managed medically in most instances, animals may
need to undergo anesthesia to place a feeding tube. Thoracotomy
for surgical correction of a persistent fourth aortic arch is necessary
if the megaesophagus is caused by this congenital vascular ring
abnormality [484,485]. Animals with congenital or acquired cleft
palate frequently have pneumonia and may require surgical
correction of the defect. Drugs used in the perianesthetic period
can reduce tone in the lower and upper esophageal sphincters,
leading to regurgitation of stomach contents, thereby predisposing
the 	patient 	to 	this 	catastrophic 	anesthetic 	complication.
Epidemiologic data from a large multicenter study involving
approximately 140,000 canine patients reported that the incidence
of aspiration pneumonia following anesthesia and sedation in dogs
(1 case for every 590 procedures) was much higher than
the incidence reported in people (1 case for every 2000 to 7100
anesthetic procedures) [270,486]. Increased odds for aspiration
pneumonia after anesthesia in dogs were observed in the presence of
patient-related factors (megaesophagus or pre-existing respiratory
or neurologic disease), anesthesia-related factors (regurgitation
during anesthesia or the use of hydromorphone for induction), and
surgical factors (laparotomy, upper airway surgery, neurosurgery,
thoracotomy, and endoscopy) [270].
Management of anesthesia
In patients with pre-existing pneumonia, anesthesia should be
delayed until clinical signs have resolved to minimize the risk of
intra- and postoperative respiratory complications. In patients with

-- 823 of 1450 --

808 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
pneumonia that require anesthesia on an urgent basis, it is impor-
tant to evaluate their preoperative condition thoroughly to initiate
appropriate therapy, and plan for postoperative supportive therapy,
including oxygen supplementation. Physical examination with thor-
ough auscultation and percussion as well as appropriate laboratory
testing based on patient signalment is recommended. Assessment
of a patient’s fluid status is particularly important as dehydration
may be present in severely affected patients and may influence
prognosis [487]. Thoracic radiography and ultrasonography, pulse
oximetry, and/or arterial blood gas analysis can provide further
information about the severity and distribution of pulmonary
disease and the degree of gas exchange impairment. As explained in
Chapter 37, pneumonia may cause areas of low V̇A
/Q̇ ratio and
varying degrees of intrapulmonary shunt resulting in lower-than-
expected PaO2 values, and even hypoxemia, or signs of ARDS in
advanced cases. Inflammatory changes in the lung parenchyma
may alter pulmonary mechanics due to poor lung/respiratory system
compliance.
In some cases, local or neuraxial anesthesia may provide
adequate conditions to permit diagnostic or therapeutic proce-
dures to be performed and may reduce the risks associated
with general anesthesia, including the progression of pneumonia.
In patients requiring general anesthesia, the anesthetist should
utilize a protocol that includes preoxygenation, rapid intubation,
and oxygen supplementation with the ability to provide ventila-
tory support if required. When mechanical ventilation is uti-
lized, a protective ventilatory strategy described above should
be employed. In brief, low V T
s with adequate PEEP to prevent
alveolar collapse should be considered. In addition to routine
hemodynamic monitoring, assessment of gas exchange and air-
way pressures should be included. Planning for postanesthetic
respiratory support, such as oxygen supplementation and/or
mechanical ventilation, should be considered for patients with gas
exchange abnormalities. If hypoxemia is present, mechanical
ventilation and ARMs may be attempted to increase the PaO 2 /
FiO 2 ratio and improve C RS . Appropriate disinfection of anesthetic
equipment should be performed after anesthetizing a patient with
pneumonia to prevent disease transmission.
In animals at risk of aspiration that require general anesthesia,
general preventive strategies to minimize the risk of aspiration
include adhering to preoperative fasting periods, using premedica-
tion agents that minimize the risk of vomiting/regurgitation, using
rapid 	anesthetic 	induction 	techniques, 	optimizing 	patient
positioning during anesthesia, and maintaining a secure airway by
ensuring a properly inflated endotracheal tube cuff from anesthetic
induction through recovery. In adult animals, standard preoperative
fasting periods should be followed based on species. Shorter fasting
periods are currently recommended for neonatal, pediatric, and
diabetic animals, while longer fasting periods are adopted for
ruminants. Upon induction of anesthesia, it is crucial that the
animal is maintained in sternal recumbency with the neck and head
kept at an elevated position to minimize the risk of regurgitation.
After rapid placement of an endotracheal tube, the cuff should be
immediately inflated before the animal is moved to another position
(e.g., lateral or dorsal recumbency) to reduce the likelihood of
aspiration in case regurgitation occurs. To minimize the risk of
aspiration after endotracheal intubation, the animal’s head should
be angled to facilitate draining of any regurgitant fluid accumulated
in the oropharyngeal cavity throughout anesthesia. If regurgitation
occurs, lavage and suction of the fluid within the oropharynx
should be carefully performed. During anesthesia, the endotracheal
tube cuff pressure should be high enough to seal the airway and
prevent any regurgitant fluid from reaching the lower airways/
lungs. It is recommended that cuff pressure should be maintained
between 20–30 cm H2
O in humans, as pressures below this range
may result in a defective seal, allowing gastric contents and bacterially
colonized oral secretions to reach the lower airways and lungs;
conversely, excessively high cuff pressures may compromise the
microcirculation of the tracheal mucosa and lead to ischemic
lesions [488,489]. Excessively high cuff pressures have been
implicated as the causative factor of postanesthetic tracheal lesions
in dogs, cats, and horses, which may range from tracheal mucosal
inflammation/irritation to tracheal rupture/necrosis [490–494].
Although veterinary anesthesiologists may consider human
recommendations (cuff pressure between 20–30 cmH2
O) as
adequate for small animal patients, this pressure range applies only
to low-pressure/high-volume cuffs found in endotracheal tubes
designed for human use, where intracuff pressure approaches the
pressure exerted by the cuff on the lateral tracheal wall. Veterinary
endotracheal tubes available for medium-sized animals (e.g., swine
and foals) and for large animals (e.g., adult horses and cattle) are
equipped with high pressure/low volume cuffs, where the
correlation between intracuff pressure and the lateral tracheal wall
pressure is unknown [492,494]. In adult horses intubated with a
30 mm internal diameter endotracheal tube, a cuff pressure of
80–100 cmH 2
O reduced the extent of tracheal mucosal damage
compared to an intracuff pressure of 120 cmH 2
O, while providing
protection against aspiration of liquid into the lungs [492]. Although
there are no recommendations for cuff pressure in large animals,
placement of an endotracheal tube with a larger internal diameter
that can be easily passed through the larynx should be encouraged
because it will require a lower volume of air within the cuff to create
a seal and minimize damage to the tracheal mucosa.
Routine measurement of cuff pressure using specific devices
that allow cuff pressure adjustment is not common in veterinary
anesthesia. Especially during prolonged procedures, there is a
tendency for cuff pressure to decrease over time and such
monitoring would allow readjusting intracuff pressures to
adequate values. Instead of inflating the cuff to a target pressure
(e.g., 20–30 cmH 2 O), prevention of air leaks between the
endotracheal tube and the tracheal lumen can be achieved by
inflating the cuff using a minimum occlusive volume. This
technique is performed while the pop-off (APL) valve is
temporarily closed. The rebreathing bag is manually compressed
to create a positive airway pressure of 20 cmH 2 O and, if an audible
air leak is perceived, the cuff is progressively inflated by adding
relatively small volumes using a graduated syringe until leakage is
no longer perceived. According to a recent study in dogs
undergoing general anesthesia, adjustment of the minimum
occlusive volume according to the technique described above
resulted in cuff pressures within the target range of 20–30 cmH 2 O
in only 14% of animals, while cuff overinflation and underinflation
were observed in 76% and 14% of patients, respectively [495].
When feasible, animals at risk of aspiration should be recovered
in a sternal position with their head elevated above the shoulders.
Removal of the endotracheal tube should be delayed until the swal-
lowing reflex is present. To remove any foreign material that may
have accumulated in the trachea proximal to the endotracheal tube
cuff (and not removed by airway suctioning), it has traditionally
been recommended that the endotracheal tube cuff remain inflated
during extubation; however, evidence to support this strategy as
being effective is limited.

Anesthesia and pulmonary hypertension
Detailed knowledge of pulmonary artery (PA) pressures at rest,
during exercise, and in disease states in different species is variable.
In dogs, pulmonary hypertension (PH) is defined as mean PA pres-
sure > 25 mmHg at rest, and similar values are currently used to
define PH in cats [496,497]. In large animals, a consensus on what
constitutes PH is not yet available; however, in the equine, mean PA
pressures > 35 mmHg at rest are considered consistent with
PH [498]. The three basic hemodynamic mechanisms that may
cause PH include: (1) increased PVR; (2) increased pulmonary
blood flow; and (3) increased pulmonary vein pressure. As
described in Chapter 37 (Fig. 37.17), PH caused by increased PVR
and increased pulmonary blood flow is classified according to its
anatomic location as precapillary PH, while postcapillary PH results
from increased pulmonary vein pressure caused by left-sided con-
gestive heart failure. On some occasions, PH can be of pre- and
postcapillary origin. Current canine guidelines divide PH into six
groups based on pathological etiology: Group 1: Pulmonary arterial
hypertension (caused by contraction of small arteries); Group 2: PH
caused by left heart disease; Group 3: PH caused by lung disease/
hypoxia; Group 4: PH caused by intraluminal PA obstruction
(pulmonary thromboembolism); 5: PH caused by parasitic disease;
and 6: PH resulting from unclear/multifactorial mechanisms [497].
PH in Groups 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 have different etiologies, although
they share a common hemodynamic mechanism (increased PVR)
and anatomic location (precapillary PH). The primary hemodynamic
mechanism involved in group 2 PH is an increase in pulmonary
vein pressures. Therefore group 2 PH is also classified according to
its anatomic location as postcapillary PH, although an increase in
PVR (precapillary PH) might also be involved [496].
In animals with precapillary PH, increased PVR has most often
been attributed to respiratory disease, parasitic disease (canine
dirofilariasis), thromboembolic disease, or multifactorial/unclear
mechanisms [496]. Increased pulmonary blood flow/increased
PVR may occur in some congenital cardiovascular defects leading
to left-to- right shunting of blood within the circulation, including
persistent ductus arteriosus, atrial/ventricular septal defects, and
aortopulmonary window [496,498,499]. Increased PVR secondary
to pulmonary disease and/or hypoxia has been recognized as a
major causative factor of precapillary PH. Hypoxic pulmonary
vasoconstriction (HPV) is a physiologic mechanism whereby a
decrease in alveolar PO 2 causes constriction of adjacent arterioles.
Although HPV aims to maintain arterial oxygenation and V̇A /Q̇
matching by diverting pulmonary blood flow from poorly ventilated
(low V̇A
/Q̇) or non-ventilated (shunted flow) alveoli to better-
ventilated lung areas, in patients with chronic respiratory diseases,
HPV can cause an overall increase in PVR and lead to PH with the
subsequent development of right-sided heart failure [498,500,501].
Within the canine population, PH secondary to respiratory disease
has been more often identified in small-breed dogs and the more
common complaints include syncope (64%), cough (56%), and
respiratory difficulty (32%) [502]. Obstructive large airway
disorders (tracheal/mainstream bronchial collapse, bronchomalacia,
and BOAS), bronchiectasis, bronchiolar disease, emphysema,
pulmonary fibrosis, neoplasia, and other parenchymal lung diseases
have been associated with PH in dogs [503]. Definitive diagnosis of
the underlying respiratory disease in dogs presenting with PH may
be challenging in some cases because of the need for more
invasive procedures requiring general anesthesia, including
tracheobronchoscopy, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cytology, and
histopathology (emphysema and pulmonary fibrosis).
The increase in pulmonary vein pressure observed in postcapillary
PH is commonly attributed to left heart disease (e.g., myxomatous
mitral valve disease [MMVD] and dilated cardiomyopathy in dogs)
or, more rarely, to compression of a large pulmonary vein, such as
could occur with the presence of an intrathoracic tumor [496,498].
The reported prevalence of PH in dogs with MMVD ranges from 14
to 53% [504–508]. In a retrospective study of 212 dogs with MMVD,
graded as B2 or C according to the American College of Veterinary
Internal Medicine, 39% of animals presented echocardiographic
signs of PH [504]. PH was more commonly observed in animals
with signs of congestive heart failure (grade C) and was associated
with poorer prognosis for long-term survival when compared to
animals with MMVD without PH [504]. Although PH has been
largely overlooked in cats, one study showed that 17% of cats with
left-sided heart disease (22 of 131 animals) also presented echocar-
diographic evidence of PH [509]. Cardiomyopathies (hypertrophic,
end-stage hypertrophic, restrictive, unclassified, and dilated cardio-
myopathy) accounted for most cases of PH in cats (n = 15), whereas
a smaller proportion of animals presented with PH associated with
congenital cardiac defects (n = 5), and the remaining two cats
showed evidence of PH associated with other causes [510].
While definitive recognition of PH may require invasive hemo-
dynamic monitoring using a PA (Swan–Ganz) catheter, echocardi-
ography is used to diagnose PH in companion animals and can
provide useful information regarding cardiac morphologic and
functional changes in the equine [496,498,510]. Diagnosis of and
classification of PH in dogs has been the focus of an American
College of Veterinary Internal Medicine consensus statement and
more recent articles have also called attention to PH in cats as a
frequently overlooked complication of several disease states [496,497].
Echocardiographic signs of PH in dogs include an abnormally
dilated PA and the presence of a pulmonic valve regurgitant jet
detected using color Doppler studies. The increase in RV afterload
caused by PH leads to eccentric dilation/hypertrophy of the right
ventricle and tricuspid valve dysplasia/regurgitation. Increased RV
afterload/pressure may cause flattening of the interventricular sep-
tum on short axis echocardiographic views. If tricuspid regurgitation
secondary to PH is present, measurement of peak tricuspid regurgita-
tion velocity (TRV) by placing the spectral Doppler over the regurgi-
tant jet ultimately allows estimation of systolic pulmonary artery
pressure (SPAP). Although SPAP derived from TRV has been tradi-
tionally used to grade the severity of PH in veterinary medicine, these
measurements are subject to several flaws and recent guidelines have
recommended using the peak TRV along with a number of different
anatomic sites with echocardiographic signs of PH (PA, ventricles,
and right atrium/vena cava) to classify the probability of PH [496].
Although data in the veterinary literature are lacking, 30-day
mortality rates in human patients with PH undergoing elective,
non-cardiac, and non- obstetric surgeries have been reported to
range between 3 and 18%, increasing to 5–50% for emergency pro-
cedures [511]. The major cause of death during the perianesthetic
period is related to RV failure. If anesthesia is to be performed in
patients with PH, outcomes may be improved by a multidisciplinary
approach aiming to provide proper preanesthetic risk assessment,
treatment optimization, and advanced perioperative planning [511].
Precapillary pulmonary hypertension
Management of anesthesia
A thorough preoperative assessment including CBC, biochemistry
profile, chest radiographs, ECG, and echocardiogram is recommended
in patients with suspected PH. In some patients, assessment of

-- 825 of 1450 --

810 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
coagulation status may also be indicated. In general, patients may be
receiving and should continue therapy prior to anesthesia to support
cardiovascular function and reduce PVR and PA pressures. Dogs
with previously diagnosed PH may be on treatment with sildenafil, a
phosphodiesterase type 5 enzyme inhibitor, which induces relaxation
of smooth muscle cells located in PA vessels, decreasing PVR and PA
pressures 	without 	significantly 	impacting 	systemic 	arterial
pressures [502,512,513]. According to one case series study, sildenafil
(target dose of 2–4 mg/kg a day) administered for 30 days in dogs
with PH associated with respiratory disease (n = 25) significantly
decreased the pressure gradient across the tricuspid valve in survi-
vors (from 83.0 ± 17.4 mmHg to 55.4 ± 17.4 mmHg) [502]. Despite
the elevated mortality rate associated with respiratory disease and
PH (32% after 1 month of therapy, 50% after 6 months, and 85%
after 5 years), and the lack of a placebo group not receiving sildena-
fil, quality-of-life scores assigned by the owners were improved after
30 days of sildenafil therapy [502]. Pimobendan has been combined
with sildenafil in the treatment of dogs that develop right-sided
heart failure secondary to PH of respiratory origin [514].
Pimobendan increases inotropism by sensitizing myocardial pro-
teins to calcium and has vasodilating properties via its actions as a
phosphodiesterase type 3 inhibitor. Although pimobendan was
shown to increase survival time and reduce the reoccurrence of pul-
monary edema in dogs with left-sided congestive heart failure
caused by MMVD [515,516], one study showed that pimobendan
combined with sildenafil in dogs with PH secondary to respiratory
disease (n = 16) did not impact long-term survival when compared
to dogs treated with sildenafil alone (n = 12) [514].
Because drugs used to treat PH and general anesthetics (e.g.,
isoflurane) can decrease SVR, the clinician should consider the use
of vasopressors to treat intra-anesthetic hypotension. Evidence sug-
gests that sildenafil, despite its pulmonary vasodilating properties,
does not appear to impact peripheral vascular tone and systemic
arterial pressure during anesthesia. In human patients with PH that
were anesthetized for valvular heart surgery, sildenafil (50 mg,
administered orally 10 min before induction of anesthesia) decreased
systolic and mean PA pressures 30 min after its administration,
without significantly altering mean arterial pressure or SVR in
comparison to a placebo control group [512]. Pimobendan has sys-
temic vasodilatory properties which could potentially contribute to
hypotension during anesthesia. A recent randomized crossover
study performed in six healthy Beagle dogs showed that one single
dose of pimobendan (0.15 mg/kg), administered intramuscularly
during isoflurane anesthesia, decreased SVR and diastolic blood
pressure in comparison to placebo controls [517]. However, these
results may not be extrapolated to the clinical scenario because ani-
mals with PH and right-sided heart failure are likely to be receiving
chronic treatment with oral pimobendan by the time anesthesia is
performed.
Table 38.3 summarizes the factors that can increase PVR and
aggravate PH, including management strategies for the perianes-
thetic period.. In addition to providing adequate sedation and anal-
gesia to avoid stress and pain, small animals should be preoxygenated
by delivery of 100% oxygen through a face mask for at least 3 min to
ensure significant increases in alveolar PO2
, to prevent hypoxemia
caused by hypoventilation during induction of anesthesia. Elevated
PaCO2 levels/respiratory acidosis are known to potentiate HPV
[500,518]. Although mechanical ventilation may prevent hyper-
capnia caused by anesthetic drugs, patients with PH may be less
tolerant of the hemodynamic effects of positive-pressure ventilation.
As discussed before (Fig. 38.29), positive-pressure breaths decrease
venous return by increasing P pl and increase RV afterload by
distending 	alveoli 	and 	compressing 	pulmonary 	capillaries.
Therefore, in patients with PH, positive-pressure ventilation has the
potential to further increase RV afterload and PVR, which could
precipitate cardiovascular collapse in a patient with right-sided
heart failure secondary to PH. To minimize the potential negative
impact of mechanical ventilation on RV function, human guide-
lines for anesthesia in patients with PH have recommended avoid-
ing high P plat and the use of low V T (5–7 mL/kg) and low PEEP
levels [511]. However, direct extrapolation of V T
s adopted in
humans to animal species might not be possible. As previously dis-
cussed, V T
s in the order of ≤ 8 mL/kg are more likely to approach
the airway deadspace volume of normal dogs and would likely
result in hypercapnia (which could also be detrimental in PH)
despite the use of high breathing rates. In the absence of veterinary
evidence, the use of a low P plat (or low P peak if only a volumetric ven-
tilator is available) is recommended in veterinary patients with PH.
Plateau pressure or P peak can be initially limited to 6–8 cmH2
O in
small animal species with PH. However, it must be acknowledged
that these adjustments may not prevent hypercapnia despite the use
of high breathing rates. Provided the animal is hemodynamically
stable, inspiratory pressures can be further increased to address
hypercapnia based on PET
CO 2 or, ideally, PaCO 2 values derived
from blood gas analysis.
Central venous pressure (CVP) monitoring has limited ability to
predict fluid responsiveness status. However, increased CVP
(> 6–8 mmHg in dogs) is expected to occur with RV failure sec-
ondary to PH, and with circulating volume overload. For more
invasive/prolonged procedures in patients with PH, insertion of a
central venous catheter for monitoring CVP along with invasive
blood pressure monitoring is advisable, as onset of hypotension/
tachycardia coinciding with increased CVP often indicates RV
failure and cardiovascular collapse [511]. Positive inotropes
(e.g., dobutamine and dopamine) may be used to treat hypotension
during anesthesia in animals with echocardiographic evidence of
right-sided heart failure [511].
Since low SVR, in addition to low cardiac output, may contribute
to hypotension during general anesthesia, and considering that
certain drugs used in the treatment of PH associated with heart
failure may also decrease SVR (e.g., pimobendan and angiotensin-
converting enzyme [ACE] inhibitors), vasopressor agents should
also be considered for treatment of hypotension. In vitro studies
support the use of vasopressin to treat hypotension during the
perioperative period because this agent does not elicit a contractile
response in the PA but is a potent vasoconstrictor of systemic arter-
ies [519,520]. However, if α1
- adrenergic receptor agonists such as
norepinephrine are used to increase SVR and treat hypotension,
their potential to increase PVR should be considered. Therefore,
α1
- adrenergic receptor agonists such as norepinephrine should
be carefully titrated to effect as higher doses may increase PVR
(Table 38.3).
General recommendations of anesthetic management should
be followed. Animals with PH secondary to respiratory disease
could present with variable degrees of respiratory distress/
hypoxemia. Therefore, mechanical ventilation with 100% oxygen
during anesthesia, along with oxygen supplementation during
the perianesthetic period is advisable. The clinician should also
consider that more invasive diagnostic procedures (e.g., bronchos-
copy and bronchoalveolar lavage) could aggravate or precipitate
hypoxemia due to limitations in providing oxygen supplementation
under these circumstances, particularly in very small patients. With
proper preanesthetic planning and discussion of the risks involved,
outcomes can be optimized.

Postcapillary pulmonary hypertension
Management of anesthesia
Canine patients with MMVD may require anesthesia for a variety of
reasons. In these cases, it should be acknowledged that the presence
of PH is a hallmark of severe left-sided congestive heart failure,
where elevated LV filling pressures and retrograde blood flow
through the degenerated mitral valve cause excessive increases in
left atrial and pulmonary vein pressures, ultimately leading to
increased hydrostatic pressure within the pulmonary capillaries
and PH. Therefore, animals with PH secondary to MMVD may be
more likely to develop hydrostatic pulmonary edema associated
with fluid overload during anesthesia.
Besides conventional therapy with diuretics and ACE inhibitors,
animals with MMVD grade B2 or above commonly receive
pimobendan treatment. Randomized controlled studies performed
in animals with MMVD have shown that pimobendan combined
with conventional therapy, compared to animals receiving only
conventional therapy, increases survival time by 1.9 to 2.5 times,
and reduces the reoccurrence of pulmonary edema [515,516]. If
echocardiographic evidence of PH is also present, pimobendan
is frequently combined with sildenafil therapy with the aim of
decreasing pulmonary arterial pressures.
While the drugs described above can ameliorate signs of heart
disease and increase long-term survival, their potential impact on
anesthesia should be considered. The use of ACE inhibitors aims to
decrease LV afterload by causing arterial vasodilation. However, in
healthy dogs, administration of the ACE inhibitor benazepril for
one week, with the last dose administered 90 minutes before
anesthesia, was reported to increase the intensity of intra-anesthetic
hypotension and the number of interventions required to correct
moderate-to- severe hypotensive crises in comparison to a placebo
control treatment [521]. As previously discussed, one single dose of
pimobendan during isoflurane anesthesia could also result in
greater decreases in SVR and lower diastolic blood pressure com-
pared to a placebo control [517]. Considering the potential of drugs
used in the treatment of MMVD to aggravate hypotension during
general anesthesia, the clinician should be prepared to rapidly
intervene with vasopressor agents (e.g., norepinephrine) or drugs
with mixed vasopressor/inotropic action (e.g., ephedrine and
dopamine) if hypotension develops following induction of
anesthesia. Unless there is clear evidence of circulating volume
deficits, administration of fluid boluses with the aim of stabilizing
arterial blood pressure should be avoided in animals with PH asso-
ciated with heart disease.
In companion animals, preference is generally given to
premedication with opioids alone, which may result in adequate
sedation 	without 	significantly 	interfering 	with 	myocardial
contractility, but combination of opioids with low doses of other
drugs (e.g., acepromazine or dexmedetomidine) may be necessary
to achieve a satisfactory level of sedation in some patients.
Preoxygenation with 100% oxygen delivered though a face mask
for at least 3 min immediately before induction of anesthesia with
an injectable agent should be routinely performed. General
guidelines for maintenance of anesthesia include an inhalant
anesthetic, 	combined 	with 	locoregional 	anesthesia 	and/or
infusions of drugs that provide intraoperative analgesia and reduce
inhalant requirements. Monitoring should include ECG, arterial
blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and capnography, and use of
mechanical ventilation is advisable to optimize gas exchange and
to prevent hypercapnia. Although data is lacking, in large animal
patients with PH, locoregional anesthesia should be considered. If
general anesthesia is required, similar principles discussed above
should be considered.

α2
- Adrenergic receptor agonists, ketamine 	Increased PVR and MPAP are observed with high doses of α2
-adrenergic receptor agonists, therefore avoid these
drugs, or use low doses, if necessary
Avoid high doses of ketamine
Low mixed-venous PO2 	Optimize tissue perfusion (inotropes, fluid therapy) to maintain mixed-venous (or central venous) PO2 > 40 mmHg

Introduction
Anesthetic management of patients with neurological disorders
undergoing diagnostic and/or surgical procedures is common in vet-
erinary medicine. Knowledge of normal anatomy and physiology as
well as pathophysiology of the central, peripheral, somatic, and auto-
nomic nervous systems allows the anesthetic provider to understand
the impact of sedation and anesthesia on normal physiology as well
as disease processes. Whether a patient is anesthetized for evaluation
or management of neurologic conditions or suffers from comorbidi-
ties related to the nervous system, a solid foundational knowledge of
the nervous system is important to ensure appropriate and optimal
patient care while decreasing patient morbidity and mortality.
Anatomy of the nervous system
The nervous system is anatomically divided into the central nervous
system, containing the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nerv-
ous system, containing the cranial and spinal nerves. Functionally,
the nervous system can be divided into somatic and autonomic
nervous system components, each with afferent and efferent fibers.
Central nervous system
The central nervous system (CNS) contains the brain and spinal cord
and is made up of gray and white matter. Gray matter is composed of
neuronal cell bodies and is located more superficially in the brain and
more deeply (i.e., centrally) within the spinal cord. There are also
some deeper regions of gray matter within the brain known as
“nuclei.” White matter is composed of nerve fibers (axons) and is
located deeper within the brain and more superficially within the
spinal cord. The meninges are composed of three layers of connective
tissue within the CNS: the dura, arachnoid, and pia mater. The dura
mater is the most superficial layer and, in the vertebral column, the
space between the bone and the dura mater is the epidural space.
Within the skull, the dura mater is fused to the periosteum and,
therefore, is considered a potential space. Because there is no epidural
space intracranially, the venous sinuses are located within the dura
mater of the brain. The arachnoid is the middle layer of the meninges
while the pia mater is the innermost layer. The pia mater is only one
cell thick and is fused to the surface of the brain and the spinal cord.
Within the vertebral canal, the subarachnoid space is located between
the arachnoid and pia mater layers and contains cerebrospinal fluid
(CSF). The meninges extend around the spinal nerve roots with some
reaching the level of the intervertebral foramina.
When CSF collection is performed, a spinal needle is inserted
into the subarachnoid space either at the level of the cerebellomed-
ullary cistern cranially, or the lower lumbar region caudally. In dogs
and cats, the L5–L6 vertebral space is recommended for obtaining
CSF. In large-breed dogs, the L4–L5 vertebral space can often be
used if obtaining CSF from the L5–L6 space is unsuccessful. Local
anesthetic and analgesic agents may be administered either in the
epidural or subarachnoid spaces; species-specific descriptions of
these techniques may be found in the local anesthetic and analgesic
techniques chapters in this text.
Brain
Anatomically, the brain can be divided into five regions: the telen-
cephalon (cerebral cortex and basal ganglia), diencephalon (thalamus,
hypothalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus, and metathalamus),

The cerebral cortex or telencephalon is where sensory informa-

smooth and lack these characteristic folds and are referred to as
lissencephalic. The presence of gyri allows a significantly increased
number of neurons without increasing the size of the cranium or
skull. The gyri are divided into lobes including the frontal, parietal,

temporal, and occipital lobes. The olfactory bulb is the most rostral
part of the telencephalon and is where the axons of the olfactory
nerves terminate.
The diencephalon, specifically the thalamus, receives all sensory
information (except olfaction) and projects to sensory areas of the
telencephalon. Efferent, or motor, pathways also course from the
cerebral cortex through the thalamus to the brainstem. The hypo-
thalamus is important in maintaining homeostasis as it is the neu-
rologic control center for the endocrine system and the autonomic
nervous system. The axons of cranial nerve II (optic nerve) termi-
nate within the diencephalon after coursing through the optic
chiasm.
The mesencephalon, or midbrain, is the most rostral part of the
brainstem. The midbrain contains sensory and motor tracts, as well
as the rostral and caudal colliculi, which are associated with visual
and auditory reflexes, respectively. The nuclei of cranial nerves III
(oculomotor nerve) and IV (trochlear nerve) are located within the
mesencephalon. The midbrain is connected to the cerebellum via
the rostral cerebellar peduncles.
The metencephalon, or pons, also contains sensory and motor
pathways and the nuclei associated with cranial nerve V (trigeminal
nerve). The cerebellum is also part of the metencephalon and is
located dorsal to the brainstem. The pons is connected to the
cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncles. The cerebellum
has two hemispheres and a centrally located vermis. It receives
sensory information directly from afferent pathways, including the
vestibular system, and motor information from the cerebral cortex.
While the cerebellum does not initiate movement, it is responsible
for integrating sensory and motor input to create smooth, controlled,
and coordinated movements.
The myelencephalon, or medulla, contains sensory and motor
tracts, as well as nuclei for the remaining pairs of cranial nerves VI
through XII, including cranial nerve X (vagus nerve), which inner-
vates organs within the thorax and abdomen. In addition, nerve
centers for vital body functions, including regulation of blood pres-
sure, heart rate, and respiration, are located within the medulla.
The blood–brain barrier (BBB) is a semipermeable membrane
made up of microvascular endothelial cells that restrict free move-
ment of particles from the blood into the brain parenchyma and
CSF. The BBB allows carbon dioxide, oxygen, small lipid-soluble
substances, and general anesthetics to cross from the blood into the
brain. The BBB is made up of pericytes, tight junctions between
capillary endothelial cells, a layer of astrocyte foot processes that
surround the capillaries, and the basal lamina (or basement mem-
brane). Several areas of the brain, including the hypothalamus, area
postrema, and the pineal gland, are outside the BBB as these regions
contain sensors for monitoring osmolarity, glucose levels, and pH,
and are important for providing information for maintenance of
homeostasis. While the BBB fulfills a protective function by pre-
venting possible toxins and limiting pathogens from entering the
CNS, it also limits therapeutic options by excluding many drugs
from entering. Permeability of the BBB may increase in the face of
inflammation or increased intracranial pressure.
The CSF is a clear, colorless fluid produced by the choroid plexus
and the ependymal lining cells within the ventricles of the brain and
is an ultrafiltrate of plasma. It is produced at a rate of 0.02 mL/min
in cats and 0.05 mL/min in dogs [2,3]. Compared to plasma, CSF
has a lower concentration of protein, glucose, calcium, and potassium
and a higher concentration of sodium, chloride, and magnesium [4].
The CSF is present within the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles of
the brain, and within the central canal and subarachnoid space of
the spinal cord. The CSF flows from the lateral ventricles, located
within the cerebral cortex, into the third ventricle, located between
the thalamus and hypothalamus. From here, it flows into the fourth
ventricle, located ventral to the cerebellum and dorsal to the
medulla. These ventricles can be clearly seen on magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) (Fig. 39.2). Caudally, the fourth ventricle becomes
continuous with the central canal of the spinal cord and bilateral
apertures within the ventricle allow CSF to flow into the subarach-
noid space. The CSF passes from the subarachnoid space through
arachnoid villi, which act as one-way valves, to the dural sinuses
where it is absorbed. The arachnoid villi are located within the
venous sinuses, as well as the spinal veins.
The blood supply to the arterial circle, or the “Circle of Willis” as
termed in human medicine, is the main arterial supply to the brain.
There are several anatomical species differences that can have clinical
implications. In dogs (and in humans), the arterial circle is formed
by the joining of the basilar artery and the left and right internal
carotid arteries. In the cow, the maxillary and vertebral arteries
form this arterial supply. In the cat and sheep, the maxillary artery,
via the rete mirabile, forms the arterial circle. The rete mirabile
is a network of branches of the maxillary artery located in the

cavernous sinus on the ventral surface of the calvarium. The blood
from the cavernous sinus drains from the nasal cavity. A counter-

(arterial) and cavernous sinus (venous) may play a role in ther-

complications associated with anesthesia, including cortical blind-

electroretinogram (ERG) and brainstem auditory evoked responses
(BAER) in anesthetized cats when mouth gags were used compared
to no changes when mouth gags were not used [8]. From the arterial
circle, the rostral, middle, and caudal cerebral arteries supply the
prosencephalon. The blood supply to the brainstem arises as
branches from the basilar artery.
The venous system including the venous sinuses and veins of
the CNS is valveless, meaning blood can flow in either direction.
Associated vessels have thin walls without muscular layers and the
veins drain into the larger venous sinuses. The cerebral cortex
contains the dorsal and ventral cerebral veins as well as the great
cerebral vein which drains the deeper cortex. The major veins of
the brainstem include the dorsal and ventral cerebellar veins,
pontine veins, and medullary veins. The dorsal sagittal sinus, straight
sinus, and paired transverse sinuses are located dorsally. Paired
rostral and caudal cavernous sinuses, as well as the sigmoid, basilar,
and petrosal sinuses, are located ventrally within the calvarium.
The venous sinuses are located within the meninges and drain
into the internal jugular, maxillary, and vertebral veins and into
the venous plexus.
Spinal cord
Rostrally, the spinal cord is continuous with the myelencephalon, or
medulla, of the brainstem and is a complex network of ascending
and descending tracts. It is located within the spinal, or vertebral,
canal and is surrounded by the meninges, which are composed of
the dura mater, arachnoid, and pia mater. The epidural space contains
epidural fat, blood vessels, and lymphatics. The CSF passes through
the central canal of the spinal cord and flows around the spinal cord
within the subarachnoid space. The pia mater is one cell thick and
lies directly on the spinal cord.
Anatomically, the spinal cord is divided longitudinally into four
major regions: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral. The caudal
(coccygeal) segments are associated with the tail and contain
nerves. Each segment of the spinal cord has a pair (right and left) of
spinal nerves that exit through the intervertebral foramen. The dor-
sal root carries sensory (afferent) information and the ventral root
carries motor (efferent) information. Just inside the intervertebral
foramina, the dorsal and ventral roots combine and exit as the asso-
ciated spinal nerve for that segment of spinal cord. The number of
vertebrae and spinal cord segments varies with species. Spinal nerve
C1 exits through a foramen in C1 and the spinal nerves C2–C7 exit
cranial to the associated vertebrae. Spinal nerve C8 exits between
C7 and T1, and spinal nerves T1–L3 exit caudal to the associated
vertebrae. The vertebrae and spinal cord segments are misaligned
to varying degrees due to differential growth rates during develop-
ment. For example, in the lumbar region of the dog, spinal cord
segments L5, L6, and L7 all lie within the region of the L4 vertebra.
In medium to large-breed dogs, the spinal cord terminates at
approximately L6–L7, and in small-breed dogs and cats, the spinal
cord terminates at approximately S1. In large animals, including
horses, ruminants, and swine, the spinal cord terminates mid-
sacrum. These anatomic differences are important to note when
considering diagnostic and therapeutic procedures involving the
subarachnoid and epidural spaces.
Clinically and functionally, the spinal cord is divided into four
segments based on innervation: C1–C5, C6–T2, T3–L3, and L4–S3.
The cervical (C6–T2 segments) and lumbosacral (L4–S3 segments)
intumescences supply the lower motor neurons to the thoracic and
pelvic limbs, respectively. Lesions within the cervical segments
(C1–C5 and C6–T2) can cause tetraparesis, hemiparesis, tetraplegia,
or hemiplegia. Cervical pain is also common with lesions in this
region but may or may not be present. Lesions within the T3–L3 or
L4–S3 segments may cause paraparesis or paraplegia and, depend-
ing on the etiology, lesions may cause back pain (Fig. 39.3).
Caudal to the lumbar intumescence, the spinal cord tapers into a
region called the “conus medullaris,” which consists of sacral and
caudal segments. The filum terminale is a strand of glial and epend-
ymal cells that extends from the end of the spinal cord. This region
is covered by a dural sac, creating a space within the subarachnoid
space filled with CSF. As the sacral and caudal spinal roots move
caudally past the conus medullaris, each exits at an intervertebral
foramen. These roots are collectively known as the “cauda equina.”
The spinal cord has an H- or butterfly-shaped center of gray mat-
ter, which is divided into the dorsal, lateral, and ventral horns
(Fig. 39.4). The dorsal horn contains sensory neurons. The lateral
horn is located in the thoracolumbar (T1–L4, specifically) and sacral
segments and contains motor neurons that innervate the viscera.
The ventral horn contains cell bodies of somatic motor neurons,
which are also called lower motor neurons. The white matter
surrounds the gray matter of the spinal cord and is divided into three
funiculi. The dorsal funiculus contains only sensory fiber tracts in
several mammalian species including the dog, while the lateral and
ventral funiculi carry both sensory and motor fiber tracts.
Cranially, the subclavian artery branches to become the vertebral
artery, which enters the vertebral canal at the atlas (first cervical
vertebra). Segmental spinal arteries enter the spinal cord via
the intervertebral foramen where they divide into dorsal and
ventral branches. The ventral branches connect via the longitudinal
ventral spinal artery (which runs in the ventral median fissure of
the spinal cord) and supply the ventral gray matter and ventral
funiculus. The dorsal branch supplies the dorsal gray matter. Other
branches of the segmental spinal arteries supply the lateral funicu-
lus. Blood flow in the gray matter of the spinal cord is four times
that of the white matter, and blood flow to the thoracolumbar
region of the spinal cord has been shown to be 40% less compared
to the cervical and lumbosacral regions [9]. There is less gray matter
in the thoracolumbar region of the spinal cord, which accounts for
the reduced blood flow.
The venous system of the CNS is valveless and vertebral veins
communicate directly with the cranial venous sinus described
above. Lying ventral to the spinal cord is the internal vertebral
venous plexus, which extends the entire length of the spinal canal.
This flat, thin-walled valveless network is paired and is a frequent
source of hemorrhage during neurosurgery. The sinus diverges at
the intervertebral foramen and then converges over the vertebral
body. At the level of the intervertebral foramen, the sinus commu-
nicates with the intervertebral veins and exits the foramen with the
spinal nerve roots where they drain into larger vessels, including the
azygous vein and caudal vena cava.
Peripheral nervous system
The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is divided into afferent
(sensory) and efferent (motor) components. Sensory neurons receive

information from peripheral receptors and transmit this informa-

tion. Sensory neurons enter the intervertebral foramen as part of
the spinal nerve and then enter the dorsal horn of the spinal cord
via the dorsal nerve root. Efferent information leaves the ventral
horn of the spinal cord via the ventral nerve root before becoming
the spinal nerve and then motor neurons. There are two divisions of
motor neurons within the PNS: somatic motor neurons, which
innervate skeletal muscle, and autonomic motor neurons, which
innervate cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and some glands.
Myelin, produced by oligodendrocytes within the CNS and by
Schwann cells within the PNS, insulates the axons of nerves and
expedites transmission of electrical activity. The nodes of Ranvier,
which are the spaces or gaps between myelin along the axon, allow
saltatory conduction to take place which greatly expedites signal
transmission. Therefore, nerves that are myelinated have consider-
ably faster conduction velocities compared to unmyelinated nerves.
In addition, large fiber nerves also have faster conduction velocities
compared to small fiber nerves. The largest and fastest nerve fibers
are called Type A and innervate somatic nerves. Type B fibers are
also myelinated but are smaller than Type A and make up the
preganglionic nerves of the autonomic nervous system. Type C
are small unmyelinated nerve fibers with the slowest conduction
velocity. Type C fibers transmit postganglionic information within

Somatic nervous system
The somatic nervous system contains both afferent (sensory) and
efferent (motor) nerves. Afferent fibers transmit environmental
and peripheral sensory information regarding pain, temperature,
and pressure, as well as sight and hearing. The cutaneous region
innervated by one specific sensory spinal nerve is called a dermat-
ome, and the presence or absence of sensation in dermatomes can
be useful to isolate a particular sensory nerve that is affected by a
lesion. Skeletal muscles contain specialized sensory receptors.
Muscle spindles provide information on muscle length and are
located within the extrafusal fibers of skeletal muscles. Golgi tendon
organs provide information about muscle tension and are located
within the tendons. All of these are examples of the information
transmitted by the general somatic afferent system.
Neuromuscular junction transmission
Motor neurons are found in both cranial and spinal nerves and
form synapses with skeletal, smooth, or cardiac muscle fibers at the
neuromuscular junction. The motor endplate is the specific region
where the nerve meets the muscle, with most muscle fibers having
one neuromuscular junction per muscle fiber. The neurotransmit-
ter acetylcholine (ACh) is released from the presynaptic neuron and
crosses the synaptic cleft to bind to receptors on the postsynaptic
muscle membrane. Depending on the strength of the stimulus
and the amount of ACh released, this action potential may cause
muscle contraction. Even without action potentials, ACh is con-
stantly being released in small amounts which causes miniature
endplate potentials.
In a resting state, there is an excess of sodium ions outside the
muscle membrane and an excess of potassium ions inside the mus-
cle membrane, creating a negatively charged environment inside
the muscle. The electrical difference between the two sides of the
membrane is 90 mV. Once a nerve is stimulated, an action potential
travels down the axon and reaches the presynaptic terminal of the
nerve where ACh is present in small synaptic vesicles. These vesicles
fuse with the presynaptic membrane and ACh is released. ACh dif-
fuses across the cleft and reaches the postsynaptic muscle mem-
brane where it binds reversibly to nicotinic receptors. There are five
subunits of the nicotinic receptor, and when two ACh molecules
bind to the two α subunits, an allosteric change in conformation of
the membrane proteins occurs. Sodium ions flow into the muscle
membrane and potassium ions flow out of the muscle membrane,
causing a change in the electrical charge, which is called depolari-
zation. If the change in charge inside the muscle membrane is
greater than 45 mV, then muscle contraction usually occurs. There
is an overabundance of ACh released by an action potential into the
neuromuscular junction, which acts as a safety margin to ensure
adequate binding. Excess ACh is broken down by the enzyme ace-
tylcholinesterase into acetic acid and choline and then recycled and
returned to the presynaptic nerve. The impulses are transmitted
through the T-tubules of the sarcolemma of the muscle membrane,
causing a release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and
muscle contraction.
In addition to the presynaptic nerve and postsynaptic muscle
receptors described above, there are other postsynaptic receptors
located outside the neuromuscular junction on the muscle mem-
brane and these are called extrajunctional (or extrasynaptic)
receptors. These receptors, which normally play a very small role in
neuromuscular transmission, proliferate after denervation or
muscle injury and may cause an exaggerated response that can be
detected after a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent
(i.e., succinylcholine) has been administered.
Autonomic nervous system
The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is responsible for regulating
the body’s internal environment and helping to maintain homeo-
stasis. Most of the functions of the ANS are under subconscious
control and include maintaining heart rate and blood pressure,
thermoregulation, controlling micturition, and managing gastroin-
testinal secretions, although the gastrointestinal tract does have
additional nervous system components. The ANS consists of afferent
pathways, CNS integration (brain and spinal cord), and two efferent
pathways: the sympathetic (flight or fight) and parasympathetic
(rest and digest) systems.
Within the diencephalon, the hypothalamus facilitates regulation
of both the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems,
along with the cerebral cortex and brainstem. Both systems are
always active, and activity can be increased or decreased to control
organ function and response. Most organs have both sympathetic
and parasympathetic innervation, creating reciprocal effects. For
example, the heart has sympathetic innervation which increases
heart rate and contractility, and parasympathetic innervation which
has opposing effects. Sympathetic innervation of the gastrointesti-
nal tract causes relaxation while parasympathetic innervation
causes contraction. Unlike the somatic system which has one effer-
ent neuron, efferent information from the ANS is conducted via
two (preganglionic and postganglionic) neurons. The preganglionic
neuron is within the CNS, and the postganglionic neuron is within
the PNS.
The general visceral afferent fibers carry afferent (sensory)
information to the CNS and that information is then used to control
internal homeostasis and bodily functions via the efferent compo-
nents of the ANS. Afferent information from cranial nerves VII, IX,
and X travels along the solitary tract within the medulla and
synapses within the solitary nucleus. Axons then travel to other
regions of the brainstem (parasympathetic system) or spinal cord
(sympathetic system) to control visceral functions or project to the
thalamus for conscious perception of sensory information. Afferent
information regarding taste travels via cranial nerves VII and IX.
Blood pressure and tissue oxygenation levels are monitored by
baroreceptors and chemoreceptors located in arteries and informa-
tion is transmitted to cranial nerves IX and X. Additionally, sensory
information from the olfactory and limbic regions is carried along
the solitary tract to the solitary nucleus to allow the ANS to respond
to smells and emotions, respectively.
ACh is the neurotransmitter for all preganglionic synapses within
the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems, as well as for post-
ganglionic synapse transmission in the parasympathetic system. In
postganglionic sympathetic synapses, norepinephrine is the main
neurotransmitter secreted; however, some sympathetic postgangli-
onic synapses, such as those that supply sweat glands and blood ves-
sels of skeletal muscles, secrete ACh. ACh receptors are either
nicotinic or muscarinic. Nicotinic receptors are found in all pregan-
glionic synapses of the ANS and at the somatic neuromuscular
junction. Muscarinic receptors are located in effector cells at post-
ganglionic synapses of the parasympathetic nervous system and in
cholinergic postganglionic synapses of the sympathetic nervous
system. A list of selected effects of sympathetic and parasympa-
thetic nervous system transmission can be found in Table 39.2.

Sympathetic nervous system
Often referred to as the “fight or flight system,” the sympathetic nerv-
ous system is most active during times of stress. It discharges as a unit,
and the effects are widespread and last longer than those of the para-
sympathetic system. ACh is the neurotransmitter between pregangli-
onic and postganglionic neurons within the sympathetic system.
Norepinephrine is the main neurotransmitter used between postgan-
glionic neurons and the effector organ within the sympathetic nerv-
ous system. Norepinephrine acts as an agonist at α1
-, α2
-, β1
-, and
β2
-adrenergic receptors. For sweat glands, the receptor is cholinergic,
except in horses where the receptor is β2
-adrenergic [10].
Visceral sensory (afferent) information travels along sympathetic
nerves to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. There, interneurons
receive information from visceral and somatic afferent nerves.
The sympathetic system has short preganglionic and long postgan-
glionic axons. The efferent preganglionic neurons of the sympathetic
nervous system are located within the gray matter of the thora-
columbar spinal cord, specifically the T1–L5 spinal cord segments
(Fig. 39.5). The axons leave via the ventral nerve root to join the
spinal nerve of the associated spinal cord segment and then synapse
in a ganglion at one of three locations. Some preganglionic neurons
synapse in the sympathetic chain ganglion located along the lateral
aspect of the vertebral column (paravertebral). These synapses can
occur within ganglia at the same segmental level of the chain, or they
may synapse rostrally or caudally which allows for multiple possible
synapses. This more diffuse distribution accounts for the widespread
effects of sympathetic innervation. The postganglionic neurons then
travel to innervate blood vessels, sweat glands, and pilomotor mus-
cles. Other preganglionic neurons travel through the sympathetic
chain without synapsing. These neurons then synapse on preverte-
bral ganglia that supply visceral organs and glands within the tho-
racic or abdominal cavities. The prevertebral ganglia include the
celiac, cranial, and caudal mesenteric ganglia.
Lastly, other preganglionic neurons of the sympathetic nervous
system travel from the thoracolumbar region of the spinal cord via
the splanchnic nerve to the adrenal medulla where they synapse on
chromaffin cells. These neurons release ACh which acts at nicotinic
receptors located on chromaffin cell membranes, stimulating
these cells to release epinephrine (80% in dogs, 60% in cats) and
norepinephrine (20% in dogs, 40% in cats) into circulation [11].
Epinephrine causes vasodilation within skeletal muscles and
bronchodilation within the airways, while norepinephrine causes
vasoconstriction, increased cardiac activity, and pupillary dilation.
Parasympathetic nervous system
The parasympathetic nervous system of the ANS also has pregan-
glionic and postganglionic neurons. In contrast to the sympathetic
preganglionic fibers, the efferent parasympathetic preganglionic
axons are long and tend to synapse either within or very near the
target organ, meaning that the postganglionic fibers are quite short.
The parasympathetic nervous system efferent nuclei are located
within the brainstem or sacral spinal cord segments, leading this
portion of the ANS to be referred to as the craniosacral component.
The preganglionic nuclei of the parasympathetic nervous system
are located within the nuclei of cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X,
adjacent to the somatic nuclei of these cranial nerves (Fig. 39.5).
The preganglionic parasympathetic nucleus (often called the
“Edinger–Westphal nucleus”) of the oculomotor nerve (cranial
nerve III) is located within the midbrain. The postganglionic neu-
ron stimulates the iris (pupillary) sphincter and ciliary muscles of
the eye to cause pupillary constriction. Postganglionic fibers from
the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves (cranial nerves VII and IX,
respectively) innervate salivary glands. The parasympathetic
nucleus of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) provides efferent
control to the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, liver, pancreas, and
gallbladder.

Physiology of the central nervous system
Brain physiology
Cerebral perfusion pressure and intracranial pressure
According to the Monro–Kellie doctrine, the brain is enclosed in
the rigid structure of the skull and an equilibrium must exist
between the volumes of brain parenchyma, interstitial and CSF
fluid, and arterial/venous blood; therefore, an increase in one com-
ponent or the addition of another (e.g., hematoma, skull fracture,
and 	tumor) 	must 	cause 	a 	decrease 	in 	the 	remaining
components [13,14]. Additionally, an increase in the volume of any
constituent can result in an increase in intracranial pressure (ICP).
Blood and CSF are the main volume buffering components; thus,
initial compensatory mechanisms such as a decrease in cerebral
blood volume (CBV), and/or a shift of CSF from the brain into the
spinal canal, or even absorption of CSF will prevent major increases
in ICP [15]. This stage is often characterized as the compensated
state of increased ICP. While changes in cerebral venous volume
occur rapidly, “spatial compensation” of CSF happens more slowly,
so its ability to mitigate acute increases in ICP is limited [14,16].
Therefore, once these compensatory mechanisms are exhausted,
marked elevations in ICP can occur leading to decreased cerebral
perfusion pressure (CPP), defined as the difference between mean
arterial blood pressure (MAP) and ICP (i.e., CPP = MAP – ICP),

and increased risk of cerebral ischemia [14,15]. Significant increases
in ICP can also result in compression of brain tissue against the
tentorium, falx, and foramen magnum and potential brain hernia-
tion, which is characterized as the decompensated state of increased
ICP [15,16].
Some causes of increased ICP include space-occupying lesions
(i.e., intracranial hemorrhage, hematoma, tumor, abscess), cerebral
edema (i.e., due to head injury, or hypoxic or ischemic encepha-
lopathy), venodilation, and a decrease in venous drainage (i.e.,
head-down position, jugular vein obstruction/compression, and
increased right heart or intrathoracic pressures) [14–17]. In addi-
tion, increased CSF production (i.e., choroid plexus tumor) or
impeded CSF reabsorption or outflow (i.e., flow obstruction by
space-occupying lesions and Chiari malformation) can result in an
increase in CSF volume and ICP [14,15].
As a result of increased ICP, a physiologic response known as the
“Cushing reflex” occurs, which has classically been reported as an
increase in systolic blood pressure, bradycardia, and an irregular
(Cheyne–Stokes) breathing pattern [18–21]; however, subsequent
studies led to refinement of Cushing’s original findings [22].
Initially, both blood pressure and heart rate may rise due to sympa-
thetic activation [22–24] as MAP increases to maintain CPP. Over
time, hypertension persists in the face of elevated ICP, but heart rate
begins to decrease. The mechanism resulting in bradycardia contin-
ues to be debated with some suggesting it is a baroreceptor reflex
while others propose it is a result of intracranial compression of the
vagus nerve [24]. Finally, once the brainstem is compressed and
the respiratory center is compromised by increased ICP, irregular
breathing and even apnea (respiratory arrest) can ensue [24]. The
Cushing reflex has also been recognized in cases of decreased CPP
(< 15 mmHg) in humans [25]. As bradycardia is a late component
of the physiologic response, focusing on this symptom may result in
the patient being subjected to a prolonged period of intracranial
hypertension prior to intervention, resulting in a higher incidence
of complications [25]. Therefore, in the human literature, monitor-
ing for systemic hypertension and tachycardia as potential early
indicators of increased ICP and impaired brain perfusion has been
recommended to facilitate earlier intervention and improved
outcomes [25].
Regulation of cerebral blood flow
The brain is an organ with high metabolic demand. Despite this
high demand for energy substrates (mainly oxygen and glucose) to
maintain homeostasis, extreme fluctuations in cerebral blood flow
(CBF) are not tolerated due to the non-compliant cranium and
meninges. Thus, tight control and regulation of tissue pressure
(i.e., ICP) is required because increases in CBV will lead to increases
in ICP, and vice versa [26,27]. Several key factors contribute to
regulation of CBF including the arterial partial pressure of carbon
dioxide (PaCO2
), MAP, cerebral metabolic rate (CMR), and the
ANS [27]. For simplicity, regulators of CBF may be classified as
chemical, myogenic, and neurogenic factors [26].
Chemical regulation of cerebral blood flow
Chemical regulation involves changes in CMR, PaCO 2
, and arterial
partial pressure of oxygen (PaO 2 ). Increases in neuronal activity
lead to increased CMR, which is directly related to the change in
CBF, a phenomenon known as “flow-metabolism coupling” [26,28].
Flow-metabolism coupling is a complex physiologic process
involving metabolic, glial, neuronal, and vascular factors [26,28].
Local by-products, including potassium ions, hydrogen ions, lactate,
adenosine, and adenosine triphosphate modulate vascular tone and
likely contribute to the mechanism of neurovascular coupling [27,29].
It is thought that neurotransmitters, especially glutamate (released
with increased or excitatory neuronal activity), are the main factors
augmenting activity-induced blood flow due to the release of nitric
oxide leading to cerebral vasodilation [27,28,30]. Oxygen concen-
tration modulates the contribution of different signaling pathways,
and reduced oxygen concentration can lead to adenosine release,
contributing to vasodilation. Additionally, astrocytes also mediate
neurovascular coupling, and nerves innervating cerebral vessels
release neurotransmitters that may also be involved in this process
[26,27,30,31]. The CMR can also be influenced by the functional
state of the nervous system (i.e., awake versus sleep), and can be
extremely high during epileptic activity, for example.
A decrease in temperature will decrease CMR and CBF in ani-
mals [32–34]. More specifically, CMR decreases by 6% per degree
Celsius drop in temperature in dogs [35]. Hypothermia has been
shown to have a consistently beneficial effect on neurologic outcomes
in small and large animals after cardiac arrest [36]. Hyperthermia is
associated with the opposite effect on CMR and CBF [35]. As such,
modest hypothermia or, more importantly, the avoidance of hyper-
thermia may be a consideration in anesthetizing patients with
conditions in which elevations of CMR or CBF may be of concern.
The cerebrovasculature is uniquely and highly sensitive to
changes in PaCO2 [27,31]. An acute decrease in PaCO2 in healthy
animals leads to an increase in cerebral vascular resistance and a
decrease in CBF; conversely, an increase in PaCO2 has the opposite
effect but is of a higher magnitude (Fig. 39.6) [31]. In monkeys, a
linear relationship between both CBV and PaCO 2 and CBF and
PaCO2 was observed when PaCO2 ranged between 15–76 mmHg
[37]. In dogs, a potential maximal cerebral vasodilatory effect
occurred at between 60–70 mmHg; however, cerebrovascular
responsiveness to CO2 seems to vary depending on species, experi-
mental design, anesthetic drugs used, and CO2 levels [38].
Additionally, while a sustained decrease in PaCO2 due to prolonged
hyperventilation (approximately 5–6 h) lowers CBF to some extent,
it may return to baseline values over time because brain interstitial
pH is one of the major regulators of CBF. Brain interstitial pH ini-
tially rises with an acute decrease in PaCO2
, but then falls during
sustained hyperventilation as lactate accumulates and bicarbonate
falls [39–41]. As such, anesthetic management of intracranial
