hypertension with modest hyperventilation (discussed later) may
only be employed as a relatively temporary strategy. Furthermore,
because of the metabolic changes associated with a decrease in
PaCO2
, patients subjected to sustained hyperventilation (hypocapnia)
may be at risk of developing intracranial hypertension with restora-
tion of normocapnia as this is accompanied by CSF acidosis,
significant increases in CBF, and ultimately increased ICP. Sustained
hypoventilation (hypercapnia), once corrected to normocapnia,
may result in a significant decrease in CBF, and the patient may,
theoretically, be at risk of ischemia [26]. The change in brain extra-
cellular pH and CBF after acute changes in PaCO 2 happens because
CO 2 diffuses across the BBB [27,31]. However, changes in pH due to
metabolic acidosis (instead of respiratory acidosis) have little effect
on CBF because hydrogen ions do not cross the BBB.
The cerebrovasculature is also sensitive to changes in PaO 2
but only in hypoxic conditions (PaO2 < 60 mmHg) (Fig. 39.6),
leading to cerebral vasodilation and a rapid increase in CBF (but
not CMR) [31]. This sensitivity to PaO 2 is dependent on the PaCO2
level. For instance, hypercapnia increases cerebrovascular sensi-
tivity to hypoxia, and both have synergistic effects, but the vasodi-
latory effect of hypoxia predominates over the vasoconstrictive
effect of hypocapnia [42]. Additionally, the changes in CBF due to
oxygen seem to be related to oxygen content rather than oxygen
tension (PaO 2 ) because decreases in oxygen content from anemia
and hemodilution also result in an increase in CBF [43,44].
The mechanism involved in hypoxia-mediated cerebral vasodila-
tion may involve neurogenic (neuraxial chemoreceptors) and local
humoral factors [26,31].
The impact of hematocrit (i.e., blood viscosity) on CBF is contro-
versial [45]. Anemia results in decreased cerebral vascular resist-
ance and an increase in CBF, but as mentioned above, this response
seems to be related to the decrease in oxygen content [43]. However,
a study in rats demonstrated that increased viscosity decreased
CBF, but only in conditions where CBF was already elevated
(i.e., not in control animals) [46].
Myogenic regulation of cerebral blood flow
Myogenic regulation of CBF is related to the local vascular smooth
muscle response to changes in intraluminal pressure in the cerebro-
vasculature. An increase in MAP leads to an increase in transmural
vessel tension resulting in depolarization of vascular smooth muscle
and a reduction in vascular diameter (i.e., constriction) [27]; con-
versely, vasodilation happens when MAP and transmural tension
decrease [16]. Autoregulation of CBF is classically defined as the
ability of the brain circulation to alter its resistance to maintain
constant CBF within a range of MAP [47]. The lower and upper
limits of CBF autoregulation likely occur at approximately 70 and
150 mmHg, respectively (Fig. 39.6). Above and below this MAP
range, CBF becomes pressure-dependent and will vary linearly with
CPP [26]. There is some controversy in the literature regarding the
lower limit of CBF autoregulation and values ranging from
50–70 mmHg of MAP have been suggested [27,31,48]. The initial
characterization of the lower limit of CBF autoregulation at approx-
imately 50–60 mmHg seems to originate from Lassen’s study in
1959 [47]. One complicating factor is that some authors use CPP
instead of MAP on the x-axis [31], which would naturally bring the
lower limit value down because CPP = MAP – ICP. There is also
significant variation between species as well as the conditions
(awake versus anesthetized) and drugs used during the studies
assessing the limits of cerebral autoregulation [49]; there is certainly
not enough evidence to form conclusions regarding all drugs and
drug combinations used clinically across all species. Furthermore,
significant interindividual variation has been reported [48,49], and
it is not valid to assume that autoregulation of CBF will be preserved
at a MAP as low as 50 mmHg in an individual, in a broader popula-
tion, or every anesthetic situation. In addition, in the normal CNS,
while there is a blood flow reserve that acts as a buffer and protects
against significant reductions in blood flow (i.e., hypotension), this
reserve may be compromised in some clinical situations [48]. As
such, defining the lower threshold of MAP below which a clinical
patient is at substantial risk of ischemic injury is not easy. The
authors prefer to use 70 mmHg as the lower limit of CBF autoregu-
lation for clinical case management (Fig. 39.6).
Newer evidence suggests this topic is much more complex than
commonly presented. Cerebral autoregulation does not always
maintain 	constant 	perfusion 	through 	the 	MAP 	range 	of
70–150 mmHg, but CBF is still directly affected by changes in per-
fusion pressure [31]. CBF is only kept constant (i.e., the “classic”
description of autoregulation) with gradual changes in blood pres-
sure, as in nocturnal MAP changes or changes due to treatment for
hypertension. For rapid changes in blood pressure (i.e., over min-
utes or seconds – such as those happening during surgery), CBF is
more unstable and can undergo large, rapid fluctuations [27]. Slow
changes in blood pressure and their effect on CBF align better with
the “static autoregulation” model, whereas the impact of faster
changes on CBF is more consistent with the “dynamic autoregula-
tion” model [27,31]. Therefore, despite normal autoregulatory
mechanisms, CBF may still vary with changes in blood pressure.
One common misconception is that chronic hypertension leads to
impairment of autoregulation (i.e., that brain vessels may become
dependent on higher MAP to maintain perfusion) but treatment to
lower MAP is not associated with a decrease in CBF [27].
Additionally, the effects of arterial blood gases and blood pres-
sure are interdependent in their regulation of CBF, and it is difficult
to determine the impact of each individual parameter when they
change simultaneously [31]. For instance, dogs with severe hypo-
tension showed no change in CBF following changes in PaCO2
because the vessels had already reached maximal dilation; there-
fore, blood pressure is a critical component of CBF [31,50].
Neurogenic regulation of cerebral blood flow
Neurogenic regulation of CBF contributes to cerebral autoregulation
and can buffer surges in perfusion pressure. The cerebrovasculature
is innervated by adrenergic fibers (with epinephrine, norepinephrine,
dopamine, and neuropeptide Y as transmitters), cholinergic fibers
(with ACh, and vasoactive intestinal peptide as transmitters), and
sensory fibers (with calcitonin gene-related peptide, substance P,
and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide as transmit-
ters) as part of the sympathetic, parasympathetic, and trigeminal
nervous systems, respectively [27,31]. The exact influence of cere-
bral vasomotor nerves is not well understood. Despite some contro-
versies, the sympathetic nervous system generally prevents increases
in CBF during resting conditions and contributes to autoregulation
of CBF during rapid changes in blood pressure [27]. However, it is
difficult to assess the effects of the sympathetic nervous system in
isolation, as many other confounding variables are usually present.
Cholinergic innervation in the brain can lead to vasodilation and
further release of nitric oxide locally, but it does not seem to play a
major role in autoregulation [27]. The influence of the sympathetic
and parasympathetic nervous systems on CBF control seems to be
species-specific [31], so caution is advised when extrapolating
across species.

Luxury perfusion
Vasomotor paralysis, which is impaired ability of vessels to respond
to PaCO 2 and perfusion pressure, or a loss of regional CBF autoreg-
ulation can happen in some pathological conditions leading to
inadequate cerebral perfusion and hypoxia (i.e., ischemic stroke
and tumor) [51–53]. Therefore, regional CBF within ischemic areas
may become passively dependent on perfusion pressure, which can
result in excessive blood flow relative to local metabolic demands in
the face of normal or high perfusion pressure, a phenomenon called
“luxury perfusion syndrome” [51,54–56]. Additionally, paradoxical
flow responses can happen in some patients with these pathological
conditions following an increase or decrease in PaCO 2 [51,57].
In the case of decreased cerebral vascular resistance (i.e., increased
PaCO 2 or drugs that cause cerebral vasodilation), blood may be
shunted away from areas of vasomotor paralysis to normal areas of
the brain, a phenomenon called “intracerebral steal syndrome” [51].
On the other hand, an increase in cerebral vascular resistance
(i.e., decreased PaCO 2
) may lead to blood shunting into areas of
vasomotor paralysis, a phenomenon called “inverse intracerebral
steal” or “Robin Hood syndrome,” which could be deleterious to
normal areas of the brain [51,54].
Spinal cord physiology
The spinal cord extends rostrally from the brainstem and ends
caudally within the lumbar or sacral spinal segments, depending
on the species. Each segment of the spinal cord contains a pair
(right and left) of spinal nerves that contain both afferent (sensory)
and efferent (motor) information. Spinal cord blood flow (SCBF) is
maintained via autoregulation when MAP is between 60–150 mmHg
[58]. When MAP falls below 60 mmHg, SCBF is significantly
reduced in dogs. Interestingly, SCBF seems to decrease with dobu-
tamine infusions that increase MAP in healthy horses, which is
concerning as low spinal cord perfusion could predispose the
animal to myelopathy [59,60]. In healthy horses anesthetized with
isoflurane, a significant decrease in SCBF was found with MAP
levels of 100 mmHg, specifically in the thoracolumbar spinal cord
region [60]. Hemodilution increases SCBF if the patient is normo-
tensive; however, in cases of hypotension, there may be increased
risk of ischemia due to limited ability to vasodilate [45]. In situa-
tions of acute blood loss representing approximately 20% of total
blood volume, no changes in SCBF were detected; however, when
tetracaine was administered in the subarachnoid space, a signifi-
cant decrease in SCBF was detected [61].
The response of SCBF to oxygen and carbon dioxide levels is very
similar to that of the brain. Hypoxia significantly increases SCBF
with maximal flow reached at PaO2 levels of 30–40 mmHg [62].
Additionally, hypocapnia decreases SCBF while hypercapnia
increases SCBF, with PaCO2 levels of 85 mmHg resulting in double
the normocapnic SCBF [9,62].
Studies evaluating the relationship between CSF and SCBF
revealed no significant change in blood flow with changes in the
volume of CSF; however, elevations in CSF pressure significantly
reduced SCBF [63].
Effects of vasoactive drugs, sedatives,
and anesthetics
Vasoactive drugs
Most drugs used to decrease blood pressure (i.e., sodium nitroprus-
side and calcium channel blockers) lead to cerebral vasodilation
but CBF may increase or be maintained [64–66]. The effects of
catecholamine agonists and antagonists on cerebral physiology
depend on baseline blood pressure, the magnitude of changes in
blood pressure, autoregulation, and the status of the BBB [26]. In
general, in cases where autoregulation is preserved but baseline
blood pressure is outside autoregulatory limits, drug-induced
increases in blood pressure will typically increase CBF. If baseline
blood pressure is within the limits of autoregulation, drug-induced
increases in blood pressure may not significantly change CBF
because of activation of normal autoregulatory mechanisms [26].
There is also significant variation in drug effects on CBF (in various
species) reported in the literature. Differences in study methodology
undoubtedly contribute to this variation and should be taken into
consideration when reviewing studies and interpreting their results.
Like anesthetics, the effect of vasoactive agents may be species-
dependent. Use of phenylephrine does not seem to change CBF
or ICP in dogs but can increase CBF in rats, rabbits, and lambs
[64,67–73]. Use of norepinephrine and epinephrine resulted in no
significant change in CBF, ICP, and cerebral oxygen utilization, but
dopamine caused an increase in all these parameters in sheep [74].
However, CBF was not changed after dopamine administration in
young rabbits and monkeys [71]. Additionally, the effect of epineph-
rine and norepinephrine on CBF and cerebral metabolic rate of
oxygen (CMRO2
) was dependent on the status of the BBB in dogs,
where no change was noted with an intact BBB but increases in CBF
and CMRO 2 were observed with increased BBB permeability [75].
The effects of β-adrenergic agonists seem to be dose- and species-
dependent. At clinically relevant doses, dobutamine and dopamine
do not seem to change CBF and CMRO2 in monkeys but cause a
dose- dependent decrease in CBF in dogs [76,77].
Sedatives and anesthetics
Anesthetic and sedative drugs can negatively interfere with CBF,
CMR, and the electrophysiology of the brain; therefore, knowledge
of these effects and how to modify them to improve clinical
outcomes is crucial for better patient care. Typically, CBF and
CBV vary in parallel; however, there are some clinical situations
(i.e., cerebral ischemia) where they can change independently [78].
Furthermore, there are some cases where the magnitude of change
in CBF may be less than that of CBV [79]. Most acute anesthetic-
induced changes in ICP occur due to changes in CBV [80]. Thus, it
is important to note that anesthetic-mediated CBF changes do not
necessarily predict their impact on ICP because they may not be
accompanied by similar changes in CBV [80,81]. Ideally, under-
standing drug-related impacts on CPP is more important than
potential isolated changes in CBF and ICP. Generally, most anes-
thetic drugs cause decreases in CBF and CMR, and autoregulation
and CO2 responsiveness are maintained with injectable anesthetics.
Opioids
Usually, the direct effects of opioids on CBF, CMRO2
, CBV, and ICP
are minimal and CO 2 responsiveness is typically preserved [82–84].
Most opioids cause a decrease in CBF and CBV and a decrease or no
change in ICP [79,82,85–87]. However, there are conflicting results
in the literature regarding the effects of some opioids, such as sufen-
tanil and remifentanil. Some studies involving sufentanil demon-
strate a transient increase in CBF and CMRO2
, but minimal effects
or a decrease in ICP [88]; others describe a decrease or no change
in CBF and CMRO 2 with no change in ICP in veterinary species
[82,86]. In humans, a dose-dependent increase in regional CBF has
been shown with remifentanil [89]. The type of anesthetic protocol
or the lack of general anesthesia (e.g., use of opioid alone or opioid

-- 848 of 1450 --

Chapter 39: Physiology, Pathophysiology, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Neurologic Disease 	833
with nitrous oxide only) may have contributed to some of this
variation and, in general, sufentanil and remifentanil are not
considered contraindicated in neuroanesthesia.
Nonetheless, indirect increases in ICP due to hypoventilation
and hypercapnia associated with opioid administration need to be
prevented in certain clinical neurological patients (i.e., traumatic
brain injury and space-occupying brain lesions). Sudden decreases
in MAP that may accompany bolus doses of potent opioids in
certain species should also be prevented or corrected as they may
be associated with transient reductions in CPP and increases
in ICP [90].
In addition, the systemic effects that may accompany administra-
tion of some opioids can have adverse impacts on the CNS. For
instance, histamine release associated with administration of mor-
phine or meperidine can result in cerebral vasodilation and an
increase in CBV and ICP, while vomiting associated with initial
administration of morphine or hydromorphone may lead to an
increase in ICP.
α2 - Adrenergic receptor agonists
Xylazine produces a dose-dependent and transient decrease in ICP
in dogs with increased ICP due to subarachnoid hemorrhage [69].
Xylazine did not change ICP in horses anesthetized with pentobar-
bital [91], and decreased ICP in conscious horses [92]. A more
recent study with normocapnic, healthy horses anesthetized with
isoflurane and lidocaine constant rate infusion demonstrated a
decrease in ICP and an increase in CPP following xylazine bolus
administration but no change in ICP following administration of
xylazine in conscious horses [93]. Lowering the head is a common
characteristic of sedation with α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists;
however, head height does not seem to correlate with ICP in the
conscious horse, likely due to active compensatory changes in cer-
ebral vascular resistance to maintain CBV and CBF [94]. In general,
one should prevent lowering of the head in anesthetized animals
because anesthetic drugs may impair normal physiologic regulation.
Lowering of the head below the level of the heart in the anesthetized
horse was associated with a significant increase in ICP and a
decrease in CBF, which could potentially predispose the animal to
ischemia; spinal cord blood flow values were very low, but unaf-
fected by head-down positioning in anesthetized horses [17].
Dexmedetomidine has been shown to decrease CBF with little to
no effect on CMRO2 in isoflurane-anesthetized dogs [95,96]. This
decrease in CBF is likely related to α2
- adrenergic receptor-mediated
vasoconstriction of cerebral vessels [95] and decreased cerebral
metabolism associated with reduced brain activity [97]. In healthy
piglets anesthetized with propofol–remifentanil total intravenous
anesthesia (TIVA), the addition of dexmedetomidine resulted in a
significant decrease in cerebral oxygenation when blood pressure
was low, but cerebral perfusion and oxygenation were not affected
when blood pressure was normal [98], again demonstrating the
importance of blood pressure on cerebral dynamics. In dogs anes-
thetized with isoflurane, no change in ICP and an increase in CPP
was reported following medetomidine administration [99].
The effects of α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists on CBF, CBV, ICP,
or CPP in animals with different underlying neurologic diseases
have not been well studied, but based on data from healthy animals,
their use seems reasonable. However, reversal with the α2
-adrenergic
receptor antagonist tolazoline has been shown to increase CBF and
ICP [69]; therefore, in situations where increased ICP is a concern,
α2 - adrenergic receptor agonists should be used with caution as
reversal of sedation may impact ICP.
Phenothiazines
The use of acepromazine in dogs with a history of seizures or those
prone to seizures (e.g., myelography) is controversial. Despite older
literature suggesting acepromazine is contraindicated in these
patients, recent studies using clinical doses of acepromazine in dogs
indicate no increased seizure risk [100–102]. However, the drug can
increase CBV (35–56% above control) in dogs [103], so its use
should be avoided in patients with high ICP. As with all anesthetic
agents, hemodynamic effects (i.e., vasodilation and hypotension)
are possible so blood pressure should be monitored, and hypoten-
sion treated to maintain MAP within a range consistent with physi-
ologic cerebral autoregulation.
Benzodiazepines
In general, benzodiazepines are considered to be safe agents with
few hemodynamic effects. At clinically relevant doses, midazolam
and diazepam decrease CBF (approximately 50–60% below control)
and EEG activity, and CMRO 2 either decreases or remains
unchanged depending on the species [87,104,105]. In a hypoxic
model in dogs, midazolam provided greater neuroprotection than
diazepam but less than pentobarbital [104].
The effects of the benzodiazepine antagonist flumazenil on CBF
and CMRO2 are transient (lasting only between 15–30 min) and
dose- dependent when administered following midazolam in
dogs [105]. At low doses (0.0025 mg/kg), administration resulted in
an increase in CSF pressure and reversal of the reduction in EEG
activity and CMRO2 produced by midazolam; while administration
of higher doses (0.01–0.16 mg/kg) resulted in decreased cerebral
vascular resistance, an increase in CBF and CSF pressure, but no
change in CPP [105]. Much higher doses of flumazenil (1 mg/kg)
can result in a more profound increase in CBF and ICP and a
decrease in MAP in dogs [106]. Use of flumazenil alone (i.e., inde-
pendent of midazolam) or in dogs that received midazolam but also
had high CSF pressure did not result in the changes noted
above [105]. In humans sedated with midazolam with traumatic
brain injury and poorly controlled ICP, flumazenil resulted in a
marked increase in ICP and a decrease in CPP [107]. Therefore,
flumazenil should be used with caution in patients for whom
increased ICP would be detrimental.
Lidocaine
Lidocaine administration results in dose-dependent decreases
in EEG activity and CMRO2 [108]. At a clinically relevant dose
(3 mg/kg), it has minimal effect on CBF and cerebral vascular
resistance and induces only a transient decrease in CMRO2 [108].
A lidocaine bolus can be used as an adjunct treatment to prevent
an acute increase in ICP during craniotomy and endotracheal tube
suctioning [109,110]. A cough reflex during endotracheal intuba-
tion may result in increased ICP [111]. In dogs, topical lidocaine
(0.4 mg/kg) applied to the larynx was insufficient to prevent the
cough reflex, but IV lidocaine (1.5–2 mg/kg) was effective [112–114];
however, IV fentanyl was superior to IV lidocaine for cough reflex
suppression [113]. In cats, an IV fentanyl bolus associated with topi-
cal laryngeal lidocaine application was more effective at decreasing
the cough reflex than topical lidocaine alone [115]. Despite the
cough-suppressing effect of lidocaine, a study in humans showed
that IV lidocaine was unable to completely prevent the increase
in ICP associated with endotracheal intubation in neurosurgical
patients [116].
Pretreatment with lidocaine has been shown to attenuate acute
hypertension and an increase in ICP, as well as increase the recovery

-- 849 of 1450 --

834 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
of neural function after acute cerebral ischemia induced by air
embolism in cats [117]. Intravenous lidocaine has also been shown
to have beneficial effects on cortical ischemia and electrophysiologic
activity in injured feline brains [118,119]. Careful attention to the
dose of lidocaine, with cautious consideration of species differences,
is necessary to avoid systemic toxicity and associated detrimental
CNS effects (i.e., seizures) [108].
Barbiturates
Barbiturates cause a decrease in CBF, CMRO2
, and ICP, and maintain
cerebrovascular reactivity to CO2
, but ventilation should be con-
trolled in patients where increases in ICP are contraindicated due to
the potential for hypoventilation/apnea leading to hypercapnia
and increased ICP [26,120–122]. Additionally, the anticonvulsant
properties of thiobarbiturates are potentially beneficial in epileptics
or in patients undergoing procedures such as myelography where
seizures are a possible complication [120]. However, barbiturate
anesthesia is commonly associated with longer recoveries from
anesthesia compared to other agents such as propofol, which may
be problematic in neurosurgical patients as it may significantly
delay postoperative neurologic evaluations.
Propofol
Propofol administration results in decreased EEG activity, CBF,
CMRO2
, and ICP, while maintaining cerebrovascular reactivity to
CO 2 similar to barbiturates [70,123–125]. However, at very high
infusion rates (0.8 mg/kg/min), propofol can result in decreased
CPP in dogs [70]. The decreased CBF and cerebrovascular reactiv-
ity to CO2 during a hypocapnic challenge from propofol was not
statistically significant when compared to isoflurane anesthesia in
dogs, though the authors suggested this could be due to small sam-
ple size [126]. In humans, a propofol bolus before endotracheal tube
suctioning in patients with severe brain disease reduced the cough
response, reduced the intracranial hypertensive response, and
improved long-term prognosis [127].
Propofol can cause myoclonus in dogs which may be related to its
antagonist actions at glycine receptors in the spinal cord and brain-
stem [128]. Propofol has been shown to be effective at managing
seizures following surgical treatment of portosystemic shunts and
may be effective at controlling status epilepticus resistant to con-
ventional therapy (i.e., benzodiazepines and barbiturates) in dogs
and cats [129,130].
The effect of different intravenous anesthetics including propofol
(as well as methohexital and ketamine) in two feline models of
brain edema revealed that all drugs studied were effective at
decreasing ICP in a space-occupying lesion model (mimicking
vasogenic brain edema), likely because a large volume of brain tis-
sue was still viable and the drug-induced decrease in CMRO2
resulted in vasoconstriction and a decrease in ICP [131]. However,
administration using a different model, cytotoxic brain edema with
diffuse intracellular damage, resulted in no drug-induced change in
ICP, likely because autoregulation of the cerebral vasculature was
impaired in this model.
Alfaxalone
Alfaxalone was previously manufactured in a formulation contain-
ing alfadolone in Cremophor EL®, and its use was discontinued
due to severe side effects. Most of the studies in the literature asso-
ciated with cerebral metabolism and dynamics involve this previ-
ous formulation and show decreases in CBF, CMRO 2
, and ICP
while maintaining cerebrovascular reactivity to CO 2 [111,132,133].
More recent studies using the current formulation of alfaxalone
(in cyclodextrin) also show a decrease in CBF [126,134]. The CBF
was significantly lower following alfaxalone total intravenous anes-
thesia (TIVA) when compared to anesthesia with isoflurane [126].
Additionally, alfaxalone TIVA was associated with greater cerebro-
vascular reactivity to CO2 during hypocapnic challenge compared
to isoflurane and propofol, which could represent an advantage
when adjustments in ventilation to decrease CO 2 are performed
under anesthesia in patients with increased ICP [126].
Etomidate
Etomidate administration results in significant decreases in CBF,
CMRO2 , and ICP, and maintenance of cerebrovascular reactivity
to CO 2 [132,135,136]. The cerebral metabolic effects (e.g., decreased
CMRO2 ) of etomidate are secondary to its effects on neuronal
function, like many other anesthetics including thiopental and
isoflurane [135,137,138]. In addition, etomidate seems to be a
potent direct cerebral vasoconstrictor, independent of its effect on
CMRO 2 [135].
Etomidate has the advantage of providing good hemodynamic
stability, seems to preserve the cerebral metabolic state even in
the face of hypotension [139], and is effective in decreasing ICP
with minimal change in CPP in patients with intracranial space-
occupying lesions and traumatic brain injury [132,140].
Myoclonus that may be observed during etomidate induction is
not associated with epileptiform activity on EEG in humans [141].
However, etomidate should be avoided in epileptic patients because
it can precipitate EEG epileptic activity in humans [142]. Furthermore,
myoclonus in some species may resemble retching, theoretically
leading to an increase in ICP. Co-administration with agents such
as benzodiazepines may prevent or attenuate these effects.
Ketamine
Compared to other intravenous anesthetics, ketamine produces
unique effects in various body systems (e.g., stimulation of the
cardiovascular system and minimal respiratory depression), and its
effects on cerebral metabolism and hemodynamics are no excep-
tion. Ketamine can cause increases in CBF, CMRO2
, and ICP but
autoregulation seems to be maintained and CO2 responsiveness
preserved [143–145]; however, its effects are not necessarily
straightforward. Increased CBF and ICP have only been demon-
strated in spontaneously ventilating animals; in animals where
ventilation was controlled, decreased CBF and variable effects
on CMRO2 (either decreased or increased) have been observed
[146–148]. In addition, when compared to other intravenous anes-
thetics such as alfaxalone, ketamine resulted in significantly higher
CBF in monkeys [134]. In healthy dogs, ketamine was reported to
increase CBF in some areas of the brain (parietal, occipital, and
thalamic regions) but not in others (frontal cortex) [149]; however,
increases and decreases in different brain regions have been reported
in various studies with different doses of ketamine in both dogs
and cats [150,151]. Regardless, potential increases in CMRO 2 and
decreases in CBF (i.e., dissociation of cerebral oxygen demand
and supply) could increase the risk of cerebral ischemia [152].
Despite the controversy in the literature regarding the impact of
ketamine on brain physiology and dynamics; some authors dis-
courage its use in patients with a history of seizures and patients
with space-occupying lesions, closed-head traumatic injuries, and
other conditions associated with high ICP [153]. However, a retro-
spective study in humans with increased ICP showed that use of
ketamine in these patients was associated with lower mortality rates

-- 850 of 1450 --

Chapter 39: Physiology, Pathophysiology, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Neurologic Disease 	835
compared to etomidate and midazolam, and the authors suggested
that its use should be considered in these patients without concern
for worsening outcomes [154]. The combination of drugs that
depress cerebral metabolism, such as midazolam or thiopental,
with ketamine, prevented the increase in CBF, CMRO 2
, and ICP but
did not change ketamine’s effect on MAP or the EEG [143,152].
Additionally, subanesthetic doses of ketamine (2 mg/kg) did not
have any significant effects on CBF, CMRO 2 , or the EEG in mechan-
ically ventilated pigs [147] and were associated with decreased ICP
and increased CPP in a feline space-occupying lesion model of
brain edema [131]. Ketamine has neuroprotective properties and its
use in combination with other sedatives has recently been proposed
as a safe and effective protocol for sedation/anesthesia and analgesia in
neurocritical human patients (e.g., traumatic brain injury) [155,156].
EEG activity increases following ketamine administration [157].
Seizure-like activity has been reported when ketamine was used in
sedation/anesthetic protocols in dogs; however, it was not possible
to rule out other causes for this abnormal activity [158,159].
Conversely, in cats, ketamine did not induce convulsant activity but
had mild antiepileptic effects instead [157]. In fact, ketamine has
been reported as a treatment for status epilepticus and cluster
seizures in veterinary patients [160–162].
Inhalation anesthetics
Inhalation anesthetics generally result in dose-dependent decreases
in CMR, however, the net effect on CBF is a balance between
decreases caused by reduced CMR and increases due to direct cer-
ebral vasodilation. This varies depending on the inhalant anesthetic
used and the concentration delivered. Typically, with isoflurane,
there is minimal effect on CBF if the inhalant concentration
remains at or below the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC);
at concentrations above 1 MAC, vasodilatory effects predominate
and CBF may increase or remain unchanged despite CMR
decreases [163–166]. Additionally, inhalation anesthetics cause a
dose- dependent decrease in MAP and CPP in dogs, cats, and horses
[166–169]. The CO 2 responsiveness of the cerebral circulation
is preserved or enhanced with inhalant anesthetics [38,170]. The
addition of nitrous oxide to other inhalant anesthetics produces an
increase in CBF and ICP and either no change or an increase in
CMRO2 in animals [171–173].
The effect on ICP is variable depending on the inhalant anesthetic
used. Enflurane above 1 MAC produced EEG and motor evidence
of seizure activity [163]. In dogs, halothane and enflurane at
approximately 1 MAC increased CBV and ICP for over 3 h [174].
On the other hand, isoflurane at approximately 1 MAC also
increased CBV for over 3 h, but the increase in ICP was short-lived
(approximately 20 min) [79]. Additionally, in an intracranial mass
model in dogs, the CSF pressure-lowering effect of 4 h of hypocap-
nia was sustained with isoflurane but not with halothane or enflu-
rane [175]. Desflurane resulted in greater increases in CSF pressure
and CBF when compared to isoflurane during normocapnia
[176,177]. In a study comparing isoflurane and sevoflurane at dif-
ferent MAC multiples (1, 1.5, and 2 MAC) in normocapnic healthy
dogs, ICP did not change significantly at different MAC multiples
and was similar between the inhalants; however, at higher concen-
trations (2 MAC), CPP was better maintained with sevoflurane
compared to isoflurane [178]. Conversely, in rats with diffuse
brain injury, sevoflurane anesthesia resulted in higher ICP and
lower CPP values when compared to isoflurane [179]. Therefore,
isoflurane or sevoflurane may be better inhalant choices for patients
at risk of intracranial hypertension, but when ICP is persistently
increased, inhalation anesthetics should be replaced by intravenous
anesthetics [180]. Injectable anesthetics, such as propofol, preserve
autoregulation better when compared to inhalants (including
isoflurane, sevoflurane, and desflurane) [181,182]. Additionally,
when isoflurane anesthesia was compared to propofol TIVA in dogs
with intracranial disease, propofol anesthesia resulted in higher
MAP (and potentially higher CPP), decreased requirements for
dopamine, and better recovery quality [183].
Neuromuscular blocking agents
Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents generally have
minimal direct effects on the CNS, although indirect effects may
occur. Laudanosine, a metabolite of atracurium, may be epilepto-
genic and is likely linked to the EEG evidence of cerebral arousal
noted in dogs following high dose of atracurium (1–2.5 mg/kg IV);
however, this cerebral stimulation was not accompanied by increases
in CBF, CMRO 2
, and ICP [184]. Atracurium has the potential to
stimulate histamine release and could, theoretically, decrease CPP
due to decreased MAP or increased ICP; however, this has not been
demonstrated in the literature [184,185]. Pancuronium, vecuronium,
and atracurium administration to anesthetized animals resulted in
no change in CBF, CMRO2
, ICP, and CPP [184,186,187]. Similarly,
rocuronium and vecuronium were not associated with changes in
ICP or CPP in human neurosurgical patients [188].
Depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents, such as succinyl-
choline and suxamethonium, can increase ICP due to muscle
fasciculations leading to increased CBF and CBV [187,189,190];
therefore, their use is contraindicated in patients at risk of intracra-
nial hypertension.
Pathophysiology and anesthetic management
of specific neurological conditions
Central nervous system conditions
Intracranial hypertension
Several neurological conditions including intracranial tumors, trau-
matic brain injury (TBI), meningoencephalitis, and hemorrhage can
present with intracranial hypertension or high ICP [191–195], and
restoration and maintenance of normal ICP and CPP are crucial to
improving outcomes [194,196]. A comprehensive discussion of the
prognostics, signs, and management of these patients is beyond the
scope of this chapter; however, the reader can find recent publica-
tions on these subjects elsewhere [193,194,197–199]. Anesthesia for
imaging and/or surgery is required for many of these patients. It is
important to note any changes in a patient’s neurological status
before anesthesia that may be indicative of increased ICP including
mentation (i.e., obtunded, stuporous, or comatose), brainstem
reflexes (i.e., abnormal pupillary light reflex with or without other
cranial nerve deficits), and gait abnormalities including opisthotonos
postures [3]. In addition, it is important to note cardiopulmonary
status in general (i.e., potential neurogenic pulmonary edema and
cardiovascular instability/arrhythmias) and measure preanesthetic
arterial blood pressure [197,200]. Often, but not always, patients
with intracranial hypertension will present with systemic hyperten-
sion (i.e., Cushing reflex, discussed earlier), which is a compensa-
tory mechanism to maintain CPP. Cerebral herniation may be
detected on magnetic resonance imaging and may occur at one of
several locations (foramen magnum, subfalcine, and rostral and
caudal transtentorial) or via a skull defect (Fig. 39.2B) [201].
Guidelines for managing blood pressure in anesthetized patients
with intracranial hypertension are scarce in the literature, especially

-- 851 of 1450 --

836 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
in veterinary medicine. In human patients following acute CNS
injury (i.e., TBI) or those with intracranial masses, it is recommended
to maintain CPP and MAP at normal or high-normal levels because
CBF may be low in certain regions of the brain and the autoregula-
tory response to hypotension may not be preserved in all areas [180].
Therefore, even MAP values in the range of 60–70 mmHg may
predispose these patients to cerebral ischemia, and higher blood
pressures may be required to ensure appropriate cerebral perfu-
sion [202–204]. On the other hand, arterial hypertension could pre-
dispose the patient to increased ICP, potential cerebral edema, and
in cases of intracranial procedures, hemorrhage in the perioperative
period [205–207].
Hypercapnia causes an increase in CBF, CBV, and ICP [37,38,
91,168]. Therefore, controlled ventilation of patients with high ICP
(to achieve low-normal PaCO 2 between 35 and 40 mmHg) is
important and should be instituted immediately after induction of
anesthesia and continued until extubation to prevent hypercapnia
and further increases in ICP with potential decreased CPP during
anesthesia. Controlled ventilation can be a useful tool to manage
ICP in patients with intracranial hypertension. Hyperventilation
(i.e., hypocapnia) can decrease CBF and ICP and help reduce acute
brain swelling, as well as prevent herniation or reduce brain bulk to
facilitate surgical access [153,180]. However, the use of hyperventi-
lation remains controversial, especially in hypotensive patients and
those with pathological brain conditions associated with inadequate
perfusion and hypoxia (i.e., ischemic stroke, tumor, and TBI).
Hyperventilation and hypocapnia can lead to increased cerebral
vascular resistance which may result in shunting of blood from
normal areas of the brain to affected areas (i.e., areas of vasomotor
paralysis); this is known as “inverse intracerebral steal” (discussed
earlier) and could potentially lead to ischemia of normal areas of
the brain [51,54,57,208]. Additionally, hyperventilation cannot
result in a sustained decrease in CBF as brain interstitial pH drops
during prolonged hyperventilation (5–6 h) due to increasing lactate
and decreasing bicarbonate levels, leading to a return of CBF to
baseline [39–41]. Furthermore, periods of sustained hyperventila-
tion may put the patient at risk of a significant increase in ICP upon
restoration of normocapnia, and the increase in PaCO2 should be
allowed to happen very gradually [180].
Along with preventing hypercapnia and maintaining adequate
blood pressure (i.e., avoiding both hypotension and hypertension),
other important strategies in patients with elevated ICP include
avoiding increases in CBF associated with inadequate oxygenation/
hypoxia which may exacerbate intracranial hypertension (Fig. 39.6).
Patients should be preoxygenated before induction of anesthesia
and administered oxygen supplementation post-extubation as
needed. In addition, mechanical increases in ICP should be avoided
through careful handling, positioning, and perianesthetic manage-
ment. This includes positioning the head above the heart, avoiding
flexion or rotation of the neck, avoiding pressure on the neck (e.g.,
neck leads or jugular venous occlusion), avoiding excessive positive
end-expiratory pressure during controlled ventilation, preventing
vomiting (after premedication and during recovery from anesthesia),
preventing coughing (during intubation, suctioning of airway,
and extubation), and providing a smooth anesthetic recovery
overall [14,17,42,111,197].
As discussed previously, most sedatives and injectable anesthetics
will contribute to decreases in CBF and ICP. In general, premedica-
tion with a non-emetogenic opioid and benzodiazepine is consid-
ered the safest option. There is some controversy regarding the use
of α2 - adrenergic receptor agonists in this patient population due to
their cardiovascular effects (i.e., bradycardia, hypertension, and
decreased cardiac output) [95,204,209]. However, dexmedetomi-
dine seems to have neuroprotective effects [210,211] and appears to
be safe in human neurocritical patients, including those with TBI
[212–214]. In dogs, dexmedetomidine has also been administered
during intracranial surgeries and resulted in similar outcomes
compared to opioid-based protocols [215]; however, further inves-
tigation in veterinary patients with high ICP is warranted.
For induction of anesthesia, the use of propofol is considered
safe in patients with high ICP; however, doses should be carefully
titrated to avoid hypotension, minimize respiratory depression,
and prevent prolonged recoveries, especially if propofol is used for
TIVA in cats [216]. While etomidate provides excellent cardiovas-
cular stability, it may cause cortisol suppression and potentially
induce myoclonus, nausea, and vomiting [217], which are undesirable
in this population of patients. Etomidate administration has also
been shown to increase the risk of cerebral hypoxia in the setting of
cerebral ischemia [218], so other options for induction of anesthe-
sia are recommended in such patients. Information on cerebral
dynamics following alfaxalone (with cyclodextrin) administration
is scarce. In a study involving healthy dogs, alfaxalone TIVA resulted
in similar CBF values to propofol TIVA and better-maintained CO2
responsiveness to hypocapnia [126]. However, further investigation
is required before alfaxalone can be recommended in veterinary
patients with high ICP. The use of ketamine remains controversial,
as described in the previous section. While not historically recom-
mended for use in this patient population, recent studies in humans
with neurological conditions causing high ICP (i.e., TBI) suggest
ketamine may be appropriate when combined with other sedatives/
anesthetics because of its positive cardiopulmonary effects, mini-
mal effect on ICP, and positive effect on CPP [155,156,209].
While more studies in veterinary medicine involving neurocritical
patients are warranted, subanesthetic doses of ketamine appear to
be safe [131,147,209].
Avoiding or minimizing agents that increase ICP and decrease
CPP (i.e., inhalation anesthetics) is advisable in patients with per-
sistently increased ICP (i.e., patients with large intracranial tumors
or signs of brain herniation and TBI patients with an expanding
mass lesion), and the use of TIVA for maintenance of anesthesia is
preferable. Administration of an IV lidocaine bolus (topical lido-
caine in cats) or IV fentanyl bolus prior to endotracheal intubation
to prevent coughing should be considered [112–115]. In addition,
the use of IV lidocaine as an adjunct intraoperatively has been
shown to prevent acute increases in ICP during craniotomy and has
other beneficial effects in models of cerebral ischemia [109,117–119].
Even though some analgesics, such as opioids, can cause respiratory
depression (hypercapnia) and an increase in ICP, it is important to
recognize that pain itself can contribute to increases in CBF and
potentially ICP, and analgesics such as opioids can attenuate this
effect [219]. Therefore, analgesics should not be withheld in painful
patients (i.e., TBI) and should be administered to those undergoing
painful procedures such as craniotomies.
Patient monitoring is critical as hypoventilation and/or hypoten-
sion resulting from the use of sedatives, analgesics, or injectable and
inhalation anesthetics could lead to further increases in ICP and
decreases in CPP [82,90,98]. Overall, use of short-acting drugs and/
or low, titrated doses in a balanced anesthetic technique is recom-
mended because some of these patients, especially those undergoing
long procedures such as craniotomies, may experience prolonged
recoveries and the antagonism of sedative agents (i.e., α2
- adrenergic
receptor agonists and benzodiazepines) may precipitate an increase

-- 852 of 1450 --

Chapter 39: Physiology, Pathophysiology, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Neurologic Disease 	837
in ICP and a decrease in CPP [69,105–107]. Even if seizures were
not previously reported, it is important to monitor for signs of
seizure activity; patients with TBI, intracranial neoplasia, or any
intracranial disease process affecting the prosencephalon may
develop seizure activity in the perianesthetic period.
Diligent monitoring of patients with suspected or confirmed
intracranial hypertension during general anesthesia is essential, and
should include body temperature, electrocardiography, capnogra-
phy, pulse oximetry, and ideally invasive blood pressure and arterial
blood gases (PaCO2 and PaO2 ). Intravenous fluid administration to
maintain euvolemia is advisable but excessive fluid administration
(leading to increased central venous pressure, decreased venous
outflow, and potentially increased ICP and decreased CPP) and use
of fluids that reduce serum osmolarity should be avoided due to the
potential risk of cerebral edema [14,220]. In the case of intraopera-
tive hemorrhage requiring administration of large fluid volumes
(e.g., during a craniotomy), the combination of crystalloids with
colloids or blood products may be appropriate [180].
Hyperosmolar therapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline is the
primary tool for pharmacologic management of acute elevations
in ICP (e.g., TBI, edema secondary to tumor, or intracerebral hem-
orrhage). These osmotic agents decrease brain tissue volume by
removing free water from normal brain tissue [194,195]. Mannitol
can have several undesirable side effects including diuresis and
volume depletion, hypotension, electrolyte disturbances (transient
decreases in sodium and chloride, and increases in potassium), and
rebound cerebral edema. With repeated mannitol use, serum osmo-
lality should be monitored and maintained at or below 320 mOsm/L,
and its use should be avoided in patients with renal disease (due to
potential risk of acute renal failure), congestive heart failure, and
hypovolemia [194,195,221,222]. The ICP lowering dose of mannitol
is 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 10–20 min and no more than three boluses
should be administered in a 24-h period to minimize side
effects [195,222]. As mannitol may crystallize at room temperature,
crystalized preparations should be warmed to approximately 37 °C
(99 °F) and administered using an in-line filter or by using filter
needles [222].
Hypertonic saline is another hyperosmolar treatment option
with several advantages over mannitol including increased
MAP and CPP, enhanced microcirculation, and anti-inflammatory
effects [194,197]. However, it can also be associated with undesirable
side effects including electrolyte disturbances (sustained hyperna-
tremia and hyperchloremia), rebound cerebral edema, and hyper-
chloremic metabolic acidosis [194,195,221]. It should be avoided in
patients with congestive heart failure and renal failure [194,195].
The recommended dose of hypertonic saline is 4 mL/kg (7.2%) or
5.4 mL/kg (3%) over 15–20 min [195,204]. Comparison of these
two hyperosmolar agents for treatment of intracranial hypertension
in humans yielded mixed results regarding efficacy with no signifi-
cant difference in clinical neurological outcome between treatments
[223–226]. In summary, there is no consensus in the literature
regarding which hyperosmolar agent is the best choice in this
patient population, but hypertonic saline is usually recommended
over mannitol in hypovolemic patients [195,197,222,227]. In any
case, careful monitoring of volume status, electrolytes, and acid–
base parameters should be performed when using hyperosmolar
agents [197,221].
The use of steroids in patients with TBI has been associated with
increased mortality and is not recommended in this population
[197,228]. Steroids, however, can limit the formation of cerebral
edema and attenuate ICP increases in patients with intracranial
tumors and are indicated for this purpose, including in the periop-
erative period (i.e., during craniotomies) [229–231].
Seizures
Generalized seizure activity is associated with a marked increase in
CBF and CMR, with systemic and cerebral acidosis and potential
decreases in PaO2 and increases in PaCO2 and ICP [232–234].
While idiopathic epilepsy is the most common cause of seizures in
dogs, other etiologies including structural epilepsy and reactive
seizures are possible [235]. Structural epilepsy includes neoplasia,
infectious and immune-mediated disease, TBI, congenital malfor-
mations, vascular lesions (strokes), and degenerative diseases.
Reactive seizures include toxin ingestion, nutritional deficits, and
metabolic derangements. A comprehensive review of etiopathogen-
esis, treatment, and prognosis of patients with seizures is beyond
the scope of this chapter, but recent publications on these subjects
are available elsewhere [199,235–238].
Anesthesia for diagnostic imaging and/or surgery may be
required for patients with a history of seizures. While seizures can
happen at any point in the perianesthetic period, they are uncommon
during the maintenance phase of anesthesia [239,240]. It is impor-
tant to know which antiepileptic drugs the patient is receiving
before anesthesia and continue these medications in the perianes-
thetic period. Some older-generation antiepileptic drugs, such as
phenytoin, phenobarbital, and primidone, have important drug
interactions relevant to the anesthetist including the induction of
cytochrome P450 enzymes, but that is not the case for the newer
antiepileptic drugs, gabapentin and levetiracetam [240]. In addition
to understanding potential drug interactions, it is also important to
know the anticonvulsant properties of sedatives and anesthetics and
take this into account when designing anesthetic protocols for these
patients. Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and propofol are safe drugs
to use in patients with a history of seizures, and they can be used
to treat status epilepticus [129,130,241]. As discussed earlier,
acepromazine use remains controversial in patients with a seizure
history, though it is generally considered to be safe. Many opioids
are associated with reports of myoclonus and/or seizures, especially
alfentanil [242–245]. Alfaxalone can produce myoclonus, but it has
been shown to have anticonvulsant effects [246,247]. Etomidate
should probably be avoided in patients with a history of seizures,
especially in epileptic patients [142,241]. The use of ketamine is
controversial, but in general, its use in patients with seizures appears
to be safe, and it can be used to treat status epilepticus and cluster
seizures [157,160–162]. Regarding inhalation anesthetics precipi-
tating seizure activity, enflurane has been most commonly impli-
cated [163]; however, seizure activity in humans has also been
reported following anesthesia with sevoflurane [248,249]. Thus,
isoflurane is probably the best choice of inhalation anesthetic in
patients with a history of seizures and has been utilized in cases of
refractory status epilepticus in humans [250].
A recent review did not find evidence to support a reduction in
the risk of late seizures or mortality rate with the prophylactic use of
anticonvulsants in humans following TBI [251]. There is no con-
sensus on this matter in veterinary medicine, but if seizures happen,
prompt treatment is required and can be accomplished with barbi-
turates, benzodiazepines, or other potent anticonvulsants such as
levetiracetam [238,240]. It is also important to ensure adequate
ventilation, oxygenation, and appropriate blood pressure to main-
tain CBF and CPP [180].
In cases where horses experience seizures in the anesthesia recov-
ery period, as may occur following myelography, administration of

-- 853 of 1450 --

838 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
benzodiazepines (0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV) and xylazine (0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV)
has been suggested as treatment. If seizures are not controlled
by these interventions, re-anesthetizing the animal has been
recommended [153,252].
Spinal cord injury and spine surgery
Specific considerations pertaining to the different advanced imag-
ing modalities are reviewed elsewhere and are largely centered
around individual patient comorbidities. Myelography can be per-
formed to confirm and localize the site of disk herniation [253]. In
these cases, the administration of contrast into the subarachnoid
space has been associated with potential seizures [102,254]. In gen-
eral, the anesthetic/sedative drug choices do not seem to influence
the likelihood of seizures post-myelography although a limited
number of drugs were used in a clinical assessment of myelography
complications [255]. Nonetheless, drugs that are associated with
seizure activity should be avoided or used with caution. Large-
breed dogs, cervical lesions, large total volumes of iohexol, and
injection into the cerebellomedullary cistern were associated with
higher risk of seizures following myelography [102,255]. The inci-
dence of seizures was also increased with shorter anesthesia times
and in dogs that did not have surgery after the myelogram, most
likely because the length of time between injection of contrast and
recovery from anesthesia was shorter [102]. Other complications
during anesthesia include apnea (likely due to contrast reaching
the brainstem), bradycardia, bradyarrhythmias, and asystole.
Complications in the postanesthetic period include intensification
of pre-existing neurologic signs, prolonged recovery, hyperthermia,
and vomiting [255,256]; therefore, vigilant monitoring of these
patients is warranted. Appropriate anesthetic depth to avoid patient
movement during manipulation of the needle is essential to prevent
further trauma to the spinal cord. In addition, hyperflexion of the
neck for cerebellomedullary cistern puncture can result in kinking
of the endotracheal tube and airway obstruction, so careful moni-
toring of ventilation is also important in these cases. After cervical
myelography, the head should be kept elevated to minimize cranial
flow of the contrast agent [257].
A discussion of the mechanisms of spinal injury, emergency care
procedures, diagnosis, and management of acute spinal cord injury
is beyond the scope of this chapter, but reviews of these topics in
dogs and cats are available elsewhere [258,259]. Some important
considerations for the anesthetist will be covered here.
In veterinary medicine, advanced imaging and/or surgery may
be required for several disease processes including intervertebral
disk herniation, fibrocartilaginous embolism, myelitis, spinal tumors,
and spinal trauma (fractures and luxation). While the location of
the lesion plays a role, general perianesthetic complications related
to spinal surgery include moderate to severe hemorrhage from the
vertebral sinus or vertebral artery and severe and/or persistent pain
(i.e., neuropathic pain) [254,260–264]. Pneumothorax/hemothorax
has been reported with surgeries in the thoracic region specifically
and careful intraoperative monitoring is necessary to identify
this complication and facilitate early intervention [260,261].
Complications specific to procedures involving a ventral cervical
approach include profound bradycardia and hypotension which
may be unresponsive to treatment (potentially due to the surgical
approach causing traction of carotid arteries and vagal trunks),
recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, aspiration pneumonia, airway
obstruction due to endotracheal tube compression by surgical
instruments, and hypoventilation leading to respiratory failure or
apnea [254,263,265–270]. Some of these complications may even
occur in anesthetized patients with cervical spinal lesions that are not
undergoing surgery. It is important to closely monitor these patients
throughout the anesthetic period and beyond recovery as many
complications may develop or worsen in the postoperative period.
Respiratory depression ranging from hypoventilation to com-
plete respiratory failure can occur in patients with cervical spinal
injuries (either on presentation or after surgery) or ascending
myelomalacia, necessitating mechanical ventilation [254,269–271].
Temporary tracheostomy may be considered for such patients as
this will allow mechanical ventilation for prolonged periods with
minimal sedation requirements [269]. The mechanisms of hypoven-
tilation are not well understood and are likely multifactorial. It is
possible that pathways (reticulospinal tracts) from the respiratory
centers in the brainstem to neurons innervating the muscles of res-
piration (diaphragm, intercostal, and extrathoracic airway muscles)
are disrupted by the spinal lesion, by surgery, or by progressive
postoperative edema from surgical manipulation [263,269,270,272].
Furthermore, the phrenic nerve may be compromised by the
pathology itself or by surgical trauma to its nerve roots leading to
impaired diaphragmatic function [263,269]. The phrenic nerve in
dogs arises from cervical spinal cord segments 5 through 7 (corre-
sponding to cervical vertebral bodies 4 through 6) [3,273]; because
projections from the reticulospinal tracts are bilateral, even unilat-
eral lesions may result in bilateral clinical manifestations of auto-
nomic motor dysfunction [273]. Patients with spinal cord lesions
cranial to the origin of motor neurons responsible for innervating
the muscles of respiration may be more likely to present with
clinical respiratory difficulties. In fact, dogs with lesions between
C2–C4 were more likely to need mechanical ventilation in a retro-
spective study [269]. In these cases, patients are unable to maintain
alveolar ventilation due to respiratory muscle paralysis or paresis
and hypoxemia develops secondary to hypoventilation [269,274].
Monitoring end-tidal carbon dioxide in the immediate postopera-
tive period while the patient remains intubated is indicated to
ensure normocapnia in patients with cervical lesions. Following
extubation, arterial blood gas assessment should be performed to
evaluate both PaCO2 and PaO2
. Additionally, patients with cervical
lesions may develop aspiration pneumonia. In such cases, the
ability to ventilate may not be compromised but patients will
present with abnormal gas exchange and hypoxemia due to lung
pathology [269,274].
Patients with severe spinal cord injuries can also experience
spinal shock, which occurs when both ascending and descending
nerve fibers caudal to the site of injury are affected, resulting in flac-
cid paralysis of the limbs and loss of reflexes [275,276]. In addition,
patients with cervical spinal cord injuries can experience impaired
sympathetic outflow (at the level of the cranial thoracic spine)
which disrupts the balance between sympathetic and parasympa-
thetic activity and results in increased parasympathetic tone. This
affects not only the respiratory system (resulting in cholinergic
bronchoconstriction and related respiratory complications), but
also the cardiovascular system leading to significant cardiovascular
instability (bradycardia, bradyarrhythmias, hypotension, ventricular
arrhythmias, and asystole) [263,270,277,278]. Therefore, in addi-
tion to complications associated with the surgical approach (traction
of carotid arteries and vagal trunks), impaired sympathetic outflow
constitutes another important cause of cardiovascular instability in
patients with cervical spinal cord injuries and may contribute to
morbidity and mortality [254,263,265,270].
Intraoperative management should be focused on addressing
individual complications as described while providing optimal,

-- 854 of 1450 --

Chapter 39: Physiology, Pathophysiology, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Neurologic Disease 	839
multimodal analgesia. Careful attention should be paid to positioning
the patient prior to placement of surgical drapes to avoid positional
interference with monitoring equipment or the anesthetic breathing
system or predisposing the patient to neuropathy or myopathy.
Fluid therapy should be tailored to the patient with the goal of euv-
olemia; hemorrhage may be managed with fluid replacement as
indicated. Hypotension in this patient population can predispose to
impaired perfusion and ischemia of the spinal cord so blood pres-
sure should be closely monitored, and hypotension aggressively
treated if it occurs [180,254,259,279,280].
Patients with suspected vertebral fractures and/or luxation may
need to be immobilized in lateral recumbency on a backboard
before induction and intubation to minimize movement and further
injury to the spinal cord [259,281]. Discussion with the neurosur-
geon prior to immobilization and/or positioning and manipulation
of the patient for these procedures is warranted. Additional consid-
erations and complications are the same as those outlined above
and are specific to the region of the spinal cord affected. Analgesia
is an important component in management of any trauma patient
and in those with painful spinal cord injuries.
Horses and cervical spondylomyelopathy
Cervical spondylomyelopathy, also known as “wobbler syndrome,”
is a spinal cord condition in horses involving compression of the
spinal cord due to cervical vertebral malformation resulting in
ataxia, dysmetria, paresis, and an abnormal gait [282,283]. Horses
with this condition may undergo anesthesia for myelography
(with radiography, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance
imaging) and/or surgery [282,284–286]. Complications associated
with cervical myelography in horses include arrhythmias and dra-
matic changes in blood pressure (decrease or increase) during the
procedure, as well as worsening of ataxia, pneumonia, neck pain,
muscle fasciculations, seizures, hyperesthesia, head shaking, obtun-
dation or dull mentation, myopathies, prolonged recoveries, and
catastrophic recoveries with fracture [252,284,287–289]. Injection
of higher volumes of contrast agent and prolonged anesthesia time
has been associated with increased risk of adverse neurological
events in a multicenter retrospective study [287]. Reported postop-
erative complications of relevance to the anesthetist include verte-
bral fracture, implant failure or breakage, pain, spinal cord edema,
postanesthetic upper respiratory tract obstruction (and pulmonary
edema), and laryngeal hemiplegia; both latter complications required
tracheostomy [282,290]. Patient positioning with overextension of
the neck seems to be correlated to postanesthetic upper respiratory
tract obstruction [282]. Supplies for an emergent tracheostomy
procedure should be available near the recovery stall in addition to
supplies to re-induce anesthesia in the event of a fracture.
Careful cardiorespiratory monitoring (electrocardiography, inva-
sive arterial blood pressure, capnography, and arterial blood gases)
and controlled ventilation during cervical myelography is recom-
mended. Changes in the positioning of the patient during radio-
graphs, such as elevation of the head and extension and flexion of
the neck after contrast administration, may be required during the
procedure [252,291]. These positional changes can result in inad-
vertent extubation or anesthesia circuit disconnection, potential
airway obstruction (especially with flexion of the neck), tracheal
injury due to endotracheal tube movement during manipulation of
the neck, and exacerbation of spinal cord injury and neurological
signs due to anesthetic-induced muscle relaxation combined with
positional changes [252,289,292]. Careful positioning, avoiding
overinflation of the endotracheal tube cuff (and potentially
deflating the cuff before moving the head and neck), keeping the
head elevated as long as possible, and diligent post-myelography
patient monitoring are important considerations [252,284,287,292].
A variety of protocols have been reported in the literature for
anesthesia of horses undergoing cervical myelography, but no sys-
tematic comparison has been performed evaluating the quality of
induction and recovery as well as the incidence of complications.
Preanesthetic evaluation should include assessment of the patient’s
degree of ataxia. Light premedication (i.e., low, titrated doses) with
xylazine (0.2–0.5 mg/kg) with or without butorphanol (0.02 mg/kg)
is typically recommended to avoid excessive ataxia or recumbency
before anesthesia induction. However, higher doses of xylazine,
other α2 - adrenergic receptor agonists, and acepromazine have also
been reported as premedication before cervical myelography in
horses [284,285]. Some horses may have to be anesthetized in their
stalls and returned to the same location for recovery due to severe
ataxia and/or recumbency, but if the horse can be safely moved to
the induction area, this should be done before administration of
any sedatives. The use of guaifenesin in combination with barbitu-
rates (thiopental or thiamylal) or guaifenesin and/or ketamine and
a benzodiazepine (midazolam or diazepam) has been reported or
recommended by different authors for induction of anesthesia
[153,252,282,285,292]. Anesthesia induction protocols involving
propofol and ketamine have been shown to produce better recovery
qualities when compared to ketamine and midazolam induction in
healthy horses anesthetized for short periods (60 min) [293];
however, it is difficult to predict if this would be the case for horses
with wobbler syndrome. Maintenance of anesthesia with inhalant
agents (preferably isoflurane or sevoflurane) is most common;
however, use of TIVA (i.e., a combination of guaifenesin, ketamine,
and an α2
-adrenergic receptor agonist) for maintenance of anesthesia
has also been reported [284,285].
During recovery, the use of ropes or other methods of assistance,
padded recovery stalls, thick foam pads, and padded helmets have
been recommended to limit potential injuries in these patients
[252,284,285]. A sling recovery system could be considered in cases
of severe ataxia or for horses that are recumbent prior to anesthesia
[153,252]. Administration of non-steroidal anti-inflammatories or
steroids has been recommended by different authors to minimize
complications [153,252,288].
Peripheral nervous system conditions
Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an acquired autoimmune neuromuscu-
lar disease characterized by autoantibody-mediated destruction of
postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors at the neuromuscular junc-
tion [294–296]. A congenital form of MG, characterized by struc-
tural or functional defects at the neuromuscular junction (without
autoimmunity), is part of a larger clinically heterogeneous group of
disorders known as “congenital myasthenic syndromes” and is now
considered a separate entity [295,297]. Both diseases (autoimmune
and congenital) result in focal or generalized clinical muscle weak-
ness and fatigability [294,296]. The focus of this section will be
anesthetic management of patients with the more common autoim-
mune version of the disease.
Hyperthyroid cats receiving methimazole can develop drug-
induced autoimmune MG [298]. Some patients with MG (cats more
frequently than dogs) have concurrent thymoma and may need
anesthesia for surgical procedures and/or radiation therapy
[296,297,299,300]. Treatment of MG patients can involve anticho-
linesterase agents (also known as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors)

-- 855 of 1450 --

840 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
such as pyridostigmine to prolong the action of ACh at the
neuromuscular junction, as well as steroids [294,296,299]. Some
authors recommend continuation of the anticholinesterase agents
until the day of surgery to avoid respiratory distress postoperatively;
however, this is controversial [301,302]. A potential side effect of
anticholinesterase therapy in MG patients is excessive accumulation
of ACh at the neuromuscular junction resulting in weakness due to
desensitization of the postsynaptic membrane, known as “cholinergic
crisis” [294,296]. The ACh will also affect muscarinic receptors,
potentially leading to bradycardia, bronchospasm, miosis, intestinal
hyperperistalsis, and hypersalivation [302].
Aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure are frequent causes
of death in cats and dogs with MG [294]. Patients with acute fulmi-
nant MG, those with worsening skeletal muscle weakness due to
surgical stress and anesthesia, or those with severe aspiration pneu-
monia may require intubation and mechanical ventilation in the
perioperative period [296]. Anesthesia for the MG patient carries a
high risk due to the presence of megaesophagus and potential
regurgitation, the risk of upper airway obstruction and aspiration
pneumonia (due to decreased laryngeal and pharyngeal muscle
function and protective airway reflexes), respiratory failure (due to
intercostal muscle and diaphragmatic weakness and/or aspiration
pneumonia), and potential drug interactions. Some drugs can
negatively affect neuromuscular transmission and should be
avoided in patients with MG including aminoglycoside, quinolone,
and macrolide antibiotics, β-adrenergic blockers, calcium channel
blockers, phenothiazines, iodinated contrast agents, quinidine and
procainamide, phenytoin, and magnesium salts [296,302,303].
Due to their compromised respiratory muscle strength and
decreased respiratory reserve, anesthetic considerations for MG
patients include selection of drugs associated with minimal res-
piratory depression, preoxygenation prior to induction of anesthe-
sia, prevention of hypothermia which can enhance neuromuscular
blockade, and provision of ventilatory monitoring and support dur-
ing and potentially after anesthesia [301,302]. Elevating the patient’s
head during induction of anesthesia, rapid endotracheal intubation
and inflation of the cuff to protect the airway, and suctioning the
esophagus as soon as possible are recommended to reduce the risk
of complications associated with regurgitation and aspiration. The
use of metoclopramide or histamine type-2 receptor antagonists
may be considered in these patients [301,302]. There is no consen-
sus in the human or veterinary medical literature on the ideal anes-
thetic protocol for MG patients to decrease the incidence of
complications or the need for ventilation in the postoperative
period [301,302,304].
Benzodiazepines can contribute to muscle weakness and their
use in MG patients is questionable [305]. Opioids provide excellent
analgesia with potential sedation but should be used cautiously.
Small doses of short-acting opioids with careful monitoring are rec-
ommended to reduce risks associated with respiratory depression
[301,302]. The use of intravenous anesthetics to rapidly induce
anesthesia and gain control of the airway (i.e., propofol, etomidate,
alfaxalone, or ketamine) is recommended [301,302]. While inhala-
tion anesthetics have potent neuromuscular blocking effects and
cause significant respiratory depressants, they facilitate rapid
adjustments in anesthetic depth and undergo rapid elimination,
making them good options for maintenance of anesthesia [306,307].
Locoregional and systemic adjunctive techniques (i.e., ketamine
constant rate infusion) can be considered to decrease inhalant
and opioid requirements. In general, local anesthetics decrease
the sensitivity of the postjunctional membrane to ACh, but
ester local anesthetics should be avoided in patients receiving
anticholinesterase agents because they are metabolized by plasma
cholinesterases. Therefore, the use of low doses of amide local
anesthetics are recommended in MG patients [301,302,305,308].
The use of anticholinergics is controversial. If an anticholinergic is
required intraoperatively to treat bradycardia in an MG patient,
atropine is recommended over glycopyrrolate because the latter
produces greater nicotinic receptor blockade and is, therefore, more
likely to affect neuromuscular transmission [309].
Neuromuscular blocking agents should generally be avoided in
MG patients as they are resistant to the effects of depolarizing
agents and potentially very sensitive to the effects of nondepolar-
izing agents, resulting in profound and prolonged blockade
[301,308,310]. If neuromuscular blockade is required, it is impor-
tant to use lower doses of a nondepolarizing agent and quantitative
monitoring of neuromuscular function (i.e., train of four with
acceleromyography) at the end of anesthesia to ensure that no
residual blockade persists [311,312]. The use of reversal agents
such as neostigmine to reverse nondepolarizing neuromuscular
blockade in MG patients is controversial [301,302].
Patients with MG are at risk of serious complications in the peri-
operative period. Cholinergic crisis, as described above, is related to
excessive accumulation of ACh (due to anticholinesterase agent
therapy) causing desensitization of the postsynaptic membrane.
Myasthenic crisis, caused by further reductions in ACh receptor
function with acute aggravation of muscular weakness, can happen
in the postoperative period due to surgery, anesthesia, pain, and
stress [301,302]. Both cholinergic and myasthenic crises result in
similar clinical signs (generalized muscle weakness and potential
respiratory failure) and emergency intubation and ventilatory sup-
port may be required. The use of an anticholinesterase agent test
(historically referred to as the “Tensilon test”) may help differenti-
ate between myasthenic and cholinergic crises because muscle
strength will improve in the case of myasthenic crisis. In the case of
a cholinergic crisis, the anticholinesterase agent test may lead to
muscle fasciculations, miosis, and exacerbation of respiratory
signs [301,302,308].
The patient’s ability to maintain appropriate spontaneous ventila-
tion with normal end-tidal carbon dioxide levels (and ideally PaCO2
)
should be assessed before extubation. Suction should always be
available in case of regurgitation. In the immediate postanesthetic
period, once the patient is extubated, the anesthetist should con-
tinue monitoring oxygenation and ventilation while watching for
signs of airway obstruction and assessing respiratory rate, breathing
pattern, appropriate chest excursions, pulse oximetry, and ideally,
arterial blood gases (PaO2 and PaCO2
). Anticholinesterase
agent therapy should be resumed as soon as possible [301,308].
Postoperative analgesia is critical, but caution is warranted to avoid
respiratory depression and exacerbation of muscle weakness;
therefore, use of balanced analgesic techniques with drugs such as
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents (if the patient is not receiv-
ing steroids), and regional anesthesia/analgesia to minimize opioid
use is important [305]. Other drugs with analgesic properties that
should be used with caution in MG patients include tricyclic
antidepressants, pregabalin, and gabapentin [305].

Introduction
The liver is centrally located between the diaphragm and abdominal
viscera and receives 20–30% of total cardiac output (CO) via the
portal vein and hepatic artery. The liver plays a vital role in homeo-
stasis and is responsible for the biotransformation and excretion of
endogenous and exogenous substances. Significant exogenous
physiologic support may be necessary for patients with clinically
relevant hepatic dysfunction. In addition, consideration must be
given to anesthetic and adjunct drug selection to avoid delayed
recovery. Anesthetic and surgical procedures involving the liver
may cause ischemia and reperfusion injury, inducing acute and
chronic hepatic dysfunction. Hence, it is crucial to maintain adequate
hepatic blood flow and oxygen delivery during general anesthesia.
Clinical application of anatomic and physiologic knowledge is
necessary to optimize anesthetic management during hepatic and
extrahepatic biliary disease interventions.
Functional anatomy and physiology
The liver is the largest gland in the body, comprising 1.5–4% of total
body weight, and is anatomically and physiologically similar among
species. The liver can be divided into four main lobes (left, right,
quadrate, and caudate lobes). The right and left lobes may be further
subdivided into separate lateral and medial lobes. A gallbladder is
present in most domestic species with the exception of the horse
and the rat, in which large bile ducts compensate for the absence of
the gallbladder. In some species, the bile duct terminates directly on
the duodenum (e.g., canine and bovine), but in others, it shares a
common duct with the pancreas (e.g., cat, horse, and small rumi-
nants). This can be of importance, as some hepatobiliary diseases
can also affect the pancreas of those species [1].
Structural organization of the liver
The hexagonal hepatic lobule is the basic anatomic unit of the liver.
Cylindrical plates of hepatocytes are separated by venous sinusoids
(fenestrated capillaries) and radiate around a central vein like
spokes in wheel. The portal triad (hepatic arterioles, portal venules,
bile canaliculi, lymphatics, and nerves) is present at each corner of
the hexagon. The perisinusoidal space (or space of Disse) lies
between the sinusoids and hepatocytes, containing plasma and
allowing hepatocytes to absorb nutrients and waste products.
Macrophage-derived Kupffer cells line the perisinusoidal space
(Fig. 40.1). These cells have phagocytic function and are active in
hepatic inflammatory responses. The hepatic arterial (HA) blood
