Pancreatitis
Although pancreatitis is not considered a endocrinopathy per se, the
disease may affect both exocrine and endocrine pancreatic
functions. While patients are not frequently anesthetized for
surgical or medical intervention of pancreatitis, it may be necessary
to anesthetize or sedate an animal with concurrent pancreatitis.
Pancreatitis is a painful condition and multimodal analgesic
protocols are paramount. Sedation with an IV opioid and an
analgesic CRI including an opioid, lidocaine, and/or ketamine are
recommended. Advanced analgesic techniques may be required due
to uncontrolled or refractory pain. A continuous TAP block using
bupivacaine administered through a catheter was reported to
reduce pain scores in dogs with acute pancreatitis and abdominal
pain [200]. The authors routinely perform a combination of caudal
intercostal nerve blocks in conjunction with bilateral, cranial TAP
blocks and/or epidural regional anesthesia for animals with
refractory pain. In people, regional anesthesia with bupivacaine and
liposomal-encapsulated bupivacaine has shown promising results
for management of pancreatitis and postoperative pain [201–203].
Anecdotally, off-label use of liposomal bupivacaine (Nocita®) for
TAP and intercostal nerve blocks can provide efficient and longer
lasting analgesia in dogs and cats, but no published data are
currently available in veterinary medicine.
Thyroid gland
The thyroid gland has two lobes, one on each side of the trachea.
Each lobe is located distal to the larynx, ventrolateral to the trachea,
and extending from the fifth to eighth tracheal rings. The thyroid
gland is composed of numerous follicles lined by epithelial cells that
produce and secrete hormones. These follicles serve as a storage
area for precursors of thyroid hormones. Interspersed between the
follicles, clusters of parafollicular or C cells are found that produce
calcitonin. The parathyroid glands are located in very close proxim-
ity to the thyroid gland [3].
The thyroid gland is regulated by the hypothalamic–pituitary–
thyroid axis, which is an endocrine negative feedback loop. When
thyroid hormone (TH) is needed, the hypothalamus releases
thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) that triggers the anterior
pituitary gland to secrete thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
(also known as “thyrotropin”). TSH stimulates the thyroid gland
to release hormones, most importantly thyroxine (T4) and triio-
dothyronine (T3) (Fig. 42.1). In the liver, kidney, brain, and skeletal
muscle, T4 is converted to T3. T3 and, to a lesser extent, T4
control the secretion of TRH and TSH through negative feed-
back [204,205]. Physiologic concentrations of TH are anabolic
and vital to nervous system development, growth, basal metabo-
lism, and thermogenesis.
Hypothyroidism
Reduction of circulating concentrations of the active thyroid
hormones T3 and T4 results in hypothyroidism. This clinical
syndrome may be congenital or acquired and occurs due to a defect
in any part of the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis. Primary
hypothyroidism occurs commonly in dogs, where it is most often an
immune-mediated disease caused by lymphocytic infiltration of the
thyroid gland with eventual destruction of thyroid tissue [206].
Idiopathic atrophy of the thyroid gland, with no associated
inflammatory component, is also described in the dog as a cause of
clinical hypothyroidism [206].
Hypothyroidism occurs most often in middle-aged to older dogs
(median age 7 years) [206–208]. There is no known sex predilec-
tion [209]. Large purebred dogs such as Doberman Pinschers, Great
Danes, Irish Setters, English Setters, and Golden Retrievers appear
to be predisposed.
Clinical presentation
Clinical signs of hypothyroidism are caused by a decrease in meta-
bolic rate. Signs are vague and non-specific and include weight gain,
hair loss, dry skin and hair coat, and decreased activity [207,210].
Other abnormalities such as pyoderma, otitis, seizures, facial
paralysis, laryngeal paralysis, megaesophagus, and myopathies have
been anecdotally observed in animals with hypothyroidism [210,211].
In severe forms of the disease, myxedema can develop. Myxedema
occurs when abnormally high amounts of mucin accumulate in the
skin and other tissues resulting in edematous skin. Myxedema
coma is a rare syndrome characterized by myxedema, severe leth-
argy, hypotension, hypoventilation, and hypothermia [212].
Clinical pathology
Mild normocytic normochromic anemia is the most common
hematological abnormality present. It is likely due to decreased pro-
duction of erythropoietin and lack of TH effects on bone
marrow [207,210,213].
Serum biochemistry findings include hypercholesterolemia and
hypertriglyceridemia [207,210,213]. These abnormalities are com-
mon in hypothyroid dogs because inadequate TH levels impact
lipid metabolism, including impaired degradation (lipolysis).
Diagnosis and treatment
Routine screening tests to assess total T4 may not be reliable. Factors
such as systemic illness (i.e., euthyroid sick syndrome) or the
administration of drugs such as corticosteroids, carprofen, and
sulfonamides, may decrease total T4 concentrations resulting in an
erroneous diagnosis of hypothyroidism [214–216]. A more accurate
test is the evaluation of serum free T4 in combination with canine
thyroid-stimulating hormone (cTSH) concentrations. However,
considerable overlap of test results may still occur in dogs with
hypothyroidism compared to dogs with non-thyroid disease [217].
Circulating antibodies against thyroglobulin may be a marker for
lymphocytic thyroiditis and could help support the diagnosis [213].
Additionally, TSH stimulation testing could also be performed, but
the expense and unavailability of TSH limits the use of this test.
Treatment of hypothyroidism involves daily supplementation
with l-thyroxine (levothyroxine, synthetic T4). Follow-up measure-
ment of total T4 approximately 6 h postadministration can be used
to monitor treatment success [210]. Therapy may also be monitored
based on clinical response and normalization of hematological and
biochemical abnormalities.
Anesthetic considerations
Prior to sedation or anesthesia for elective procedures, hypothyroid
animals should be appropriately treated with synthetic hor-
mones [2]. Blood work should be performed to assess the possible
presence of mild to moderate anemia. In most cases, however, the
anemia observed in animals with hypothyroidism is not clinically
significant [218]. Severe hypothyroidism resulting in profound

-- 924 of 1450 --

Chapter 42: Physiology, Pathophysiology, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Endocrine Disease 	909
cardiovascular and/or neurological effects is rare, but stabilization
of these patients prior to anesthesia is critical [4,218]. Stabilization
of cases of myxedema coma involves administration of IV thyroid
supplementation and cardiovascular support [219].
Muscle weakness and obesity are often present, which may
compromise the animal’s ability to ventilate spontaneously and
oxygenate appropriately during the perioperative period. Markedly
obese dogs have reduced function residual capacity and compression
and absorption atelectasis due to increased thoracic fat deposition
can exacerbate ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) mismatch during
anesthesia [220,221]. Positioning the patient in sternal recumbency
is recommended when feasible as dorsal recumbency may result in
further V/Q mismatch [222]. Ideally, mechanical ventilation should
be available to support ventilation intraoperatively when needed.
Hair thinning or alopecia is common in hypothyroid animals,
which may result in marked intraoperative hypothermia if
thermoregulatory support is not provided. Temperature should be
closely monitored, and active warming devices utilized.
Dogs with hypothyroidism may also have comorbidities such as
laryngeal paralysis and megaesophagus, making them more prone
to regurgitation and aspiration pneumonia [27]. Adequate fasting
prior to any procedure and rapid airway capture following induc-
tion of anesthesia is recommended. Appropriate equipment such as
suction canisters with tubing should be readily available to manage
regurgitation if it occurs.
Untreated and inadequately treated hypothyroid patients have
reduced metabolic rates and decreased hepatic metabolism of
drugs, which could potentially prolong recovery after sedation or
anesthesia [2,27]. Recoveries may be further delayed in hypother-
mic patients.
Anesthetic management
No specific drug protocol is contraindicated in well-managed,
otherwise healthy animals that are euthyroid at the time of
anesthesia. However, patients with poorly controlled or uncontrolled
hypothyroidism may present with comorbidities that necessitate
anesthesia. Short-acting drugs that are rapidly metabolized or
reversible are usually preferred. Especially in a lethargic geriatric
animal, an opioid such as methadone or hydromorphone combined
with a benzodiazepine such as midazolam generally produces
adequate preanesthetic sedation. Acepromazine is an irreversible
drug that can exacerbate hypotension and hypothermia; thus, it
should not be administered to hypovolemic and/or anemic animals.
α2
- Adrenergic 	receptor 	agonists 	may 	cause 	or 	exacerbate
hypothermia, bradyarrhythmias, and decreased cardiac output.
Since cardiac output may already be impaired in dogs with poorly
controlled hypothyroidism due to reduced myocardial contractility,
α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists are not usually a first-line choice in
these patients [209]. For stable, previously hypothyroid animals,
acepromazine and dexmedetomidine are often administered in
conjunction with an opioid.
In obese animals, body composition changes may affect the
pharmacokinetics 	and 	pharmacodynamics 	of 	administered
drugs [223]. Reduction of anesthetic drug dose or dose calculation
based on lean/ideal body weight should be considered in obese
hypothyroid dogs [224,225]. Heavy sedation in obese dogs results in
poor oxygenation variables and, thus, should be avoided [221], or
supplemental oxygen should be provided. Prior to induction of
anesthesia, preoxygenation of the hypothyroid dog is recommended.
Preoxygenation with a tight-fitting face mask has been shown to
prolong the time to desaturation [70,71].
Although it is likely that most anesthetic agents have been used in
hypothyroid animals without any perceived increase in anesthetic
risk, propofol or alfaxalone and inhalant agents are often
recommended 	for 	anesthetic 	induction 	and 	maintenance,
respectively [2]. Isoflurane produces similar dose-dependent
decreases in cardiac output and blood pressure in both euthyroid
and hypothyroid dogs and, thus, is a suitable anesthetic in these
patients. As with any patient, isoflurane-induced cardiovascular
depression can be minimized by using balanced anesthetic
techniques [226]. Halothane, though no longer available in many
countries, has direct myocardial depressant effects and should be
avoided to preserve cardiac output [2,227]. Studies have shown that
the MAC of halothane and isoflurane in both euthyroid and
hypothyroid dogs are clinically similar [226,228]. Anecdotally,
hypothyroid dogs appear to have reduced requirements for
anesthetic drugs. This clinical impression may be related to
hypothyroid dogs being more prone to hypothermia, which has
MAC-sparing effects, as well as inadvertent administration of
higher doses of injectable drugs in obese patients. Euthyroid obese
dogs have been shown to require smaller effective propofol doses
for induction of anesthesia compared to ideal weight dogs when the
dosage was calculated based on total body weight [226].
Continuous monitoring of heart rate and rhythm, blood pressure,
ventilation, oxygenation, and temperature is important for the
anesthetic management of these patients. Fluid therapy rate may be
adjusted based on ideal body weight in obese patients [229,230].
Sinus bradycardia, low QRS amplitude, inverted T waves, and
decreased left ventricular function have been observed in
hypothyroid dogs [210]. Bradycardia and hypotension are common
intraoperative 	complications 	and 	should 	be 	treated 	with
anticholinergics, crystalloid or synthetic colloid fluid therapy, and
positive inotropes [2,4]. Rewarming hypothermic patients may also
improve or correct bradycardia and hypotension. Hypoventilation
is common, especially when obesity is present, and mechanical
ventilation may be required to maintain normocapnia and adequate
oxygenation. Thermoregulatory support should be provided to
prevent and treat hypothermia.
Slow recoveries may occur as mentioned previously. Diligent
monitoring with pulse oximetry, provision of ventilatory support,
oxygen supplementation, and active warming, when indicated, are
vital during the recovery period. Patients with myxedema coma
may require IV hormone replacement therapy with l-thyroxine
postoperatively [27,231].
Hyperthyroidism
Excessive circulating concentrations of active T3 and T4 result in
hyperthyroidism. This clinical syndrome is usually caused by
poorly controlled hypersecretion of TH from autonomously hyper-
functional nodules of the thyroid gland [232]. The etiology of this
disease is unknown but, similar to human patients with toxic nodu-
lar goiter, activating mutations of TSH receptors may be
involved [233].
In cats, the most common thyroid gland disease resulting in
hyperthyroidism is benign adenomatous hyperplasia [234,235]. In
rare cases (only 1–2% of cats with thyrotoxicosis), thyroid carcinoma
is the cause. Hyperthyroidism occurs much less commonly in dogs
compared to cats, and thyroid carcinoma is the most common cause
in this species. Hyperthyroidism is documented in less than 20% of
dogs diagnosed with thyroid carcinoma [236]. In contrast to thyroid
adenomas in cats, thyroid carcinomas in dogs are usually large and
invasive [237].

-- 925 of 1450 --

910 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
Hyperthyroidism is one of the most common disorders of
middle- aged and older cats (mean age 12 years) [238,239]. There is
no sex or breed predilection [234,238,239].
Clinical presentation
Clinical signs of hyperthyroidism are multisystemic and caused
by pathologically high metabolism due to sustained excessive
circulating TH concentrations. High levels of TH are catabolic
and cause increased gluconeogenesis, protein breakdown, and
nitrogen wasting. Common clinical signs include weight loss with
normal or increased appetite, polyphagia, vomiting, diarrhea, PU/
PD, hyperactivity, and behavioral changes that can range from
depression to aggression.
Hypertension, myocardial hypertrophy, chronic cellular malnutri-
tion, hepatocellular stress, and decreased gastrointestinal transit time
are also observed in animals with hyperthyroidism [234,238,239].
Physical examination findings include poor body condition, tachy-
cardia, heart murmur, gallop rhythm, palpable unilateral or bilateral
thyroid nodules, and an unkempt hair coat (Fig. 42.8) [238,239].
Thyrotoxic storm, described as a syndrome of severe hyperthy-
roidism, occurs rarely in cats and dogs [240–242]. This life-
threatening manifestation of the disease results in severe
tachycardia, fever, gastrointestinal signs, and CNS signs. Thyrotoxic
storm is not well described in veterinary medicine, and specific
triggers are unknown.
Clinical pathology
Mild erythrocytosis is the most common hematological finding in
cats with hyperthyroidism [239]. This is likely mediated through
TH effects (β-adrenergic stimulation) on the bone marrow and an
increase in oxygen consumption resulting in increased erythropoi-
etin levels.
Serum biochemistry findings include mild to marked elevation
of liver-derived enzyme activity, a mild increase in BUN without a
concurrent increase in creatinine concentrations, and hypokalemia.
Elevations in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and/or serum ALP
activity are found in approximately 75% of hyperthyroid cats. A
study of hyperthyroid cats with severe elevations in liver enzymes
showed normal liver function [243]. Increased BUN occurs due to
increased protein catabolism. Elevations in both BUN and creati-
nine levels may indicate the presence of concurrent renal dis-
ease [234,235,239,243,244]. Hypokalemia may be observed in
hyperthyroid cats due to movement of potassium from the extracel-
lular space into the intracellular space stimulated by high TH levels
and stress-induced release of catecholamines [245,246].
Animals with thyrotoxic storm have similar clinical pathology
findings to those described above. However, these animals also pre-
sent with extremely high concentrations of TH [242].
Diagnosis and treatment
Enlargement of one or both thyroid glands can be detected during
physical examination in many cats with hyperthyroidism; however,
this is not a pathognomonic finding. Diagnosis is based on clinical
presentation, as described above, and measurement of total
T4 levels. High serum total T4 concentration confirms the diagnosis
in most cases [247]. Some hyperthyroid cats may have occult
hyperthyroidism with normal total T4 concentrations. This may be
due to fluctuations in hormone concentrations or concurrent non-
thyroidal disease. In these cases, other diagnostic tests such as
measurement of free T4, repeated measurements of total T4, thyroid
scintigraphy, or T3 suppression testing may be required [247,248].
Heart murmurs and gallop sounds are often detected during
physical examination of cats with hyperthyroidism and concurrent
comorbidities such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) may
be present. Therefore, thoracic imaging and echocardiography may
be useful in assessing the cardiovascular system of these patients.

The cardiac biomarkers N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide
(NTproBNP) and cardiac troponin I were elevated in cats with
hyperthyroidism before treatment but were not able to distinguish
between thyrotoxic myopathy and primary feline HCM [238]. In
hyperthyroid dogs, thoracic radiographs are recommended to
investigate the presence of pulmonary metastases. Abdominal
ultrasound may be performed in hyperthyroid cats to assess renal
architecture and size, although further renal testing may better
define renal function.
The treatment of choice for feline hyperthyroidism is radioiodine
therapy. It is non-invasive, has few side effects, and is effective in
most cases [249]. Another effective treatment option is medical
management with methimazole or carbimazole [250]. However,
these antithyroid drugs often cause side effects such as vomiting,
self-induced facial excoriation, and anorexia. Surgical thyroidectomy
is less common in cats but is still performed in some cases [246].
Surgical complications include iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism,
laryngeal paralysis, and hypothyroidism. Approximately 30% of cats
with hyperthyroidism develop mild but stable renal failure following
medical treatment [251]. β-Adrenergic receptor antagonists,
amlodipine, or ACE inhibitors may be used to manage tachycardia
and hypertension in cats with hyperthyroidism [27,156,252].
Management of thyroid carcinoma in dogs is dependent on the
size and stage of the tumor [236]. Surgery may be a viable option for
small non-invasive tumors. Large or non-resectable tumors may
require radiation and chemotherapy; however, treatment is rarely
curative.
Although uncommon, thyroid storm is usually treated with
antithyroid drugs to decrease hormone synthesis. TH secretion may
be inhibited by administration of iodine (oral potassium iodide,
oral ipodate, or IV sodium iodide). Additionally, corticosteroids
may be administered to inhibit the peripheral conversion of T4 to
the active hormone T3. Hyperthermia should be treated and fluid
therapy used to correct dehydration. If the patient presents in heart
failure, appropriate management (e.g., diuretic agents) should be
initiated. Tachyarrhythmias may be treated with β-adrenergic
blockers.
Anesthetic considerations
Whenever possible, hyperthyroidism should be treated prior to
sedation or general anesthesia. Medications including methimazole
can be administered on the morning of surgery. A preoperative
thyroid panel can confirm a euthyroid state. If total T4 or free T4
are above the reference range, elective procedures should be
postponed, and treatment with carbimazole or methimazole for
6–12 weeks may be indicated to minimize anesthetic and surgical
complications [253].
A thorough examination should be performed to assess the
cardiorespiratory system and hydration status. Blood work will help
assess hydration (PCV and TS) and renal function (BUN and
creatinine) and reveal any electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., potassium
and calcium) [156]. Baseline ECG and blood pressure measurements
should be obtained, especially if a heart murmur, gallop rhythm,
HCM, or azotemia is present or suspected. Hypertension may be
seen in animals with untreated or unregulated hyperthyroidism
and/or with chronic kidney disease (CKD). In hypertensive animals
with CKD, renal autoregulatory mechanisms that normally stabilize
GFR over a wide range of blood pressures (80–180 mmHg) may be
impaired and shifted to a higher range. Therefore, even mild
decreases in blood pressure during anesthesia may decrease renal
blood flow and GFR. The authors recommend maintaining the
arterial blood pressure within 20% of resting blood pressure
measurements as a goal. Additionally, preanesthetic fluids to restore
normovolemia and hydration may be considered [254], but caution
is advised in animals with cardiac abnormalities. Correcting
dehydration preoperatively and preserving cardiac output through
use of anesthetic-sparing techniques may help reduce episodes of
intraoperative hypotension.
Intraoperative hypotension may be exacerbated in hypertensive
animals treated with drugs such as atenolol, amlodipine, or ACE
inhibitors. A study in healthy dogs treated with enalapril showed
increased severity of intraoperative hypotension. Extrapolating
from these data, withholding ACE inhibitors for 24 h prior to the
scheduled procedure could be considered [60].
Hemorrhage during surgical excision of thyroid tumors may
occur. Many of these tumors are highly vascularized and, especially
in dogs, they are often large and invasive. Patients with larger
tumors should be blood typed and crossmatched prior to anesthe-
sia, and blood products should be readily available to manage intra-
operative blood loss.
A possible postoperative complication, especially following bilat-
eral thyroidectomy, is the development of transient hypocalcemia.
Hypocalcemia may occur due to removal, damage, or local edema of
the parathyroid glands. Postoperative measurement of calcium levels
is advised, and supplementation may be required [246,255,256].
Anesthetic management
If emergency surgery is required in an untreated hyperthyroid cat,
cardiovascular stabilization is paramount. Fluid resuscitation and
electrolyte supplementation may be required, especially in cats
experiencing PU/PD and vomiting. Cats with concurrent hyper-
trophic cardiomyopathy, tachyarrhythmias, or hypertension should
be managed as described previously.
No specific drug protocol is contraindicated in treated, otherwise
healthy cats that are euthyroid on the time of anesthesia. However,
many cats with hyperthyroidism are presented with comorbidities
requiring specific anesthetic management. When sedating or
anesthetizing these animals, the goal should be to minimize
increases in oxygen consumption, hypertension, tachycardia, and
arrhythmias. Pain- and stress-induced catecholamine release should
be avoided or minimized; therefore, multimodal analgesia and low-
stress handling techniques are paramount.
Premedication 	of 	hyperthyroid 	cats 	generally 	includes
administration of an opioid. Opioids cause dose-dependent
decreases in heart rate and, thus, myocardial oxygen consumption. If
dogs and cats are undergoing non-painful procedures, butorphanol
is often the agent of choice. For surgical or painful procedures, a full
μ-opioid receptor agonist is generally used. Benzodiazepines or
acepromazine may be included in the preanesthetic protocol [257].
Benzodiazepines are good choices for sick, unstable animals due to
minimal cardiorespiratory effects, but in healthy animals, paradoxical
excitement or disinhibition may ensue. Acepromazine, an α-
adrenergic receptor antagonist, causes vasodilation and could help
counteract pre-existing hypertension. It may also reduce the
sensitivity of the myocardium to catecholamines thus decreasing the
occurrence of catecholamine-induced arrhythmias. Acepromazine,
however, has long-lasting, irreversible effects and may worsen
intraoperative hypotension. Its use should be avoided when the
patient is hypovolemic, on antihypertensive medication, or when
tumors are large or invasive with increased risk of blood loss. In cats
with HCM, acepromazine is usually avoided because it may reduce
preload and increase the pressure gradient across the left ventricular

-- 927 of 1450 --

912 	Section 5: Physiology and Anesthetic Management
outflow tract in these patients. Low doses of α2
-adrenergic receptor
agonists such as dexmedetomidine may increase preload, reduce
heart rate, and enhance diastolic filling in some patients with
HCM [258], but this must be weighed against the potential for
reduced cardiac output. In fractious cats, alfaxalone could be added
to the preanesthetic protocol to improve sedation. It causes dose-
dependent 	immobilization 	with 	minimal 	cardiorespiratory
depression [258–260].
Intravenous propofol or alfaxalone are common agents used to
induce anesthesia but can cause dose-dependent hypotension and
hypoventilation [261]. Etomidate can also be used, especially for
cats with advanced heart disease. This agent has minimal
cardiovascular effects and is usually co-administered with a
benzodiazepine. However, etomidate may not be the drug of choice
for systemically ill patients undergoing invasive procedures due to
its transient suppression of cortisol secretion. Propofol and
alfaxalone can also be co-administered with a benzodiazepine,
which reduces the required dose of the primary anesthetic agent,
potentially reducing side effects [262].
Induction doses of dissociative, sympathomimetic anesthetic
agents such as ketamine stimulate sympathetic output resulting in
an increase in heart rate and a decrease in ventricular filling [2,257].
Telazol® also increases sympathetic tone resulting in an increase in
heart rate and mean arterial pressure [263]. Drugs known to
increase heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand or consumption
should be avoided or used with caution in hyperthyroid cats, espe-
cially if HCM is also present. Chamber induction of anesthesia with
an inhalant agent is also not recommended due to the high stress
levels associated with this technique, environmental contamina-
tion, and limited monitoring ability.
Anesthesia is generally maintained with inhalant anesthetics
such as isoflurane or sevoflurane. Halothane, though no longer
available in many countries, was historically avoided in these
patients as it could sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines and
produce arrhythmias [264]. A balanced anesthesia protocol with
short-acting opioid infusions and locoregional anesthetic tech-
niques will help maintain adequate anesthetic depth, supplement
analgesia, and avoid exaggerated sympathetic nervous system
responses [27].
Blood pressure, heart rate, and ECG should be closely monitored.
Invasive (direct) blood pressure monitoring is considered the gold
standard and should be performed in patients that are critically ill,
have renal or cardiac disease, or are undergoing surgery for large or
invasive tumor resection. Fluid rates should be tailored to the
patients’ health status; they should be decreased in patients with
cardiac disease or congestive heart failure, or marginally increased
in patients with renal disease [265]. The increased metabolic rate
associated with feline hyperthyroidism increases demand for oxy-
gen and glucose, and production of carbon dioxide. This, combined
with poor body condition and possible muscle weakness, makes
these animals more prone to hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and hypo-
thermia. Preoxygenation, provision of thermoregulatory support,
continuous monitoring with pulse oximetry and capnography, and
ventilatory support are recommended.
Hyperthyroid animals, especially if receiving antihypertensive
drugs, may have refractory hypotension intraoperatively, requiring
positive inotropes. In cats with nonobstructive HCM, dopamine
was reported to increase cardiac output. However, in HCM cats with
outflow tract obstruction, positive inotropes may increase
obstruction to blood flow further decreasing cardiac output.
Management of hypotension in cats with HCM is often
challenging [266]. Phenylephrine was reported to increase blood
pressure in cats with HCM but did not increase cardiac output [266].
If profound bradycardia and hypotension persist despite adequate
anesthetic depth, normothermia, and provision of MAC-sparing
drugs, a low-dose dobutamine infusion or anticholinergic may be
required. Anticholinergics may reduce diastolic filling due to
tachycardia [267] and are usually avoided by the authors, except in
emergency situations. These agents cause parasympathetic blockade
leading to an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption and
increased arrhythmogenicity. Dobutamine in hypovolemic patients
or at high infusion rates may result in tachyarrhythmias and should
be used with caution. However, dobutamine may be a more
favorable option in this situation due to its short duration of action.
Anesthetic recovery should occur in a quiet place and sedation
may be administered. To smooth recovery and decrease stress-
related catecholamine release, a low dose of a sedative such as
acepromazine (0.005–0.01 mg/kg IV) may be administered if there
are no contraindications. Thyrotoxic storm may be seen in the
postanesthetic period. This is rare but may occur in untreated or
poorly managed hyperthyroid patients. Monitoring of heart rate
and rhythm, respiratory rate, blood pressure, body temperature,
and, ideally, pulse oximetry should be continued throughout
recovery.
Thyroid neoplasia
In dogs, most thyroid tumors are non-functional carcinomas, and
they do not secrete excessive TH. Pulmonary metastases are com-
mon, and local invasion of tissues such as the trachea, esophagus,
musculature, and vasculature may occur [268]. Dogs with thyroid
tumors usually present with a large space-occupying lesion in the
ventral cervical region (Fig. 42.9).
Clinical signs are associated with the size of the thyroid tumor
and secondary damage to the cervical tissues. These may include
stridor, dyspnea, coughing, gagging, dysphagia, anorexia, weight
loss, and concurrent laryngeal paralysis [268,269].
Diagnostic evaluation of thyroid tumors includes biopsy of the
mass and serum TH measurement. Thoracic radiographs are indi-
cated to identify pulmonary metastases [268]. Other imaging
modalities, such as CT or MRI, may identify the extent of local
invasion. Thyroidectomy is preferred for mobile, well-differentiated
tumors, whereas unresectable tumors can sometimes be treated
with radiation or radioactive iodine-131 [268].
Anesthetic considerations and management
Maintenance of a patent airway, provision of analgesia, and readi-
ness to manage possible sudden blood loss are the main goals of
anesthesia. Hemorrhage has been reported as the most common
intraoperative complication in thyroidectomies [268]. Blood prod-
ucts should be available and, ideally, preanesthetic evaluation
should include a coagulation panel, blood type, and cross-
match [270]. Aspiration pneumonia has been the most reported
postoperative complication following tumor resection [269].
Laryngeal paralysis may be identified postoperatively; therefore,
airway examination at the time of intubation and extubation is
warranted [269].
Combinations of dexmedetomidine or acepromazine with
hydromorphone or butorphanol have been studied for provision of
sedation 	while 	maintaining 	laryngeal 	function 	for 	airway
evaluation [271,272]. Heavy sedation should be performed
cautiously in patients with respiratory compromise, and equipment
for intubation along with an injectable induction agent, such as

-- 928 of 1450 --

Chapter 42: Physiology, Pathophysiology, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Endocrine Disease 	913
propofol, should be readily available. Although full μ-opioid
receptor agonists can cause dose-related respiratory depression,
they are routinely administered for invasive and/or painful
procedures and are still considered the gold standard for analgesia.
However, 	opioids 	associated 	with 	high 	incidences 	of
gastroesophageal reflux and/or regurgitation, such as morphine and
hydromorphone [273,274], may be best avoided.
Prior to induction of anesthesia, preoxygenation is recom-
mended to prolong the time to desaturation [71]. If tracheal inva-
sion is present, multiple endotracheal tubes, guarded endotracheal
tubes, and tracheostomy supplies should be available. Propofol or
alfaxalone is often administered for induction of anesthesia, espe-
cially if airway evaluation is being performed prior to endotracheal
intubation [272]. Alternatively, a ketamine–benzodiazepine combi-
nation may be administered to induce anesthesia and will provide
additional analgesia. All induction agents should be administered
to effect as they cause dose-dependent respiratory depression.
Inhalant anesthetics such as isoflurane or sevoflurane are typically
used for maintenance of anesthesia.
Direct arterial blood pressure, pulse oximetry, ECG, and
capnography should be monitored intraoperatively. Volume
resuscitation during acute hemorrhage may include isotonic
crystalloids, artificial colloids, and/or blood products, preferably
whole blood transfusion, depending on the magnitude of blood
lost [106]. Hypertonic saline 7.5% (4 mL/kg IV over 10–20 min) has
been shown to improve hemodynamic performance without
inducing signs of volume overload in a canine model of hemorrhagic
shock 	[108]. 	Multimodal 	analgesia 	and 	anesthetic-sparing
techniques will allow reduction of delivered inhalant concentrations
and thereby minimize adverse cardiovascular side effects.
Alterations in renal blood flow and renal injury may occur in
patients 	receiving 	NSAIDs 	that 	experience 	hypotension/
hypovolemia during anesthesia [275]. Therefore, it is recommended
to delay NSAID administration until the postoperative period when
the patient’s hemodynamic status has been re-evaluated and
determined to be stable.
Complications during recovery may be related to laryngeal
paralysis, aspiration pneumonia, tracheal compression, and
hemorrhage. To reduce the incidence of aspiration pneumonia
during extubation and promote adequate ventilation, the patient
should recover in sternal recumbency with the head slightly
elevated. A strong swallow should be evident before removing the
endotracheal tube. If regurgitation is observed or suspected, leaving
the endotracheal tube cuff partially inflated during extubation may
further protect the airway from gastric contents. Supplies for
induction of anesthesia and rapid re-intubation should be readily
available in the event of airway obstruction.
Hypocalcemia may develop in cases where the parathyroid gland
was not preserved, requiring supplementation with calcium and
vitamin D [276]. Serial measurements of ionized calcium should be
considered in cases where preservation of the parathyroid gland
was not possible or is uncertain.
Parathyroid gland
The parathyroid glands are located near the thyroid gland [3]. Dogs
and cats have four parathyroid glands, two embedded near the cau-
domedial pole of each lobe of the thyroid and two external glands
typically on the cranial dorsolateral surface of the thyroid lobe.
Ectopic parathyroid tissue is common in cats, less so in dogs [277].
The parathyroid glands have densely packed cells surrounding cap-
illary vessels [3].
Parathyroid glands produce and secrete parathyroid hormone
(PTH) in response to decreased serum calcium concentrations. There
are no PTH releasing or stimulating hormones. PTH increases serum
calcium via three main mechanisms: (1) it stimulates activity of

osteoclasts to reabsorb bone; (2) it results in absorption of calcium
from the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) via the activated form of vitamin
D, which is produced in the kidney; and (3) it reduces excretion of
calcium in the urine [3]. In healthy animals, normal or increased
serum ionized calcium (iCa) concentrations have a strong negative
feedback effect on PTH secretion and also stimulate the thyroid to
release calcitonin which has opposite effects of PTH (Fig. 42.1).
Hyperparathyroidism
Increased concentrations of circulating PTH result in hyperparath-
yroidism. When excessive amounts of PTH are produced, persistent
hypercalcemia occurs and calcification of soft tissues, with resultant
dysfunction 	of 	affected 	structures 	or 	organs, 	ensues.
Hyperparathyroidism can be a primary or secondary disorder.
Primary hyperparathyroidism is generally caused by a singular
benign adenoma of an extracapsular parathyroid gland. Parathyroid
adenomas 	autonomously 	secrete 	PTH, 	causing 	hypercalce-
mia [278,279]. Parathyroid adenocarcinomas are very rare.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is an adaptive increase in PTH
induced by hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia associated with
CKD or an unbalanced diet [280]. The following discussion is
focused on primary hyperparathyroidism in the dog.
Primary hyperparathyroidism is an uncommon disorder of
middle-aged and older dogs (mean age 10.2 years) and is a rare con-
dition in cats. There is no known breed or sex predilection [278,281–
283]. However, a genetic predisposition for parathyroid tumors has
been found in Keeshonds [284].
Clinical presentation
Clinical signs of primary hyperparathyroidism are often lacking. In
many cases, an incidental finding of increased total calcium (tCa)
concentration on routine blood work warrants further investigation
and measurement of ionized calcium (iCa) concentration. Ionized
calcium is the physiologic active form and is a superior measure-
ment compared with tCa in patients with hyperparathy-
roidism [285]. Furthermore, prediction of iCa based on tCa
concentration was less accurate in patients with concurrent diseases
such as CKD [285]. On physical examination, parathyroid adeno-
mas are small and rarely palpable in dogs, but they may be palpable
in cats [286,287]. Some animals may display mild clinical signs
because of severity or chronicity of hypercalcemia.
Polyuria and polydipsia are the most commonly reported clinical
signs. Hypercalcemia interferes with the ability of the kidneys to
concentrate urine resulting in polyuria. There is an impaired
response to ADH due to calcium interference with vasopressin V 2
receptors in the renal tubules. Activation of calcium-sensing recep-
tors decreases reabsorption of sodium, potassium, and chloride and
causes downregulation of aquaporin-2 water channels. Polydipsia
follows to compensate for fluid loss from frequent urina-
tion [278,288]. In severe cases, or with chronic hypercalcemia, ani-
mals may present dehydrated or hypovolemic.
Lower urinary tract inflammation and urolithiases (calcium-
containing urinary stones) in the bladder, ureters, or kidneys may
also be identified in animals with hyperparathyroidism. In addi-
tion, hypercalcemia affects intestinal function, and animals may
present for vomiting, weight loss, constipation, or anorexia.
Clinical pathology
Hypercalcemia is the most consistent finding in animals with
hyperparathyroidism. High calcium causes increased excretion of
other electrolytes such as phosphorus, sodium, and potassium.
Serum biochemistry may reveal hypophosphatemia and azotemia.
Urinalysis may reveal low USG. These findings may be due to the
diuretic effects of hypercalcemia; however, chronic hypercalcemia
may cause renal damage resulting in CKD in some dogs [27,279].
Acid–base status and urea and creatinine concentrations should be
assessed in patients with suspected CKD.
Diagnosis and treatment
Diagnosis of hyperparathyroidism is based on elevated iCa, a history
of PU/PD, a low or low-normal serum phosphorus concentration,
and an inappropriately high serum concentration of PTH. A “normal”
concentration of PTH in the presence of hypercalcemia is also
indicative of hyperparathyroidism because PTH secretion should
be suppressed by increased levels of calcium [289]. PTH has been
reported to be within the normal reference range in cats with
hyperparathyroidism [285]. Cervical ultrasonography correlates well
with direct tumor measurements and has been recommended [287,290].
Urinalysis and abdominal ultrasound often reveal urinary tract
infections, cystic calculi, and renal mineralization [278,287].
Initial 	treatment 	of 	hypercalcemia 	includes 	intravenous
administration of 0.9% sodium chloride (100–125 mL/kg/day)
aimed at improving GFR, increasing renal calcium and sodium
excretion, and thus decreasing calcium reabsorption [291,292].
Additionally, some animals may also be hypovolemic due to urinary
and gastrointestinal water losses, and fluid resuscitation is
paramount. Water ad libitum should be available to animals with
hypercalcemia. Once normovolemic, furosemide, a loop diuretic,
can be administered (2–4 mg/kg twice or three times daily) to help
increase renal calcium excretion. To further decrease calcium
concentrations 	in 	animals 	with 	persistent 	hypercalcemia,
prednisolone or dexamethasone may be used to reduce bone and
intestinal absorption of calcium and increase renal calcium
excretion (Table 42.4) [27,291,293]. In cases with life-threatening
hypercalcemia [tCa > 17–20 mg/dL (4.3–5.0 mmol/dL)], sodium
bicarbonate, administered IV as a slow bolus, can decrease iCa by
promoting binding of calcium to albumin [279].
Surgical parathyroidectomy is curative and is the most com-
monly performed treatment option. It allows for direct excision of
the tumor while sparing the thyroid gland and the remaining
healthy parathyroid gland. Ultrasound-guided ethanol ablation is a
minimally invasive alternative to surgical parathyroidectomy, but

ethanol may not destroy the entire tumor and repeat administration
may be needed. Percutaneous ultrasound-guided radiofrequency
heat ablation has also been reported and resulted in few short- or
long- term complications [288,294]. Coughing, change in bark, and
Horner’s syndrome have been reported as postoperative complica-
tions after ethanol and heat ablation [294].
Anesthetic considerations and management
Although administration of calcitriol (active vitamin D metabolite)
3–5 days prior to anesthesia has been reported, a more recent
retrospective study found no protective value in its prophylactic
administration to prevent hypocalcemia in the postoperative period
(48 	h) 	after 	parathyroidectomy 	[279,295]. 	If 	calcitriol 	is
administered, careful monitoring of serum calcium and clinical
signs 	should 	be 	performed, 	and 	therapy 	discontinued 	if
hypercalcemia worsens [291].
A thorough preanesthetic evaluation is required, and hydration
status and electrolyte imbalances corrected. Serum calcium concen-
tration should be measured, and symptomatic animals treated
appropriately, as described above. Anesthesia should be postponed
when tCa is greater than 15–16 mg/dL (3.75–4 mmol/L) due to the
increased risk of side effects such as arrhythmias. Although there
are conflicting data regarding predictors of postoperative hypocal-
cemia, high iCa concentrations may increase the risk of postopera-
tive hypocalcemia after surgical removal or heat ablation in dogs
with primary hyperparathyroidism [283,291,296,297].
Absolute hypovolemia due to volume depletion in addition to the
relative hypovolemia caused by drug-induced vasodilation can
greatly affect maintenance of normal blood pressures intraopera-
tively. The presence or suspicion of CKD is another reason to main-
tain adequate hydration status and ensure normovolemia before
anesthesia [56]. Perioperatively, a calcium-free isotonic crystalloid
solution is preferred (e.g., Normosol-R®) in animals with high iCa.
If renal dysfunction is present, fluid rates up to 20–30 mL/kg/h dur-
ing anesthesia may be required [298,299]. The authors usually
maintain fluid rates at approximately 10 mL/kg/h. Especially in
dogs with higher preoperative calcium concentrations, renal failure
may be unmasked postoperatively, and renal values should be
closely monitored [279]. Consider placing a urinary catheter to
measure urine output intra- and postoperatively.
Anesthetic drug choices should be based on the animal health
status and concurrent comorbidities. There are no anesthetic drugs or
techniques specifically contraindicated for euvolemic dogs with
primary hyperparathyroidism undergoing elective procedures.
Animals with a history of vomiting may benefit from administration
of an antiemetic agent such as maropitant 30–60 min prior to opioid
premedication. Alternatively, opioids associated with lower incidences
of vomiting, such as methadone, meperidine, and fentanyl, could be
used as part of the premedication protocol. Full μ-opioid receptor
agonists are generally administered to provide appropriate
analgesia. α2
-Adrenergic receptor agonists, such as dexmedeto-
midine and medetomidine, benzodiazepines, and/or phenothiazines
(acepromazine), are often included in the intramuscular protocol to
provide sedation. Induction of anesthesia can be accomplished with
propofol, alfaxalone, ketamine–benzodiazepine, or etomidate, and
anesthesia is generally maintained with an inhalant anesthetic.
Constant rate infusions of lidocaine, dexmedetomidine, ketamine,
and/or short-acting full μ-opioid receptor agonists may be delivered
intraoperatively for MAC-sparing effects. For further multimodal
analgesia, NSAIDs may be beneficial in animals without renal
dysfunction and that are not receiving glucocorticoids. Although
there are no reports in the veterinary literature, humans with
hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia required higher doses of
vecuronium than patients without hyperparathyroidism [297].
However, non-depolarizing muscle relaxants are rarely required for
parathyroidectomies in veterinary patients.
Heart rate, ECG, and blood pressure should be closely monitored.
Hypercalcemia is associated with increased myocardial contractil-
ity and, in severe cases, can progress to incomplete or complete
atrioventricular block and cardiac arrest. ECG changes are charac-
terized by slowed conduction and include bradycardia, a prolonged
PR interval, a widened QRS complex, and a shortened QT inter-
val [291,293]. Blood gas analysis is warranted to monitor electro-
lytes and acid–base status and may be indicated intraoperatively if
ECG and/or blood pressure changes are noted.
Invasive (direct) blood pressure monitoring is preferred for
hemodynamically unstable patients, those with concurrent renal
disease, and those with large tumors. Respiratory rate and effort,
end-tidal carbon dioxide, and pulse oximetry should also be moni-
tored continuously. Although parathyroid tumors are usually not
large, hemorrhage and airway compromise are still possible compli-
cations of parathyroidectomy. Hypertonic saline and blood products
should be available to manage hemorrhage. Multiple large bore IV
catheters or a central line are recommended if a large or invasive
tumor is present. Ventilation should be closely monitored whenever
surgery is performed in the vicinity of the larynx or trachea. Damage
to the recurrent laryngeal nerve is possible due to its proximity to the
thyroid and parathyroid glands [300]. Pulse oximetry monitoring
should be continued until the animal is fully recovered.
Intraoperative PTH measurements can help confirm successful
tumor excision. A > 50% decrease in PTH concentrations 20–45 min
post-excision indicates removal of the affected tissue [301,302].
The most common complication following parathyroidectomy is
hypocalcemia due to hypercalcemia-induced atrophy of the remain-
ing parathyroid gland. Therefore, inadequate serum PTH concen-
tration results in hypocalcemia that is usually transient [283,296,297].
The median time to the lowest calcium concentration reported was
at 48 h and clinical hypocalcemia developed on average 4 days post-
operatively [303]. Mild postoperative hypocalcemia without clini-
cal signs is usually not treated. However, acute decreases in calcium
levels, tCa < 6 mg/dL (< 1.5 mmol/L), and development of clinical
signs such as muscle cramping or tremors, seizures, tetany, ano-
rexia, pain, and coma must be treated. Parenteral or oral calcium
supplementation and administration of calcitriol are common
treatments for animals with hypocalcemia [279,297]. Intravenous
calcium should be administered slowly to effect via a dedicated IV
catheter. Calcium gluconate (10%) solution can be administered at
0.5–1.5 mL/kg/h, while heart rate and ECG are closely monitored.
Infusion rates should be decreased or discontinued if bradycardia,
shortening of the QT interval, or development of arrhythmias is
observed. Frequent monitoring of iCa is required in these patients
postoperatively [291].

Introduction
The kidneys receive and require 20–25% of cardiac output to
appropriately perform their intricate and multifaceted role in the
maintenance of physiologic homeostasis. By its nature, general
anesthesia alters hemodynamics and organ perfusion, thus
inherently posing specific potential risk to healthy kidneys and
even more so to diseased or compromised kidneys. Renal disease
and functional impairment occur frequently in veterinary patients,
particularly in geriatric ones, with a 1–3% overall prevalence in
cats, up to 20% of cats having chronic kidney disease (CKD)
during their lifetime, and 35–80% of cats older than 15 years
affected [1–3]. The prevalence of CKD in dogs is lower and has
been reported at 0.05–3.74% depending on inclusion criteria, with
the largest and most recent study reporting a 0.21–0.37% overall
prevalence [4]. Histopathologic examination of the kidneys of
nonazotemic cats shows chronic degenerative changes including
glomerulosclerosis, tubular atrophy, interstitial inflammation, and
fibrosis that increases in severity with age [5]. Similar chronic
changes have been shown in aged canine kidneys as well,
suggesting that geriatric patients may be at heightened risk of
renal damage from nephrotoxic drugs and hemodynamic shifts,
even when these patients are nonazotemic [6].
Equine and ruminant patients have a much lower overall
prevalence of renal disease than cats and will be discussed less
in this chapter. The overall prevalence of CKD in horses is
0.12% with a prevalence of 0.23% in horses older than 15 years of
age, increasing to 0.51% in stallions older than 15 years of age [7].
Acute kidney injury occurs more commonly than CKD in horses,
with 23% of horses presenting for colic having evidence of injury
and as many as 25% of neonatal foals presenting for intensive
care [8].
Because animals with renal disease will routinely require anesthesia,
clinicians must have a working knowledge of renal physiology and
pathophysiology, as well as a thorough understanding of both the
potential renal effects of the sedative, analgesic, and anesthetic drugs
they select and how best to protect kidney health and function during
their use.
Normal anatomy and physiology
A complete in-depth overview of the anatomy and physiology of
the renal system is beyond the scope of this chapter; the reader is
referred to medical anatomy and physiology textbooks for further
detailed descriptions [9–11].

Anatomy of the urinary tract
Grossly, the urinary system can be divided into the kidneys, the
ureters, the urinary bladder, and the urethra. The kidney can be
further divided into the cortex, medulla, and renal pelvis. The renal
pelvis is essentially the expanded proximal portion of the ureters,
which carry urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder. Between
species, there are several anatomic differences that exist within the
kidney. Dogs, cats, horses, and small ruminants have unilobar
kidneys that contain a renal crest or basin within the renal pelvis
that collects urine and empties into the proximal urethra.
Additionally, gland-like structures in the wall of the horse’s renal
pelvis secrete a mucous-like substance that is responsible for
the cloudy and foamy nature of normal horse urine. Swine and
bovine kidneys are multilobar kidneys that contain renal papillae
(medullary extensions or pyramids) that empty into cup-like
calyces that then empty into the renal pelvis. The gross shape of the
kidney is fairly similar in that most species have the classic kidney
shape with a smooth surface and two poles. The exceptions are the
right kidney of the horse, which tends to have a heart-like shape,
and the lobulated kidneys of the bovine species, due to incomplete
fusion of the kidney lobes. The ureters are smooth muscle-lined
tubes that carry urine from the kidney to the bladder. The urinary
bladder can be anatomically divided into the body and the neck or
trigone region. The body consists of a compliant three-layered
muscular wall that can accommodate incoming urine for storage
and later voiding. This allows the bladder to vary greatly in shape,
size, and position within the pelvis and abdomen. The urethra is a
muscular tube that connects the bladder to the genitals, allowing
transit of urine from the bladder to the external environment.
Anatomic variations of the urethra exist based on gender
and species.
The functional units of the kidneys are nephrons (Fig. 43.1),
which consist of a renal corpuscle and associated tubule, span the
cortex and medulla of the kidney, and exist within a vital milieu
called the renal interstitium. The renal interstitium is composed
of cellular components (“interstitial cells”) residing in a loose
glycosaminoglycan matrix. The majority of interstitial cells are
specialized fibroblasts that structurally stabilize the kidney by
weaving around and between nephrons, and by connecting to each
other via intermediate-like junctions. These fibroblasts have very
well developed rough endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, and Golgi
apparatus to support their many synthetic functions. A smaller
population 	of 	marrow-derived 	cells 	migrates 	through 	the
interstitium; in healthy kidneys, most of these are major
histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II-expressing dendritic
cells, but in disease states, particularly inflammatory states, invasion
by other mononuclear cells (e.g., lymphocytes, monocytes/
macrophages, and other dendritic cells) is common. The interstitial
matrix is a living interconnection among the three chief functional
components of the kidney, that is, the vasculature, the tubules, and
the glomeruli, and serves as a thoroughfare between the renal
tubules and the peritubular capillaries. Solute and water transport
occurs from the tubular lumina through the interstitium and into
the peritubular capillaries, while oxygen and nutrients travel from

the capillaries through the interstitium to nourish the tubular

Renal tubules are responsible for modification of plasma filtrate
into urine and are described in functional segments termed the
proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, and collecting duct.
Tubules comprise the substantial majority of renal mass, with blood
vessels, interstitium, and renal corpuscles present in much smaller
quantities. The cortex contains the corpuscles, which are tight,
spherical convolutions of glomerular capillaries surrounded by a
specialized proximal tubular outpouching called Bowman’s capsule.
Initial filtration of plasma occurs at the glomerulus across the
glomerular filtration barrier (described later in the chapter); the
filtrate then flows into Bowman’s capsule and from there into the
proximal renal tubule. The cortical parenchyma consists of renal
tubules and capillaries packed around glomeruli in seemingly
random fashion, surrounded by small amounts of intercalated
interstitium. The medulla consists entirely of tubules, arterioles,
capillaries, and interstitium, packed tightly together with the
tubules and vessel networks arranged radially in near-parallel
formation within the parenchyma and in much more organized
fashion than in the cortex. The final tubular product, urine, flows
into the renal pelvis in transit to the ureter, which then propels the
urine by peristaltic waves into the bladder [13].
Physiologic function
The kidneys govern or play a significant role in a myriad of homeo-
static processes, chiefly maintaining water and electrolyte balance,
acid–base regulation, systemic blood pressure management, extra-
cellular fluid volume composition, excretion of dissolved foreign
substances and metabolic wastes, vitamin D production and calcium–
phosphorus balance, hormone secretion, metabolism and excre-
tion, erythrocyte production, and even gluconeogenesis. They
accomplish many of these functions through generation of urine by
the processes of filtration, reabsorption, and secretion and receive
about 25% of the cardiac output in order to do so. In fact, the renal
arteries branch directly from the caudal aorta, providing the high
percentage of cardiac output necessary to facilitate filtration and
maintain the kidneys’ high metabolic activity (i.e., very high oxygen
and substrate consumption). Kidneys, especially the proximal
tubules, are particularly susceptible to hypoxic damage and even
short-term renal ischemia can lead to acute kidney injury (AKI).
Renal blood flow (RBF) is regulated by extrinsic nervous and
hormonal control and by intrinsic autoregulation. The renal vascu-
lature is highly innervated by sympathetic constrictor fibers origi-
nating in the spinal cord segments between T4 and L1, yet the
kidneys lack sympathetic vasodilating fibers and parasympathetic
innervation. Dopamine receptors in the renal vasculature and
tubules help regulate vasodilation and blood flow. There are two
known subtypes of dopamine receptors, D 1 and D2
. Both of these
receptors have been identified in dogs, rats, rabbits, and other ani-
mals. It was thought that cats did not possess renal dopamine recep-
tors; however, in 2003, a D1
- like receptor was identified that is
considered to be different from receptors found in rats, dogs, or
humans [14]. Intrinsic autoregulation of RBF is demonstrated by a
constant flow when the mean arterial blood pressure ranges from
80 to 180 mmHg. When the mean arterial blood pressure is in this
range, the kidney can control blood flow via alteration of resistance
in the glomerular afferent arterioles. Although the exact mechanism
of renal autoregulation is not known, the phenomenon protects glo-
merular capillaries during hypertension and preserves renal func-
tion during hypotension. In addition to renal autoregulation,
extrinsic forces (e.g., neural, hormonal, and pharmacologic) and
intrinsic forces (e.g., kidney disease) may cause alterations in RBF.
Catecholamines are major hormonal regulators of RBF. Epinephrine
and norepinephrine cause dose-dependent changes in RBF. Low
doses increase arterial blood pressure and increase RBF through
increased cardiac output, whereas higher doses cause a decreased
RBF through increased vascular resistance. The renin–angiotensin–
aldosterone system, discussed later in this chapter, is also an
important regulator of RBF. In addition, prostaglandins play an
important role in the regulation of RBF. Prostaglandin-E 2 (PGE2
)
and prostaglandin-I 2 (PGI2 or prostacyclin) cause vasodilation
within the kidney. Generation of PGE2 and PGI2 occurs through the
upregulation of cyclo-oxygenase enzymes; in particular, the cyclo-
oxygenase-2 (COX-2) enzyme plays a largely constitutive and
protective role. The COX-2 enzyme is found mainly in the macula
densa but can also be found in other areas of the cortex and the
medulla. During low blood flow or hypotensive states, COX-2-
derived prostaglandins promote natriuresis, renin release, and vas-
odilation of afferent arterioles to preserve RBF.
Although the kidney receives a high percentage of the cardiac out-
put, blood flow is not evenly distributed throughout the kidney. The
renal cortex receives the majority of the blood (90–95%), thus leav-
ing the medulla relatively hypoperfused and hypoxic. This dichoto-
mous blood flow strategy maximizes flow-dependent activities in
areas of the kidney that specialize in high-efficiency filtration.
Hydrostatic pressure drives plasma filtration across the glomerular
filtration barrier and into the proximal convoluted tubules. The filtra-
tion barrier consists of the glomerular capillaries, the glomerular base-
ment membrane, and specialized epithelial cells called “podocytes.”
The glomerular capillaries consist of a single layer of endothelial cells
with small fenestrations that provide the filtration surface and allow
only fluid, very small proteins, and electrolytes to be filtered. Under
these cells is the glomerular basement membrane, an acellular, trilam-
inar structure composed of various proteins and proteoglycans, that
provides a scaffold for the epithelial cells and a negatively charged bar-
rier that excludes larger negatively charged molecules (chiefly pro-
teins). The last layer of the glomerular filtration barrier is formed by
the network of extensively branching podocytes that cover the entire
glomerular surface. The tiny spaces between the interdigitating pro-
cesses of these cells are specialized junctions called “slit pores” or “slit
diaphragms,” which provide the most size-restrictive portion of the
filtration barrier. With the exception of albumin and larger proteins,
the glomerular filtrate received by Bowman’s capsule is very similar in
composition to plasma (Table 43.1).
The rate of formation of the filtrate, or glomerular filtration rate
(GFR), is a measurable parameter that can be evaluated clinically to
determine renal excretory function. GFR is expressed as milliliters of
glomerular filtrate per kilogram of body weight formed per minute
(mL/kg/min). Blood flow into the glomeruli for filtration is under
pressure and is regulated by afferent (preglomerular) and efferent
(postglomerular) arterioles. The amount of filtrate formed is directly
related to the pressure across the capillaries, and this pressure can be
described mathematically using Starling’s equation:
Q 	K 	P 	P	f 	c 	i 	c 	i
where Q is the net fluid movement across the capillaries, Kf is the
filtration coefficient (which depends on the permeability and length
of the filtration surface), Pc is the capillary hydrostatic pressure, Pi is
the interstitial hydrostatic pressure, σ is the reflection or filtration
coefficient, πc is the capillary oncotic pressure, and πi is the
interstitial oncotic pressure. When measured at the afferent arteriole

Chapter 43: Physiology, Pathophysiology, and Anesthetic Management of Patients with Renal Disease 	925
end of the glomerulus, the net filtration pressure is about 10 mmHg,
resulting in a net outflow. When measured at the efferent arteriole
end of the glomerulus, the net filtration pressure is about 0 mmHg,
resulting in zero net outflow.
RBF and, thus, usually GFR are maintained within a consistent
range in spite of changes in systemic blood pressure by an
autoregulation system controlled in large part by the renin–
angiotensin–aldosterone hormone system (RAAS). When blood
pressure and subsequent renal perfusion decrease, the enzyme
renin is released from specialized juxtaglomerular cells located in
the walls of the afferent arterioles, just proximal to the glomeruli.
Renin acts on angiotensinogen (produced by the liver) to release
angiotensin I, which is swiftly converted to angiotensin II (AT-II, a
potent vasoconstrictor) by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE).
This conversion occurs chiefly while blood flows through the small
vessels in the lungs, since most ACE is produced by the pulmonary
small vascular endothelium. The kidneys and other blood vessels
also produce some ACE and generate a smaller amount of AT-II
locally. AT-II directly increases blood pressure through constriction
of smooth muscle in arterioles but also has multiple endocrine and
paracrine effects. Locally within the kidney, AT-II activates sodium
uptake in the tubules of the nephron, promoting fluid retention and
increased blood volume. At the adrenal gland, AT-II increases
release of the steroid hormone aldosterone, which promotes sodium
conservation, potassium elimination, and increased fluid retention
and blood pressure. At the pituitary gland, AT-II enhances
vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone) release, which
increases water reabsorption in the kidneys through the insertion
of water channels (aquaporin-2) into the membrane of the distal
tubules of the nephron. Vasopressin also has direct vasoconstrictive
properties through G-protein-coupled V receptors in vascular
endothelium. Additionally, AT-II induces intrarenal release of the
vasodilating prostaglandins PGE2 and prostacyclin (PGI2 ) that
counteract the vasoconstricting effects of AT-II, thereby preventing
excessive intrarenal vascular resistance and local ischemia. A
second intrinsic system, called “tubuloglomerular feedback,” also
contributes to the autoregulatory system that helps maintain GFR.
A distinct group of epithelial cells within the distal convoluted
tubule (DCT), the macula densa, contact the glomerulus between
the afferent and efferent arterioles as part of the juxtaglomerular
apparatus (JGA). Osmoreceptors within the macula densa cells
sense decreased sodium concentrations within the tubular lumen
and initiate a cascade of events resulting in renin release from the
juxtaglomerular cells. Alternatively, increased sodium chloride
concentrations result in an undefined cascade of events that
suppresses renin release and leads to production of vasoactive
factors (nitric oxide, adenosine triphosphate, prostaglandins) that
reduce GFR and promote free water conservation.
Filtered fluid that leaves the glomerulus next enters the proximal
convoluted tubules (PCTs). The major function of the PCT is to
reabsorb the majority of the filtrate; in fact, more than 60% of the
filtered substances are reabsorbed in the PCT. Transport across the
PCT membrane into the interstitial tissues and then into the vascu-
lar space occurs via both active and passive transport with Starling’s
forces dictating the passive phases. The majority of ions filtered at
the glomerulus (Na +
, K +
, Ca 2+
, Cl –
, and HCO 3
– ) are reabsorbed in
the PCT so that filtrate leaving the PCT and entering the loop of
Henle has lower levels of electrolytes than plasma. Water passively
follows the active reabsorption of electrolytes so that the osmolality
of the tubular fluid is similar to that of plasma at both ends of the
PCT. Organic low-molecular-weight proteins (insulin, glucagon,
parathyroid hormone, etc.) that were filtered are also actively reab-
sorbed in the PCT. Secretion of substances also occurs in the PCT.
Organic ionic wastes are eliminated via secretion into the filtrate;
these include protein-bound exogenous substances that are not fil-
tered at the glomerulus, for example, endotoxins, antibiotics, and
anesthetic and analgesic drugs such as morphine and ketamine, and
endogenous wastes such as bile salts, urates, and prostaglandins.
PCT secretion is exceptionally important for endogenous waste
removal in birds and reptiles. In mammals, one of the main waste
products from muscle metabolism is urea, which is freely filtered at
the glomerulus; however, uric acid is the waste product from mus-
cle metabolism in birds and reptiles. Uric acid is not filtered at the
glomeruli, and its removal is dependent upon active mechanisms in
the PCT in these species.
Next, the remaining filtrate enters the descending loop of Henle
(DloH). Metabolic activity within the DloH is minimal, and little to
no active transport process occurs. Pure water reabsorption and
minimal solute drag occur as the filtrate travels through the DloH
to the highly active ascending (AloH) or thick portion of the loop of
Henle.
The AloH is one of the most metabolically active parts of the
tubule and the entire kidney. It is composed of simple cuboidal
epithelium with many mitochondria, which provide the energy for
high-capacity active transport. Here, the filtrate is further modified
as the majority of electrolyte reabsorption within the loop of Henle
takes place in the AloH. An abundant concentration of Na +
- K+
ATPase pumps can be found on the luminal surface of the tubules,
which are responsible for the active transport of Na +
, K +
, and Cl−
into the cell and out of the filtrate. Other ions such as Mg 2+ and Ca 2+
move down a cation-selective paracellular pathway into the
interstitium. In the case of K + in particular, hyperkalemia can result
in electrical conduction pathology, and therefore, both apical and
basolateral K + channels exist to increase secretion into the filtrate
for eventual removal in the urine. As the AloH is highly metabolically
active, it has a high demand for substrates such as oxygen and,

therefore, has increased sensitivity to damage during hypoxemia or

effects both therapeutically and pathologically at the AloH. For
example, furosemide works as a diuretic by inhibiting Na+
- K+
