intermittent pressure release phase [70,71]. More specifically, APRV
is better described as applying continuous airway pressure (Phigh
)
identical to CPAP to maintain adequate lung volume and promote
alveolar recruitment, with a time-cycled release phase to a lower pres-
sure (Plow
) very transiently. Mechanically, this is not too dissimilar
from the early APV mode used on dolphins, however, APV uses a Plow
of 0 cmH2
O and time sufficient for alveoli to collapse. APRV was
developed to maintain functional residual capacity (FRC, the volume
of gas remaining in the lung after a normal expiration) at a level that
would optimize gas exchange and lung compliance in the spontane-
ously ventilating patient in respiratory failure. Unfortunately, when
APRV is applied to the unconscious, non-spontaneously ventilating
patient (e.g., marine mammals), it allows lung volume to drop below
FRC and may promote the development of atelectasis.
Apneustic anesthesia ventilation (AAV) was developed to
maintain lung volume at a level slightly greater than FRC. In this
mode of ventilation, tidal ventilation occurs when airway pressure
is transiently reduced from P high (CPAP) to P low (the release pres-
sure), allowing lung volume to decrease to no lower than FRC and
supporting partial inflation of alveoli (Fig. 56.1). Immediate reap-
plication of P high leads to the alveoli remaining partially inflated
(at a volume above FRC) prior to the lung volume increase. This
intermittent pressure release and reapplication permits tidal
breathing to occur without allowing development of atelectasis.
Target P high and P low are determined by optimizing compliance and
the desired tidal volume. Note that mechanically, AAV and APV
modes of ventilation are similar. However, the key distinction is
that exhalation to lower airway pressures for a longer duration
during APV can result in atelectasis, decreased compliance,
derangement of ventilation and perfusion (V/Q mismatch), and
hypoxemia. During AAV application, V/Q matching is main-
tained at baseline levels in anesthetized patients, and lung
mechanics are normalized [72–74]. Of note, published studies in
horses indicate AAV should not be applied in a static mode and is
best used clinically as a dynamic mode of ventilation involving
regular adjustments [74]. That said, it might better be described as
a continuum of recruitment maneuvers. When applied in this
dynamic mode, the advantages of AAV over other modes of venti-
lation include lower mean intrathoracic (pleural) pressure, aug-
mented venous return, improved cardiovascular performance,
and better distribution of inspired gas flow resulting in improved
ventilation–perfusion matching [75]. The AAV mode is specifi-
cally indicated in patients with low lung and thoracic compliance,
as may be the case in large marine mammal species, particularly
the “beached,” anesthetized dolphin.
APV, APRV, and AAV will each mimic the breathing patterns of
conscious, actively breathing marine mammals, and live subject test-
ing is needed to elucidate their role in the target marine mammal
population. Of these modes, AAV would be anticipated to provide
superior ventilatory support to the anesthetized, non-spontaneously
ventilating marine mammal and is actively under evaluation in
California sea lions and bottlenose dolphins [76]. Additional testing
of these modes of ventilation, including the evaluation of lower
inspired oxygen concentrations, is currently underway and is pro-
ducing promising results in both terrestrial and marine mammal
species [68,74,76,77].
Permissive or intentional hypercapnia
In theory, “lung protective” ventilation strategies that utilize lower
tidal volumes may limit alveolar overdistension and minimize
lung injury; however, they will concurrently lead to hypercapnia,
commonly referred to as “permissive hypercapnia” in medical lit-
erature [78]. Fundamentally, when properly performed, AAV will
produce a degree of intentional hypercapnia. Both intentional
hypercapnia (whereby hypercapnia is intentionally implemented as
part of the ventilation mode such as in AAV) and permissive hyper-
capnia (whereby hypercapnia is accepted in avoidance of poten-
tially negative ventilatory effects) are generally well tolerated and
are described in greater detail elsewhere in this textbook.
Allowing a degree of intentional or permissive hypercapnia will
allow implementation of lung protective ventilatory strategies and
can both increase cardiac output and promote offloading of oxygen
to tissues if held to a reasonable level. Although one may rationalize
a degree of benefit of hypercapnia, recent work has suggested that
high levels of CO2 are not beneficial to pinnipeds and indicate a
need for enhanced monitoring and support [79]. If intentional or
permissive hypercapnia is used, the following parameters are sug-
gested limits: PaCO2 < 80 mmHg; pH > 7.20; and PaO2 > 80 mmHg.
The authors apply both intentional hypercapnia and eucapnia, situ-
ationally dependent. Since hypercapnia increases cardiac output
and blood pressure, individuals accustomed to use of permissive
hypercapnia who achieve eucapnia, as a choice or out of necessity,
may need to be prepared to manage hypotension they may not rou-
tinely observe. Additionally, hypercapnia may increase pulmonary
vascular resistance of the ventilated lung, which can result in
increased shunt fraction. Interestingly, sea lions appear to undergo
hypoxic pulmonary vasodilation rather than vasoconstriction, per-
haps increasing shunt fraction in improperly ventilated marine
mammal species under anesthesia [80].
Preanesthetic assessment and planning
The first step in any sedation or anesthetic event is determination
of whether chemical restraint is even necessary. Many minimally
invasive procedures (e.g., blood sampling and diagnostic imaging)
can be completed under behavioral control alone and addition of
simple local anesthetic blocks may even facilitate more invasive
procedures (e.g., tissue biopsy). If needed, this can be combined
with mild sedation for short, minimally invasive procedures.
Immobilization or general anesthesia will be warranted for longer
or more invasive procedures (e.g., surgery), in free-ranging species
or those without behavioral control, or with large, potentially haz-
ardous marine mammal subjects. While true anesthetic risk is still
largely unknown for the vast majority of marine mammal species,
it is likely higher than traditional domestic species due to a number
of factors, including unknown health status, extrapolated phar-
macology, and challenges with monitoring; a single retrospective
study reported a perianesthetic mortality rate of 4.3% for free-
ranging pinnipeds undergoing sedation or anesthesia at a renowned
rescue and rehabilitation facility [81].
In managed populations where a voluntary preanesthetic health
assessment is feasible, examination and laboratory tests can provide
an overview of the animal’s current health status and identify con-
current disease states. This is especially relevant when considering
that many anesthetic procedures in managed populations are per-
formed on geriatric patients. Where possible, this should include, at
minimum, a physical examination, complete blood count and
serum chemistry panel with a urinalysis, and imaging (e.g., radio-
graphs, abdominal ultrasound, and echocardiography) performed
where appropriate. Trainers must be vigilant to maintain necessary
medical behaviors, but the anesthetist must recognize how disease
(e.g., decreased vision), pain, and medications (e.g., preoperative

-- 1111 of 1450 --

1096 	Section 7: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia
opioids) can alter or lead to loss of medical behaviors. In situations
in which a preanesthetic health assessment is limited (e.g., behavio-
rally non-compliant patients, and free-ranging subjects), visual
inspection from a distance and interview of the managing trainers
and veterinarians where possible should be performed. A limited
preanesthetic assessment could put subjects at greater risk for nega-
tive outcomes and the anesthetist should prepare accordingly.
When tailoring an anesthetic protocol, the anesthetist must con-
sider the species, size, age, demeanor, training, as well as the work-
ing environment. Anesthesia of marine mammals requires a balance
of behavioral, mechanical (physical), and chemical restraint.
Though often useful, excessive reliance on mechanical restraint
may lead to physical injury to the patient (e.g., improper desensiti-
zation, “off behaviors” due to illness), hyperthermia, or exertional
myopathic conditions [82]. Similarly, even though darting an ani-
mal with ultrapotent anesthetic agents to cause immobilization can
be efficacious, it may result in severe negative physiologic effects.
As such, emphasis should be placed on preprocedural behavioral
training for voluntary medical procedures whenever time and
resources exist, as these may reduce the need for mechanical or
aggressive chemical restraint. When mechanical restraint is needed,
desensitization training to mechanical restraint devices, such as
netting, slings, and squeeze cages is recommended. With proper
desensitization training and chemical sedation, mechanical devices
may be used to improve the safety of anesthetic procedures for both
the patient and personnel, without undue added risk.
The choices of anesthetic and perianesthetic drugs applied to
marine mammal species have actually been rather limited, yet have
been reviewed many times over the years, with focus primarily
on immobilization cocktails and field applications of anesthetic
drugs [83–90]. Induction of anesthesia of marine mammals requires
a balance of behavioral, mechanical, and chemical restraint (Fig. 56.2).
For instance, the process of anesthesia for pinnipeds has ranged
from heavy mechanical restraint by lasso of juvenile Stellar sea lions
followed by dowel and board squeeze/entrapment and mask induc-
tion with inhalation anesthetic alone [91,92], to solely chemical

restraint by various potent and efficacious combinations of anes-
thetic agents delivered by dart, to remarkable behavior control by
training for mask induction with an inhalation anesthetic agent
alone under trainer command. In any situation, the concept of bal-
anced anesthesia (use of a combination of drugs and techniques at
lower individual doses to minimize dose-dependent side effects)
should be employed. Additionally, for marine mammals, a balanced
approach to anesthesia usually includes considerations beyond
anesthetic drug selection. For example, with sufficient personnel, it
is feasible to manually restrain small cetaceans and sirenians, but
pinnipeds of size will require additional tools for restraint.
The rationale for the anesthetic protocol begins with assessment
of behaviors. Behaviors are useful responses taught to marine mam-
mals by qualified trainers. Desensitization training and voluntary
medical behaviors contribute in no small part to more positive out-
comes in managed populations, eliminating the need for aggressive
restraint methods or potent cocktails with severe physiologic conse-
quences. Skilled trainers and animal handlers are necessary to sup-
port safe anesthesia, and they must be given both the opportunity
and time required for training where possible. Examples of useful
medical behaviors are holding on target for injections by hand, toler-
ance of mechanical restraint in a squeeze cage, self-beaching of dol-
phins, or acceptance of an anesthetic mask for inhalation anesthetic
delivery. Even in subjects that could be very difficult to restrain, such
behaviors can be sufficiently robust to allow free-standing applica-
tion of anesthetic agents without physical restraint. Without medical
behaviors, there is greater reliance on both mechanical restraint,
which can become dangerous and lead to injury, and chemical
restraint, which often needs to be more profound.
With chemical restraint, ut est rerum omnium magister usus or,
experience is the best teacher [93]. Anesthesia methods applied to
free-living subjects are highly variable and often depend on the
experience of the personnel, as well as the historical success of the
method applied. For example, though less commonly used in man-
aged species, the combination of tiletamine and zolazepam (Telazol®
or Zoletil®) is still the preferred immobilization method for free-
living elephant seals. As most free-living subjects are anesthetized
to facilitate study of the species as a whole, these subjects are usually
healthy individuals that may better tolerate the physiological chal-
lenges of a broader range of necessary mechanical and chemical
restraint methods. On the contrary, rescued free-living subjects are
often debilitated or otherwise unhealthy and are at greater risk of
negative outcomes in the face of immobilization methods necessary
for the safety of human caretakers. The authors recognize the broad
range of sedation and anesthesia methods applied to the wide vari-
ety of marine mammal species over the past many decades, and
offer only to provide some general, repeatable methods in hopes of
improved outcomes for all the species under our care, particularly
the growing geriatric populations.
Protocol selection
Historically, drugs used in the anesthetic and perianesthetic period
in marine mammals have been quite limited. These have been
extensively reviewed in other texts and primarily focus on immobi-
lization cocktails and field applications of anesthetic drugs [83–86].
To tabulate that historical information again here would not serve
the anesthetist well and, instead, a brief summary of common drug
choices for each species is provided below. As noted previously,
anesthesia of marine mammals requires a balance of behavioral,
physical/mechanical, and chemical restraint, although various
combinations of the above have been used. Managed populations
do not generally require aggressive restraint methods or potent
cocktails for induction, especially if preprocedural behavioral train-
ing is implemented. When selecting an anesthetic protocol, the
risk-benefit ratio for each drug and technique should be carefully
considered and the anesthetist should be reminded that, “There are
no safe anesthetic agents; there are no safe anesthetic procedures;
there are only safe anesthetists” (Robert Smith) [94,95]. The impor-
tance of vigilant perianesthetic monitoring and support in conjunc-
tion with any anesthetic protocol cannot be overstated and will be
discussed further.
While specific drugs will not be discussed in detail, α2 - adrenergic
receptor agonist use in pinnipeds warrants discussion. One of the
most commonly administered drug combinations in this cohort
involves various combinations of midazolam, butorphanol, and
medetomidine, and has proven effective in field immobilization of
young, healthy otariids for short procedures [96]. While useful in
certain situations, the authors have anecdotally appreciated a higher
incidence of negative outcomes in some managed populations with
use of an α2
- adrenergic receptor agonist. Medetomidine was used in
> 50% of induction protocols reported in a retrospective assessment
of anesthetic mortality in a cohort of rescued, untrained, free-living
otariids of variable disease condition and severity; perianesthetic
mortality in that study was 4.3% [81]. Additionally, a high negative
outcome rate (e.g., ciliary body hemorrhage, hyphema, and death)
was anecdotally reported in pinnipeds following medetomidine or
dexmedetomidine administration for ophthalmologic procedures.
In a series of 13 prolonged ophthalmologic procedures on geriatric
California sea lions (median age 22.5 years) immobilized with a
combination of midazolam, butorphanol, and dexmedetomidine,
one subject vomited, two had arrhythmias, two had prolonged
recoveries, and three died during anesthesia or within 72 h of recov-
ery [86,97]. For these reasons, α2
-adrenergic receptor agonists,
despite their reversibility, may not be a reasonable choice in geriat-
ric marine mammals or those undergoing lengthy procedures, and
would be ill-advised in phocids and odobenids [98]. This is not to
say the α2 - adrenergic receptor agonists are not effective or on occa-
sion necessary; however, the anesthetist must recall Maslow’s
Axiom that “it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to
treat everything as if it were a nail” [99]. While it is easy, and some-
times necessary, to dart an animal with potent efficacious anesthetic
agents (including α2 -adrenergic receptor agonists), all options
should be explored and the physiologic consequences for this con-
venience should be considered. That being said, more judicious use
of α2 - adrenergic receptor agonists may yet prove beneficial.
Sedation and anesthesia
Relatively few pharmacologic agents have gained acceptance for use
in managed populations of marine mammals. In brief, benzodiaz-
epines (diazepam 0.05–0.3 mg/kg PO, IM, IV; midazolam 0.05–
0.3 mg/kg IM, IV) are commonly used, often in combination with
opioids (butorphanol 0.1–0.4 mg/kg IM; meperidine 0.1–2 mg/kg
IM) to produce sedation or neuroleptanalgesia. Immobilization can
be achieved with the addition of medetomidine (0.01–0.03 mg/kg
IM) or dexmedetomidine (0.002–0.01 mg/kg IM) in some otariid
pinnipeds, but not cetaceans or sirenians. Concentrated versions of
midazolam, butorphanol, and medetomidine assist with remote
delivery by dart or pole syringe by minimizing volume. Alternatively,
alfaxalone (0.5–2 mg/kg IM, IV) has been introduced for immobili-
zation where larger volumes or multiple intramuscular injections are
feasible in pinnipeds. An experimental, concentrated (40 mg/mL)

-- 1113 of 1450 --

1098 	Section 7: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia
alfaxalone formulation, RD0387, which allows for reduced volumes
has recently been used successfully for immobilization of large otari-
ids in lieu of medetomidine [100]. Other parenteral anesthetic agents
have been used for immobilization or induction of general anesthe-
sia. The cyclohexamines, ketamine (1–10 mg/kg IM, IV), or tileta-
mine (in Telazol® or Zoletil®; 1–2 mg/kg IM, IV), have been used but
are not reversible and are less favored. The phenolic compound
propofol (1–6 mg/kg IV) is used routinely in the extradural vein for
induction of anesthesia of phocids and odobenids for rapid airway
control and ease of intubation in preference over slower mask induc-
tion with inhalation anesthetics. Behaviorally non-compliant patients
can be injected remotely by pole syringe or dart, but it is imperative
the drug is delivered into muscle and not fat, or uptake will be poor.
Repeat dosing from presumed “failed delivery” can lead to eventual
cumulative drug uptake and overdose with sudden onset of CNS
depression and respiratory depression.
Inhalation anesthetics (e.g., isoflurane and sevoflurane) have
been used successfully in marine mammals. They are low-solubility
agents and are minimally metabolized. For mask induction, sevo-
flurane has a faster onset and lesser pungency, thus, it has become
preferred. The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of inhalant
anesthetics has not yet been determined for any marine mammal
species, making comparison of equipotent concentrations to other
species imprecise. However, the effect of inhalation anesthetic
agents is well preserved over the wide variety of mammalian species
tested, so the dose of inhalation anesthetic for marine mammals
will likely differ little from other mammalian species. Anecdotally,
the authors use MAC estimations of 1.3% for isoflurane and 2.3%
for sevoflurane. In the authors’ experience performing marine
mammal anesthesia over the past decade, with similar preanes-
thetic drugs (i.e., benzodiazepine and opioid), the end-expired
sevoflurane concentration usually needs to be maintained at
approximately 1.8 to 2.0% to prevent gross, purposeful movement
in response to a surgical stimulus.
An in-depth discussion of anesthetic agents and their effects to
be used for all orders of marine mammals is beyond the scope of
this chapter. Instead, a brief summary of commonly used agents
and their administration in each order is presented below.
Cetacean anesthesia
The first attempt to anesthetize a dolphin was made in the 1930s in
which a dolphin was administered “ether by cone” over the blowhole,
became apneic, and died [101]. After concurrent dolphin deaths
associated with intraperitoneal barbiturate anesthesia [102], Nagel
successfully developed an endotracheal intubation method and
induced a state where the dolphins were “largely insensitive to nox-
ious stimuli” with nitrous oxide (N2
O) and O2 (70%:30%) delivered
by a ventilator and using neuromuscular blockade with succinylcho-
line [63,69]. Although this method appeared “safe,” it was inadequate
for major surgery. Ridgway and McCormick used combinations of
inhaled halothane and intravascular thiopental for induction and
maintenance of anesthesia sufficient for major surgery [65,66].
However, uncertain about the effects of injectable agents, the early
successful anesthetic inductions involved manual restraint and con-
scious intubation followed by halothane administered via endotra-
cheal tube. This produced excitement and dysphoria characterized by
significant swimming motions, a physical response less commonly
observed with current methods of balanced anesthesia.
In managed care settings, cetacean sedation and anesthesia are
heavily supported by behavioral training. These intelligent species
are amenable to desensitization or other behavioral training and,
ideally, this is incorporated into routine medical or husbandry train-
ing. Fasting of food for at least 12 h duration is typically practiced as
regurgitation can occur. The target animal is often separated from
conspecifics and preanesthetic sedation is often used to reduce stress
and facilitate patient compliance. Currently, benzodiazepines alone
(either diazepam 0.25 mg/kg PO or midazolam 0.08 mg/kg IM) or in
combination with opioids (butorphanol 0.1 mg/kg IM or meperi-
dine 0.1 mg/kg IM) are used for preanesthetic sedation. Midazolam
0.1 mg/kg IM (0.05–0.2 mg/kg IM) with butorphanol 0.1 mg/kg IM
(0.1–0.3 mg/kg IM) has provided sedation for minor procedures in
bottlenose dolphins, killer whales, and even 20,000 kg North Atlantic
right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) [103,104]. Propofol (2–3 mg/kg
IV) is used, often with supplemental midazolam (0.02 mg/kg IV) for
induction of anesthesia in the lateral caudal subcutaneous vein
(LCSV). Anesthesia of dolphins has been maintained with the
inhalation anesthetics halothane, isoflurane, and more recently,
sevoflurane in oxygen [31,64,65,105–108]. Controlled mechanical
ventilation (CMV) has been applied with variable success, as well as
the alternative mode, apneustic anesthesia ventilation (AAV), which
is currently undergoing clinical trials.
Pinniped anesthesia
Phocid anesthesia
Similar to other marine mammals, desensitization and behavioral
training when possible are keys to phocid health in managed care;
this includes desensitization to use of a “blood collection box” for
extradural anesthetic drug administration and, for larger pinni-
peds, use of a squeeze cage. In brief, benzodiazepines are very effec-
tive in tranquilizing phocids. In wild captures, intravenous
diazepam 0.25 mg/kg in combination with mechanical restraint
using a simple hoop-net prior to mask induction with inhalation
anesthetic is not uncommon. In managed populations, subjects can
be trained to accept an intramuscular injection of midazolam and
inhalation anesthetic via mask under behavioral restraint alone.
Free-living phocids remain somewhat excitable with a concurrent
elevated respiratory rate, resulting in successful mask induction
using inhalant anesthetics. In contrast, animals in managed popula-
tions tend to breath-hold, which can delay induction. These sub-
jects can also become apneic from anesthetic exposure before
sufficiently relaxed for smooth intubation, thus, induction with IV
anesthetic agents is often pursued. This usually includes behavioral
or mechanical restraint (e.g., blood collection box) for extradural
venous puncture and IV administration of propofol (1–2 mg/kg
titrated to effect); this is often in combination with IM premedica-
tion (e.g., midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IM and butorphanol 0.2 mg/kg IM)
to reduce induction drug requirements. Butorphanol is often suffi-
cient for the purpose of control without significant respiratory
depression; however, full μ-opioid receptor agonists (e.g., meperi-
dine) have been used for greater sedation of larger phocid species
where there is inadequate behavioral control. Due to the likelihood
of apnea following any induction protocol, the anesthetist should be
prepared for prompt intubation, usually performed under direct
laryngoscopy. In field settings where inhalation anesthesia may not
be readily available, heavy sedation can be maintained for longer
procedures with repeated dosing of midazolam, butorphanol, and
ketamine IV, alone or in combination.
Otariid anesthesia
Training robust medical behaviors is crucial to reducing anesthetic
risk in otariids. Behaviors, such as free-standing anesthetic induc-
tion by mask, have been trained even in extremely large otariid

-- 1114 of 1450 --

Chapter 56: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia – Marine Mammals 	1099
species. Benzodiazepines are anxiolytic, but further sedation with
opioids is generally needed for most otariid subjects, even when
properly trained for mechanical restraint. A scissor-style squeeze
cage is commonly used for mechanical restraint in managed popu-
lations, and has been used for some free-living capture and longer-
term holding situations [109,110]. Subjects are trained to accept
temporary restraint by squeeze allowing for injection of sedative
agents. Accurate intramuscular delivery of drugs is necessary, or
uptake will be poor. The intramuscular sedative combination
(midazolam 0.2 mg/kg and butorphanol 0.2 mg/kg or meperidine
2 mg/kg) is administered, and time allowed for uptake and full
effect (20–25 min). Sedation is followed with mechanical restraint
by squeeze to facilitate mask induction. Mechanical restraint sig-
nificantly enhances control and human safety but is not without
risk. Inadequately trained or sedated subjects may attempt to resist
mask induction or bite at the bars, the latter of which can break
teeth and fracture jaws. Even subjects known to tolerate a squeeze
cage can become intolerant when ill. Only properly designed
squeeze cages with padded bars should be used for this method of
restraint. Boat bumpers and rolled towels can be used to center the
head for mask induction and act as safe bite “toy.” It is preferred
that the anesthetic mask be malleable to move between cage bars,
if necessary, mold to the face of the subject, and tolerate biting
without injury to the subject. A modified traffic cone has proven
ideal for this purpose [111]. The combination of intramuscular
midazolam (0.2–0.3 mg/kg) and meperidine (1–2 mg/kg) may
produce neuroleptanalgesia in some species, such as southern sea
lions, and result in marked sedation. A squeeze cage is not always
available or may be of inadequate size for larger subjects making
mechanical restraint impractical and improvised squeezes have
been created, but efficacy and response are often variable. Large
custom walrus restraint nets can be effective for large sea lions and
fur seals. Where mechanical restraint is not possible, a greater reli-
ance is placed on pharmacologic agents. A combination of concen-
trated intramuscular midazolam 0.2 mg/kg, butorphanol 0.2 mg/
kg, and medetomidine 0.01 mg/kg is commonly used, but results in
bradycardia, vasoconstriction, and a reduction in cardiac output,
complicating vascular access and challenging debilitated and geri-
atric patients physiologically. A combination of medetomidine and
the peripheral α2 -adrenergic receptor antagonist vatinoxan
(Zenalpha®) has recently been used in otariids, but clear benefit is
not yet evident. Alternatively, the combination of concentrated
intramuscular midazolam 0.2 mg/kg, butorphanol 0.2 mg/kg, and
alfaxalone 1 mg/kg is currently under review with promising
results [100].
Odobenid anesthesia
Walrus subjects in managed population can be very well trained
such that delivery of intramuscular midazolam (0.2 mg/kg) or even
direct extradural or saphenous venous needle placement for deliv-
ery of propofol (2–4 mg/kg) can be performed under behavioral
control. However, most walruses will need additional intramuscu-
lar sedation and analgesia using an opioid, particularly when not
participating in medical behaviors due to illness and/or discomfort;
meperidine (2 mg/kg) is often chosen, but butorphanol (0.2 mg/kg)
has also been used. In young patients, the combination of mida-
zolam and meperidine can produce a state of neuroleptanalgesia
sufficient to permit intubation. If this combination is not sufficient
for intubation, the authors have used a low dose of alfaxalone (<
0.5 mg/kg) to bridge control, but further evaluation is needed
before recommending this drug. As noted previously, induction is
performed using propofol (0.5–4 mg/kg) delivered in the extradural
or saphenous vein. Intubation is performed blindly via manual pal-
pation and, as these species often experience apnea following
propofol administration, the anesthetist must be well prepared for
intubation.
Sirenian anesthesia
To our knowledge, no dugong has ever undergone anesthesia and
most anesthesia experience has been with the Florida manatee
(Trichechus manatus latirostris). Many manatees needing anesthesia
for surgical procedures come from rescue and rehabilitation facili-
ties that perform lifesaving work on untrained subjects. It is recom-
mended that only trained personnel participate in the handling and
restraint of sirenians, and we emphasize here that quality trainers
and animal handlers are necessary for safe anesthesia of these
marine mammals. The strong thrust of sirenian tails and large body
size make injury to both handlers and animals possible. For this
reason, it is preferred that manatees are removed from the water for
procedures and personnel wear helmets for safety. In captive envi-
ronments, physical restraint is accomplished by corralling the ani-
mal using nets, dry-docking within a pool by draining the water, or
raising a medical pool floor above the water level; the animal is then
placed within a stretcher for transport.
As the sole obligate herbivores of the marine mammal world,
preanesthetic fasting is often extended to 24 h. Historically, mana-
tees were sedated with midazolam (0.08 mg/kg IM) and mask
induced with isoflurane via a modified 5-gallon plastic water bot-
tle [112,113], but this was tedious and time consuming. Currently,
midazolam (0.05–0.2 mg/kg IM) has been used in combination
with butorphanol (0.05–0.15 mg/kg IM) to achieve neuroleptanal-
gesia sufficient to facilitate conscious nasotracheal intubation.
When necessary, this can be supplemented with sevoflurane via a
nasal mask, as manatees are obligate nasal breathers. Meperidine
(0.05–0.2 mg/kg) had been used in place of butorphanol for greater
analgesia but has fallen from favor as, anecdotally, there has been
prolongation in the time to achieve a level of recovery sufficient for
the manatee to raise its head to breathe when submerged.
Vascular access
Cetacean vascular access
There are several peripheral sites from which blood may be col-
lected in the cetacean. The arteriovenous nature of the peripheral
vasculature in these species, however, means very few of these sites
allow rapid drug or fluid administration or clear differentiation of
arterial and venous blood. Consequently, true venous and arterial
access are desirable, and have become increasingly attainable as
imaging and vascular access methodology have improved. In this
section, we describe common clinically accessible sites for blood
sampling and both arterial and venous catheter placement.
Braun’s 1905 angiograms of the arteries of the fluke and pectoral
flipper of the harbor porpoise helped begin documentation of the
extensively branching network of the peripheral vasculature of ceta-
ceans [114]. In 1941, the complex arterial and venous blood supply
of the dolphin and manatee were described [115] and, in 1951,
Tomilin first described the closely adhering venous reticulum asso-
ciated with the arteries involved in temperature regulation which he
called “complex vessels” [116]. We now know these as the periarte-
rial vascular rete (PAVR). Shortly thereafter, the countercurrent
heat exchange function of this “artery-within-vein arrangement” of
the PAVR was first hypothesized [117]. The radiographic, gross,

-- 1115 of 1450 --

1100 	Section 7: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia
and histologic anatomy of the PAVR was further detailed via
corrosion casting of its architecture (Fig. 56.3C) [118].
Armed with this knowledge, it must be noted that when per-
forming “venipuncture” at a PAVR location, it is the artery (sur-
rounded by the venous reticulum, the periarterial venous rete) that
is most probably penetrated by the needle. This may be evidenced
by rapid passive outflow of blood. Depending on the location and
angle of incidence, the needle lumen may communicate with the
artery, venous reticulum, or the perivascular space or channels
through the firm collagenous matrix surrounding the PAVR. This
imprecise positioning, and the likelihood of needle migration, can
result in blood source mixing and possible perivascular leakage.
With proper aseptic technique, this is an acceptable location for
blood collection and delivery of isotonic crystalloid fluids, but cau-
tion is advised in delivering other medication. Arteries are muscu-
lar and will respond to changes in pH or osmolarity, direct
cytotoxicity, or known vasopressor activity through vasospasm,
thrombosis, or direct vascular injury. Accordingly, there are a num-
ber of anecdotal reports of fluke injury and circumferential slough-
ing after delivery of medications, such as insufficiently diluted
antibiotics, into the peduncle or fluke PAVR [119]. As noted above,
it is documented that drugs of extreme pH (e.g., the barbiturate
anesthetic thiopental) will cause vascular injury and severe compli-
cations when injected into arteries [120]. That said, thiopental
delivery has been reported (10 mg/kg IV, 50 mg/mL) in the pedun-
cle PAVR without complication on multiple occasions [61,64–66].
However, it should be noted that these injections were usually deliv-
ered in crystalloid perianesthetic fluids, thus, diluting the drug
prior to entry into the PAVR [personal communication: Dr. Sam H.
Ridgway, 2020]. Common anesthetic drugs administered intravas-
cularly in cetaceans include midazolam and propofol. There are
some reports of vasculitis and vascular impairment after
intraarterial delivery of the midazolam in human subjects, but
symptoms resolved without sequelae with no specific intervention.
Propofol is well known to cause pain on injection, but it has not
been associated with any vascular injury when inadvertently deliv-
ered intraarterial. If true venous access is not acquired for anes-
thetic drug delivery, we advise careful drug selection and use of
crystalloid fluids during induction for the purpose of dilution. True
venous access in the lateral caudal subcutaneous vein as described
below is now routine and will enhance safety.
Lateral caudal subcutaneous vein
First proposed in 1997 and attempted in 1998 [107,121], catheteri-
zation of the lateral caudal subcutaneous vein (LCSV), also known
as “lateral subcutaneous caudal vein” and historically referred to as
the “caudal ventral peduncle,” “caudal superficial peduncle,” “super-
ficial caudal peduncle vein,” or “superficial lateral peduncle vein,”
was not perfected until 2011 [122]. The LCSV is now the first choice
for true venous access in the dolphin and catheterization of this ves-
sel is a routine procedure. It is commonly performed with the ani-
mal in modified sternal recumbency, with the peduncle tilted
approximately 10–15 degrees from midline to expose the area of
interest (Fig. 56.3B). The authors have had the greatest success cath-
eterizing the LCSV with ultrasound guidance using a linear trans-
ducer (10-5 MHz) and a single lumen, 4 to 5 French micro-introducer
catheter kit utilizing a modified Seldinger method [123]. When
necessary, longer peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs)
with one or more lumens can be placed. In a transverse ultrasound
view, the ventral branch of the LCSV lies just dorsolateral to the
levator ani (pubocaudalis) muscle and ventromedial to the hypaxi-
alis lumborum (supracoccygeus) muscle. In the longitudinal view,
the vein travels caudal to cranial under the blubber, becoming
larger and diving deeper as it travels craniad. Further caudad, as the

depth (more superficial), vessel diameter (larger), and minimized
perivascular connective tissue. Even in more cranial locations,
perivascular connective tissue is quite dense, making a stiffened
micro-introducer dilator cannula preferred for placement. For
patient comfort and compliance, a local anesthetic block (subcuta-
neous lidocaine) with or without sedation is used prior to catheter
placement. Pressure cranial to the site of venipuncture may help
increase the diameter of the vessel and facilitate cannulation as can
warm wet towels placed over the vessel. Attempts have been made
to maintain an LCSV catheter in the postanesthetic aquatic envi-
ronment, with some limited success [124].
Median artery
It is feasible to catheterize many arteries of the cetacean PAVR.
Used for collection of blood in early studies, the median artery of
the pectoral flipper of dolphins is now a commonly acceptable loca-
tion for cannulation [125,126]. The median artery sits snuggly
between the radius and ulna, slightly palmar, under the dense con-
nective tissue of the flipper (Fig. 56.3A). Doppler flow probes
and ultrasound can facilitate identification and cannulation of the
median artery, but the location is also digitally palpable. The authors
have had the greatest success catheterizing the median artery
with ultrasound guidance using a linear transducer (10-5 MHz) and a
4 to 5 French micro-introducer catheter kit utilizing a modified
Seldinger method similar to those used for venous access. For
placement, the dolphin is positioned in lateral recumbency, and the
dependent pectoral flipper is pulled laterally and slightly cranial
for placement. In a transverse view across the palmar surface of
the flipper, the artery sits slightly superficial to the notch formed
by the convergence of the radius and ulna. To maintain patency of
the cannula, 2–5 unit/mL of heparinized 0.9% NaCl is used to regu-
larly flush the catheter. Modern disposable blood pressure trans-
ducers with integrated, pressurized flush mechanisms can be used
to simplify maintenance of the catheter. The transducer is zeroed to
the level of the right atrium (physiologic zero) and invasive blood
pressures are continuously monitored. Blood can also be collected
from this site for analysis of arterial blood gases or other hemato-
logic or biochemical indices.
Pinniped vascular access
Vascular access is feasible in pinnipeds, with ultrasound facilitating
visualization in the majority of locations. Venipuncture of the
extradural vein of phocids and odobenids can be performed using
a spinal or Tuohy needle inserted perpendicularly between the
dorsal spinous processes of lumbar vertebrae 3 and 4. The needle
can be maintained throughout a procedure or converted to a small-
diameter cannula using commercially available epidural catheter
kits. Though small in diameter, thus limiting fluid volume delivery,
such extradural venous catheters have been aseptically maintained
for up to a week postoperatively for drug delivery. Venous access of
the external jugular vein, though visible on smaller subjects, is facil-
itated by ultrasound and is more commonly performed in otariids
than phocids and odobenids (Fig. 56.4A). Commercially available
longer PICCs may be more easily maintained in the jugular vein of
larger subjects. Cannulation of pectoral and pelvic flipper veins is
also possible and most often performed with the animal positioned
in lateral or modified dorsal recumbency. Visualization of the pec-
toral flipper antebrachial vein (also referred to as the “brachial vein”
or “superficial palmar vein”) and occasionally the cephalic vein do
not require ultrasound, but this tool can be useful, especially in
hypotensive, hypovolemic, or smaller patients (Fig. 56.4B).
Branches of the pelvic flipper medial saphenous veins (Fig 56.4C),
particularly in phocids and odobenids, are best visualized with

digitally palpable. Standard over-the-needle catheters can be used
to cannulate both arteries and veins to reduce cost, but modern
micro-introducer kits using a modified Seldinger technique sim-
plify and expedite cannulation. Venous cannulation of pinnipeds,
ultrasound-guided or otherwise, may be complicated by α2
-adrenergic

Manatee vascular access
As Fawcett wrote, “The most characteristic feature of the circula-
tory system of the manatee is the complete subdivision of the larger
arteries, usually near their sources, into great numbers of small
arteries which run parallel for considerable distances without any
significant diminution in caliber.” This is “most highly developed in
the vascularization of the pectoral limb” and “resembles rather the
arrangement of a broom” [115]. As such, the typical site for blood
sampling in manatees of all ages is the interosseous space between
the radius and ulna, which contains a vascular bundle of veins and
arteries (Fig 56.5B). It can be accessed from the medial or lateral
sides of the pectoral flippers, usually based on personal preference,
using an 18 gauge, 5 cm (2 inch) needle in adults or a 20 gauge,
3.75 cm (1.5 inch) needle in juveniles [128]. Cannulation of the bra-
chial vascular bundle is complicated by the perpendicular place-
ment of the needle relative to the arteriovenous plexus. A vascular
bundle is also available for venipuncture under the fluke (paddle) in
the ventral vertebral arch. This technique is particularly useful in
younger animals where pectoral vessels are small, but has also been
used in anesthetized adult manatees using spinal or Tuohy needles.
While these techniques have been used in conscious individuals,
subjects can move and displace the needle or produce explosive for-
ward thrust of the fluke and injure the phlebotomist as well as the
vascular bundle. Perivascular leakage of drugs can also occur in
these vascular bundle venipuncture sites, potentially resulting in
local tissue inflammation or necrosis.
“Cephalic” and “caudal” veins have also been described and dia-
gramed for the pectoral flipper of manatee (Fig. 56.5A) [129]. The
cephalic vein was cannulated using a “cut-down” technique and a
standard over-the-needle catheter during anesthesia of one Florida
manatee [113]. However, in recent years, transcutaneous cannula-
tion has become feasible in the palmar digital veins, as well as the
median artery of the manatee pectoral flipper (Fig. 56.5D). Similar
to other discussed species, the median artery sits snuggly in the
interosseous space between the radius and ulna, slightly palmar on
the flipper, under the thick dermis and connective tissue. Doppler
flow probes or ultrasound are mandatory to facilitate identification
and cannulation of the artery, as it is not externally palpable. The
authors have had success catheterizing the median artery of six
adult Florida manatees with ultrasound guidance using a linear
transducer (10-5 MHz) and a 4 to 5 French micro-introducer cath-
eter kit utilizing a modified Seldinger technique, similar to methods
used for vascular access in other marine mammals.
Airway management
Orotracheal or nasotracheal intubation should be considered in
every immobilized or anesthetized marine mammal for reasons
similar to other species, including maintenance of airway patency,
delivery of assisted ventilation, and protection from regurgitation.
Unique risk factors in marine mammal species, including redun-
dant pharyngeal tissue and risk of apnea with induction agents, fur-
ther emphasize the importance of rapid intubation. This is especially
true if using remotely delivered drugs or mechanical restraint

devices that may logistically delay “hands-on” access to the patient
or in situations in which airway patency is compromised. Regardless
of induction technique, careful observation for both continued
spontaneous ventilation and airway patency is necessary and will
guide the urgency of intubation. Proper airway management
requires consideration of the logistics of anesthetic induction,
knowledge of airway anatomy and the physical condition of the tar-
get species, as well as preparation of necessary equipment. Many
species are obligate nasal breathers (e.g., Cetaceans and manatees),
which may influence the approach to both intubation and extuba-
tion. Tools used in intubation such as elongated laryngoscopes,
malleable stylets, and flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopes must be
available as required; in some species, alternate methods of airway
management, such as nasotracheal intubation, must also be consid-
ered. Similarly, as many marine mammals may become apneic prior
to sufficient relaxation for simple intubation, advanced planning for
and experience in alternative options for airway management is
necessary.
Cetacean intubation
Endotracheal intubation of adult bottlenose dolphins and larger
odontocete species is usually performed using an oral approach to
the larynx (Fig. 56.6). While less ideal, this can be accomplished in
a conscious animal in an emergency situation, but is preferably
performed following heavy sedation or anesthetic induction. Size
16 to 30 mm ID endotracheal tubes with inflatable, high-volume,
low- pressure cuffs are appropriate for most adult bottlenose dol-
phins. Soft, rolled towels are used to hold open the mandible and
maxilla and the larynx is accessed blindly by palpation. The elon-
gated epiglottal and cricoarytenoid cartilages of the larynx (“goose-
beak”) are manually displaced from their connection to the
nasopharyngeal sphincter and oriented in a rostral direction. Two
fingers of one hand are placed into the glottis and, using the other
hand, the endotracheal tube is guided through the glottis. Care
should be taken to shield the cuff with the palm and forearm when
advancing the endotracheal tube to prevent cuff damage by the
sharp teeth. Tracheal intubation should be confirmed using a cap-
nograph. The trachea is very short in most odontocetes and a right-
sided accessory bronchus precedes the carina [131]; awareness of
the depth of insertion is necessary to prevent blockade of this bron-
chus. Use of a flexible endoscope can both facilitate intubation and
assure proper depth of insertion. Once positioned in place, similar
to terrestrial mammals, the tube should be secured to the maxilla
using a tie, and the cuff inflated to a minimum occlusive volume.
Intubation through the blowhole is possible, but usually reserved
for smaller odontocetes in which the oral approach is prohibitive
due to their small mouth and oropharynx. Similar to orotracheal
intubation, this technique can be performed in conscious, sedated,

and anesthetized animals. In all situations, a relatively smaller
endotracheal tube is inserted into the blowhole and advanced
through the left or right nasal cavity into the trachea. This approach
is greatly facilitated by the use of a flexible endoscope for both visu-
alization of the laryngeal opening and as a stylet to guide advance-
ment of the tube. While this method seems straightforward, it is
subjectively more complicated than oral intubation due to redun-
dant tissue and muscular folds between the blowhole and larynx
that are used for vocalization and echolocation. Not surprisingly,
this limits the size of the tube that can be used. While it has not been
attempted to the authors’ knowledge, theoretically, intubation of the
blowhole could be maintained in a conscious animal beyond anes-
thetic recovery if necessitated by the animal’s medical needs. That
said, prolonged blowhole intubation could create inflammation or
result in abnormal blowhole function, which would be problematic
once the animal is returned to the water. Blowhole intubation has
been used in small dolphins (Stenella styx and Delphinus delphis)
under experimental conditions at sea [132]. To facilitate laryngeal
anesthesia for conscious intubation, lidocaine (2%) was applied to
the blowhole, nasal passages, and larynx using a small metal can-
nula prior to passing the uncuffed endotracheal tube.
Pinniped intubation
Subjectively, compared to other marine mammal species, the ade-
quately anesthetized pinniped is less difficult to intubate since the
larynx can be visualized and the vocal cords are relatively immobile.
Cuffed endotracheal tubes of sizes 8 to 22 mm ID are suitable. An
oral approach is used. After induction of anesthesia, the patient is
positioned in sternal recumbency with the mandible and maxilla
pulled apart with rope or webbing material and the neck extended
in a straight orientation. Care should be taken not to twist the head
or neck as this can distort the normal anatomy, particularly in larger
pinnipeds. A laryngoscope should be used, but a good light source
(e.g., headlamp) can be useful. The laryngoscope blade is placed
underneath the epiglottis at the base of the tongue and gently forced
downward; this stretches the hypoepiglottic ligament, dropping the
epiglottis and exposing the glottic opening. If needed, a second
laryngoscope blade rotated 180 degrees or similar device (e.g., sili-
cone spatula) can be used to push upwards on the soft palate and
improve visualization; this can also be achieved with the tip of the
endotracheal tube. Advancement of the tube timed with inspiration
(e.g., abduction of the arytenoid cartilages) may ease the process.
Larger pinnipeds often have excessive soft palate and pharyngeal
tissues and physically heavy heads, both of which can impede posi-
tioning and visualization. In these situations, blind intubation via
palpation is usually selected and is similar to intubation of domestic
large animal species such as cattle. An appropriate level of anesthe-
sia is crucial for safety, but a bite block can also be used to protect
the individual’s arm. With the animal positioned as described
above, the anesthetist’s hand is cupped around the distal aspect of
the endotracheal tube and inserted into the oropharynx. The epi-
glottis is digitally retracted, the arytenoids are identified, and the
endotracheal tube is manually guided into the trachea. In larger
species or with smaller arms, this can be accomplished using a two-
hand technique and the digits can be used to gently hold the aryte-
noids open. In lieu of this palpation method, fiberoptic intubation
scopes can be used to improve human safety, but may be logistically
complicated. Using either technique, tracheal insertion should be
confirmed with a capnograph. If unavailable, bilateral thoracic aus-
cultation should be performed to confirm placement and concur-
rently rule out one-lung intubation. The tube should also be secured
to the maxilla using a tie and the cuff inflated to a minimum occlu-
sive volume.
Manatee intubation
The manatee has several anatomic characteristics that make visuali-
zation of the caudal pharynx and larynx using an oral approach
extremely difficult, including a curved angle of the tongue, a nar-
row buccal cavity, and a long soft palate. As a result, oral intubation
is generally unsuccessful and, instead, the glottis and trachea are
best accessed from the nasal cavities. While nasotracheal tubes have
occasionally been passed blindly with success, dependable tracheal
intubation is best accomplished with endoscopic assistance
(Fig. 56.7). This visualization helps in wild sirenians which are

inflated to a minimum occlusive volume.
Monitoring and support
The importance of vigilant monitoring during marine mammal
anesthesia cannot be overstated and this extends throughout all
four phases of the anesthetic episode (premedication, induction,
maintenance, and recovery), during any sedation episode, and dur-
ing any period of mechanical/physical restraint. Monitoring is a
challenging, complex process which requires superb critical think-
ing skills and should involve at least one dedicated anesthetist.
Arguably, the most important monitor is the anesthetist themself as
a wealth of information can be collected using the human eyes and
ears and a basic stethoscope (e.g., anesthetic depth, mucous mem-
brane color, respiratory rate and effort, and auscultation). Even dur-
ing situations of limited patient access, observation of the thoracic
wall can confirm both ventilation and myocardial contraction (e.g.,
apex beat). Productive ventilation and a patent airway are impor-
tant to confirm, particularly when using aggressive immobilization
cocktails, with physically large species, or with fully aquatic species
(cetaceans, sirenians) that are “beached,” as partial or complete air-
way obstruction can occur. In some situations, subjects will flare
their nostrils and attempt to move their diaphragm and thoracic
wall, but ventilation will be suboptimal and consistent with partial
or complete airway obstruction. Thus, ventilation with evidence of
air flow must be monitored from the time of first handling to after
full recovery. Monitoring should be continuously performed, and
physiologic values ideally recorded every 5 min. The anesthetist
should understand acceptable or “normal” physiologic parameters
for the target species prior to the anesthetic event. Historically, most
anesthetic monitoring in marine mammal anesthesia was non-
invasive in nature. While this is appropriate in some situations (e.g.,
sedation), advances in technology and vascular access techniques
have laid the groundwork for routine use of more invasive monitor-
ing techniques (e.g., invasive blood pressure and arterial blood gas
analysis).
In addition to visual assessment of the patient as discussed above,
additional non-invasive monitoring tools (i.e., electrocardiogram,
pulse oximetry, temperature, end-tidal gas analysis, and non-
invasive blood pressure) should be considered for every sedation or
anesthetic event. The decision to exclude a monitoring tool should
be based on patient compliance and the consideration for personnel
safety, among other factors. A 3-lead electrocardiogram allows
assessment of heart rate and rhythm and should be placed as soon
as access to the patient is safe. The marine mammals discussed here
have a type 2/category B cardiac conduction system, similar to the
horse, with a diffuse Purkinje network and an overall axis of depo-
larization that is different than domestic dogs and cats [78]. As
such, a modified base apex lead is frequently used in larger subjects
to simplify electrode placement and optimize the ECG tracing.
Pulse oximetry probes provide an assessment of the oxygen satura-
tion of hemoglobin; as this technology relies on pulsatile arterial
flow, a concurrent pulse rate is also obtained and should always be
compared to the heart rate generated on an ECG. Reusable clip-
type transmittance probes (originally designed for the human ear)
are frequently placed on the tongue or mucous membranes of the
oral or urogenital regions with reflectance probes allowing place-
ment in additional areas (e.g., dorsal aspect of the rectal cavity).
Hypoxemia is a potential anesthetic complication, especially in
spontaneously ventilating or larger marine mammals, thus, contin-
uous assessment of oxygenation is a necessity. Monitoring of tem-
perature is paramount in both managed care and free-ranging
settings as hypo- or hyperthermia can frequently occur. Temperature
probes should be inserted at least 30 cm into the esophagus or rec-
tum and, thus, hand-held style thermometers common in domestic
animal anesthesia are usually not sufficient. While often forgotten
until well into the anesthetic episode, prioritization of temperature
assessment and thermoregulatory support should occur. End-tidal
gas analysis (i.e., CO2
, O2
, and inhalant concentration) can provide
a wealth of information (e.g., confirm intubation, assess ventilation
and perfusion, and guide vaporizer management during induction,
maintenance, and recovery) and is discussed in detail in
Chapters 14, 15, and 16. Both intubated and non-intubated patients
should have a gas analyzer attached between the breathing circuit
and the patient, as even a tight-fitting facemask will usually allow
assessment of ventilatory trends through gas analysis. Blood pres-
sure measurement is performed to obtain an objective measure-
ment of systemic perfusion and is standard of care in veterinary
anesthesia. Non-invasive blood pressure assessment is limited by
patient size and limb anatomy, among other factors. While non-
invasive blood pressure monitors have yet to be validated in marine
mammal species, the use of oscillometric cuffs on the pectoral and
occasionally pelvic flippers of small to medium-sized pinnipeds
have been used to identify trends and contribute to assessment of
the overall clinical picture. With that in mind, if an appropriate cuff
size is available (i.e., width of the cuff approximately 40% of the
circumference of the limb) for the target species, the authors
encourage its use in pinnipeds. Even in situations in which invasive
blood pressure monitoring is planned, cannulation of an artery
takes time and may not always be successful, thus, non-invasive
blood pressure measurement should still be used. Unfortunately, no
non- invasive blood pressure measurement has yet proven success-
ful in cetaceans or sirenians. “Normal” arterial blood pressure val-
ues in marine mammal species are largely unknown, but the authors
anecdotally define hypotension as a mean arterial pressure (MAP)
< 70 mmHg in pinnipeds and sirenians and < 90–100 mmHg in
cetaceans (conscious MAP range 115–142 mmHg) [136,137].
Invasive blood pressure monitoring has become a standard of care
for marine mammals in managed care, but can be technically chal-
lenging in manatees and small phocids [137]. Placement of arterial
catheters is discussed in the vascular access section of this chapter.
This monitoring tool should be used whenever possible in immobi-
lized or anesthetized marine mammals, especially for longer proce-
dures, compromised or geriatric patients, or when significant
anesthetic or procedural complications are expected (e.g., hypoxemia
and hemorrhage). Principles of hypotension management are similar

1106 	Section 7: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia
to domestic species and include a reduction in inhalant delivery,
techniques for MAC reduction, volume loading where appropriate,
and intravenous use of inotropes (e.g., dobutamine 0.2–2 μg/kg/min,
ephedrine 0.05–0.1 mg/kg) or vasopressors (e.g., phenylephrine
0.1–1 μg/kg/min, norepinephrine 0.01–0.1 μg/kg/min).
Similar to invasive blood pressure monitoring, blood gas, elec-
trolyte, and lactate analyses should be used whenever possible in
immobilized or anesthetized marine mammals, especially for
lengthy anesthetic procedures, in compromised or geriatric sub-
jects, or when significant anesthetic or procedural complications
are expected (e.g., hypoxemia and hypotension). Interpretation of
blood gas data is reviewed elsewhere in this textbook. However,
early testing of even venous blood can warn of excessive exertion
during the process of anesthetic induction and the potential for
developing rhabdomyolysis [82].
Cushioning with thick (4 to 8 inch) medium-density, open-cell
foam padding similar to that used for large terrestrial mammals is
necessary to minimize development of myopathy and neuropathy,
especially during longer procedures [138]. Waterproof closed-cell
foam padding provides minimal cushioning and should be reserved
for short procedures. The insulating effect of foam padding also
minimizes conductive heat loss. As discussed previously, thermoreg-
ulatory support is necessary as hypo- or hyperthermia may occur.
Control of environmental temperature (if possible), minimization of
stress or excitement in the preanesthetic period, use of external
patient warming devices (i.e., circulating warm water or forced air
blankets), and dry-docking or towel-drying patients prior to anes-
thesia can be useful adjuncts. For cetaceans, near-neutral buoyant
liquid suspension systems have been used [61] and are currently
being reevaluated for positioning support and thermoregulation.
Dive reflex
When discussing the dive reflex or dive response in marine mam-
mals handled for sedation and anesthesia, it is generally directed at
concerns for breath-holding and circulatory adjustments, specifi-
cally apnea, bradycardia, and regional vasoconstriction. Studies
have convincingly proven that pinnipeds demonstrate a profound
“dive reflex” when forced to dive [139]. Furthermore, these same
animals when allowed to dive voluntarily do not demonstrate the
same degree of bradycardia as when forced into a dive [140–142].
As such, the normal dive response of pinnipeds appears to be more
graded and under conscious control while the response is more
exaggerated if the animal does not know when the dive will end.
Importantly, none of the studied animals died as a result of the dive
reflex during forced or voluntary dives, and there is no evidence to
suggest this is a potential outcome (as long as they are allowed the
opportunity to surface and breathe). There is also no evidence that
the dive reflex remains intact in pinnipeds during chemically
induced unconsciousness. On the contrary, there is evidence that
anesthesia depresses or eliminates the dive reflex [143,144]. A
wealth of anecdotal evidence supports the notion that the heart rate
of a marine mammal stabilizes during general anesthesia when
proper physiologic support is provided. Although activation of the
dive reflex has quite often been blamed for negative outcomes in
marine mammal anesthesia over many decades, it is more likely
that the lack of a dive response is the issue. That is, during drug- and
disease-induced physiologic derangements (e.g., apnea, hypoxemia,
vasodilation, and hypoperfusion), the lack of this elegant reflex
control and lack of ability to direct blood flow to vital organs may
precipitate negative consequences. Indeed, an intact dive response
might well enhance the probability of positive outcomes in anesthe-
tized pinnipeds. This significantly underscores the need for mind-
ful anesthetic monitoring and support of sedated or anesthetized
marine mammals.
There are some physiologic reflexes, including the laryngeal,
oculocardiac, and other trigeminocardiac and vagally induced
reflexes that may occur in the anesthetized marine mammal, espe-
cially at light planes of anesthesia (e.g., induction and recovery).
Occurrence of these reflexes and resultant bradycardia may well be
confused with a “dive reflex.” Bradycardia during sedation, immo-
bilization, or anesthesia can also result from inadequate respiratory
support in that severe hypoxemia and myocardial hypoxia can
cause terminal bradycardia. While the true occurrence of a “dive
reflex” during general anesthesia of marine mammals is questiona-
ble, monitoring for bradycardia of any etiology or other physiologic
disturbances is important.
Anesthetic recovery
Anesthetic vigilance, monitoring, and support do not end just
because the anesthetic vaporizer has been turned off as anesthetic
complications can occur into and beyond the recovery period. This
is especially important to highlight in situations involving free-
ranging or dangerous animals where monitoring capabilities and
human safety are sometimes at odds. Ventilatory support (e.g.,
mechanical ventilator, manual resuscitator bag, and demand valve)
may be necessary well into recovery. As alluded to earlier, monitor-
ing the end-expired anesthetic concentration in recovery can guide
administration of reversal agents. More specifically, the authors
administer reversal agents when the inhalant anesthetic is at a con-
centration that is expected to produce minimal effect on awareness
(approximate MAC awake of isoflurane < 0.4%, sevoflurane < 0.8%);
this strategy theoretically promotes arousal at a timepoint when
unwanted dysphoria from the inhalant is minimal.
Limited pharmacokinetic data on opioids and non-steroidal anti-
inflammatory drugs in marine mammals suggest the half-life of
many useful anesthetic and perianesthetic drugs will have a surpris-
ingly long duration of action when compared to terrestrial spe-
cies [145–148]. For this reason, it is preferable to use anesthetic
drugs that can be eliminated easily without metabolism (i.e., inhala-
tion anesthetics) or are reversible. As such, it is common to reverse
benzodiazepines, opioids, and α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists to
speed recovery and promote the return of effective spontaneous
ventilation in marine mammals.
Full reversal of clinically used benzodiazepines, on a milligram-
for-milligram basis, requires 1 part flumazenil for every 13 parts of
midazolam or every 26 parts diazepam [149]. The functional half-
life of flumazenil can be estimated from terrestrial animal models as
at least one hour. As intravenous administration may result in an
abrupt and excitable recovery and large volumes are often needed,
the authors recommend half the calculated dose of flumazenil be
delivered intramuscularly and, 5 min later, half the calculated dose
is administered intravenously. The response is then evaluated
before any redosing.
Full reversal of opioids can be achieved with naloxone 0.01 mg/
kg or naltrexone 0.05–0.1 mg/kg (0.5–1 mg/kg for ultrapotent opi-
oids). The half-life of naloxone is variable in terrestrial species but
can be approximated at 20–30 min, where naltrexone can be antici-
pated to have a much longer species-dependent half-life of 7–8 h
and a slow terminal elimination-phase half-life of around 24 h.
Naloxone can be used at a full or partial dosage to attenuate the

-- 1122 of 1450 --

Chapter 56: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia – Marine Mammals 	1107
level of opioid-induced postoperative depression, theoretically
allowing return of residual opioid analgesia. Where analgesia is not
necessary, or the subject is perceived to have excessive opioid-
induced respiratory depression, naltrexone can be used to provide
sustained reversal of opioid effects. The authors use a partial IM
and IV strategy as described above for flumazenil. As, anecdotally,
opioid reversal tends to greatly increase arousal, it is usually admin-
istered as the final drug in any IV reversal strategy.
Reversal of concentrated medetomidine is dependent on the
ratio of milligrams of antagonist drug to milligrams of α2 - adrenergic
receptor agonist, not the volume. Atipamezole is delivered at 5
and 10 times the milligram dose of medetomidine and dexmedeto-
midine, respectively, for full reversal via the intramuscular route
to avoid rapid arousal and/or potential hypotension. When
α2
- adrenergic receptor agonists are absolutely necessary for induc-
tion of anesthesia, but the cardiovascular effects of the α2 - adrenergic
receptor agonists are deemed undesirable for the target patient, the
authors will administer atipamezole after achieving an appropriate
end-expired anesthetic level and, preferably, after gaining vascular
access for provision of necessary support.
The endotracheal tube should be maintained in the airway as
long as possible within the safety guidelines for the species involved.
Protective contact restrictions for large pinnipeds can influence this
decision-making process in favor of human safety. Subjects will
routinely attempt to extubate prematurely or cough and inadvert-
ently extubate as they regain reflex control of their airway. Given
the respiratory depressant effect of anesthetic agents in marine
mammals, it is possible for these species to extubate prematurely
and either develop airway obstruction or become apneic; this is par-
ticularly true of phocids, cetaceans, and sirenians. For this reason,
the authors try to maintain IV access as long as safely possible into
the recovery period as reintubation may not be possible without
reinduction of anesthesia. It is also advisable to have an additional
endotracheal tube (usually one size smaller) on hand as well as both
drugs and tools for reintubation. Phenylephrine (0.5–1%) nasal
spray can be used to reduce nasal cavity edema that can develop
from recumbency and endotracheal tube ties around the muzzle.
Respiratory stimulants, such as the nonspecific central nervous
stimulant doxapram (1 mg/kg IM, IV), are generally unnecessary,
but worthy of mention as a tool for managing respiratory depres-
sion when there is lack of airway control in a semi-conscious ani-
mal. Unfortunately, this only increases cerebral oxygen consumption
in the face of inadequate ventilation and may do more harm than
good in most instances.

Introduction
Reptiles, amphibians, and fishes are unique animal classes
encountered in veterinary medicine and are very different in
terms of anatomy, physiology, and behavioral adaptations from
the more familiar mammals. Regardless of the differences among
these animal classes, by using sound anesthetic principles reason-
ably safe and effective anesthesia can be performed, even in the
absence of species-specific information. In the following sections,
emphasis has been placed on providing comparative anatomic
and physiologic information relevant to the anesthetic manage-
ment of each class of animals. A comprehensive review of the
anesthetic and analgesic literature is beyond the scope of this text
but is available elsewhere and should be consulted for additional
detail [1–6].
Reptile anesthesia
Anesthetic management of reptiles is associated with many chal-
lenges. Reptilia represents a diverse class of animals in terms of
size, environmental requirements, behavior, physiology, and
anatomy. There are over 7800 species represented by four main
orders (Crocodylia, Testudines, Squamata, and Rhynchocephalia).
Compounding the difficulties created by these inherent species
differences, historically there was relatively little peer-reviewed
research investigating anesthesia and analgesia in reptiles and
much of the earlier literature is anecdotal in nature and persists as
accepted fact despite contradictory evidence. Fortunately, there
has been considerable interest in this area recently and scientific
studies investigating anesthesia and analgesia in reptiles are
becoming more available.
Applying generalized anesthetic recommendations to such a
large and varying group of animals is difficult. Clinical application
of various techniques is often ascribed to one of the three principal
orders: the crocodilians (crocodiles and alligators), the chelonians
(tortoises and turtles), and the squamates (snakes and lizards). An
understanding of normal physiology, pathophysiology, the action
and disposition of anesthetic and related drugs, and a familiarity
with the design and use of related anesthetic equipment are impor-
tant considerations. A thorough preanesthetic assessment and care-
fully designed anesthetic plan with attention to premedication,
induction, maintenance, monitoring, supportive care, recovery, and
ongoing postoperative support and analgesia all contribute to the
reduction of risk associated with anesthesia.
Anatomy and physiology
Reptiles have long been considered to be the class of vertebrates
that reflect the evolutionary transition between the aquatic and
amphibious ectothermic vertebrates, and endothermic birds
and mammals. Reptiles arguably represent one of the most ancient,
successful, and well-adapted classes of animals, with some species
surviving essentially unchanged for hundreds of millions of years.
Recent investigations recognize reptilian physiologic evolutionary

adaptations as “optimal or advantageous,” enabling exothermic
animals to inhabit almost all of the available non-polar ecological
niches.
Although many aspects of reptilian physiology are similar
to those of endothermic vertebrates, significant differences are
present. Such differences may alter both the action and disposition
of anesthetics and analgesics.
Metabolism and thermoregulation
The ectothermic nature of reptiles and their generally lower meta-
bolic rates are probably the two most striking differences between
mammals and reptiles that impede extrapolation of anesthetic prin-
ciples and practices between the two groups. Reptiles derive much
of their body heat from the surrounding environment and use
behaviors such as basking or burrowing to regulate their body tem-
peratures. Reptiles can also alter their body temperature through
changes in their cardiovascular physiology. During periods of
warming, some reptiles increase their heart rate and the degree of
right-to- left cardiac shunting to increase the fraction of blood flow
that is directed to the periphery for heating and ultimate return to
the body core [7]. This adaptation facilitates more rapid and effi-
cient warming of the animal.
Reptiles will tend to choose a preferred optimal temperature
zone (POTZ) maintaining a body temperature that is presumably
ideal for the animal. In most instances, reptiles undergoing anesthe-
sia should be maintained at the average or the high end of their
POTZ to ensure optimal metabolic function. Species-specific
ranges can often be found in general husbandry references or
extrapolated from known species, which are found in similar natu-
ral habitats. In general, 20–25 °C is recommended for most aquatic
and temperate reptile species, and 25–35 °C for most tropical
species [8].
Although ambient temperature is one of the main determinants
of metabolic rate in resting reptiles, and consequently the metabo-
lism and excretion of drugs [9], there are significant interspecies
and intraindividual variations. Minimum and maximum oxygen
consumption rates of individual reptilian species range from almost
zero to values similar to a resting mammal [10]. The oxygen con-
sumption of any individual is a function of the species, the tempera-
ture, and the individual. In general, the varanid and lacertid lizards
tend to have relatively high metabolic rates, and boid snakes and
chelonians have lower rates. Surface-dwelling squamates have
higher metabolic rates than burrowing species, and species of liz-
ards that eat insects or other vertebrates have higher metabolic rates
than herbivorous species [11]. Those species with higher inherent
metabolic rates may be expected to more rapidly metabolize and
excrete drugs compared to those with lower metabolic rates, but
this has not been demonstrated conclusively.
Cardiovascular system
The non-crocodilian reptile heart has three chambers: two com-
pletely separate atria and a single anatomically continuous ventri-
cle. The crocodilian heart is more typical of that seen in mammals
and birds with two completely divided atria and two ventricles. In
the crocodilian heart, the foramen of Panizza allows for some intra-
vascular shunting under circumstances of breath holding, such as
diving. In non-crocodilian reptiles, the ventricle is divided into two
main chambers by a septum-like structure called the “Muskelleiste”
or “muscular ridge” (Fig. 57.1). This ridge originates from the ven-
tral ventricular wall and runs from the ventricular apex to the base,
dividing the ventricle into two anatomically defined but connected
chambers: the cavum pulmonale and the cavum dorsale [12,13],
comparable in function to the right and left ventricles of mammals,
respectively. The cavum dorsale is sometimes further subdivided
into the cavum venosum and cavum arteriosum. The dorsolateral
border of the muscular ridge is free, permitting the flow of blood
between the cavum pulmonale and cavum dorsale. However, dur-
ing ventricular systole, the muscular ridge presses against the dorsal
wall of the ventricle and separates the cavum pulmonale from the
cavum dorsale; thus, in a functional sense, the heart is capable of
acting as a two-circuit pump. The pulmonary artery arises from the
cavum pulmonale, and two aortic arches arise from the cavum
venosum of the cavum dorsale. The left aortic arch becomes the
dorsal aorta while the right aortic arch forms the subclavian and
carotid arteries and a third branch joins the dorsal aorta. However,
there is considerable anatomic variation among species.
Cardiac shunting occurs commonly in reptiles [14–16]. Cardiac
shunts can occur in both directions, and under some circum-
stances may occur simultaneously in both directions [14,17,18].
The direction of the net shunt determines whether the systemic or
pulmonary circulation receives the majority of the cardiac output.
Intracardiac shunting has three important functions. First, shunting
serves to stabilize the oxygen content of the blood during respira-
tory pauses. Second, the right-to- left shunt is partly responsible for
facilitating heating by increasing systemic blood flow. Third, a
right-to- left shunt directs blood away from the lungs during breath
holding.
During anesthesia, cardiac shunting can affect systemic arterial
oxygen content and the uptake and elimination of inhaled anes-
thetics. The size and direction of the shunts are ultimately con-
trolled by pressure differences between the pulmonary and
systemic circulations and the washout of blood remaining in the
cavum venosum (an anatomic subchamber of the cavum dorsale
described in many reptiles) [14,16,18,19]. The pressure differ-
ences are principally controlled by cholinergic and adrenergic fac-
tors that regulate the vascular resistance of the pulmonary and
systemic circulation [14,20–25].
