Hypoventilation makes it difficult to control the plane of anes-
thesia, and it can have a variety of adverse effects on cardiac func-
tion. For example, unifocal and multifocal cardiac arrhythmias
occurred in 50% of ducks anesthetized and maintained at a constant
end-tidal halothane concentration of 1.5%, and in which PaCO2
was varied from 40 to 80 mm Hg through addition of CO 2 to the
inspired oxygen [233]. The mean PaCO2 at which arrhythmias
developed was 67 ± 12 mm Hg; in five of six ducks, the arrhythmias
disappeared after CO 2 inhalation was terminated [233]. To avoid
the adverse effects of hypercarbia on cardiac function in anesthe-
tized birds, ventilation should be supported by maintaining a light
plane of anesthesia and, when possible, by assisting or controlling
ventilation.
Adjuncts to general anesthesia
Nitrous oxide
Nitrous oxide can be used as an adjunct to general anesthesia but is
not suitable as the sole anesthetic [234]. Nitrous oxide (50%) may
decrease the concentration of isoflurane necessary to maintain a
suitable plane of anesthesia by only 11% [235]. As with other anes-
thetic gases and vapors, nitrous oxide is not uniquely sequestered or
concentrated in the air sacs. The considerations for using nitrous
oxide are the same as for its use in mammals, such as adequate pul-
monary function and delivery of sufficient oxygen to meet the
patient’s metabolic demands. Thirty percent oxygen is generally
accepted as the minimum fraction of inspired oxygen that should
be provided. Nitrous oxide may pose problems in some birds with
normal subcutaneous air pockets [236]. For example, pelicans have
subcutaneous pockets of air that do not communicate with the
respiratory system and the use of N 2 O in these birds can result in
subcutaneous emphysema [237].
Neuromuscular blocking drugs
Neuromuscular paralytic drugs have two purposes in birds: whole-
body skeletal muscle paralysis to facilitate surgical procedures,
and to produce mydriasis. The neuromuscular and cardiovascular
effects of atracurium used as a muscle paralytic, have been reported
in chickens [238]. The effective dose associated with 95% twitch
depression in 50% of the birds (ED 95/50 ) was 0.25 mg/kg IV, and the
ED 95/95 was calculated by probit analysis to be 0.46 mg/kg IV. The
duration of action for the 0.25 mg/kg and 0.45 mg/kg doses was
34.5 ± 5.8 and 47.8 ± 10.3 min, respectively, and these durations
are similar to those reported in dogs [239,240]. Edrophonium
(0.5 mg/kg IV) reversed muscle paralysis. There were small but
statistically significant changes in cardiovascular variables (i.e.,
heart rate decreased, and blood pressure increased) after adminis-
tering atracurium, but these changes were considered clinically
unimportant [238].
Avian pupillary diameter is controlled primarily by skeletal muscles
and neuromuscular blocking drugs may be applied topically to
produce mydriasis with two notable exceptions, alcuronium and
pancuronium, which do not produce safe or consistently effective
mydriasis in some species [241]. In adult cockatoos (Cacatua sul-
phurea), gray parrots (Psittacus erithacus), and blue-fronted Amazon
parrots (Amazona aestivate), vecuronium (injectable formulation;
0.8 mg/mL) alone and diluted in sterile sodium chloride solution
(0.9% NaCl), consistently produced the greatest pupillary dilation,
and did so with few systemic side effects with one notable excep-
tion – a cockatoo collapsed and died soon after a combination of
vecuronium and saponin (a surface-acting penetrating agent) was
topically applied to its eye [242]. This suggests that vecuronium
administered topically as a mydriatic should not be combined with
an agent that promotes corneal penetration, as enhanced systemic
uptake may have potentially fatal effects. It also reinforces the real-
ity that avian species differ significantly in their responses to any
given drug. For neuromuscular blocking drugs, a contributing fac-
tor may be the tremendous variation in acetylcholinesterase levels
from one avian species to another: from 0.87 μmol of substrate
hydrolyzed/min/mL in cormorants to 7.89 μmol of substrate hydro-
lyzed/min/mL in mallard ducks [243].
In juvenile double-crested cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus),
vecuronium alone or in combination with atropine and phenyle-
phrine was evaluated as a mydriatic [244]. The drug combination
produced the most consistent and greatest dilation and longest aver-
age duration; no side effects from vecuronium were observed [244].
However, in a study involving adult double-crested cormorants,
vecuronium by itself produced much better dilation than was
observed in the juvenile double-crested cormorants [244]. The
difference between the juvenile birds and the adults was the very
blue irides of the adults compared to the brown irides of the young
cormorants; the authors speculated that the ability of melanin to
bind drugs may explain the difference in response [244]. Indeed, a
study investigating the mydriatic effect of rocuronium in pigeons
reported that the iris of birds with grayish brown-colored irides
(“bull eye”) did not dilate after a single application of rocuronium
and only two out of eight did so after a second application [245].
In European kestrels (Falco tinnunculus), rocuronium (0.12 mg
in each eye) [246], or vecuronium (4 mg/mL; two drops in each eye,
three times, at 15-min intervals) [241], effectively produced mydri-
asis. Rocuronium has been shown to be effective in a number of
raptorial species, including common buzzards (Buteo buteo;
0.40 mg in each eye), little owls (Athene noctua; 0.20 mg in each
eye) [247], tawny owls (Strix aluco; single topical administration of
0.35 mg in each eye) [248], and scops owls (Otus scops; 0.15 mg in
each eye) [249]. Rocuronium also significantly decreases intraocu-
lar pressure in kestrels and little owls [250].
Rocuronium produces mydriasis in Hispaniolan Amazon par-
rots (Amazona ventralis) [251,252]. In the study by Baine et al.,
topically applied rocuronium (0.15 mg per eye) rapidly produced
mydriasis and had a prolonged duration of action; 24 h after treat-
ment 2 of the 10 birds had superficial corneal ulceration as deter-
mined by fluorescein staining [251]. The authors speculated that
the low pH of the rocuronium solution could account for the ulcer-
ation. In the Petritz et al. study, rocuronium (20 μL/eye, 10 mg/mL
solution) applied topically produced mydriasis lasting up to
360 min after drug administration with minimal adverse effects
noted other than three birds having transient inferior eyelid paresis
that resolved within 24 h [252]. Baine speculated that in addition to
acidic pH, eyelid paresis could be a contributing causative factor of
the corneal ulceration [251].
Drugs of historical interest
In the past, barbiturates, the combination drug Equithesin, and
α-chloralose have been used for sedating or anesthetizing birds,
sometimes in clinical settings, but more often in research or field
situations. Surgical anesthesia can be maintained for relatively long
periods of time (1 to 12 h) by using intermediate- to long-acting
barbiturates or combinations of drugs with intermediate durations
of effect. Pentobarbital, when injected intravenously, requires 10 to
15 min for full onset of action and produces anesthesia lasting sev-
eral hours [178]. Because of its slow onset of action, the drug should

-- 1159 of 1450 --

1144 	Section 7: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia
be administered initially as a bolus consisting of half the total dose
and the remainder titrated over several minutes until the desired
plane of anesthesia is achieved. Phenobarbital is a long-acting bar-
biturate that produces anesthesia lasting up to 24 h when adminis-
tered intravenously [178]. Its onset of action is very slow, requiring
as much as 30 min before surgical anesthesia is achieved.
Equithesin is a combination of pentobarbital, chloral hydrate,
and magnesium sulfate. It does not produce a surgical plane of
anesthesia when used alone but produces surgical anesthesia lasting
as long as 90 min when combined with diazepam [253].
α-Chloralose, a general depressant and tranquilizer, is used to
capture birds in the wild, such as cranes, crows, storks, wild turkeys,
and Canada geese. The drug is usually mixed with a bait that is
attractive to the birds to be captured. When using corn to capture
cranes, each kernel is drilled out and the α-chloralose is packed into
the kernel, not sprinkled on top of the corn as the cranes will not eat
it. The amount of drug mixed with the bait depends on the avian
species to be captured and the number of birds at the bait site that
are likely to eat the baited food. For some species, date, time of day,
temperature, and humidity must be taken into consideration when
planning bait-and-capture sessions [254–256]. Capture myopathy
has occurred after α-chloralose baiting and physical capture of san-
dhill cranes during a banding study [257].
Anesthetic management
Airway management
Intubation may be difficult in species with unique oropharyngeal
anatomy, or very small birds. For example, psittacine species, such
as budgerigar parakeets (Melopsittacus undulatus), can be difficult
to intubate because of the difficult-to-visualize location of the glot-
tis at the base of the humped, fleshy tongue [258]. Appropriately
sized Cole endotracheal tubes can be used in small birds, and com-
mercially manufactured (Jorgensen Labs®) endotracheal tubes as
small as 1.0 mm ID for budgerigars and 1.5 mm ID for lovebirds do
exist. Red-rubber catheters can also be cut-to-size and used for
intubation. However, compliant tubes < 2 mm ID are often highly
flexible and kink easily, so they must be secured properly to prevent
occlusion. Intravenous catheters can be used as endotracheal
tubes [259] but are a less desirable alternative for intubating and
delivering inhalant anesthetics to very small birds because of their
lack of flexibility that can cause tracheal trauma. If an IV catheter is
used for intubation it must be appropriately sized and secured to the
head with the neck extended to prevent injury to the trachea [259].
Another hazard of small-diameter endotracheal tubes is the
resistance they impose on gas flow, a hazard that increases when
tubes become partially or completely obstructed as a result of
mucus accumulation or plugs. Resistance to flow through a tube is
inversely proportional to the tube’s radius raised to the fourth
power. For example, decreasing the radius from 3 to 2 mm or 2 to
1 mm would increase resistance approximately 5 and 15 times,
respectively. Mucus production during anesthesia can be copious
and the cold, non-humidified fresh gas used to deliver inhalant
anesthesia has a drying effect that makes the mucus thick and tena-
cious. Endotracheal tube obstruction can be detected by observing
the bird’s pattern of ventilation. As the airway becomes progres-
sively occluded, the expiratory phase becomes prolonged. An artifi-
cial sigh of the bird usually confirms the presence of an obstruction
because the keel will move and the abdominal wall will expand in
a seemingly normal manner, but they will return slowly or not at
all to their end-expiratory positions. Airway noises, especially
gurgling, may be heard as the tube becomes more obstructed with
mucus. Airway obstructions must be corrected quickly either by
extubating the bird, cleaning the tube, and re-inserting it, by replac-
ing it with a fresh tube, or by gently suctioning it with a small red-
rubber tube. An anticholinergic, such as atropine (0.04 mg/kg) or
glycopyrrolate (0.01 mg/kg), administered intramuscularly, may
reduce mucus production and lessen the risk of developing mucus
plugs, but it may also increase mucus viscosity thus making it
harder to clear secretions from the tube.
If a cuffed endotracheal tube is used, the cuff should either not be
inflated or must be inflated with extreme caution; in small birds, it
is better not to inflate the cuff. Because of the complete cartilagi-
nous tracheal rings, an overly inflated cuff will injure the tracheal
mucosa, or rupture the tracheal rings at the site of the cuff; when a
cuff is over inflated, the tracheal rings tend to rupture longitudi-
nally rather than circumferentially. On average, intubation-induced
tracheal trauma and obstruction becomes evident 16 days post-
intubation when the processes of healing and fibrotic narrowing of
the trachea cause signs of dyspnea [260].
As mentioned previously, flamingos with their ventroflexed
beaks and large fleshy tongues, can be difficult to intubate. One
strategy is to reduce the amount of equipment in the mouth during
intubation. This can be accomplished by shining a transilluminator
light from the outside of the mouth into the oral cavity; a cotton-
tipped applicator can be used to bring the tongue forward so as to
visualize the laryngeal opening into which the endotracheal tube is
inserted [personal communication: Dr. Noha Abou-Madi, Cornell
University; November 1, 2012].
The double trachea in jackass penguins (Spheniscus demersus)
poses a challenge for intubation. One technique for intubating these
birds is to use two Cole tubes attached to a double-pronged circuit
adapter, the type used for double-lumen endotracheal tubes [per-
sonal communication: Dr. Frank Golder; July 2, 2013]. Ostriches
can be intubated using endotracheal tubes with internal diameters
of 10 to 18 mm, while emus generally require endotracheal tubes
measuring 9 to 14 mm [261]. Careful inflation of the cuff is usually
necessary to enable effective ventilation of adult ratites. The tra-
cheal cleft in emus does not complicate intubation, but makes
effective positive-pressure ventilation difficult, a problem overcome
by wrapping a towel snuggly around the middle and distal thirds of
the neck [261].
Breathing circuits and fresh gas flows
Nonrebreathing circuits, such as the Bain circuit or Norman elbow,
rather than circle breathing circuits, are ideal for use in small birds
with small tidal volumes because they do not have to overcome
the resistance to ventilation imposed by unidirectional valves. An
additional advantage of all-plastic nonrebreathing circuits is their
light weight, a desirable feature when used in very small birds.
Oxygen flow for a nonrebreathing circuit should be two to three
times minute ventilation, or 150 to 200 mL/kg/min. For larger
birds, such as ratites, the breathing circuit should be commensu-
rate with the size of the bird. Emus and ostriches weighing less
than 130 kg can be maintained on a small animal breathing circuit
while larger ostriches can be maintained on a large animal breathing
circuit [261].
Induction methods
The number and variety of techniques for inducing gas anesthesia
in birds are only limited by the anesthetist’s imagination. Birds can
be induced with commercially available small animal masks, or

-- 1160 of 1450 --

Chapter 58: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia – Birds 	1145
with homemade masks fabricated from plastic bottles, syringe
cases, syringes, or breathing hose connectors. Mask induction tech-
niques can be used in a wide variety and sizes of birds, from the very
small up to and including the emu. Mask inductions are unsatisfac-
tory in adult ostriches [261].
Other techniques include the use of plastic bags or chambers.
Birds can be induced by inserting their heads into plastic bags (pref-
erably clear plastic) into which oxygen and anesthetic vapor are
introduced via a nonrebreathing circuit. Plastic bags have been used
to completely enclose a bird cage in order to induce anesthesia in a
difficult-to- manage bird [262].
An anesthetic chamber can be used to induce anesthesia. A
disadvantage of this technique is that the anesthetist is not in
physical contact with the bird and is unable to get a feel for how
the bird is responding to the anesthetic. In addition, birds
can injure themselves as they pass through stage 2 (involuntary
excitement) anesthesia.
Whatever technique is used, the anesthetist must take precau-
tions to control and eliminate anesthetic gas pollution in the work
environment. If a mask is used it should fit snugly over the bird’s
beak and face, or over its entire head. If a plastic bag or chamber is
used, it should be free of leaks. Once induction is completed, the
bag or chamber must be removed from the area without the con-
tents being released into the workplace environment.
Monitoring and support
The 2008 Confidential Enquiry into Perioperative Small Animal
Fatalities provided some data regarding perianesthetic mortality in
birds [3]. In that study, the perianesthetic mortality rate was 3.94 %
for parrots which is approximately 20 times higher than rates for
dogs and cats. The mortality rate was 16.3% for budgerigars, and
1.76% for “other birds.” That study did not provide further informa-
tion as to what species were included as “other birds,” the health
status of the patients, anesthetic protocols, or degree of monitoring
and support during the procedures. A subsequent study found that
3.4% of birds died during anesthesia [4]. Unfortunately, none of the
variables investigated in that study were associated with an
increased risk of anesthesia-related death; absent such information
makes it difficult to predict which birds might have an anesthesia-
related death [4]. A 2021 study defined anesthesia-related mortality
in birds as those deaths occurring during anesthesia and up to
7 days post anesthesia; by this definition, anesthesia-related mortal-
ity was 3.88% [5]. Birds with an abnormal health status had a 15.53-
fold increased risk of death compared with those with a normal
health status. The duration of anesthesia was a statistically signifi-
cant risk factor in the univariable analysis, but not when combined
with health status [5]. A more recent study looked at avian mortal-
ity rate based on ASA physical status [263] and found that patients
assigned an ASA status of I and II had a rate of 0% (95% CI 0.0–0.2)
and 0.6% (CI 0.2–1.3), respectively, while patients assigned a status
of III, IV, and V had rates of 5.9% (CI 4.3–8.0), 18.8% (CI 13.4–
25.7), and 50.0% (CI 29.9–70.1), respectively. Investigation into
timing of death showed that the majority of patients died following
cessation of general anesthesia (81.48%), with a majority of postan-
esthetic deaths occurring within 3 h of anesthetic recovery.
Avian anesthesia is fraught with challenges, not the least of which
is size; it is difficult to obtain preoperative blood work, secure the
airway, obtain IV access, and monitor blood pressure in very small
patients. Nonetheless, the above-cited studies make a strong case
for monitoring birds during and following anesthesia. Physiologic
variables to monitor include respiratory rate and tidal volume,
oxygenation, expired CO2
, heart rate and rhythm, body tempera-
ture, and muscle relaxation.
Central nervous system
Anesthetic depth can be assessed by checking muscle tone and vari-
ous reflexes. The loss of muscle tone in the legs or wings can denote
transition from a light to a medium plane of anesthesia. The with-
draw reflex in response to a toe pinch is lost when the bird is in a
medium (surgical) plane of anesthesia. Palpebral reflexes are usu-
ally lost at a medium plane of anesthesia, but corneal reflexes persist
until a deep plane of anesthesia. Heart and respiratory rates increase
when birds experience pain, or when the depth of anesthesia is too
light; conversely, they may decrease at a deep plane of anesthesia,
signaling the need to lighten the plane of anesthesia.
Respiratory system
The gas exchange efficiency of the avian lung is not limited to O 2
and CO 2
, but also applies to the exchange of inhalant anesthetics.
The avian lung lacks a significant functional residual volume, a
feature that limits how long a bird can remain apneic during anes-
thesia. This is a concern during induction of anesthesia of birds,
especially waterfowl, because apnea and bradycardia can occur and
may last for up to five minutes. Although referred to as a “dive
response,” in diving ducks under experimental conditions it is a
stress response mediated by stimulation of trigeminal receptors in
the beak and nares [264–267]. Anesthetic gases are not required to
elicit this response as it can be triggered by placing a mask snugly
over a bird’s beak and face. During this stress response, blood flow is
preferentially distributed to the kidneys, heart, and brain [268,269].
This stress response makes safe induction of anesthesia challenging
and raises the question, would premedicants such as butorphanol or
midazolam ameliorate or eliminate the dive response and shorten
the time to intubation in birds likely to experience a dive response,
such as waterfowl? In non-divers, specifically adult Hispaniolan
Amazon parrots (Amazona ventralis), butorphanol did not shorten
the time between induction with sevoflurane and intubation com-
pared to birds not sedated with butorphanol [100]. Other indicators
of stress in birds due to manual restraint include increases in body
temperature and respiratory rate. Using those measures of stress,
Hispaniolan Amazon parrots sedated with midazolam (2 mg/kg)
administered intranasally had a slower rate of rise in cloacal tem-
perature compared to the same birds when administered saline, and
mean respiratory rates were significantly lower for up to 12 min [58].
In mammalian species, it is well recognized that anesthetics,
through their effects on the central nervous system and peripheral
chemoreceptors, significantly depress ventilatory responses to hypoxia
and hypercapnia [270–272]. Since birds have many of the same mech-
anisms for controlling ventilation, one must assume that anesthetics
will similarly depress avian ventilatory control mechanisms. Several
studies have shown that inhalants depress the responsiveness of
a number of peripheral control mechanisms in birds, including
intrapulmonary chemoreceptors, that directly or indirectly affect
ventilation [273–275].
General anesthesia disrupts ventilatory control mechanisms
in birds, thus whenever possible a bird’s ventilation should be
assisted or controlled so as to minimize or prevent anesthesia-
induced hypoventilation. During positive-pressure ventilation, the
direction of gas flow within the avian lung may be reversed, but
the efficiency of the cross-current and multicapillary serial arteri-
alization system is independent of the direction of air flow relative
to blood flow [19]. Studies of mechanically, bi-directionally

-- 1161 of 1450 --

1146 	Section 7: Comparative Anesthesia and Analgesia
ventilated birds from which arterial blood samples were collected
and analyzed, did not show adverse effects of mechanical ventila-
tion on gas exchange [217,276,277].
Because of the flow-through nature of the avian pulmonary sys-
tem, it is possible to ventilate birds by flowing a continuous stream of
gas through the trachea and lungs, and out through a ruptured or
cannulated air sac [217,276–279]. It is also possible to cannulate an
abdominal or caudal thoracic air sac and flow inhalant anesthetic
through the air sac, across the lung, and out via the trachea. This
same technique can be used to induce and maintain anesthesia in
birds [269,278,280,281] and offers a unique, effective means by
which to maintain anesthesia for procedures that require full, unim-
peded access to the head. This technique has been used in birds as
small as zebra finches [282]. In one study of ducks in which arterial
blood gases were compared before and after cannulation of the clav-
icular air sac, both PaO2 and PaCO2 remained unchanged, but tidal
volume increased, and minute ventilation doubled [283]. However, a
study involving sulphur-crested cockatoos (Cacatua galerita)
reported that anesthesia could not be maintained in this species
when isoflurane was insufflated through the clavicular air sac [280].
This suggests that there may be species differences as to which air
sac is best cannulated for delivery of inhalant anesthetics.
Monitoring respiratory rate and tidal volume by visually observing
the frequency and degree of motion of the sternum or movements
of the breathing circuit reservoir bag, give a general sense of the ade-
quacy of ventilation and the depth of anesthesia. However, assessing
the adequacy of ventilation solely on respiratory frequency can be
misleading. High respiratory frequencies in an anesthetized bird do
not necessarily indicate the bird is light and hyperventilating but are
often associated with small tidal volumes and a greater proportion
of deadspace ventilation than effective ventilation [217].
In general, halothane, isoflurane, and sevoflurane, in a dose-
dependent manner, depress ventilation in birds [217,225,229,230,
284–287]. The anesthetic or apneic index (AI) is a measure of the
tendency of an inhalant anesthetic to cause respiratory depression
and apnea. It is derived by dividing the end-tidal concentration of
an anesthetic at apnea by the MAC for the anesthetic [288]. The
lower the AI for an anesthetic, the greater its depressant effect on
ventilation. In ducks anesthetized with halothane the AI was
1.51 [229] and for isoflurane it was 1.65 [230], values considerably
lower than those reported for dogs (2.5) and cats (2.4) [289], and
horses (2.3) [290]. This suggests that isoflurane depresses ventilation
more in birds than in mammals. However, in a study of isoflurane
in chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus), AI was similar to that reported
for mammals [291]. Species differences (ducks versus chickens)
or differences in how apnea was assessed may account for the
differences in results.
Capnography should be used to monitor ventilation in anesthe-
tized birds, while understanding its limitations. In birds, capnogra-
phy measures the partial pressure of end-expired carbon dioxide
(PE CO2
), not end-tidal carbon dioxide (PET
CO2
), and it provides
information regarding ventilatory status. Accurate sampling of air-
way gas may require adjustments in sampling flow rate or tech-
nique [292]. In intubated birds during positive-pressure ventilation,
there is acceptable correlation between PE CO2 and PaCO 2 , with
PE CO2 slightly exceeding PaCO 2 [292,293]. A PE CO2 of 30 to 45 mm
Hg indicates adequate ventilation during inhalation anesthesia in
most birds and approximates a normal physiologic range of 25 to
40 mmHg for PaCO 2 in awake birds. In contrast, during air sac
insufflation anesthesia of chickens, PE
CO2 was not strongly associ-
ated with PaCO 2 [294]. This latter study also demonstrated that
PE CO2 cannot be used to determine optimum insufflation gas flow
rates solely based on weight and previously derived values for min-
ute ventilation [294]. When feasible, arterial blood gases, specifi-
cally PaCO2
, should be the preferred method for monitoring CO2
during air sac insufflation anesthesia to verify patient ventilation
(Table 58.4).
Respiratory pauses longer than 10 to 15 s should be treated by
lightening the plane of anesthesia and, when possible, ventilating
the bird by either periodically squeezing the reservoir bag or using
a positive-pressure mechanical ventilator. Intermittent positive-
pressure ventilation (IPPV) is recommended at 2 breaths/min in
spontaneously ventilating birds, and 10–20 breaths/min in apneic
birds. A maximum pressure of 10–20 cm H2
O is recommended to
prevent air sac volutrauma. If used in combination with capnogra-
phy, IPPV rate should be adjusted to maintain PE CO2 between 30
and 45 mmHg.
Pulse oximetry can be used to monitor oxygenation, but typical
pulse oximeters are designed to measure oxygenated and deoxygen-
ated mammalian hemoglobin, not avian hemoglobin. Critical inci-
dents in birds, such as cardiac dysrhythmias, severe blood loss, or
movement artifacts, cause fluctuations and discontinuity of dis-
played values and failure to record actual values [296]. Oximeters
also tend to underestimate oxygenation levels at high oxygen satu-
ration levels and overestimate oxygenation levels at lower saturation
levels [296]. Recent development of pulse oximeters for use in small
animals, such as mice, has addressed some of the shortcomings of
early pulse oximeters [297]. The adequacy of cardiopulmonary
function and oxygenation can also be assessed visually by noting
the color and capillary refill time of mucous membranes, the color
of the cere, beak, or bill, as well as coloration on the head where
there is a lack of feathers.
An early study reported that dorsal recumbency of anesthetized
chickens, especially of “heavy breeds,” may adversely affect ventila-
tion [298]. At least two factors may explain this phenomenon:
(1) the weight of the abdominal viscera may compress the abdomi-
nal air sacs thereby effectively reducing a bird’s tidal volume; and
(2) during anesthesia there is some degree of muscle relaxation such

that a bird with large, heavy pectoral muscles may not be able to
generate sufficient muscular effort to lift the keel against gravity,
again reducing tidal volume. In a computed tomographic study of
isoflurane-anesthetized red-tailed hawks (Buteo jamaicensis), one
that did not measure physiologic variables, such as PaCO 2 and
PaO2 , mean partial air sac volume was smallest in dorsal recum-
bency compared to lateral and sternal recumbency [299]. Sternal
recumbency resulted in the greatest lung and air sac volumes and
lowest lung density compared to right lateral or dorsal recum-
bency [299]. In another study that measured respiratory rate and
volume as well as physiologic variables in isoflurane-anesthetized
red-tailed hawks, dorsal recumbency did not compromise minute
ventilation or oxygen transport more than when the birds were in
lateral recumbency [300]. However, the birds hypoventilated
in both positions, and PaCO 2 differed with time, and the position
by time interaction. Despite similar minute ventilation in both
positions, birds in dorsal recumbency hypoventilated more yet
maintained higher PaO 2 , suggesting parabronchial ventilatory or
pulmonary blood flow distribution changes with position [300].
The effect of body position has also been investigated in isoflurane-
anesthetized Humboldt penguins (Spheniscus humboldti) where air
sac volume was lowest in dorsal recumbency, and lung density was
highest compared to lateral recumbency [301]. All of these studies
suggest that body position during anesthesia may affect the avian
pulmonary system. Thus, as with any anesthetized patient, to over-
come ventilation problems in birds associated with anesthesia-
induced muscle relaxation, it is reasonable to provide IPPV.
Cardiovascular system
The heart is an electromechanical pump. Its function can be
assessed by monitoring heart rate and rhythm, mucous membrane
color and refill time, palpation of peripheral pulses, ECG monitor-
ing, and indirect or direct arterial blood pressure monitoring.
A stethoscope can be used to monitor heart rate and rhythm, and
an esophageal stethoscope can facilitate this mode of cardiac moni-
toring. The esophageal probe should be inserted into the thoracic
esophagus using digital manipulation to bypass the crop. The ultra-
sonic Doppler flow detector can be used to monitor heart rate and
rhythm by placing the sensor over one of several arteries: the cra-
nial tibial artery, palpable on the cranial aspect of the hock joint; the
superficial ulnar artery, palpable on the ventral surface of the elbow
joint; the deep radial artery, palpable on the ventral surface of the
distal radius near the carpal joint; or the palatal artery in the dorsal
oropharynx.
Standard bipolar and augmented limb leads can be used to moni-
tor and record the avian ECG. To assure adequate skin contact for
an interference-free signal, ECG clips can be attached to hypoder-
mic needles inserted through the skin at the base of each wing and
through the skin at the level of each stifle. An alternative technique
is to attach the ECG clips to stainless steel wires that have been
inserted through the prepatagium of each wing and the skin at the
lateral side of each stifle. The wire size selected depends on the size
of the bird. 20 or 22 gauge wire can be used in birds larger than 500 g.
Appropriately sized hypodermic needles are used to insert the wires
through the skin.
The morphometry of the normal avian ECG has been mistaken
for ventricular tachycardia (Fig. 58.11) [48] so it is incumbent on an
anesthetist to be familiar with avian electrocardiograms in order
to distinguish between normal and abnormal cardiac rhythms
encountered during anesthesia. Electrocardiograms have been
described for a number of avian species, including gray (Psittacus
erithacus) and Amazon (Amazona spp.) parrots [302], Pekin
duck [303], peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus brookei) [304],
Eurasian kestrel, griffon vulture, little owl, and Eurasian eagle
owl [305], and golden (Chrysolophus pictus) and silver (Lophura
nycthemera) pheasants [306].
The effect of halothane on blood pressure can be variable. In
chickens and ducks, increasing concentrations of halothane can
cause a decrease in mean arterial blood pressure [225,307], or no
change [229]. In contrast, isoflurane appears to consistently cause
a 	dose-dependent 	decrease 	in 	mean 	arterial 	blood 	pres-
sure [217,230,307,308], possibly because of isoflurane-associated
peripheral vasodilation. Sevoflurane has been reported to decrease
blood pressure in chickens in a dose-dependent manner during
controlled ventilation [227,286], but not during spontaneous
ventilation probably because of hypercapnia due to hypoventila-
tion [286]. In crested caracara (Caracara plancus), sevoflurane
moderately depressed blood pressure and did so without producing
cardiac arrhythmias [284]. In red-tailed hawks anesthetized with
sevoflurane, blood pressure was significantly lower compared to
when they were awake and physically restrained [309].
In mammals, positive-pressure ventilation depresses mean arte-
rial blood pressure by creating positive intrathoracic pressures that
compress the great vessels, thus impeding the venous return of
blood to the heart. In sandhill cranes anesthetized with isoflurane,
mean arterial blood pressure was actually higher during positive-
pressure ventilation than during spontaneous ventilation [217].
Blood pressure can be monitored and measured either indirectly
or directly, but avian anatomy and physiology make either tech-
nique challenging. Indirect methods include using a Doppler flow
probe (Parks Electronics, Aloha, Oregon, USA) to monitor pulsa-
tile blood flow in small birds, or blood pressure when used with
a sphygmomanometer in either moderate or large-size birds.
However, in awake birds representing 17 commonly kept psittacine
species weighing between 230 and 1263 g, Doppler-derived blood

pressure measurements were imprecise [310]. Attempts to meas-
ure blood pressure with an oscillometric device in Hispaniolan
Amazon parrots (Amazona ventralis) proved unsuccessful [311].
In those same birds, there was substantial disagreement between
indirectly measured blood pressure obtained with a Doppler device
and directly measured systolic arterial blood pressure [311]. In
anesthetized and awake red-tailed hawks, the results of a study
comparing Doppler and oscillometric methods of indirect blood
pressure measurement with direct arterial measurement indicated
that the oscillometric technique was unreliable [309]. Using a
Doppler device and a cuff of 40–50% of limb circumference, meas-
urements obtained from either the pectoral or pelvic limbs yielded
values closer to mean arterial blood pressure than systolic arterial
blood pressure [309].
Arterial catheterization is required for direct arterial blood pres-
sure monitoring. For birds less than 200 g, the preferred catheteri-
zation site is the superficial ulnar artery, one that is prominent but
very mobile where it crosses the elbow, thus making catheteriza-
tion technically challenging without causing a hematoma [312].
Furthermore, the anatomy of the wing makes it difficult to secure a
catheter at this location. For medium to large birds, the deep radial
artery is the preferred site [312,313] due to its minimal mobility as
it lies between the tendons of the extensor digitorum longus and the
flexor digitorum profundus in the distal wing of most birds [312].
Catheterization should occur where the artery is most superficial at
the ulnar carpal bone or the distal head of the ulna [312]. For
aquatic or long-legged birds, the cranial tibial or dorsal metatarsal
arteries can be catheterized [313]. The external carotid artery can
be catheterized, but surgical dissection is required for visualization
and catheterization [294].
Monitoring a physiological variable such as arterial blood pres-
sure implies that action will be taken if blood pressure differs from
the expected. This touches on the concept of action limits: in an
anesthetized patient, what blood pressure requires intervention?
What constitutes hypotension, and what constitutes hypertension?
For birds, there are no clear answers since cited blood pressures
vary across avian species. For example, direct blood pressure meas-
urements are higher in psittacines, cranes, raptors, and owls than
in pigeons, chickens, and ducks [314]. In chickens, normal mean
arterial blood pressure (MAP) is approximately 84 ± 13 mm Hg,
and in conscious red-tailed hawks, it is 187 ± 42 mm Hg [314]. In
humans, a 30% decrease from baseline MAP is one indicator of
hypotension [315], and this metric has been used to define hypo-
tension in birds [314]. As such, hypotension in chickens would be
a MAP ≤ 59 mmHg, and ≤ 131 mmHg in red-tailed hawks, both of
which would require intervention, such as lightening the plane of
anesthesia, administering fluids, and cardiac inotropes, including
dopamine or dobutamine.
In general, birds tend to have a higher plasma osmolality
compared to mammals [316]. For this reason, fluids with an osmo-
larity close to 300–320 mOsm/L, such as Normosol®-R, Plasma-
Lyte®-R, Plasma-Lyte®-A, and 0.9% NaCl, have been recommended
for fluid therapy in birds, specifically parrots [178], and are reason-
able choices for fluid support of any bird during anesthesia [316].
In a dose-dependent manner, dobutamine at 5, 10, and 15 μg/kg/
min and dopamine at 5, 7, and 10 μg/kg/min increased arterial
blood pressure in Hispaniolan Amazon parrots [314]. However,
4 out of 12 parrots receiving dobutamine at 15 μg/kg/min devel-
oped marked second-degree atrioventricular block accompanied
by a dramatic decrease in blood pressure, a situation that quickly
resolved after the dobutamine infusion was discontinued [314].
Body temperature
Body temperature must be monitored as hypothermia is the most
commonly encountered problem during anesthesia [317]. The
stress associated with anesthesia and surgery is minimized when
birds are maintained at or near their normal body temperature
which is 40 to 41 °C (104 to 106 °F) [318]. During anesthesia, it is
not unusual to see major fluctuations in body temperature, but
hypothermia decreases the amount of anesthetic needed to main-
tain anesthesia, causes cardiac instability, and prolongs recovery.
In well-insulated birds (feathers, drapes, and warming devices),
hyperthermia can also occur and cause cardiac instability and
increased oxygen demand. Body temperature can be monitored
with an electronic thermometer and a long flexible thermistor
probe inserted into the esophagus to the level of the heart.
Temperature monitored via the cloaca can vary significantly over
time owing to cloacal movements that affect the position of the
thermometer or thermistor probe.
Methods for warming birds during anesthesia include convective
(forced warm air), conductive, and radiant heat sources. In anesthe-
tized Hispaniolan Amazon parrots (Amazona ventralis) covered
with a clear plastic drape, a forced air warming device was used to
maintain body temperature. The device did not prevent an initial
drop in core body temperature, but it maintained body temperature
within a clinically acceptable range [319]. A disadvantage to using a
forced air warming device is that it can blow air into the surgical
site. The type of anesthetic delivery system, with or without heated
air, does not appear to affect core body temperature in isoflurane-
anesthetized pigeons [320]. Electric heating pads and gloves filled
with hot water are not appropriate warming methods for birds as
they can cause thermal injury.
Recovery
Precautions should be taken to protect birds while they recover
from anesthesia. During recovery, birds should be in a warm (25
°C/77 °F) incubator until fully recovered. Birds must be kept from
flopping around, as this can lead to serious neck, wing, or leg inju-
ries. Struggling and flopping behavior can be prevented by lightly
wrapping a bird with a towel but wrapping poses its own hazards. If
a bird is wrapped too tightly, sternal movements will be impeded,
and breathing will be difficult if not impossible. Wrapping can lead
to excessive retention of body heat and cause hyperthermia. If a bird
has not been fasted prior to anesthesia, regurgitation can occur dur-
ing recovery. Keeping a bird intubated during the recovery phase
helps to maintain a patent airway.

Veterinary Anesthesia and Analgesia: The Sixth E dition of Lumb and J ones. Edited by Leigh Lamont, Kurt Grimm, Sheilah Robertson, Lydia Love and Carrie Schroeder.
© 2024 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Published 2024 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
Companion website: www.wiley.com/go/lamont/anesthesia
Introduction
The selection of a particular anesthetic plan is predicated upon the
patient’s physical status and temperament, the type of procedure for
which anesthesia is being considered, anticipated degree of periop-
erative pain, the familiarity of the anesthetist with the anesthetic
drugs, the type of facility and equipment available, the personnel
available for assistance, and the cost of anesthetic drugs [1,2]. There
is no single best method for anesthetizing dogs or cats, and famili-
arity with just one anesthetic technique at best limits a veterinarian’s
ability to perform the myriad of surgical and diagnostic procedures
commonly performed in a modern veterinary practice and at worst
results in unnecessary risk to the patient. A debilitated dog or cat
undergoing extensive repair of a fractured limb will require a differ-
ent anesthetic regimen than one undergoing routine neutering, one
requiring short-term restraint for radiography, or a geriatric patient
requiring extensive dental surgery.
General anesthesia is characterized by muscle relaxation, uncon-
sciousness, amnesia, and analgesia. It is difficult for a single drug to
provide all of these elements without causing significant distur-
bances to patient homeostasis. Inhalant anesthetics come closest to
satisfying all of these conditions, but even they are more useful when
co-administered with anesthetic adjunctive drugs such as sedatives,
opioids, local anesthetics, or hypnotics. As a general rule, when
formulating an anesthetic plan, it is best to consider using relatively
low doses of several different drugs rather than a large dose of a sin-
gle drug. For example, apnea resulting from a large bolus of propofol
can be eliminated, or its duration shortened, by prior administration
of opioids, acepromazine, benzodiazepines, or α2
-adrenergic receptor
agonists, which allows administration of a lower propofol dose [3].
The opioid drugs, while important components of modern anes-
thetic regimens, by themselves do not produce general anesthe-
sia [4]. Muscle rigidity, salivation, and long recoveries associated
with large dosages of ketamine can be lessened when the latter is
combined in reduced doses with opioids, α2
-adrenergic receptor
agonists, and hypnotic drugs such as benzodiazepines [5].
Any plan for procedural sedation or general anesthesia must
include a provision to control pain if it is present or anticipated. A
good analgesic regimen should include drugs sufficient to ensure
analgesia during and after the procedure. The one aspect that
should not vary among anesthetic procedures is the degree of vigi-
lance associated with monitoring an anesthetized dog or cat. Early
warning of impending anesthetic difficulty is the single most
important factor responsible for decreasing anesthetic-related
morbidity and mortality.
Consideration should also be given to the use of anesthetic
checklists to improve patient outcomes [1].

1158 	Section 8: Anesthesia and Analgesia for Domestic Species
Preanesthetic considerations
Recording a thorough history and conducting the physical and
laboratory evaluation are the most important components of a
preanesthetic evaluation. Even young, seemingly healthy, animals
presenting for routine procedures, such as neutering, require both.
These animals may have never been examined previously by a
veterinarian, and congenital disorders, severe parasitism, or heart-
worm disease may be discovered.
Signalment
Review of patient signalment is a key preanesthetic consideration
(Box 59.1). Anesthesiologists are often questioned about “sensitivity
to anesthesia” in a variety of dog and cat breeds. Although several
breed-associated anesthesia concerns (e.g., predisposition to heredi-
tary diseases that increase anesthetic risk) have been documented, all
breeds have been successfully anesthetized by using standard anes-
thetic regimens, and most reports of “sensitivities” are anecdotal. An
assessment of the validity of information relating to anesthesia in
dogs on the World Wide Web reported that information was often
incomplete, and that breed sensitivities mentioned were not sup-
ported by scientific evidence [6]. One well-documented breed-
associated anesthetic concern is the altered pharmacokinetics of
barbiturates and propofol in certain sighthounds, which is associated
with a mutation in cytochrome P450 CYB2B11 enzyme expres-
sion [7–9]. Another is brachycephalic breeds and their associated
airway anatomic malformations. This presents a concern for ensur-
ing a patent airway throughout the perianesthetic period. There is
also evidence that these breeds possess greater resting vagal tone,
heightening the concern for anesthetic-induced bradycardia [10].
Anesthetic risk has been shown to increase in these breeds as body
weight decreases and as duration of anesthetic increases, with the
incidence of intra- and postoperative complications being 1.6 and 4.3
times greater than in non-brachycephalic dogs, respectively [11].
Since toy breeds have a greater surface area to body mass ratio and
have a relatively greater metabolic rate, they require careful attention
to maintenance of body heat and blood glucose concentrations.
Additionally, they require a relatively greater dose of drugs on a per-
kilogram basis than larger dogs. Reduced doses of some drugs (ace-
promazine, butorphanol, maropitant, and ondansetron) should be
used in breeds that are known to have the ABCB1 gene (formerly
known as “MDR1”) [12]. Further information about canine breed-
specific anesthetic considerations is available in Chapter 50.
Generally, there are no sex-related differences in the response to
anesthesia. However, a history of the estrus cycle will often identify
recent estrus and thus alert the clinician to the concerns associated
with an enlarged and vascularized uterus. This would potentially
cause concern regarding blood loss during an ovariohysterectomy.
Additionally, the owner of an intact female animal should be queried
about the possibility of their animal being pregnant because the stress
of surgery and anesthesia may adversely affect the fetus(es), and preg-
nancy can affect multiple body systems (see Chapter 45).
Age is an important anesthetic consideration. Generally, the very
young (less than 8 weeks old) and the aged (more than 80% of their
expected lifespan) do not metabolize anesthetic drugs as rapidly as
healthy adult animals [13]. Healthy geriatric patients may only
require 25–50% of the dose of sedatives, hypnotics, tranquilizers,
and opioids given to comparable young, healthy animals.
History
In addition to questions concerning organ system function
(Box 59.1), the owner should also be asked about any previous anes-
thetic episodes, past and present illnesses, and past and current
medication history, including history of heartworm prophy-
laxis [14]. The time elapsed since the last feeding should be noted.
Physical examination
The preanesthetic physical examination should be thorough, with
all body systems considered (Box 59.2). Any abnormality discov-
ered by physical examination or suggested by the medical history
should be followed with appropriate laboratory or other suitable
diagnostic testing. The assessment of an animal’s temperament is
critical. Vicious or aggressive animals will require a different
approach to anesthesia than quiet, cooperative individuals.
Laboratory evaluation
There is no objective evidence supporting age-based or American
Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical-status-based (see
below) 	minimum 	laboratory 	evaluation 	requirements 	[1].
Regardless, the minimum preanesthetic laboratory data suggested
for young, healthy dogs are hematocrit and plasma protein. These
tests are easy, quick, and inexpensive to perform. Hematocrit is an
indicator of hemoglobin concentration, which directly relates to the
ability of the blood to transport oxygen to tissues. As a general rule,
a hematocrit of less than 20% indicates the need for perioperative
administration of blood. Hemoglobin concentration (g/dL) can be
approximated by dividing the hematocrit by three.
For elective procedures in middle-aged to older animals, or ani-
mals treated chronically with medications that could alter liver or
renal function (e.g., non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, pheno-
barbital, or antineoplastic chemotherapeutics), a complete blood
count, urinalysis, and biochemistry profile is recommended. Other
laboratory tests should be performed (e.g., thoracic radiographs and/
or echocardiography, abdominal radiographs, and/or ultrasound) if
the history or physical examination suggests specific organ system
disease. A minimum laboratory database prior to emergency anes-
thesia for a debilitated dog or cat should include packed cell volume,
total protein, and electrolytes (sodium, potassium, and chloride).

Physical status
Many factors (e.g., age, breed, concurrent disease, surgical proce-
dure, surgeon skill, and available equipment) contribute to the over-
all anesthetic risk for a given patient. One risk factor is the physical
status of the patient. A convenient system of status classification for
veterinary patients has been adapted from the ASA [1]. In general,
physical status I and II patients appear to be at less risk for anes-
thetic complications. Physical statuses III–V are usually at greater
anesthetic risk. However, this is not to imply that category I and II
patients are at no risk from unanticipated anesthetic mishaps
(Table 59.1).
Patient preparation
Fasting
Healthy dogs and cats should be fasted for 4–6 h prior to being anesthe-
tized, if possible [1]. Water can be allowed until just prior to anesthesia
for most procedures. Dogs and cats less than 8 weeks old should not be
fasted longer than 1–2 h because they are at a greater risk for perianes-
thetic hypoglycemia. They should receive dextrose-containing intrave-
nous (IV) fluids during any prolonged anesthesia (longer than 15 min)
and/or serial blood glucose measurements until fully recovered.
Patient stabilization
When possible, life-threatening physiological disturbances should
be medically addressed prior to anesthesia (Box 59.3). This may,
however, not always be possible, and anesthesia should never be
delayed if immediate surgical or medical intervention is needed to
save the patient’s life.
Anesthetic and analgesic plan
Several aspects should be considered when formulating an anes-
thetic plan (Box 59.4). In general, techniques for procedural seda-
tion or general anesthesia rely primarily on local anesthesia,
injectable anesthesia, or inhalation anesthesia. Regardless, these pri-
mary techniques are typically supplemented with some degree of
drug-induced sedation and systemically administered analgesics.
Techniques frequently overlap. For example, inhalant anesthesia is
usually initiated with injectable anesthetics. Local anesthetic nerve
blocks are typically performed under general anesthesia or
sedation.
The remainder of the discussion regarding the choice of anes-
thetic and analgesic drugs assumes that the reader has reviewed
and is familiar with the clinical pharmacology of the various anes-
thetic drugs as presented elsewhere in this text. Although the drug
combinations described are suitable for a variety of patients, the
reader should refer to the appropriate sections of this text or con-
sult a veterinary anesthesiologist if questions remain about how to
anesthetize and monitor specific patients. Drug availability can be
an issue, so it is best to become familiar with a variety of
techniques.
Short-term anesthesia (less than 15 min)
By themselves, sedative–opioid combinations are suitable for
short-term restraint for minimally invasive procedures or those
procedures not requiring general anesthesia, such as radiography
or physical examination in an intractable animal (Tables 59.2
and 59.3). An advantage is that one or both of these components are
reversible, allowing a rapid return to preanesthetic mentation and

Currently, propofol is widely used for short-term immobilization
in cats and dogs. Because of its rapid plasma clearance, multiple
boluses of propofol, or a propofol constant rate infusion (CRI), can
be used to prolong the duration of restraint without significantly
prolonging the duration of recovery [15]. Respiratory depression
may be significant and ventilatory assistance should be available.
Alfaxalone is a neurosteroid anesthetic drug that produces hypnosis
and muscle relaxation by enhancing conduction of the GABAA recep-
tor. Immobilization is characterized by excellent muscle relaxation
and hypnosis in dogs and cats. Although labeled in the United States
for IV induction of anesthesia, it can also be administered intramus-
cularly (IM) for sedation of dogs and cats. Alfaxalone administered
either as a single agent (IM or IV) or combined with other sedatives at
higher dosages (5 mg/kg IM) is not recommended given its poor
recovery quality [17–19]. However, when lower dosages (1–3 mg/kg
IM) combined with additional sedatives are used, these effects are
much improved [20–22]. Its duration of action is dose-dependent, and
it provides good cardiovascular stability in healthy patients [23,24].
Like propofol, it is compatible for use following commonly used pre-
anesthetic sedatives and tranquilizers to maintain general anesthesia
as a CRI [25,26]. Respiratory depression may, however, be significant,
and ventilatory assistance should be available [25,26].
A combination of ketamine and midazolam produces less muscle
relaxation than propofol, alfaxalone, or propofol–ketamine. In dos-
ages typically used, ketamine–midazolam is also associated with
increased salivation and dysphoria upon recovery [5]. However,
dissociative anesthetic combinations generally produce less respira-
tory and cardiovascular depression than other available short-
acting injectable anesthetics. Muscle relaxation and recovery quality
are improved, and salivation is lessened when dissociatives are
given with, or preceded by, a sedative or tranquilizer [5].

1162 	Section 8: Anesthesia and Analgesia for Domestic Species
While thiopental is no longer available in a number of countries,
including the United States, it is relatively inexpensive and suitable
for short-term restraint of most healthy dogs and cats. A disadvan-
tage to its use as a sole anesthetic is that relatively large doses are
required, full recovery can take up to 1 h, and recovery can be
associated with ataxia and disorientation. These undesirable char-
acteristics are reduced when its administration is preceded by a
tranquilizer such as acepromazine or a sedative such as dexmedeto-
midine. Another disadvantage is that it must be administered IV, a
problem with fractious or uncooperative animals. Perivascular thi-
opental administration is associated with local tissue inflammation,
pain, and potential tissue necrosis. Perivascular administration
should be attended to by infiltrating the area with a crystalloid fluid
(e.g., 0.9% sodium chloride) at a volume equal to 3–5 times the vol-
ume of perivascularly administered thiopental. Additionally, a local
anesthetic such as lidocaine and an anti-inflammatory (e.g., meth-
ylprednisolone) may be infiltrated near the site of perivascular
injection. Another important side effect of thiopental is the signifi-
cant respiratory depression that can accompany its use.
The relatively cumbersome nature of inhalation anesthetic deliv-
ery makes it inconvenient for use in very short procedures, and its use
solely for routine induction of unconsciousness and anesthesia is not
recommended. On occasion, it can prove useful for chamber induc-
tion of feral or fractious cats. It can also be useful for short-term
anesthesia in neonates or those animals with severe organ system
compromise and a reduced ability to clear drugs through the kidney
or liver. Mask induction with inhalant anesthetics should be preceded
by preanesthetic administration whenever possible to reduce the
stress and anxiety (and catecholamine release) associated with ini-
tial inspiration of high concentrations of inhalant anesthetics. Care
should also be taken to minimize environmental contamination and
subsequent exposure of veterinary staff to inhalant anesthetic.
Intermediate-term anesthesia (15 min to 1 h)
For procedures of intermediate duration that do not require
significant analgesia, the previously discussed drugs suitable for
short-term restraint can be used and re-dosed to effect. Typically,
one-third to half of the induction dose is administered slowly to pro-
long the anesthetic effect. Thiopental and ketamine–midazolam
should not be re-dosed multiple times. Their initial duration of
action following bolus administration depends primarily on redis-
tribution away from the brain to other tissues, such as muscle.
However, when these tissues are saturated with drug, redistribution
greatly slows, and metabolism becomes the rate-limiting factor for
awakening. Propofol and alfaxalone, because of their relatively rapid
clearances and large volumes of distribution, can be administered
repeatedly to dogs by using small boluses or by CRI (Table 59.5).
Invasive surgical procedures such as canine and feline gonadec-
tomy typically require 15 min to 1 h of anesthesia, accompanied by
good perioperative analgesia. Several options are available. Total
injectable anesthesia, where a drug combination is injected IV or
IM and will last for the duration of the procedure, is suitable for
short-term anesthesia in healthy animals, and is frequently used in
cats for procedures such as castration and wound care (Table 59.7).
A combination of Telazol®, ketamine, and xylazine is suitable for
cats, although its use has been associated with relatively prolonged
recoveries and it provides minimal postoperative analgesia [27].
An alternative is the combination of dexmedetomidine, ketamine,
and an opioid agonist. Inclusion of dexmedetomidine in the combi-
nation facilitates antagonism of the α2
- adrenergic agonist’s hypnotic
and analgesic effects with atipamezole, if required. Inhalation
anesthesia following sedation and induction of anesthesia with a
rapidly acting injectable drug such as propofol is also appropriate
for procedures of intermediate duration and may be the most con-
venient and most controllable option. Inhalant anesthetic delivery
of this duration usually requires endotracheal intubation and care-
ful monitoring but offers the benefit of enabling a rapid adjustment
of anesthetic depth should anesthetic conditions change unexpect-
edly (e.g., loss of blood or respiratory arrest).
Long-term anesthesia (longer than 1 h)
Long procedures are best managed by maintenance with inhalation
anesthesia. Awakening from sevoflurane and isoflurane anesthesia
is predictably rapid. Even sick and debilitated patients recover from
prolonged periods of inhalation anesthesia relatively quickly, and
liver or renal impairment does not preclude drug clearance. As an
alternative, injectable anesthesia using drugs administered IM or
IV has been described (see above) [25–31].
Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) can also be used for longer-
term anesthetic maintenance. Techniques that involve infusion of
propofol or alfaxalone, often in combination with opioids and/or
reversible sedatives, are most suited for prolonged anesthesia
because propofol and alfaxalone undergo rapid and predictable
clearance. Techniques involving infusion or repeated administra-
tion of longer-acting, non-reversible drugs, such as Telazol®, are less
suited for long procedures as they result in protracted recoveries.
Most anesthetic techniques are associated with some degree of res-
piratory depression and a loss of the protective swallowing reflex, so
tracheal intubation and a means to assist ventilation are essential for
reducing anesthetic risk.
Premedication
While inhalation anesthesia can be initiated without premedica-
tion, administration of a sedative or tranquilizer often in combina-
tion with an opioid is recommended prior to induction of anesthesia
(Tables 59.2 and 59.3). Preanesthetic drugs aid in restraint, reduce
apprehension, decrease the quantity of potentially more depressant
drugs used to produce general anesthesia, facilitate induction,
enhance perioperative analgesia, and reduce arrhythmogenic auto-
nomic reflex activity. Premedications are usually administered IM
or SC 15–30 min before induction. The choice of premedication
depends on signalment, temperament, physical status, concurrent
disease, the procedure to be performed, drug availability, and per-
sonal preference (Table 59.6). For procedures associated with post-
operative pain, premedication should include an analgesic such as
an opioid and possibly a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug.
Fewer analgesics are typically needed postoperatively when analge-
sics are administered preemptively [32]. Repeated and frequent
patient assessment following surgery is needed to assess the ade-
quacy of analgesia. Additional analgesics should be administered
when needed (see Chapter 47).
Induction
Induction of anesthesia is most easily accomplished in most cats
and dogs with propofol, alfaxalone, ketamine–midazolam, propofol–
ketamine, or etomidate (Table 59.5). Advantages of an IV method of
induction include rapid loss of consciousness and ability to intubate
the trachea quickly. Alternatives to these rapid IV induction
protocols include administration of a higher dose IM dissociative
(cyclohexamine) anesthetic–benzodiazepine combination (e.g.,

-- 1178 of 1450 --

Chapter 59: Dogs and Cats 	1163
Telazol®), chamber or mask inhalant induction, or high-dose IV
opioid induction. These techniques can be useful in special circum-
stances, but for routine use in healthy dogs and cats, their disadvan-
tages generally outweigh their advantages.
Chamber or mask inhalant induction
One disadvantage to chamber and mask induction is the associated
waste-gas pollution. Another is the struggling and associated stress
that some animals experience during the induction phase [33]. Mask
induction is most easily accomplished in moribund animals and
small tractable dogs. Prior tranquilization or sedation enhances the
quality and speed of induction, as does the use of a non-rebreathing
system to deliver the anesthetic agent initially [34]. Chamber induc-
tion is most useful in intractable cats and very small dogs. Isoflurane
and sevoflurane are the most suitable inhalants for this technique
because they produce a relatively rapid induction [35]. Relatively
high oxygen flow rates (4 L/min for chamber and 3 L/min for mask)
and vaporizer settings (3–5% isoflurane and 5–7% sevoflurane in
healthy animals) are used. The use of nitrous oxide is not necessary
during chamber or mask induction with currently used agents [36].
With chamber induction, once the animal has lost its righting reflex
and is unresponsive to the chamber being tilted from side to side, it
is removed from the chamber and induction is continued using an
appropriately sized mask. Mask induction is begun by exposing the
animal to the mask and oxygen. The inhalation concentration is
slowly increased to 3–5% for isoflurane and 5–7% for sevoflurane.
This is accomplished with a non-rebreathing or rebreathing circuit by
gradually increasing the vaporizer setting over 2–4 min. Use of a non-
rebreathing anesthetic system to deliver gas to the chamber or mask
will facilitate rapid induction because exchange of the room air,
which is present in the reservoir bag, breathing circuit, and carbon
dioxide absorber prior to starting induction, with anesthetic-laden
gas from the vaporizer is not necessary.
Intravenous high-dose opioid induction
A disadvantage to opioid induction is the accompanying relatively
slow loss of consciousness. Advantages include good cardiovascular
stability (although severe bradycardia may be seen when anticho-
linergics are not co-administered) and the attenuation of the stress
response associated with anesthesia and surgery. Opioid induction
works best in debilitated dogs and is not recommended in cats or
young, healthy dogs that are not well sedated. Incremental doses of
an opioid agonist (Table 59.3) are alternated with small incremental
doses of midazolam (Table 59.2) until the dog can be intubated.
This technique does not always result in a patient that can be intu-
bated; therefore, an IV induction agent should be available, and
given to effect if needed.
Anesthetic maintenance
The maintenance phase of anesthesia begins when unconsciousness
is induced and ends with discontinuation of anesthetic delivery.
After the loss of consciousness, a properly sized, cuffed endotra-
cheal tube or alternative airway (e.g., supraglottic airway device) is
usually inserted to allow assisted ventilation, if necessary, and pro-
tect against aspiration of oropharyngeal contents. Adequate cardio-
vascular function is rapidly verified, and the anesthetic vaporizer is
turned on. The initial and subsequent anesthetic vaporizer settings
(percentage concentration of inhalant) vary with the condition of
the patient, the type of breathing circuit used, and the fresh-gas flow
rate (Table 59.8). The relatively high fresh-gas flow rate and
vaporizer setting that are initially used after induction are decreased
to maintenance settings when the patient nears the desired anes-
thetic plane (usually when palpebral reflexes disappear, and the
heart rate begins to decrease). The vaporizer setting is adjusted
according to signs of anesthetic depth. The most useful signs of
anesthetic depth in dogs and cats include a combination of ocular
signs (palpebral reflex and position of the globe), muscle tone
(assessed by opening the mouth to its full extent), heart and respira-
tory rates, and systemic arterial blood pressure. Other monitors
that may be used include a pulse oximeter and a capnometer. Pulse
oximetry non-invasively provides an estimate of hemoglobin’s oxy-
gen saturation (normal is greater than 95%). This information
along with packed cell volume or hemoglobin concentration indi-
cates the oxygen content of arterial blood. A capnometer non-
invasively assesses ventilation by monitoring respiratory rate and
end-tidal expired carbon dioxide (CO 2
) partial pressure, which is
related to arterial CO2
. End- tidal CO2 monitors can also identify
problems with the gas delivery system such as rebreathing due to
malfunctioning one-way valves and exhausted CO 2 absorbent,
especially when graphic display of the CO 2 time profile is provided
(i.e., a capnogram). Additional information on patient monitoring
is available in Chapters 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16.
The anesthetic record
This is part of the patient’s permanent record and should include
notation of patient status, the anesthetic drugs used (including time
of administration, dose, and effect), duration of the surgery, and
notation of significant perioperative events. Ideally, heart rate, res-
piratory rate, blood pressure, and any other variables monitored
should be recorded at regular intervals (every 5 min). Recording
these data at regular intervals creates a visual aid that assists in deter-
mining the change in patient status during the anesthetic period. For
example, a steadily increasing heart rate accompanied by a steadily
decreasing blood pressure during a 15-min interval could signal
hypotension caused by fluid loss or excessive anesthetic depth. This
is easily observed on the anesthetic record but may not be noticed
without the visual prompt of the data recorded over time.
Perioperative analgesia
Concurrent administration of various analgesic drugs during inha-
lation anesthesia is useful to enhance intraoperative and postopera-
tive analgesia. These drugs can be continued into the postanesthetic
period to maintain analgesia. Infusions of low doses of ketamine,
lidocaine, opioids, and their combinations have been described as
adjuncts to inhalation anesthesia [37–39] (Table 59.9). When using
these drugs, the concentration of inhalant anesthetic can often be
significantly reduced. Increased respiratory depression is a concern,

and the adequacy of ventilation should be closely monitored, with

Local and regional anesthetic techniques can and should be used
when indicated to enhance analgesia and decrease general anes-
thetic requirements intraoperatively. Many different techniques are
available for dogs and cats with reasonable safety and efficacy and
are presented in Chapter 60.
Recovery
Recovery begins when the procedure for which a patient has been
anesthetized is finished and the anesthetic drugs have been
discontinued. Patient status should be monitored regularly during
recovery until the patient is conscious and extubated, and heart
rate, respiratory rate, and body temperature have returned to
normal. Young, healthy animals undergoing routine procedures
usually do not need supplemental oxygen during recovery,
although it should always be immediately available. Continuous
use of pulse oximetry is helpful to identify unexpected
postanesthetic hypoxemia. Hypoxemia caused by respiratory
depression, atelectasis-related ventilation–perfusion mismatch,
and/or rapidly decreased fraction of inspired oxygen (e.g., near
100% oxygen when attached to an anesthetic breathing system to
21% when breathing room air) is easily addressed if detected early.
If nitrous oxide was used during anesthetic maintenance, the
breathing system should be repeatedly filled with oxygen, and the
patient allowed to breathe an oxygen-enriched gas mixture for
5–10 min after discontinuation of nitrous oxide. This helps
prevent the diffusion hypoxia that can develop if the inspired
oxygen concentration suddenly decreases while nitrous oxide is
rapidly moving from the blood into the alveolar gas. Sick or
debilitated dogs and cats benefit from supplemental oxygen
during recovery, particularly if hypothermic, because shivering
can significantly increase oxygen consumption. The endotracheal
tube cuff should be partially deflated and endotracheal tube
untied when a patient is disconnected from the anesthetic
machine. This permits extubation in the event that the patient
rapidly awakens and begins chewing, but care should be exercised
when moving the animal to the recovery area so premature
accidental extubation does not occur. At this time the animal’s
nose should be positioned downwards slightly to allow drainage
of any accumulated oral or pharyngeal fluid that accumulated
during the procedure. If an esophageal stethoscope or temperature
probe was used, it should be removed prior to terminating
anesthetic delivery. Dogs and cats should be extubated as soon as
swallowing occurs, unless there is a specific contraindication to
removing the endotracheal tube at this time (e.g., brachycephalic
airway syndrome). Dogs and cats should never be left to recover
unobserved. Patients should recover in a well-ventilated area to
minimize pollution of the workspace by exhaled anesthetic gas.
Occasionally, a dog or cat will suddenly awaken from anesthesia
disoriented and will vocalize, paddle, and appear incoherent. This
sudden arousal can be caused by emergence delirium, opioid dys-
phoria, or pain, and it is important to distinguish between them.
Emergence delirium occurs most frequently in poorly or non-
premedicated animals and in particular those awakening rapidly
from inhalant anesthesia. With emergence delirium, the dog or cat
will become quiet and more comfortable, usually within 10 min.
A quiet, reassuring voice and gentle restraint can guide the animal
through this period of excitement. Alternatively, a low dosage of
IV propofol (0.25–1 mg/kg) can dramatically lessen the dysphoric
behavior, allowing a smooth recovery. Occasionally, a low dose of
dexmedetomidine (0.5–1 μg/kg IV) or acepromazine (0.005–0.02
mg/kg IV) is necessary to quiet an excited, dysphoric animal. If pain
is believed to be the cause of the rough recovery, rapidly acting opi-
oid analgesics (e.g., fentanyl) should be administered IV.
Postoperative pain control is managed best with preanesthetic
analgesic administration of relatively long-lasting analgesics, perio-
perative analgesic infusion, local anesthetics, and attention to signs
of pain. Dogs and cats can become dysphoric during recovery,
related to perioperative opioid administration [40]. Opioid dyspho-
ria can be diminished with partial opioid reversal using the opioid
antagonist naloxone (1–2 μg/kg IV).
Dogs or cats receiving perioperative fluids can develop a fully
distended or overdistended urinary bladder that can cause signs of
discomfort. If a full bladder is palpated, it can be gently expressed
prior to recovery.
Delayed anesthetic recovery
Occasionally, a dog or cat that received several drugs (especially
opioids) during the anesthetic episode will remain mildly
hypothermic and unresponsive. In these instances, consideration
should be given to antagonism of reversible drugs (α2 -adrenergic
receptor agonists or opioids) that were given as part of the
anesthetic regimen. Relatively small IV boluses of naloxone (1–2
μg/kg) can be used to reverse the central nervous system (CNS)
and thermoregulatory depression associated with the opioids

Severe hypoglycemia is an easily corrected problem that can
result in delayed anesthetic recovery. Blood glucose concentration
should be measured if hypoglycemia is suspected, and IV dextrose-
containing fluids given until blood glucose concentrations normal-
ize. Arterial hypotension associated with blood loss or poor cardiac
function can cause altered mentation and slow recovery. Periodic
measurement of arterial blood pressure during recovery, especially
in debilitated patients, is warranted. Hypercapnia (PaCO 2 approach-
ing 100 mmHg) associated with respiratory-depressant anesthetic
and adjunctive drugs may cause severe mental impairment and
possibly respiratory arrest. Use of capnometry or arterial blood gas
analysis during the anesthetic maintenance and recovery period
helps facilitate early detection and correction of respiratory depres-
sion. Occasionally, animals with undiagnosed, compensated CNS
disease (e.g., hydrocephalus) may decompensate under anesthesia,
resulting in impaired brain function. Prevention of hypercapnia,
hypoxemia, and hypotension, and rapid implementation of resusci-
tative measures (e.g., mannitol and controlled positive-pressure
ventilation) may limit brain injury and speed recovery. Many prob-
lems that lead to delayed recovery from anesthesia can be prevented
or otherwise managed with appropriate patient monitoring during
and after anesthetic drug delivery.

Introduction
Local and regional (locoregional) anesthetic and analgesic techniques
are a cornerstone of modern veterinary anesthetic and analgesic
protocols. However, the relevance of locoregional anesthesia
extends beyond the perioperative setting to include applications in
interventional pain management, both acute and chronic. Due to
their unique mechanism of action targeting voltage-gated sodium
channels along nerve fibers, local anesthetics interrupt transmis-
sion of neural impulses along axons and contribute significantly
to decreasing nociceptive traffic along the pain pathways in
both the peripheral and central nervous systems. The benefits of
incorporating local or regional blocks into analgesic protocols are
many, ranging from profound surgical anesthesia and analgesia,
inhibition of central sensitization, a decreased reliance on systemi-
cally administered opioids and their associated adverse effects, low-
ering of inhaled anesthetic requirements for maintenance of a
desired surgical plane of anesthesia and, ultimately, a potential for
better surgical outcomes with a significant decrease in patient mor-
bidity and mortality.
Locoregional anesthetic techniques range in complexity, from
simple local infiltration techniques needing minimal equipment
and training (e.g., ventral midline infiltration or “line blocks,” ring
