Techniques
Several different techniques have been described to provide regional
anesthesia of the eye and orbital tissues, which vary in their ability
to produce akinesia of the globe. These techniques may be classified
as extraconal or intraconal (outside or within the musculofascial
cone), or retrobulbar or peribulbar (behind or around the eye).
Retrobulbar blocks are more invasive and carry a risk of damaging
the optic nerve; therefore, they are almost exclusively performed for
enucleation, while less invasive peribulbar techniques or topical
anesthesia are preferred for other types of ophthalmic procedures.
Classically, a retrobulbar block is performed by inserting a
curved needle at the junction of the middle and temporal third of
the lower eyelid, directing the tip behind the globe until a popping
sensation is appreciated and the eye rolls dorsally, indicating punc-
ture into the musculofascial cone. Volume of injectate is dependent
on the size of the patient, ranging from approximately 2–3 mL of
0.5% bupivacaine [143]. Alternatively, a supratemporal approach
modeled on the technique used in horses has also been developed
in dogs [146]. In this technique, the needle is inserted between the
posterior aspect of the orbital ligament and the zygomatic process
of the temporal bone and advanced ventromedially until the mus-
culofascial cone is punctured. Deposition of local anesthetic within
the musculofascial cone results in complete analgesia and akinesia
of the globe. It is important to note that the optic nerve sheath con-
tains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) that is contiguous with intracranial
CSF; accidental injection of local anesthetic within the optic nerve
sheath can result in severe complications, such as total brainstem
anesthesia [147–149]. As with all regional anesthetic techniques,
cautious needle advancement and aspiration prior to injection of
local anesthetic should be used.
Peribulbar and extraconal techniques are less invasive than intra-
conal techniques and carry a lower risk of damage to the optic
nerve. They rely on diffusion of local anesthetic from the extraconal
space into the intraconal space and may produce akinesia less reli-
ably than intraconal techniques. Using a blind technique, the needle
is inserted percutaneously at the anterior dorsomedial and ventro-
lateral margins of the eye and advanced until the tip of the needle is
level with the equator of the globe, being careful not to puncture the
globe itself [150]. Ultrasound guidance may aid the operator in
positioning the needle within the extraconal space. An ultrasound-
guided in- plane peribulbar technique has been described in canine
cadavers, in which the ultrasound transducer is positioned caudal
to the orbital ligament, and the needle is introduced caudally, guid-
ing the tip into the extraconal space. Peribulbar spread of injectate
was successful in all attempts [151]. A similar posterior ultrasound-
guided approach with the transducer oriented transversely was less
consistent in delivering injectate to the targeted structures [152].
Sub-Tenon’s anesthesia refers to infiltration of local anesthetic
within Tenon’s capsule, the fibrous sheath surrounding the eyeball.
It requires a specialized sub-Tenon’s cannula, several different types
of which have been described with similar characteristics [153].
Sub-Tenon’s anesthesia, described in depth elsewhere, has been
reported to produce analgesia and akinesia for cataract surgery in
dogs [154].
Auricular techniques
Anatomy
Nerve blocks of the auricular region may be indicated for pain
management or surgeries involving the ear canal, tympanic bulla,
or pinna. Sensory innervation of the external ear canal is provided
by the auriculotemporal nerve and the auricular branches of the
facial nerve, while the pinna is innervated by the caudal auricular
and the greater occipital nerves [150]. The auriculotemporal nerve
arises from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V 3 ),
running cranially to the external ear canal along the caudodorsal
border of the masseter muscle and in close proximity to the facial
nerve. The caudal auricular nerve is a branch of the facial nerve,
and the greater occipital nerve is the largest branch of the second
cervical spinal nerve.
Techniques
A blind approach to the great auricular nerve has been described in
which the needle is inserted ventral to the transverse process of the
atlas and advanced 0.3 cm ventromedially toward the jugular
groove [155]. The auriculotemporal nerve can be blocked by insert-
ing a needle perpendicular to the skin at the caudolateral border of
the zygomatic arch and advancing toward the temporomandibular
junction [155]. Alternatively, ultrasound guidance may be used to
block the auriculotemporal and caudal auricular nerves; an ultra-
sound transducer is positioned in the coronal plane over the parotid
salivary gland, perpendicular to the ramus of the mandible [150].
The auriculotemporal and caudal auricular nerves can be visualized
between the external acoustic meatus and parotid salivary gland
caudally and the condyloid process of the mandible cranially. The
needle is introduced out-of- plane ventral to the transducer and
advanced dorsomedially at an approximately 45° angle until the tip
is positioned caudal to the condyloid process. The great auricular
nerve is located superficially, cranial to the bifurcation of the jugu-
lar vein into the maxillary and linguofacial veins. It is easily visual-
ized on ultrasound with the transducer oriented in the transverse
plane at the level of the atlas. The great auricular nerve is a small,
oval structure dorsal to the maxillary vein and mandibular salivary
gland. Blocking the great auricular nerve provides analgesia to the
skin overlying the caudal ramus of the mandible and on the dorsal
surface of the pinna. Akinesia of the eyelid is possible due to the
relationship between the auriculotemporal nerve and the facial
nerve and should be treated with ophthalmic lubricants until palpe-
bral function has returned.
Trigeminal nerve block
Ultrasound-guided trigeminal nerve block has been reported in a
dog undergoing extensive head surgery involving exenteration,
caudal maxillectomy, and zygomatic arch resection [156]. Proximal
blockade of the trigeminal nerve provides a broad area of desensiti-
zation in a single injection site, including areas innervated by the
ophthalmic branch (V1
) such as the orbit and nasal septum.
However, the block is technically challenging compared to more
peripheral techniques. The needle is introduced in-plane to the
ultrasound transducer immediately caudal to the orbital ligament
and advanced ventrally toward the caudal pterygopalatine fossa,
where the three branches of the trigeminal nerve and the maxillary
artery can be visualized lateral to the frontal bone and overlying the
sphenoid bone [150,156]. Doppler ultrasonography can aid in iden-
tification of the maxillary artery. The volume delivered is 0.1 mL/cm
of the cranium length from the inion to the nasion.
Blocks of the thorax and abdomen
Dependent upon the region that requires blockade, there are a
number of techniques that may be used to provide regional anes-
thesia to the thoracic walls, with or without visceral analgesia. In
general, the innervation of the thorax and abdomen is provided by

-- 1194 of 1450 --

Chapter 60: Canine and Feline Local Anesthetic and Analgesic Techniques 	1179
branches of spinal nerves. Dorsal branches of thoracic spinal nerves
extend dorsally and divide into medial and lateral branches to
innervate the epaxial muscles and the skin near the dorsal midline.
The sensory innervation of the lateral and ventral thoracic wall is
provided by the ventral branches of the thoracic spinal nerves via
the intercostal nerves [125]. The skin of the thorax is innervated
by dorsal, lateral, and ventral cutaneous branches of the spinal
nerves [157].
Thoracic paravertebral block
The thoracic paravertebral space in dogs has been described as a
wedge-shaped area bordered ventrally by the parietal pleura, medi-
ally by the vertebral bodies, intervertebral discs, and foramina, lat-
erally by the intercostal muscles, and dorsally incompletely by the
costotransverse ligament [158]. Ventral branches of the spinal
nerves travel distally via the dorsal compartment of the thoracic
paravertebral space. Before the advent of technologies such as neu-
rostimulation or ultrasonography to guide injections of local anes-
thetics, the standard approach to the thoracic paravertebral space
consisted of a blind technique guided by anatomical land-
marks [159]. Loss of resistance to injection performed with a loss of
resistance syringe and the characteristic pop-like feeling perceived
by the operator once the endothoracic fascia is pierced by the tip of
a Tuohy needle were long considered confirmatory for locating the
thoracic paravertebral space. Portela et al. described a nerve
stimulator-guided method for injections into the thoracic paraver-
tebral space; however, this technique was associated with a compli-
cation rate of 20%, which included instances of epidural spread and
intrapleural migration of injectate from accidental puncture of the
parietal pleura [158]. This technique, though imperfect, brought
about a level of objectivity beyond that of blind injections where the
subjective pop-like feeling of the needle through the internal inter-
costal membrane guided the injection. The sonoanatomy of the
canine thoracic paravertebral space in dog cadavers was subse-
quently described, along with a method to perform a thoracic para-
vertebral block with ultrasound guidance, further decreasing risks
associated with the thoracic paravertebral block [160,161]. In addi-
tion to enabling the use of a lower volume of injectate, ultrasound
guidance afforded a superior level of safety as direct visualization of
the needle during injection prevented the puncture of the parietal
pleura. Single injection points of diluted dye injectate in cadaveric
studies resulted in staining beyond the thoracic paravertebral space
despite correctly located injections, suggesting that local anesthetic
spread outside of the immediate paravertebral space may play a role
in the regional anesthesia observed with this technique. Based on
inconsistent staining of multiple levels of spinal nerves under
cadaveric conditions, complete thoracic anesthesia may require
injection at multiple spaces.
Another canine cadaveric study suggests the utility of this tech-
nique may extend beyond the thorax. Spinal nerves originating
from T10 to L1 contribute sensory innervation to the cranial
abdomen; caudal thoracic paravertebral spaces can also be
injected to provide somatic and visceral analgesia at the level of
the cranial abdomen [162]. Though this technique was associated
with mediastinal contamination in 80% of injections, no other
complications were noted.
Clinically, a single injection at the level of the caudal thoracic para-
vertebral space has been shown to provide adequate analgesia in radi-
cal mastectomy [163], lateral thoracotomy [164], and adrenalectomy
via midline laparotomy [165]. The thoracic paravertebral block
was also described in other animal species (Vulpes vulpes) [166].
Together, the evidence suggests thoracic paravertebral blocks are
useful for the provision of perioperative analgesia in thoracic and
cranial abdominal surgeries. It is important to note that ultrasound-
guided thoracic paravertebral block is a technically challenging
technique and is recommended for more advanced practitioners of
ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia.
Intercostal nerve block
Caudal to each rib, the intercostal nerve runs as part of a neurovas-
cular bundle that also includes the intercostal artery and vein
(Figs. 60.9 and 60.10). The neurovascular bundles are bordered by
the endothoracic fascia medially and the internal intercostal mus-
cles laterally [125]. The intercostal nerves provide sensory and
motor innervation to the parietal pleura and lateral thoracic body
wall and give rise to the lateral and ventral cutaneous branches that
supply the skin of the mid- to ventral thorax [157]. Intercostal nerve
blocks have been described as a technique to provide superior anal-
gesia for dogs undergoing thoracic surgery [167–169].
The safety and utility of intercostal blocks is well supported in the
literature. Berg and Orton compared the effects of different analge-
sic modalities on the respiratory function of dogs following thora-
cotomies [170]. Intravenous administration of opioids caused
significant respiratory depression in dogs due to a concomitant
decrease in minute volume and respiratory frequency and led to
clinically significant hypoventilation and hypoxemia; however, a
treatment group that received intercostal nerve blocks with bupiv-
acaine exhibited no such respiratory depression in the immediate
postoperative period. Similarly, Thompson and Johnson compared
selective intercostal nerve blocks to interpleural instillation of bupi-
vacaine and systemic morphine administration in dogs undergoing
lateral thoracotomies and assessed respiratory function and analge-
sia postoperatively [168]. Dogs treated with systemic opioids expe-
rienced more complications than dogs in the other treatment
groups such as perioperative hypothermia, with slower return to
normal temperature and blood gas alterations suggestive of poor
respiratory function. Though all groups showed a downward trend
in PaO2 , only the morphine and interpleural bupivacaine groups
had significantly lower PaO 2 compared to baseline. Another study
of the effect of intercostal nerve blocks on arterial blood gas ten-
sions in dogs that underwent thoracotomies noted that PaO 2 and
PaCO 2 were not different before and after treatment at 4 and 8 h
postoperatively, suggesting that intercostal nerve blocks with bupi-
vacaine afforded postoperative analgesia sufficient to normalize
respiratory function in dogs [169].
As innervation of the cranial abdomen involves thoracic dermat-
omes, the addition of selective (e.g., T8–T10) intercostal nerve
blocks may provide adjunctive coverage to other abdominal
regional anesthetic techniques. A study comparing the analgesic
efficacy of a combination of intercostal nerve blocks and spinal
anesthesia to a sufentanil constant rate infusion in cats undergoing
unilateral radical mastectomies showed that both intraoperative
and postoperative analgesia was superior in patients that received
locoregional anesthesia as part of their anesthetic protocol [171].
The sternum and associated tissues may be blocked via various
ultrasound-guided parasternal blocks, described elsewhere [172,173]
These techniques aim to desensitize the terminal branches of the
intercostal nerves, distal to where the lateral cutaneous branches
bifurcate off the intercostal nerves, thus providing analgesia solely at
the level of the thoracic ventral midline (i.e., for median sternoto-
mies). In theory, this technique would be expected to spare intercos-
tal muscle function and preserve ventilatory function, though

clinical trials have yet to be conducted to assess the clinical efficacy
of this technique in veterinary patients.
In order to decrease the risks of block failure secondary to inac-
curacy of blind injections and reduce the risks of complications
associated with potential pleural puncture, Thomson et al. studied
the sonoanatomy of the intercostal space and described a novel
ultrasound-guided technique for intercostal nerve blocks [35].
Though slightly more time consuming than blind injections, the
authors reported a significant improvement in the accuracy of
intercostal nerve staining with ultrasound guidance compared with
the blind technique with 68/70 (97%) successful injections versus
45/70 (64%).
Interpleural regional analgesia
Interpleural regional analgesia involves infiltration of a local anes-
thetic solution into the potential space between the parietal and
visceral pleura. Multiple studies in dogs have shown that inter-
pleurally administered local anesthetics work by diffusion across
the parietal pleura to block the underlying intercostal nerves,
resulting in multidermatomal blockade [174]. The distribution of
blockade is gravity-dependent and corresponds with the lowermost
part of pleural space where pooling of the local anesthetic solution
occurs [175]. Interpleural administration of local anesthetics has
proven useful for providing pain relief not only for thoracic surger-
ies, but also for painful disorders of the cranial abdomen (e.g.,
pancreatitis) [176].
While effective, it is important to note the possible complications
of this technique. The large surface area of the pleura can potentially
result in rapid absorption of the administered local anesthetic solu-
tion and high plasma levels of the local anesthetic can result, poten-
tially leading to local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) [177]. No
adverse cardiovascular effects were reported when local anesthetic
was administered interpleurally to patients with or without an open
pericardium [178]. While direct lung trauma is unlikely with careful
technique, a small volume of air can be aspirated into the pleural
space due to the negative intrathoracic pressure. This can result in an
insignificant pneumothorax and is not considered to be of clinical
significance. Potentially more significant is a potential loss of dia-
phragmatic function on the injection side after administration of
interpleural bupivacaine [179]. Dogs that received bilateral blockade
demonstrated paradoxical respirations and generated negative intra-
abdominal pressures upon inspiration. Patients at increased risk of
cardiovascular and respiratory complications may be better treated
with alternative methods of pain relief (e.g., intercostal nerve blocks
and thoracic epidural anesthesia).
With the patient positioned in lateral recumbency, an over-the-
needle catheter connected to a syringe filled with 2–3 mL of saline
via a three-way stopcock is advanced onto the lateral aspect of the
seventh or eighth rib at its midpoint between the dorsal and ventral
midline. The needle is then walked off the cranial border of the rib
until it can be advanced through the intercostal space. Entering the
thorax at the cranial border of the rib helps minimize the risk of
traumatizing the intercostal nerve and vascular bundle that lies cau-
dal to each rib. Once the parietal pleura has been penetrated (often
with a palpable “pop” or “click”), the column of saline in the syringe
will slowly decrease in volume as the negative interpleural pressure
aspirates the saline into the interpleural space. Once the needle tip
has been confirmed to be in the interpleural space, the catheter is
gently advanced off the needle stylet into the interpleural space
(Fig. 60.11). The preloaded syringe with local anesthetic solution is
then attached to the catheter and the calculated volume of local
anesthetic is slowly injected over 1–2 min into the interpleural
space. Following injection of the local anesthetic, the catheter is
withdrawn and the patient is positioned with the operative side
down for at least 10 min, allowing the local anesthetic to pool and
block the underlying intercostal nerves.

Alternatively, an indwelling catheter or chest tube can be placed
into the interpleural space to facilitate repeated injections. Catheter
dislodgement can occur whenever an indwelling catheter is placed
at any site in the body; after correctly positioning the catheter in the
interpleural space, it should be secured to the patient by means of
adhesive patches, tissue glue, suture, and/or bandages. Subcutaneous
tunneling of larger gauge interpleural catheters can be used as a fur-
ther means to reduce the likelihood of dislodgment and to prevent
air from inadvertently entering the interpleural space around the
catheter. A C-clamp or other similar device may be used to reduce
the possibility of air being aspirated through the chest tube or cath-
eter following inadvertent dislodgment or other issues.
Fascial plane block techniques
Fascial plane blocks represent a relatively novel class of ultrasound-
guided regional anesthetic techniques in veterinary medicine. They
rely on the deposition of higher volumes of dilute local anesthetic
into a fascial plane that contains nerves, rather than targeting dis-
crete nerves. In both human and veterinary medicine, there has
been an explosion of descriptions of novel techniques with accom-
panying cadaveric studies. In most cases, prospective, controlled
trials are lacking yet many practitioners of regional anesthesia uti-
lize these techniques frequently as part of a balanced analgesic plan.
Each technique described below has been detailed in initial cadav-
eric studies; the reader is directed to the referenced literature for
more complete descriptions of individual techniques.
Serratus plane block
The serratus plane block, also known as the serratus ventralis or
serratus anterior plane block, is a fascial plane block that was origi-
nally proposed in human patients as an alternative method to pro-
viding locoregional anesthesia to the thoracic body wall via
desensitization of the lateral cutaneous branches of T2 to T9 [180].
A veterinary adaptation of this ultrasound-guided technique has
been described in canine cadavers [181]. The technique consists of
injecting a volume of local anesthetic solution in the fascial plane
between the serratus ventralis thoracis and the latissimus dorsi
muscles or, in the alternative deep technique, between the serratus
ventralis thoracis and the external intercostal muscles. As it is usu-
ally recommended to desensitize up to two dermatomes cranial and
caudal to the site of surgery due to the significant overlap in recep-
tive fields on the thorax, the serratus plane block is expected to only
produce partial thoracic anesthesia involving the cranial thoracic
dermatomes based on spread of injectate in cadaver subjects.
Despite questionable efficacy for complete thoracic anesthesia in
cadaveric studies, there is clinical evidence that suggests effective
perioperative analgesia may be afforded by a combination of the
transversus abdominis plane block with the serratus plane block in
dogs undergoing unilateral radical mastectomy [182]. While pro-
spective randomized clinical trials evaluating the clinical efficacy of
this technique in thoracic surgery are lacking, two case series
describe the effective use of serratus plane block as part of a multi-
modal analgesic protocol for lateral thoracotomies for a variety of
surgical conditions [183,184]. Prospective blinded and appropri-
ately controlled studies are needed to assess the utility of this locore-
gional technique in veterinary species.
Quadratus lumborum block
Upon exiting through their respective intervertebral foramina, the
ventral rami of the twelfth and thirteenth thoracic spinal nerves
(T12, T13) run within the bundles of the quadratus lumborum
(QL) muscle while the first three lumbar spinal nerves (L1–L3)
course between the QL muscle and the psoas muscle. Lumbar spi-
nal nerves course through the transverse fascia that separates the
retroperitoneum from the sublumbar musculature. They penetrate
the transversus abdominis muscle to continue their course within
the fascial plane that exists between the transversus abdominis
muscle and the internal abdominal oblique muscle. Together with
the caudal thoracic spinal nerves (T9–T13), these lumbar spinal
nerves provide motor and sensory innervation to the abdomen. In
addition, sympathetic ganglia are present alongside the vertebral
bodies from T13–L5 and are responsible for autonomic innerva-
tion of the abdominal viscera [185]. There are several different
approaches that may be utilized to deposit local anesthetic into the
fascial planes that surround the QL muscle to provide regional
anesthesia suitable for abdominal procedures. These have been
described extensively in the human literature and have more
recently been described and evaluated in veterinary patients.
An initial canine cadaveric study provided a thorough assess-
ment of the anatomy and sonoanatomy of the canine QL plane and
evaluated the feasibility of an in-plane ultrasound-guided injection
technique [185]. Injections of 0.3 mL/kg of dye–lidocaine injectate
performed at the level of L1 were associated with successful cranial
lumbar nerve and splanchnic nerve staining. However, inconsistent
staining was found for more cranial (i.e., T13) spinal nerve seg-
ments, indicating that surgery of the cranial abdomen may require
either a higher volume of injectate or that the QL block would need
to be combined with another technique. Furthermore, injections
into the intermuscular plane between the psoas major and the QL
muscles using the described technique were less likely to be feasible
in larger breed dogs due to the excessive depth. Two alternative
approaches to delivering injections lateral to the QL were then
assessed, the transverse or longitudinal needle approaches [186].
The authors determined that a transverse approach to the lateral QL
plane with 0.3 mL/kg of injectate per hemiabdomen was feasible
and resulted in more consistent spread of injectate. No complica-
tions such as intra-abdominal or epidural contamination were
noted in either technique. In both studies, the approach to the QL
was performed from a ventrolateral to dorsomedial direction.
Due to concern about the risk of making an intra-abdominal
injection or causing inadvertent injury to adjacent abdominal
organs, another approach to the QL block was described whereby
the needle was advanced in a dorsolateral to ventromedial trajec-
tory targeting the medial aspect of the QL [187]. This technique
yielded results similar to those described previously and no ectopic
abdominal or epidural injectate was observed. When assessed by
CT, however, there were important differences noted in the cranio-
caudal injectate spread. Another study evaluated use of a higher
volume of injectate consisting of dye and a radiopaque contrast
agent (0.6 mL/kg) and also found distinct patterns of reach as
assessed by anatomic dissection and CT evaluation [188]. These
findings illustrate how different evaluation methods (e.g., dissec-
tion versus advanced imaging) or injectate solution types (e.g., dye
versus local anesthetic combined with contrast agent) can be an
important source of variation in studies of ultrasound-guided
blocks, and that the relationship between cadaveric studies involv-
ing contrast media or tissue dyes may not equate to clinical block
efficacy when techniques are performed in live patients using dif-
ferent local anesthetic solutions.
Cadaveric studies in cats have also been performed and, similar
to previous studies in dogs, the results varied between assessment
techniques and found staining that could potentially be associated

-- 1198 of 1450 --

with incomplete regional anesthesia of the abdomen [189,190]. A
QL block as part of multimodal analgesia protocol was described in
a case report involving a cat undergoing exploratory laparotomy
and cystotomy [191]. Those authors reported the need for intraop-
erative administration of rescue analgesia at the beginning of sur-
gery, but none thereafter, and the patient was reportedly comfortable
with pain scores consistently below the suggested intervention
threshold using a validated pain scoring instrument. Like many fas-
cial plane techniques, no clinical studies have been published to
date evaluating the efficacy of QL blocks in companion animals for
perioperative analgesia, and more research is needed to bridge the
gap between the findings of laboratory cadaveric studies and pain
management in clinical cases.
Transversus abdominis plane block
The abdominal wall is innervated by thoracolumbar spinal nerves
including T9 to T12, the costoabdominalis nerve (T13), and the
three most cranial lumbar nerves (iliohypogastricus cranialis
nerve [L1], iliohypogastricus caudalis nerve [L2], and ilioingui-
nalis nerve [L3]). Nerves course along the fascial plane in between
the internal abdominal oblique muscle and the transversus
abdominis muscle, underneath a thin sheet of connective tissue
that is tightly adhered to the transversus abdominis muscle [192].
Thus, sensory blockade to the abdominal wall can be achieved by
injecting local anesthetic solution in the intermuscular plane
known as the transversus abdominis plane (TAP). Occasionally,
additional thoracic nerves located more cranially may be found in
the TAP.
Several cadaveric studies aimed at characterizing the spread of
injectates within the TAP have been published [193–196]. Variable
staining of sensory nerve fibers with even the highest volumes of
injectate tested (0.25–1 mL/kg of 0.25% bupivacaine and dye solu-
tions) suggest that a combination of a subcostal and mid or caudal
abdominal approach may be necessary to effectively desensitize
the ventral abdominal midline. Interestingly, most studies appear
to indicate that a ceiling effect exists. While craniocaudal spread
increases up to a volume of 0.5 mL/kg; doubling the volume to
1 mL/kg does not result in a greater reach. Interestingly, one study
reported no significant difference in number of ventral spinal
nerves stained between dogs receiving a single-point TAP block
per side as compared to two injections per side, though the area of
injectate spread did differ significantly between groups [197].
Beyond the volume of the injectate, variables that may affect
spread include cadaver condition, position, and duration between
injection and dissection. Additionally, the composition of the dye
may account for interstudy variability since the physical and
chemical properties of the solutions may change their ability to
penetrate tissues [198]. Different injection techniques have also
revealed different patterns of staining, with a combination of
subcostal and lateral injections yielding a better craniocaudal
staining pattern than a combination of cranial and caudal lateral
injections [199].
To perform an ultrasound-guided TAP block in canine and feline
patients undergoing exploratory laparotomy with incisions extend-
ing from the xiphoid to the caudal abdomen, the authors recom-
mend a four-point technique combining the lateral and subcostal
approaches. The authors’ preference is to draw up 0.35 mL/kg of
bupivacaine 0.5%, diluted in a 1:1 ratio with sterile saline 0.9%.
Dexmedetomidine can be added to the final solution in a ratio of
1 μg/mL of solution. The resulting solution is split evenly to per-
form a total of four injections.
For the lateral approach, a linear high-frequency transducer is
placed in either a transverse or longitudinal orientation, midway
between the last rib and the iliac crest, and midway between the
ventral and dorsal midline (Fig. 60.12). The body wall is identified
as the first hyperechoic line superficial to the peritoneum. The
muscle immediately superficial to the peritoneum is the trans-
versus abdominis which lies deep to the internal abdominal
oblique muscle. The TAP is the potential space between these two
muscles, appearing as a hyperechoic line that can be hydrodissected
by injecting a local anesthetic. The procedure is repeated on
both sides.
For the subcostal approach, the transducer is placed in a trans-
verse orientation, perpendicular to the linea alba just caudal to the
xiphoid process. The probe is then rotated 10–15° with the marker
located cranially. The resulting position of the transducer is parallel
to the costal arch and oblique to the midline. The rectus abdominis
and transversus abdominis muscles are visualized, and the perito-
neum is again identified as a thick hyperechoic structure separating
the peritoneal cavity and the body wall. The overlying transversus
abdominis muscle is separated from the more superficial rectus
abdominis muscle by the fascia of the transversus abdominis mus-
cle (superficial), which can be identified as a characteristic triangle.
When these structures have been identified, the needle is inserted
from the cranial aspect of the transducer, using an in-plane tech-
nique, with a 20° angle, so that the tip is located in the fascial plane
between the rectus abdominis and transversus abdominis muscles.
The first report of clinical use of a TAP block in a veterinary spe-
cies described an uneventful anesthetic event to facilitate the surgical
excision of a gastrointestinal foreign body in a Canadian lynx [200].
In that report, the bilateral TAP block was performed with one
injection of 0.4 mL/kg of 0.125% bupivacaine on each side (a total of
1 mg/kg) as part of a multimodal analgesic plan. The patient exhib-
ited no signs of discomfort up to 10 h postoperatively. A retrospective
study evaluated the use of a cranial and caudal TAP block (0.3 to
0.35 mL/kg per injection) combined with intercostal nerve blocks in
dogs undergoing mastectomy [201]. The combination of TAP and
intercostal blocks as part of a balanced multimodal analgesic protocol
in combination with low doses of systemic opioids produced ade-
quate intraoperative and immediate postoperative analgesia. In an
assessment of duration of analgesic effect, TAP blocks were per-
formed with either a liposome-encapsulated formulation of bupiv-
acaine or 0.25% bupivacaine potentiated with dexmedetomidine
[202]. The authors did not find a significant advantage to liposome-
encapsulated bupivacaine in that the duration of analgesia afforded
by the technique was equivalent in each group and was limited to
approximately 24 h. It is important to consider that, given the low
fraction of free bupivacaine in the commercially available liposome-
encapsulated bupivacaine suspension, its use in preoperative locore-
gional blocks may not provide sufficient intraoperative analgesia.
Consequently, consideration may be given to mixing the suspension
with standard bupivacaine (though no other agents should be com-
bined with liposomal formulations of bupivacaine).
Though locoregional blocks are best performed in the context of
preemptive analgesia, TAP blocks may be performed postopera-
tively in certain situations where time is of the essence and perfor-
mance of a preoperative block is not feasible (e.g., such as emergent
celiotomies for rapidly bleeding abdominal masses or cesarean sec-
tions where fetal stress is documented) or when ultrasound equip-
ment is not readily available. However, in such cases, the presence
of a pneumoperitoneum may cause a mirroring artifact that would
make the identification of the TAP more difficult and may lead to

abdominal puncture and/or organ damage if the artifact is not
correctly recognized [120]. An alternative to ultrasound-guided
blocks consists of an open surgeon-assisted approach where local
anesthetic solution is injected at the level of the aponeurosis of the
transversus abdominis muscle [203].
Erector spinae plane block
Motor and sensory innervation to the epaxial muscles and dorsum
is provided by the dorsal rami of the thoracic and lumbar spinal
nerves while the lateral branches of the dorsal rami provide motor
innervation to the longissimus thoracis, levatores costarum, and
iliocostalis thoracis muscles. These lateral extensions are known as
dorsal cutaneous branches, and they supply sensory innervation
from the dorsal midline to the lateral axillary limit of the thoracic
body wall [157]. Motor innervation to the transversospinalis
muscle group and sensory innervation to the vertebral laminae,
ligaments, and facet joints are derived from the medial branches of
the dorsal rami of the spinal nerves [204].
The erector spinae plane (ESP) block is a fascial plane block in
which a local anesthetic is deposited deep to the erector spinae
muscles, resulting in spread of local anesthetic solution in the
epaxial compartment that involves the lateral and medial branches
of the dorsal rami [205]. The original landmark for ESP injections
is the dorsolateral edge of the transverse process, which corre-
sponds to the ventromedial aspect of the longissimus thoracis mus-
cle. Single injections along the thoracolumbar spine result in
variable and unpredictable craniocaudal spread according to the
results of various cadaver studies [206–208]. Medial and lateral

branches of the dorsal rami are consistently targeted by ESP injec-
tions and the injectate appears to remain confined to the epaxial
compartment. More recently, a cadaveric study comparing injec-
tions aimed at the lateral process or mamillary processes of the
thoracolumbar spine caudal to T11 indicated that medial branches
of the dorsal branches of the spinal nerves were more reliably
stained when the needle is directed at the mamillary processes [209].
This technique is thus preferred since innervation of the vertebral
laminae, facet joints, and epaxial muscles of dogs comes from the
medial branches. Cadaveric canine studies of the ESP block have
only rarely identified hypaxial spread of injectate, and epidural and/
or thoracic paravertebral space contamination have not been
reported in cadaveric studies involving thoracic ESP blocks [206–
208]. Epidural migration was observed in 11.7% of cadavers injected
with a transverse approach to the L4 vertebra [208] and may be
responsible for rare complications such as sympathetic blockade
and subsequent sinus arrest when performed at the T13 or L1 seg-
ment in dogs [210]. It is thus anticipated that ESP blocks would
provide regional anesthesia to the dorsolateral aspect of the body
wall and would be a suitable technique to use in the context of neu-
rosurgery such as hemilaminectomies. This is supported by the
findings of a retrospective study in dogs in which there was a sig-
nificant reduction of perioperative opioid administration and more
stable cardiovascular status in patients undergoing hemilaminecto-
mies that received an ESP block [211].
Further support for application of this block comes from a case
report of a dog undergoing opioid-free anesthesia for hemilaminec-
tomy surgery [212]. The ESP block may also prove useful in the
context of interventional pain management practice for treatment
of chronic pain associated with vertebral articular facet degenera-
tion [207]. The potential versatility of this block was highlighted in
a case report involving a dog with acute pancreatitis and intractable
pain despite systemic infusions of fentanyl, lidocaine, ketamine,
and dexmedetomidine that responded favorably to ESP block [213].
A small retrospective study evaluating the addition of ultrasound-
guided ESP block at T5–T9 to multimodal analgesic protocols in
dogs undergoing median sternotomies suggested the technique
may also be of some benefit in this context [214]. Since anatomic
studies have not identified a clear path for distribution of injectate
toward the ventral branches of the spinal nerves, the exact mecha-
nism whereby the ESP block may provide analgesia for cranial
abdominal pain remains unknown.
Blocks of the thoracic limb
Anatomy of sensory innervation
Spinal nerves emerge from the intervertebral canals of the cervical,
thoracic, and lumbar vertebral column as postganglionic fibers that
contain both sensory and motor nerves that originate from the dor-
sal and ventral horns of the spinal cord, respectively. Except in the
thoracic region, the ventral branches of the spinal nerves form
plexi, networks of nerve fibers that ultimately combine to form the
specific motor and sensory peripheral nerves that serve the thoracic
and pelvic limbs.
While species and individual variations may exist, the brachial
plexus is generally formed by the ventral branches of the C6 to T1
spinal nerves [215]. Although early anatomic studies of the canine
brachial plexus identified occasional contributions from the C5 and/
or T2 nerves, more recent studies have failed to corroborate these
observations [216]. The brachial plexus includes the following nerves
(with respective contributing cervical ventral rami): pectoral (C6),
suprascapular (C6 and C7), subscapular (C6 and C7), musculocuta-
neous (C7 and C8), axillary (C7 and C8), radial (C7, C8, and T1),
median (C7, C8, and T1), ulnar (C7, C8, and T1), long thoracic (C7),
thoracodorsal (C8 and T1), and lateral thoracic (T1) nerves [215,216].
Various approaches may be utilized to provide regional anesthesia to
the brachial plexus and its distal branches (Fig. 60.13).
The brachial plexus provides motor, sensory, and autonomic
innervation to the thoracic limb, including four extrinsic muscles.
The ventral rami of the cervical spinal nerves emerge from their
respective intervertebral foramina and pass through the intertrans-
versarius muscles to course distally between the scalenus and sub-
scapularis muscles. The phrenic nerve, which supplies motor
innervation to the diaphragm, primarily originates from the ventral
branches of C5, C6, and C7 and thus is anatomically related to the
brachial plexus [125]. The spinal nerve T1 emerges from the first
thoracic intervertebral space and contributes a primary branch to
the brachial plexus that innervates the elbow and antebrachium, and
a minor branch that innervates the first intercostal space. The T2
spinal nerve rarely contributes fibers to the brachial plexus. Instead,
its ventral ramus forms the intercostobrachial nerve that innervates
the pectoral ventral dermatomes and its dorsal ramus innervates the
caudal cervical region. Lateral cutaneous branches of T2 provide
sensory innervation to the lateral aspect of the shoulder.
The radial, ulnar, musculocutaneous, and median nerves course
distally through the axilla in a sheath of connective tissue bordered
cranially by the biceps brachii and coracobrachialis muscles, medi-
ally by the pectoralis muscle, and laterally by the triceps muscle.
Within the axillary sheath, multiple layers of connective tissues
separate individual components of the neurovascular bundle.
Beyond the proximal third of the humerus, the radial nerve sepa-
rates from the median, ulnar, and musculocutaneous nerves to
assume its final position between the brachialis muscle and the tri-
ceps. The median, ulnar, and musculocutaneous nerves remain
with the brachial artery and vein, deep to the pectoralis muscles and
the thin fibrous sheet that serves as an insertion tendon to the
humerus for the deep pectoralis, latissimus dorsi, cutaneous trunci,
and tensor fascia antebrachii muscles, medial to the triceps.

branches into a medial and a lateral superficial radial nerve on
either side of the cephalic vein. The median nerve travels alongside
the median artery and vein, caudal to the pronator teres, and cranial
to the flexor carpi radialis. The ulnar nerve courses laterocaudally
deep to the flexor carpi ulnaris and gives off lateral and palmar
branches at the carpus to innervate the dorsolateral and palmar
aspects of the manus.
Cervical paravertebral block
The cervical paravertebral block in dogs is an advanced-level tech-
nique originally described by Lemke and Dawson that provides sur-
gical anesthesia to the thoracic limb’s most proximal structures
including the scapula, the shoulder, and the humerus which cannot
be blocked with the traditional axillary approach to the brachial
plexus [130]. Since then, revised techniques have been proposed
using alternative landmarks, neurostimulation, and ultrasound
guidance, but most have failed to yield significant improvements in
accuracy and safety [217–226]. Overall, the technique appears to be
associated with an unacceptably high rate of complications relative
to the potential benefits of the block. Anatomic landmark (i.e.,
“blind” approaches) and nerve stimulator-guided techniques are
associated with inherent risks, including technical failure, nerve
damage from direct needle trauma, or inadvertent puncture of blood
vessels in the area. Although ultrasound guidance allows for direct
visualization of the target nerves and surrounding structures and
thus may be considered safer, ultrasound-guided paravertebral bra-
chial plexus blocks can be associated with Horner’s syndrome
(caused by epidural spread of local anesthetic or blockade of the cer-
vicothoracic ganglia); in addition, extraneous injectate spread
involving the mediastinum or the phrenic nerve is also possible
leading to hemidiaphragmatic paralysis [224,225]. Potentially dele-
terious complications include epidural spread of injectate, intravas-
cular injection with associated local anesthetic toxicity, and
pneumothorax secondary to needle penetration into the thoracic
inlet. Based on these risks and the ability to use other, safer tech-
niques to achieve comparable levels of anesthesia and/or analgesia
for procedures of the thoracic limb, use of cervical paravertebral
blocks is not recommended.
Subscalenic brachial plexus block
Before reaching the axillary space, the ventral branches of the C6,
C7, C8, and T1 spinal nerves course caudoventrally within a fascial
plane that is bordered by the scalenus muscle and the longus colli
muscle. Using ultrasound guidance, the more proximal aspect of the
brachial plexus can be blocked by injecting local anesthetic solution
within the fascial plane at this location with minimal risk of epi-
dural, mediastinal, or intrapleural spread [227]. The extent of block-
ade would be expected to include all parts of the thoracic limb distal
to the scapulohumeral joint; indications for this technique may
include forelimb amputation and surgical approaches to the humerus
and elbow. Potential risks of this technique include incidental block-
ade of the phrenic nerve and Horner’s syndrome [228].
Axillary brachial plexus block
The traditional “blind” approach to performing a brachial plexus
block consists of manually palpating the axillary artery and the
greater tubercle of the humerus and injecting a solution of local
anesthetic in the general vicinity of the nerves that make up the bra-
chial plexus. This technique was originally described by Tufvesson
in 1951 [229]. Many years later, Futema et al. described the use of
nerve stimulator guidance to perform axillary brachial plexus blocks
in dogs undergoing surgical procedures of the mid-humerus [230].
A prospective, randomized, controlled study demonstrated that suc-
cessful surgical anesthesia of the thoracic limb could be achieved in
dogs undergoing carpal arthrodesis or surgery of the radius/ulna
following nerve stimulator-guided axillary brachial plexus blocks
with mixtures of local anesthetics [231]. Dogs that received brachial
plexus blocks with a local anesthetic required lower postoperative
rescue analgesia and lower intraoperative opioid administration
guided by autonomic nociceptive responses or absence thereof.
Following these landmark studies, assessments of nerve stimulation
to guide brachial plexus blockade continued to develop. The neuro-
stimulation of individual nerves of the brachial plexus and associ-
ated muscular responses were meticulously mapped in dogs [232]. A
subsequent evaluation of nerve staining with different volumes of a
lidocaine and methylene blue solution injected via neurostimulation
guidance in the axillary space revealed satisfactory staining of the
target nerves with the use of at least 0.3 mL/kg in medium-sized
dogs (16–40 kg, median 22 kg) [233]. Indeed, in a comparison of the
clinical features of nerve stimulator-guided brachial plexus block
with a traditional approach guided by anatomical landmarks, it was
concluded that neurostimulation improved the success rate of this
block in dogs [234].
Subsequently, Campoy et al. performed a terminal prospective
study to describe a new combined nerve stimulator- and ultrasound-
guided technique to block the brachial plexus at the level of the
axilla [235]. Their technique differed from previous descriptions in
that the dogs were positioned in dorsal recumbency and the needle
inserted in a craniocaudal direction, in-plane with the ultrasound
probe (Fig. 60.14). With this technique, though the nerve roots of
C7 to T1 were consistently stained with a low volume of lidocaine
and methylene blue solution (0.15 mL/kg), the root of C6 was
missed or insufficiently stained in most cases. A subsequent ana-
tomic (i.e., “blind technique”) evaluation of the axillary brachial
plexus performed via anatomic landmarks with twice the volume
of dye–local anesthetic solution only achieved complete staining of
main nerves (musculocutaneous, ulnar, median, and radial) or of
the ventral nerve rami from which these nerves originate (C7, C8,
and T1) in 58% of cases [216]. These findings support the use of
ultrasound guidance to increase success rates as well as reduce the
volumes of local anesthetic that are required to achieve successful
axillary brachial plexus blocks.
The sonoanatomy of the brachial plexus is dependent on patient
positioning because neurovascular bundles that course through
sheaths of connective tissue between musculofascial planes are
somewhat mobile [236]. In a study assessing the location of the
nerves of the brachial plexus with canine subjects positioned in
dorsal recumbency, the radial nerve was located caudolateral to the
axillary artery, the median and ulnar nerves caudomedial to the
axillary artery (in more than 90% of cases), and the musculocutane-
ous nerve was consistently located cranial to the axillary artery.
These findings highlight the importance of patient positioning
when it comes to successful ultrasound identification of nerves and
the advantage of placing patients in dorsal recumbency rather than
lateral recumbency for this block as the musculocutaneous nerve
was more easily identified. Similarly in cats, despite direct visualiza-
tion of the nerve roots by ultrasound, patient positioning was found
to significantly impact the success of the block. Axillary brachial

-- 1202 of 1450 --

Chapter 60: Canine and Feline Local Anesthetic and Analgesic Techniques 	1187
plexus blockade in cats positioned in dorsal recumbency with the
limb held in abduction at a 90° angle had more success as compared
to positioning in dorsal recumbency with the thoracic limbs
extended caudally [237].
Clinically, the axillary approach to the brachial plexus can also be
performed with the use of anatomic landmarks, without advanced
equipment such as ultrasound or nerve stimulators, yielding clini-
cally acceptable success rates when higher volumes of local anes-
thetics are used [238]. The increase in sophistication of the
technique may come at the cost of efficiency when inexperienced
operators perform the techniques, but evidence toward increased
safety such as decreased risks for vascular puncture or direct nerve
trauma supports the use of combined techniques. Akasaka et al.
compared ultrasound-guided and nerve stimulator-guided axillary
brachial plexus blocks in dogs and found that though the success
rates did not differ between each group, ultrasound guidance
resulted in faster blocks compared to nerve stimulator guid-
ance [239]. Complications may still occur despite ultrasound guid-
ance or nerve stimulation. There are isolated reports of serious
complications including life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias fol-
lowing nerve stimulator-guided axillary brachial plexus block [240],
in addition to pneumothorax [241], and phrenic nerve blockade
with resulting hemidiaphragmatic paralysis [237]. More likely
potential complications include direct nerve damage or vascular
puncture with subsequent hematoma formation. As with all tech-
niques, diligent patient monitoring during and after the block is
performed is recommended.
As duration of motor blockade may last longer than sensory
blockade, inference of the analgesic effects of nerve blocks should
not be made on the basis of continued motor deficits. Rather, pain
scoring using a validated pain assessment instrument is recom-
mended. To provide an extended duration of analgesia, catheteriza-
tion of the axillary brachial plexus has been described in awake
dogs; though feasible, concerns about dislocation of the catheter
and evidence of local anesthetic channeling resulting in uneven dis-
tribution among target nerves have curbed the enthusiasm of clini-
cians for this technique [242].
Proximal radial, ulnar, median,
and musculocutaneous nerve block
The radial, ulnar, median, and musculocutaneous (RUMM) nerves
can be blocked at the level of the proximal medial humerus within
the axilla (proximal RUMM block or distal brachial plexus block).
This provides motor and sensory block of the elbow and distal tho-
racic limb. At this location, these four nerves are contained within a
connective tissue sheath, the axillary sheath, that is derived from
the deep cervical fasciae. In a preliminary cadaver study, due to the
presence of the axillary sheath, the four target nerves contained
within the sheath were adequately stained without extravasation of
the dye solution into the surrounding tissues or complications such
as phrenic nerve or intrathoracic contamination [243]. In a cohort
of 15 client-owned dogs, an in- plane approach to an ultrasound-
guided injection of local anesthetic solution (0.15 mL/kg of 0.5%
ropivacaine) provided intraoperative analgesia associated with sig-
nificant opioid-sparing effects and postoperative analgesia for up to
8 h [243]. The approach described in this study is performed distal
to the axillary brachial plexus block and specifically targets the
RUMM nerves as opposed to the spinal nerve roots located more
proximally.
In cats, an ultrasound-guided lateral approach to block the
radial, ulnar, median, and musculocutaneous nerves was recently
described. A single injection technique was unsuccessful at consist-
ently blocking the musculocutaneous nerve when the tip of the nee-
dle was directed at the radial nerve, and a second injection directed
at the musculocutaneous nerve proved necessary due to the pres-
ence of interrupted layers of connective tissue that separate the
different components of the neurovascular bundle [244].

Distal radial, ulnar, median, and musculocutaneous
nerve block
An alternative to the traditional axillary brachial plexus block con-
sists of targeting individual RUMM nerves at the level of the mid- to
distal humerus (distal RUMM block). This technique was initially
evaluated in dogs in a study that involved anatomic evaluation of
injectate distribution in canine cadavers followed by a placebo-
controlled, prospective, crossover clinical evaluation of the tech-
nique [245]. The radial nerve courses laterally and separates from
the ulnar, median, and musculocutaneous nerves at the level of the
proximal third of the humerus and thus, this technique was
described as two separate injections in order to successfully reach
all of the target nerves. Though their pilot study demonstrated ade-
quate staining of all but one of targeted nerves when sufficient vol-
umes of injectate were used (0.1 mL/kg and 0.15 mL/kg for the
lateral and medial approach, respectively), complete sensory block-
ade was not obtained in all limbs tested. They found that the degree
and duration of sensory deficits varied across the different dermat-
omes that were tested and the extent and duration of motor deficits
differed from the sensory blockade.
The distal RUMM block technique can be performed with nerve
stimulation guidance; the successful application of this technique
was described in a clinical case report as part of a multimodal anal-
gesic plan consisting of systemic opioids and regional anesthesia
(0.5% bupivacaine) for a muscle biopsy in the distal thoracic limb
of a dog in which general anesthesia was considered to have an
increased risk of complications [246]. Descriptions of ultrasound-
guided mid-humeral RUMM block techniques in dogs undergoing
distal limb surgical procedures have also been published [247,248].
An ultrasound-guided lateral approach to the RUMM block in
cats has been described and found that target nerves were more
successfully stained with 0.4 mL of methylene blue using an in-
plane approach [249]. The clinical efficacy of the technique remains
to be confirmed in cats.
Radial, ulnar, and median nerve block (ring block)
To selectively block structures distal to the elbow, perineural injec-
tions of local anesthetics around the radial, ulnar, and median
(RUM) nerves can be performed anywhere along the course of the
nerves. However, surgical procedures involving the manus and/or
digits do not require the entire thoracic limb to be blocked. While
regional anesthetic techniques applied more proximally will result
in acceptable analgesia, they typically also result in motor blockade,
which is often unnecessary for procedures involving the distal limb
and can result in trauma due to decreased mobility and propriocep-
tive deficits.
The somatic organization of individual nerve fibers within plexi
is such that afferent nerve fibers from the distalmost aspects of a
limb are found in the center of nerves, while the more peripheral
fibers innervate more proximal dermatomes. Furthermore, the size
of nerves can adversely influence the success and duration of sen-
sory blocks. This theoretically raises the issue that attempting to
block the manus with a brachial plexus or proximal RUMM block
may carry a greater risk of failure, though no study exists compar-
ing the intensity or duration of analgesia at the distal limb with ring
blocks versus more proximal blocks [250]. For this reason, the
radial, ulnar, and median nerves are commonly blocked at a loca-
tion immediately proximal to the carpus by means of a four-point
block that will selectively desensitize the superficial branches of the
radial nerve (dorsomedially), the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve
(laterally), the palmar branch of the ulnar nerve (palmaromedially),
and the median nerve (palmarolaterally) (RUM block). The tech-
nique can be simplified to a ring block where the target nerves are
all successfully blocked following a circumferential subcutaneous
infiltration of local anesthetic proximal to the carpus, as previously
described [251,252].
Blocks of the pelvic limb
Until relatively recently, local anesthetic techniques for the pelvic
limb of small companion animals were limited mainly to epidural
or spinal anesthesia or intra-articular injections. However, periph-
eral nerve blockade can provide highly effective analgesia with
potentially less morbidity than neuraxial anesthesia [254]. When
compared with epidural anesthesia, peripheral nerve blockade of
the pelvic limb for orthopedic surgery provided similar require-
ments for postoperative analgesia with a lower incidence of intra-
operative hypotension and postoperative urinary retention in
dogs [254,255].
Bupivacaine (0.5%) with or without dexmedetomidine (0.5–2
μg/mL of injectate solution) is commonly used to provide surgical
anesthesia, although 0.5% ropivacaine may also be used. The addi-
tion of 50 μg of dexmedetomidine to a 50 mL vial of 0.5% bupiv-
acaine will create a solution that contains 0.5% bupivacaine and
dexmedetomidine at a concentration of 1 μg/mL. When bupiv-
acaine alone (0.15 mL/kg) was used for femoral and sciatic nerve
blocks, the duration of action for sensory blockade was found to be
15 and 10 h, respectively [256]. The addition of dexmedetomidine
may further prolong sensory blockade; however, this has not been
demonstrated in all studies [257,258].
Anatomy
The pelvic limb is served by two nerve plexi (lumbar and sacral)
and both must be partly or entirely blocked to provide surgical
anesthesia and analgesia to the entire pelvic limb (including the
hemipelvis). The lumbar plexus supplies the lateral femoral cutane-
ous nerve (L3, L4), the genitofemoral nerve (L3, L4), the femoral
nerve (L4, L5, L6), and the obturator nerve (L4, L5, L6) [259]. The
sacral plexus supplies the sciatic nerve (L6, L7, S1), the cranial and
caudal gluteal nerves (L6, L7, S1), and the caudal cutaneous femoral
nerve (S1, S2) [256].
Blocking the femoral nerve (or its distal sensory continuation,
the saphenous nerve) will provide anesthesia of the femur (mid-
diaphysis to distal), the femorotibial joint (medial aspect of the
femorotibial joint capsule and intra-articular structures), the skin of
the dorsomedial tarsus, and the first digit. Blocking the sciatic nerve
alone is sufficient to perform surgery involving the foot or hock.
Components of both nerves (femoral and sciatic) must be blocked
for almost any stifle or proximal tibial surgical procedure (e.g., tib-
ial plateau leveling osteotomy).
Lumbar plexus block
The lumbar plexus is formed via the ventral branches of L4, L5, and
L6 within the psoas compartment, a sheath formed by the iliopsoas
and psoas minor muscles [260]. Regional blockade of the nerves of
the lumbar plexus can be achieved using either nerve stimulator or
ultrasound guidance [42,45]. When a psoas compartment block is
combined with a parasacral lumbosacral trunk block, regional
anesthesia to the entire limb can result, sufficient for pelvic limb
amputation, hip surgery, or femur surgery [259].
Three different approaches to nerve stimulation-guided lumbar
plexus blocks have been described: a single-injection paravertebral

-- 1204 of 1450 --

Chapter 60: Canine and Feline Local Anesthetic and Analgesic Techniques 	1189
approach [233], a three-point paravertebral approach [261], and a
lateral pre-iliac approach [260]. Using the single-injection paraver-
tebral approach, a stimulating needle is introduced through the
epaxial muscles at the L5–L6 intervertebral level toward the iliop-
soas muscle until a quadriceps femoris muscle twitch is elic-
ited [233]. Epidural and abdominal spread of contrast injected at
this location occurred in a small proportion of subjects [233];
indeed, in a retrospective study examining this technique, one of 95
cases showed bilateral motor deficit, consistent with epidural
spread [262].
While the single-injection approach utilizes a large volume of
local anesthetic (0.4 mL/kg) to desensitize the lumbar plexus, the
three-point approach aims to utilize a smaller volume (0.05 mL/kg)
at each of three sites to block the individual ventral branches of the
L4, L5, and L6 nerve roots prior to them forming the lumbar
plexus [261]. Using this approach, when combined with a parasa-
cral lumbosacral trunk block, less rescue analgesia was needed for
pelvic limb amputations in dogs [42].
The lateral pre-iliac approach aims to block the femoral nerve
caudally within the psoas compartment where it is further from the
vasculature [260]. This approach utilizes a stimulating needle
inserted through the lateral aspect of the lumbar muscles, cranial to
the wing of the ilium. Comparison of the effect of blocking the lum-
bar plexus via the sagittal paravertebral or lateral pre-iliac approach
in dogs undergoing pelvic limb orthopedic surgery failed to show a
statistically significant difference in success rate (74.7% versus
82.3%) or rescue analgesia (33.7% versus 27.1%), although the vol-
ume used for the paravertebral approach was lower than that previ-
ously described (0.15 mL/kg versus 0.4 mL/kg) [262]. The
lumbosacral plexus block, when combined with sciatic nerve block,
has also been shown to be effective in cats undergoing hindlimb
orthopedic procedures [263].
The lumbar plexus block can also be achieved via combined
ultrasound–nerve stimulator guidance or under ultrasound guid-
ance alone. In either situation, a linear, high-frequency transducer
is positioned on the ventral aspect of the abdomen and lumbar
muscles, cranial to the iliac crest. At this location, the femoral
nerve can be identified as a hypoechoic, round structure within the
body of the iliopsoas muscle [259]. The needle can be advanced
toward the femoral nerve using several different approaches in
dogs; however, when introduced from the lateral aspect of the lum-
bar muscles there is less risk of inadvertent vascular puncture (e.g.,
the external iliac artery) [264]. When combined with a sciatic
nerve block, ultrasound-guided lumbar plexus block improves
analgesia and recovery quality for dogs undergoing tibial plateau
leveling osteotomy [265].
Using nerve stimulation and/or ultrasound guidance, the sciatic
nerve may also be blocked more proximally utilizing a parasacral
approach at the lumbosacral trunk. At this location, anesthesia/
analgesia can be provided to the proximal femur and pelvis that is
sufficient for hind limb amputation and hip and femur surgery
when combined with a lumbar plexus block [42,259].
Femoral/saphenous nerve block
At the caudal aspect of the iliopsoas muscle, the femoral nerve exits
the muscle and courses across the femoral triangle (Fig. 60.15). The
femoral triangle is demarcated by the iliopsoas muscle cranially, the
pectineus muscle caudally, and the sartorius muscle cranially. Within
the triangle, the femoral nerve is located cranial to the femoral artery
and vein, running deep to the caudal belly of the sartorius muscle. At
this level, the femoral nerve gives rise to the saphenous nerve and
the lateral circumflex vessels originate from the femoral artery and
vein. These vessels cross the femoral triangle in a craniocaudal
direction, disappearing between the vastus medialis and rectus fem-
oris muscles. The femoral nerve then continues distally, entering the
quadriceps muscle between the vastus medialis and rectus femoris.
The saphenous nerve is the sensory branch of the femoral nerve and,
when it is blocked in combination with a sciatic nerve block, anes-
thesia for stifle surgery will be achieved while still preserving quadri-
ceps muscle function [259]. While other branches of the femoral and
obturator nerve may contribute some sensory innervation to the
stifle in dogs [266], a recent retrospective analysis found no differ-
ence in intraoperative or postoperative analgesic requirements
between a saphenous–sciatic and a lumbar plexus–sciatic nerve
block in dogs undergoing stifle surgery [254].
For nerve stimulator-guided blockade of the femoral nerve, the
patient should be positioned in lateral recumbency with the limb to be
blocked positioned uppermost. The limb should be abducted 90° and
extended caudally, making it easier to palpate and identify the
pectineus and iliopsoas muscles and to palpate the pulse of the femo-
ral artery. Since the femoral nerve will be located cranial to the femoral
artery, the puncture site is located cranial to the femoral artery within
the femoral triangle (Fig. 60.16). An insulated needle (e.g., 22 gauge,
50 mm) is advanced toward the iliopsoas muscle, maintaining a
20–30° angle with respect to the skin. As the needle is advanced, the
fascia iliaca will be penetrated (a “pop” can usually be appreciated).
Once the tip of the needle is near the femoral nerve, contractions of
the quadriceps muscle will result in stifle extension. Bupivacaine
(0.5%, 0.1 mL/kg) combined with dexmedetomidine (0.5 μg/mL) pro-
vides approximately 14 (range 6–24) h of effect until rescue analgesia
may be needed following stifle surgery [255,267,268].
Alternatively, nerve stimulation can be combined with ultra-
sound with the transducer placed over the femoral triangle in a
craniocaudal direction. Doing this will provide a short-axis view of
the femoral artery and the nerve. Since it is usually compressed by
the pressure that is being exerted by the ultrasound transducer, the
femoral vein is rarely seen adjacent to the artery (Fig. 60.17). The
femoral nerve is located cranial and deep to the femoral artery and
is identifiable as a small, hyperechoic structure directly beneath the
thin caudal belly of the sartorius muscle and the fascia iliaca

(which appears as a thin hyperechoic line superficial to the femoral

aspect of the thigh (cranial belly of the sartorius muscle) in-plane
with the transducer (Fig. 60.18). The recommended volume to be
injected is 0.1 mL/kg [235]. However, the final injection volume can

The saphenous nerve may be blocked distally along the medial
femur to minimize motor blockade of the quadriceps. As this nerve
is sensory, nerve stimulator-guidance is not feasible. Instead, the
saphenous nerve may be identified under ultrasound guidance at the
level of the middle-third of the femur, in a triangular fascial plane
located immediately cranial to the femoral artery (Fig. 60.19) [36,123].
Sciatic nerve block
The sciatic nerve courses from its points of origin distally down
the pelvic limb between the greater trochanter of the femur and the
ischiatic tuberosity (Fig. 60.20). In this region, the sciatic nerve
gives rise to muscular branches that supply the semitendinosus
and semimembranosus muscles. The caudal gluteal vessels lie just
caudal to these muscular branches and must be avoided when the
needle is placed close to the sciatic nerve at this location.
Immediately distal to the greater trochanter and ischiatic tuberos-
ity, the sciatic nerve lies between the biceps femoris muscle later-
ally, and the semimembranosus/semitendinosus muscles caudally,
and the adductor muscle medially. The sciatic nerve then divides
into its two main branches, the tibial nerve medially and the com-
mon peroneal nerve laterally. The location of this division is vari-
able and can occur anywhere from the level of the hip joint to just
proximal to the stifle joint.
Sciatic nerve blocks may be performed utilizing nerve stimula-
tion and/or ultrasound guidance. For either technique, the patient
should be positioned in lateral recumbency with the limb to be
blocked positioned uppermost in a natural position. For a nerve
stimulator-guided approach, the greater trochanter and ischiatic
tuberosity should first be identified. The puncture site is located at
a point between the cranial and the middle thirds of a line that
could be drawn between these two bony landmarks. An insulated
needle (22 gauge, 50 mm) is inserted through the skin and is
advanced ventromedially at a 45° angle to the skin (Fig. 60.21).
Once the tip of the needle is near the sciatic nerve, dorsiflexion or
plantar extension of the foot will be elicited. The recommended
volume to be injected is 0.1 mL/kg. Contractions of the semimem-
branosus or semitendinosus muscles should not be considered an
acceptable endpoint. If stimulation of the hamstring muscles is
observed without movement of the foot, the needle is likely stimu-
lating the muscular branches of the sciatic nerve and not the sciatic
nerve itself. Injection of a local anesthetic at this location will miss
the sensory components of the sciatic nerve and may result in
block failure.
If performing the sciatic nerve block using ultrasound guidance,
the transducer should be placed in a craniocaudal orientation
over the biceps femoris muscle on the lateral aspect of the thigh,
distal to the ischiatic tuberosity (Fig. 60.22). Using this approach, a
short-axis view of the sciatic nerve should be obtained (Fig. 60.23).
An insulated needle (22 gauge, 50–100 mm) will enter the skin from
the caudal aspect of the thigh, in-plane with the ultrasound trans-
ducer. The needle should be advanced toward the sciatic nerve in a

ultrasound guidance, plantar extension (from tibial nerve stimula-

foot will be elicited when the needle approaches the sciatic nerve.
The recommended volume of local anesthetic to be injected is
0.1 mL/kg, although the final injection volume can be assessed by
monitoring the ultrasound image [235].
Intra-articular blocks
An additional strategy for pain management following joint surgery
is the intra-articular administration of analgesics such as local anes-
thetics or opioids. The intra-articular injection of local anesthetics
desensitizes intra-articular structures only and may reduce the dose
and interval for administering supplemental analgesic therapy [269].
Stifle technique
The patient is positioned in dorsal or lateral recumbency. The stifle
joint is held in a flexed position. The needle is inserted lateral to the
patellar ligament, midway between the cranial pole of the patella
and the tibial tuberosity, and the hub of the needle is observed for
the presence of synovial fluid (confirming correct needle position).
However, absence of synovial fluid does not necessarily rule out

The stifle may also be blocked utilizing ultrasound-guided local
anesthetic injection of the popliteal fossa utilizing the “infiltrating
around genicular structures” or “FLAGS” technique, described in
dogs [270]. This technique may provide sufficient analgesia for sti-
fle surgery while maintaining motor function; however, further
studies are needed to assess its clinical safety and utility.
Coxofemoral joint technique
The patient should be positioned in lateral recumbency with the
coxofemoral joint to be injected uppermost; the limb should be
slightly flexed, with the stifle in a neutral position. The puncture
site is located cranial and proximal to the greater trochanter. Once
the needle has entered the joint, the hub of the needle should be
observed for evidence of synovial fluid to confirm correct needle
positioning. However, absence of synovial fluid does not rule out
correct needle positioning. Depending on the size of the patient,
1–6 mL of local anesthetic solution can be injected into the
joint [271]. Lack of resistance during injection confirms correct
intra-articular position of the needle tip and excludes injection into
periarticular soft tissue or a fat pad.
Neuraxial techniques
The administration of agents with analgesic properties via the
epidural or spinal routes provides effective anesthesia and analgesia
for procedures involving the pelvis and pelvic limbs, as well as the
tail, perineum, and caudal abdomen. In addition, the use of epi-
dural anesthesia for blockade of thoracic segments in dogs has been
extensively studied [272]. Epidural analgesia can also be extended
by using an indwelling catheter.
The lumbosacral approach (L7–S1) to performing epidural anes-
thesia in dogs and cats is technically straightfoward to perform
owing to the relatively wide intervertebral space at this location,
although more cranial approaches in dogs have also been
described [273,274]. Alternatively, a sacrococcygeal approach to the
epidural space has been described in cats to minimize the risk of
dural puncture and help facilitate urethral catheterization in
blocked cats [275,276] and a sacrococcygeal approach in dogs has
been described to minimize the risk of accidental dural puncture, as
a high frequency of “subarachnoid contamination of contrast” was
reported in one study of lumbosacral epidurals [31]. Under experi-
mental conditions in canine cadavers, the cranial extent of contrast
spread in the epidural space appears similar between the lumbosa-
cral and sacrococcygeal locations [277].
Contraindications
There are several contraindications to the use of epidural anesthesia
in small animal patients. Alternatives to epidural anesthesia should
be considered in patients with bleeding disorders (e.g., thrombocy-
topenia). Since placing a needle in the vertebral canal can result in
inadvertent puncture of an epidural venous sinus, hemorrhage may
result in the formation of an epidural hematoma compressing neu-
ral structures such as the cauda equina, different spinal nerve roots,
dural sac, or even the spinal cord. Epidural anesthesia using a local
anesthetic should be avoided in patients with uncorrected hypov-
olemia and hypotension since they will be at further risk due to
vasodilation following sympathetic nerve blockade. Opioids may
continue to be used in these patients. Finally, epidural anesthesia
should be avoided in patients with skin infections or presence of
neoplasia or other lesions at the site of injection. In these patients,
alternative routes for performing the epidural injection (e.g., sacro-
coccygeal route) or selection of a different regional anesthetic tech-
nique should be considered. Potential complications associated
with neuraxial administration (single dose or continuous infusion)
and strategies to avoid them are summarized in Table 60.1.
Anatomy
The vertebral canal contains the epidural space and the intrathecal
structures. The roof of the canal is formed by the vertebral laminae
and the interarcuate ligament (also known as the ligamentum fla-
vum or yellow ligament). This ligament widens at the level of the
intervertebral openings. The epidural space in the dog is largest
at the lumbosacral level where the dural sac tapers (Fig. 60.24).
