Protection of the contralateral eye
For unilateral procedures, the dependent eye is padded to protect
against physical injury. Prior to surgery, lubrication of the non-
surgical eye must be performed periodically to avoid corneal desic-
cation and ulceration. Other methods for preventing corneal drying
and exposure include temporarily taping the eyelids closed or tem-
porary tarsorrhaphy.
Neuromuscular blockade and anesthetic
monitoring
The nondepolarizing NMBA should be administered immediately
before corneal or intraocular surgery is started and mechanical ven-
tilation is recommended throughout surgery. In addition to routine
anesthetic monitoring, the degree of paralysis can be closely moni-
tored using a peripheral nerve stimulator or acceleromyography
(see Chapter 26). These drugs cause a centralized globe (Fig. 67.5)
independent of anesthetic depth, which makes anesthetic monitor-
ing more challenging. Anesthetists must focus on changes in heart
rate and blood pressure to assess the anesthetic depth and adequacy
of analgesia. Measurement of expired volatile agent concentrations
can also be useful when available. In diabetic patients, serial blood
glucose monitoring should be performed perioperatively to deter-
mine glucose trends, diagnose extreme abnormalities, and assess
response to any administered treatments (see Chapter 42).
Recovery, extubation, and emergence
Recovery is initiated only after neuromuscular function has been
completely restored, either by reversal of the NMBA or by sponta-
neous recovery, based on neuromuscular monitoring. Once muscu-
lar function resumes, non-essential monitoring can be removed
and the patient should be moved to a comfortable position before
the anesthetic is discontinued. Gagging or coughing should be pre-
vented during tracheal extubation. Recovery needs to be smooth
and should occur in a quiet environment. Emergence delirium, dys-
phoria, and excitement should be controlled using sedatives to pre-
vent sudden changes in IOP with ocular hemorrhage or trauma. An
Elizabethan collar must be carefully placed to prevent the patient
from scratching or rubbing the operated eye. Additional analgesia
should be provided if required.
Anesthesia-related ocular complications
In humans, dogs, and horses, the most common ocular complica-
tion of general anesthesia is corneal abrasion [279–281]. Causal
factors include damage caused by face masks, surgical drapes, spill-
age of solutions, ocular injury from loss of protective reflexes and
lack of pain sensation, and dry eye from reduced tear produc-
tion [281]. Therefore, during anesthesia, it is prudent to tape the
eyelids closed, apply protective goggles, and lubricate eyes with
petroleum-based ointments or aqueous-based solutions. Other
ocular complications reported in humans are chemical injury,
photic injury, visual disturbances, retinal ischemia, hemorrhagic
retinopathy, acute glaucoma, cortical blindness, and ischemic optic
neuropathy [282]. Postanesthetic blindness in cats has been associ-
ated with the use of spring-held mouth gags and consequent com-
pression of the maxillary artery during non-ocular procedures [283].
Out of the 20 feline cases, a mouth gag was used in 16 cats.
Neurological deficits were seen in 17 cats in addition to blindness,
and 3 cats suffered from cardiac arrest during anesthesia. Moreover,
maximal opening of the mouth interrupts maxillary artery blood
flow as evaluated with magnetic resonance angiography and
dynamic computer tomography [284]. The use of a smaller mouth
gag was recommended in cats as it produced minimal alterations in
the maxillary artery blood flow [285].
Special considerations for equine ophthalmic
patients
Ophthalmic procedures that require equine patients to be com-
pletely immobilized are performed under general anesthesia.
However, there are surgical procedures of the eye that can be per-
formed on a standing horse using sedatives and analgesics com-
bined with local anesthetic techniques. The decision largely
depends on the ophthalmologist’s personal preference, cost, dispo-
sition and medical condition of the horse, and available facilities.
Some surgeons prefer a standing sedation technique for selected
procedures to reduce the risk associated with general anesthe-
sia [246]. Detomidine can be given in intermittent boluses as
needed, or as a CRI. For detomidine infusion, a 7.5 μg/kg IV load-
ing dose is administered followed by a 0.6 μg/kg/min CRI. This
rate is halved every 15 min until the rate of 0.15 μg/kg/min is
reached. The horse is given IV boluses of detomidine (1–2 μg/kg)
as needed [286]. This is accompanied by an effective locoregional
anesthetic technique as described elsewhere in this chapter.
Horses with a non-visual eye should be approached from the
visual side. If approach from the non-visual side is necessary, it
should be accompanied by words of reassurance and gentle hand
contact. If an increase in IOP will jeopardize the primary ocular
problem of the horse, steps should be taken to minimize factors that
can potentially increase IOP during the physical examination.
Horses that are excited or stressed are more difficult to handle and
tend to have more fluctuations in IOP, which may be deleterious to
an eye with pre-existing intraocular hypertension [287]. Hence, it is
better to sedate such horses with xylazine or detomidine during the
ophthalmic examination to prevent sudden increases in IOP. When
examining a sedated horse, an effort should be made to raise the
head above the level of the heart as a lowered head results in an
increase in IOP [24]. Prior to anesthesia, it is advisable to administer
sedation before flushing the horse’s mouth out to prevent excitement-
associated increases in IOP.
Effective premedication is important in ensuring a smooth anes-
thetic induction. An α2
-adrenergic receptor agonist administered IV
will provide profound sedation, as well as analgesia and muscle relax-
ation. Some horses may need a supplemental dose of α2
- adrenergic
receptor agonist to achieve adequate sedation. Administration of an
opioid following an α2
-adrenergic receptor agonist will provide addi-
tional sedation and analgesia. To prevent excitement, it is good prac-
tice to give the opioid after signs of sedation from the α2
-adrenergic
receptor agonist are observed, which generally occur about 2–3 min
after its administration. Butorphanol is the most commonly used
opioid in equine practice. The IV dose for butorphanol ranges from
0.02–0.05 mg/kg. Morphine may be used in place of butorphanol,
given IV at 0.2–0.6 mg/kg. Hydromorphone and methadone are also
excellent alternatives [288,289]. Recommended IV doses for the α2
-
adrenergic receptor agonists and opioids are shown in Table 67.5. The
tranquilizer acepromazine can be incorporated into the premedica-
tion. It has been shown that acepromazine is associated with lower
mortality in equine elective cases when used as part of the anesthetic
plan [290]. It is given IV at 0.02 mg/kg 30 min before, or at the same
time as, the α2
-adrenergic receptor agonist. Acepromazine can also be
administered IM before or during anesthesia. Since acepromazine
has a long duration of action, its effect will last until the recovery
period, which may contribute to a better recovery.

The choice of anesthetic induction agents for equine patients
depends largely on the quality of induction associated with the
injectable agents and the effect of the induction agents on IOP.
Presently in the United States, induction of anesthesia in equine
patients has been limited to ketamine combined with a benzodi-
azepine, propofol or guaifenesin, and Telazol®. When an α2 -
adrenergic receptor agonist is used as premedication, propofol
may be an acceptable induction agent in foals. Telazol® can also be
used for induction like a ketamine–benzodiazepine combination.
It is imperative that profound sedation from an α2 -adrenergic
receptor agonist be observed before inducing anesthesia with
either of these induction protocols to ensure smooth induction
and minimize the effect on IOP.
When a nursing foal needs general anesthesia, the mare should
be present during the induction of anesthesia to minimize stress on
the foal. Conversely, if the mare is undergoing anesthesia, it is
important that the foal be near to facilitate sedation of the mare and
ensure a smooth induction. Mask induction for foals may not be an
option if the mask rubs or presses on the eyes, and struggling of the
patient during induction with a face mask may increase IOP or
potentiate eye rupture. Nasotracheal intubation in a conscious foal
requires physical restraint and may be accompanied by coughing
and gagging, which may increase IOP and further compromise the
globe. Appropriate sedation may help calm the foal and decrease
the amount of physical restraint that is needed, as well as decrease
the potential for additional eye trauma or increases in IOP.
Endotracheal intubation should be accomplished quickly once
the horse is in lateral recumbency. Adult horses rarely gag or cough
during endotracheal intubation, making a sudden increase in IOP
less likely. Movement of equine patients to lateral recumbency after
induction should include careful control of the head to prevent
additional trauma to the eyes. In addition, lower positioning of the
head relative to the body during hoist transport could result in
increased IOP and may be responsible for intraocular hemorrhage
observed shortly after induction in horses with traumatized
eyes [21,22]. Supporting the head to keep it level with the heart dur-
ing transport is recommended to avoid such an occurrence. The
normal eye can be lubricated with eye ointment during hoisting.
Complex ophthalmic procedures such as penetrating kerato-
plasty in horses may require extended anesthesia time. Partial intra-
venous anesthesia (PIVA) is a technique that may be implemented
to reduce the amount of inhalation agent needed to maintain anes-
thesia, provide intraoperative analgesia, and minimize the cardio-
pulmonary depressant effects of inhalation agents. This technique
utilizes injectable agents that are administered as single-drug or
multi-drug CRIs, thereby permitting reduction of the vaporizer
setting over time while still maintaining an adequate plane of
anesthesia. Injectable agents commonly utilized for this technique
include ketamine, lidocaine, butorphanol, and α2
- adrenergic recep-
tor agonists. Administration of CRIs requires close attention to
detail especially when multiple drugs are utilized. The PIVA tech-
nique has been associated with better recoveries and fewer attempts
to stand in horses [291,292].
Analgesics administered during anesthesia may reduce inhalant
requirements and improve recovery as the horse regains conscious-
ness without the stimulus of postoperative pain. Analgesic options
in equine ophthalmic patients include NSAIDs, opioids, lidocaine,
ketamine, and appropriate nerve blocks. One commonly adminis-
tered NSAID for horses with ocular inflammation related to the
primary disease or because of surgery is flunixin meglumine. It is
administered at 1.1 mg/kg IV preoperatively. It is repeated postop-
eratively using the same dose every 12–24 h, with frequency of
administration dependent on the ocular problem. Butorphanol,
morphine, hydromorphone, and methadone are opioids available
for use in horses. They can be administered as part of the premedi-
cation and may be re-dosed postoperatively. Lidocaine CRI has
been used for intraoperative pain management in horses. A bolus
dose of 2 mg/kg can be administered over 15 min, followed by a
CRI of 3 mg/kg/h. The CRI should be discontinued 30 min before
recovery to minimize incoordination associated with lido-
caine [293]. Infusion of an α2 - adrenergic receptor agonist or keta-
mine can be used as PIVA to enhance analgesia, and the analgesic
effect may extend into the postoperative period. Nerve blockade
from local anesthetic injection may provide analgesia both during
surgery and postoperatively.
The main goal of recovering anesthetized horses that have under-
gone an ophthalmic procedure is to have smooth and injury-free
recoveries similar to other equine cases. This becomes more impor-
tant after intraocular procedures or corneal transplants. Recovery
efforts should include preventing trauma to the eyes as the horse
attempts to stand. Duration of anesthesia should be minimized to
decrease the risk of postanesthetic complications as the possibility
of rough recoveries is higher in horses with ocular problems [294].
Many suggestions have been made to achieve quiet, predictable,
and smooth recoveries in horses but there is not any one single rec-
ommendation that will ensure this outcome. Administration of
sedatives in recovery has been advocated to improve recovery.
α2
- Adrenergic receptor agonists may be administered before the
horse is moved to the recovery stall or when the horse reaches the
recovery area. The recovery dosages for these drugs are listed in
Table 67.6. Note that these dosages are lower than those used for
premedication. Acepromazine has also been given with or without
the α2
- adrenergic receptor agonist. It should be given intravenously
at 0.01–0.02 mg/kg at least 30 min before recovery because of its
delayed onset of action compared with the α2
- adrenergic receptor
agonists.
As discussed previously, effective analgesia will help improve
the quality of recovery, and ideally, should be administered before
the horse regains full consciousness. Passing a urinary catheter in

the recovery stall to empty the urinary bladder will also help
improve recovery quality. Horses that received an NMBA during
general anesthesia should be evaluated closely for muscle strength.
Return of neuromuscular function as determined by the nerve
stimulator does not rule out muscle weakness due to persistent
low-level neuromuscular blockade. Horses with muscle weakness
that attempt to stand are more prone to limb injuries. Muscle
strength can be judged by determining the negative pressure that
the horse can generate during inspiration when the connection to
the rebreathing bag is occluded. A negative pressure of at least
15 cmH2
O indicates acceptable muscle strength. Conversely, signs
of muscle weakness may include muscle fasciculations when the
horse attempts to stand, inability to keep its head up, and failure to
close its eyelids tightly. When signs of muscle weakness are evident,
and the reversal agent was not administered because the nerve
stimulator indicated return to normal neuromuscular function,
neostigmine should be administered. One way to avoid administer-
ing atropine or glycopyrrolate before administering neostigmine is
to give it very slowly.
To protect the eye during recovery, a padded hood may be placed
on the head, with a halter secured over the hood to keep it in place.
However, a hood may not be tolerated by some horses, and may
lead to premature attempts to rise. Weak attempts to rise may be
controlled by kneeling on the horse’s neck and lifting its muzzle up.
Additional sedation may prevent horses with active nystagmus
from attempting to rise. A head-and-tail rope technique assists
horses that are making strong attempts to rise and helps them
remain standing in recovery. Ideally, there should be three individ-
uals to execute this recovery technique. Ropes are tied to the tail
and to a strong, reliable halter, and then passed through metal rings
on the walls of the recovery stall. When the horse makes a strong
attempt to rise, the person on the tail will forcefully pull the rope to
assist the horse to rise. The person on the head rope will simply
guide the head of the horse, rather than pulling forcefully on the
rope and disorienting the horse. Once the horse stands, the third
person will push the horse against the wall of the recovery stall for
support. If this technique is to be used, recovery stalls should be
constructed so that there are readily accessible exit routes, and the
personnel handling the ropes will be outside the stall to avoid the
hazards of an uncoordinated horse attempting to stand. Quiet sur-
roundings and a darkened recovery stall may minimize any stimu-
lus that may excite a horse recovering from anesthesia. When the
horse is standing and steady on its feet, a hard cup hood may be
placed over the affected eye for additional ocular protection. A
higher incidence of colic has been reported in horses with ocular
disease [295] and such patients should be observed very closely
postoperatively for signs of abdominal pain.

Introduction
Young animals have physiologic and anatomic characteristics that
can make them challenging to anesthetize. In addition to their small
size, these patients tend to have limited body system reserves, can be
more sensitive to the sedative effects of some agents, such as opioids,
and are vulnerable to anesthetic complications, such as hypothermia.
Fortunately, with careful attention to these considerations, most
pediatric patients can be anesthetized safely and successfully.
Definition of pediatric and neonatal periods
In cats and dogs, the neonatal period extends from birth to weaning
(4 to 6 weeks of age) and the pediatric period can be defined as the
period between 6 weeks (which marks the end of the neonatal
period) and 12 weeks of age [1,2]. Puppies and kittens can be
defined as dogs and cats less than 6 months of age. The most impor-
tant physiologic differences for foals exist between 48 and 72 h after
birth, but they are considered physiologically mature by 4 to 6 weeks
of age [3]. Ruminants (cattle, sheep, and goats) and camelids are
considered neonatal until 4 weeks of age and physiologically mature
by 4 to 6 weeks of age.
Anesthetic risk for young patients
Because of their relatively small size, lack of physiologic reserves,
incomplete immunity, and susceptibility to the stress of handling
and separation from their dam, all puppies and kittens should be
considered a special category of anesthesia patient until at least
3 months of age. The risks of anesthesia are not increased in young
healthy animals undergoing elective procedures which are per-
formed rapidly and efficiently [4]. In contrast, a large study in
general veterinary practices found that the risk of anesthetic death
in cats weighing less than 2 kg was over 15 times greater than that of
cats between 2 and 6 kg [5]. In addition, the risk of anesthetic death
was higher in dogs weighing < 5 kg compared to dogs weighing
5–15 kg suggesting size is a risk factor that is independent of age [6].
Foals less than 1 month of age have increased risk of mortality
during anesthesia [7,8].
Circumstances warranting anesthesia
Early spay-neuter is an accepted practice for population control and
is endorsed by the American Veterinary Medical Association [9]
and the Association of Shelter Veterinarians [10,11]. The rationale

for early spay-neuter has been reviewed elsewhere [12–15] but, in
addition to the benefits for population management, surgery in
young, healthy animals is generally associated with good outcomes
and, at least in cats, may be less painful [16]. For elective procedures
(sterilization), it is preferred that puppies and kittens are ≥ 1 kg.
However, puppies and kittens may present at a very early age and
under 1 kg for emergency procedures such as abdominal surgery,
diaphragmatic hernia, fractures, and other accidental injuries, and
good outcomes can be achieved with careful anesthetic and analge-
sic management.
Foals and young ruminants are not commonly anesthetized for
castration during the pediatric period, but ruminants may present
for routine husbandry procedures such as disbudding. Emergency
surgeries in foals such as patent urachus surgery or septic joints are
common. These species may present at a young age for the correc-
tion of congenital abnormalities (e.g., limb malformations) or with
traumatic injuries such as fractures.
Patient characteristics
The unique physiologic features of pediatric cats and dogs have
been reviewed [17,18]. Pediatric patients of all species have limited
reserves of all body systems and a limited ability to respond to
events that challenge homeostasis. The role of a high resting basal
metabolic rate in determining the pediatric patient’s response
to anesthesia should not be underestimated and can lead to fast
metabolism of drugs and the need for redosing. Anatomic charac-
teristics that are relevant to anesthesia include a high body surface
area-to-mass ratio and a high lean body mass compared to body fat.
These features can predispose the pediatric patient to hypothermia,
which is perhaps the most devastating complication of anesthesia
for young animals. In addition, the tissues are delicate requiring
gentle handling.
Cardiovascular system
The pediatric heart is relatively small for the size of the patient,
ventricular compliance is low, and stroke volume is relatively fixed.
Low cardiac reserves are accompanied by a high cardiac index
(volume of blood pumped per minute indexed to body size:
L/min/m2
) leading to an overall decreased ability to compensate for
or respond to fluid losses and hypotension. Because the stroke
volume of a pediatric patient is relatively fixed, these patients are
particularly dependent on heart rate for the maintenance of cardiac
output (heart rate × stroke volume) and organ perfusion [17,19].
The neonate is unable to increase cardiac contractility in response
to increased demand, unlike the adult [20]. Because cardiac output
is determined by heart rate, any decrease in heart rate in a pediatric
patient can have serious consequences, and it should be noted that
one of the most common causes of bradycardia is hypothermia. In
addition to the lack of reserves, the autonomic nervous system,
especially sympathetic control, is thought to be poorly developed in
pediatric patients leading to poor vasomotor control and responses.
Baroreceptors are immature until 12 weeks of age leading to an
inadequate response to a fall in blood pressure [17]. Lastly, persis-
tent fetal circulation may be present in some pediatric patients lead-
ing to right to left anatomical shunting and hypoxemia, especially if
systemic hypotension develops.
Respiratory system
Like the pediatric cardiovascular system, the pediatric respiratory
system is also characterized by a lack of reserve capacity. While tidal
volumes are similar to those of the adult animal (10–15 mL/kg), the
pediatric respiratory rate is two to three times higher in order to
provide an appropriate minute ventilation (tidal volume × respira-
tory rate) [21]. An important clinical consequence of a faster res-
piratory rate is a shorter induction time in neonates when inhalant
agents are used, although this effect may be counteracted by their
high cardiac output and may be less obvious when using today’s less
soluble inhalant agents such as isoflurane and sevoflurane. With a
high resting metabolic rate, a high oxygen demand, and high base-
line minute ventilation, pediatric patients are at increased risk of
developing hypoxemia and have limited ability to adapt to decreases
in oxygen delivery. The heart is entirely dependent on aerobic
metabolism; therefore, any decrease in oxygen supply results in
rapid decompensation. The nares and tracheas of pediatric patients
are small and susceptible to obstruction; the small airways and
alveoli are also prone to collapse [17]. The extremely pliant rib cage
increases the work of breathing in pediatric patients which can
predispose to ventilation fatigue and further increase the risk of
hypoxemia. Ventilation of pediatric patients should be monitored
and supported when necessary.
Airway anatomy can pose a challenge. The pediatric patient has
small nares and the tongue is proportionally large for the size of
the mouth. Intubation can be difficult, and when performed, great
care must be taken to avoid airway trauma resulting in postopera-
tive swelling and obstruction. However, the small trachea creates
increased resistance to airflow, and intubation and ventilatory sup-
port may be necessary.
Renal and hepatic systems
By 8 weeks of age most physiologic processes related to renal and
hepatic function should be relatively normal, although organ
reserves may still be limited. The cytochrome P450 enzyme system
is immature after birth but develops during the neonatal period
[22–24]. After the age of 6 weeks, there is no rationale for altering
drug doses in animals to account for hepatic clearance [25].
Herbivores have better-developed drug metabolism and excretion
at younger ages than do dogs and cats. Hepatic development is
largely mature in foals by 2 weeks of age. However, hepatic glycogen
stores are low and gluconeogenesis is decreased, factors which
increase the risk for hypoglycemia, especially if the patient is fasted
for more than a short period. Pediatric dogs and cats and very
young foals (under 4 days of age) have immature renal function,
which can result in delayed clearance of renally metabolized
drugs, potentially increasing their duration of action. Young ani-
mals have decreased glomerular filtration rates, decreased renal
blood flow, and decreased concentrating ability. Decreased renal
clearance rates may also increase the risk of fluid overload in the
young patient [24].
Central nervous system
The blood–brain barrier is immature in young animals and there-
fore profound sedative effects may be noted with drugs such as opi-
oids and benzodiazepines. In foals under 3 weeks of age, diazepam
is profoundly sedating, and this may in part be due to the increased
permeability of the blood–brain barrier. In this age group, benzodi-
azepines will induce deep sedation and muscle relaxation, with
patients often becoming recumbent [26]. In contrast, when used in
older foals and adults, benzodiazepines often result in excitement
and ataxia but not recumbency.
Pain management in young animals is very important in order to
prevent permanent changes to the central nervous system [27,28].

The decreased function of the thermoregulatory center contributes
to the risk of hypothermia.
Hematologic system
Young patients have less capacity for hematopoiesis [29]. In addi-
tion, they have lower levels of erythropoietin, lower packed cell vol-
ume, and fewer circulating red blood cells. This resulting anemia
means they are less able to compensate for hemorrhage. Moreover,
hematopoiesis does not commence until after 15 weeks of age [30].
Other hematologic variabilities include decreased albumin, blood
urea nitrogen, and creatinine, as well as increased phosphorus.
Anesthetic management
Patient preparation
Pediatric patients are likely more susceptible to the effects of stress
than adults. Studies in neonatal rat pups demonstrate that the
increased plasticity of the neonatal brain may increase vulnerability
to stress and anxiety disorders later in life [27]. Pediatric animals
may be presented for surgery during their critical socialization
period. It is essential to protect these patients from the risk of fear
imprinting when a bad experience could translate into a lifetime of
fearful or fractious behavior during veterinary visits. Puppies and
kittens should be gently handled. Littermates should be housed
together during transport if possible and should be kept together in
the cage until the time of premedication. If still with their dam, they
should not be separated from her.
Fasting times for younger animals should be short (under 2 h) to
account for their decreased glycogen stores.
As with all surgery patients, a thorough presurgical physical
exam should be conducted prior to sedation or anesthesia. It is
especially important to perform a thorough auscultation in case
cardiac murmurs have gone undetected. The animal should also be
checked carefully for other congenital abnormalities that might
affect anesthesia or surgery such as pectus excavatum, hernias
(inguinal or umbilical), and undescended testicles. Lastly, an accu-
rate weight is very important as all drugs should be dosed on a mg/kg
or mg/m 2 basis; “guesstimates” of weight that are off by a small
amount with respect to grams can represent a large percentage of a
very small patient’s body weight, resulting in drug overdose and an
adverse response and outcome.
Monitoring
Pediatric patients should be monitored while sedated and anesthe-
tized in a similar fashion to adult patients [11]. Doppler ultrasound
equipment is versatile and can be used on even the smallest of
patients. A Doppler unit can be used to monitor heart rate (placed
directly on a shaved area over the heart), pulse rate (placed on the
caudal aspect of the carpus), and blood pressure can be measured
when the probe is placed on a limb and a blood pressure cuff applied
proximally.
Pulse oximeters should be used, and their use decreases the risk
of anesthetic-related fatalities in cats [5]. In dogs and cats, the pre-
ferred placement site is the hind paw [31] and a toe can be shaved to
help improve contact. The tongue is also commonly used but may
increase the risk of spreading infection between patients, so if this
site is used the probe must be cleaned and disinfected thoroughly
between cases. Surgery and fluorescent lighting can interfere with
the functioning of pulse oximeters so the light-emitting diode
(LED) and the sensor should be covered.
If “alligator clips” are utilized to apply electrocardiogram leads,
they should have their sharp edges filed down, the spring loosened,
and a small square of gauze placed between the clips and the skin to
avoid damage to delicate skin. Alternatives include “duckbill clips”
without teeth and electrode patches placed on the paw pads. The
patient’s mucous membrane color, capillary refill time, anesthetic
depth, and temperature should also be assessed at 5-min intervals
as outlined in the American College of Veterinary Anesthesia and
Analgesia Guidelines [32], though continuous physical monitoring
may allow for early detection of physiologic abnormalities.
Guidelines for monitoring are also available from the American
Animal Hospital Association [33].
Supportive care
Intravenous catheter placement can be greatly facilitated if topical
local anesthetics are applied over the catheter site and covered with
an occlusive dressing (plastic plus a flexible wrapping) during the
time between sedation and catheter placement. A eutectic mixture
of lidocaine and prilocaine or lidocaine (4%) topical can be used
and, though systemic absorption is minimal, the time to onset can
be up to 1 h [34]. In children, liposomal lidocaine 4% cream resulted
in a higher success rate for intravenous cannulation compared to
placebo and was effective after a contact time of 30 min [35].
When IV fluids are given, crystalloids are used and administered
at a rate of 3 mL/kg/h in cats and 5 mL/kg/h in dogs in accordance
with the American Animal Hospital Association’s fluid therapy
guidelines, though attention should be paid to total fluid dose
delivered (e.g., a young cat that receives 3 mL/kg/h for 15 min may
benefit from continued IV fluids or subcutaneous fluids in recovery).
Monitoring glucose levels in neonatal and pediatric patients of all
species is recommended, particularly for sick patients or for longer
procedures. Routine administration of dextrose without monitor-
ing may lead to hyperglycemia [36].
Thermoregulatory support
The single most important thing the anesthetist can do for a pediat-
ric patient is to avoid hypothermia. Hypothermia will decrease the
minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) and therefore increase
the risk of inhalant anesthetic overdose. Hypothermic patients
will become bradycardic, leading to decreased cardiac output and
hypotension. Decreasing core temperature also increases the risk of
myocardial irritability and arrhythmias. Clot formation is slower at
low temperatures, potentially increasing the risk of bleeding [37].
Hypothermic patients have an increased surgical infection rate as
well as decreased immune response [38]. Drug elimination will be
prolonged and recovery may be delayed. Postoperative shivering
increases oxygen demand and myocardial oxygen consumption
which is particularly detrimental in pediatric patients due to their
higher oxygen requirements.
Patient warming devices such as a forced air heating system,
warming blankets, and circulating warm water blankets can be
used. Kittens and puppies should never be placed on a cold surface
and should be covered whenever possible; a good technique is to
use one fleece blanket which travels from start to finish with the
patient. Electric blankets, warm fluid bags, heated disks, and rice
bags can burn patients and should not be placed in direct contact
with patients. Perioperative thermoregulation and heat balance are
discussed in detail in Chapter 17.
Recovery
Recovery should take place in a warm, quiet, and safe environment.
As soon as possible the patient should be returned to his litter or
herd mates and/or dam as appropriate. In addition, the animals

should be offered a small amount of soft food as soon as they can
swallow. If recovery is slow or prolonged (> 30 min), hypothermia
should be investigated, and if temperature is low more aggressive
warming strategies should be applied. Dextrose 50% or high-fructose
corn syrup can be applied to the gums or placed under the tongue
and anecdotally will often arouse puppies and kittens. However,
recent research indicates corn syrup is ineffective at raising kitten
blood sugar levels and moreover kittens were not hypoglycemic
after anesthesia that included dexmedetomidine, so routine appli-
cation of corn syrup for kittens is not necessary [39]. Nursing
animals should be returned to their dam as soon as they are able
to swallow.
Summary of pediatric drug metabolism
and pharmacokinetics
Drug metabolism and excretion are somewhat less of a concern in
herbivores because metabolism is more well developed at an early
age. Older foals will have faster clearance of both injectable and
inhaled anesthetics because they have higher extracellular fluid vol-
umes than adult horses (43% of body weight versus 22% in adult
horses) [40]. Highly protein-bound molecules such as NSAIDs are
more extensively distributed in young animals and adult levels of
cytochrome P450 are not reached in small animal species until
5 months of age [23]. The increased body water content of young
animals leads to an increased initial volume of distribution for water-
soluble drugs and conversely, their decreased percentage of body fat
leads to a decreased volume of distribution for lipid-soluble drugs.
Drugs
Sedatives and tranquilizers
Most sedatives provide good sedation in young patients, particu-
larly in neonates. Low doses are recommended. It has often been
stated that α2
-adrenergic receptor agonists should be used with cau-
tion due to cardiovascular effects, but this class of drugs is commonly
used in combination protocols for pediatric patients in high-quality,
high- volume spay-neuter (HQHVSN) programs [11,15].
The cardiopulmonary effects of xylazine (1.1 mg/kg IV) have
been studied in foals at 10 and 28 days of age [41]. Marked brady-
cardia (a 19–27% drop) was reported. Short-lived increases in
blood pressure were followed by a decrease below baseline values
(a 23–28% drop). One of the most striking respiratory effects in this
group of foals was marked changes in airway flow and intermittent
upper airway obstruction creating loud respiratory noise for 20 min
after administration. However arterial blood gases did not change
in the 2 h after administration. It is hypothesized that the airway
obstruction is due to profound pharyngeal muscle relaxation. All
foals were sedate and ataxic and some became recumbent. There
were no significant differences in the results obtained at 10 and
28 days of age.
Acepromazine is often avoided in the very young due to lack of
reversibility and since it may promote hypothermia due to its vaso-
dilatory actions. Benzodiazepine effects are discussed in the central
nervous system section above.
Opioids
Opioid medications are reversible, have minimal cardiovascular
effects (mostly limited to bradycardia), and are generally well toler-
ated by healthy pediatric patients. As previously mentioned, and
discussed further below, adequate analgesia is central to humane
and effective perioperative care of young animals.
Induction drugs and techniques
Care should be taken with mask induction with an inhalant agent as
it tends to increase the risk of anesthetic death in dogs and foals [6,8].
In addition, environmental contamination will occur, and person-
nel may be exposed to waste anesthetic gases. Mask induction can
be considered for very young animals if intravenous access cannot
be achieved but they should be sedated to decrease stress and reduce
inhalant anesthetic requirements. If induction with an inhalant
agent is chosen, sevoflurane is the preferred agent as, compared to
isoflurane, induction time is shorter in dogs and cats [42,43].
Intravenous techniques titrated to effect are preferable, especially
in compromised patients. Acceptable agents for induction include
propofol, alfaxalone, and ketamine–benzodiazepine combinations.
Anesthetic maintenance
Some procedures (e.g., castration and ovariohysterectomy in
puppies and kittens) can be completed under injectable anesthesia
(with oxygen supplementation and possibly intubation). If additional
time is required to complete a procedure, anesthesia is generally
maintained with inhalant agents administered to effect.
Suggested protocols for puppies and kittens
There are numerous anesthetic protocols for kittens and puppies
and the reader is referred to other resources for details [44].
The “kitten quad” comprises a mixture of medetomidine or dex-
medetomidine, ketamine, buprenorphine, and midazolam and is
used widely in shelter neutering programs [45,46]. Recovery time
can be reduced by administering atipamezole and kittens recover
faster than adult cats [45]. Cats under 6 months of age that received
“quad” with dexmedetomidine and then atipamezole 40 min after the
initial injection attained sternal recumbency at 51 ± 5 (mean ± SD)
min and were standing at 62 ± 19 min after the initial injection [45].
Pain management
Contrary to earlier beliefs, young patients do experience pain and
its effects may have far-reaching adverse consequences [47]. Pain
experienced at a young age may lead to dynamic changes in the
nociceptive pathway and result in altered responses to noxious
stimuli and chronic pain later in life [27,28,48]. In addition to these
negative effects, pain has adverse physiologic effects resulting in
tachycardia, hypertension, ileus, and immunosuppression.
A balanced anesthetic protocol, including multimodal analgesia
should be used in pediatric patients. The most practical and com-
monly used combinations are opioids and NSAIDs, and the con-
comitant use of these does have benefits over using either group of
drugs alone [49]. Opioids are generally very well tolerated in pedi-
atric patients, although an opioid-free protocol has been found to
provide adequate analgesia in kittens (not adult cats) [50]. As dis-
cussed earlier, the use of NSAIDs in very young puppies and kittens
is controversial [51]. Moreover, label indications for available
NSAIDs vary and some are not labeled for dogs and cats less than 4
to 6 months of age. Meloxicam is approved for use in cattle and is
commonly used in calves for dehorning and castration.
The use of local anesthetics is encouraged; these can be injected
into the testicles [52–54] or via incisional blocks. In dogs, intrates-
ticular lidocaine decreased the cardiovascular responses to castration
[53] but did not have an impact on postsurgery pain scores [54].
Intraperitoneal bupivacaine (2 mg/kg) was minimally absorbed
into the systemic circulation and was beneficial in cats undergoing
ovariohysterectomy [55,56].

-- 1367 of 1450 --

1352 	Section 9: Anesthesia and Analgesia for Selected Patients
There are several non-pharmacologic methods that can be used
to address pain [47], for example, oral sweet solutions are analgesic
in pediatric humans and so human infants are often given some-
thing sugary at the time of procedures involving noxious stimuli.
It is not known if this effect occurs in dogs and cats, and cats
are thought not to be able to taste sweet flavors. Other non-
pharmacologic strategies can be applied to veterinary patients such
as cuddling or swaddling. Swaddling and contact with the mother
(“kangaroo care”) can diminish pain [57]. Warmth has also been
shown to be analgesic in human infants [58]. Pain is driven by
inflammation, therefore minimizing surgical trauma and using the
smallest possible incisions will decrease pain in the postoperative
period [59].

Introduction
A large study that included 8.9 million dogs and 2.4 million cats
reported that life expectancy for both species increased between
2013 and 2019 [1]. Clinicians are anesthetizing more older pets and
it is important to understand the specific changes that occur with
age, and how these impact perioperative care and clinical outcomes.
Biological aging can be defined as “the progressive accumulation of
changes with time associated with or responsible for the ever-
increasing susceptibility to disease and death” [2,3]. The American
Animal Hospital Association (AAHA) has proposed the following
life stages in dogs: puppy, young adult, mature adult, senior, and
end of life [4]. The Association of American Feline Practitioners
(AAFP) and AAHA, place cats into five life stages: kitten, young
adult, mature adult, senior, and end of life [5]. These stages are
somewhat arbitrary, especially in dogs, because they are based on
chronological age and not biological age. Both organizations have
recently published senior care guidelines, which delve deeper into
defining senior and geriatric patients [6,7]; details are shown in
Table 69.1. In dogs, the term senior is used to describe the last 25%
of estimated lifespan through to the end of life [4]. Because the
lifespan of dogs varies greatly based on breed and size, it has
been difficult to accurately allocate dogs into this life stage [8].
Life expectancy tables based on size, sex, and body condition
confirm that life expectancy is decreased for the largest sizes of dogs
compared to the smallest and provide life expectancy data for toy,
small, medium, large, and giant dogs [1]. These life expectancy
tables allow for the correct allocation of any size of dog to the life
stage of “senior.” The term geriatric is a statement of health status
and not a specific age [3,6]. McKenzie et al. have proposed the
concept of the canine geriatric syndrome, which includes physical,
behavioral, metabolic, and functional changes, frailty, clinical
disease, and quality of life to facilitate the recognition of aging as a
risk factor for negative health outcomes [3].
Anesthetic management encompasses the pre-, intra-, and
postoperative period. Successful anesthetic management of older
patients requires careful planning and includes an evaluation of
comorbidities, functional status, frailty, nutrition, and a review
of current medications. Older dogs and cats may have a variety of
overt diseases (single or multiple) such as cardiac, renal, and hepatic
disease. These disease processes require specific anesthetic manage-
ment, which is covered elsewhere in this book. Access to a drug
interaction checker (e.g., Plumb’s drug interaction checker: https://
plumbs.com/features/drug-interaction-checker/) is extremely helpful
due to the number of drugs some older patients may have been pre-
scribed. Patient care does not stop in the immediate recovery period;
arrangements must be in place for postoperative care, which includes

Physiologic changes related to age
The physical and functional changes associated with aging in dogs
and cats are well described [8–14]. Veterinary geroscience is an active
area of research with a goal of developing therapies to mitigate age-
related dysfunction [3,15–17]. With respect to anesthesia in older
animals, the key factor is understanding the impact of decreased
functional or physiologic reserve in major body systems. In people,
functional reserve in vital organs is reported to decrease by 1%
every year after the age of 40 [18]. “Robustness” and “resilience” are
terms that enhance the understanding of the aging process [19].
McKenzie encourages the use of “robustness” (the ability to resist
deviation from an original or optimal state) and “resilience” (the
ability to return to this state after deviations induced by external
stressors) when assessing aging dogs [3,15]. These terms are easy to
understand, and most clinicians know when they see an animal that
is neither robust nor resilient and this may prompt a change in the
anesthetic plan for these patients.
The following section and Table 69.2, describe and summarize the
age-related changes in major body systems and their potential impact
on anesthetic management; many detailed studies are available
in humans, and it is assumed that similar changes occur in all
mammalian species. The reader is referred to an excellent open-
access clinical review by Lim and Lee [20].
Cardiovascular changes
Similar to humans, cardiac reserve is decreased with increasing age
in dogs. Cardiac output (CO) is decreased by up to 30% in older
dogs, maximum heart rate and oxygen consumption in response to
exercise are reduced, ventricular contraction is reduced, and myo-
cardial stiffness is increased [21–23].
In aging humans, blood pressure is higher and CO lower than in
young populations due to changes in connective tissues resulting in
stiffness of blood vessels and the myocardium [24]. Age-related
changes in blood pressure have been reported in both dogs and
cats [8,10,13,14,25].
Clinical implications
Preanesthetic measurement of blood pressure is recommended as a
reasonable step in older dogs and cats [26] so that changes from
normal values can be detected and managed appropriately during
anesthesia. Cats may have anxiety and stress-related elevations in
blood pressure but these can be partially mitigated by using feline-
friendly handling techniques [27].

1356 	Section 9: Anesthesia and Analgesia for Selected Patients
A decrease in CO will result in an increase in the injection site to
brain circulation time; therefore, it is essential that intravenous
anesthetic drugs are given slowly, allowing sufficient time for drugs
to reach the brain and exert an effect before additional drugs are
administered. Reduced cardiac reserve leaves older patients less
able to respond to acute changes in blood volume (loss or overload)
and hypotension compared to younger animals. Intravenous fluids
should be administered to meet pre-existing needs and ongoing
losses. Close cardiovascular monitoring is required, and inotropes
and vasopressors should be available. Animals with a rightward shift
in autoregulation due to chronic hypertension should be maintained
within ~30% of their presenting blood pressure to ensure that perfu-
sion to vital organs is maintained throughout the anesthetic event.
Pulmonary changes
Chest wall compliance decreases with age while lung compliance
increases, increasing functional residual capacity (FRC) and the
work of breathing [28]. Closing capacity also increases but faster
than FRC and may eventually equal FRC, such that at normal tidal
volume, areas of low or zero ventilation to perfusion ratios may
exist. The surface area for gas exchange decreases; there is a reduc-
tion in diffusion capacity across the capillary–alveolar membrane;
and respiratory muscle strength weakens [28]. Elderly humans
(aged 65–79 years) have an approximately 50% reduction in venti-
latory response to hypoxia and hypercapnia compared to young
subjects [29]. Older humans have decreased pharyngeal muscle
tone and less effective upper airway reflexes. This is likely true in
dogs based on their incidence of aspiration pneumonia (see later).
Laryngeal paralysis (a component of geriatric onset laryngeal paral-
ysis and polyneuropathy [GOLPP]), a disease of older dogs, puts
them at risk of aspiration and airway obstruction. Low-grade chronic
inflammation (“inflamm-aging”) has been reported in humans
and is associated with an increased incidence of morbidity and
mortality [30]. This is also likely to affect our aging veterinary
patients. Using sterile endotracheal tubes, appropriate inflation of
the endotracheal tube cuff, and suctioning of the oral cavity prior to
extubation are some measures that can be used to help protect
these animals.
In awake elderly patients, PaCO 2 and PaO 2 are usually well
maintained, but when challenged by sedation and anesthesia
involving respiratory depressant drugs, the lack of pulmonary
reserve, decreased respiratory drive, and poor muscle strength ren-
der these patients at risk of hypoxemia and hypercapnia [31].
Clinical implications
Older dogs and cats should be closely monitored perioperatively
using a pulse oximeter, and capnography intraoperatively to
determine if ventilation is appropriate. Respiratory support using
manual or mechanical ventilation may be needed, especially when
patients are in dorsal recumbency. Preanesthetic administration of
antinausea and antiemetic medications is advised [32]. Oxygen
supplementation prior to induction of general anesthesia and in the
postoperative period until the animal is able to maintain normal
oxyhemoglobin saturation on room air is recommended [33].
Neurocognitive and behavioral assessment,
postoperative delirium, and cognitive impairment
There are three distinct clinical problems associated with cognition
in the postoperative period. Emergence delirium refers to restlessness
in the immediate postoperative period and can occur in any age
group, is usually short-lived, can be managed with sedation, and
has no long-term effects. Postoperative delirium is defined as a
“short-term and transient” issue and is characterized by changes
in consciousness and cognition, disorientation, anxiety, and fear
which may fluctuate [34]. A diagnosis of frailty before surgery is
associated with an increased risk of postoperative delirium in human
patients [35]. Postoperative delirium can occur in any age group,
but elderly patients are at the highest risk. It appears between the
second and seventh day following anesthesia, and the pathophysi-
ology is poorly understood [34]. This syndrome likely occurs in
animals but may go undetected because animals do not need to
function at a high level of cognition, and we are unlikely to monitor
for this in the extended postoperative period. However, there are
enough reports by owners of their pets being “different” after
anesthesia that this warrants further investigation. Interventions
including frequent orientation, noise reduction, early mobilization,
and attention to hydration are effective at reducing postoperative
delirium in humans, all of which can be applied in veterinary
medicine [34].
Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) refers to longer-term
changes in cognition after surgery. It occurs in up to 12% of all
patients and is usually self-limiting [34,36]. The elderly and patients
with pre-existing cognitive impairment before surgery may show a
dramatic decline after surgery [36]. No specific anesthetic drug or
technique has been shown to cause or prevent POCD and the
mechanism that triggers it is unknown [36]; however, some authors
suggest that benzodiazepines should be avoided in elderly patients
at high risk of developing POCD [20]. The majority of studies
comparing POCD after general versus regional anesthesia fail to
show a difference, suggesting that its etiology is complex and
multifactorial [37].
Cognitive dysfunction (CD) is documented in dogs and cats and
may affect up to 35% of aging dogs and more than 50% of cats over
the age of fifteen [38–42]. Canine and feline CD are analogs of
human Alzheimer’s disease; therefore, postoperative delirium and
worsening of cognition are likely to occur. Reports of cognitive
decline after anesthesia in older dogs and cats are anecdotal but
some clinicians state that owners should be informed of this possi-
bility and that it is more evident in animals that have cognitive
impairment prior to anesthesia [43]. Confusion, anxiety, disturbed
sleep/wake cycle, and decreased interaction with owners are all
common clinical signs of canine CD and these can be exacerbated
by a hospital stay. Diagnosis of CD is not straightforward but older
animals should at least be screened for CD prior to anesthesia so
that clinicians can prepare for the recovery period; assessment tools
are available for dogs and cats [6,44].
Failing vision and hearing in older patients may add to confusion
in the postoperative period. Changes in environment are poorly
tolerated by older animals, especially those with CD. Whenever
possible these patients should be scheduled as outpatients; when
creating the day’s operating list, assign them the first slot so they can
be cared for when the hospital is fully staffed and discharged at the
end of the day.
Renal changes
There is a gradual decline in renal function with increasing age;
however, a significant loss of functional nephrons must occur
before this is detectable with routine testing. The dangers of reduced
renal reserve related to anesthesia are real. Perioperative dehydra-
tion, hypovolemia, and hypotension are not well tolerated in older
patients, and animals with reduced renal reserve may suffer acute
kidney injury. Many older dogs and cats are prescribed non-
steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for maladaptive pain
states putting them at a higher risk of renal insult. Cyclo-oxygenase- 1

-- 1372 of 1450 --

Chapter 69: Aging Patients 	1357
and 2 are constitutively expressed in the kidneys and the products
of these pathways include prostaglandins (PGs) and thromboxanes,
which are involved in the regulation of glomerular filtration rate
(GFR) [45]. In the face of decreased renal perfusion (e.g., decreased
circulating volume), renal PGs play a vital compensatory role,
including vasodilation to enhance renal blood flow and GFR [46].
NSAIDs block the ability of the kidney to autoregulate.
Measurement of GFR is not a routine clinical test, though it may
be reduced in patients with normal serum creatinine values [47].
Not knowing the GFR in older animals makes dosage adjustments
of renally excreted drugs difficult. Gabapentin is a renally excreted
drug and marked differences in serum concentrations were reported
in normal cats compared to those with IRIS stage 2 and 3 chronic
kidney disease (CKD) [48]. In the same study, serum gabapentin
concentrations were correlated with serum creatinine and symmetric
dimethylarginine, but it is not known if serum drug concentrations
are correlated with GFR.
CKD is common in older pets, especially cats [6]. Perioperative
management of patients with CKD is discussed in Chapter 43.
Clinical implications
Maintaining euvolemia and renal perfusion pressure during anes-
thesia is essential when renal reserves are reduced, therefore fluid
therapy, blood pressure monitoring, and treatment of hypotension
are primary considerations in this population. Renally excreted
drugs should be used with caution in older patients.
Hepatic changes
In humans, liver mass and blood flow decrease with age [49,50].
Drugs that are processed via phase I reactions (involving the
cytochrome P450 system) are “flow limited” and are likely to be
cleared more slowly in older patients. Phase II elimination involves
conjugation and drugs dependent on this pathway are less affected
by age [50]. This is a simplistic approach and drug elimination is
dependent on multiple factors; further details are available in
Chapter 19. Liver enzymes do not reflect hepatic function, and
hepatic function tests may be normal in older animals, yet their
ability to clear drugs may be compromised.
Clinical implications
Due to the difficulty in predicting how an aging patient will process
a specific drug, it is recommended that the anesthetist uses drugs
that can be titrated to effect, have a high therapeutic index, and are
reversible.
Immune function
Immunosenescence, which is defined as changes in the immune sys-
tem associated with age, has received a lot of attention in humans,
with increased vulnerability to infection and decreased immune
response to vaccinations being recognized as contributing to mor-
tality [51]. There is some, albeit limited, evidence that age-related
changes in immune function occur in dogs and cats [15].
Age-related changes in the canine immune system are summarized
by Bellows [10].
Clinical implications
Older animals should be considered at higher risk than young
patients for developing perioperative infections. Urinary retention
is a risk factor for infection in older humans but the use of indwell-
ing urinary catheters, which are not without risk, must not be used
as a substitute for good nursing care [20]. Animals should have
their bladders expressed at the end of the procedure and provided
opportunities to void voluntarily in the postoperative period – this
requires assisting large dogs to stand and providing suitable litter-
boxes to cats. If urinary catheters are used, they must be placed in a
sterile fashion and properly maintained.
Changes in body composition
With increasing age, there is loss of muscle mass and an increase in
adipose tissue in humans, dogs, and cats [15,50,52]. In dogs, these
changes vary among different breeds and sizes [52]. Changes in the
mass, structure, and function (increasing weakness) of skeletal
muscle result in the clinical condition termed “sarcopenia,” which is
seen in all mammalian species as they age [15]. The loss of muscle
mass decreases the ability of older patients to generate heat, leaving
them vulnerable to hypothermia. Muscle also acts as an important
“sink” for drugs prior to metabolism or excretion; therefore,
older animals may maintain higher plasma concentrations of drugs
for longer periods. Total body water, plasma, and intracellular
volume are reduced in older patients. The consequence of these
changes is a decrease in the central compartment and central
volume of distribution. After a bolus of intravenous drugs, plasma
concentrations are higher and can lead to more profound central
nervous system effects.
Clinical implications
Muscle weakness must be addressed in the perioperative period;
patients with sarcopenia may need help getting up and are more
likely to slip and fall, resulting in injury. Due to pharmacokinetic
changes induced by body composition differences, induction doses
of anesthetics should be reduced to prevent deep levels of anesthesia
and hypotension.
Thermoregulation
A decrease in metabolic rate occurs as dogs age [52] and this,
combined with a decrease in muscle mass, makes aging patients
vulnerable to hypothermia. Perioperative hypothermia is common
in all dogs and cats irrespective of age, resulting in delayed recovery,
altered coagulation, bradycardia, and decreased CO, and may be
linked to postoperative wound infection [53–55]. Hypothermia
decreases inhalant anesthetic requirements [56,57]. During recov-
ery, hypothermic animals will shiver to generate heat, but this
capacity is limited in older animals. Shivering during recovery can
significantly increase oxygen consumption [33] and may lead to
hypoxemia, lactic acidosis, and catecholamine release, all of which
would be detrimental in patients with limited organ reserves [58,59].
People describe postoperative shivering as a highly unpleasant
experience and we can assume this is the same in veterinary
patients [60,61].
Clinical implications
Every effort should be made to prevent perioperative hypothermia
(see Chapter 17). Oxygen supplementation should be in place until
patients are normothermic.
Frailty
In humans, frailty is a predictor of postoperative outcomes, includ-
ing morbidity, length of hospital stay, and mortality [35,62–66].
McIsaac et al. stated that the use of frailty instruments provides
meaningful increases in accuracy when predicting postoperative
outcomes for older people [67]. Frailty is distinct from comorbidity
and disability, is not synonymous with aging, and is an important

concept because there can be significant differences in health status
between individuals of the same chronological age [68]. Diagnosing
frailty allows the clinician to identify patients who are significantly
more vulnerable compared to other individuals of the same age [64].
When anesthesiologists understand the concept of frailty, they can
play a key role in improving clinical outcomes in this vulnerable
patient population [69]. Frailty can be described as a multidimen-
sional syndrome characterized by decreased physiologic reserve,
a diminished resistance to stressors, a state of vulnerability, or a
“deficit of homeostatic capabilities” [64,70]. In older patients, frailty
should be assessed in addition to comorbidities when developing a
perioperative plan. Frailty is a relatively new concept in human
medicine with the frailty phenotype first being described by Fried
et al. in 2001 [71]. In human medicine, many instruments have
been developed to assess levels of frailty and work is being done to
assess which tools are most relevant in patients scheduled for
surgery [35,65,67]. The frailty phenotype model assesses fatigue,
and measures muscle strength and walking speed. The frailty
index counts the number of deficits in multiple domains, including
physiological, psychological, and cognitive [64,68]. Assessments
can alert the care team to the special needs of an individual and if
surgery is elective, prehabilitation can be used to improve a patient’s
functional reserve and reduce risk [66,69].
Frailty and its impact on healthspan and mortality risk in com-
panion animals is an area of active research in dogs [3,72–74] and is
receiving attention in cats [6]. A five-component frailty phenotype
(chronic undernutrition, poor mobility, exhaustion, low physical
activity level, and weakness) has been described in dogs and con-
firms that frailty is a risk factor for death and that the number of
components present is predictive of increased risk [72]. A clinically
based frailty index tool has been developed for dogs and a question-
naire is included in the publication by Banzato et al. [73]. Chen
et al. demonstrated validity of this tool; frailty scores increased with
age and were correlated with a decrease in health-related quality of
life [74]. The AAFP has developed a phenotype frailty scale and an
index frailty scale that are easy to use in cats [6]. In human medi-
cine, many groups including the American Society of Surgeons and
the Association of Anesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland recom-
mend frailty assessment before surgery; however, these are not yet
performed routinely [35]. In addition to assigning an ASA score,
veterinarians are encouraged to assess frailty in patients scheduled
for surgery.
Risk of anesthesia related to age
Morbidity and mortality risks associated with anesthesia are covered
in detail in Chapter 2. Morbidity and mortality specifically related to
age will be discussed here. An increased risk of anesthetic-related
death with increasing age, and independent of patient physical sta-
tus, has been reported in dogs and cats [75–79]. Although analyzing
data based on chronological age alone is problematic in dogs,
increasing age is consistently flagged as a risk factor. In a study of
mortality related to general anesthesia and sedation in dogs in pri-
mary practice in the United Kingdom, dogs over nine years of age
were 12 times more likely to die than those between six months
and 1.5 years [79]. Brodbelt et al. reported that cats over the age of
12 were 2.1 times more likely to die than cats aged six months to five
years [76]. In a more recent study in primary care veterinary hospi-
tals in the United States, Matthews et al. reported that the odds of
death in a cat aged nine years were more than twice that of one four
years of age [78].
The key question for clinicians is “can the risks associated with
anesthesia in older animals be mitigated and what interventions are
effective?” Risk factors related to increasing age include gastroe-
sophageal reflux (GER) and aspiration pneumonia, and these risks
can be mitigated.
GER, regurgitation, aspiration pneumonia, and vomiting are
common adverse events associated with anesthesia in dogs and can
result in devastating outcomes; mortality from aspiration pneumo-
nia can be as high as 25% with increasing patient age correlated
with non-survival [32]. GER during anesthesia is significantly asso-
ciated with age [80]. Postoperative regurgitation and vomiting
(PORV) were reported in 12.3% of all dogs undergoing non-elective
surgery [81]. The risk of developing aspiration pneumonia was
higher in dogs over the age of eight and those with laryngeal disease
(e.g., GOLPP) [82,83]. Galatos and Raptopoulos reported an overall
incidence of GER of 17.4 % of dogs in their study, with increased age
being associated with an increased incidence of gastric acidity [84].
In people, the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery [ERAS®]
(www.erassociety.org) program permits patients to consume solid
food for up to 6 h and a carbohydrate supplement drink for up to
2 h prior to surgery. The ERAS program demonstrated that this
guideline reduces the risk of complications caused by aspiration
during the induction of anesthesia, significantly improves discom-
fort (from hunger and thirst), and maintains lean body mass after
surgery [85].
There are conflicting reports on the effect of preoperative fasting
times on gastric acidity and GER in dogs, likely due to the multiple
different anesthetic protocols used [84,86,87]. There is some evi-
dence to support shorter fasting times (under 5 h) with one study
reporting the incidence of GER to be significantly lower if dogs
were fed half their daily ration of canned food 3 h before anesthesia
compared to 10 h [87]. However, another clinical study reported
that 61% of dogs fed a partial daily ration of canned food 3 h prior
to anesthesia had GER compared to 43.9% of dogs fasted for
18 h [80]. Since no fasting strategy can prevent GER, other meas-
ures should be implemented.
Maropitant and famotidine appear to be effective at mitigating
some of these adverse events; of 105 dogs over the age of eight
premedicated with maropitant and famotidine, none vomited,
two regurgitated (1.9%), and one (1%) developed aspiration pneu-
monia [32]. Other studies strongly support that changes to anesthetic
protocols [88], the use of higher doses of metoclopramide [89], or
the use of esomeprazole and cisapride [90] can reduce the risk of
aspiration pneumonia. It should be noted that GER is “silent” and
often goes unnoticed; therefore, it is advised that the esophagus be
suctioned and flushed after induction and before recovery [91].
Preanesthetic testing
Preanesthetic blood screening is not required for every patient
(Chapter 2). It should be noted that reference ranges for many labo-
ratory tests only incorporate approximately 95% of the population;
therefore, 1 in 20 animals will show results outside a “normal”
range, yet these may be of no clinical significance. Blood work in
one hundred “apparently healthy senior and geriatric dogs” revealed
increased serum creatinine, hypophosphatemia, increased ALP,
increased ALT, and leukopenia in 32, 29, 27, 25, and 23 dogs,
respectively [8]. Results of serum biochemistry and hematologic
tests in older dogs and cats should be compared to age-dependent
laboratory reference ranges to differentiate healthy aging from
disease [8,9,12,14].

Chapter 69: Aging Patients 	1359
Joubert recruited 101 dogs over the age of seven that were to be
anesthetized to assess whether hematologic and biochemical analy-
ses were of value in this population [92]. In 30 dogs, a new diagnosis
was made (e.g., neoplasia and hyperadrenocorticism) as a result of
blood work, and 13 of these had their procedure canceled. However,
Joubert suggested that there was little evidence to show that blood
results impacted the anesthetic management of dogs that did pro-
ceed to surgery. In another study, the results of routine non-targeted
blood testing in dogs and cats over the age of eight were predicted
by anesthetists in most cases and did not result in major changes in
anesthetic management [93]. In a United Kingdom study of prean-
esthetic blood testing in dogs and cats (mean age 9.6 and 11.6 years
respectively), abnormal blood results raised concerns by clinicians
in approximately 8% and 16% of dogs and cats, respectively,
although only 1% of these results were unexpected based on the
animal’s history and physical examination [94]. Abnormal blood
results led to postponement of some cases and adjustments to the
anesthetic management in 4% of dogs and 9% of cats [94].
Clinical implications
Blood work results should be compared with animals within the
same age group and considered in conjunction with the patient’s
history and clinical examination.
Age-related changes in response to drugs
The pharmacologic concerns related to anesthesia drug use in older
humans are similar to those in the aging veterinary population and
focus on the increased sensitivity to drugs in this population [95].
Opioids
Elderly humans are at greater risk than younger patients of adverse
events and unpredictable responses related to opioid administra-
tion [96]. The reasons are multifactorial but include altered
pharmacokinetics due to changes in body composition and organ
function, and altered pharmacodynamics secondary to impaired
neurotransmitter production and altered receptor affinity [95,96].
Senior and geriatric patients require perioperative analgesics and
may be at risk of inadequate treatment because of the fear of adverse
effects and because many in this population already suffer from
maladaptive pain (e.g., osteoarthritis).
Age-related changes in the pharmacokinetics of pethidine
administered postoperatively have been reported in dogs [97].
Compared to young dogs, the rate of absorption of pethidine from
intramuscular sites was slower (Tmax delayed), Cmax was lower, and
elimination half-life was significantly longer in dogs over the age
of 10 [97,98]. Plasma clearance was not different between the
two age groups, suggesting that the distribution of the drug is
altered in the older population [97].
Propofol
The induction and infusion doses of propofol in humans show
age-related changes [99]. At the same plasma concentration, the
reduction in blood pressure is greater, whereas the time to reach a
specific depth of anesthesia and the time to recovery are longer in
older versus young patients [95,100]. A failure to age-adjust dosages
may contribute to hypotensive episodes, which can have serious
consequences in a population with reduced reserves [95].
The pharmacokinetics of propofol have been studied in dogs 8.5
to 10.5 years of age and, as these dogs weighed 29 ± 7.4 kg (mean ±
SD), they could be classified as senior [101]. Despite a lower
induction dosage (5 mg/kg), apnea occurred in four out of six (66%)
dogs after induction, which is higher than the reported 25% in
younger dogs given 6.5 mg/kg, by the same investigators [102]. The
blood levels of propofol were higher despite the lower dosage, and
the clearance was slower in older dogs compared to young
dogs [101,102].
Alfaxalone
Alfaxalone has a high therapeutic index compared to propofol
[103–105] but is not devoid of cardiopulmonary depressant effects
and should be given slowly and titrated to effect.
Ketamine
Ketamine has a high therapeutic index as well as anesthetic-sparing,
antinociceptive, and antihyperalgesic properties, which may make
it a good choice for older patients, especially those with chronic
pain [106,107]. It also mitigates postanesthetic hypothermia [108].
Constant rate infusions preceded by a subanesthetic loading dose
may be especially beneficial as these are associated with fewer
cardiovascular changes (tachycardia and increased blood pressure)
than anesthetic doses [109].
Inhalant agents
The influence of age on the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)
of inhalant agents is well documented in humans, decreasing by
approximately 6% per decade after the age of 40 [57,110]. The
increased sensitivity to inhalant agents is thought to be caused by age-
related changes in the brain, including changes in receptor numbers
or function. The MAC of isoflurane in 2- to 3-year-old and
11-year-old Beagles was reported as 1.82 ± 0.8% (mean ± SEM) and
1.45 ± 0.6%, respectively; when adjusted for altitude, the mean MAC
values at sea level were 1.53% and 1.22% in young and older dogs,
respectively [111]. Binding of glutamate to the excitatory receptor N-
methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) in multiple brain regions was decreased
in older dogs, and the change in NMDA receptors was associated
with an increased sensitivity to isoflurane [111]. This study could not
determine if the changes in binding were due to changes in affinity or
a decrease in binding sites. Another study using Beagles determined
the MAC of sevoflurane to be 2.25 ± 0.15% (mean ± SD) at age two
and 1.86 ± 0.9% at eight to ten years of age [112]. Dogs in the older
age group showed mild to moderate cardiorespiratory depression
(lower heart rate, indirect blood pressure, and SpO2
) than younger
dogs at an equipotent dose of sevoflurane, indicating that close moni-
toring is essential in older patients [112].
Body temperature also influences MAC, with hypothermia
decreasing anesthetic requirements; an approximately 4–5% decrease
in MAC occurs for each 1 °C fall in temperature [57]. Older animals
are susceptible to hypothermia; therefore, a combination of age-
related changes and hypothermia puts them at risk for anesthetic
overdose. Vaporizer settings or inspired concentrations of inhalant
agents should be adjusted based on a critical evaluation of the
patient’s depth of anesthesia (see Chapters 10 and 16).
Clinical implications
The extent of increased sensitivity to anesthetics in aging patients is
underappreciated by many practitioners but is also unpredictable.
Preference should be given to drugs that are reversible and those
that can be titrated to effect. Vaporizer settings or inspired concen-
trations of inhalant agents should be adjusted based on a critical
evaluation of the patient’s depth of anesthesia.

1360 	Section 9: Anesthesia and Analgesia for Selected Patients
Neuromuscular blocking agents
The pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of neuromuscular
blockade are altered in elderly human patients with postoperative
residual curarization (PORC) predisposing to hypoxemia and upper
airway obstruction in this population [113–115]. The differences in
response to neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) in elderly
humans appear to be related to altered pharmacokinetics (e.g., age-
related alterations in distribution, metabolism, and excretion) rather
than pharmacodynamics because the physiology of the neuro-
muscular junction is not significantly altered by age [113,114].
Some authors however suggest that the variability in recovery from
neuromuscular blockade in the elderly may also be related to
neuromuscular junction dysfunction [95]. Although there are no
similar studies in dogs and cats, the risks of PORC in the aging dogs
and cat populations should be taken seriously.
Clinical implications
Close neuromuscular monitoring and pharmacologic reversal are
key components to prevent PORC and are discussed in Chapter 26.
Anesthetic case management
An appropriate anesthetic and analgesic protocol for aging animals
should be based on an assessment of the animal’s physical and
health status and utilize drugs that best fit the needs of the animal,
as described above. There is no one protocol that should be used
for all older animals, however, it is recommended to use drugs
that are reversible, have a high therapeutic index, and are titratable
to effect.
Care with positioning of these patients is important to prevent
postoperative discomfort. In humans, one of the risks for position-
related pain after surgery is the presence of preoperative pain [116].
Many older veterinary patients will have osteoarthritis-related pain
and care should be taken to place them in neutral positions to pre-
vent exacerbation of joint and muscle pain postoperatively.
Analgesic considerations
As with all patients, providing perioperative analgesia is an impor-
tant component of an anesthetic plan. The analgesic drugs and
techniques covered in other chapters are all applicable to aging
patients.
Supportive care
Nutrition
In people, nutritional support can have a large impact on postop-
erative outcomes, including decreasing the length of hospital stay,
shortening the “time to eat,” less weight loss, and fewer medical
complications [117]. Nutritional care is a key component of the
ERAS® global initiative (www.erassociety.org). The role of periop-
erative nutritional care is likely underestimated in older dogs
and cats and deserves investigation. Short fasting times, the use of
antiemetic and antinausea medication, appetite stimulants, and
provision of palatable and easily digestible food should all be con-
sidered in a comprehensive plan for aging pets. Administration of
maropitant in dogs given morphine resulted in an earlier return to
feeding and increased calorie intake after surgery but this effect
was not reported when non-emetic opioids such as buprenorphine
were used [118].
Environmental stressors
Older patients may have a degree of cognitive decline and impaired
hearing and vision, which can lead to confusion during a hospital
stay. Limiting external stimuli (noise, light) may aid in a more rest-
ful environment, and limiting the number of people interacting
with the patient may decrease confusion and allow the pet to bond
with one or two team members. Owners should be encouraged to
bring familiar objects from home to leave with their pets. The use of
low-stress techniques such as feline-friendly nursing [119] will
enhance recovery. As previously stated, early return to a familiar
environment should be prioritized and it is advisable to schedule
this population as outpatients whenever possible.
